articles.text: At its meeting on Monday, December 19, the Piedmont City Council swore in newly elected members Tom Ramsey, Betsy Andersen, and Jennifer Long and named a new mayor, Jennifer Cavenaugh, and new vice mayor, Betsy Andersen. Following the City Council’s verification of the November election results which were certified on December 8 by the Alameda County Registrar of Voters, outgoing mayor Teddy Gray King received farewell remarks from councilmembers. articles.text: Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson were formally announced as new members of Piedmont School Board on Monday, December 19. They were sworn into office by City Clerk John Tulloch at a regularly scheduled City Council meeting held in the Community Hall instead of City Hall. The venue change allowed for a reception afterwards in celebration of new and departing elected officials from the School Board and City Council. Medhekar, the top vote getter for the school board election, received 4,291 votes (43% of the vote), and Thomasson received 3,951 votes (40%). They succeed Amal Smith and Megan Pillsbury on the board and begin four-year terms of office. Pillsbury, a former 2nd and 1st grade teacher at Havens and Wildwood schools, served one four-year term on the board. Smith termed out after almost nine years of service. After the swearing in, Medhekar said, “I can’t imagine that [Amal and Megan] knew what was coming four years ago and what they would have to guide us through. And so, I thank them for their service.” “I think about the long-storied history of the people on the dais. articles.text: The Initial Study-Negative Declaration (IS-ND) for the City of Piedmont’s 6th Cycle Housing Element is available for public review and comment through January 8, 2023. The statement is available for download and review on the City’s website at the following link: bit.ly/3FDqFhg. Physical copies of the documents are available for review at Piedmont City Hall (120 Vista Avenue). Community members who wish to provide feedback may send comments in writing to Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov, or by mail at 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. This study is the next step in the City’s Housing Element update, a process that has been underway since Spring 2021. As part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the City to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 – a number assigned to Piedmont by regional authorities. Adopting a Housing Element does not require these homes be built. Rather, the purpose of the document is to demonstrate that the City has a plan for how it could support this growth. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. articles.text: As the Piedmont Post celebrates its 25th year of publication as the community’s newspaper, some kind words have been received from our readers. A sampling is printed below. Editor: Thanks again for the terrific job you keep doing with the Piedmont Post, probably the best neighborhood paper in the U.S. –Eric Behrens Hillside Avenue Editor: Thank you for all you do to keep our community in touch with each other. Happy Holidays. –Christina and Eric Hsia Editor: The Piedmont Post truly is a great community paper. Thank you for all you are doing. –James Pell and Siow Fang Tan Oakland Avenue Editor: Thank you for helping with publicity for the important concert with Oakland Symphony. I think the article captured the important aspects of the music and the people making it. You and the Piedmont Post have done a good thing, and I join the choirs and the community in gratitude. –Bob Geary Founding Artistic Director Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir Editor: You have always been so helpful, and I am a proud subscriber to the Post. Thanks also for all the work you do for the Piedmont Center for the Arts. –Sandra Cook Editor: Thanks for all the great reporting and service to the community. –Dean and Karen Barbieri Editor: For decades you have kept our community informed about schools, city government and “what’s up”. There is always some good news in Piedmont, and it is nice to hear when things go well. Kids learn how to handle the attention, and our community feels proud. However, equally important is the Post’s willingness and ability to dig into areas where we aren’t doing well, and we do have things like that as well. Sometimes your focus is painful. However, we all need to stay informed about our great city. Thank you for all you do for Piedmont. –David Brown Editor: We love the Post and are happy to help support our community paper. Thanks for all that you do. –Kristin Ogles 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com REVIEWERS

articles.text: The Piedmont Public Works Department received feedback last week from AC Transit on Piedmont’s proposed bulb-outs and changes in bus stops on Oakland Avenue. The City’s initial bulb-out plan involved the net loss of 10 parking spaces; the modified plan has three. If the City is unable to address these concerns in a new draft, it would amount to a net loss of four. AC Transit expressed concern that buses in the westbound (downhill) direction on Oakland Avenue at Jerome Avenue would project across the intersection with Latham Street. “I am very optimistic that the City will reach an agreement with AC Transit, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “These back-and-forth iterations are typical, and it’s realistic that we’ll resolve them in January.” In the meantime, the City continues to work with residents to develop a plan which is agreeable for those affected. Gonzales said he has received requests from some residents for the City to paint the affected curbside areas in order to make it clear where the new bus stops will be. When the initial plan for bulbouts on Oakland Avenue at the intersections of Jerome and El Cerrito Avenues was approved by the City on October 4, 2021 and presented to the public recently on November 1, “there was pushback from many parties,” confirmed Gonzales. In addition to permanent bulbouts – where the sidewalk extends and the street shrinks, to make the pedestrian crossing shorter and safer – the plan provided for high-visibility crosswalks, pedestrian ramps, yellow flashing beacons, new street paint, and new signs at each intersection. There was opposition to the loss of parking spaces which would result from relocating bus stops on Oakland Avenue near the affected intersections. Accordingly, the City created a modified bulb-out plan. The new plan addresses a majority of the concerns voiced by residents and involves a net loss of three parking spots – one on El Cerrito Avenue in the downhill direction, and two at Jerome Avenue. “As we work with AC Transit to maintain the modified plan while keeping to their safety guidelines,” said Gonzales, “we’ve also made sure to be very proactive in working with those affected by this plan.” Residents with questions about the bulb-out plan may e-mail Daniel Gonzales at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov, or call 510-420- 3061. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

The City of Piedmont is soliciting bids from contractors for a street striping project on Moraga Avenue. The project involves the installation of new traffic lane striping, curb markers, and crosswalk markings on La Salle Avenue, Moraga Avenue, and the intersection at Lincoln and Sheridan Avenues. Two new bike lanes on Moraga Avenue would be added from Coaches Field eastward (uphill) to the city limits near Maxwelton Road. articles.text: The American Red Cross will have a blood drive on Saturday, December 24, from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. in the Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue. Blood donations are fewer during the winter holidays due to travel, illness, and weather, but the need for blood is constant. Volunteer donors are the only source of blood for trauma and cancer patients, accident and burn victims, people with blood disorders, and more. Blood donors must be at least 18 years old (16-17 with parental consent), weigh at least 110 pounds, and wait a minimum of eight weeks between making donations. To make an appointment, visit redcrossblood.org/give.html/finddrive and use the sponsor code “Piedmont”. To learn more about donating blood, visit donateblood.org/ faqs/#who-can-donate. Parental consent forms can be found online at bit.ly/3HF715S.
articles.title: Blood drive in Piedmont on December 24

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s highly-anticipated White Elephant Sale will return next year beginning with a preview sale on January 29. The sale, touted as Northern California’s “biggest and best rummage sale,” is organized and operated by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board and a legion of volunteers, many working throughout the year to make the sale a success. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the museum to support its art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, and capital improvements. The sale has many volunteers from Piedmont, most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The preview sale begins at 12 p.m. on Sunday, January 29. Visit https://museumca.org/event/ white-elephant-preview-sale/ to purchase tickets and to learn how to donate.
articles.title: Oakland Museum White Elephant Preview returns in January

articles.text: Renovation of the steps connecting the Piedmont Community Hall with Guilford Avenue will begin on January 4. The Public Works Department issued a notice earlier this month to proceed with the project. The $155,000 renovation project was approved by City Council on September 6, 2021, with the understanding that $55,000 of the cost will be funded by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and the Piedmont Garden Club. Piedmont Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales estimated that work could be completed in mid-March. “The main priority of this project is safety,” he stated. The city will replace the current steps — which are currently wooden railroad ties of varying sizes — with colored concrete steps and landings, and add metal handrails on both sides of the steps and landings. Further additions will include benches, trees, and a small plaza with a permeable-pavement floor to accommodate for groundwater runoff. The Highland/Guilford Steps project plans can be found at bit. ly/3jlK65z, and all City projects out for bid can be found at piedmontplanroom.com. Residents with questions may e-mail Daniel Gonzales at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov, or call 420-3061. Current plans for renovation of the Highland/Guilford steps. business hours.

articles.text: Dear PUSD Community: The Holiday Season is here and so much has happened in a month. The district is moving along with the Superintendent Search and community engagement has been completed. In addition to parent, staff and community meetings with the search firm, over 400 individuals completed a survey identifying qualities they would like to see in the next superintendent. The position has been posted and applications will be brought to the Board on February 1 for review. Thank you to everyone for your feedback and assistance in this process. In our School Board community engagement meetings in October, there were parents who felt strongly that rigor and excellence needed to be addressed in the District’s Vision, Mission and Core Values. But what became clear was we all have different definitions of what those values are and how to represent them both in the district and classroom. Does that mean that Piedmont needs to have a certain number of Advanced Placement courses? Does this mean we need to hit a certain mark on State standardized tests? Finally, does rigor and excellence go beyond academics to include social and emotional welfare as well as equity and inclusivity? Getting everyone on the same page is important. To do this, I will be meeting with teachers, administrators and the Superintendent’s Community Advisory Committee to develop an operating definition of rigor and excellence. I will then bring parents into the conversation through several community meetings. Following this dialogue, I will bring to the Board a plan of what rigor and excellence looks like in Piedmont. My goal is to have all stakeholders on the same page and operating under the same definitions. This will become part of a foundation on which we can build and sustain as our district moves forward under the next superintendent. Yesterday, the state released data as part of its accountability reporting system known as the California School Dashboard. The Dashboard is an online tool to help communities identify strengths and weaknesses and pinpoint student groups that may need support. In its sixth year, it reports status on multiple measures of academic and school climate. The Dashboard also focuses on the state priority of closing the performance differences among student groups’ (e.g. race/ethnicity, socioeconomically disadvantaged, English Learners [ELs]) performance. Piedmont continues to demonstrate excellence across multiple measures. With the impact of the pandemic changing the landscape of learning, communities are encouraged to consider these results a new baseline and to reflect and engage with their districts in moving forward to support all students. You can review the dashboard at Caschooldashboard.org. PUSD’s results will be presented to the Board on January 11. We just completed our 1st Interim Budget Report. The report gives us a clearer picture of where our finances are. After giving 7.5% salary increases, a $1,500 one-time bonus and an increase in health care benefits to all staff, we were still able to receive a positive certification. A positive certification means that we are able to meet all of our financial obligations this year and the two subsequent years. You can read more about the background of the report at Simbli. eboardsolutions.com/Meetings/ Attachment.aspx?S=3603037 3&AID=398174&MID=17392 and view a slidedeck from Wednesday’s Board presentation at Docs.google.com/presentation/d/1CXXcsIMG3BhE9GYQ1E70ZGnPNhZ8h9mb/edit Over the past six months, I have enjoyed meeting with the many amazing organizations that work tirelessly to support our students and staff. I want to take a moment to especially thank the Piedmont Education Foundation that has impressed me beyond belief. Its impact on PUSD can be seen on every campus and in every classroom, and felt by every student and staff member. As its 2022 Giving Campaign comes to a close this month, I invite you to consider making a donation and see the difference it can make. Visit Piedmontedfoundation.org/donate for more information. Finally, as Winter Break approaches, I ask for your help in continuing to provide a safe environment for students and staff. With COVID cases on the rise, we are asking families to test their students prior to returning to school on January 9. Schools will be distributing tests to all students next week. Please plan to test on January 7-8 and report any positive cases on the District’s COVID self reporting form at Tinyurl.com/pusdgotcovid and on Primary. I wish you all a happy and safe Holiday season. Enjoy your break and we’ll see you in the New Year! Sincerely, Donald Evans Interim Superintendent Saturday, February 11. and early ticket sales. coffee, and cocktails.

articles.text: Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans On Wednesday, December 14, community members gathered at the Piedmont Center for the Arts for a discussion with Piedmont School District Interim Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans and Chief Financial Officer Ruth Alahydoian. The Giving Campaign team facilitated and hosted the event, which focused on an overview of PUSD funding sources and expenses, and the financial challenges that the district faces. Emily Chang Stull, an award-winning author and Bloomberg producer and host, moderated the event. Dr. Evans highlighted the unique nature of what Piedmont schools offer students compared to many other public school districts, thanks to community fundraising efforts like the Giving Campaign. “If you go up and down the state (of California), you don’t see fully structured art programs,” he said. “You don’t see structured music programs or technology programs. You don’t see fully operational libraries. Even in some of the highest achieving districts, you will not see all those things…like you see here.” Ruth Alahydoian presented information about how the state funding model works and the expenses involved in running PUSD. “It was so illuminating,” said Giving Campaign co-chair Katie Sharafi. “California gives us only 50% of what we need to operate our schools. The rest we need to find through local sources and fundraising.” Alahydoian also highlighted the importance of reflecting community priorities in funding decisions. “The dollars that we get in donations… it’s important that we spend it as people ask us to spend it,” she noted. Piedmont Education Foundation’s Heather Frank shared information about how the district allocates funds raised by PEF. “Every year, we convene a grants committee that includes a representative from every parent’s club and support group in the district, along with community and PEF board members, the district superintendent, assistant superintendent, and CFO,” she said. “The committee reviews grant spending from the prior year and then determines what community priorities are for distributing funds for the upcoming year.” Questions from the audience ranged from how the district prioritizes areas for funding cuts to the most significant upcoming expenses for the district. Superintendent Evans noted that healthcare costs for PUSD employees CFO Ruth Alahydoian continue to skyrocket and are completely out of the district’s control. Dr. Evans, who has worked in public school districts of all sizes throughout California, feels that Piedmont is unique in the strength of its teaching community. “I am so grateful for what we have here,” he said “Our PUSD teachers are really invested in their classroom and their kids and so committed to their work. That is not true everywhere. What we have here is really exceptional.” He noted that while this year’s 7.5 % teacher raise (made possible by last year’s Giving Campaign fundraising and state distributions) was much higher than raises given by many other districts, the district needs to remain competitive with benefits as well. “To…keep teachers, and give the salaries we want to give them, you have to cut! And what goes out are those things… (art, music, and STEAM programs) that really define us here, that we take for granted.” As the 2022 Giving Campaign comes to a close, it has raised just short of $3 million. But as much as the amount, the team is focusing on participation – parent participation is still under 50%. “Every dollar counts,” says Sharafi. “But getting the community involved is what we’re most focused on right now.”
articles.title: Giving Campaign hosts Supt. Evans, CFO Alahydoian

articles.text: After a week of competition Piedmont Middle School’s 2022 Spelling Bee concluded on Friday, December 16, with 6th grader Sophia Li standing alone as the champion. On the final day of scholastic competition Li outlasted two worthy competitors, 7th grader Emahn Sheikh and defending champion Zoe Snyder, The Bee is organized and hosted by 7th grade teacher Ted Scherman in his classroom Students who advanced to the fourth day of competition on Thursday were deemed finalists. Sixth grader finalists included Rosemary Li, Sophia Li, Rohan Seshan, Francesca Clark, and Jai Ramakrishnan. Seventh grade finalists included Olivia Bailey, Ava Casalaina, Emahn Sheikh, and Maggie Eidt. Eighth-grade finalists participating in their final Spelling Bee included Jia Ramakrishnan, Livi Britt, Zoe Snyder, and Aliya Vora. “Mostly what I thought was, ‘wow, the pressure is on,’” said Li after winning the contest. “These words aren’t easy, I didn’t know ‘barrister’ was a word, I didn’t know ‘Whist’ existed and I never would have of guessed ‘accede’,” add Li. Li asked for the language of origin on a couple of occasions, including on the championship word “Lupus,” which is Latin. “Sometimes with the language of origin, if you study the roots for how the language typically spells certain things, it can help you,” she explained. For winning the Piedmont Bee, Li will is eligible for an online test to qualify for the San Ramon Valley Rotary Regional Spelling Bee in March. 6th grader Sophia Li is the winner of this year’s Piedmont Middle School Spelling Bee. Last year’s Spelling Bee champion Zoe Snyder congratulates Sophia Li as this year’s winner. Zoe Snyder (left), Sophia Li, and Emahn Sheikh with Middle School teacher and Spelling Bee guru, Ted Scherman. 1980 Mountain Boulevard, #212 510-339-9313

articles.text: transition from classroom to school board was significant. “I felt a huge responsibility, because I knew how important the decisions at the school board level were for people who work at our sites, and most importantly for our students,” said Pillsbury. Megan Pillsbury completed her final school board meeting on December 14 after a fouryear term. Pillsbury’s impact on the district began much earlier. She moved to Piedmont in 1987, raised three children who graduated from Piedmont High School, and taught 1st and 2nd grade students at Havens and Wildwood schools for 16 years – from 1998 to 2014. Pillsbury easily won a seat on the board as top vote getter in 2018 with 31.7% of the vote. In Piedmont, retired teachers are a rarity on the board, primarily due to the high cost of living which prohibits many former teachers from being able to afford living in Piedmont. Pillsbury explained why the – Megan Pillsbury “I think many people who have a desire to become a school board member have the misconception that they can come in and make a direct impact on the disMegan Pillsbury (right) lobbying with Sarah Pearson (left) and Cory Smegal at the State Capitol for increased funding for public education. Megan Pillsbury with dog Harvey trict,” Pillsbury explained. “It’s not true. 1: You’re one of a five-part governance team and the decisions are made by the team. 2: You have no direct impact on what’s happening on our sites; you only have direct impact on directing the superintendent, who is the sole employee of the board, in setting policy,” she added. Pillsbury chose not to pursue re-election in 2022 as she and her husband plan to move to Inverness in West Marin. In her farewell comments to the school board, she said, “Tonight I want to particularly call out the role of our teachers, because as I leave, that is one perspective that will be missing from our board. I implore you all and our new board members, to continue what many of you have begun now that our schools have opened up. Spend time observing in our classrooms, get to know staff at each site, dig deep, ask questions about lessons,
articles.title: Megan Pillsbury reflects on four years on school board

articles.text: Volunteers at Chabot Space & Science Center do incredible things. They assist educators in workshops to inspire students, run scientific demonstrations to educate visitors and donate their time every Friday and Saturday night to offer free telescope viewing to the public. One rockstar, Gabrielle Stewart, is a Chabot Observation Deck volunteer and UC Berkeley student. She has discovered more than 450 supernovae since February this year, and recently made a particularly rare find on August 1. In the constellation Ophiuchus (the Serpent Bearer), a Type 1a supernova awaited its discovery. With a magnitude of around 19, it wasn’t visible to the naked eye. You’d need a powerful telescope to see it, like the 36-inch reflector on Chabot’s Observatory Deck. For Stewart, this exploding star jumped off the page in photos from the 48-inch telescope at Palomar Observatory near San Diego. What makes this discovery so unique is the fact that this supernova’s brightness is enhanced by gravitational lensing – where a massive object, like a galaxy, has bent the light on its long-distance journey to Earth. Similar to what a lens would do, this effect has made the supernova appear brighter than it normally would. This is only the third such object ever discovered, and the first in six years. A team of astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope was able to capture a picture of the supernova. The lensing is what creates an image that appears to be four objects. Now officially designated SN Zwicky, around these parts we’ll be referring to this discovery as Gabby’s Supernova. Volunteer at Chabot Join a dynamic team dedicated to creating a fun and interactive science experience. No science or astronomy background needed, just a willingness to inspire and educate visitors of all ages about our Planet Earth and the UniChabot Observation Deck volunteer and UC Berkeley student Gabrielle Stewart spots the Supernova Sn Zwicky. verse. If you are comfortable interacting with the public, enjoy engaging children and adults, and have eight hours of your time to give per month, consider becoming a volunteer at Chabot Space & Science Center. Visit Chabot Space & Science Center – Oakland’s Home For Science (https:// chabotspace.org/) Annie McShane is Volunteer Manager at Chabot Space & Science Center, located at 10000 Skyline Boulevard in Oakland. articles.text: The Piedmont Diversity Film series will return on January 19 with a free screening of Through the Night. The documentary is an intimate cinema verité portrait of working mothers whose lives intersect at a 24-hour daycare center: a mother working the overnight shift at a pediatric hospital, another holding 3 jobs to support her family and the woman who cares for their children whose parents have nowhere else to turn. The film won the New York Times Critics Pick in 2020, and the Hollywood Critic Top 10 from Tribeca and South by Southwest Film Festival. The film is being presented as an inspirational film in advance of Martin Luther King Jr. Day. The film will be shown on Thursday, January 19 at 7:00 p.m. at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, 325 Highland Avenue. This 76-minute film will be followed by a discussion of current East Bay childcare services led by Bananas Child Care Director Kym Johnson. The film series is sponsored by the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee, the Piedmont Adult School, the City of Piedmont, and the Piedmont Chapter of the League of Women Voters. The free screening of Through the Night will be on January 19.

pages.text: Wednesday, December 21, 2022 7 Megan Pillsbury reflects on four years on school board transition from classroom to school board was significant. “I felt a huge responsibility, because I knew how important the decisions at the school board level were for people who work at our sites, and most importantly for our students,” said Pillsbury. By Jay Russell Megan Pillsbury completed her final school board meeting on December 14 after a fouryear term. Pillsbury’s impact on the district began much earlier. She moved to Piedmont in 1987, raised three children who graduated from Piedmont High School, and taught 1st and 2nd grade students at Havens and Wildwood schools for 16 years – from 1998 to 2014. Pillsbury easily won a seat on the board as top vote getter in 2018 with 31.7% of the vote. In Piedmont, retired teachers are a rarity on the board, primarily due to the high cost of living which prohibits many former teachers from being able to afford living in Piedmont. Pillsbury explained why the “No matter what role I take on, I am, and will always be, an educator at heart.” – Megan Pillsbury “I think many people who have a desire to become a school board member have the misconception that they can come in and make a direct impact on the disMegan Pillsbury (right) lobbying with Sarah Pearson (left) and Cory Smegal at the State Capitol for increased funding for public education. Megan Pillsbury with dog Harvey trict,” Pillsbury explained. “It’s not true. 1: You’re one of a five-part governance team and the decisions are made by the team. 2: You have no direct impact on what’s happening on our sites; you only have direct impact on directing the superintendent, who is the sole employee of the board, in setting policy,” she added. Pillsbury chose not to pursue re-election in 2022 as she and her husband plan to move to Inverness in West Marin. In her farewell comments to the school board, she said, “Tonight I want to particularly call out the role of our teachers, because as I leave, that is one perspective that will be missing from our board. I implore you all and our new board members, to continue what many of you have begun now that our schools have opened up. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: With a sleigh full of toys – and Saint Nicholas, too. And then in a twinkling, I heard on the roof ’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that Saint Nicholas soon would be there. The children were nestled all snug in their beds, While visions of sugar plums danced in their heads; And mama in her kerchief, and I in my cap Had just settled our brains for a long winter’s nap. When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, Tore open the shutter and threw open the sash. The moon on the breast of the new-fallen snow Gave a luster of midday to objects below; When to my wondering eyes should appear But a miniature sleigh and eight tiny reindeer. With a little old driver, so lively and quick, I knew in a moment it must be Saint Nick! More rapid than eagles his coursers they came, And he whistled and shouted and called them by name: “Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer! Now, Vixen! On, Comet! On, Cupid! On Donder and Blitzen! To the top of the porch, to the top of the wall, Now dash away, dash away, dash away all.” As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle mount to the sky. So up to the housetop the coursers they flew, The prancing and pawing of each little hoof. As I drew in my head and was turning around, Down the chimney Saint Nicholas came with a bound. He was dressed all in fur from his head to his foot, And his clothes were all tarnished with ashes and soot. A bundle of toys he had flung on his back, And he looked like a peddler just opening his pack. His eyes, how they twinkled! His dimples, how merry! His cheeks were like roses, his nose like a cherry! His droll little mouth was drawn up in a bow, And the beard on his chin was as white as the snow. The stump of a pipe he held tight in his teeth, And the smoke, it encircled his head like a wreath. He had a broad face and a little round belly That shook when he laughed like a bowl fully of jelly. He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf, And I laughed when I saw him in spite of myself. A wink of his eye and a twist of his head Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread. He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work, And filled all the stockings; then turned with a jerk, And laying a finger aside of his nose, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose. He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle, And away they all flew like the down of a thistle. But I heard him exclaim, ’ere they drove out of sight, “Happy Christmas to all, and to all a good night!” PLEASE JOIN US AS WE CELEBRATE

articles.text: On a cold Christmas Eve in 1818, pastor Joseph Franz Mohr walked the three kilometers from his home in the Austrian village of Oberndorf bei Salzburg to visit his friend Franz Gruber in the neighboring town of Arnsdorf bei Laufen. Mohr brought with him a poem he had written two years earlier. He desperately needed a carol for his Christmas Eve midnight mass that evening. He hoped his friend Gruber, a school teacher who also served as the church’s choir master and organist, could set his poem to music. In a matter of a few hours, Franz Gruber composed the “Stille Nacht” melody for Mohr on that night of December 24, 1818. Flooding of the nearby Salzach River had put the church organ out of commission, so Gruber composed the music for guitar accompaniment. A few hours after Gruber finished the composition, he and Mohr stood before the altar at St. Nicholas Church in Oberndorf to perform the work. A local choir sang the new composition, breaking the silence of that “stille nacht.” Silent Night, Holy Night Mohr; English trans. by John Freeman Young. Silent, night, holy night, All is calm, all is bright. ’Round yon virgin, mother and child Holy infant so tender and mild, Sleep in heavenly peace, Sleep in heavenly peace. Silent night, holy night, Shepherds quake at the sight. Glories stream from heaven afar,

articles.text: If you want to watch some great basketball this winter, head to Binks Rawlings Gym in Piedmont. The Highlanders’ girls’ team was just named the top-ranked team in SportsStar Magazine’s North Coast Section rankings. The No. 1 spot came after PHS notched one of its biggest regular season wins in the last decade with a 60-56 victory over previously No. 1 ranked ArchPerseas Gioukaris is a guard with tough on-ball defense and speed in transition. bishop Mitty of San Jose. In addition to its core of Trinity Zamora, Maddie Hill, and Natalia Martinez, the three lead players throughout last year, a major part of Piedmont’s 6-0 start to the season is the addition of three transfer students. Eva Levingston, Perseas Gioukaris, and Adrienne Blackwell, all seniors, they are making their debut at PHS. In addition, junior Samantha Smith is scheduled to play her first game for PHS against California High this Friday, December 23. Both Levingston and Gioukaris were on the roster last season but had to sit out a year as active players as they waited to be cleared after transferring. They rooted from the bench as Piedmont finished as runners up in the league, in the North Coast Section finals, and advance to the second round of the Div. 2 State Playoffs. All that has only made them eager to do their part on the court. “Honestly, last year was very hard for Perseas and I to sit out. We worked out in the summer coming into last season and were really anxious to play. Sitting on the bench and helping out in practice, sort of as a coach during games. gave me a different perspective,” said Levingston. This is our season and we’re coming for more. Watching those tight games last season was tough because you want to help out. I was very proud of my team,” added Gioukaris. Levingston has already proven a contributor in the low post and as a ball handler. Coach Gardere describes her as a “Draymond Green” type of player. “Bryan says I’m like the Draymond Green on the court. I love being aggressive, and at the same time getting the ball to my teammates,” said Levingston. Levingston comes to Piedmont after playing at St. Joseph in Alameda as a freshman and at Alameda High as a sophomore. Gioukaris is very much the sparkplug described by coach Bryan Gardere. She may be one of the smallest players on the court, but she’s one of the fastest. Her vertical leap makes her an aggressive rebounder to go along with skill as a defender. “I’m very aggressive,” confirmed Gioukaris. “I talk more on the defensive side than offensive. I’m a defensive player first, but I like to push the ball up the court fast.” She played at St. Joseph as a freshman and sophomore. Blackwell is proving to be a skilled shooting guard who can knock down 3-pointers and also drive to the basket. “It’s great to be on this team. We have a target on our backs, and I think we can keep that No. 1 spot with our ability and skillForward Eva Levingston is a key player on Piedmont’s No. 1 ranked team. set,” said Blackwell. She played at St. Mary’s in Stockton as a freshman and at Santiago High in Corona as a sophomore and briefly as a junior before having shoulder surgery. “I’m bringing defensive energy, great communication, and leadership. It feels great to be on the court, I’m also coming back from injury so it’s really a relief,” said Blackwell. Gardere is also excited about Smith, a tall forward. “This is definitely a big step up for me. This is a very talented group, and I haven’t had an opportunity to play with people like this other than playing on a travel team over the summer. I like doing all the little things, so I’m hoping to help us win games,” said Smith. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, December 21, 2022 Sports By Jonathan Comeaux If you want to watch some great basketball this winter, head to Binks Rawlings Gym in Piedmont. The Highlanders’ girls’ team was just named the top-ranked team in SportsStar Magazine’s North Coast Section rankings. The No. 1 spot came after PHS notched one of its biggest regular season wins in the last decade with a 60-56 victory over previously No. 1 ranked ArchPerseas Gioukaris is a guard with tough on-ball defense and speed in transition. Dave Perez… ...a uality guy He was a friend, neighbor, and the ultimate car whisperer — fixing Piedmonters’ cars since 1979. Quality Body & Fender lives on... through Dave's children, Jacqueline & Michael, who have maintained the high-quality of work and the revered reputation their father created. PHS girls named No. 1 in North Coast Section Levingston, Gioukaris, Blackwell, Smith help team’s ascent bishop Mitty of San Jose. In addition to its core of Trinity Zamora, Maddie Hill, and Natalia Martinez, the three lead players throughout last year, a major part of Piedmont’s 6-0 start to the season is the addition of three transfer students. Eva Levingston, Perseas Gioukaris, and Adrienne Blackwell, all seniors, they are making their debut at PHS. In addition, junior Samantha Smith is scheduled to play her first game for PHS against California High this Friday, December 23. Both Levingston and Gioukaris were on the roster last season but had to sit out a year as active players as they waited to be cleared after transferring. They rooted from the bench as Piedmont finished as runners up in the league, in the North Coast Section finals, and advance to the second round of the Div. 2 State Playoffs. All that has only made them eager to do their part on the court. “Honestly, last year was very hard for Perseas and I to sit out. We worked out in the summer coming into last season and were really anxious to play. Sitting on the bench and helping out in practice, sort of as a coach during games. gave me a different perspective,” said Levingston. This is our season and we’re coming for more. Watching those tight games last season was tough because you want to help out. I was very proud of my team,” added Gioukaris. Levingston has already proven a contributor in the low post and as a ball handler. Coach Gardere describes her as a “Draymond Green” type of player. “Bryan says I’m like the Draymond Green on the court. I love being aggressive, and at the same time getting the ball to my teammates,” said Levingston. Levingston comes to Piedmont after playing at St. Joseph in Alameda as a freshman and at Alameda High as a sophomore. Gioukaris is very much the sparkplug described by coach Bryan Gardere. She may be one of the smallest players on the court, but she’s one of the fastest. Her vertical leap makes her an aggressive rebounder to go along with skill as a defender. “I’m very aggressive,” confirmed Gioukaris. “I talk more on the defensive side than offensive. I’m a defensive player first, but I like to push the ball up the court fast.” She played at St. Joseph as a freshman and sophomore. Blackwell is proving to be a skilled shooting guard who can knock down 3-pointers and also drive to the basket. “It’s great to be on this team. We have a target on our backs, and I think we can keep that No. 1 spot with our ability and skillStaff Photos Forward Eva Levingston is a key player on Piedmont’s No. 1 ranked team. set,” said Blackwell. She played at St. Mary’s in Stockton as a freshman and at Santiago High in Corona as a sophomore and briefly as a junior before having shoulder surgery. “I’m bringing defensive energy, great communication, and leadership. It feels great to be on the court, I’m also coming back from injury so it’s really a relief,” said Blackwell. Gardere is also excited about Smith, a tall forward. “This is definitely a big step up for me. This is a very talented group, and I haven’t had an opportunity to play with people like this other than playing on a travel team over the summer. I like doing all the little things, so I’m hoping to help us win games,” said Smith. She played at Dublin when they reached the semifinals of the Division 1 NCS Playoffs last year. “At Dublin I contributed with defense and energy. That’s what I wanted to bring here,” said Smith. The goal for all players on Gardere’s talented team is to finish at the top. “We work hard every single day. We’re going to keep going. Just being on the court is like a dream come true. I’ve been waiting to play for a long time and now I have the opportunity in front of me,” said Levingston. The Highlanders play this Friday, December 23, at 2:30 p.m. against California HS at Binks Rawlings Gym. Shortly after Christmas the team heads to Washington state for a threeday invitational tournament, the Top of the Peak Classic in Snohomish, from December 27-29. Before returning home they will play Renton HS near Seattle on December 30. Their league schedule in the East Bay begins with a game at San Leandro on Wednesday, January 4. articles.text: Piedmont traveled to Alhambra in Martinez on Tuesday, December 13, and came home with a satisfying 70-59 win against the Bulldogs. The win brings the Highlanders’ record to 8-2. Its final game before winter break is this Friday, December 23 in a home game against Campolindo. The victory over Alhambra marks the school’s second win over a Division 3 North Coast Section opponent. “Another big win for us against a D3 team, we’re now 2-0 versus schools in our division, which will help our ranking,” explained coach Ben Spencer. “It was another gritty win for us and we battled from behind. I love the fight in our group.” A.J. Harris, Brit Burden, and Matthew Riordan had strong performances. Harris finished the night with a double-double – 20 points and 10 rebounds – while Burden had nearly identical numbers with 20 points and nine boards. Riordan was critical from beyond the arch, scoring 14 points including three 3-pointers. “Matt had a really good game and knocked down some big threes in the second and fourth quarters,” said Spencer. Piedmont had to crawl out of a big hole after falling behind 21-10 in the first quarter. They rallied for 21 points in the second quarter to cut the deficit to 35-31 by halftime. Both teams put up 14 points in the third quarter to make it 45-41 Alhambra entering the fourth. But Piedmont’s defense cranked up the pressure on Alhambra in the final going, outscoring the Bulldogs 25-10 to claim a n impressive 70-59 comefrom-behind victory. After the first quarter, Piedmont made four 3-pointers – two by Riordan, one from Arjun Bornstein, and one by Harris. Burden in the low post scored eight points. Both teams traded Staff Photos A.J. Harris scored 20 points and had 10 rebounds against Alhambra. points back and forth in the third quarter with Harris scoring six points and Burden scoring four points. Trailing 45-41 at the start if the fourth quarter, Piedmont came out hot with Bornstein assisting Burden on an inbounds play. Bornstein put PHS ahead after Matteo Costa made a steal then sent it up court to Bornstein for a layup plus a free throw. And suddenly Piedmont had a 46-45 lead. Riordan knocked down a 3-pointer to continue the run. The two teams traded points until PHS held a 59-55 lead with 1:02 left. The Bulldogs resorted to fouls resulting in the Highlanders scoring eight points from the free throw line. Harris and Riordan both made 3-point shots in the final quarter, two by Harris and one by Riordan. Final stats: Harris had 20 points and 10 rebounds. Burden had 20 points and nine rebounds. Riordan had 14 points, Bornstein scored 11, Ravi Silverberg had three points, and Costa had two. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-2) hosts Campolindo this Friday, December 23 at 7:00 p.m. in Binks Rawlings Gym on the Piedmont campus. It will be their final game prior to Winter Break. Brit Burden had 20 points and nine boards against Alhambra. The PHS boys’ basketball team gained its second win against a Div. 3 opponent.

articles.text: The Highlanders’ boys’ soccer team continued its strong start to the season with a pair of shutout wins, blanking San Leandro 5-0 at Witter Field on Wednesday, December 14, and beating Mt. Eden 3-0 in Hayward two days later. The pair of wins comes against Foothill Division opponents, and improved Piedmont’s record to 3-1-1. Their only loss through five matches was a 1-nil game with Berkeley. Their one tie, 0-0, came against Bishop O’Dowd. This is the team’s first season in the WACC upper division. “If you think about the previous league games we played, we deserved to get something out of the Berkeley match and we got a draw out of O’Dowd. San Leandro just tied with O’Dowd and we beat them 5-0, so there are loads of positives to take at the moment. They are a Div. 1 team, so it’s a great result,” said coach Todd Sullivan. “But we have to play these teams again,” he cautioned, “so we have to make sure we’re on top of it when we see them again,” The San Leandro match proved to be a big game for senior William Daniel, who scored twice. “Will had a busy first half. The energy really caught San Leandro early and before you know it we’re three goals up and were cruising. We got a little complacent towards the end of the first half but the second half was probably better even though we only scored twice,” said Sullivan. Piedmont goals against Mt. Eden came from Jack Nelson, a penalty kick by Enzo Bernales, and an own goal by their opponent. “Against Mt. Eden, we looked pretty comfortable. We scored early on but Mt. Eden had some good counterattacks in the first half and gave us a good game. In the second half, the boys really showed up and were a lot tougher. Staff Photos William Daniel scored two goals against San Leandro. Enzo Bernales had a goal against San Leandro and converted a penalty kick against Mt. Eden. They made fewer mistakes and had more quality in the final third,” added Sullivan. 5-0 over San Leandro In a rocket start, Piedmont scored three goals in the first 20 minutes of action against San Leandro. Will Daniel scored early, followed by Aiden Woolwine a couple of minutes later, and Daniel’s second goal at the 20th minute. Piedmont nearly scored again in the 25th minute, but it was called offside. Piedmont controlled possession In the second half, but didn’t Team captain T.J. O’Neil celebrates after a goal against San Leandro. get on the board until late in the game at the 75th and 80th minutes with goals by O’Neil and Enzo Bernales. In the 44th minute, Max Schleuning had two shots on goal; one hit the post and the other hit the crossbar a few minutes later. Sam Shelby had a shot on target in the 50th and also had a shot ring off of the post in the 57th. O’Neil’s goal in the 75th was a perfectly placed shot from the top of the box after dribbling around a defender to create shooting space. Bernales’ goal in the final moments was a product of a good buildup into the penalty area. 3-0 over Mt. Eden Piedmont scored its first goal in the 25th minute on a shot by Jack Nelson for a 1-0 lead at halftime. The Highlanders gained their second score five minutes into the second half thanks to an own goal by the Monarchs. The final goal came on a penalty kick by Bernales after Shelby drew a foul in the at the 60th minute. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-1-1 overall, 2-1-1 league) hosts San Lorenzo at Witter Field tomorrow, Thursday, December 22, at 6:00 p.m. in the final match before winter break.

articles.text: The Piedmont Post is seeking interns to cover Junior Varsity sports for the winter season – boys’ and girls’ basketball and soccer. The position offers budding sports journalists professional experience in covering events, learning the trade – and seeing their byline in print. Interns will work remotely with the Posts’ sports reporter, Jonathan Comeaux, who will advise and give feedback to interns wanting to publish their first articles. Those interested do not require playing experience in any sport, only an open mind and eagerness to learn. Jonathan will give young writers tips on how to cover sporting events, profile players, and utilize interviewing skills. Parents or PHS students may contact the newspaper at news@piedmont-post.com, or contact Comeaux by e-mail at JonathanCX525@gmail.com.

articles.text: With an enrollment of roughly 900 students, it is more common than not for Piedmont students to compete on two sports teams, sometimes three. Here is look at three athletes competing in multiple sports. JACK NELSON Football, Soccer, Lacrosse Jack Nelson, a senior, is among the only three-sport athletes at the school as an influential member of the football team in the fall, soccer team this winter, and lacrosse in the spring. Staff Photo Michaela Bini was a four-year varsity starter on the tennis team, and has competed in soccer the last two years. She’s pictured here scoring in Piedmont’s recent game with Oakland Tech. of the field. The team is off to a 3-0-1 start and 2-0 against league competition in the Foothill Division. Bini scored against Oakland Tech on December 16 and in a season-opening 3-2 loss against Miramonte on November 28. MICHAELA BINI Tennis & Soccer Jack Nelson played football in the fall, soccer this winter, and will be a marquee player on the WACC Championship lacrosse team in the spring. Last fall, Nelson was a marquee player on the football team as a running back and a linebacker before the varsity program was canceled after four games. He had over 100 yards against Seaside and had a kickoff return for a touchdown against Pierce. This winter, Nelson is a big part of Todd Sullivan’s soccer team and can line up at striker, on the wing, and as a midfielder. He scored once against Justin-Siena on November 30 and put one in recently against Mt. Eden on December 16. In the spring of 2022 he earned a first-team All-League selection for helping the lacrosse team capture its sixth consecutive WACC title and a berth in the Division 1 North Coast Section playoffs. In Piedmont’s league championship game against Bishop O’Dowd, Nelson scored one goal with three assists but his most critical play was forcing a ground ball on O’Dowd’s last possession, recovering it, and killing the clock for the win. DECLAN LINNANE Water Polo & Basketball Senior Michaela Bini was a four-year starter on the varsity tennis team and received an AllLeague selection as a doubles player. She helped Piedmont finish its season with a 16-3 overall record and a perfect 10-0 against league teams, It was the team’s first league title since 2018. This winter she is on Dan Chubbock’s soccer team primarily as a winger, often seen sprinting down the right side Declan Linnane helped the water polo team post a 20-7 record in the fall and win its second-consecutive WACC Championship. They reached the North Coast Section Semifinals where they lost 6-5 to No. 2 Marin Academy, including three goals in the fourth quarter. She helped Piedmont finish its season with a 16-3 overall record and a perfect 10-0 against league teams, It was the team’s first league title since 2018. This winter she is on Dan Chubbock’s soccer team primarily as a winger, often seen sprinting down the right side Declan Linnane helped the water polo team post a 20-7 record in the fall and win its second-consecutive WACC Championship. articles.text: Messi finally leads Argentine to the championship What a dramatic and amazing World Cup this was. In the end, Argentina captured its first title since 1986 and Lionel Messi solidified himself as the greatest player of the modern generation. Sunday’s f inal between Argentina and France eventually became one of the best World Cup Finals of all time. Completely outplayed by Argentina in the first half, Les Bleus stormed back from a 2-nil deficit, and again from a 3-2 disadvantage in overtime to force a penalty kick shootout of the ages. It became just the third championship game to reach penalties. The early ones were Brazil vs, Italy in 1994, and Italy vs, France in 2006. There were so many illustrious and awe-inspiring moments from this year. Here’s a recap of some of the best. • Lionel Messi cements his legacy Lionel Messi has now done it all; he is a 10-time La Liga winner at Barcelona, a winner of Ligue 1 with Paris St. Germain last year, winner of seven Cope del Reys, a four-time Champions League winner, winner of the Copa America, and now finally, at age 35, is now a World Cup Champion. He scored seven times in this year’s tournament, one behind France’s Kylian Mbappe, and bagged two goals in the final against France. He made the case for the greatest of all time. • Kylian Mbappe revives France Kylian Mbappe, at age 24, was extraordinary in only his second World Cup, He won the Golden Boot award as the leading scorer in the Cup with eight scores, including the first ever hat trick in the finals. He personally revived France after halftime when down 2-0, for a 3-3 tie late in the second period of overtime vs. Argentina. Mbappe is clearly the next great generational talent. With 12 World Cup goals, he is already tied for sixth-place on the all-time list with Brazilian legend Pele, • The magic of Morocco Morocco became the first ever African nation to reach the World Cup semifinals in the tournament’s 92-year history, shocking team after team through the tournament. The Atlas Lions did so by using patience and a stifling Photo courtesy of The Japan Times Morocco celebrates manager Walid Regragui after it became the first African nation to reach the World Cup semifinals. Photo courtesy of Sky News Croatia defeated Brazil in a dramatic PK shootout. Argentina and Lionel Messi lift the 2022 World Cup trophy. defense, knocking off world powers like No. 2 ranked Belgium 2-0 in the group stage to win Group F. They followed up by upsetting No. 7 Spain in penalty kicks in the Round of 16, blanking the Spaniards and bagging three PKs. And then came their dramatic 1-0 quarterfinals win over No. 9 Portugal, sending Ronaldo home to Lisbon. Following their win over Spain, Morocco players tossing manager Walid Regragui into the air became one of the most memorable images of this year’s games. • Croatia knocks out No. 1 Brazil Everyone knew walking into the quarterfinals that Brazil was the hands-down favorite, perhaps of the entire tournament with the No. 1 seed. But Croatia had other plans, and relied on its defense to force penalty kicks against the Canaries. It was the same blueprint that helped Croatia advance to the Finals in 2018. In PKs, Brazil opted to not use its superstar, Neymar, and it came back to bite them. Croatia won 4-2 in penalty kicks after Brazilian opted for center back Marquinhos to take the final attempt—ringing his shot against the post. • Japan falling by PKs in Round of 16 Japan winning Group F over Spain and Germany was the stuff of legend. Their group stage 2-1 win over Spain on December 1 featured one of the most controversial goals of the tournament when Kaoru Mitoma sent a pass with a fraction of the ball Photo courtesy of the Toronto Star Photo courtesy of 13thmansports.ca Kylian Mbappe brought France back from the brink in the Finals with a hat trick against Argentina. He won the Golden Boot trophy as the top scorer in the World Cup with eight goals. still on the goal line, sending it to Ao Tanaka for the eventual game-winner in the 51st minute.. They battled their way to penalty kicks against Croatia in the Round of 16 after ending regulation and overtime in a 1-1 draw. However, the Croatians won 3-1 in PKs. • Ronaldo’s last dance This year’s World Cup was most likely the last appearance of several players in their mid-to late 30s, including Messi, Croatia’s Luka Modric, Brazil’s Neymar, and Portugal’s Cristiano Ronaldo. Ronaldo’s time with Portugal this World Cup was less than anticipated and only polarized his diminishing product. Going into the games, Ronaldo bad-mouthed Manchester United in a shocking interview. He was sent to the bench in two games for Portugal at the World Cup. It wasn’t the glorious ride into the sunset Ronaldo envisioned. • Saudi Arabia upsets Argentina Argentina’s World Cup didn’t start as anticipated, losing 2-1 to Saudi Arabia in the opening game on November 22. The Argentines became the first team since Spain in 2010 to lose their first group stage match to eventually lift the trophy. Saudi Arabia fans went viral following the match, asking Where is Messi? They may have not made it out of the group stage, but that upset will live on forever. Photo courtesy of 13thmansports.ca Saudi Arabia’s upset of Argentina in the opening game was one of the most unexpected wins in World Cup history.

articles.text: Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside to see the 16-acre estate lit up for holidays. The non-profit historical landmark will be celebrating “Holidays at Filoli” through January 2. Take photos with Santa on December 23 from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Afterwards view a dozen festooned Christmas trees inside the estate. Filoli has a designated holiday decor team responsible for installing decorations inside and outside the mansion, and miles upon miles of string lights that drape the interior. Last year, the team installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreates the original holiday placement that is indicative of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents. The Bourns decorated with natural materials from the gardens, including pinecones and evergreen wreaths. Realistic artificial trees and garlands were not yet available in the early to mid-1900s. More original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene, one of her favorites, is displayed in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively in the daylight. Daytime admission gains you access to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://filoli.org/ events/holidays/. unique pieces for you & everyone on your list! ®
articles.title: Filoli House & Garden light display through January 2

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre reimagines Emily Brontë’s gothic masterpiece Wuthering Heights in a new play by Emma Rice. The play is showing onstage now through January 1. The 1847 novel tells the story of the Earnshaws and Lintons, two families living on the West Yorkshire moors, and the compelling relationship between the characters Catherine and Heathcliff. Heathcliff is rescued from the Liverpool docks as a young child, adopted by the Earnshaws and taken to live at Wuthering Heights. He strikes a friendship with Catherine Earnshaw and soon a fierce love ignites. Leah Brotherhead performs the lead role as Catherine. Her theater credits include Gulliver’s Travels (Unicorn Theatre), Lands (Bush Theatre/Summer Hall Edinburgh Fringe), and Two Gentlemen of Verona (The Globe Theatre/Liverpool Everyman). Liam Tamne will perform the role of Heathcliff. His extensive discography includes The Prince of Egypt (Dominion Theatre), Bonnie and Clyde (Theatre Royal Drury Lane). To obtain tickets, visit https:// www.berkeleyrep.org/shows/ wuthering-heights/. Berkeley Rep is located at 2025 Addison Street in Berkeley. Call the box office for tickets at (510) 647-2949, or purchase online at www.berkeleyrep.org.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s Wuthering Heights ends on January 1

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony musicians will perform alongside a screening of the movie Elf tonight and tomorrow. San Francisco Symphony musicians will perform the music from the 2003 holiday movie Elf with a screening of the film tonight and tomorrow Wednesday, December 21, and Thursday, December 22. This family-friendly event showcases the talent of symphony musicians performing the original score by John Debney. Elf is a comedy film directed by Jon Favreau, written by David Berenbaum, and starring Will Ferrell as Buddy the elf, a human living in the north pole who ventures to New York City to find his real family. Elf inspired the 2010 Broadway musical Elf: The Musical and NBC’s 2014 stop motion animated television special “Elf: Buddy’s Musical Christmas.” The Wednesday performance begins at 7:30 p.m.; the Thursday performance begins at 2 p.m. Let us help you find great gifts for family, friends, clients, and yourself: Champagne & fine wine, artisanal spirits, and holiday beers.

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s holiday favorite, Nutcracker, will be performed one more week at War Memorial Opera House, with a final show on December 27. This new adaptation is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks like the Painted Ladies by Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. San Francisco Ballet premieres the production every year and features “a kaleidoscope” of more than 150 dancers within the company to tell the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco, accompanied by a live orchestra that performs Tchaikovsky’s familiar score. A diverse array of instruments are played during performances, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani — all played by a group of three musicians. The Scenic Design is by Michael Yeargan, costume Design is by Martin Pakledinaz, lighting Design is by James F. Ingalls, and projection design by Wendall K. Harrington. Nutcracker is appropriate for children aged five and older; no children under age three will be permitted. The ballet runs two hours with one intermission. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker-dec-2022/. articles.text: SF Jazz will host trumpeter Chris Botti at Miner Auditorium in a weeklong engagement, January 3-8. An American trumpeter and composer, he is best known as a contemporary jazz musician. He gained popularity for his 2001 recording of his “Night Sessions” album, which fused pop and jazz genres, then won a Grammy Award a decade later for his album “Impressions.” Botti’s SFJazz shows have become a New Year tradition and routinely sell out. This year, he is joined by a number of talented artists, including Chad Lefkowitz-Brown (saxophone), Leonardo Amuedo (guitar), Sandy Cameron (violin), Holger Marjamaa (piano), Reggie Hamilton (bass), Lee Pearson (drums), and Sy Smith and John Splithoff on vocals. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/chris-botti-2223/. Jazz trumpeter Chris Botti will perform in San Francisco January 3-8.

articles.text: The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn verges of being a heartwarming allegory about a mysterious man named Noah Dearborn (Sidney Poitier) who lives alone on a bucolic farm on the outskirts of a small southern town. He is a gifted carpenter, woodworker, generous to a fault, and seems ageless. soon becomes clear that the denizens of the town keep Noah’s presence a well-kept secret, understanding that it’s his preference to live quietly, go about his work, and be left undisturbed. Actually, in countless ways, his life is so spare and timeless, it seems as if the 20th century has passed him by. And so it has, that is until a cohort of land developers arrive and decide that in order to build a shopping center they need Noah’s acreage. Driven by greed, they set up an office in town and send slick and fashionable Christian Nelson (George Newbern) out to pay Noah a visit, prepared to make him an offer for his property that, given the amount, he certainly cannot refuse. Of course, Noah does that very thing: he insists he has no interest in selling his farm, no matter the offer. Nelson points out that Noah could retire, move into town and relax in his golden years. But all Nelson hears in response is a polite “no.” He returns to his office suite and discusses the result with his Mary-Jane Parker and Sidney Poitier in The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn. partners, searching for a scheme to get the property, deciding that perhaps there’s a way to get Noah declared mentally incompetent; after all, who in his right mind would turn down the well-over market price they are prepared to pay? Nelson, whose fiancé, Dr. Valerie Crane (Mary-Louise Parker), is a psychologist, gets the idea for her to drive down from the city and pay Noah a visit, the intent being to evaluate him professionally and determine if he is unable to manage his own affairs. Which she does. What nelson is unprepared for is the magic that defines not only Noah, but his farm, especially his residence, which is the second floor of his weathered barn. Valerie is smitten with Noah and grows suspicious regarding her fiance’s plan. And so the story develops, filled with charming moments and outstanding performances by Poitier and Dianne Wiest. She was nominated for an Emmy for Best Supporting Actress, delivering a superb portrayal of Sarah McClelland, a neighbor who lives just down the road from Noah and constantly searches for reasons to have him repair something while thanking him with a homemade pie. And no surprise, Mary-Louise Parker who, in her role as Valerie, displays an abundance of talent. The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn. Directed by Greg Champian. Starring Sidney Poitier, Dianne Wiest, Mary-Jane Parker. I hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 1999. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn a quiet gem with Sidney Poitier, Dianne Wiest

articles.text: They were a dynamic duo. Each was a star in the musical firmament, but oh, so different. One of them had a very quiet demeanor. He dressed in black and was known as “the man in black”. The other was much more flamboyant. Perhaps you are thinking of Johnny Cash as the man in black and the more flamboyant musician as Elvis Presley (“Elvis the Pelvis” as he was known). They had a friendly rivalry and even tried to imitate each other. Nothing could be funnier. Elvis’s rock and roll music wasn’t for Johnny Cash and vice versa for Cash’s country music. But… History frequently repeats itself, so let’s go back. The names are different, but the story is familiar. This time we’re talking about classical musicians. The original “man in black” was violinist-composer Arcangelo Corelli and the flamboyant character was the famous German composer George Frederick Handel. Corelli was a rather somber guy and, like Johnny Cash, he liked the low registers of music. He had good connections despite a rather sordid past. In some ways, Presley was quite a bit like George Frederick Handel. Both traveled a lot, wore flashy clothes and were binge eaters. Let’s go back to Rome in 1706. Corelli was rehearsing a composition by Handel. He was having some trouble because of the high register. Handel was present at the rehearsal and became annoyed. Having an assertive nature, he walked up to Corelli and said: “May I borrow your violin? Let me show you how the music goes.” After Corelli got his violin back, being very diplomatic, he said: “Maestro Handel, you must excuse me. articles.text: Crazy Rich Asians is a highgloss romantic comedy, based on the best-selling novel by Singaporean author Kevin Kwan. The story is familiar fare: Nick (Henry Golding), a handsome and successful Asian born New Yorker, brings his girl friend, Rachel (Constance Wu), a Chinese American university econ professor, to his home in Singapore for his best friend’s wedding. What he fails to tell her, though they’ve dated for more than a year, is that he is a scion of one of the wealthiest families in Southeast Asia. They are, without hyperbole, crazy rich. Actually “crazy rich” doesn’t begin to describe the incredibly high-thread-count wealth Nick’s family possesses, a reality that at first stuns, then takes Rachel’s breath away, given that she comes from a modest background and was raised by a hard-working single mom. Recall that in every solid romcom there has to be a roadblock (often comedic) to the couple’s union. In Crazy Rich Asians it is quickly obvious that Nick’s family is a matriarchy wherein his mother, Eleanor (Michelle Yeoh), and his grandmother, Ah Ma (Lisa Lu), steadfastly believe in endogamy and are both committed to sabotaging the couple’s relationship. Not only does Eleanor’s mien suggest her displeasure, but her barbed-tongue rejection of Rachel is voiced with a quiet, almost malevolent hurtfulness. And it is with dripping sarcasm that Nick is reminded by his mother that his girlfriend is Chinese-American with the emphasis on “American.” Michelle Yeoh, Henry Golding and Constance Wu in a sceen from Crazy Rich Asians. It is soon obvious that Rachel – a generous, kind-hearted woman – is overwhelmed not only with the family’s intimidating wealth (I would argue that this lily is far too gilded) but with the countless cultural cues that she can’t quite sort out and which contribute to her sense of unease. Some might call it culture shock lite. Clearly, Nick, in all his good-natured naiveté, has failed to prepare her for what she will have to absorb. What distinguishes Crazy Rich Asians from its antecedents is that the cast is 100 percent Asian, a fact that has been lavished with praise given that Asians are underrepresented in Hollywood. Here is a film that clearly attempts to right this deficit and mirrors much of the discussion that took place when Black Panther was released. Crazy could have been set in any city where the stereotypical conceits of wealth and social class – old money vs. nouveau riche – are concerned. The essential story is pretty much universal. Regarding the outcome, well, in most rom-coms the basic question posed is, “Will love conquer all?” You can, of course, guess at the ending, which brings to mind the Cinderella fairytale. Crazy Rich Asians. Directed by Jon M. Chu. Starring Constance Wu, Henry Golding, Michelle Yeoh. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv.

articles.text: Ignore those who might say that Five Feet Apart relies on a bevy of “sick-lit” tropes. That’s lazy criticism. All narratives rely on the familiar and the vagaries of the human condition. The good ones find new and nuanced ways to construct characters and plots that are compelling. This film does that, intending not only to emotionally reach the audience – in this case the demographic is teen/tween – but it is also meant to educate regarding a harrowing, incurable disease known as Cystic Fibrosis. The setting of Five Feet Apart is a large urban hospital somewhere in the U.S. Stella Grant (Haley Lu Richardson), 17-18, has just returned to what is called the “CFer” ward for what she stoically refers to as “tune-up.” This is not her first visit, for she has chronic CF. She is spirited, resilient, and quick to smile, and she suffers from this incurable, rapacious respiratory disease with a sincere, direct understanding of her circumstances. Mere decades ago, children born with CF likely did not live past their tenth year. Now, medicine and research pushes the expanding edges of the envelope ever outward, well beyond that first decade. Hence adolescents such as Stella are fully cognizant of the challenges that confront them. Stella’s room is hospital cheerful, with a med cart and books and a full bulletin board of getwell cards. Always nearby is her portable oxygen machine that is connected by a plastic tube that is hooked around both ears and inserted in her nose. Monitoring Stella’s care is the ward nurse, Barb (Kimberly Herbert Gregory), who runs a tight ship, insisting that her charges remain six feet apart. Always. Or risk contracting from another CF patient a lethal microbe called B.cepacia. It’s on the ward that Haley meets Will Newman (Cole Sprouse), also newly arrived, and also hooked up to an oxygen tank. Like Stella, he has CF and is in the hospital to participate in a clinical drug trial. When they first meet it’s oil and water, with an overlay of chemistry. Stella studiously ignores him and his questions, with a dash of salt, which, in Stella speak, means that Cole Sprouse and Haley Lu Richardson star in Five Feet Apart. she finds him interesting. So, they circle one another while stalked by their medical reality that frames their days – at times oppressively so. She is structured and obsessively organized and is on a lung transplant list. Will, whose disease is a bit more advanced and is therefore disqualified for a transplant, resists the drug trial, the meds, and the intrusiveness of his treatment. He would rather sketch or sit outside on the edge of the hospital roof, looking out at the horizon. Given all that is mentioned above, Five Feet Apart is essentially a charming romance. A love story. And therefore, like all such tales, there are exigent circumstances that must be overcome if a relationship is to bloom. Those barriers are expressed in the admonition by nurse Barb that Stella and Will cannot violate the six-foot rule. Their lives depend on it and they will not die on her watch. Naturally, they whittle it down to five feet, which is about the length of a pool stick, one actually carried around by Stella. I found the writing to be excellent – even with a dash of melodrama in act three – and the performances by Richardson and Sprouse extraordinary. They each inhabit their characters fully, especially Richardson who is radiant, her portrayal heartfelt and will definitely draw the tween/teen demographic into her and Will’s world. The sustained struggle of both Stella and Will is to survive another day. They face a reality that dictates that every breath they take is framed by a constant awareness that it requires effort and that what is almost a cliché – life is short – is a truth to be faced every day and is never an abstraction. Five Feet Apart is also about courage. Remarkable courage. CF is an anvil placed on young shoulders, theirs to confront and this film resists any temptation to exploit this disease for fanciful fairytale outcomes. Five Feet Apart. Directed by Justin Baldoni. Starring Haley Lu Richardson, Cole Sprouse, Kimberly Herbert Gregory. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Released in 2019. Now streaming on VUDU/Netflix/ Prime.
