articles.text: A scene from Luck. Luck is a vibrant computer animated film about an 18-yearold girl named Sam Greenfield who has spent all of her life at the Summerland School For Girls orphanage, wishing year after year that she would find a “forever family.” Sadly, no one ever appeared and now Sam has aged out of the orphanage and must go out into the world and live on her own, meaning she has to say goodbye to her young friend Hazel (Adelynn Spoon) who also hopes daily that a “forever family” will come to Summerland and take her home. Sam considers never having found a family as an example of being someone who has constant bad luck. Random objects fall on her, she slips and trips, and almost everything she touches breaks. So on her must-leave-Summerland day, she is driven to a new apartment by a cranky social worker who informs her that she can only visit Hazel on visitors’ day. She gets a job at Flowers & More, but on her first day, of course, oversleeps; her bathroom door sticks; and she drops her toast on the floor, jelly-side down; her bicycle tire has a flat, hence she arrives late for work. Her kind-hearted boss, Marv, tells her that the next day will be better, but does assign her to the cart patrol where she can’t wreck stuff. She also visits Hazel, but finds her despondent, still wishing for a family. Sam promises to bring her a lucky penny. Sam goes about settling in and visits a bustling café where she spots a black cat and begins to chat the critter up. And it’s while she’s there she spots a shiny penny and thinks of Hazel. Having the penny in her possession, things unexpectedly begin to go right: her socks match, the toast doesn’t fall upside down and the bathroom door opens with ease. But in a moment of bad timing she drops the penny in the toilet. She returns to the café looking for another penny, and encounters the same black cat that apparently can talk and tells her his name is Bob (Simon Pegg). The cat takes off through the streets and Sam follows and sees Bob pass through a strange portal. Sam is right behind Bob and discovers she is in a place called Land of Luck. And thus begins her very remarkable adventure. Land of Luck is filled with strange creatures: leprechauns, floating elevators, and even an anxiety-driven dragon (Jane Fonda). The head of Land of Luck is a woman named the Captain (Whoopi Goldberg). There are lots of surprises, and Sam does indeed learn a great deal about good luck and bad luck in the upside-down land, knowledge that she uses to help Hazel. Luck. Directed by Peggy Holmes. Skydance animated. With voices of Eva Noblezada, Simon Pegg, Whoopi Goldberg. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Released in 2022. Now streaming on Apple tv+.
articles.title: Luck and an upside down world

articles.text: Piedmont residents wanting a new community pool don’t have to hold their breath any longer. A groundbreaking ceremony for the city’s new community pool drew a crowd of hundreds on Saturday morning, December 17. Residents showed up in support and to applaud speeches from those most involved. Speakers at the groundbreaking ceremony included community members, and city official who have been working on building a new pool for more than 20 years, including resident Clarence Mamuyac, whose firm, ELS Architecture and Urban Design of Berkeley, was selected to design a new aquatic facility. “It’s a place to carve out a little bit of joy in our overcrowded and stressful schedule. That’s what this community pool means,” said Mayor Teddy Gray King. “This pool will change people’s lives. And for all of us here who supported measure UU, this is your legacy. I am so deeply appreciative.” she added. Hundreds of Pedometers braved the cold winter morning to formally acknowledged the beginning of pool construction.
articles.title: City rallies for groundbreaking of new community pool

articles.text: Swim practice was canceled last Saturday so that more than 100 members of the Piedmont Swim Team, their parents and coaches could converge at Piedmont Park for a photo prior to the groundbreaking ceremony of the new Piedmont Community Pool. “I’m super excited,” said Swim Teach coach Colby Price. ”It’s making everything a whole lot more real. The pool has been empty a long time, and it’s exciting to see that we are starting this project.” 11-year-old Amor Rodriguez has been on the swim team for eight months and while she loves the coaches and the team, she says having a home pool will make it even better. “I’m excited about the swimming pool because now we can have our own place to swim so we don’t have to go to different pools,” she said. “The new pool seems really cool, and I like it,” said Mason Armstrong. Nathan Judy said the swim team, provides him a sense of community and has become a second family for him. “We need a home pool right now. We’re a Piedmont swim team and we don’t have a pool. It would be nice to have one [within walking distance],” said Judy. Paige Arnold, who will be swimming for Amherst College next fall, was seven years old when she started swimming at the Piedmont Pool. She has fond memories of it being a fun community spot. While she was sad to see it close, she is looking forward to this next chapter. “I’m hoping that kids can have the same journey as mine; they’re at the age when I started swimming at the pool. I’m excited for them to have a community pool Young Piedmont Swim Team members Eva Stolicny (left) and Maia Saxena hold up their sign at the ceremony Photos by Lisa Carnazzo Event organizers acknowledged the large number of kids from the Piedmont Swim Team and asked them to have a photo taken. rather than going to Mills College and other pools.” Piedmont Swim Team member Zafar Majid said he misses the days when he could walk to swim practice right after school. “I’m excited about this new pool, because it takes a long time to drive to one pool and back. It’ll be nice to have a pool in our community.” After a brief ceremony the Piedmont Swim Team was asked to come up for a photo because the event organizers were blown away by how many members showed up. Piedmont Swim Team members Asher Takazawa (left), Cole Carnazzo, and Evan Byun take one last look at the old pool. Piedmont Swim Team members gathered at Piedmont Park ahead of the groundbreaking ceremony on Saturday, December 17.
articles.title: Piedmont Swim Team, bursting at the seams, eagerly awaits new pool

Piedmont Swim Team, bursting at the seams, eagerly awaits new pool By Lisa Carnazzo Swim practice was canceled last Saturday so that more than 100 members of the Piedmont Swim Team, their parents and coaches could converge at Piedmont Park for a photo prior to the groundbreaking ceremony of the new Piedmont Community Pool. “I’m super excited,” said Swim Teach coach Colby Price. ”It’s making everything a whole lot more real. The pool has been empty a long time, and it’s exciting to see that we are starting this project.” 11-year-old Amor Rodriguez has been on the swim team for eight months and while she loves the coaches and the team, she says having a home pool will make it even better. “I’m excited about the swimming pool because now we can have our own place to swim so we don’t have to go to different pools,” she said. “The new pool seems really cool, and I like it,” said Mason Armstrong. Nathan Judy said the swim team, provides him a sense of community and has become a second family for him. “We need a home pool right now. We’re a Piedmont swim team and we don’t have a pool. It would be nice to have one [within walking distance],” said Judy. Paige Arnold, who will be swimming for Amherst College next fall, was seven years old when she started swimming at the Piedmont Pool. She has fond memories of it being a fun community spot. While she was sad to see it close, she is looking forward to this next chapter. “I’m hoping that kids can have the same journey as mine; they’re at the age when I started swimming at the pool. I’m excited for them to have a community pool Young Piedmont Swim Team members Eva Stolicny (left) and Maia Saxena hold up their sign at the ceremony Photos by Lisa Carnazzo Event organizers acknowledged the large number of kids from the Piedmont Swim Team and asked them to have a photo taken. rather than going to Mills College and other pools.” Piedmont Swim Team member Zafar Majid said he misses the days when he could walk to swim practice right after school. “I’m excited about this new pool, because it takes a long time to drive to one pool and back. It’ll be nice to have a pool in our community.” After a brief ceremony the Piedmont Swim Team was asked to come up for a photo because the event organizers were blown away by how many members showed up. Piedmont Swim Team members Asher Takazawa (left), Cole Carnazzo, and Evan Byun take one last look at the old pool. Piedmont Swim Team members gathered at Piedmont Park ahead of the groundbreaking ceremony on Saturday, December 17.

articles.text: Betsy Andersen (left), Teddy King, Sara Lillevand and Daniel Gonzalez get the work started at the new community pool’s ground breaking ceremony. Mayor Teddy Gray King addresses the large crowd for the momentous occasion. City Administrator Sarah Lillevand introduced the speakers of the morning, all of whom were vital to the new pool project to the groundbreaking moment. Each speaker emphasized that replacing the old pool, constructed in 1964, is a once in a generation effort. Mamuyac described how he and residents Josh Bernstein and future mayor Abe Friedman began some preliminary planning of a new pool in the early 1990s. In addition to leading the efforts of the current design, Maymuyac was instrumental in creating the 2017 conceptual master plan which was used as a basis to begin the campaign for fundraising for the Measure UU bond in 2020. “Mayor Bob McBain and the rest of the council decided to go for this bond right in the middle Piedmont resident Clarence Mamuyac, architect for the new community pool, addresses a large crowd gathered for a groundbreaking ceremony on December 17. of a pandemic – and it passed,” Mamuyac said with a smile. But the journey was not completed with the passage of the $19.5 million bond in 2020. Inflationary construction costs forced a change in the design of the pool facility from two stories to one. Even after shrinking the aquatics building, a gap of more than $2 million between project cost estimates and available funds still presented itself. The proposition of having to decrease the sizes of the two pool was reluctantly floated. “To be honest, I think PRFO (Piedmont Recreation Facilities Organization, led by Steve Collins) saved this project,” said Lillevand. “To move to this point, to implement Clarence Mamuyac’s wonderful design, would not have happened without PRFO, who stepped up in August, when things were pretty uncertain.” she added. As of December 5, PRFO was halfway to its goal of raising $2.1 million for the completion of the new community pool as designed, with a main pool big enough for regulation water polo and both pools completely heated by electricity. The event brought the community together, including more than 100 members of the burgeoning Piedmont Swim Team. Breakfast and coffee were served, and graphics were displayed outlining the project. After the ceremonial shoveling of dirt, residents were invited to enter the old pool, sans water, for one last lap down memory lane. The City of Piedmont aims for the pool to be completed by the summer of 2024. For more information on the new pool, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool .

articles.text: Russian-Ukrainian war. Outdoor terrace heaters are banned in France. Unfortunately, their popularity is now growing outside Europe, such as in the U.S. The city’s monster trucks rumbled through Parisian streets in early April collecting the steely heat-servants that proprietors valiantly placed at the curb, and the haulers crushed them on the spot. The sound was deafening, I couldn’t hear my friend Terrance over the prolonged metal gnashing and grinding while we sat at a sidewalk table having lunch at Les Philosophe’s. What a sad, sickening saga to watch: the heaters looked brand new, and this was a wretched climax to three decades of cozy café life any day, every season, when patrons were kings, smoking and sipping a coffee or Kir Royal, and people-watching. Smokers were a prime reason that outdoor seating grew popular, when consciousness laws in the 1990s began protecting food workers exposed to second-hand smoke. Restaurant owners happily attracted customers with grand awnings and enclosures warmed by giant metallic heaters wondrously engineered for comfort. Regulars need not shed their coats, perhaps unbuttoning of outer layers, and they sat for hours, and quite a few diners huddled over laptops upon finding the outdoor café to be a convenient office. The December sun sets before 5 p.m., so the night is long for restaurants serving until midnight or later. Seated at an outside table View to the west of Tuileries and its Marché Noël from the grand Pont Alexander III. Coupole at Les Galeries Lafayette, Haussmann Boulevard. at nightfall in 30º temperatures is a delightful memory, but it’s not yet known how the sacrifice we make will impact the restaurant business that makes Paris the café society of the world. Time will tell. And as President Macron is fond of saying, when it comes to the environment and climate change, there is no Planet B. Vive la Paris. articles.text: It was another beautiful, cold, clear day last Wednesday for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. Melba Yee filled in for activity leader Dick Carter with a big group of 50 walkers and three K-9 best friends were on hand. Among the first-time walkers were local architect Rebecca Schnier, Phil Witte’s wife, and Joyce Bailey, a recent arrival to Piedmont. Piedmont architect and urban planner Will Adams led the walkers on a 1.6 mile loop on the familiar hilly streets around Exedra Plaza viewing and discussing the numerous architectural styles close to the center of town. These included Mission Revival, Craftsman, Victorian, Tudor, several Contemporary styles, Spanish Revival, Colonial Revival, and Art Nouveau. The group stopped at nine locations to review 12 buildings. It was astutely pointed out that there is an interesting richness to the city texture that results from so many different building styles. Some pointed out that what unites the different styles is the landscaping, especially the rows of mature street trees that connect and soften the differences of the buildings. The walk ended with the group being made privy by Will to a secret shortcut on their way back to the Exedra Plaza. On December 21 Melba Yee and Mike Henn will take the group down the hill to Zachary’s Pizza on Grand Avenue for a holiday lunch. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. A large group of Wednesday Walkers stopped for a photo on hazel Lane during their walk led by Will Adams in central Piedmont on Wednesday, December 14.
articles.title: Wednesday Walkers see range of architecture in walk led by Will Adams

articles.text: One of our favorite fall and winter fruit combinations is pears and cranberries. This cake speaks of the seasons and is welcomed on a dessert table for brunch, coffee or teatime, and dinner. I enjoy its simplicity but use your imagination on how to serve it according to the situation. A simple dusting of confectioner’s sugar or a dollop of softly whipped cream will go nicely. Or sliced as is won’t compromise its visual appeal. Choose either d’Anjou or Bosc pears if available, as they will hold up during the hour or so of baking, retaining both shape and some texture when fully baked. In comparison Bartlett pears can turn very soft and mushy. I usually load up on fresh cranberries as soon as I see them in stores. I keep a bag out for immediate use and toss the rest in the freezer, so cranberries are usually available at our house. If you don’t happen to have this small quantity on hand, substitute with raspberries or other fruit. Using frozen is fine, also. Pear Cranberry Cake Adapted from Back from Scratch INGREDIENTS • 1 cup unsalted butter, softened • 1 cup granulated sugar • 3 large eggs, room temperature • 2 cups all-purpose flour • 1 teaspoon baking powder • 1/2 teaspoon baking soda • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt • 1/3 cup milk or half and half, room temperature • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1/2 teaspoon almond extract • 1 large pear, d’Anjou or Bosc, cut into 12 wedges • 1/4 cup cranberries, whole • 1/4 cup sliced almonds INSTRUCTIONS 1. Position an oven rack in the center position. Preheat oven to 350° F. Generously butter the sides and bottom of a 9-inch spring form pan. 2. In a small bowl, whisk together the flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt. Set aside. 3. In a large mixing bowl, cream the softened butter and sugar on medium speed until light and fluffy, 3 – 4 minutes. Scrape the sides of the bowl as needed. Add eggs, one at a time, beating well after each addition. Add vanilla and almond extracts and beat to incorporate. 4. Add about one-third of the flour mixture to the butter mixture, then half of the milk. Repeat with another one-third of the flour, the remaining milk, and finally the remaining flour; mixing just until combined after each addition. Do not over mix. 5. Transfer the batter into the prepared pan, smoothing the top to an even level. Arrange the pear slices in a decorative fashion, then distribute the cranberries. 6 Bake until lightly browned, about 30 minutes. Sprinkle with sliced almonds, and continue baking another 30 minutes, or until a wooden pick inserted in the center comes out clean. 7. Let cool in the pan for about 10 minutes, remove the sides of the springform and continue to cool slightly. The cake may be served warm or at room temperature. Add a dusting of confectioner’s sugar or softly whipped cream to serve. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. Original published in the Piedmont Post on December 1, 2021
articles.title: Pear Cranberry Cake – a holiday treat for all

articles.text: On Saturday, December 17, Sacha Grippando, an independent jewelry appraiser and resident of Piedmont, gave an insightful and detailed talk at Piedmont Center for the Arts about jewelry from the Gilded Age. She began by outlining the history of the Gilded Age, talking about the rise of families like the Vanderbilts, Astors, Morgans and Rockefellers and how jewelry was used as a signifier of wealth and status. She went on to speak about the American heiresses or “dollar princesses” as they were referred to and how they brought their wealth to Europe, particularly to England, by marrying into old aristocratic and cash poor families who needed an injection of money to upkeep their massive ancestral palaces. She then moved on to talk about the highly influential coronations that occurred during this period that warranted the commissioning of some fabulous pieces of jewelry as well as how influential figures like Queen Alexandra and Maria Feodorovna, the Empress of Russia had on the style and types of jewelry that were popular. She also discussed the change in fashion from the voluminous hooped Victorian skirts to the tighter bustle dresses of the 1880s. She described how the evolution of fashion affected the types of jewelry that could be worn, and the rise of global luxury brands, Sothebys devant decorsage Sacha Grippando speaks at the Piedmont Center for the Arts about the jewelry from the Gilded Age. the notably Cartier, and their influence on the jewelry of the period. She recounted the humorous tale of how Cartier ended up with their flagship American store on 653 5th Avenue by swapping it for two strands of natural pearls. The next section of the talk focused on the jewelry; the manufacture, choice of gemstones and precious metals and the types that were popular. She examined the enormous effect of the Diamond Rush in South Africa in the late 19th century thus creating an abundance of diamonds on the market. She also discussed innovations made in metalsmithing and the rise in the use of platinum as well as talking about innovations in diamond cutting. She concluded with a discussion of the famous Hope diamond and its illustrious Gilded Age owner, the socialite and heiress Evalyn Walsh McLean. The lecture provided a delightful overview of a period of time that glittered and sparkled through the amazing jewelry that was created and worn. Grippando plans to host more jewelry lectures in 2023. The next one will be on jewelry from the Art Deco period.
articles.title: Grippando speaks at Center for the Arts

articles.text: Is your New Year’s resolution to be more sustainable in 2023? Here are eight actions you can take to lower your carbon footprint this year! 1. Go zero waste: Swap out single-use items in your home for reusable or zero waste options. In the kitchen, you can exchange plastic wrap for beeswax wrap and zip-top bags for reusable silicone bags. Make the switch to eco-friendly and low-waste personal hygiene products. For example, try using a bamboo toothbrush or a shampoo bar. Check out nearby refill stores like Fillgood and Re-Up to get started today. 2. Start Composting: When organic waste decomposes in a landfill without oxygen, it produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. By composting your food scraps, you can easily reduce your ecological footprint. Piedmont residents can request a free 1.5-gallon kitchen scrap pail by emailing sustainability@piedmont.ca.gov. 3. Electrify your home: Here in Piedmont, residential buildings account for nearly half of in-territory greenhouse gas emissions. An overwhelming majority of these emissions come from natural gas used for heating and cooling. Swapping out gas appliances for electric appliances has the potential to significantly reduce your home’s greenhouse gas emissions. To help your electrification journey, the City of Piedmont is launching an Electrification Rebate Program in January. Residents will be eligible for cash rebates to support the purchase of electric appliances such as heat pumps and heat pump water heaters. This rebate can be stacked on top of the many existing rebates available from the region, state, and federal government. Check out SwitchIsOn.org and RewiringAmerica.org/app/ira-calculator to learn more about available rebates. 4. Don’t buy anything new: Every product we buy has its own carbon footprint from the materials used to create it, the manufacturing process, the packaging, and its delivery. See how long you can go without buying anything (other than food and necessities). You might be surprised at how hard it is to go even a couple of days without making a purchase. When it’s time to buy something, see if you can get it second hand. Try a local thrift store or a Buy Nothing group on Facebook. 5. Drive less: Make a commitment to walk, bike and take public transit whenever possible this year. When you do drive, make sure that your tires are inflated and perform regular maintenance to maximize efficiency. If public transit isn’t accessible for your commute, consider carpooling. articles.text: Starting on Tuesday, January 3, 2023, the City of Piedmont will offer rebates for the removal of existing gas appliances and for their replacement with certain electric appliances. Rebates will be available for single family and multi-family properties. Eligible low-income applicants may qualify for additional funding. Rebates will only be issued for existing buildings; new construction is not eligible for this program. Rebates can be applied to equipment and installation labor for projects applying for a Building Permit on or after January 3. Here are some frequently asked questions about the program: Why is the City of Piedmont offering this program? The City is offering this rebate program to incentivize homeowners to electrify their homes. Building electrification has the potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in Piedmont and help meet the City’s goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions 40% by 2030, as set by the Piedmont Climate Action Plan 2.0, which is available at bit. ly/3FI54mE. Will installing electric appliances increase monthly utility bills? The exact costs and savings will vary depending on your individual situation. Switching from a gas to electric-powered appliance may increase your electricity bill, while decreasing your gas bill. Nonetheless, using an efficient heat pump can lower your heating bills dramatically, especially in Piedmont where winters do not get too cold. If I can only afford to make one change, which appliance would be best for me to swap out first? As with many things, it depends on your home and your energy use. Traditionally, heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems (HVAC) are often the biggest energy consumers, followed by water heating systems. It also may be best to swap out the oldest appliance that is most in need of being replaced. Are there any additional or hidden costs to electrification? Besides the labor and appliance cost there may be costs to upgrade your home’s electrical system, depending on its age and condition. Fortunately, California has introduced a number of rebates and incentives that make electrifying your home more affordable than ever. Visit switchison.org/incentives to learn more. What happens to my old gas appliances when I make the switch to electric? Consider donation or resale before recycling. Appliances may be recycled with Republic Services. Call Republic Services at 800-320-8077 to schedule a special bulky item pickup. In order to be hauled away, all doors must be sealed with duct tape and appliances must be empty. Appliances may also be recycled through the retailer. Confirmation will have to be documented on the receipt as recycled. Funding for the program is limited and applications will be accepted until funding is exhausted. To learn more about qualification for the program, rebate amounts, and eligible electric appliances, please visit the following link: piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/planning___building/about_building_/rebates_and_incentives. Find the answers to more frequently asked questions about the rebate program at bit.ly/3YCKZXg.

pages.text: Wednesday, December 21, 2022 25 Grippando speaks at Center for the Arts On Saturday, December 17, Sacha Grippando, an independent jewelry appraiser and resident of Piedmont, gave an insightful and detailed talk at Piedmont Center for the Arts about jewelry from the Gilded Age. She began by outlining the history of the Gilded Age, talking about the rise of families like the Vanderbilts, Astors, Morgans and Rockefellers and how jewelry was used as a signifier of wealth and status. She went on to speak about the American heiresses or “dollar princesses” as they were referred to and how they brought their wealth to Europe, particularly to England, by marrying into old aristocratic and cash poor families who needed an injection of money to upkeep their massive ancestral palaces. She then moved on to talk about the highly influential coronations that occurred during this period that warranted the commissioning of some fabulous pieces of jewelry as well as how influential figures like Queen Alexandra and Maria Feodorovna, the Empress of Russia had on the style and types of jewelry that were popular. She also discussed the change in fashion from the voluminous hooped Victorian skirts to the tighter bustle dresses of the 1880s. Here are eight actions you can take to lower your carbon footprint this year! 1. Go zero waste: Swap out single-use items in your home for reusable or zero waste options. In the kitchen, you can exchange plastic wrap for beeswax wrap and zip-top bags for reusable silicone bags. Make the switch to eco-friendly and low-waste personal hygiene products. For example, try using a bamboo toothbrush or a shampoo bar. Check out nearby refill stores like Fillgood and Re-Up to get started today. 2. Start Composting: When organic waste decomposes in a landfill without oxygen, it produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. By composting your food scraps, you can easily reduce your ecological footprint. Piedmont residents can request a free 1.5-gallon kitchen scrap pail by emailing sustainability@piedmont.ca.gov. 3. Electrify your home: Here in Piedmont, residential buildings account for nearly half of in-territory greenhouse gas emissions. An overwhelming majority of these emissions come from natural gas used for heating and cooling. Swapping out gas appliances for electric appliances has the potential to significantly reduce your home’s greenhouse gas emissions. To help your electrification journey, the City of Piedmont is launching an Electrification Rebate Program in January. Residents will be eligible for cash rebates to support the purchase of electric appliances such as heat pumps and heat pump water heaters. This rebate can be stacked on top of the many existing rebates available from the region, state, and federal government. Check out SwitchIsOn.org and RewiringAmerica.org/app/ira-calculator to learn more about available rebates. 4. Don’t buy anything new: Every product we buy has its own carbon footprint from the materials used to create it, the manufacturing process, the packaging, and its delivery. See how long you can go without buying anything (other than food and necessities). You might be surprised at how hard it is to go even a couple of days without making a purchase. When it’s time to buy something, see if you can get it second hand. Try a local thrift store or a Buy Nothing group on Facebook. 5. Drive less: Make a commitment to walk, bike and take public transit whenever possible this year. When you do drive, make sure that your tires are inflated and perform regular maintenance to maximize efficiency. If public transit isn’t accessible for your commute, consider carpooling. If you’re planning on purchasing an electric car this year, there are many rebates and incentives available! Check out DriveClean.ca.gov and RewiringAmerica.org/app/ ira-calculator to learn more. 6. Participate in “Veganuary”: Veganuary is a challenge to eat plant-based for the month of January. A study done by the University of Oxford found that cutting meat and dairy products from your diet could reduce an individual’s carbon footprint from food by up to 73%! If you don’t want to commit to a whole month, try eating vegan one day a week. 7. Conserve water: Commit to reducing your water usage in 2023. The East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) has free water saving devices like efficient showerheads and faucet aerators. EBMUD also has rebates available for flowmeters, graywater diversion systems and those who convert their lawns to be drought resilient. Learn more at EBMUD. com/water/conservation-and-rebates/rebates. 8. Find a way to engage with your community: Vote, sign petitions, submit public comments, volunteer, or join a community group. Big environmental changes are possible when we work together. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps AmeriCorps Fellow with the City of Piedmont. sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov READ IT IN THE POST Sothebys devant decorsage Sacha Grippando speaks at the Piedmont Center for the Arts about the jewelry from the Gilded Age. the notably Cartier, and their influence on the jewelry of the period. She recounted the humorous tale of how Cartier ended up with their flagship American store on 653 5th Avenue by swapping it for two strands of natural pearls. The next section of the talk focused on the jewelry; the manufacture, choice of gemstones and precious metals and the types that were popular. She examined the enormous effect of the Diamond Rush in South Africa in the late 19th century thus creating an abundance of diamonds on the market. She also discussed innovations made in metalsmithing and the rise in the use of platinum as well as talking about innovations in diamond cutting. She concluded with a discussion of the famous Hope diamond and its illustrious Gilded Age owner, the socialite and heiress Evalyn Walsh McLean. The lecture provided a delightful overview of a period of time that glittered and sparkled through the amazing jewelry that was created and worn. Grippando plans to host more jewelry lectures in 2023. The next one will be on jewelry from the Art Deco period. articles.text: There are many reasons that someone becomes a caregiver: they have been caring for a family member and discovered their strengths in being compassionate; they are following a path into nursing or related medical field and want some hands-on experience; they enjoy helping others and developing meaningful oneon-one connections. As caregiving becomes a high in-demand career with more people living longer in the comfort of their own homes, there can also be financial incentives to consider this job. The need for quality caregivers has perhaps never been greater. Yet there are reasons that caregiving can be more than just a job. We’d like to share five of them: 1. Transferable skills. The skills gained in a caregiving job can apply to all kinds of other roles, including some in the home care agency office. Things like being compassionate, being a good listener, showing patience, and other qualities used to assist people whose abilities have changed due to illness or age can be used in all other personal and professional situations to your benefit. 2. Training. At Homewatch CareGivers, caregivers have the opportunity for additional training via the Homewatch CareGivers University which can empower them to grow professionally. These courses may include dementia care, behavioral health, instructions on caring for people who are living with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and much more. Once you start learning, there is no telling how far you can go in a career. 3. Flexibility. Caregivers often have scheduling flexibility, much different than a traditional 9 to 5 type of job, which means they have the ability to pick and choose what suits them and their own families while earning money from their career. 4. Making a difference. Yes, a smile can change someone’s world. Many people who need in-home care services have become isolated from a life that brought them joy. Symptoms of chronic conditions may limit their abilities to engage in certain activities or socialize as they once did. A friendly caregiver who provides transportation for errands, plays a fun board game, gives medication reminders, and much more, can alleviate their feelings of loneliness, helplessness, and boredom. 5. Each day is new. Caregiving may have challenges and surprises and that can help you to grow personally and professionally, as well as bring laughs and new life skills. Each client is unique and brings their own life story and needs to the relationship, and a chance to learn more. Homewatch CareGivers is located at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmonters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com.

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Macmama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security, says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include everything, so make sure you really trust them! As our lives become more technically involved, so must our preparation for access to this technology postmortem. And as one who has struggled to settle the estate of a loved one, and been frustrated with no access to necessary passwords for the countless accounts we had to close, I have become committed to making sure my own family will have an easier time after I am gone. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com

articles.text: If you’re a Boomer grandparent and your child is a Millennial parent, you’ve no doubt noticed one or two differences between your parenting style and your child’s style. In many families, these differences can be a source of friction, and that friction can effectively drain much of the joy out of family time. Does it need to be this way? What steps can a grandparent take to improve the situation? Childrearing recommendations have never been static. Parenting norms change with the times and reflect both new factual information from medical and psychological experts, as well as societal changes and cultural developments that influence family life. So, in the broad sense, societal shifts in parenting rules and recommendations have reasonable explanations; they can be explained by new data, medical advice, and community trends. For an individual family welcoming a new baby, however, these societal shifts can cause little tremors that can shake a Boomer grandparent’s expectations of what this time of their life was going to look like. For the Millennial new parent, the effort to bring their parents to a place of understanding and acceptance can be exhausting. Can’t we all just get along? What’s stopping us? Why is it hard for a grandparent who raised their children in the freewheeling 80’s or 90’s to accept that their adult children are raising their own children quite differently? Millennial parents strongly believe in validating childhood emotions, supporting a child’s independent choices, and tend to stress acceptance and tolerance over shame. Your grandchildren may be breast fed for two or more years, sleep at specific times and always with a sound machine, have limited time in front of screens, eat nothing but farm fresh organic foods, and be asked their opinion on absolutely everything from whether or not they want a hug, to what they want to wear to school, to how they want their sandwich cut. Boomers might not get this. But, why does it matter? Why do you feel it necessary to say to your grandchild’s parents: It seems so odd that you do X. Why don’t you do Y like I did? You turned out just fine, didn’t you? The world today looks nothing like the world you raised your children in. You had far fewer resources to learn from and fewer competing bits of information to analyze. Many of the skills that you taught your children simply aren’t needed anymore and you may be completely ignorant about many of the skills they need today. Your adult children are not criticizing what you did in raising them. They just want to do it their way with all of the information they now have. What if you asked yourself: What am I willing to do to ensure future happiness and harmony with my family? What if you actually asked yourself that question every time you were tempted to point out what seems odd or ill-advised to your adult child? What if you thought about how a seemingly innocent comment or question may come across to them? Take some time to ask yourself how you want to be remembered after you’re gone. Do you want to be remembered as the grandparent who had to be right all the time, who had to win or come out on top every time there was a discussion, or whose advice had to be followed otherwise you felt disrespected? Grandparenthood is your chance to lead by example, to be a role model, to be the wise elder. It’s the time that you can celebrate the successes of the younger generation in your family, and be there as a safety net in times of real challenge. You can decide to be a lifelong learner, and watch your grandchildren grow while trusting your adult children to know what is best for them. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com. Find us on Facebook.

articles.text: All Aboard! Piedmont Seniors are about to board the train from the Jelly Belly factory in Fairfield to its newly opened museum. Pictured are Penny Robb, Carole Jones, Greg Jurin, Mona Jamieson, Sandra Curach, Irene Westler, Yorkman Lowe, Martin Rosson, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Jim Ayotte, and Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein. On November 9, a group of Piedmont Seniors was eager to get a head start on the holiday shopping frenzy. They visited the Vacaville Outlet stores with dozens of stores eager to welcome the group. The stores even offer a Senior discount upon request. After they were shopped out, the group had a filling lunch at Black Bear Diner in Vacaville, where they particularly enjoyed huckleberry ice cream. The last stop of the day was a visit the recently remodeled Jelly Belly Factory in nearby Fairfield, complete with a new museum. The Jelly Belly Factory has an interesting history. Formerly called the Herman Goetlitz Candy Company, the company, founded in 1919, moved from Oregon to Oakland on 61st Street near Emeryville in 1922. The company’s growth accelerated quickly after it sent its jelly bellies to California Governor Ronald Reagan to sample. Reagan was trying to quit smoking and decided that eating candy was a better alternative. Reagan even used to place these now-famous candies on conference tables for all his meetings, and after becoming President, he had a bowl of jelly beans in the suites at Blair House, Washington D.C.’s guest residence. The Jelly Belly factory offers daily self-guided walking tours where visitors can learn all about making jelly beans. Jelly Bellies were first produced in 1976. There is an attractive café for casual dining, where you will find jelly bean-shaped hamburgers and pizzas. The inviting gift shop has a huge assortment of all different kinds of candies. The factory routinely ships its jelly beans to all corners of the world. After shopping at the Jelly Belly store they took a short ride on the Jelly Belly Express to the newly opened museum, part of every tour. It recently opened and has large decorative jelly beans hanging from the ceiling. The museum shows the evolution of candy making equipment from 100 years ago to the present day, where robots do much of the work. All in all, the Piedmont Seniors had a very fun-filled outing. The group’s next excursion will be to the Chabot Space & Science Center in the Oakland hills on Wednesday, January 11, 2023. To participate in Piedmont Seniors activities, including monthly meetings at the Piedmont Community Hall, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov for further information, or call the Piedmont Recreation Department at 510- 420-3070. Piedmont Seniors in front of a giant Jelly Belly poster: Jim Ayotte, Janet Epstein, Irene Westler, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, and Martin Rosson. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

articles.text: The City of Piedmont and the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) invite community members to a groundbreaking ceremony for the new Piedmont Community Pool at 11 a.m. this Saturday, December 17. Refreshments will be served. The event, which will take place behind the Recreation Department at the site of the former pool, will celebrate the City Council’s recent hiring of a contractor to build an aquatic facility at a cost of approximately $23,870,000. Construction of the new pool is expected to begin in early 2023, and the new pool could open as soon as spring 2024. City officials and PRFO leaders will be joined by pool users young and old to thank the many volunteers, community advocates, and generous donors who have worked tirelessly over the years to make this project a reality. Olympic swimmer Dana Vollmer will be on hand for greetings and photos with her five gold medals. “This is a very exciting time for aquatic lovers and the entire Piedmont community,” said Steve Collins, President of PRFO. “Holding an inclusive event really represents what this effort is about. Not just for the water aspect, the Pool facility is also a perfect destination for birthday parties, social events, team get-togethers and all other types of gatherings. It will be an essential part of Piedmonters’ lives for decades.” To date, PRFO has raised over $1 million towards a fundraising goal of $2.1 million to complete the community pool as designed. PRFO initiated a capital campaign in partnership with the City in August 2022 to bridge a funding gap created by a sharp rise in construction costs. This effort builds on the success of previous PRFO fundraising in support of Hampton Park and the Corey Reich Tennis Center. Primary funding for the pool replacement project comes from Measure UU, approved by Piedmont voters in November 2020. Measure UU authorized the sale of $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to fund a new community pool. The City of Piedmont, Piedmont City Council, and PRFO thank the many generous donors who have contributed to support the new pool, including the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and the Piedmont Education Foundation, and remain grateful to the entire community for their ongoing support for this project. For more information on the new pool, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ newpool. To contribute to the capital campaign, visit prfo.org/ piedmont-community-pool.
articles.title: Groundbreaking ceremony for new pool this Saturday, December 17

articles.text: Editor: Congratulations are in order. First of all to the Piedmont Post on 25 years of service to the community! Well done! Secondly, to the City of Piedmont for pushing the new pool project closer to the finish line! Betsy Andersen has been working tirelessly for many years on our new pool after our original group initiated the project 25 years ago. Along with Mayor Teddy King and other recent City Council members and administrators, today’s generation of leaders is turning our vision into reality, and the community is so grateful. Thank you also to PRFO for helping to fill the funding gap. Now what do we have to do to make the new facility even more inclusive with a gym and a jacuzzi? Hats off to all! –Josh Bernstein, DDS PHS Class of 1975, Alumnus of Piedmont Swim Team
articles.title: Some congratulations, please

articles.text: On a warm, sunny day about 10 years ago, I sat on the edge of the pool next to Betsy Andersen. I’ve known Betsy since she was a teenage lifeguard with our younger daughter. She said she was going to spearhead another attempt to build a new pool, after repeated prior attempts had failed. I wished her luck and said I’d support her every step of the way, but that to make it happen, we had to build a facility that worked for the whole community, and we had to get all the aquatics stakeholders on board pushing for that pool. I jokingly made her promise to get it done before I turned 80. The City hired a firm to help us come up with a conceptual design. Multiple community meetings were held and by the end of 2016 a conceptual design master plan was approved. A 2017 study showed that the plan was financially viable. A community survey in 2018 showed that just over 50% of the community would support a bond issue to fund the new pool, far below the 2/3 needed to pass it. In 2020, the political consultants said there was no way you could bridge the gap from 50% to 2/3 to pass a bond measure, but we did it anyway in the middle of a pandemic, when no one could meet or campaign door to door. Then, in 2021, the City hired ELS to design the actual pool facilities. They met with the community again to perfect the conceptual design, they told us the main pool in that design wouldn’t fit in the available space and came up with an alternative that would fit, one that everyone was even more excited about than the original design. In January, that design was approved, but two months later we were told the high construction inflation caused by the pandemic made it too expensive to build.
articles.title: New Pool getting closer, but we’re not there yet

This time the low bid was close enough that we could go forward and finally build the pool if we could close a $2.1 million funding gap. PRFO stepped forward and said they would raise the money, and the City entered into a construction contract. As I write this, PRFO has already raised over $1 million. Later this month, I will turn 80. There is nothing I can do about that, even in the quest for a new pool we’ve been talking about building for more than 20 years. But I can donate to PRFO to help bridge the funding gap and so can you. Aging aside, we have overcome every obstacle to building this facility. This is Piedmont. We can do this. Please join me in donating to the PRFO campaign. I can’t wait to swim in the new pool. Jon Sakol was a longtime active member of Piedmont Swim Club. OF THE QUOTE WEEK “In the depth of winter I finally learned that there was in me an invincible summer.” – Albert Camus 1913-1960 French philosopher, author, dramatist, and journalist.

articles.text: After receiving extensive feedback from residents affected by the prospective loss of parking spaces, the City has drafted a modified plan for bulb-outs on Oakland Avenue at the intersections of Jerome and El Cerrito Avenues. The city is now waiting for approval from AC Transit. When the initial bulb-out plan was approved by the City more than one year ago, on October 4, 2021, it was then presented to the public at an on-site meeting on November 1 last month. According to Piedmont Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, there was “pushback from many parties.” In addition to permanent bulb-outs — where the sidewalk extends and the street shrinks, to make the pedestrian crossing shorter and safer — the plan provided for high-visibility crosswalks, pedestrian ramps, yellow flashing beacons, new street paint, and new signs at each intersection. There was support for the four bulb-outs, but considerable opposition to a plan that would eliminate parking spaces by relocating of bus stops. As a result, they are working on new plans, with continual feedback from AC Transit. The new plan, said Gonzales, addresses a majority of the concerns of neighbors. Instead of a net loss of 10 parking spots, the newer revised plan would only involve three parking spaces, and in modified locations – one on El Cerrito Ave. in the downhill direction, and two at Jerome Avenue. “We were trying to figure out how much flexibility their [AC Transit’s] safety guidelines allowed for,” said Gonzales. “We found that we could keep the bus stops where they were. Ironically, there was enough space for the buses to pull in and out as a result of the curb changes presented by the bulb-outs. While the revised bulb-out plan is not yet finalized, it is currently under review by AC Transit. “We are optimistic about the results,” said Gonzales, “and most importantly about keeping the bus stops in their existing configuration. Now we’re just waiting for AC Transit to sign off.” After the new plan is finalized, Gonzales plans to hold a second informational public meeting about the bulb-outs to receive comments, questions, and other feedback from residents. Those with questions about the new bulb-out plan may send an e-mail to Gonzales at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov, or call 420-3060.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont has released an Initial Study and Negative Declaration for its proposed 6th Cycle Housing Element. The report is available for public review and comment through January 8. This is the next step in the City’s Housing Element update, a process that has been underway since Spring 2021. Part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the City to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 – a number assigned to Piedmont by state and regional authorities. Adopting a Housing Element does not require these homes be built. Rather, the purpose of the document is to demonstrate that the City has a plan for how it could support the growth. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. A review of the City’s Draft Housing Element based on these guidelines determined that, as a policy document, the Housing Element alone will not have adverse physical impacts on the environment. Physical changes that would result from the implementation of policies and programs proposed in the Housing Element are currently being studied as part of a programmatic Environmental Impact Report (EIR) covering updates to the City’s General Plan and changes to the City Code that would happen after the Housing Element is adopted. The Initial Study and Negative Declaration is available for download and review on the City’s website at the following link: https://bit.ly/3FDqFhg. Physical copies of the documents are available for review at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. Background The City submitted its proposed Draft Housing Element to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for review on November 18, 2022. HCD will review the City’s Draft Housing Element for compliance with State law. If reviewers determine that changes are needed, Planning staff will work with HCD to develop any necessary amendments, then bring the proposed updates to City Council for approval. After the City Council adopts the Housing Element, the City will have three years to implement a substantial number of the proposed programs and regulatory changes outlined in the document. This process involves additional environmental review. This review is already underway – the City is currently in the process of preparing a programmatic EIR that studies the impacts of the new homes and residents that could come to Piedmont once implementation is complete. Community members who wish to provide feedback may send comments in writing to City Planner Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov, or by mail at 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. The comment period ends Sunday, January 8, 20023. Information about the Housing Element update is available at PiedmontIsHome.org. For questions write to PiedmontIsHome@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Housing Element comments due January 8

articles.text: After performing exclusively online in 2020 and 2021, Piedmont Community Church will perform its popular annual Christmas concert in the Sanctuary this Saturday and Sunday, December 17 and 18, at 7:30 p.m. This marks the 12th year for the concert. The concert, which consists of the full choir and soloists accompanied by a full professional orchestra, is conducted by the church’s Music Director, Stephen Main. Stephen, winner of the John Ness Beck Award for Best American Choral Composition, is a well-known composer. Among his many accomplishments, he has composed scores for several movies and wrote the Centennial Fanfare for the City of Piedmont. The beautiful interior of the church, which was designed by Piedmont’s most prominent architect, Albert Farr, enhances the concert experience. Following the concert, audience members are invited to a gala reception in Guild Hall with hot and cold gourmet hors d’oeuvres served with wine and non-alcoholic punch. The concert, For All this Night, will reprise the very first concert of the series. The text for the music comes mainly from the 15th and 16th centuries, “one of the first of several golden ages in English carol-writing”, explained Dr. Main. “Carols were the music of common people rather than of liturgical professionals,” he said. “They offered an opportunity to flesh out the biblical stories, which by themselves are often quite spare in the details of Jesus’ birth. For example, in one of the movements of For All this Night, there is an imaginative dialogue between Mary and her newborn son.” Inspired by these Renaissance era carols, Main has composed fresh melodies for them. All are invited to be part of this holiday tradition. Give yourself, or someone on your Christmas list, the gift of beautiful music, good cheer and good food this weekend. Tickets are $50 for general admission and $150 for patron tickets with seating in a reserved section. To purchase, visit Piedmontchurch.org/concert. Piedmont Community Church is located at 400 Highland Avenue. articles.text: Ozell Thompson joined the Piedmont Fire Department as a firefighter last November 7. Thompson began his career as a firefighter for Cal Fire in Fresno, where he was raised. He recalled that the work “got a lot more fun season after season. It was all new to me, and as you learn more, you can do more.” He began working for Cal Fire (the State Fire Agency) through the California Conservation Corps, where he trained for three months. After seven seasons in Fresno, he moved to North Carolina where he worked as a firefighter in Greensboro and Charlotte. By 2020 he decided that he “wanted to come back home and be close to the family. here “for as long as they’ll let me. It’s a good place where the people are warm, and the Fire Department’s certainly got a lot of new guys lately. It’s nice that we’re all on the same spectrum — just trying to be better day by day, building camaraderie.” When he was younger he wanted to play football “for the rest of my life,” he said. His high-intensity work as a firefighter has always been a source of happiness and comfort more than one of stress. Thompson added, “There’s no other way to build a strong connection and familiarity among the people working here.” It’s a connection certainly reflective of what he’s found among locals throughout the city since moving to Piedmont. Staff photo Ozell Thompson is a newly hired firefighter with Piedmont Fire Department. “I applied here to Piedmont and got very, very lucky,” he said. Thompson envisions staying

articles.text: Amal Smith will term out of office following the Piedmont School Board meeting tonight, December 14, after nearly nine years as a volunteer board member. Smith took some time to catch up with the Post about how the position and the school district has changed over time, the future of PUSD, what it was like to be President of the Board at a time when COVID changed everything. A 25-year resident of Piedmont, Smith won her seat on the school board in February 2014 as the top vote getter. In 2018 former teacher Megan Pillsbury, took the election by storm, and garnered the most votes from Piedmont residents. As an incumbent seeking reelection, Smith won over Julie Caskey by 47 votes. “I don’t like knocking on people’s doors because I don’t like people knocking on my door at the end of the day. [The strategy] worked,” Smith said about the 2018 campaign. Smith was at the helm of the Board when COVID hit, and the basic delivery method of education had to be rethought. For the last six years Smith has worked as Associate Dean for Financial Affairs at the UCSF School of Medicine. “There was this interesting synergy or alignment because what I learned daily at UCSF could help shape what I was thinking about what we needed to do as a school district,” she said. Smith oversaw the school board through some of the district’s toughest times. The school campuses closed and previously routine board meetings turned into six-hour marathons. Cory Smegal succeeded Smith as board president in December 2020. In thinking of her time on the board, Smith pointed to two areas in which she takes significant pride: board policy on sexual harassment, and the work done towards Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEI-B). “I think we’re moving in the right direction,” Smith said. “I want to not lose sight of this idea of social-emotional wellness; and hold that in the same place as we hold academic excellence. You cannot have lifelong learners if you don’t help kids feel they are in a place where they can learn.” “What I’m really interested in is how do we learn and get better at the things we need to get better at. I think our community is really wrestling with and actively working on [DEI-B] issues. I think we are headed in the direction of being more open and recognizing that experiences do vary,” Smith said. Thompson began his career as a firefighter for Cal Fire in Fresno, where he was raised. He recalled that the work “got a lot more fun season after season. It was all new to me, and as you learn more, you can do more.” He began working for Cal Fire (the State Fire Agency) through the California Conservation Corps, where he trained for three months. After seven seasons in Fresno, he moved to North Carolina where he worked as a firefighter in Greensboro and Charlotte. By 2020 he decided that he “wanted to come back home and be close to the family. Ozell Thompson joins Piedmont Fire Department here “for as long as they’ll let me. It’s a good place where the people are warm, and the Fire Department’s certainly got a lot of new guys lately. It’s nice that we’re all on the same spectrum — just trying to be better day by day, building camaraderie.” When he was younger he wanted to play football “for the rest of my life,” he said. His high-intensity work as a firefighter has always been a source of happiness and comfort more than one of stress. Smith took some time to catch up with the Post about how the position and the school district has changed over time, the future of PUSD, what it was like to be President of the Board at a time when COVID changed everything. A 25-year resident of Piedmont, Smith won her seat on the school board in February 2014 as the top vote getter. In 2018 former teacher Megan Pillsbury, took the election by storm, and garnered the most votes from Piedmont residents. As an incumbent seeking reelection, Smith won over Julie Caskey by 47 votes. “I don’t like knocking on people’s doors because I don’t like people knocking on my door at the end of the day. [The strategy] worked,” Smith said about the 2018 campaign. Smith was at the helm of the Board when COVID hit, and the basic delivery method of education had to be rethought. For the last six years Smith has worked as Associate Dean for Financial Affairs at the UCSF School of Medicine. “There was this interesting synergy or alignment because what I learned daily at UCSF could help shape what I was thinking about what we needed to do as a school district,” she said. Smith oversaw the school board through some of the district’s toughest times. The school campuses closed and previously routine board meetings turned into six-hour marathons. Cory Smegal succeeded Smith as board president in December 2020. In thinking of her time on the board, Smith pointed to two areas in which she takes significant pride: board policy on sexual harassment, and the work done towards Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEI-B). “I think we’re moving in the right direction,” Smith said. “I want to not lose sight of this idea of social-emotional wellness; and hold that in the same place as we hold academic excellence. The use of trails in the park skyrocketed during the pandemic, resulting in the trails being heavily used and in much need of maintenance. articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Pioneers, a First Tech Challenge robotics team. Piedmont Pioneers, a middle school First Tech Challenge robotics team, recently participated in a qualifying tournament in Saratoga. The team includes several team members from Piedmont. Their members are Aliya Vora, Dylan Wallway, Ed Balasingham, Elliott Briggs, Elsa Wallway, Grey Sanford, Max Carter and Sam Charslon. As one of the few all-middle school teams, the Pioneers competed on December 4 in Saratoga with mostly high schoolers. The competition format allows for multiple robot matches, which then lead to semifinals, then finals. There is also a presentation to the judges, where the teams discuss team strategy. In preparation for the tournament, the Pioneers ramped up practices to four times a week in order to get in more practice driving the robot and running through speeches, as well as making any last-minute coding or building adjustments. They woke up early Sunday morning to head to the event. After passing robot and field inspection with the tournament officials, they gathered with all competing teams to watch the opening ceremony. Then, the Pioneers completed the presentation, which consisted of speeches, a discussion of outreach events, engineering portfolio, and giving a run-through of the robot’s design. After finishing the interview, the team went back to watch the early robot matches and analyze other teams’ designs. After watching the first few rounds, the Pioneers stepped up to the field, robot in hand, ready for their first match. They started off strong in the autonomous period, but their alliance team’s robot malfunctioned and ended up barely losing the match for the Pioneers’ alliance. However, it was a good starting match, and allowed them to get in extra practice completing the tasks real-time on the field. During the next couple of matches, the team got used to the competition environment and started to hit their stride. With the help of their alliance partners, they managed to win three matches in a row. The last qualifying match started out well, but during the beginning of the match, the arm, a crucial component of the robot, broke. However, due to the help of their alliance partners, they were still able to win the round. The Pioneers ended up fourth overall for the robot game and were designated as an alliance captain. They chose two other teams that would be their alliance partners and competed in the elimination round as the third seed. The Pioneers were able to win two matches in a row, and with their alliance partners, continued on to the finals. After doing last minute checkups on all three robots, the two alliance teams competing in the finals were called to the stage. They set their robots down and the countdown began. The Pioneers’ alliance took off quickly and had a strong start, but the opposing alliances’ autonomous worked perfectly, allowing them to score a lot of points. In the driver-controlled period, they lost the match by a few points. The team won the Finalist Alliance Captain award, along with being named runner-up for the Motivate Award. Overall, the team learned a lot and now has knowledge it will use in its next competition on January 8.

articles.text: 7th grader Zayd Mahmood (right) correctly spells the word “bruise,” given by Spelling Bee Host Ted Scherman as 7th grader Colt Hitchcock watches in anticipation. At 1:07 p.m. on Monday, December 12, most students were racing down the steps for lunch at Piedmont Middle School. For 40 students, however, the lunch bell signaled the start of stiff competition in Ted Scherman’s classroom for Day One of the 2022 Spelling Bee. Only three of 40 students were eliminated in the first round of the week-long competition. Participation has increased in Scherman’s second year of hosting the event which normally draws an average of 20 participants. “Lots of kids signed up this year, possibly because there are fewer avenues available to compete academically,” said Scherman, a veteran 7th grade teacher. He plans on reviving the equally popular Geography Bee in the spring. It is no longer sponsored by National Geographic. “[The Spelling Bee] is a great way to test your smarts and it’s also super satisfying when you get a word correct,” said 8th grader Mira Sen, who finished third last year. Whizzed, cottonwood, slather, and M-U-R-A-L-S were all easily handled by the students. With little difficulty, 8th graders Eliza Berry and Emahn Sheikh spelled It was a packed and tense house for round one of the Spelling Bee in Ted Scherman’s class on Monday, as contestants easily outnumbered chairs. 8th grader Mira Sen finished in third place last year and has advanced to the 2nd round this year. out “joggled,” and “squinched” respectively. The school’s reigning champion, 8th grader Zoe Snyder, breezed into round two after confronted with “probably.” The three words that ousted some contestants were: “decide,” “orca,” and “constant.” “Spelling bees can be cruel and unusual; you can make one mistake and you are out,” warned Scherman at the start of the first day of competition. Last year’s Spelling Bee went for 14 rounds in six days of lunchtime competition before declaring a champion. This year, the winner of Piedmont’s Spelling Bee will be invited to an online test to qualify for the San Ramon Valley Rotary Regional Spelling Bee in March.

articles.text: I’ve been reading Michelle Obama’s new book, The Light We Carry, which starts out with a chapter on how knitting helped get her through the worst of the pandemic. How, in the moments when she couldn’t do anything else, she taught herself to knit, and it brought her a moment of ease and a sense of accomplishment that then helped her tackle the bigger challenges. She talks about how knitting gave her a break from her brain doing all the thinking and instead, let her hands just take over for a little while. I see this description as an absolutely perfect explanation of why creative play is so critical for all of us at all times of our lives, not just during a complete shutdown due to a worldwide pandemic. So much of our stress comes from over saturation of the stories and questions that our minds fixate on: Will my kindergartner learn how to read? Will my toddler ever potty train? How can I ensure that my kids have a good relationship with their grandparents? What does work/ life balance look like when I go back to work after my maternity leave and I’m still expected to work 60 hours per week? How am I supposed to fight climate change when I can barely remember that I provide snacks on Tuesdays for aftercare? These types of worries, and so many more like them that swirl Knitting, and other activities like it, relax the mind. in all of our heads day in and day out are legitimate and important concerns. But, if we live in those concerns and allow them to take over, we are, in essence, forever living in the future–a future that does not yet exist. We need an opportunity for quiet. We need an emergency break for our racing thoughts. Michelle Obama found this in her knitting needles, but any kind of creative play can have this powerful effect. While Michelle was knitting, I was learning to use watercolor pencils for the first time in my life. Others were baking sourdough bread or dancing in their living rooms. But, we can’t lose touch with the things we tried over the past 2+ years. Now that we are back to a somewhat normal existence, how can we ensure that we still have that outlet to shut down our minds and let our hands, feet,

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Highlanders blank Bishop O’Dowd, Alameda 1-0 Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team opened its league season in strong fashion, defeating two local rivals, both by scores of 1-0. It posted a shutout of Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, December 7 in a road game, and produced the same result against the Alameda Hornets in front of their fans at Witter Field on Monday, December 12. “They are always tough teams to break down. Even when 1-nil down they sat and defended and made themselves difficult to beat,” said PHS coach Dan Chubbock. “Both teams were really just looking for that one chance and we didn’t give it to them.” Against Alameda, the Highlanders kept a high press and rarely let the Hornets out of their own defensive half. Alameda relied on long balls down the wings and trying to earn corner opportunities. But they finished without any shots on target and only a few shot attempts. Piedmont looked like the superior side in both victories, but a one-goal advantage never leaves players and coaches with any sense of security. They know that the results can change in a flash. “One goal never feels like it’s enough, so I did feel a little anxious that they needed just one chance to change the game. We controlled possession and controlled the chances. We looked in control, but we only scored one goal,” said Chubbock. “1-0 isn’t ideal but we were able to keep it out of our half and prevent them from creating chances. I think defensively, we’ve done well. I think there are some things we can do better offensively,” added senior Audrey Lam, who made an appearance during the summer with the U.S. Under-17 Women’s National team. Piedmont scored its lone goal against Alameda when freshman Miranda Liu sent a pass through to Lam for an easy one-on-one goal against the Hornets’ keeper. Liu also scored the game-winner against Bishop O’Dowd in the second half. Liu has been the starting striker in Chubbock’s attack, making a clear impact with the team. She scored and had an assist in Piedmont’s 3-2 loss to Miramonte in the season-opener on November 28. “It’s a great community. Everyone is really supportive, I knew some freshmen on varsity, and they really want to help me fit in,” said Liu. 1-0 win vs. Alameda Piedmont’s game-winner came in the 20th minute on a nice holdup play by Liu with two defenders on her, flicking a through pass to Lam all alone a few yards in front of the keeper. The Highlanders had several more chances to score in the first half and also had opportunities in the second half. After the goal, Emily Fitzgerald and Lam had shots on target in the 25th and 26th minutes that led to corner kicks. Michaela Bini also had a shot on target in the 28th minute and nearly scored in the 30th minute after Liu made a turn around a defender to find Bini, but her shot went wide as the keeper rushed out to make the block. In the second half, Piedmont continued the pressure to force turnovers in Alameda’s half. Staff Photos Audrey Lam scored against Alameda in the first half of Monday’s game. Freshman Miranda Liu scored against Bishop O’Dowd and had the assist against Alameda.
