articles.text: Highlanders beat Archbishop Mitty by 4 points in final For just the second time in its 12-year history, Piedmont High has won its own Paris Twins Classic invitational tournament after narrowly beating Archbishop Mitty of San Jose 60-56 on Saturday, December 10. The tournament is named for twins Courtney and Ashley Paris, who led Piedmont to consecutive State championships in 2004 and 2005. Mitty received the SportsStar Magazine’s preseason No. 1 ranking in Northern California. Cardinal Newman of Santa Rosa, who PHS beat 66-34 on Friday, is ranked No. 17. This year’s Piedmont team is ranked No. 5 in Northern California. “It feels amazing just for us to win our own tournament. We haven’t gotten to match up against Mitty and we’ve always wanted to play them. For us to win means a lot. It feels like we’re a main target right now; it’s a lot of pressure but we’re ready to take it on,” said senior and team captain Trinity Zamora, who recently committed to play at San Diego State next year. Natalia Martinez led against Mitty with 20 points. Junior guard Natalia Martinez notably has already scored more than 1,000 points in less than three seasons. Making a debut on the team this year are transfer students Eva Levingston and Perseas Gioukaris. Their additions have allowed the Highlanders to have their most fluid offense in several years. ”It’s my comeback season and this feels like a year for our team to have a lot of success,” said Levingston. Championship game vs. Mitty Piedmont trailed Mitty 11-10 to end the first quarter but scored 20 points to take a 30-24 lead by halftime. PHS kept a five-point advantage going into the fourth quarter and closed out with a 4-point victory, 60-56. Mitty was playing without two of SportsStar Magazine’s preseason All-NorCal honorees, Morgan Cheli and Elana Weisman. Martinez started Piedmont’s scoring rally in the second quarter for an 18-13 lead, but Mitty scored six straight to regain the lead 19-18. The two sides traded the lead until PHS led 23-21 following a 3-pointer by Adrienne Blackwell. The Highlanders then scored seven of the next 10 points for a 30-24 lead at the break. Mitty narrowed Piedmont’s lead to 40-39 in the third period. With the score at 42-40, Maddie Hill knocked down a 3-pointer on an assist by Gioukaris. PHS and Mitty traded points until Piedmont took a 59-56 lead. In the final minute and after a series of fouls, Zamora hit one of two free throws for the 60-56 final. Final stats: Martinez had 20 points, four rebounds, and three steals. Hill had 10 points, three rebounds, one steal, and an assist. Gioukaris had 10 points, two rebounds, one steal, and two assists. Levingston had eight points, 11 rebounds, three assists, two blocks, one steal. Zamora had eight points, 10 rebounds, five steals, two blocks, and one assist. Adrienne Blackwell had five points, three rebounds, and two assists. 66-34 over Cardinal Newman Piedmont jumped ahead 22-11 by the end of the first quarter and maintained a 13-point cushion, 35-22, by halftime. Piedmont’s defense held Cardinal Newman to just four points in the third quarter and scored 14 to lead 49-26 to start the fourth, closing out with 17 points, 66-34. Final scorers: Zamora had 15 points, Levingston and Dorothy Nemeth had 12 points, Martinez had 11 points, Adrienne Blackwell had six, Gioukaris had four, Hill had three. 76-4 over Damonte Ranch It was a one-sided 76-4 victory in the opening game against

They know that the results can change in a flash. “One goal never feels like it’s enough, so I did feel a little anxious that they needed just one chance to change the game. We controlled possession and controlled the chances. We looked in control, but we only scored one goal,” said Chubbock. “1-0 isn’t ideal but we were able to keep it out of our half and prevent them from creating chances. I think defensively, we’ve done well. I think there are some things we can do better offensively,” added senior Audrey Lam, who made an appearance during the summer with the U.S. Under-17 Women’s National team. Piedmont scored its lone goal against Alameda when freshman Miranda Liu sent a pass through to Lam for an easy one-on-one goal against the Hornets’ keeper. Liu also scored the game-winner against Bishop O’Dowd in the second half. Liu has been the starting striker in Chubbock’s attack, making a clear impact with the team. She scored and had an assist in Piedmont’s 3-2 loss to Miramonte in the season-opener on November 28. “It’s a great community. Everyone is really supportive, I knew some freshmen on varsity, and they really want to help me fit in,” said Liu. 1-0 win vs. Alameda Piedmont’s game-winner came in the 20th minute on a nice holdup play by Liu with two defenders on her, flicking a through pass to Lam all alone a few yards in front of the keeper. The Highlanders had several more chances to score in the first half and also had opportunities in the second half. After the goal, Emily Fitzgerald and Lam had shots on target in the 25th and 26th minutes that led to corner kicks. Michaela Bini also had a shot on target in the 28th minute and nearly scored in the 30th minute after Liu made a turn around a defender to find Bini, but her shot went wide as the keeper rushed out to make the block. In the second half, Piedmont continued the pressure to force turnovers in Alameda’s half. See Girls’ Soccer on page 32 Natalia Martinez led against Mitty with 20 points. Junior guard Natalia Martinez notably has already scored more than 1,000 points in less than three seasons. Making a debut on the team this year are transfer students Eva Levingston and Perseas Gioukaris. Their additions have allowed the Highlanders to have their most fluid offense in several years. ”It’s my comeback season and this feels like a year for our team to have a lot of success,” said Levingston. Championship game vs. Mitty Piedmont trailed Mitty 11-10 to end the first quarter but scored 20 points to take a 30-24 lead by halftime. PHS kept a five-point advantage going into the fourth quarter and closed out with a 4-point victory, 60-56. Mitty was playing without two of SportsStar Magazine’s preseason All-NorCal honorees, Morgan Cheli and Elana Weisman. Martinez started Piedmont’s scoring rally in the second quarter for an 18-13 lead, but Mitty scored six straight to regain the lead 19-18. The two sides traded the lead until PHS led 23-21 following a 3-pointer by Adrienne Blackwell. The Highlanders then scored seven of the next 10 points for a 30-24 lead at the break. Mitty narrowed Piedmont’s lead to 40-39 in the third period. With the score at 42-40, Maddie Hill knocked down a 3-pointer on an assist by Gioukaris. PHS and Mitty traded points until Piedmont took a 59-56 lead. In the final minute and after a series of fouls, Zamora hit one of two free throws for the 60-56 final. Final stats: Martinez had 20 points, four rebounds, and three steals. Hill had 10 points, three rebounds, one steal, and an assist. Gioukaris had 10 points, two rebounds, one steal, and two assists. Levingston had eight points, 11 rebounds, three assists, two blocks, one steal. Zamora had eight points, 10 rebounds, five steals, two blocks, and one assist. Adrienne Blackwell had five points, three rebounds, and two assists. 66-34 over Cardinal Newman Piedmont jumped ahead 22-11 by the end of the first quarter and maintained a 13-point cushion, 35-22, by halftime. Piedmont’s defense held Cardinal Newman to just four points in the third quarter and scored 14 to lead 49-26 to start the fourth, closing out with 17 points, 66-34. Final scorers: Zamora had 15 points, Levingston and Dorothy Nemeth had 12 points, Martinez had 11 points, Adrienne Blackwell had six, Gioukaris had four, Hill had three. 76-4 over Damonte Ranch It was a one-sided 76-4 victory in the opening game against See Girls’ Basketball on page 32 Staff Photos Audrey Lam scored against Alameda in the first half of Monday’s game. Freshman Miranda Liu scored against Bishop O’Dowd and had the assist against Alameda.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team took a 1-nil loss to Berkeley at Witter Field on Wednesday, December 7. The Yellowjackets scored the game’ only goal in the ninth minute on a penalty kick. Ironically, Piedmont controlled the action and allowed Berkeley no clear looks on goal. “The [players] followed our game plan really well, Berkeley capitalized the one time we got caught out of position. After that moment, I’d argue we were the better team. We created the better opportunities to score another goal. We just can’t seem to get it over the line against Berkeley,” said coach Todd Sullivan. Looking like the better side against Berkeley, the defending WACC Foothill Division champions, is an encouraging sign for Piedmont as it begins competing in the league’s upper division. “My message to the team is to keep playing how they are. I’d argue that Berkeley is one of the best teams in our league and we’re competing with the best teams in a new league. It bodes well for the rest of the season,” said Sullivan. Piedmont finished the night with nine shots but just one on target, while Berkeley’s only shot on target was the penalty kick goal. Among the Highlanders’ strong points through three games has been their work from set pieces, and despite accumulating seven free kicks, they had no corners on the night. “We like the set plays. We’re very big, strong, and committed when in the air. It’s just a case of whether we can make something happen. We didn’t have any corners, but we were a threat on our set plays,” said Sullivan. The Highlanders had the first look of the night with a free kick in the first minute of action, resulting in a shot on target from distance. Berkeley drew the penalty kick on a long ball from midfield into the PHS penalty area, resulting in a Piedmont defender making contact with the Yellowjackets’ forward. Following the goal, Piedmont’s Sam Shelby had a shot trail wide in the 17th minute. Midfielder William Daniel also had shot attempts go over the net and wide of the mark in the 33rd and 38th minutes. articles.text: It’s the winter season when basketball takes center stage at most colleges. In this article the Post looks at three former Piedmont High basketball stars, JoJo Murphy at Chico State, Ashley Gao at the University of Chicago, and Maddy Meadows at William Jessup.University. Ashley Gao University of Chicago Ashley Gao, PHS Class of 2019, is a senior at the University of Chicago, and a starter on its basketball team, currently undefeated at 8-0. Gao has appeared in all eight games, averaging 17 minutes per game. She’s scored 16 total points, including 23 rebounds, 14 assists, one block, and eight steals. Her best performance this season was in a 71-48 victory over Eureka on November 30, in which she had six points, two steals, an assist, and four rebounds. In 2021-22 as a junior, Gao played in 21 games and averaged 15.3 minutes for 49 total points, 34 assists, 49 rebounds, 14 steals, and 12 blocks. She was a four-year starter at Piedmont High and was named to the All-League first-team. Maddy Meadows William Jessup U. Maddy Meadows, PHS Class of 2020, is a junior at William Jessup University in Rocklin after transferring from Biola University following her sophomore year in college. Meadows has appeared in 13 games and is averaging 14 minutes per game. She has scored 57 total points thus far, to go along with 27 rebounds, seven assists, and six steals. Her best performance was scoring 13 points against Lincoln, including a pair of 3-pointers, and seven rebounds. Meadows played one year at Piedmont High as a senior, helping them to a 21-7 overall record with a second-team All-League selection. In 2019-20, Piedmont reached the quarterfinals of the Div. 4 North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 5 seed. Photo courtesy of Chico State Athletics JoJo Murphy, PHS Class of 2022, is a starter for Chico State and recently earned his league’s Player of the Week honors. JoJo Murphy Chico State JoJo Murphy, PHS Class of 2022, is having a remarkable freshman season for Chico State and was recently named the California Collegiate Athletic Association Player of the Week. Murphy has started in five games and is averaging 20.6 points per game, shooting more than 50% from the field, .442 on 3-pointers, and .833 from the free throw line. He has scored at least 30 points over the last three games for Chico State. He had 30 points and five assists in an 83-77 win over San Marcos, 32 points and three assists in an overtime 116-112 win over Humboldt State, and 30 points and five assists in a 78-69 loss to Sonoma State. He finished his career at Piedmont with 1,488 points and was the WACC’s Player of the Year as a senior. articles.text: This treasure of California is among the best wintertime hikes in the Sierra Nevada. Donner Pass, an abandoned railway that was originally constructed in 1867 for the Central Pacific Railroad’s portion of the First Transcontinental Railroad. The trek takes you through hollowed out mountain tunnels and snow sheds through the pass above Donner Lake. Aside from the obvious historic railway, the mountain pass is the same area where the Donner Party tragically met their fate in the fierce winter of 1846— becoming the namesake of the lake and surrounding state park. The walk through the train tunnels is brief at just 2.1 miles to the final snow shed, but it gives you the magic of the Tahoe winter without being knee deep in snow. It’s a great place for children, families, or beginning snowshoers. During the warmer weather, you can walk past the last snow shed and continue to Donner Peak. From our starting point, we took the same route as our 2018 summer visit from McGlashan Point over a Native American petroglyph site that can be seen in warmer months. For now, it’s a popular sledding site with fresh snow. The Central Pacific Railroad created its route through Donner Pass in the spring of 1868 after a near three-year construction effort, accomplished Staff Photos A view of Donner Lake and the Donner Pass snow sheds appropriately covered in snow. China Wall is a platform created by Chinese workers to create the Central Pacific Railroad in 1868. through the efforts of Chinese railroad workers. The Donner Pass trail’s starting point, the China Wall, is a handmade construction that was the platform for the railroad leading into the starting tunnel. Inside the 1,659 foot Tunnel #6, hikers can spot a second Chinese Wall with boulders piled neatly up to the roof. A frozen wall of ice creates a surreal sight inside a snowshed. The entire walk has graffiti-covered walls inside the snow sheds. Some are distinctly graffiti art, such as the one on the right. Through the hollowed out mountains, some large icicles glisten through the tiny peaks of light along the roof and walls. Even some large frozen sections of water created massive blocks of ice that are clear as a piece of glass. You’ll find few sites that combine history and artwork with graffiti covering each wall of the sheds — some pieces magnificent in detail. Peeking around unsuspecting corners and behind walls, walkers with keen eyes can find some of California’s most prominent urban artists and large murals. Proper hiking gear is required in some ice-covered areas to prevent slipping and falls. With limited parking at the entrance lot to the tunnels, some may have to park n the sside of Donner Pass Road or at the Donner Lake Overlook. In our five miles of hiking, we passed just 27 hikers. Another 13 were huddled around the starting area’s sledding hill toward the China Wall. To access this area, hikers can punch in Donner Pass, Summit Haus, or Donner Lake Overlook on their GPS devices for common starting areas. Remember to return in the summer to see petroglyphs along McGlashan Point and fr a hike to Donner Peak. Originally printed in the Piedmont Post on January 27, 2021.

articles.text: The Piedmont Post is seeking interns to cover Junior Varsity sports for the winter season – boys’ and girls’ basketball and soccer. The position offers budding sports journalists professional experience in covering events, learning the trade – and seeing their byline in print. Interns will work remotely with the Posts’ sports reporter, Jonathan Comeaux, who will advise and give feedback to interns wanting to publish their first articles. Those interested do not require playing experience in any sport, only an open mind and eagerness to learn. Jonathan will give young writers tips on how to cover sporting events, profile players, and utilize interviewing skills. Parents or PHS students may contact the newspaper at news@piedmont-post.com, or contact Comeaux by e-mail at JonathanCX525@gmail.com.

articles.text: The Argentines have pushed their way to the 2022 World Cup Final on Sunday, December 18, after defeating Croatia 3-nil yesterday, December 13. They now await today’s result between France and Morocco. How amazing has this World Cup been? In last week’s Post, I wrote that Brazil and France were looking like the favorites, but that was until Croatia powered past the Canaries in penalty kicks. Morocco, meanwhile, has made magic as this year’s Cinderella story, defeating Portugal 1-0 in the quarterfinals. In next week’s Post, we’ll recap the tournament and all of the amazing moments from this Kylian Mbappe and France are the clear favorite walking into Wednesday’s semifinal. year’s games. Until then, here’s looking into tomorrow’s semifinal between France and Morocco, and the prospective final with Argentina. No. 4 France vs. No. 22 Morocco If you can tell by this writer’s last name, I’m going for France and will be wearing my Les Bleus jersey on Wednesday – and hopefully on Sunday as well. articles.text: American Conservatory Theater (ACT) continues its popular holiday production of the Dickens classic, A Christmas Carol, with performances through December 24. The play is based on Charles Dickens’ famous story that captures the zeitgeist of the mid-Victorian era, with main character Ebenezer Scrooge at its center. Dicken’s novella has been recounted onstage and in film for nearly a century; ACT’s production is adapted by Carey Perloff and Paul Walsh and directed by Peter Kuo. Music is by Karl Lundenberg with choreography by Val Caniparoli. The cast is once again led by James Carpenter, with Anthony Fusco in alternating performances as Ebenezer Scrooge. Dan Hiatt plays the Ghost of Jacob Marley, Jomar Tagatac and Sarita Ocón are cast as Bob and Anne Cratchit; Brian Herndon and Sharon Lockwood are Mr. and Mrs. Fezziwig; B Noel Thomas is the Ghost of Christmas Past; and Catherine Castellanos as the Ghost of Christmas Present. Also featured are Tasi Alabastro, John Chukwudelunzu, Evangeline Edwards, Steven Flores, Cindy Goldfield, Jeremy Kahn, Adam KuveNiemann, Paige Mayes, James WDL Mercer II, Emily Newsome, Amanda Le Nguyen, Anna Marie Sharpe, and Howard Swain. Photo by Kevin Berne James Carpenter performs the role of Ebenezer Scrooge in ACT’s production of the Dickens’ classic, A Christmas Carol. A Christmas Carol has been included in ACT’s repertory for decades, and Carpenter’s performance as Scrooge for 15 seasons, has become his signature role. Performances will take place at the newly-named Toni Rembe Theater at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Tickets are available at: https://www.act-sf.org/whatso n / 2 0 2 2 2 3 - s e a s o n /c h r i s tmas-carol/. The production uses theatrical haze and lighting that may not be appropriate for photosensitive groups. A sensory-friendly performance of A Christmas Carol will be performed on December 18 at 6 p.m.
articles.title: ACT’s well-loved Christmas Carol in SF through Dec. 24

articles.text: Tap Dancing Christmas Trees perform this Sunday at exhibit Frequent visitors to Golden Gate Park will remember the Entwined installation, back at Peacock Meadow for the third year. New to this year’s art installation are live performances twice a week. The illuminate twice-a-week exhibit began in 2020 at the height of the COVID pandemic as a way to encourage people to come to Golden Gate Park. San Francisco artist Charles Gadeken created a whimsical, brightly lit wonderland where visitors can explore paths and sit under a grove of three entwined sculptural trees. Gadeken, an industrial artist, has worked in the creative field for over 25 years, and whose monumental interactive public artworks reimagine the world “post-nature.” His artwork commissions include Black Rock Arts Foundation, City of SF, Insomniac Events, Coachella, Absolut Vodka, City of Palo Alto, City of Calabasas, City of Los Altos, Stanford University, and more. Many of Charles’ works have been exhibited internationally. Entwined will remain in Golden Gate Park through March 2023 and remains illuminated until 10 p.m. each night. The project is sponsored by the San Francisco Parks Alliance. This Sunday, December 18, see the Tap Dancing Christmas Trees perform alongside the installation. For nearly three decades, the Oakland-based group of three dancers has performed at the Tree Lighting Ceremonies for San Francisco, Oakland, Hayward, Emeryville and Alameda under the direction of Pamm Drake. The Trees recently performed at the opening of the Piedmont Scout Christmas Tree Lot on November 26. The Trees will perform in Golden Gate Park on December 18 at 5 p.m. To learn more about the installation and its history, and the various performances now through March, visit https://sanfranciscoparksalliance.org/projects/ entwined/. Entwined at Golden Gate Park.
articles.title: Entwined public art installation returns to Golden Gate Park

articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse’s current production of Matilda the Musical, based on the popular children’s book by Roald Dahl, will continue through December 23. Titular character Matilda is an extraordinary girl with a big imagination. Despite her unique and empathetic wit she is looked down upon by her family and wicked school headmistress Miss Trunchbull. Matilda’s closest confidante and friend is her sweet teacher Miss Honey, who fosters the little girl’s big personality. Gregory Lynch is cast as Miss Trunchbull; Mark Robinson and Mary Kalita play Matilda Wormwood’s wayward parents. Chanel Tilghman is Miss Honey. Miranda Klein and Ozzie Schaffer are co-cast as the young Matilda. The show is directed and choreographed by Dane Paul Andres, with vocals directed by Camden Daly and an orchestra conducted by Jessica Igarashi. Performances are Friday through Sunday and select weekday evenings. Tickets are available online at www.berkeleyplayhouse.org, or by calling (510) 845-8542, extension 351. Cast members of Matilda the Musical at Berkeley Playhouse.
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse’s Matilda the Musical ends Dec. 23

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet will introduce its first-ever sensory friendly performance of Nutcracker on Wednesday, December 21. The event is presented in collaboration with the San Francisco Bay Area Autism Society. Special accommodations have been made to the ballet for the December 21 performance that are friendly to those who experience sensory processing disorders, autism, post-traumatic stress disorder, and all neurodiverse audiences. It takes place in a relaxed and “shushfree” setting and is appropriate for all ages. Designated quiet areas will be available for guests. “As a musician, and parent of an autistic son, I’m especially sensitive to how much music and dance can touch the hearts of people with autism and special needs,” said Stephen Prutsman, President of Autism Society San Francisco Bay Area. “The holiday season can be stressful and isolating for autism and special needs families, so for a world-class company like San Francisco Ballet to open its doors and welcome our community is a landmark for the entire ballet world, and a tremendous gift for us.” This special version of Nutcracker is open to all audience members; but because it is adapted specifically to accommodate individuals with sensory sensitivities, guests are encouraged to familiarize themselves with the adjustments of the Sensory Friendly Performance. The performance begins at 7 p.m. Visit https://www.sfballet. org/nutcracker-sensory-friendly-performance/ to purchase tickets and to learn more about sensory friendly performances.
articles.title: SF Ballet introduces sensory friendly performance of Nutcracker on Dec. 21

articles.text: Sacha Grippando in talk at Center for the Arts this Saturday W i l l i a m S h a k e s p e a r e famously wrote “all that glitters is not gold”. This statement could not better sum up the Gilded Age, a period from 1870-1914 in America. This was a time of immense political, economic and social change and unrest. On the surface it was a time of glamor, innovation and immense wealth, the likes and scale of which had never been seen in the U,S. What better way to show one’s power than through the most dazzling jewelry ever made? Innovations in metalsmithing and lapidary coupled with the discovery of diamonds in South Africa heralded an era of jewelry made with superior craftsmanship and brilliance. Piedmont resident Sacha Grippando, a graduate gemologist from the Gemological Institute of America, is giving a free talk this coming Saturday, December 17, at Piedmont Center for the Arts at 5:00 p.m. Her lecture will focus on the history, the jewelry and some of the characters from this fascinating time period. It is the first in a series of planned lectures on jewelry. What better way to kick off the festive season than with a talk filled with glitter and sparkle? Doors open at 4:30 p.m. Light beverages and snacks will be served following the talk. A Cartier tiara, circa 1912
articles.title: All that glitters – Jewelry from the Gilded Age

articles.text: Weekends through Dec. 18, 11 a.m.– 2 p.m. Michael Stehr Art Exhibit This year’s exhibition, entitled Lost in the Shadows – Considering Light and the Absence of It... will be open this weekend through December 18, 2022, and includes forty-two new works, many of which explore the power of shadow in painting. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, December 14, 2022 All that glitters – Jewelry from the Gilded Age Sacha Grippando in talk at Center for the Arts this Saturday W i l l i a m S h a k e s p e a r e famously wrote “all that glitters is not gold”. This statement could not better sum up the Gilded Age, a period from 1870-1914 in America. This was a time of immense political, economic and social change and unrest. On the surface it was a time of glamor, innovation and immense wealth, the likes and scale of which had never been seen in the U,S. What better way to show one’s power than through the most dazzling jewelry ever made? Innovations in metalsmithing and lapidary coupled with the discovery of diamonds in South Africa heralded an era of jewelry made with superior craftsmanship and brilliance. Piedmont resident Sacha Grippando, a graduate gemologist from the Gemological Institute of America, is giving a free talk this coming Saturday, December 17, at Piedmont Center for the Arts at 5:00 p.m. Her lecture will focus on the history, the jewelry and some of the characters from this fascinating time period. It is the first in a series of planned lectures on jewelry. What better way to kick off the festive season than with a talk filled with glitter and sparkle? Doors open at 4:30 p.m. Light beverages and snacks will be served following the talk. articles.text: The following recommendations of Young Adult Thrillers comes from novelist Faridah Abike-Iyimide. The list appeared in the December 11 edition of the New York Times. “My favorite Young Adult thrillers are the ones that provide unexpected answers to big, terrifying questions about our world, our future and our fears. I love how they manage to electrify audiences while folding in beloved Y.A. tropes, like swoon-worthy high school romance, found family and, of course, young people forced to fix problems left to them by older generations,” wrote Abike-Iyimide. somewhere other than the West interest you, this book might just be your new favorite read. Her review is available at Nytimes.com/2022/12/11/books/ review/young-adult-thrillers. html. The Cousins by Karen M. McManus Though she’s known for her series One of Us Is Lying, my favorite novel from Karen M. McManus’s impressive catalog is her 2020 book, The Cousins. The novel is about three cousins who one summer are unexpectedly summoned to work for their wealthy but scornful grandmother, a matriarch who previously shunned her family. At the request of their parents, the cousins bend to their grandmother’s will for a chance to reclaim their inheritance and figure out what happened all those years ago that caused the rift in their family. Parts of this book rendered me speechless. This is a story steeped in generational secrets, filled with sharp and witty dialogue, and it features a unique and unforgettable twist. The Red Palace by June Hur Eighteenth-century Korea is the backdrop for this bloody historical thriller. The Red Palace follows a young nurse as she attempts to uncover the truth behind the murders of four women. Hur is known for her stunning female-centered historical Y.A. novels, and this is arguably her darkest book yet. It’s a story about the violence that society so often sweeps under the rug, but a closer look reveals many additional layers: “The Red Palace” is also about relationships — both distant and dear — and the family we choose. If slow-burn romances, well-paced plots and historical fiction set The Girls I’ve Been by Tess Sharpe The protagonist of The Girls I’ve Been, Nora, was raised by a con artist mother and brought up in a world of violence and deceit. It’s a life Nora has tried to escape, but when she finds herself in a bank robbery-hostage situation at the start of the book, she must tap into her past, and her index of false identities, to get everyone out of the situation alive. Y.A. often features strong female characters, and Nora is no different. While I loved Nora’s resilience, I admired even more the way Sharpe stressed the importance of giving survivors of all kinds of abuse the chance to love and be loved. Grown by Tiffany D. Jackson In this harrowing thriller, Tiffany D. Jackson manages to craft a story that is not only deeply heartfelt and relevant but also incredibly entertaining. The narrative follows Enchanted “Chanty” Jones, a 17-year-old aspiring musician whose dreams come true when she captures the interest of the musical superstar Korey Fields. Korey seems to be Enchanted’s ticket to stardom, but nothing is as it seems. The novel explores important topics, including the dark corners of the music industry, the adultification of Black girls and the consequences of abuses of power. This is a book that is filled to the brim with shocking twists and turns, but in “Grown,” Jackson also centers Black girls in conversations about abuse, discussions they are so often erased from. Death Note by Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata This genre-bending manga offers readers an imaginative take on the Y.A. mystery thriller by showcasing an untraditional hero-villain dynamic. When 17-year-old Light Yagami gets hold of a notebook (the titular death note) that allows him to kill others by simply writing their names inside, he jumps at the chance, killing high-profile criminals in secret to rid the world of evil. Light begins to feel invincible until he finds himself under the scrutiny of the genius detective L. The story quickly becomes a game of cat and mouse, leaving readers at the edge of their seats anticipating whether or not Light will be caught. This story completely blew my mind and forever changed what I thought about thrillers as a genre. (I’d recommend Death Note for readers ages 14 and up — it sounds darker than it is, and it doesn’t get too graphic.) We Were Liars by E. Lockhart Before it became a BookTok obsession, We Were Liars was long a cult favorite in the Y.A. thriller space. I picked up this strangely structured yet beautifully written thriller shortly after it was published in 2014 and inhaled it in one sitting. The story follows the tortured mind of a teenage girl, Cady Sinclair, and the many secrets both she and her entire family harbor. I adored the unconventionality of this story, from the prose to the big revelations at the end. Lockhart’s lyrical thriller continues to enthrall readers years after its initial release, marking this novel as a future classic in the genre.
articles.title: Young Adult Thrillers featured in NY Times

articles.text: The race to the end of the year is off with a big bang. Rain and storms and mountains of snow. Nature is making up for lost time. A big snafu in Piedmont gave us an embarrassment of riches over the weekend. And off we go… Publicists love the word “big”. Where would we be without it? That great promoter, Ed Sullivan, always gave us a “big show.” For the circus it was the big top. And for politicians it is the big picture. Perspective is everything. Local artist and lecturer Michael Stehr tells art lovers that shadow is a part of light. The big snafu in Piedmont resulted in two great concerts over the weekend. Berkeley Symphony presented its stellar brass ensemble in concert in the Community Center. They took the opportunity to appreciate the many wonderful things that Gray Cathrall has done for the community and for Berkeley Symphony in particular. At the very same time, the Diluvian String Quartet played a concert for an enthusiastic audience in the Piedmont Center for the arts. I learned long ago to appreciate events in small venues. The immortal violinist Jascha Heifetz actually preferred to play in small concert halls. I will never forget his numerous concerts in Hancock Auditorium at USC in Los Angeles. It was so much better to hear him up close rather than in the Hollywood Bowl. Festive holiday concerts are everywhere, and indeed ‘tis the season. There are sing-along Messiahs and balletic Nutcrackers everywhere. I hope that our Piedmont Chamber Orchestra will present a holiday concert. Some of my favorite presentations are the holiday concerts presented by Cantare con Vivo. The programs themselves are lots of fun, but there is a big side story to Cantare. Its music directors, David Morales and Julie Haydon, contribute mightily to the musical health of our area. They have established a musical organization which gives music lessons to some 3000 students in the East Bay. Some of these musical kids performed in the concert. Piedmont‘s favorite guitarist, Jaume Torrent, offered some philosophy on modern life. As he approaches his 70th birthday, he has been reevaluating all aspects of musical art. Torrent noted that the artists of the past probed the depths of music. Every artist of the past cultivated an individual personality. But at the same time they realized that “personality” must not defeat innate musical creativity. The composer and our musical art was all important. Jaume points out that commercialism has trampled those ideals of the past. We now have an acrobatic circus. Time marches on. At the same time we must keep in mind that music is a savior in all aspects. It is a unifying force which educates us in a way that anticipates a world liberated from stupidity, selfishness, and corruption. Catalonian classical guitarist and composer Jaume Torrent.
articles.title: Small venues producing big rewards

articles.text: Part 58 in a biweekly series Religious buildings all over the world have been constructed on a grand scale both to celebrate the faith they represent, and often to inspire awe. From the giant Grand Mosque at Mecca ($100 billion cost) to Barcelona’s Sagrada Familia (under construction for 140+ years). to Jerusalem’s Great Beth Midrash Gur synagogue (20,000 seating capacity), to the local Cathedral of Christ the Light at Lake Merritt (in Oakland (built of wood requiring its own new building code), these buildings have been among the most expensive and impressive ever built. But apart from these famous and spectacular venues, thousands of small religious buildings of various kinds have historically been an integral part of the heart of villages, towns, and cities. With constant use from lifeevents such as weddings, funerals, baptisms, bar mitzvahs, as well as regular worship services, they form the center of energy in many communities. Although the large increase of secularism in much of the world culture has changed this to a degree, there seems to be a strong role for many of the great number of religious buildings throughout our built environment. Statistics on the number of religious venues such as churches, synagogues, and mosques in the US are confusing. But one that is especially interesting to me is that a number of cites (such as Seattle for example) have a very high percentage of residents with a stated “no religious affiliation” who strongly support a large number of religious venues. Putting aside the philosophical question of spirituality vs religion, this suggests that at least some aspects – the service, community Photos by Will Adams The interdenominational Piedmont Community Church sits right in the heart of town. A wonderful mix of Spanish revival and Mission style architecture, the elegance of the southeast elevation along Mountain Avenue in the historic photo is no longer fully visible because of mature landscaping. This wonderful Albert Farr designed historic facility has been modified, added to and upgraded a number of times over the 100+ years of its life. articles.text: The first time I tried a glass of sherry was when a friend handed me a glass of cold Fino style. Taken aback by the astringent taste, I replied “Whoa. That is bitter!” It is hard for me now to relate to that experience. 25 years later there is nothing that so perfectly marks the end of a workday and the beginning of a relaxing evening than a glass of frigid, dry, fino sherry. I suppose you could say it is an acquired taste, but it is certainly one I am glad I acquired. But to speak in the singular of sherry is to speak a falsehood. Sherry is not one drink but a world of varied tasted experiences – ranging from the driest, most austere liquid you can put in your mouth, to the most unctuous, sweet, treacly indulgence that you can pour over ice cream if you don’t want to drink it. Here is a brief rundown on four of the major types of Sherry. Manzanilla Manzanilla is a dry white wine made from palomino grapes and aged under a layer of yeasts know as veil de flor. It is produced exclusively in the bodegas of Sanlúcar de Barrameda. The special climatic conditions of the town, situated at the mouth of the river Guadalquivar, favor the formation of a special kind of veil of flor which gives the wine its uniquely distinctive characteristics. A very bright, pale straw-colored wine. A sharp, delicate bouquet with predominant floral aromas reminiscent of chamomile, almonds and dough. Dry, fresh and delicate on the palate, light and smooth in spite of a dry finish. Light acidity produces a pleasant sensation of freshness and a lingering, slightly bitter aftertaste. Fino Fino is a dry white wine made from palomino grapes, which, as is the case with Manzanilla, is aged under a layer of yeasts which make up the veil of flor. It is stored and aged in American oak butts using the traditional solera y criaderas system in the bodegas of Jerez de la Frontera and El Puerto de Santa María. Ranging from bright straw yellow to pale gold in color. A sharp, delicate bouquet slightly reminiscent of almonds with a hint of fresh dough and wild herbs. Light, dry and delicate on the palate leaving a pleasant, fresh aftertaste of almonds. Fino wine has the extraordinary ability to stimulate taste buds. Due to this, it’s an ideal aperitif for preparing the palate to better enjoy food. Additionally, the savory nature of this type of Sherry intensifies all flavors in a dish; as such, any food is better understood if it’s accompanied by a glass of Fino. Oloroso Oloroso is a wine made from palomino grapes. The special structure that it demonstrates at an initial tasting destines it for oxidative ageing. For this reason alcohol is added to 17°, thus preventing the development of the veil of flor and allowing the wine to age while exposed to oxygen. The result is a wine both structured and complex. Ranging from rich amber to deep mahogany in color, the darker the wine the longer it has been aged. Warm, rounded aromas which are both complex and powerful, predominantly nutty bouquet (walnuts), with toasted, vegetable and balsamic notes reminiscent of wood, tobacco and autumn leaves. There are noticeable spicy, animal tones suggestive of truffles and leather. It is full flavored and structured in the mouth, powerful, well-rounded and full bodied. Smooth on the palate due to its glycerin content, it lingers in the mouth, with complex aromas of wood creating an elegant dry finish. Taken aback by the astringent taste, I replied “Whoa. That is bitter!” It is hard for me now to relate to that experience. 25 years later there is nothing that so perfectly marks the end of a workday and the beginning of a relaxing evening than a glass of frigid, dry, fino sherry. Here is a brief rundown on four of the major types of Sherry. Manzanilla Manzanilla is a dry white wine made from palomino grapes and aged under a layer of yeasts know as veil de flor. It is produced exclusively in the bodegas of Sanlúcar de Barrameda. The special climatic conditions of the town, situated at the mouth of the river Guadalquivar, favor the formation of a special kind of veil of flor which gives the wine its uniquely distinctive characteristics. A very bright, pale straw-colored wine. A sharp, delicate bouquet with predominant floral aromas reminiscent of chamomile, almonds and dough. Dry, fresh and delicate on the palate, light and smooth in spite of a dry finish. Light acidity produces a pleasant sensation of freshness and a lingering, slightly bitter aftertaste. Fino Fino is a dry white wine made from palomino grapes, which, as is the case with Manzanilla, is aged under a layer of yeasts which make up the veil of flor. It is stored and aged in American oak butts using the traditional solera y criaderas system in the bodegas of Jerez de la Frontera and El Puerto de Santa María. Ranging from bright straw yellow to pale gold in color. A sharp, delicate bouquet slightly reminiscent of almonds with a hint of fresh dough and wild herbs. Light, dry and delicate on the palate leaving a pleasant, fresh aftertaste of almonds. Fino wine has the extraordinary ability to stimulate taste buds. Due to this, it’s an ideal aperitif for preparing the palate to better enjoy food. Additionally, the savory nature of this type of Sherry intensifies all flavors in a dish; as such, any food is better understood if it’s accompanied by a glass of Fino. Oloroso Oloroso is a wine made from palomino grapes. The special structure that it demonstrates at an initial tasting destines it for oxidative ageing. For this reason alcohol is added to 17°, thus preventing the development of the veil of flor and allowing the wine to age while exposed to oxygen. The result is a wine both structured and complex. Ranging from rich amber to deep mahogany in color, the darker the wine the longer it has been aged. Warm, rounded aromas which are both complex and powerful, predominantly nutty bouquet (walnuts), with toasted, vegetable and balsamic notes reminiscent of wood, tobacco and autumn leaves. There are noticeable spicy, animal tones suggestive of truffles and leather. It is full flavored and structured in the mouth, powerful, well-rounded and full bodied. Smooth on the palate due to its glycerin content, it lingers in the mouth, with complex aromas of wood creating an elegant dry finish. Although the Olorosos sometimes reach relatively high alcohol levels, even above 20%, it is simply the result of the long ageing process. The cask allows for the evaporation of a good amount of water that the wine contains, thus concentrating not only the alcohol content, but also the rest of the components that contribute to the aromas, flavors, and complexity of the wine. Pedro Ximenez Pedro Ximénez is obtained from the overly ripe grapes of the same name which are dried in the sun to obtain a must with an exceptionally high concentration of sugar. Its ageing process, which is exclusively oxidative, gives the wine a progressive aromatic concentration and greater complexity, whilst fully preserving the characteristic freshness of the variety. A dark, ebony colored wine with pronounced viscosity and thickness. In the nose its bouquet is extremely rich with predominantly sweet notes of dried fruits such as raisins, figs and dates, accompanied by the aromas of honey, grape syrup, jam and candied fruit, at the same time reminiscent of toasted coffee, dark chocolate, cocoa and licorice. Velvety and syrupy in the mouth and yet with enough acidity to mitigate the extreme sweetness and warmth of the alcohol leading to a lingering, tasty finish. Pedro Ximénez is probably the sweetest wine in the world, yet despite this, its complexity of aroma and flavor make it fresh and harmonious on the palate as a result of the natural process of raisining by “asoleo” – drying the grapes in the sun. This concentrates the sugars but also the natural acidity of the grapes. articles.text: It’s that time of the year when holiday shopping, gift giving and home decorating are top of mind. But maybe it’s time to take a step back and think about what and how we buy, wrap, give and decorate. Maybe there’s a better way that fills our holiday needs and at the same time, offers the biggest gift of all: helping save our climate, our environment, our future! Here are a few ideas: “Thrifting” Instead of ordering another new shirt, sweater, dress, or purse, check out local thrift shops where you can find clothing in excellent shape for bargain prices, as well as unique items that will find new life again and be treasured for years to come. Here’s a list of thrift store near us: https://www.piedmontconnect. org/thrifting. Reusable gift wrap Republic Services can recycle tissue paper but not coated, glossy or embellished wrapping paper or gift bags, plastic ribbons, bows or cellophane. Instead, save and reuse these items as well as gift boxes, for next year. Wrap presents in reusable gift wrap made of stretchable fabric, Kraft paper, or recycled wrapping paper. Get creative by wrapping presents in old maps or recruit children to draw magical pictures on recyclable paper bags or newspapers, and tie gifts with reusable fabric ribbons. Give experiences Instead of purchasing gift items, offer family and friends an enjoyable experience. Delight youngsters with a trip to the Oakland Zoo, Chabot Observatory, Academy of Sciences, Exploratorium, a ferry ride on the Bay, or any of dozens of Bay Area activities. Let children choose a non-profit organization to donate to in their name. Give the adults in your life tickets to a theater, concert or ballgame, dinner at a favorite restaurant, a local wine tasting venture, a museum exhibit. There are a plethora of diverse activities to select from in the Bay Area. Real vs. artificial trees Is it better to buy a real live Christmas tree every year or an artificial one that can be reused year after year? Studies have found that a real Christmas tree generates fewer environmental impacts than an artificial tree unless the artificial tree is reused for at least five years, at which point it has a smaller environmental impact than a real tree. Artificial trees are made from plastic and steel, take more energy to produce, many are shipped from China, and they cannot be recycled. Christmas tree farmers, on the other hand, replant a new tree for every one they harvest, and Republic Services collects and recycles them. Earth Friendly Tips also suggests a dozen ways to recycle or reuse your tree, yourself, from making coasters out of the wood and air fresheners from the pine needles to creating wildlife habitat from the entire tree. Or what about buying a living tree to plant in your yard? And there’s always the choice of creating your own artistic tree. However you decorate, be sure to use LED bulbs or solar powered lights in holiday lighting. It turns out there’s no need to be a Grinch by “going green” for the holidays. From buying second-hand to choosing sustainable products, there are plenty of ecofriendly ways to show your family, friends and the planet, lots of holiday love. Marjorie Blackwell is a Board Member of Piedmont Connect, a collaborative community organization supporting resident initiatives and city efforts to build a sustainable future. For more ideas on how to have an eco-friendly holiday, visit Piedmont Connect at https://www. piedmontconnect.org/eco-friendly-holidays.
articles.title: Going green for the holidays

articles.text: Have you ever had to throw away food that’s gone bad, even though you had every intention of eating it? According to a study published in the American Journal of Agricultural Economics, the average U.S. household wastes 32% of its food. Wasted food is a major contributor to climate change. The production and transportation of food generates carbon emissions and when food is thrown into landfills, it generates methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Luckily, there are simple steps you can take to reduce your food waste at home, and in turn save money and lower your carbon footprint. The first step in reducing food waste is to buy only what you know you’ll eat. Next, choose the freshest produce. This means greens that aren’t wilted or yellowing at the edges, apples without brown spots, and potatoes that are firm. The freshest fruit will feel heavy for their size. If you have lots of produce in the fridge but aren’t sure what to make, try using the app Plant Jammer. It takes the ingredients you have and provides recipes that incorporate those ingredients. Storing food correctly can significantly impact its longevity. Many foods stay fresh for longer when stored outside the fridge. Tomatoes and bananas should be stored on the counter. Potatoes should be stored in a cool, dry, dark place in an open container for airflow. Onions and garlic don’t need to be kept from the light but should also be stored in a cool dry place with air flow. Other root vegetables, like carrots, parsnips, beets, turnips, and radishes, can last 3 weeks if stored in a crisper drawer on high humidity. Fresh herbs do well in a glass of water and greens are best stored unwashed in a zip-top bag. Additionally, cut carrots, celery, potatoes, and apples can be kept crisp when stored in cold water in the refrigerator. Even avocado halves can be kept fresh in water! To prolong freshness even more, change the water every few days. Fruits like apples, pears and bananas give off ethylene gas as they ripen, which in turn causes the produce around them to ripen faster. Lettuce, carrots, and broccoli will deteriorate rapidly if exposed to ethylene and should be stored away from apples. Lots of commonly disregarded food scraps are edible. Carrot, beet and radish greens are versatile and delicious. If you collect your veggie scraps and peels in the freezer, you can use them to make vegetable stock. Lettuce and green onions are particularly easy to grow from scraps. Even if you buy food with intention and store your produce perfectly, you’ll inevitably have some inedible food scraps. You can reduce your environmental impact by composting. Unlike when food decomposes in the landfill, compost does not produce methane. Putting your food scraps in the green bin is one of the easiest ways to lower your carbon footprint.
articles.title: How to reduce food waste

GOOD THROUGH JANUARY 2023 GOOD THROUGH JANUARY 2023 GOOD THROUGH JANUARY 2023 GOOD THROUGH JANUARY 2023 How to reduce food waste By Sophie Roberts Have you ever had to throw away food that’s gone bad, even though you had every intention of eating it? According to a study published in the American Journal of Agricultural Economics, the average U.S. household wastes 32% of its food. Wasted food is a major contributor to climate change. The production and transportation of food generates carbon emissions and when food is thrown into landfills, it generates methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Luckily, there are simple steps you can take to reduce your food waste at home, and in turn save money and lower your carbon footprint. The first step in reducing food waste is to buy only what you know you’ll eat. Next, choose the freshest produce. This means greens that aren’t wilted or yellowing at the edges, apples without brown spots, and potatoes that are firm. The freshest fruit will feel heavy for their size. If you have lots of produce in the fridge but aren’t sure what to make, try using the app Plant Jammer. It takes the ingredients you have and provides recipes that incorporate those ingredients. Storing food correctly can significantly impact its longevity. Many foods stay fresh for longer when stored outside the fridge. Tomatoes and bananas should be stored on the counter. Potatoes should be stored in a cool, dry, dark place in an open container for airflow. Onions and garlic don’t need to be kept from the light but should also be stored in a cool dry place with air flow. Other root vegetables, like carrots, parsnips, beets, turnips, and radishes, can last 3 weeks if stored in a crisper drawer on high humidity. Fresh herbs do well in a glass of water and greens are best stored unwashed in a zip-top bag. Additionally, cut carrots, celery, potatoes, and apples can be kept crisp when stored in cold water in the refrigerator. Even avocado halves can be kept fresh in water! To prolong freshness even more, change the water every few days. Fruits like apples, pears and bananas give off ethylene gas as they ripen, which in turn causes the produce around them to ripen faster. Lettuce, carrots, and broccoli will deteriorate rapidly if exposed to ethylene and should be stored away from apples. Lots of commonly disregarded food scraps are edible. Carrot, beet and radish greens are versatile and delicious. If you collect your veggie scraps and peels in the freezer, you can use them to make vegetable stock. Lettuce and green onions are particularly easy to grow from scraps. Even if you buy food with intention and store your produce perfectly, you’ll inevitably have some inedible food scraps. You can reduce your environmental impact by composting. Unlike when food decomposes in the landfill, compost does not produce methane. Putting your food scraps in the green bin is one of the easiest ways to lower your carbon footprint. ADVERTISE IN THE POST

Once again, the Walking on Wednesdays group had great weather for their weekly walk on December 7. The group has had good weather all year and December 7 was no exception. There was a near record turnout of 45 walkers and four K-9 best friends. Piedmont Recreation Department supervisor Eva Phalen told the group about classes available for older adults, including a line dancing class. Melba Yee will organize walks for the next several weeks in the absence of Dick Carter, with urban planner and architect Will Adams leading today’s walk, December 14. Melba Yee and Mike Henn will take the group down the hill to Zachary’s Pizza on Grand Avenue for a Holiday lunch on December 21. Part of the focus last week was on the history Sharon Avenue. A few years ago, Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi devoted almost an entire issue of the society’s publication to William E. Sharon, his family, and estate. The group decided it would walk to Sharon Avenue, discuss its history, and then continue on up to Sea View Avenue to see the Christmas decorations in some of the front yards. The walkers crossed Highland Avenue, went up Piedmont Court to a path that took them to Mountain Avenue, as its corner with Dormidera Avenue the Sharon history was shared. Born in 852, William Sharon grew up on an Ohio farm. In 1872 he came to San Francisco, and went to Virginia City, Nevada to work for his uncle, a successful banker and oner of a silver mine. Sharon married Lillian Mygatt there in 1876. He was elected to the Nevada State Senate in the 1880s. After the birth of the first three of their seven children but they wanted them to attend better schools and bought a home in Oakland in 1890. In 1893 the Sharons purchased nine acres in the Piedmont hills on Mountain Avenue. In 1897 they hired Frederic Voorhess to design a home in Piedmont, a magnificent threestory house that they called Casa Montana. The Sharons with seven children, her mother, a housekeeper, cook, and gardener moved into Casa Montana in 1898. In 1914 the City of Piedmont, then 7 years old, imposed a new property tax based on the size of the property, and the Sharons’ taxes increased dramatically. In 1915 they subdivided their land into 20 lots in a development they called Sharon Terrace. The driveway to Casa Montana became Sharon Avenue, and the address changed from Mountain Avenue to 37 Sharon Avenue. Lots from the subdivision have frontages on Mountain, Sharon, Dormidera, and Pacific Avenues. William Sharon died at his home in 1926, but Casa Montana continued as a family home with seven family members and two servants living there. Lillian Sharon continued to live in the mansion until 1934 when she moved to Oakland. Developer George Windsor purchased the remaining land and built his own home at 11 Sharon and the house at 7 Sharon on spec. He later also built homes at 40 and 44 Sharon. he demolished Casa Montana in 1936. The grand mansion was replaced by three homes at 27, 33, and 37 Sharon. Today, only three Sharon family members’ houses remain on the former Casa Montana property, 235 Mountain (1908), 56 Sharon (1921), and 52 Sharon (1922). articles.text: ⊲ JUST SOLD ⊳ “I found Lisa a year before we were ready to start making offers. Piedmont was our first choice and we wanted to work with a Realtor who knew the area well and who could maximize our chances of getting into Piedmont. Lisa was responsive and assured us we could get into Piedmont at our price point. Over the course of a year, we kept in contact with her until we were ready to make offers. When we were, Lisa never pressured us to make an offer; instead, she encouraged us to only make offers on homes where we imagined that we’d be happy for the long term. How refreshing! We looked for three months before we found a house we really wanted. Our offer was accepted! articles.text: Our City deserves credit for managing the contract award for construction of the new Piedmont Community Pool project. After issuing bonds at very favorable interest rates, Piedmont ran into the same buzz-saw of construction cost inflation experienced by all of us, from professional contractors to DIY homeowners. In response, the City cut approximately 20% from the project by prioritizing the pool size and reducing the square footage of the associated building. Unprecedented cost inflation was not the last of the challenges. A lack of competition in the first round of pre-qualified bidding resulted in a low bid that was $3 million above the City’s already-reduced cost estimates. The City decided to reject the first bids, and cast a wider net to rebid the project. That bold decision paid off with four bidders submitting in the second round and two significantly below the first round low bid. On Monday night this week, the City Council awarded the construction contract to Wickman Development and Construction, the low bidder from the second round, at $21.35 million in construction costs, an amount in alignment with the City’s current cost estimates and more than $3 million less than the low bid from the first round. The City has done its part; now it’s time for us to do ours. Even with this successful bid process the City’s available funding remains $2.1 million short of what is necessary for the essential features we want in the recreational centerpiece of our City. These include a 27-meter x 25-yard deep water pool with a diving well; a scoreboard, electronic timing system, and toe ledges; more than 3000 square feet of shallow recreation water with zero beach entry and three additional 25-yard lap lanes; and a poolside multipurpose room. We should be mindful that this is a 50-year investment in our City and in Piedmont school athletics. articles.text: Deadline for Oakland Planning Commission appeal is Dec. 14 On Wednesday, November 30, the Oakland Planning Department conditionally approved the issuance of a permit for Ohana Growers, a marijuana dispensary, at 3838 Grand Avenue, a quarter block from the Piedmont city border with Oakland. A public hearing on the application was held on Monday, Oct. 24 via Zoom. Ohana Growers first submitted an application in 2017, in response to the Oakland City Administrator’s request for applicants to operate eight new dispensaries in the city. Four applicants were selected after review by a panel of City staff, and an additional, including Ohana, were selected as runners-up. Pledges to Oakland by Ohana included 90-100% of its employees were to be Oakland residents; over half of its employees would be formerly incarcerated Oakland residents, The city pledged to provide three years of free rent to five equity businesses with the understanding that over 50% of its cannabis products would come from Oakland equity businesses. Under the Oakland Municipal Code, equity cannabis businesses (as distinguished from general businesses) qualify for application fee waivers, technical assistance, and financial assistance based upon income level and residential location. The can nabis business Root Sixty-Four, owned by Ron Leggett, Oakland’s first Native-American verified equity applicant, scored in the top four in 2017, but informed the City in September this year it was forfeiting its selection in order to partner with Ohana. Ohana subsequently moved forward with the site-selection process, and identified 3838 Grand Avenue, two doors from the intersection with Boulevard Way, as the site for their proposed dispensary. Prior to the public permit application hearing on Oct. 24, the Special Activity Permits Division received about a dozen emails from locals opposing the proposed dispensary. Their grounds for opposition included the dispensary’s proximity to two nearby preschools, Little People and Wildwood Children’s School, both near the intersections of Grand and Wildwood Avenue, and Grand and Boulevard Way. Other complaints were an incompatibility with nearby residential use; a perceived increase the dispensary would bring in traffic and crime; and also that the site exceeded Oakland Planning Code limits on retail square footage. At the hearing, Ohana was represented by its company President Nasser Azimi, Community Development Director Rob Fong, and Leggett. Azimi shared his experience operating Ohana dispensaries in Emeryville and Sacramento, his security plan for the proposed Oakland site, and his intention to work with neighbors and initially limit evening hours to 7 or 8 p.m. Two speakers voiced support of the proposal. They noted that the dispensary would bring more foot traffic to the neighborhood and argued that building’s reinforced concrete and windows limited potential for the burglary that has occurred at other dispensaries. Seventeen speakers voiced their opposition to the proposal. This opposition included concerns of late-night (10 p.m.) dispensary operation, insufficient customer parking, proximity to schools and residences, increased crime, the hiring of formerly incarcerated people, and ineffective security measures. Individuals who object to Oakland granting an occupancy permit for the dispensary may appeal by filing a written notice

articles.text: Jeremiah Loser, Tariq Harless join city as firefighters Piedmont’s newest firefighters, Jeremiah Loser (left) and Tariq Harless. Tariq Harless and Jeremiah Loser joined the Piedmont Fire Department as firefighters last February 22 and August 30, respectively. Tariq Harless Harless, raised in San Diego, first began his career as an EMT in 2005 after a few years working in the food and beverage industry. Toward the end of his time in the service industry, he began itching “for something more to do.” He became a paramedic in 2008 and continued working in San Diego for five years, after which he moved north to the Bay Area in 2014 to complete his bachelor’s degree in Legal Studies at UC Berkeley. His time working in San Diego with his Emergency Medical Services union, said Harless, stoked his interest in legal work. After finishing his degree in 2016, Harless thought about going to law school, but firefighting pulled him back in. “Working in law and policy is certainly an essential way of contributing to society, but the act of helping people day-to-day, on the frontlines as a firefighter, felt much more real to me,” he said. “I think about the most intense calls we’ve gotten — rushing to hospitals, performing live-saving rescues,” said Harless. “It would be hard to experience the same thing writing pleadings as a legal assistant. I have no doubt I’ll continue in this job.” “From the moment I started here, I’ve been embraced not only by the department but by the city and its citizens,” he said. He earlier worked in Oakland as a Paramedic Supervisor for three years. Jeremiah Loser Born and raised in Placerville, Loser learned all about rescue operations as a Coast Guard helicopter rescue swimmer for six years in North Carolina. He performed boat rescues during hurricanes along the East Coast, including Hurricane Katrina. A few years later, he decided to join the US Air Force Special Operations Command, and served all over the world, including Afghanistan, Iraq, and Africa. In 2012, he decided to return Staff photo to the U.S. and began working as a firefighter-paramedic with Berkeley Fire Department. His first officer in Berkeley was the current Piedmont Fire Chief, Dave Brannigan. He continued part-time work with the Special Ops, and was re-deployed to Afghanistan two months after completing training at the fire academy. Loser continued to switch back and forth between part-time work at the Berkeley Fire Department and Air Force Special Ops pararescue until 2017, when he began working in pararescue fully and exclusively. When he learned that Piedmont was hiring, he was ready for the stability of a single, fulltime job. “You’re not really paid for what you might be doing any particular moment. You are paid for what you can do. The time may be three in the morning, and the next thing you know you’re in the back of an ambulance with all the sirens blaring and lights flashing just trying to keep someone alive. In that sense it’s a high-intensity job, going from making dinner at home to doing IVs for a patient.” Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Osher Lifelong Learning at UC Berkeley is offering a free talk this Friday, December 9 at 10:30 a.m. on the current events of the invasion of Ukraine by Russia, and what lies ahead. It has been nine months since Russia invaded Ukraine. Join an illuminating conversation with Anastasia Edel and Michael Baker in a free zoom event. Edel, a Piedmont resident and a Russian-American, is an acclaimed writer, social historian, and New York Times contribuPiedmont writer, lecturer and social historian Anastasia Edel. tor. She’s the author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, a concise guide to Russian history, politics and culture. Baker retired after 40 years as a general and trauma surgeon. He served 30 years in active duty with the U.S. Navy and retired as a Rear Admiral. He has been in Kyiv multiple times over the past few months, teaching Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) to Ukrainian physicians. RSVP at OLLI.berkeley.edu.

Toward the end of his time in the service industry, he began itching “for something more to do.” He became a paramedic in 2008 and continued working in San Diego for five years, after which he moved north to the Bay Area in 2014 to complete his bachelor’s degree in Legal Studies at UC Berkeley. His time working in San Diego with his Emergency Medical Services union, said Harless, stoked his interest in legal work. After finishing his degree in 2016, Harless thought about going to law school, but firefighting pulled him back in. “Working in law and policy is certainly an essential way of contributing to society, but the act of helping people day-to-day, on the frontlines as a firefighter, felt much more real to me,” he said. “I think about the most intense calls we’ve gotten — rushing to hospitals, performing live-saving rescues,” said Harless. “It would be hard to experience the same thing writing pleadings as a legal assistant. I have no doubt I’ll continue in this job.” “From the moment I started here, I’ve been embraced not only by the department but by the city and its citizens,” he said. He earlier worked in Oakland as a Paramedic Supervisor for three years. Jeremiah Loser Born and raised in Placerville, Loser learned all about rescue operations as a Coast Guard helicopter rescue swimmer for six years in North Carolina. He performed boat rescues during hurricanes along the East Coast, including Hurricane Katrina. A few years later, he decided to join the US Air Force Special Operations Command, and served all over the world, including Afghanistan, Iraq, and Africa. In 2012, he decided to return Staff photo to the U.S. and began working as a firefighter-paramedic with Berkeley Fire Department. His first officer in Berkeley was the current Piedmont Fire Chief, Dave Brannigan. He continued part-time work with the Special Ops, and was re-deployed to Afghanistan two months after completing training at the fire academy. Loser continued to switch back and forth between part-time work at the Berkeley Fire Department and Air Force Special Ops pararescue until 2017, when he began working in pararescue fully and exclusively. When he learned that Piedmont was hiring, he was ready for the stability of a single, fulltime job. “You’re not really paid for what you might be doing any particular moment. You are paid for what you can do. The time may be three in the morning, and the next thing you know you’re in the back of an ambulance with all the sirens blaring and lights flashing just trying to keep someone alive. In that sense it’s a high-intensity job, going from making dinner at home to doing IVs for a patient.” Piedmont Post news racks at 2 locations Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at Mulberry’s Market, and Piedmont Shell at Grand & Wildwood Ave. Copies of the paper may be purchased for $1 at all locations during business hours. articles.text: The Piedmont Neighbors & Newcomers Club will hold its annual Holiday Party at the home of Shonnon and Martin Schey on Friday, December 9 at 7 p.m. The event will feature catered appetizers and desserts, wine and beer, and special holiday cocktails. Festive or cocktail attire is appropriate. Shonnon, the President of the PNNC Board for four years, said that the holiday party will be the club’s first large event in three years. Despite a slow few years, many new members have joined since 2019. “The best thing about PNNC is there’s something for everyone,” she said. “Many people who joined during the pandemic weren’t Piedmont newcomers at all, but locals interested in a deeper, broader connection with neighbors both new and old.” Concurrently with the re-introduction of larger events like the Holiday Party and their Supper Club (which currently boasts 135 members), Schey hopes to keep holding smaller gatherings like Girls’ and Guys’ Nights Out, children’s play groups, and book club gatherings. The Annual PNNC Holiday Party is open to PNNC members and non-members, but limited to adults only. Those interested may purchase a ticket for $50 until 9 a.m. on Thursday, December 1. and $60 after December 1 at piedmontpnnc. org/events-upcoming/2022/12/9/ holiday-party.
articles.title: PNNC Annual Holiday Party on December 9

articles.text: All those looking for viable, effective, trusted organizations to support as a part of your holiday season giving are invited to participate in Piedmont Community Church’s annual Alternative Gift Market this Sunday, December 11 from 11 a.m. to 12 noon. For nearly 20 years, Piedmont Church has sponsored this program as an opportunity for people to support local, national and international organizations dedicated to helping people in need. All groups are vetted by the church and chosen to maximize effect and result for all donations. All money received goes directly to the organizations you select. Gifts may be purchased in honor of a friend or relative, allowing donors to notify them with gift descriptions. Contributions are made at a separate station staffed by church volunteers receiving cash, checks, and credit cards. Complimentary coffee and pastries will be served. For an overview of the approximately 20 organizations involved, view the online catalog at PiedmontChurch.org/AGM where gifts can also be purchased. Everyone is encouraged to come in person to the Market. There is a feeling of excitement, a sense of spirituality and a shared joy of giving at this popular event. Visit PiedmontChurch.org/ AGM or contact the church at (510) 547-5700. Piedmont Community Church is located at 400 Highland Avenue. articles.text: Ground-breaking ceremony to be held December 17 The Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) has announced that it has raised over $1,000,000 towards a goal of $2.1 million for the Community Pool. PRFO congratulates the City of Piedmont on awarding a contract for construction of the new facility to Wickman Development & Construction. Construction is set to begin in early 2023, with a ground-breaking ceremony scheduled for December 17. It has been a long road from the City approval of the master plan and the passage of the Measure UU bond, to a global pandemic and the resulting cost impact. PRFO commends the City of Piedmont for the dedication and thoughtfulness they have put into this project. It is now full steam ahead and PRFO is asking for community support to raise the additional funds needed to complete the vision. “As with our past projects at Hampton Field and the Corey Reich Tennis Center, we are dedicated to ensuring the City has the funds needed to complete this project,” said Steve Collins, President of PRFO. “Funding will ensure that our student athletes and advanced swimmers finally have a practice and competitive aquatic center in town that includes a deep-water pool with diving well and three (3) additional 25-yard lap lanes.” With PRFO funding, the new Pool project will also include 3,000 square feet of shallow recreation water ensuring the youngest community members have the space to swim and learn water safety while creating a Recreational Center for the entire community. “This will be a centerpiece of our city to last for generations, but we are only halfway to our goal. Community support is needed to make it happen.” PRFO is thankful for the support from organizations like the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and the Piedmont Education Foundation and to the families who have generously donated to date. With the year-end approaching, PRFO’s fundraising efforts are ramping up and hope the community will visit PRFO.org to learn more and donate. PRFO and the City of Piedmont will be celebrating the start of construction with a ground-breaking ceremony on Saturday, December 17th, at 11:00 am. The entire Piedmont community is invited to join in the celebration and learn more about the project. oped by the city of South San Francisco, and a fourth for the city of Oxnard. articles.text: On November 28 classified employees of Piedmont School District (CSEA) reached an agreement during a special school board meeting that states the district will contribute modest amounts to CSEA’s rising healthcare cost. Depending on individual health care plans, the amounts will range from $250-$625 per year, $250 for a single employee, $600 more for an “employee plus one” and $625 for family plans to account for upcoming increases to out-of-pocket health care expenses which could amount to $2400 per year for full-time staff. “While it is important progress, this current agreement is barely a Band-aid for the larger crisis in education,” said CSEA President Christine Petersen. “We are in crisis,” she added. Effective January 1, 2023, the school district will increase its contribution to employee Health Benefits from on-going Measure H funds. During 2022, teachers became vocal and visible by waving signs at student drop off in the morning at school campuses. articles.text: With just a few weeks remaining, the Giving Campaign has raised $2.7 million toward the $3.5 million goal. As the 2022 Giving Campaign enters its final few weeks and the holiday season accelerates, principals at Piedmont’s schools have expressed their gratitude for the muchneeded support that the Giving Campaign provides. As Piedmont School District’s largest annual fundraiser, the Giving Campaign keeps Piedmont class sizes small and funds a broad array of student needs, from wellness to classroom aides, to libraries and the arts. “Thanks to the Giving Campaign, we have the counseling staffing we need to address our students’ social emotional needs, the intervention staff to meet academic needs, and the incredible luxury of being able to provide timely and robust professional growth opportunities for our teachers and paraprofessionals,” said Anne Dolid, principal of Havens Elementary School. Shannon Fierro, principal of Millennium High School, concurs. “The resources the Giving Campaign gives the district allow us to provide our kids with smaller classes, supplemental programming, and opportunities that enhance their experiences and learning. I am sincerely grateful for the generosity of our community to support our schools.” So far this year the Giving Campaign has raised over $2.7 million and is working to reach its goal of $3.5 million. This year, Piedmont educators received a 7.5% salary increase, and the school district relied heavily on funding from PEF to meet this need. It will continue to rely on the Giving Campaign to meet future budget obligations. Funds raised through the Giving Campaign help build a school system that consistently delivers high reading and math scores, and strong college preparedness. Piedmont High School principal Sukanya Goswami said, “Parent donations not only fund many of the programs and courses at Piedmont High School, but also class materials, online curriculum, and smaller class sizes. The Giving Campaign fills an essential gap in what we can provide at the high school in terms of a challenging, competitive, and well-rounded education to all our students. Karyn Shipp, the principal of Piedmont Middle School, says that the funds raised by the Giving Campaign are critically important. “We are so fortunate that the Piedmont community comes together to support education and provide things like professional development, online resources, and so many other programs.” To learn more about the Piedmont Education Foundation or to donate, visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org.
articles.title: School principals express gratitude for Giving Campaign
