By adding part-time employees as fractions to full-time CSEA employees, the district pays for 134.5 full time salaries, for a total of approximately 150 classified employees. The salary increases for the 150 CSEA employees will cost the district $450,000 and the bonuses around $200,000. By contrast, the 7.5% salary increases for the 22 administrators cost the district $200,000 this year. CSEA and PUSD have been in negotiations for months. Much of the fight for the 7.5% raise was pushed by CSEA’s colleagues, the teachers’ union. During 2022, teachers became vocal and visible by waving signs at student drop off in the morning at school campuses. CSEA was looking for a bit more of a boost to help with increased health care costs from Kaiser, which the district is only partially covering. Negotiations broke down earlier in November when the district offered an additional $300 increase to the salary schedule. CSEA initially understood that to mean monthly, as the salary schedule posted on the website is given in hourly and monthly pay. However, the district meant annually, and back to negotiations the two parties went. “We are pleased that we were able to come to an agreement regarding pay and benefits,” said Petersen. “However, educators have been raising the alarm about the difficulty of staying for awhile now. Because of the low pay and high stress of this work, the reality is that fewer young people are choosing to work in schools, and the demand for school workers is extremely high.” PUSD will use funds from Measure H and draw from the ongoing record-breaking increase in funding for education authorized in the 2022-23 State Budget Act put forth by Governor Gavin Newsom. In the agreement an ominous statement made by the district may foreshadow what it has in mind for next year. “The District will continue to monitor enrollment and class sizes to right-size See CSEA Employees on page 30 School principals express gratitude for Giving Campaign With just a few weeks remaining, the Giving Campaign has raised $2.7 million toward the $3.5 million goal. As the 2022 Giving Campaign enters its final few weeks and the holiday season accelerates, principals at Piedmont’s schools have expressed their gratitude for the muchneeded support that the Giving Campaign provides. As Piedmont School District’s largest annual fundraiser, the Giving Campaign keeps Piedmont class sizes small and funds a broad array of student needs, from wellness to classroom aides, to libraries and the arts. “Thanks to the Giving Campaign, we have the counseling staffing we need to address our students’ social emotional needs, the intervention staff to meet academic needs, and the incredible luxury of being able to provide timely and robust professional growth opportunities for our teachers and paraprofessionals,” said Anne Dolid, principal of Havens Elementary School. Shannon Fierro, principal of Millennium High School, concurs. “The resources the Giving Campaign gives the district allow us to provide our kids with smaller classes, supplemental programming, and opportunities that enhance their experiences and learning. I am sincerely grateful for the generosity of our community to support our schools.” So far this year the Giving Campaign has raised over $2.7 million and is working to reach its goal of $3.5 million. This year, Piedmont educators received a 7.5% salary increase, and the school district relied heavily on funding from PEF to meet this need. It will continue to rely on the Giving Campaign to meet future budget obligations. Funds raised through the Giving Campaign help build a school system that consistently delivers high reading and math scores, and strong college preparedness. Piedmont High School principal Sukanya Goswami said, “Parent donations not only fund many of the programs and courses at Piedmont High School, but also class materials, online curriculum, and smaller class sizes. The Giving Campaign fills an essential gap in what we can provide at the high school in terms of a challenging, competitive, and well-rounded education to all our students. Karyn Shipp, the principal of Piedmont Middle School, says that the funds raised by the Giving Campaign are critically important. “We are so fortunate that the Piedmont community comes together to support education and provide things like professional development, online resources, and so many other programs.” To learn more about the Piedmont Education Foundation or to donate, visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org. articles.text: Chelsea Yi stopped by the Getty Museum while visiting UCLA over the summer. High school seniors wishing to attend University of California (UC) colleges or California State University (CSU) were faced with a November 30 deadline for submitting college applications. Students grappled with the deadline, which is earlier than most private and out-of-state schools whose deadlines typically are in December and January. The CSU application consists of grades, courses, and extracurriculars, but UC adds another layer of complexity, asking for four personal insight essays. These 350-word essays are an opportunity for students to share challenges and accomplishments that can’t be seen through grades. Fall is always a stressful time for high school seniors; balancing applications while maintaining high grades is no easy task. In recent years pressure upon applicants has increased as colleges have become more selective. COVID caused students who would normally have entered college in 2020 or 2021 more likely to defer, take a gap-year and wait until in-person classes returned. As a result, there are more applicants this year and admission rates have significantly decreased. In addition to the increased selectivity, Piedmont’s rigorous academic appetite and high average grade point average (GPA) leave students in intense competition against their classmates for spots in prestigious four-year Seniors Ginger Gardner (left) and Heather Stoneman hand out Girl Scout cookies. Finding a balance between extracurriculars and academics is another college application challenge. colleges. “There are so many people at Piedmont applying to the CSUs and UCs, so there’s more competition and there’s more high-level competition, too,” said senior Ginger Gardner. “I got a college counselor fairly early on, at the end of my sophomore year, so I feel like I’ve thought about [college] for a long time.” Gardner’s dream school is UC Berkeley where she hopes to major in Political Science. Teachers also have seen the effects of added pressure and the specific pressure seen in Piedmont. “It’s always shocking to me every year how we have freshmen talking about college, and freshman year grades and how that will affect them. It used to be that freshman year grades didn’t matter,” said Piedmont High School teacher Hayley Adams. “I start to talk about college with my sophomore year students. I feel like I actually put pressure on students by doing that, but I know that they have the anxiety already.” Adams added, “I believe that whatever college you go to, is going to be a great college because it’s really about you. It doesn’t have to do with rankings. But kids at Piedmont have a much different definition of what’s good for them. They have a high standard that’s usually coming from their parents or their legacies.” Legacy and monetary factors are very real for selective private schools. “I’m competing against a lot of individuals who have legacy. When admission offices are looking at our school and the school profile, they are going to be aware of these individuals with legacy,” explained senior Chelsea Yi, “That’s always been a little bit of pressure, but it’s been something that I had to come to terms with.” As the application process comes to an end and after being put to the final test with hours of essays, students begin to show signs of relief after years of anxiety and excitement to start a new chapter. “It’s a relief to be done. I am ready to expand my horizons,” said Yi.
articles.title: Piedmont students meet deadline for UC college applications

articles.text: Historically, I’ve always felt energized by social connection, and when Thanksgiving came, I looked forward to time with family and friends: hours of games, dinner, and conversation. However, when the festivities came to an end, I found myself depleted. Being constantly “on,” navigating personalities, and filtering out background noise was exhausting. After the festivities, I relished the quiet. This is how young people experience school each day. As a result of the social isolation during the pandemic, it has become clear that, for many, the cognitive bandwidth for faceto-face interaction is limited. We’re seeing increased sensitivity, a lower tolerance for frustration, and more avoidance behaviors. These changes are more pronounced in teenagers because their isolation occurred during some of the most formative years of development. Their need to develop a sense of self among peers, away from home and parents, was delayed. Before the pandemic, we were seeing a steady increase in anxiety among school-aged children. The pandemic then compounded what was already an upward trend. Having access to a constant stream of information hasn’t helped, either. For parents, trying to enforce limits on screen time has been an exercise in futility. Getting back to in-school learning hasn’t changed that. The Give students the space and time to learn how to interact face-to-face in the classroom again. regular stressors in a full day of school seem more draining than they used to be, and students use their phones to avoid the stress. The problem is that the tendency to avoid normal everyday school tasks has a cost. The teenage years are an important time to develop executive functioning skills (e.g. initiating, planning, and sustaining attention), and engaging in hard tasks is essential to building these skills. Schools and parents must work together to meet today’s students where they are and gradually build their capacity for engaging in purposeful activities. This includes facilitating face-to-face interactions, setting limits on cell phone use (e.g. placing phones in pouches during class), building self-awareness, and creating time and space to rest when cognitive systems get overtaxed (e.g. frequent breaks built into each student’s schedule). To be clear, this is not a list of snowplow parenting strategies; it’s the opposite. Students should be allowed to work through hard things and navigate social situations so they build executive functioning pathways in the brain. Our role is to empathize with their struggle, not to fix problems for them. We need to resist the desire to make them feel better, and, instead, create opportunities for them to build their capacity for engaging with the in-person world around them. Their future success at “adulting” may well depend on it. Nancy Rowland is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small, independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at nancy@orindaacademy.org.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. articles.text: PHS defeats Spanish Springs, Reno, McQueen Photo courtesy of PHS Basketball Instagram Piedmont is off to a hot start to the season after winning the Winter Tip-Off Tournament in Nevada. Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team kick started their season with three dominant wins at the Winter Tip-Off Tournament in Reno. Hosted by Spanish Springs and Reno High Schools, the tournament went from Thursday through Saturday, December 1-3. The Highlanders opened with a 63-13 win over Spanish Springs, defeated Reno 65-31 the following day, and closed with a third one-sided game, 67-14 over McQueen. Piedmont never trailed in any of the games. “It was a great tournament for us – a great way to start the year. We showed some great energy and effort, and everyone got involved,” said coach Bryan Gardere. It was a big tournament for new starter Eva Levingston, who sat out last season due to transfer policies. She scored 18 points against Spanish Springs, 16 points against Reno, and 12 in the game with McQueen. “Eva brings some size, toughness, grit, and ability to finish at the basket. She’s a strong, physical player, and can also handle the ball,” said Gardere of Levingston. 63-13 romp vs Spanish Springs Piedmont beat up on Spanish Springs by just allowing four points in the first quarter to take a 14-4 lead. They led 30-9 by halftime. The Highlanders held their scoreless in the third quarter to lead 47-9 at the start of the fourth quarter, then closed it out strongly with 16 more points in the final going. Final stats: Levingston had a huge game with 18 points, 16 rebounds, and four assists. Trinity Zamora scored eight points, 12 rebounds, and six assists. Natalia Martinez had 16 points, eight rebounds, and seven steals. Perseas Gioukaris scored eight points, Adrienne Blackwell had eight points, and Maddie Hill scored seven. 65-31 over Reno In another one-sided win, Piedmont scored 15 points in the first quarter, 17 in the second quarter, and closed out with a strong 20-point fourth quarter. Seven players scored for PHS. Final stats: Martinez led with 20 points, six rebounds, and six steals. Zamora had 12 points, 11 rebounds, and seven assists. Levingston had 16 points and 12 rebounds. Gioukaris had seven points, Blackwell had five, Katarina Melian had two, and Hill had three. 67-14 over McQueen Piedmont bashed McQueen in the final game, jumping out with 24 points in the first quarter, and adding 18 in the second. All Highlanders scored. Final stats: Martinez led with 19 points, seven rebounds, and six steals, Zamora had 14 points, 11 rebounds, and eight assists. Levingston had 12 points and 10 rebounds.. Hill scored six, Blackwell had nine, Gioukaris had four, and Melian had three. The 12th annual Paris Twins Classic kicks off tomorrow at Binks Rawlings Gym on the Piedmont campus.
articles.title: Piedmont dominates Winter Tip-Off Tournament in Nevada

articles.text: The PHS boys’ soccer team started its season with a bang, shutting out Justin Siena 5-0 on Wednesday, November 30 on their home turf, Witter Field. The victory comes against a Division 4 North Coast Section foe, which is critical for Piedmont this season after being bumped up to the Foothill Division in league play. PHS similarly defeated Justin 5-0 in last year’s NCS Quarterfinals. “Moving up divisions means we’ll probably take a hit in our league record this year, so we need to perform well against Div. 4 schools in order to make the playoffs. This is a good start,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. Piedmont’s first goal came in the 27th minute following a free kick, when Evan Manolis sent a pass from 26 yards out to Jack Nelson, who stormed toward the net, and sent the ball into goal after the first bounce. It didn’t take long for Piedmont to strike again. One minute later Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai bolted down the right side and worked his way around a defender by the corner flag. Zirkelbach-Ngai then flicked a cross to William Daniel for a header goal. Piedmont struck again in the 40th minute moments before halftime when Jordan Miller sent a through-ball to Max Schleuning on the right side of the penalty area. Schleuning sent his shot across the face of the keeper to Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai had a goal and assist against Justin-Siena. William Daniel scored with a header in the 28th minute. the far post for a 3-0 advantage. In a clinical first half, Piedmont had 11 shots on goal, with eight of them on target. Justin-Siena only had shot go wide of the mark in the 32nd minute. Piedmont continued to maintain possession to create opportunities in the second half. The fourth goal, scored in the 59th minute, was the most impressive of the game. On a corner kick, Enzo Bernales lobbed a cross into the box to Soren Dixon standing free. Dixon didn’t allow the ball to touch the ground, hitting a volley shot into the back of the net. Piedmont nearly scored again in the 70th minute when Jacques Saldanha had a shot attempt trickle through the keeper’s legs before he stopped it on the goal line. The fifth and final goal came in the 77th minute when Rylan Nelson instinctively pounced on a loose ball on the left side of the penalty area, sending a cross to Zirkelbach-Ngai unmarked in the box. Zirkelbach-Ngai took a right footed shot on the volley to the corner of the net. In the final 40 minutes of action, Piedmont had seven shot attempts with four on target while their high-pressing action kept Justin-Siena without any shot attempts in the second half. Piedmont now looks ahead to the start of its league schedule in the Football Division of WACC this week, hosting Berkeley tonight, traveling to Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, and facing San Leandro next week on December 14. Of those schools, Piedmont lost to Berkeley 1-0 last year but defeated Bishop O’Dowd 1-0 and San Leandro 2-0. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0) hosts Berkeley today, Wednesday, December 7 at 6:00 p.m. at Witter Field. They have another league match on Friday, December 9 at Bishop O’Dowd, at 7:30 p.m.
articles.title: Piedmont shuts out Justin-Siena 5-0 in season-opener

articles.text: The Piedmont Post is seeking interns to cover Junior Varsity sports for the winter season – boys’ and girls’ basketball and soccer. The position offers budding sports journalists professional experience in covering events, learning the trade – and seeing their byline in print. Interns will work remotely with the Posts’ sports reporter, Jonathan Comeaux, who will advise and give feedback to interns wanting to publish their first articles. Those interested do not require playing experience in any sport, only an open mind and eagerness to learn. Jonathan will give young writers tips on how to cover sporting events, profile players, and utilize interviewing skills. Parents or PHS students may contact the newspaper at news@piedmont-post.com, or contact Comeaux by e-mail at JonathanCX525@gmail.com.

articles.text: The winter season is upon us, with basketball taking center stage in collegiate athletics. In this article, we look back at three former Piedmont High basketball stars and Piedmont Post Athlete of the Year recipients, including Luke Barrett at St. Mary’s, Kai Johnson at Weber State, and Luke Harris at Carleton College. Luke Barrett St. Mary’s College Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020, is a junior on the St. Mary’s men’s basketball team and has appeared in eight games so far this season. Last year as a sophomore, Barrett made an appearance in the Gaels’ 82-53 win over Indiana in the first round of the NCAA Tournament. This year, Barrett has played 110 total minutes and has knocked down 10 shots with a shooting percentage of .526, including six 3-pointers in 10 attempts. On November 10 he converted three consecutive 3-point attempts against Vermont. He’s a member of Piedmont’s 2020 D4 NCS Championship winning team and was the Post’s’ Athlete of the Year as a senior. Kai Johnson Weber State Kai Johnson, PHS Class of 2021, was a four-year starter at Piedmont High, who currently is in her sophomore year at Weber State. So far this season, Johnson has appeared in eight games and has played 87 total minutes, recording 12 points, eight rebounds, two assists, two steals, and a block. As a freshman, she played in 26 games for 135 minutes, 19 points, 14 steals, 16 rebounds, three assists, and one block. She was team captain at. PHS in her final two high school years. Johnson was a major part of a strong four-year run for the girls’ basketball program, finishing with records of 23-7 in 2017/2018, 20-11 in 2018/2019, 21-7 in 2019/2020, and 15-3 in 2021’s shortened pandemic season. Luke Harris Carleton College Luke Harris, PHS Class of 2021, was named Athlete of the Year in 2021 by the Post and was the leading scorer on the 2020 NCS Championship team. He’s currently a sophomore at Carleton College in Northfield, Minnesota and was an all-conference player as a freshman. Photo courtesy of SMC Athletics Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020, is currently a junior on St. Mary’s basketball team. Photo courtesy of Weber State Kai Johnson, PHS Class of 2021, is earning minutes as a sophomore at Weber State. So far this season, he’s appeared in and started all six games for 181 total minutes. He’s currently second on the team in points with 114 and is shooting for a high percentage at .616 from the field by converting 45 of 73 attempts. He is also seven of 15 from 3-pointers, to go along with 32 rebounds, 14 assists, six steals, and a block. As a freshman, he shot 47 percent from the field and converted 17 of 46 three-point attempts to finish with 283 points, 72 assists, 21 steals, and five blocks. He finished his high school career as a three-year starter with over 1,200 points scored. He was a part of three successful years. The team was 21-11 when he was a sophomore, it won the NCS Championship in 2020 and finished with a 24-6 record. During the pandemic shortened season in 2021, the team was 11-5. Photo courtesy of Carleton College Luke Harris, PHS Class of 2021, is a starter at Carleton College in Minnesota.

articles.text: The 2022 World Cup has now pushed through the Round of 16 and the quarterfinals are set. Croatia will face Brazil on Friday morning, while the Netherlands takes on Argentina later in the day. On Saturday, Portugal will square off with the tournament’s Cinderella team, Morocco. Later in the day, defending champion France will take on England in what is shaping up to be the most star-studded game of the batch, and a matchup that many had hoped to see as the tournament‘s championship game. When we return in next week’s Post, the World Cup will be one match through the semifinals. Here’s taking a look at each of the quarterfinals’ games and how the teams got there. No. 1 Brazil vs. No. 12 Croatia (Friday, 7 a.m.) Starting the quarterfinals will be Brazil versus Croatia with the Canaries looking like the tournament favorites after bashing South Korea 4-1 in the Round of 16 on Monday, December 5. Croatia, meanwhile, defeated Japan in penalty kicks 3-1 after ending overtime in a 1-1 tie. It’s hard to predict anything other than a Brazil win here given they might be in the best form of any team in the tournament. Brazil’s team carries an astonishing €1.14 billion value, compared to Croatia’s €377 million. Crazier upsets have hapThe Moroccans have been the story of this year’s tournament, winning Group F over Croatia and helped send No. 2 ranked Belgium home in the group stage by defeating them 2-nil on November 27. In Tuesday’s Round of 16 penalty kick shootout win over Spain, they stood on stout defense to allow just one shot on target against the Spaniards, They forced a shootout, and goalkeeper Yassine Bounou was a star by stopping three straight penalty kicks. However, Portugal walks into the match hot off its best performance in a 6-1 win over Switzerland in Tuesday’s Round of 16. Interestingly, Portuguese moved superstar Cristiano Ronaldo to the bench at halftime, and his role going forward has yet “to be defined,” per coach Fernando Santos. Portugal enters as 4/1 favorites and it’s hard to see a dip in quality from the 6-1 win. I’m going 1-0 Portugal with a spirited second half by the Moroccans. No. 4 France vs No. 5 England (Saturday, 11 a.m.) Saturday’s match of France taking on England, for many will be the best matchup of the tournament. It’s a star-studded affair with France’s Kylian Mbappe Photo courtesy of Marca.com The Samba Kings of Brazil look like the favorites, but must get through Croatia. Can they become the first No. 1 ranked team to win the World Cup? Photos courtesy of SportingNews.com Argentina made the quarterfinals with a narrow 2-1 win over Australia. They next will face a tough Netherlands side. pened, like Japan winning Group E over Spain and Germany—but the Samba Kings have outscored opponents 6-1 so far. I’m going with a 2-0 win for Brazil. It’s worth mentioning that a No. 1 ranked team has never won the World Cup. Can Brazil be the first? I had them winning it in my predictions at the start of the tournament. No. 3 Argentina vs. No. 8 Netherlands (Friday, 11 a.m.) Argentina entered the tournament as a favorite to win the whole thing, but have looked shaky at best through their four appearances. The Netherlands, meanwhile, played their best match of the tournament when defeating the United States 3-1 in the Round of 16. The Americans had no answer for the Dutchmen on Saturday, December 3, trailing 2-0 at the half and conceding the third goal just five minutes after Haji Wright scored for the U.S. In the 76th minute. Argentina, meanwhile, nearly took an exit in the Group Stage but managed to beat Poland 2-0 to win Group C. Even in the Round of 16, they unconvincingly defeated lowly ranked Australia 2-1. If we’re making a prediction based on current form, I’m undoubtedly giving Netherlands the edge despite Argentina currently being the favorite with odds makers. But, I’m a victim of being sentimental for Lionel Messi in his final World Cup; I’m going 2-1 for Argentina but wouldn’t be surprised to see the Dutch move on. No. 9 Portugal vs. No. 22 Morocco (Saturday, 7 a.m.) Morocco has a chance to keep its Cinderella mantle and have a good chance against an erratic Portuguese team. currently leading the Golden Boot race with five goals, and England with a deep roster that includes veteran striker Harry Kane and sensational rookie midfielder Jude Bellingham. The two teams carry a market value of over €1 billion with their players available. Mbappe has been nothing short of brilliant in every game. He already has nine career World Cup goals in his two tournaments of action, which ties him at No. 14 All-Time with Messi. He scored twice in France’s 3-1 win over Poland in the Round of 16 and has a lot of talented players around him, notably Antoine Griezmann, Ousmane Dembélé, and striker Olivier Giroud. Against Poland, Les Bleus recorded 16 shots with eight on target. England enters after a dominant 3-0 win over Senegal. English fans are saying “the World Cup is coming home.” They’ll need a larger contribution from Kane, who scored his first World Cup goal against Senegal, and from wingers Bukayo Saka, Phil Foden, and Marcus Rashford. I’m going with a high-powered 3-2 victory for France. It’s worth mentioning that I predicted France to face off with Brazil for the trophy and I still think that will be the case. Photo courtesy of SkySports France faces England on Saturday in a star-studded match with the fourth and fifth ranked teams in the world. Photo courtesy of CTV News Morocco has been the story of this year’s tournament after upsetting Spain in penalty kicks on Tuesday.

articles.text: Winter is here and the hours of daylight are limited. It is a great time to take in a beautiful sunset from the summit of Mission Peak, overlooking the Bay Area with sunset shortly before 5 p.m. in early December. Among the most popular trails in the East Bay, the area can become a highway of foot traffic, bikers, families, and dog walkers making their way to the Mission Peaker Summit Pole for photo opportunities. Making your way to the Mission Peak Trailhead in the late afternoon allows a more secluded trek and provide a striking view of a burning orange sunset over the Bay Area as the sun departs below the mountains surrounding the San Mateo Peninsula. Summiting Mission Peak requires 3.25 miles of hiking and 2,500 feet of elevation gain. The average hiker should allow two hours to reach the top. Arriving in mid-afternoon should allow you ample time to get situated for a remarkable sunset. Standing at the Summit Pole the view overlooks Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge with the Dumbarton Bridge and Fremont further to your right. You can watch the lights flicker down through Union City and Hayward, with a glimpse of the San Mateo Bridge and San Francisco off in the distance. To the South are Milpitas and the cityscape feeding toward San Jose and the remaining Mission Peak Regional Preserve. Turning to the East are the rolling hills of the Sunol Regional Wilderness and Ohlone Regional Wilderness. A visit to the 2,520-foot summit, such as when we did it in The rolling hills of the Mission Peak Regional Park. This hill means you’ve hit the home stretch towards the summit of Mission Peak. Hikers routinely pass by cows and calves grazing in the fields. Rocky cliffs of Mission Peak Regional Park near the summit of Mission Peak.

Turning to the East are the rolling hills of the Sunol Regional Wilderness and Ohlone Regional Wilderness. A visit to the 2,520-foot summit, such as when we did it in The rolling hills of the Mission Peak Regional Park. This hill means you’ve hit the home stretch towards the summit of Mission Peak. Hikers routinely pass by cows and calves grazing in the fields. Rocky cliffs of Mission Peak Regional Park near the summit of Mission Peak. The view from the Mission Peak Summit Pole with Fremont off in the distance. Staff Photos The sun creeps below the mountains surrounding the Peninsula. A view of the Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge, Dumbarton Bridge, and a golden California sky. March 2020 made it difficult to maintain a 6-foot distance back at. a time when everyone was trying to confirm to the latest Covid rules in place. This time, however, it wasn’t difficult to keep ample space from fellow patrons on the wide gravel trail despite passing 170 hikers on the way up. Instead of the usual mass gathering at the Summit Pole, the pack was never more than 10, giving the Post a surprising opportunity to snap a few shots. A dozen night-owl hikers were still trekking their way to the summit on our way back down, meaning we spanned an average of 30 hikers per mile in the 6.5- mile day. Older hikers and beginners can find several places to stop on the way up to the 2,500-foot peak. With a flashlight in hand, A view of the East Bay after the streetlights went on. there was never a point when we would get too far ahead or too far behind other hikers. Be sure to pack a good-sized water bottle to stay hydrated, some granola or source of energy, and a charged battery for taking videos of an unforgettable sunset. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco opened its newest exhibition, The New Black Vanguard: Photography between Art and Fashion, last month. It will be on view through March 5, 2023. The exhibition enjoys its West Coast premiere at MoAD and highlights the work of 15 contemporary fashion photographers from London, Lagos, New York, Johannesburg, and more. Each artist’s work showcases a fresh perspective on fashion, beauty, race, gender, and aesthetics The New Black Vanguard is curated by Antwaun Sargent and organized by Aperture, New York. Visitors will see over 100 select works from international artists and photographers, including Tyler Mitchell, the first Black photographer hired to shoot a cover story for American Vogue. To learn more and to purchase tickets, see https://www.moadsf. org/exhibitions/the-new-blackvanguard. A museum patron views the newest exhibit at MoAD The New Black Vanguard. articles.text: Santa available for photos December 10-23 Meet and take photos with Santa at Filoli House. Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside throughout the month to see the 16-acre estate illuminated for the holidays. The non-profit and historical landmark will be celebrating Holidays at Filoli through January 2. Meet and take photos with Santa on December 10-11, 17-18, and Dec. 23 from 10 a.m. to 4 www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223 p.m. Afterwards, view more than a dozen Christmas trees inside the estate. Filoli’s holiday decor team has installed decorations inside and outside the mansion, with miles of lights that drape the interior. Last year, the team installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The reception room’s 18-foot ceiling creates an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreates the original holiday placement that is indicative of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents. The Bourns decorated with natural materials from the gardens, including pinecones and evergreen wreaths. Realistic artificial trees and garlands were not yet available in the early to mid- 1900s. More original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene, one of her favorites, is displayed in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively in the daylight. Daytime admission offers access to explore the estate trail before sundown to admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. To learn more and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/ events/holidays/.
articles.title: Celebrate the holidays at Filoli now through Jan. 2

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony will perform alongside a screening of the classic holiday film How the Grinch Stole Christmas on Friday and Saturday, December 16-17. The film, directed by Ron Howard with music by James Horner, is a vibrant 2000 adaption of the Dr. Seuss classic. The modern, live-action adaptation features the reclusive green Grinch, played by Jim Carrey, and all the citizens of Whoville, including Cindy Lou Who. This is a family-friendly performance and appropriate for all ages. Joshua Gersen leads the orchestra in both performances. Gersen served as assistant conductor of the New York Philharmonic, where he made his debut in 2017. He has also appeared as guest conductor with Chicago Symphony and Detroit Symphony. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2022-23/How-theGrinch-Stole-Christmas.
articles.title: SF Symphony to perform How the Grinch Stole Christmas Dec. 16 & 17

articles.text: Post-show discussion tomorrow, December 8 Berkeley Repertory Theatre (Berkeley Rep) reimagines Emily Brontë’s gothic masterpiece Wuthering Heights in a new play by Emma Rice. The play is onstage now with performances through January 1. The 1847 novel tells the story of the Earnshaws and Lintons, two families living on the West Yorkshire moors, and the compelling relationship between the characters Catherine and Heathcliff. Heathcliff is rescued from the Liverpool docks as a young child, adopted by the Earnshaws and taken to live at Wuthering Heights. He strikes a friendship with Catherine Earnshaw and soon a fierce love ignites. Leah Brotherhead is cast as Catherine; her theatre credits include Gulliver’s Travels (Unicorn Theatre), Lands (Bush Theatre/Summer Hall Edinburgh Fringe), and Two Gentlemen of Verona (The Globe Theatre/Liverpool Everyman). Liam Tamne plays Heathcliff and also has an Photo by Steve Tanner The cast of Wuthering Heights. extensive discography including The Prince of Egypt (Dominion Theatre), Bonnie and Clyde (Theatre Royal Drury Lane). A post-show discussion with Berkeley Rep’s staff will take place tomorrow, Thursday, December 8, and on Tuesday, December 13. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/shows/wuthering-heights/ to obtain tickets.
articles.title: Wuthering Heights at Berkeley Rep through January 1

articles.text: A scene from Captain Fantastic. Review by Chris Honoré Captain Fantastic, written and directed by Matt Ross, finds a complex and revelatory sweet spot and expands on it. In so many ways this film is sublimely poetic while remaining firmly grounded as it probes the many facets of what it means to be a parent. It is also an engaging and captivating character study. At the film’s center is Ben, portrayed by Viggo Mortensen, a gifted, nuanced actor who inhabits Ben completely as he grapples with all of the subtle and overt challenges of being a single parent to six very independent children. But their collective lives are not lived in a suburban two-story home somewhere on the west coast; rather, home is a camp or sorts, nestled in the verdant forest of the Pacific Northwest. They live in a place apart, off the grid, and their existence, that of the children, mirrors the values of their father. He strives to instill in them a fearlessness toward life, to think for themselves, to let their minds engage in the seminal questions of purpose and existence, questions that dominate their days and, with the urging of Ben, fill their evenings as they search for answers in books and more books, from literature to philosophy to biology and history; his oldest son, Bodevan (George McKay), has recently decided he is a Maoist, a declaration that prompts a smile from Ben. As well, they are schooled to be survivalists, to engage in extreme rock climbing, hunting, hand-to-hand combat, and they find together a harmony and web of support and concern that so often eludes families surrounded by the trappings and distractions of a consumer-driven pop culture saturated with electronics. What tests (nee fractures) this harmony is the death of their mother in a hospital in New Mexico where she was taken for treatment. The children, at first devastated, argue strongly, against the wishes of Ben, that they want above all else to attend their mother’s funeral. Ben fears the journey could have unintended consequences; however, he finally relents. And suddenly these children of the forest, with all of their attendant skills, are confronted with a culture steeped in all that Ben has attempted to shield them from: television, Gameboy, Walmart and a funeral, organized by their grandparents (Frank Langella and Ann Dowd), a religious ceremony that they know is against the wishes of their mother. This immersion is both humorous and revealing and for most of the children jaw-dropping. These are not feral children, but neither are they, for all of their resilience, children of this century. Painfully, gradually, Ben is faced with a truth that he has tried to avoid: while his children are supremely prepared for a good part of life, they are also woefully lacking in so many other aspects of what it means to live in a complete world. His didacticism – embedded with his values and convictions and love – has been his gift to them. But the revelation that haunts him is that their lives have been unexpectedly truncated, their prism while wide and encompassing and rich has also been too narrow. Perhaps Ben has loved his children too much. Captain Fantastic is a beautifully crafted film, a story that is life-affirming and lovely, thanks in great part to exceptional writing by Ross and a fine ensemble of actors, all wonderful. Surprisingly, this story comes along at a time when so much of our lives can feel disjointed, and our values seemingly inadequate to the issues that confront us. In essence, our contemporary grid can sometimes seem frayed, at times empty and unfulfilling. And so, Thoreau’s simplicity beckons, the quiet voice that urges us to wander off the grid; it can feel so seductive, the vision/ fantasy seemingly idyllic. But there are larger truths involved than simply leaving the grid. And it is those truths that gradually begin to confront Ben and challenge his vision of the ideal. And it is those truths and their inherent cost that make up the thematic structure of this wonderful film. Captain Fantastic. Directed by Matt Ross. Starring Viggo Mortensen, Frank Langella and Kathryn Hahn. 2 hrs. Rated R. Released in 2016. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Captain Fantastic a sweet story of what it means to be a parent

articles.text: Stan & Ollie is an understated, touching story about Laurel and Hardy, one of the most celebrated comic duos of a generation, a partnership that spanned some 37 years in film and vaudeville. I’m assuming that, as their remarkable story searches for an audience, there will be those who only vaguely remember them, if at all. And to watch their nuanced, subtle routines is to realize that a great deal has changed regarding popular comedic entertainment. The coarsening of society, meaning what it takes to make us laugh, also comes to mind. Much of what they did as they performed their established signature routines – Stan (Steve Coogan) almost Chaplinesque in his movements and head scratches, and Ollie (John C. Reilly), given to a slow burn of frustration, while reaching deep for that last reserve of patience – was elegant in its simplicity, while layered with a subtle humor that demonstrates a disguised genius. The film opens in 1937, in the dressing room of Stan and Ollie as they sit and discuss their troubles: ex-wives, alimony, contracts and salaries. The camera then follows them in a long tracking shot to a crowded soundstage where they do a soft-shoe dance before a screen depicting a western town; it’s a scene for their movie, Way Out West. Now cut to 16 years later. Its 1953, over a decade past their peak popularity, and the duo is booked for a tour in England, staying in second-tier hotels and performing in small variety halls. Their practiced routines, lifted from their films, are polished and familiar; however, the audiences are small, even in Glasgow and Newcastle. And so the two begin to grapple with an encroaching reality: something has changed, the laughter seems a bit brittle, and those vignettes (many written by Stan) that once filled theaters, seem to lack a punch. As well, television is the newest, greatest thing as are the fresher comic duos such Abbott & Costello. But to their credit they rally; they need the money, there is a promised movie at the end of the tour, and so they agree to do publicity events advertising their shows. To their delight, larger halls are scheduled with accompanying larger audiences. And it’s at this point in the narrative that the filmmakers make an artful decision: while Stan & Ollie is, to be sure, a tribute film to their on stage career, it is also far more and the story shifts to an examination of the vagaries of their friendship as well as their respective idiosyncrasies. At first blush, it’s obvious that their strength as a duo was in part due to the contrast in their appearance: Stan was blade thin, his face narrow and angular. Ollie was pear-shaped, his diminutive nose lost in his bulging cheeks atop a second and third chin. And there’s that narrow mustache. But they were also very different in outlook. Stan was bottom line, sitting behind his typewriter; Ollie was easygoing, loved betting on the horses, and his onstage tie twiddles reflective of his demeanor off stage. They were also married to two very different women, played wonderfully by Shirley Henderson and Nina Arianda, who arrive in London as the tour is winding down. But looking past those decades when Laurel & Hardy were enthusiastically embraced, there is a universal story to be told beneath the period patina and that is the sadly sweet realization that what once was can never be again. Time and age have overtaken them (Ollie’s heart is also problematic) and the culture of comedy is beyond their grasp, both literally and figuratively. The curtain is slowly beginning to descend on an era they once defined. One last point: Steve Coogan and John C. Reilly deliver marvelous performances. The film ultimately is dependent on their ability to step into the personas of Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy and literally vanish. It’s what superb acting is all about, and it’s also never easily achieved. They manage to do it with brilliance. Stan & Ollie. Directed by Jon S. Baird. Starring Steve Coogan, John C. Reilly, Shirley Henderson. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG. Released in 2019. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Stan & Ollie a wonderful story of 2 brilliant comics

articles.text: Paddington 2 is a family-friendly, live-action, CGI comedy, directed by Paul King, and based on the stories by Michael Bond. As a general rule, sequels don’t have the pizazz of the first film; however, if anything, this is a far better movie. Two words capture the narrative: “decency” and “kindness.” The story opens with Paddington Bear (Ben Wishaw) still living happily with the Brown family – matriarch Mary (Sally Hawkins) and her husband Henry (Hugh Bonneville) – in London’s Windsor Gardens, a model of diversity. Due to his gregariousness and friendly demeanor, he is popular with his community, and never fails to greet the Gardens’ denizens. He works odd jobs such as washing windows and is in the process of saving his earnings to buy a pop-up book of London for his aunt Lucy (Imelda Staunton), who lives in a retirement home in Peru; she is soon to be 100-years old. Paddington spotted the book in Mr. Samuel Gruber’s (Jim Broadbent) antique shop, and just as he’s preparing to buy it a thief breaks in and steals the book. Knowing Paddington’s interest in the book, he is accused of being the robber and surprisingly is sent to prison. Of course, the Browns are convinced that the bear is innocent (there are many in the Gardens who aren’t so sure), and so begins the family’s attempt to find out who the real thief is. And though doing time in jail, he never loses his friendly manner, even when surrounded by a group of hardened meanies, led by the snarling prison cook, Knuckles McGinty (Brendan Gleason). P, ever friendly, eventually wins the cranky cook over. In P’s world, even the inmates have some inherent goodness and can be better people if they try. As aunt Lucy once told him, “If you’re kind and polite, the world will be right.” Meanwhile the search for the robber continues, and as far as the Browns are concerned it just might be the slimy, egotistical actor Phoenix Buchanan (Hugh Grant), who is also a resident of the Gardens. However, he has claimed that it was Paddington who took the book. Paddington 2 is a charming film with an outstanding cast, lots of cavorting, chase sequences, and a steam train that delights. Kids will no doubt fall under the spell of this very special bear, and who could be a better role model? Paddington 2. Directed by Paul King. articles.text: A scene from Pixar/Disney Animation’s Coco. The story of Coco follows a 12-year-old boy named Miguel Rivera (Anthony Gonzalez) who lives in the small Mexican town of Cecilia. He dreams of one day becoming a musician, exactly like the legendary Ernesto De La Cruz (Benjamin Bratt), an iconic guitar player. Miguel secretly practices while studying video footage of Ernesto. There is, however, a problem, and it is not a small one: the Riveras are shoemakers, part of the artisan trade community, and theirs is a tradition that has been proudly passed along from one generation to the next. The expectation is that Miguel will be what the Rivera men were before him – shoemakers. Playing music is not a consideration. Meanwhile, Miguel yearns to participate in a talent show to be held in the town plaza on the Dia De Muertas, a day when those who are deceased visit the living. His ancient great grandmother, Coco (Ana Ofelia Marguia), the strict matriarch of the Rivera family, and the daughter of Miguel’s great-great grandmother, Imelda, sternly supports the family’s ban on music playing. In preparation for the Dia De Muertas, the Riveras have created an elaborate shrine with the photos of deceased family members. If he going to be in the talent show, Miguel realizes he will need a guitar. He goes to the tomb of Ernesto and there finds Ernesto’s original guitar, which he steals. It’s that moment that Miguel is transported to the Land of the Dead, where he meets all of his past relatives who are preparA scene from Pixar/Disney Animation’s Coco. ing for their journey on this very special day. When he meets up with his great-great grandmother, Imelda (Alana Ubach), who has a dark history with musicians, makes it clear that he must quit music. During his adventure, Miguel hooks up with a scallywag called Hector (Gael Garcia Bernal), and also has a sidekick, a spifffy dog. There is one caveat to Miguel’s family reunion with those who have passed away: he must return to the Land of the Living by dawn or he will remain forever in the Land of the Dead. All he needs is a blessing from a deceased relative. And so his journey continues. This is a beautifully animated feature film, one of Pixar’s best, filled with vibrant colors, cultural themes, wonderful songs, and amazing alebrijes (folk art sculptures). The embedded importance of family runs throughout the story, as well as the importance of following your dreams, all of it leading Miguel to finding peace in the Land of the Living. Coco. Pixar/Disney Animation. Directed by Lee Unkrich. Starring Anthony Gonzalez, Gael Garcia Bernal, Benjamin Bratt. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Released in 2017. Now streaming on Disney+/Prime/VUDU.

articles.text: Photo by Erik Tomasson Helgi Tomasson’s production of Nutcracker begins on December 8 at the War Memorial Opera House. San Francisco Ballet’s holiday favorite, Nutcracker, premieres on Thursday, December 8, at the War Memorial Opera House. The ballet will be performed through December 27. This special production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks like the Painted Ladies by Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s 90-year history. San Francisco Ballet performs the production every year, with a kaleidoscope of 150 dancers telling the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco. San Francisco Symphony will perform the familiar score of Tchaikovsky. A diverse array of instruments are used by the Symphony, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani – all played by only three musicians. Scenic design is by Michael Yeargan; costume design is by Martin Pakledinaz; lighting design is by James F. Ingalls, and projection design by Wendall K. Harrington. The ballet is especially appropriate for children aged five and older. No children under age three will be permitted. The performance Nutcracker runs two hours with one intermission. Tickets are selling quickly for performances on Christmas Eve, December 24. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker-dec-2022/.

She enters an intimate relationship with one of them, who’s also haunted by his past. This richly layered book explores the nature of grief, how it can stretch or compress time, reshape memories and make us dream up alternate realities. “I don’t want to tell you what happened,” the narrator says. “I want to tell you how it felt.” Trust by Hernan Diaz Diaz uncovers the secrets of an American fortune in the early 20th century, detailing the dizzying rise of a New York financier and the enigmatic talents of his wife. Each of the novel’s four parts, which are told from different perspectives, redirects the narrative (and upends readers’ expectations) while paying tribute to literary titans from Henry James to Jorge Luis Borges. Whose version of events can we trust? Diaz’s spotlight on stories behind stories seeks out the dark workings behind capitalism, as well as the uncredited figures behind the so-called Great Men of history. It’s an exhilarating pursuit. The Candy House by Jennifer Egan You don’t need to have read Egan’s Pulitzer-winning “A Visit From the Goon Squad” to jump feet first into her much-anticipated sequel. But for lovers of the 2010 book’s prematurely nostalgic New Yorkers, cerebral beauty and laser-sharp take on modernity, The Candy House is like coming home – albeit to dystopia. This time around, Egan’s characters are variously the creators and prisoners of a universe in which, through the wonders of technology, people can access their entire memory banks and use the contents as social media currency. The result is a glorious, hideous fun house that feels more familiar than sci-fi, all rendered with Egan’s signature inventive confidence and – perhaps most impressive of all – heart. The Candy House is of its moment, with all that implies. Checkout 19 by Claire-Louise Bennett Bennett, a British writer who makes her home in Ireland, first leaped onto the scene with her 2015 debut novel, Pond. Her second book contains all of the first’s linguistic artistry and dark wit, but it is even more exhilarating. Checkout 19, ostensibly the story of a young woman falling in love with language in a working-class town outside London, has an unusual setting: the human Strangers to Ourselves: Unsettled Minds and the Stories That Make Us by Rachel Aviv In this rich and nuanced book, Aviv writes about people in extreme mental distress, beginning with her own experience of being told she had anorexia when she was 6 years old. That personal history made her especially attuned to how stories can clarify as well as distort what a person is going through. This isn’t an anti-psychiatry book – Aviv is too aware of the specifics of any situation to succumb to anything so sweeping. What she does is hold space for empathy and uncertainty, exploring a multiplicity of stories instead of jumping at the impulse to explain them away. Under the Skin: The Hidden Toll of Racism on American Lives and on the Health of Our Nation by Linda Villarosa Through case histories as well as independent reporting, Villarosa’s remarkable third book elegantly traces the effects of the legacy of slavery – and the doctrine of anti-Blackness that sprang up to philosophically justify it – on Black health: reproductive, environmental, mental and more. Beginning with a long personal history of her awakening to these structural inequalities, the journalist repositions various narratives about race and medicine — the soaring Black maternal mortality rates; the rise of heart disease and hypertension; the oft-repeated dictum that Black people reject psychological therapy — as evidence not of Black inferiority, but of racism in the health care system. We Don’t Know Ourselves by Fintan O’Toole O’Toole, a prolific essayist and critic, calls this inventive narrative “a personal history of modern Ireland”. It’s an ambitious project, but one he pulls off with élan. Charting six decades of Irish history against his own life, O’Toole manages to both deftly illustrate a country in drastic flux, and include a sly, self-deprecating biography that infuses his sociology with humor and pathos. You’ll be educated about increasing secularism, the Celtic tiger, human rights, but you’ll also be wildly, uproariously entertained by a gifted raconteur at the height of his powers.

articles.text: An Immense World: How Animal Senses Reveal the Hidden Realms Around Us by Ed Yong Yong certainly gave himself a formidable task with this book — getting humans to step outside their “sensory bubble” and consider how nonhuman animals experience the world. But the enormous difficulty of making sense of senses we do not have is a reminder that each one of us has a purchase on only a sliver of reality. Yong is a terrific storyteller, and there are plenty of surprising animal facts to keep this book moving toward its profound conclusion: The breadth of this immense world should make us recognize how small we really are. But the enormous difficulty of making sense of senses we do not have is a reminder that each one of us has a purchase on only a sliver of reality. Yong is a terrific storyteller, and there are plenty of surprising animal facts to keep this book moving toward its profound conclusion: The breadth of this immense world should make us recognize how small we really are. Stay True: A Memoir by Hua Hsu In this quietly wrenching memoir, Hsu recalls starting out at Berkeley in the mid-1990s as a watchful music snob, fastidiously curating his tastes and mercilessly judging the tastes of others. Then he met Ken, a JapStrangers to Ourselves: Unsettled Minds and the Stories That Make Us by Rachel Aviv In this rich and nuanced book, Aviv writes about people in extreme mental distress, beginning with her own experience of being told she had anorexia when she was 6 years old. That personal history made her especially attuned to how stories can clarify as well as distort what a person is going through. This isn’t an anti-psychiatry book – Aviv is too aware of the specifics of any situation to succumb to anything so sweeping. What she does is hold space for empathy and uncertainty, exploring a multiplicity of stories instead of jumping at the impulse to explain them away. Under the Skin: The Hidden Toll of Racism on American Lives and on the Health of Our Nation by Linda Villarosa Through case histories as well as independent reporting, Villarosa’s remarkable third book elegantly traces the effects of the legacy of slavery – and the doctrine of anti-Blackness that sprang up to philosophically justify it – on Black health: reproductive, environmental, mental and more. Beginning with a long personal history of her awakening to these structural inequalities, the journalist repositions various narratives about race and medicine — the soaring Black maternal mortality rates; the rise of heart disease and hypertension; the oft-repeated dictum that Black people reject psychological therapy — as evidence not of Black inferiority, but of racism in the health care system. We Don’t Know Ourselves by Fintan O’Toole O’Toole, a prolific essayist and critic, calls this inventive narrative “a personal history of modern Ireland”. It’s an ambitious project, but one he pulls off with élan. Charting six decades of Irish history against his own life, O’Toole manages to both deftly illustrate a country in drastic flux, and include a sly, self-deprecating biography that infuses his sociology with humor and pathos. You’ll be educated about increasing secularism, the Celtic tiger, human rights, but you’ll also be wildly, uproariously entertained by a gifted raconteur at the height of his powers. articles.text: Montclair Village Association will host its 20th Annual Montclair Village Holiday Stroll tomorrow, Thursday, December 8, from 5:30 to 8:30 p.m. The heart of the event is located at 2050 Mountain Boulevard in charming Montclair Village, nestled in redwood groves unique to Oakland’s hills. Festivities include live performances from local artists, professional photos with Santa, giant puppets, children’s crafts and activities, Oakland Fire Department parade rig and toy drive, choirs and live music performances, feasts and libations, and holiday shopping at over forty businesses. Free admission for all ages. Highlights include: • Winter Wonderland including professional photos with Santa for the kids. • Giant Puppets Save the World entertainment by a collaboration between puppeteers, builders, and performance artists. • A family-friendly holiday festival presenting the ideal kick off to the holiday season. • Live performances with local youth and school groups including Pacific Boychoir Academy, Jazz Education Ensemble, Edna Brewer Band Carolers, and Montera Cheer Squad. • Holiday entertainment provided by The Tap Dancing Christmas Trees, Oakland Ballet Company, Renegade Orchestra, and more. • Special discounts and promotions offered at over 40 locally-owned, independent merchants who stay open late to greet guests with music, food, and drinks. Santa visits the Montclair Village Holiday Stroll Photo by Melissa Rivers • Opportunity to donate a toy to the “Random Acts Toy Drive” hosted by the Oakland Fire Department, attending with their parade rig. The Holiday Stroll celebrates its 20th year of transforming Montclair Village into Santa’s Winter Wonderland, a whimsical and magical holiday experience for all ages to enjoy. Decked out in bright lights and cheerful decorations, Mountain Boulevard and Antioch Court — and its many inviting boutique shops — are sure to fill you with the holiday spirit. Montclair Village provides a picturesque setting for sharing the holidays with family, friends, and community. The biggest draw for younger visitors is meeting Santa Claus himself and having their keepsake snapshot taken by a professional photographer. Adults will enjoy delicious food and libations while visiting over forty shops open late with special offers, unique holiday gifts, and stocking stuffers. Jam-packed with entertainment, all ages will be elevated with joy by the youth choirs, live music, and performance artists. Pacific Boychoir Academy, a Grammy Award winning independent choir school for boys in grades 3-8, will perform holiday classics. Giant Puppets Save the World is a live art demonstration magically dancing overhead like large-scale mobiles. The Tap Dancing Christmas Trees are a Holiday Stroll tradition, delighting all ages with choreographic tap dance routines in tree costumes. Visit MontclairVillage. com for the full entertainment lineup. “Our Holiday Stroll is designed to bring people together, to support the mom and pop, and community connected businesses, the community groups, artists, and Oakland schools.” Executive Director Daniel Swafford said. “It reminds us how important the people in our lives are and what community means.” Holiday Stroll is an ideal family tradition creating lasting memories of celebrating the holidays together. Montclair Village has everything you need to complete your shopping list with plenty of opportunities to find unique gifts that will bring joy to recipients. Shop Montclair Village during the Holiday Stroll, throughout the season, or visit the curated gift guides at MontclairVillage.com for gift ideas. If you are able, donate a new toy during the event at the Oakland Fire Department’s Toy Drive for a local family in need. The Holiday Stroll is an opportunity to support Oakland’s locally owned businesses whose collective efforts and donations create community events that thousands of people enjoy. If you’re interested in supporting public events in Montclair, consider joining the Montclair Cares Club and help bring more arts and cultural activities to the neighborhood.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Parmesan Rosemary Shortbread a perfect snack for the holidays. These savory shortbread cookies would be right at home on your cheese board where I’d also nestle a few roasted almonds nearby. We enjoy these from lunch time to cocktail time, anytime the mood strikes. And they go dangerously well with a flute of bubbly for celebratory cheer. While the recipe sounds a bit fussy to make, the techniques are very straightforward and easy to track with a kitchen timer. A bench scraper with a measuring scale on the edge makes things easier to cut in the pan and later spread out for the second bake. You can change the size and shape of the cookies as you prefer. Just be aware they are a bit crumbly when you are cutting them as they are still warm. Parmesan Rosemary Shortbread Makes one 9ʺ x 13ʺ pan; 35 pieces, 1-3/4ʺ x 1-3/4ʺ squares. INGREDIENTS 1-1/2 cups (12 oz) unsalted butter, room temperature, very squishy soft 3/4 teaspoon sea salt 3/8 cup, scant (2.25 oz) granulated sugar 1-1/2 tsp. black pepper, freshly ground 3-3/8 cups (14-3/4 oz.) all-purpose flour 3 oz. finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano 3 Tbs. fresh rosemary (1/2 oz), finely minced Course sea salt for finishing, about 3/4 teaspoons sprinkled all over INSTRUCTIONS Center rack in oven. Preheat the oven to “Convection Setting” 300°F. Line the pan with sheet of parchment paper, with some overlap on at least one of the 9-inch sides. Place the butter in a large mixing bowl. The butter must be very soft—the consistency of mayonnaise. Add the salt to the butter and mix well with a wooden spoon so that it dissolves completely before adding the remaining ingredients. Add the granulated sugar and black pepper and mix just until combined. Add the flour mixture all at once, along with the Parmesan and rosemary; and mix until evenly incorporated but dough is still crumbly. Pat gently and evenly into the prepared pan, making sure edges and corners are neat. Do not press down too hard. Bake 40 - 45 minutes until pale, golden brown. After initial baking, remove from oven, keeping oven on. Let rest for 5 minutes. Using a bench scraper, cut straight down through the dough at 1-3/4ʺ intervals, making five strips along 9ʺ side of pan. Give the pan a quarter turn and repeat cutting at 1-3/4ʺ intervals, making 35 squares. Sprinkle lightly with course sea salt, distributing evenly with a few grains on each square. Return to oven for 10 minutes. After 10 minutes, remove from oven, and reduce the temperature to 250°F. Let rest for 5 minutes. Have a large cookie sheet ready (without sides makes things easier). Carefully tip and pull an edge of the parchment paper lining the pan, transferring the shortbread onto the cookie sheet. Using a bench scrapper, carefully cut through the shortbread squares completely and separate, allowing at least 1/4ʺ between squares for air circulation. Return to the 250°F oven for another 10 minutes for final baking to dry and crisp the shortbread. Remove shortbread from oven and cool completely before handling and storing. Store at room temperature for up to 5 days. They can be re-crisped in a 300°F oven in about 5 – 10 minutes and are delicious eaten when slightly warm.
articles.title: Try some Parmesan Rosemary Shortbread for the holidays

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group continued to live a charmed life on November 30. The weather forecast was for heavy rain on Thursday, but Wednesday was a beautiful, mild, sunny morning. A solid turnout of 35 veteran walkers and three K-9 best friends were at the Exedra to enjoy their weekly walk. Piedmont Recreation Department Supervisor Eva Phalen was there to tell the group about new classes for older adults. The group has an informal objective of walking every safe-walking street in Piedmont each year, and there remain only a few they haven’t gotten to. One little pocket of streets was Cambrian Way and parts of Jerome and Howard Avenues. The group wanted to see them and along the way see Hillside Court off Magnolia Avenue, which they have passed many times on walks, but hadn’t gone to in a couple of years. When Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi read about the walk, she responded with some excitement, “You are in for a treat. The house at the bottom of Hillside Court (415) is a real gem with a river rock base. The designer was Verb Strang who designed a handful of distinct houses in Piedmont.” Gail went on, “Also, if you walk Jerome north of Oakland Avenue, you’ll see a cluster of Queen Anne houses, some of the oldest houses in Piedmont dating back to the 1890s. Lots of choices.” The walkers headed off down Magnolia Avenue past the high school, to the top of Hillside Court. They went down its steep hill to 415, a house built in 1904. It is a charming home with a base made of large river rocks. As the group was admiring it, John Randolph, the long-time owner, came out and talked with the walkers about his home. Verb Strang designed and lived in the home. He designed some other homes in Piedmont, and many more in Alameda. Randolph said the house is beautiful, but like most older homes, is a “maintenance sink.” As the group started back up the hill, neighbor Mike Costello, also a longtime resident on Hillside Court and Magnolia, was there to share more neighborhood history. First, he pointed out that the telephone pole at the bottom on the street does not have a cell phone signal booster, as was once proposed. That’s because Mike was able to show the pole is curiously on the private property of one of the residents, not on public land. Mike also shared more history of the street, including how the City bought the land, which went all the way down to what is now Witter Field, for one piece of gold. The group continued to Jerome, passing Frosty the Snowman and crossed Oakland Avenue looking for a set of early homes near Cambridge Way. Architects Jim Kellogg and Bob Wong, who were on the walk, provided some background information on the Queen Anne homes in the neighborhood. They are Victorian-style houses that have specific features, including asymmetrical facades, wraparound porches, towers and turrets, multicolored palettes, steep roofs with cross gables or large dormers, and expansive porches with decorative wood trim. The home at 31 Jerome seemed to be the oldest on the street, built in 1894. Some years back the new owner took on the significant job of restoring the home with its brick foundation. There was also a dilapidated horse stable on the back of the property that was falling down. They were saved. The house next door was built in 1895. The group went on to Cambridge Way, crossed Grand Avenue and continued up Cambridge to its end at Howard Avenue, overlooking Beach School. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. pages.text: Wednesday, December 7, 2022 25 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers visit Hillside Court By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group continued to live a charmed life on November 30. The weather forecast was for heavy rain on Thursday, but Wednesday was a beautiful, mild, sunny morning. A solid turnout of 35 veteran walkers and three K-9 best friends were at the Exedra to enjoy their weekly walk. Piedmont Recreation Department Supervisor Eva Phalen was there to tell the group about new classes for older adults. The group has an informal objective of walking every safe-walking street in Piedmont each year, and there remain only a few they haven’t gotten to. One little pocket of streets was Cambrian Way and parts of Jerome and Howard Avenues. The group wanted to see them and along the way see Hillside Court off Magnolia Avenue, which they have passed many times on walks, but hadn’t gone to in a couple of years. When Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi read about the walk, she responded with some excitement, “You are in for a treat. The house at the bottom of Hillside Court (415) is a real gem with a river rock base. The designer was Verb Strang who designed a handful of distinct houses in Piedmont.” Gail went on, “Also, if you walk Jerome north of Oakland Avenue, you’ll see a cluster of Queen Anne houses, some of the oldest houses in Piedmont dating back to the 1890s. Lots of choices.” The walkers headed off down Magnolia Avenue past the high school, to the top of Hillside Court. They went down its steep hill to 415, a house built in 1904. It is a charming home with a base made of large river rocks. As the group was admiring it, John Randolph, the long-time owner, came out and talked with the walkers about his home. Verb Strang designed and lived in the home. He designed some other homes in Piedmont, and many more in Alameda. Randolph said the house is beautiful, but like most older homes, is a “maintenance sink.” As the group started back up the hill, neighbor Mike Costello, also a longtime resident on Hillside Court and Magnolia, was there to share more neighborhood history. First, he pointed out that the telephone pole at the bottom on the street does not have a cell phone signal booster, as was once proposed. That’s because Mike was able to show the pole is curiously on the private property of one of the residents, not on public land. Mike also shared more history of the street, including how the City bought the land, which went all the way down to what is now Witter Field, for one piece of gold. The group continued to Jerome, passing Frosty the Snowman and crossed Oakland Avenue looking for a set of early homes near Cambridge Way. Architects Jim Kellogg and Bob Wong, who were on the walk, provided some background information on the Queen Anne homes in the neighborhood. They are Victorian-style houses that have specific features, including asymmetrical facades, wraparound porches, towers and turrets, multicolored palettes, steep roofs with cross gables or large dormers, and expansive porches with decorative wood trim. The home at 31 Jerome seemed to be the oldest on the street, built in 1894. Some years back the new owner took on the significant job of restoring the home with its brick foundation. There was also a dilapidated horse stable on the back of the property that was falling down. They were saved. The house next door was built in 1895. The group went on to Cambridge Way, crossed Grand Avenue and continued up Cambridge to its end at Howard Avenue, overlooking Beach School. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The $118 million and 8-year project, San Francisco’s Presidio Tunnel Tops, opened in July this year for the public to enjoy every day and for free. The newest park, a 14-acre space in San Francisco, is an innovative use of the land on top of and adjacent to the Presidio Parkway tunnels on Highway 101 which lead to the Golden Gate Bridge. Presidio Tunnel Tops has unique views of the Golden Gate, play spaces for kids, picnic areas, sprawling lawns and links the Golden Gate National Recreation Area to Crissy Field. The possibility for the space, which connects and extends nature spaces for public use, was born in 2012 when the elevated highway connecting San Francisco to the Golden Gate Bridge was demolished and replaced with tunnels. In 2014, The Partnership for the Presidio started asking the public for input on what the space could become. While the Presidio Tunnel Tops has plenty to offer visitors of all ages, it will be tough to drag kids away from the expansive playground called Outpost. An authentic water pumping station for trellised gold mining fun is not to be missed, nor are the huge structures to balance, swing, and climb upon. The sweeping lawns are impressive and ripe for any gathering, with lawn chairs, picnic tables and barbeques installed Aerial View of Tunnel Tops in San Francisco. and available for reservation. Accessibility was a key aspect in the design of the space. The free Presidio Go Downtown Shuttle offers direct service from Embarcadero BART, Transbay Terminal, and Van Ness and Union Streets. Paid parking is available at large lots near the Presidio Visitor Center at 210 Lincoln Boulevard. This new outdoor area is a destination capable of providing a full day of fun and is also a convenient starting point for other Presidio activities. Food vendors and restrooms are available on site. Presidio Tunnel Tops is open 9:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m. through March. Visit Presidiotunneltops. gov to plan your trip. Q: Soon after you moved here, in 1990, you became a licensed architect. What was your career trajectory, and when did you start the community-based involvements that you’ve kept going? A: I have owned an architectural firm in Oakland for 18 years. Today, I’m the Vice President of a national real estate project management and development company, Project Manager Advisors, Inc. I’m an owner’s representative, meaning that I oversee the client’s scope, schedule, and budget. I really got serious with my volunteer work in Piedmont when I joined the Planning Commission about seven years ago, because it aligned heavily with what I loved doing as a career. Before that, I’d also volunteered for various design and public school committees, and I led low-income housing repair projects with local students under the Piedmont Community Service Crew. Q: What about the Planning Commission work aligned with your values as an architect? A: I love spending my career helping people design and build projects in the Bay Area.
