Given that connection of my volunteer work to my experience in building and planning, when I started working with volunteers, attorneys, and architects on the Planning Commission, there seemed to be a very natural connection. The next thing I know, it’s been seven years! Q: Your focus on keeping local control of infrastructure upgrades has been a common factor across the various committees over the course of your career. What has presented the largest difficulty to this goal, in your experience. Has it changed over the years? A: It’s not a good or bad thing in itself, but we are very cautious as a town – and rightfully so, especially given our approach to budgets. If it’s a difficulty, I don’t think it’s one that gets in the way. However much we may differ in opinions, I believe that we all generally have the same goals. We all like where we live, and like the perspectives we have to offer each other. So while we’re often quite cautious when it comes to change, I think that is often quite a good thing. Q: The recently passed Housing Element was a great litmus test for that sort of caution, and City Council certainly made concerted efforts to make sure that Piedmonters could voice their concerns. What do you believe to be the most essential factor in maintaining that communication between local government and residents? A: It’s certainly essential to have the information published, widely distributed, and readily available. I think that the conversations we were having – like the Open Houses that the city held – were very helpful. People were able to hear the background and history of the Housing Element and able to hear about the experience of other cities in California submitting theirs. Piedmont has some unique challenges. We’re a small town, we’re fully built out. I think it was necessary we understood that, along with every other city and county in California, we had to reckon with them – that the Element was a mandate of state law. That kind of communication was critical to understanding the reasoning behind the Planning Commissioners’ and City Council members’ decisions. Q: The ongoing Community Pool Project is another case where communication between local government and residents has been critical. What has been the most essential factor in dealing with the project’s surprises? A: This is a great collective and volunteer effort. I think that Bob McBain’s letter (in the Nov. 23 edition of the Post) put it very succinctly: Piedmont deserves a first-class facility, and Piedmont’s schools deserve to use a firstclass facility. We haven’t had that in our city’s entire history. After we acknowledged this need, I think that the response was also critical. More than just a pool, we regarded this project as the social hub in the town’s center, particularly given that the Rec Department was to be next door. So I’m glad that the City Council rejected the first bids; it was good timing, and certainly a gutsy move to aspire to be a leader in sustainability and opt for electrification. In order for Piedmont to meet its climate goals and have that gradual changeover from gas to electric, we need the participation of all residences. It certainly would have been difficult for Piedmont to encourage residents to do that if the city itself didn’t walk the talk. In short, it’s been critical that we experienced no disconnect in our commitments there, even in the face of greatly inflated costs. Q: What do you hope to change in your own commitments here, day-to-day? A: I want to be more of a bike commuter. While we’re not 100% back to the office post-pandemic, it sure seems that way when you’re driving around in rush hour. articles.text: Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King During her eight years on Piedmont City Council and with the city government, Mayor Teddy Gray King has trailblazed initiatives in the health, education, housing, and environmental sectors. A recent interview reveals her proudest moments and most meaningful contributions. Q: When did your civic involvement in Piedmont first begin? A: I moved to Piedmont from San Francisco in 2003. By 2005 I was on the Park Commission, and then I was on the Recreation Commission. After that I was named to the Environmental Task Force by Abe Friedman, the mayor. Climate Action Plans are commonplace now, but when I was serving on the Task Force, we developed the very first one. Q: Your involvement in government began much earlier. You worked for a member of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors and had a mayoral-appointed Staff photo position working for a San Francisco municipal department. What drew you here? A: I was first drawn to the amazing school district here, as my children were very young at the time. At the same time, I grew up in San Francisco, and I remain a very urban person; I found that Piedmont had this unique blend of close-knit residential communities with all the urban dynamism that you want. Public services are my first love, and I have a very communitarian perspective of government, so I wanted to bring my perspective and previous work experience to this dynamic. I have a deep belief that government changes people’s lives for the better. – Teddy Gray King Teddy Gray King......................1 Turkey Trot . .............................1 Scout Tree Lot opens. ..............1 Letters. .....................................2 Question Man..........................4 Tree Lighting . ..........................5 PHS Dance Concert.................6 FLIP. .........................................9 PPD Blue. .................................9 Turkey Trot Results...............10 Sports....................................12 Museums. ..............................16 Music, Dance. ........................17 PCA events............................19 Movies...................................20 Wine Corner. ..........................23 Seniors. ..................................24 Obituary . ...............................26 Real Estate............................27 Where in the World. ...............32 Q: What was an initial focus of your platform? A: One of the reasons that I first ran was the miscommunication that was happening between the school district and the city a decade ago. I saw many missed opportunities for collaboration, and I was very fortunate that Paul Benoit, our former City Administrator, took it upon himself to work with me and fix that. I’ve also been involved with the City-School Liaison Committee, because there are so many areas where these institutions can come together for the benefit of our citizens. articles.text: A total of 2300 runners, walkers and jogger participated in this year’s Turkey Trot, a 5-kilometer workout on city streets on Thanksgiving morning, November 24. Piedmont’s 21st annual Turkey Trot had repeat winners in both the men’s and women’s divisions. Walter Teitelbaum, a 22-year-old Piedmont alum, who competes for UC Santa Cruz, won for the second year in a row with a time of 16:02 (16 minutes, 2 seconds) on the 5-kilometer course. The top female runner was Jessica Freeman, also a repeat winner and the wife of Crosby Freeman, the all-time race winner. A new mother, she ran solo, while Crosby pushed their son Spencer in a stroller the length of the race. Her winning time was 19:49
articles.title: Teitelbaum, Mrs. Freeman win 2022 Turkey Trot

articles.text: The 55th Annual Piedmont Scout Tree Lot opened to the public bright and early on Saturday morning, November 26, and stayed busy throughout the weekend. The lot, located at Coaches Field next to the city’s Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue, will be open seven days a week until all trees are sold – typically by December 20. Advance orders for Silver Tips, Noble Firs, and Douglas Firs are currently available online at scouttreelot.org. Freshcut wreaths, cedar garlands, and mistletoe are also available. Due to heavy early snows in Northern California and Oregon where many trees are sourced, the supply of Silver Tips is reduced to about 60% of last year’s supply. Silver tips at four-, six-, and seven-foot sizes are still available. The Tree Lot organizers have split the incoming tree supply into more truckloads than usual, in order to allow for the ability to restock. Piedmont Scout Council Executive Director Kate Benson stated that she expects a new supply of tall Noble Firs to arrive today, November 30. With many families traveling during Thanksgiving week, sales Staff photos Piedmont Community Service Crew members volunteering at the Scout Tree lot on opening weekend: Dave Feinberg (left), Ashley Ronen, Ken Li, Samantha Ronen, Ishaia Goldberg-Berman, Bruno Banuelos, Kyra Dang, and Holland Feinberg.
articles.title: Scout Tree Lot sees high sales in opening week

articles.text: Most residents know that the venerable Piedmont Community Pool had exceeded its useful life. It no longer served the needs of our community and was terribly dated. For many years the community reviewed, discussed and debated the issue of the aged community pool. As Mayor and with support of the City Council, I believed it was important that the community make the decision about the future of the Piedmont Community Pool. They made that decision decisively in November 2020 and told the City Council to move forward on a new aquatic facility. Many thought Measure UU could not pass; I believed that if any community could support such a measure, it would be Piedmont. The proposed pool will serve the varied aquatic and recreational needs of the Piedmont Community. As well, it will become a great venue for community and family events. The project fulfills all the requirements that the city and community asked for in a new pool facility. It will provide space for the community to gather and greatly enhanced recreational opportunities. Piedmont USD aquatics will also greatly benefit. The swimming and water polo programs are very successful and continually growing. Student-athletes in the aquatics programs deserve to have a facility that serves the programs as all other sports teams do. Along with the newly renovated Corey Reich Tennis Center, the Piedmont Center for the Arts and the new performance center at Piedmont High School, the Community Pool will be a great addition that enhances our community. The City Council moved quickly on the project. Bonds were issued at low interest rates. Plans were finalized and an outstanding architect and project management team assembled. That’s the good news. The cost environment, however, has been the bad news. Inflation is not news to any of us and it has led to increased costs. These increased costs are not cost overruns: they are the result of cumulative increases in materials and labor that have impacted projects across the state. This has created a funding gap of $2.1 million. This gap represents the amenities and capacity of the pool as currently proposed and those of a scaled-back version; a multi-purpose activity room is an example that would need to be cut. Our community deserves the best facility we can build: Piedmonters have and should expect the best. We need the community’s help to bridge the funding gap. The Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization is actively fundraising. Many of our neighbors have already donated. My family and I have pledged to support this effort. I hope you will consider making a donation to help build a great pool and community facility. It will serve us well for many decades to come. As with Measure UU, I’m confident that Piedmont can get this done. Bob McBain is the former Mayor of Piedmont. 460 Boulevard Way, Oakland, CA 94610 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org REVIEWERS

articles.text: The American Red Cross of Northern California needs special volunteers to deliver blood products to hospitals in local communities and provide the vital link between blood donors and patients who need blood products. Volunteers in the blood transportation specialist position have two important assignments — to transport blood from our blood collection sites to our labs throughout the region for testing and processing and to deliver blood products to hospitals in the area using a Red Cross-owned vehicle. WHAT DOES IT TAKE? These crucial volunteers will be asked to fill two to four shifts in their region each month, and the assignment usually taking about four hours to complete. The need for these transports may be scheduled during the day, in the evening, and on weekends. If you have a valid state driver’s license and at least three years of licensed driving experience, you can choose regular routes, stand-by emergency deliveries or both. This is a great volunteer opportunity for individuals, couples, friends or family members. Volunteers must be able to lift as much as 45 pounds. Training is provided by the Red Cross. Blood transportation specialists can schedule their own hours while helping patients in need. “It only takes a few hours each week to have an impact on someone’s life. When you join us, as a member of our Blood Transportation Team, you’ll serve as a critical link in getting blood donations to those who need them,” said Patty Montmorency, Blood Services Transportation Team Lead. “Training is free, but the blood you deliver is priceless.” Hear firsthand why others For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken. have volunteered in this role (ht t ps://w w w.yout ube.com / watch?v=X-hTsLecWDk): When Red Cross volunteer Mark Merz is asked why he serves as a Blood Transportation Specialist, he says he gets motivated “just knowing that someone is in hospital and might need a transfusion.” Since he is semi-retired, Mark does a shift every other week, picking up boxes of blood donations from blood drives and transporting them to hospitals. What is his impression of the Red Cross since he started volunteering in December 2021? “It’s a top-notch organization,” he says. If helping hospital patients who need blood and blood products during their battle back to health is of interest to you, visit https://www.redcross.org/volunteer/become-a-volunteer/urgentneed-for-volunteers.html for more information.

articles.text: Community support for the Piedmont Community Pool project continues to grow with more families donating to ensure that key elements of the City’s plan for the new Pool Center are included in the project. The Piedmont Recreational Foundation (PRFO) has a target of raising $2.1 million. “We really appreciate the generosity of the Piedmont families who have donated to the Piedmont Community Pool Project Campaign. The success of this campaign is a tribute to our community’s commitment to our athletic and recreational facilities,” said PRFO President, Steve Collins. The funds raised by PRFO will help ensure key elements of the project will be included. This includes funds needed for the competitive-sized pool to be built at a regulation length and depth for water polo play and competitive swimming, a diving well with two diving boards, a scoreboard, timing system, sports lighting, and starting blocks and toe ledges. Funds could also cover three (3) standard-length lap lanes and a shallow area for play and swim lessons in the Activity Pool, and a poolside room for parties and gatherings. Community members who make a donation by December 31 will be included in the PRFO donor list published in local papers and will also be able to take advantage of 2022 tax deductions. Many companies offer end-of-year corporate matching, which can increase donor impact. For those who have not yet made their gift, remember that this is an instance where giving is more than its own reward! Every dollar contributed to the campaign directly benefits our community, student athletes, and our city. PRFO encourages the community to visit their website at PRFO.org to learn more about the project and to make a tax-deductible donation. being clear about why that was irresponsible and why it wouldn’t work. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host its Annual Holiday Luncheon at Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, this Friday, December 2. The cost is $40 for LWV members and $45 for guests. This year’s event will feature guest speaker Shannon Olivieri Hovis, Director of NARAL ProChoice California, who will discuss the role of California in the fight for reproductive rights after the Supreme Court’s recent Roe v. Wade decision. Hovis is a civil rights policy expert with fifteen years of experience in state and local government, classrooms, electoral campaigns, and political advocacy. While at NARAL, Hovis played a critical role on the California Future of Abortion Council, leading a legislative package of 16 bills in 2022, including a constitutional amendment to specifically enshrine the right to abortion and contraception in the California state Constitution. This year has been the worst year for reproductive freedom on record. In June, the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, ending the constitutional right to abortion and allowing states to enforce total bans on abortion. This decision eviscerated federal constitutional protections for abortion access, sending a clear and terrifying message to Americans: Freedom to determine if, when, and how to start or grow a family is now gone for many people across the country. Emboldened Shannon Olivieri Hovis, Director of NARAL Pro-Choice California, is the guest speaker at the Piedmont League of Women Voters Holiday Luncheon. by the Supreme Court decision, anti-choice lawmakers are racing to ban abortion in roughly half of the United States, with more than a dozen states already enforcing total or extreme bans. California is leading the fight to protect and expand access for all people. California has long played an outsized role in ensuring that all people can access the critical abortion care they need. Even before Roe v. Wade was overturned, California was home to one in four healthcare facilities in the country that provide abortion care. Now, as providers and clinics in states across the United States are forced to stop providing care, that percentage is increasing exponentially. This will be the first fundraiser and first in-person event for the League of Women Voters in three years. To sign up for the luncheon, see: lwvpiedmont.org.

articles.text: Starting on Tuesday, January 3, 2023, the City of Piedmont will offer rebates for the removal of existing gas appliances and replacement with certain electric appliances. Rebates will be available for single family and multi-family properties. Eligible low-income applicants may qualify for additional funding. Rebates will only be issued for existing buildings; new construction is not eligible for this program. Rebates can be applied to equipment and installation labor for projects applying for a Building Permit on or after January 3, 2023. Funding is limited and applications will be accepted until funding is exhausted. To learn more about qualification for the program, rebate amounts, and eligible electric appliances, please visit the following link: piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/planning___building/about_building_/rebates_and_incentives.
articles.title: Appliance Electrification Rebate program starts Jan. 3

articles.text: The Curative COVID-19 testing station in the Community Hall parking lot will close permanently this week on Friday, December 3. The kiosk has provided over 11,000 tests in Piedmont since opening in November 2021. Originally open only two days per week, the site expanded to Monday through Friday service in January 2022. Demand has waned in recent months, and Curative has cited low use numbers as the reason for the site’s closure. “I’m proud that we’ve been able to provide this service to our community for over a year at no cost to the public,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Bringing a test site to our civic center last winter – when testing lines stretched around the block throughout the region – gave Piedmont residents a critical tool to navigate last year’s Omicron surge. Since then, the site has supported thousands of community members as they resumed elements of pre-pandemic life, including return to offices, attending large events, and enjoying long-delayed travel plans.” In contrast to when the site opened last year, COVID-19 tests are now widely available through many sources, including: • At-home tests: Home antigen tests are now easy to purchase at pharmacies and online. Additionally, the FDA has extended the expiration dates for many brands of home test kits, so tests you already have may still be good even if the printed expiration date has passed. • Public testing locations: Use the California Department of Public Health interactive map and search tool at myturn. ca.gov/testing to find local testing options. This site provides information about community clinics sponsored by Alameda County Public Health as well as sites run by private testing providers. The tool allows you to filter results to display only free testing sites, or locations that offer both testing and treatment.
articles.title: COVID testing station in Piedmont to close Dec. 3

articles.text: The Piedmont Beautification Foundation and City of Piedmont invite community members to kick off the holiday season with its annual tree lighting ceremony next Wednesday, December 7 at 7:00 p.m. in front of Piedmont Community Hall. This year’s event, called Lights Up!, represents an expansion of the celebration which dates to 1969. Longstanding traditions, including the illumination of the 80-foot redwood tree and a cappella serenades by Piedmont High School’s Troubadours will continue, enhanced by new additions intended to create a more inclusive and welcoming event that celebrates the diversity of Piedmont. In the depths of winter, celebrations centered around light are common to cultures across the globe. Building on this theme, Lights Up! will include new lighting around the park, the lighting of a menorah concurrently with the tree, and an activity hosted by Piedmont Girl Scouts inviting attendees to document how they plan to share their own inner light in the new year. A person named by the Make-A-Wish Foundation will flip the switch to turn on the lights on the redwood tree. Piedmont Scouts will serve warm apple cider and hot cocoa generously provided respectively by Piedmont Grocery and Heafey Baum Group. Chabad Oakland will add to the festivities this year with a latke station. Santa Claus will be available for photos inside Community Hall, and children are invited to write letters to Santa and deposit them in a special mailbox addressed to North Pole. Santa will read every letter. Children with special needs will be able to see Santa starting at 6:00pm. About PBF The Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) obtains, maintains, installs, and removes the colorful LED lights that adorn the illuminated tree each year. Throughout the year, PBF partners with the City to provide research and funding for projects that increase safety, beauty, and function of Piedmont’s extensive and unique public facilities. Community members can support these efforts by donating at piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/donate. A donation to PBF this time of year provides an opportunity to extend warm wishes to friends and neighbors as part of the group’s 54th Annual Holiday Greeting Campaign by way of names of donors being listed in the Post and the Exedra. For questions contact Barbara Love at pbf.piedmont@gmail. com.
articles.title: Tree lighting ceremony, Lights Up!, set for December 7

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department is currently conducting its annual Toys for Tots Drive, with bins at the Fire Department ready for people to drop off new, unwrapped toys through December 9. The donation bins are located in the Fire Department adjacent to City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. The Toys for Tots Drive is organized by the U.S. Marine “The Piedmont Fire Department is proud to partner with the Alameda County Marine Toys for Tots Foundation,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Every year the generosity of the Piedmont community brings hope and joy to children throughout Alameda County.” “The intent of the program is to provide toys for children whose parents wouldn’t be able to afford them otherwise.,” explained Fire Capt. John Fitzpatrick. “Since it takes the Marines several weeks to distribute the gifts, he urged community members to donate by the second week of December. We always do our best to distribute last-minute gifts, “but the sooner, the better.” In a longstanding tradition, each member of the Piedmont City Council will donate a toy to the Toys for Tots program. Their donations will take place at the City Council meeting on Monday, December 5 in City Hall. For more information on donating a toy in Piedmont, please call Fire Captain Jon Fitzpatrick at (510) 420-3030, or email him at jfitzpatrick@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Annual Toys for Tots drive is underway

articles.text: The Piedmont Neighbors & Newcomers Club will hold its annual Holiday Party at the home of Shonnon and Martin Schey on Friday, December 9, at 7 p.m. The event will feature catered appetizers and desserts, wine and beer, and special holiday cocktails. Festive or cocktail attire is appropriate. Shonnon, the President of the PNNC Board for four years, said that the holiday party will be the club’s first large event in three years. Despite a slower time, many new members have joined since 2019. “The best thing about PNNC is there’s something for everyone,” she said. “Many people who joined during the pandemic weren’t Piedmont newcomers at all, but locals interested in a deeper, broader connection with neighbors both new and old.” Concurrently with the re-introduction of larger events like the Holiday Party and their Supper Club (which currently boasts 135 members), Schey hopes to keep holding smaller gatherings like Girls’ and Guys’ Nights Out, children’s play groups, and book club gatherings. The Annual PNNC Holiday Party is open to PNNC members and non-members, but limited to adults only. Those interested may purchase a ticket for $50 until 9 a.m. on Thursday, December 1. and $60 after December 1 at piedmontpnnc.org/events-upcoming/2022/12/9/holiday-party.
articles.title: PNNC Annual Holiday Party on December 9

Jessica Pomey confirmed that as part of the city’s Toys for Tots Drive, red donation bins will be in the Community Hall during the event for people to donate new, unwrapped gifts to children in need. articles.text: All those looking for viable, effective, trusted organizations to support as a part of your holiday season giving are invited to participate in Piedmont Community Church’s annual Alternative Gift Market on Sunday, December 11 from 11 a.m. to 12 noon. For nearly 20 years, Piedmont Church has sponsored this program as an opportunity for people to support local, national and international organizations dedicated to helping people in need. All groups are vetted by the church and chosen to maximize effect and result for all donations. All money received goes directly to the organizations you select. Gifts may be purchased in honor of a friend or relative, allowing donors to notify them with gift descriptions. Contributions are made at a separate station staffed by church volunteers receiving cash, checks, and credit cards. Complimentary coffee and pastries will be served. For an overview of the approximately 20 organizations involved, view the online catalog at PiedmontChurch.org/AGM where gifts can also be purchased. Everyone is encouraged to come in person to the Market. There is a feeling of excitement, a sense of spirituality and a shared joy of giving at this popular event. Visit PiedmontChurch.org/ AGM or contact the church at (510) 547-5700. Piedmont Community Church is located at 400 Highland Avenue.
articles.title: Annual Alternative Gift Market returns to Piedmont Community Church Dec. 11

articles.text: Filmmaker Shakti Butler met with Piedmont and Millennium High School social justice student leaders on November 14 for an insightful discussion on racial equity. Butler is a visionary educator that has produced documentaries and provided professional consulting in equity and anti-racism teachings. Marguerite Vanden Wyngaard, Piedmont School District’s Director of Diversity, set up the meeting. Butler also delivered a speech that evening for Piedmont Education Foundation as part of its Education Speaker Series. Topics during the discussion included the systems of inequity in the world and the roles students can play in creating change. Butler also discussed the work she has done at World Trust, an organization she founded in 1998 which promotes social justice and racial equity. “Getting the chance to meet with Dr. Butler was really a gift to all of us,” said PHS senior Shakti Butler speaks to Piedmont students on November 14. Elena Stevens. “She is so knowledgeable in her field and has a very open style of teaching that allows everyone to interact and participate,”. Invitations went to all of Piedmont High’s 40 clubs and all students at Millennium HS as well. Members of 12 student clubs participated, with a total of 31 students and 8 advisors in attendance. Questions included: How does change happen and how can a new vision arise for our families and communities? “The conversation actually raised more questions for students as we spent the time thinking about and meeting the challenge of transformative change,” said Wyngaard. Students and school staff with Shakti Butler.
articles.title: Racial equity pioneer Shakti Butler meets PHS students

PHS Symphonic and Jazz Bands Wednesday, December 7, 7:00 p.m. Directed by Andria Mullan the bands will perform music ranging from Brahms to Duke Ellington to Trombone Shorty. They will also perform an arrangement of John Phillip Sousa’s “Manhattan Beach March.” Piedmont Middle School Band Thursday, December 8, 7:00 p.m. Four middle school bands – two from 6th grade and one each from 7th and 8th grade – will perform the music of Duke Ellington, Herbie Hancock, and Sonny Rollins, as well as several marches and the popular “Jolly Old St. Nicholas”. A $5 suggested donation for adults will be requested at the door. All students are free.

articles.text: It’s the time of year when gift giving is top of mind, especially for parents searching for toy ideas for their tots. Since play is the foundation for robust learning, many parents are looking for toys that will be fun as well as infused with learning potential. How do we evaluate the quality of a toy in terms of a beneficial learning edge as well as the fun factor? What do we look for in a toy? We can look to the research for a few guiding principles. Regarding quantity, research shows that a bit less is best. For some children, the overload of all the play items can be overwhelming and distracting, causing the child to pick up one toy, drop it and move on. Regarding quality, research would have us remember the value of the simple “open-ended” toy which can be used in multiple ways. For example, hardwood blocks can be for building, or a make-believe car, or pretend food. Conversely, “closed-ended” toys (which consumers tend to gravitate toward when gift giving) tend to have a “right way” to play, and include such toys as a cash register, Mr. Potato Head, or Legos. Beyond these general principles of quantity and quality, what should be our toy buying guide? To foster problem solving, look to toys such as blocks, instruments or simple board games (or consider keys and containers with lids which you do not have to purchase). To tap into the child’s experimental tendencies, consider toys such as a sand or water table (or look to flashlights, colanders, or a whisk to use in the bath which you do not have to purchase). To encourage communication, doll houses and books are excellent choices (or introduce dress up or rhyming games for similar effects without a price tag). Cognitive development can be fun with toy items such as matching/memory and sorting picture cards, but can also be enjoyed with sorting of silverware, clothing or small household items using a muffin tin for a non-retail option. Creative kids will enjoy gifts of silly putty, paint or other art supplies (tape, paper towel rolls, paper plates and cotton balls can also be creative fun without additional purchases). Motor development can be enhanced with gifts such as puzzles, balls and shape sorters. And don’t forget that the same fun and developmental stimulation can be had with common kitchen items such as measuring cups, mixing bowls, plastic cups, etc. Regarding social/emotional based toys, dolls and puppets can’t be beat, and a mirror can do the trick for a no purchase option. Collaborative toys are always a good idea, such as a construction set or play kitchen. If you want to get the same effect without the specific toy purchase, the laundry basket, sheets and pillows can become a wonderful collaborative fort building experience. Have a wonderful gift-giving season. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

pages.text: Wednesday, November 30, 2022 7 Racial equity pioneer Shakti Butler meets PHS students By Jay Russell Filmmaker Shakti Butler met with Piedmont and Millennium High School social justice student leaders on November 14 for an insightful discussion on racial equity. Butler is a visionary educator that has produced documentaries and provided professional consulting in equity and anti-racism teachings. Marguerite Vanden Wyngaard, Piedmont School District’s Director of Diversity, set up the meeting. Butler also delivered a speech that evening for Piedmont Education Foundation as part of its Education Speaker Series. Topics during the discussion included the systems of inequity in the world and the roles students can play in creating change. Butler also discussed the work she has done at World Trust, an organization she founded in 1998 which promotes social justice and racial equity. “Getting the chance to meet with Dr. Butler was really a gift to all of us,” said PHS senior Shakti Butler speaks to Piedmont students on November 14. Elena Stevens. “She is so knowledgeable in her field and has a very open style of teaching that allows everyone to interact and participate,”. Invitations went to all of Piedmont High’s 40 clubs and all students at Millennium HS as well. Members of 12 student clubs participated, with a total of 31 students and 8 advisors in attendance. Questions included: How does change happen and how can a new vision arise for our families and communities? “The conversation actually raised more questions for students as we spent the time thinking about and meeting the challenge of transformative change,” said Wyngaard. pages.text: 8 Wednesday, November 30, 2022 Scout Tree Lot Continued from page 1 were slightly less than last year’s record numbers. On the opening weekend the Lot generated $50,000 in sales, with an additional $30,000 in online sales the month before the Lot’s opening. The Scout Council anticipates sales to be “about $6,000 to $10,000 a day on weekdays Staff Photos A sign explains the weatherrelated shortage of Silver Tip trees this year. and $20,000 to $25,000 a day on weekends — less, of course, if the weather is bad,” said Benson. In recent years, the Scouts have sold about 1,800 trees annually — a grand testament to the popularity of the Lot, given that there are only about 4,000 houses in Piedmont. Benson affirmed that the Scouts have been seeing similar trends so far this year. Proceeds from the lot comprise about 15% of the Council’s annual budget, which supports nearly 1,000 Piedmont children involved in Scouts, Cub Scouts, Explorers, and Venturers, including the High Adventure and Community Service crews. Since its earliest days in the Corpus Christi parking lot in the late ‘60s, the Scout Tree Lot has been what Benson called “an amazing opportunity for our Scouting family to connect with the larger Piedmont community.” This year, as in past years, the Tap Dancing Christmas Trees Tree Lot manager Tom Smegal (right) with Matt Sprague, a Troop 11 Eagle Scout and recent graduate working at the lot this year to oversee the use of the chainsaw. Siow Fang Tan and a Cub Scout help a customer and his children at the Tree Lot. Piedmont BSA Council board members Anne Hauss Davies and Ken Li help out as cashiers on Sunday during the Tree Lot’s opening weekend. A Scout volunteer carries a tree to the check-out stand at the Tree Lot. A buyer loads a newly purchased tree onto the top of his car. A Scout ties a tree onto the car of a customer at the Tree Lot. Cole Venner helps set up the stand of wreaths. returned to the Lot on opening day. The Tree Lot Committee begins planning and preparing for the operation as early as June, as members begin preparing permits, hiring drivers, organizing Troop participation, gathering equipment, setting up lighting, working on marketing, training board members to cashier, and setting up Wi-Fi. The Lot preparations are accomplished by hundreds of Scouts and volunteers, with many of the adults involved being Scout veterans themselves. “That’s the best part of it,” said Benson – “all of the older generations which take part in this program alongside the younger kids and newer recruits.” Benson has been the Executive Director of Piedmont Scouts for two years and has been with the national Scouting program for 20 years. “There’s nothing like the experience of smelling the freshcut trees, seeing the kids giving back – it’s tangible, it’s real, and it’s been part of this community for decades,” Benson added. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. articles.text: Piedmont opened its season with a strong 73-35 victory over Marin Catholic. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team opened its season in a big way, bashing Marin Catholic 73-35 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Saturday, November 26. The victory comes against a Marin Catholic side that went 23-10 last season, advancing to the NCS Finals, and reaching the second round of the CIF State Tournament. The Wildcats lost just two seniors from last year’s team. “I thought we did pretty well with the game plan. The coaching staff had a great scouting report on Marin Catholic,” said assistant coach Shamaree Worley who was filling in for coach Ben Spencer out due to illness. “The kids executed well on what we wanted them to do. Our defense was pretty solid; we held them for nearly two points for an entire quarter. We moved well offensively as well, and nearly our entire roster scored,” said. Senior A.J. Harris led the way with 26 points and 10 rebounds, and junior Brit Burden had 19 points and nine rebounds. “Our leaders A.J. and Brit showed up big time with scoring, getting rebounds, and making sure the team is upbeat,” said Worley. Burden will be a major part of this year’s team after playing a smaller role last season. The Piedmont coaching staff has often praised Burden for his development over the offseason and has long expected him to become a focal point as their big man. “I believe that Brit can be a 20-10 guy for us in points and rebounds. We’re expecting a lot from him because we know what we’re getting from A.J. We need that second-punch coming from him. He’s a junior now and he already has next-level expectations of himself.” A.J. Harris scored 26 points and had 10 rebounds. Brit Burden had 19 points and pulled down nine rebounds. Staff Photos Piedmont led 21-10 by the end of the first quarter and 36-23 at halftime. From there, the Highlanders allowed just 12 second-half points by way of six points conceded in both the third and fourth quarters. PHS scored 22 points in the third to lead 58-29 by halftime and 15 in the fourth to win it 73-35. Piedmont had 10 of its 11 players score points. Worley reflected on Piedmont’s lock-down defense in the second half. “I thought our defense and our communication was great. I think we have the ability to have any player guard anyone at any position,” said Worley. It was an impressive performance by sophomore guard and first-year varsity starter Raji Silverberg, who scored 10 points with five assists and five steals. “It’s his first time playing point guard. We’re expecting good things from him but also hope he can limit those mistakes that typically come from younger players like sophomores. I think he’s going to be a great player coming up, he’s strong defensively and gets in the passing lanes,” said Worley. Final scorers include: Harris with 26 points and 10 boards. Burden had 19 points and nine rebounds. Theo Evans made a 3-pointer, while Matthew Riordan, Alex Anderson, Teagan Haddawy, Arjun Bornstein, Matteo Costa, and Declan Linnane had two points. Tuesday at Bellarmine Piedmont traveled to Bellarmine Prep in San Jose on Tuesday, November 29. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0) will host its 32nd annual PHS Invitational Varsity Tournament from Thursday through Saturday, December 1-3. It opens against Richmond on Thursday at 8:30 p.m. Northgate, which were last year’s NCS Open Division semifinalists. Windsor will play Hamilton HS from Los Angeles. Acalanes takes on Archie Williams, which also competes in Division 3 against Piedmont and made last year’s semifinals.

articles.text: Staff Photo Skylar Best placed 64th place at the State meet and was the 11th fastest freshman in the state. Piedmont High freshman Skylar Best was the lone qualifier from the cross-country team to qualify for the CIF State Championship on Saturday, November 26, at Woodward Park in Fresno. She finished 64th out of 201 runners with a time of 19:56.2, and was the 11th fastest freshman in the state. “I’m really proud to even make it there as a freshman. The competition was really tough but that inspires me to improve and train hard to get back there next year. It definitely meant a lot to me personally to race there. The environment was amazing and I just had a great time,” said Best. Piedmont has now sent at least one runner to the prestigious event for 34 consecutive years. It was just Best’s second time competing on a 5K course, eclipsing her previous best of 22:14.1 at a league meet at Oyster Bay in San Leandro on October 19. “This was a 5K instead of a three-mile that we usually raced this season,” explained Best. “It felt like a great end to the season. I had a really fast first mile and wanted to try and stay in the front area of the pack. The course had a lot of rolling hills and two steep hills.” they were freshmen, including Sophia Zalewski (2016, 20:06.3) and Ellie Black, (2018, 20:37.7). Piedmont’s varsity team should have a large slate of returners in 2023 after featuring junior Jamie Schwarz, sophomores Ella Yasar and Caroline Taylor, and some standout freshmen like Cora Chun, Elia Kwong, Quincy Antaya, Amina Green, and, of course, Best. Her time at Woodward Park was better than several previous star runners from Piedmont when Skylar Best, the only Piedmont cross-country runner to qualify for the State meet, was consistently the lead runner for the girls’ team throughout the season. Photo courtesy of NCS Skylar Best (second from right) shown after qualifying for the State Meet at the North Coast Section Championship.

articles.text: Photos by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team opened the season with a 3-2 loss to North Coast Section foe Miramonte. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team began its season with a 3-2 loss to Miramonte at Witter Field on Monday, November 28. The Highlanders were still without several players with the club soccer season not over. “We were still missing a few players but that’s usually the case at this time of the season with players finishing the club season and doing showcases,” said coach Dan Chubbock. Still the Highlanders played well against the Matadors and held the lead twice before halftime when the score was tied at 2-2. Miramonte scored the eventual game-winner around 10 minutes into the second half. The Matadors, notably, competes in Division 3 of North Coast Section while Piedmont plays one division below them. “We actually played well in the second half but they managed to get the goal and we just couldn’t quite find the finishing touch,” said Chubbock. Piedmont’s Michaela Bini, who also is a member of the tennis team, struck first for the Highlanders just a few minutes into the start of the game on an assist from freshman Miranda Liu. However, Miramonte didn’t take long to tie the game, requiring another few minutes to make it 1-1 in the first 10 minutes of action. Later on in the first half, Liu scored the first goal of her high school career on a long ball over the defenders from Charlotte Davies. However, Miramonte closed the action with a goal from a corner where the corner-taker sent her ball in for a goal. Ten minutes into the second half, Miramonte scored the go-ahead goal after another corner kick. Piedmont was without goalkeeper Morgan Hunt due to illness and brought up Clio Salzer from the junior varsity team. Piedmont had some scoring chances in the remaining time of the second half. Liu had a shot that just trailed wide after receiving a pass from Bini, while Cameron Lorin also had an opportunity in the box in the late minutes before she nearly drew a penalty, but the referee didn’t award the spot kick. Chubbock wants the team to focus on keeping the tempo high and moving the ball with more acceleration in advance of the league opener at Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, December 7. “We have to keep up the temp and move the ball a little bit quicker. We can also move the ball a little bit longer and just take our chances when they are there,” said Chubbock. NEXT UP Piedmont (0-1) plays at Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland on Wednesday, December 7 at 6:00 p.m. Michaela Bini (left) celebrates with Miranda Liu after the two connected for a goal and assist. Miranda Liu (6) scored and had an assist in her Piedmont debut.

Ten minutes into the second half, Miramonte scored the go-ahead goal after another corner kick. Piedmont was without goalkeeper Morgan Hunt due to illness and brought up Clio Salzer from the junior varsity team. Piedmont had some scoring chances in the remaining time of the second half. Liu had a shot that just trailed wide after receiving a pass from Bini, while Cameron Lorin also had an opportunity in the box in the late minutes before she nearly drew a penalty, but the referee didn’t award the spot kick. Chubbock wants the team to focus on keeping the tempo high and moving the ball with more acceleration in advance of the league opener at Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, December 7. “We have to keep up the temp and move the ball a little bit quicker. We can also move the ball a little bit longer and just take our chances when they are there,” said Chubbock. articles.text: The 2022 World Cup is shaping up with its usual upsets and Cinderella tales. The Group stage wraps up this week with Groups A and B officially settled. The U.S. fought down to the wire against Iran to overtake them 1-0 on Tuesday to send the Stars and Stripes onto the Round of 16. After posting ties in its first two games, it marked the team’s first win. It tied Wales 1-1 in the Cup opener on November 21, and then did well to hold tournament favorite England to a scoreless draw last Friday. Here’s a recap of how the World Cup is shaping up. Group B: No. 5 England (7 points, clinched), No. 16 USA (5 points, clinched), No. 20 Iran (3 points), No. 19 Wales (1 point) The Americans got the job done. The stress from watching may have taken some years off of our lives, but they are through to the Round of 16. Christian Pulisic scored the only goal – arguably the most important goal of his U.S. career º in the 38th minute against Iran, but had to leave the game at halftime after suffering an abdominal injury The U.S. sat deeper in the latter 45 minutes but did well to not concede any goals. They allowed just one shot on target throughout the night. Iran argued for a penalty in the waning minutes of second-half stoppage time, but the ref ruled Iranian forward Mehdi Taremi went down too easily (called a flop). Looking ahead, the Americans are now set to face No. 8 ranked Netherlands. The two sides have played five times, with the Dutchmen dominating the series at 4-0- 1. They. haven’t faced each other since June 2015, where Holland won a friendly 4-3. The Netherlands will be tough with one of the more balanced rosters in the tournament, led by a stout defense with Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk and Bayern’s Matthijs de Ligt. For what it’s worth, I picked the Dutch making the Quarterfinals, but I also had the U.S. not getting out of the group. Group A: No. 8 Netherlands (7 points, clinched), No. 18 Senegal (6 points, clinched), No. 44 Ecuador (4 points), No. 50 Qatar (0 points) The Dutch opened with a 2-0 win over Senegal, tied 1-1 with Ecuador, and beat Qatar 2-0 to solidify the top spot. Senegal, meanwhile, overtook Ecuador on Tuesday for the second spot with a big 2-1 win. It marks the first time the Senegalese reach the Round of 16 since 2002 when they made the quarterfinals. Netherlands faces the U.S. on December 3 at 6:00 a.m., while Senegal will be the underdogs against England the following day at 11:00 a.m. Group C: No. 26 Poland (4 points), No. 3 Argentina (3 points), No. 51 Saudi Arabia (3 points), No. 13 Mexico (1 points) Today’s Group C matches have both qualification spots up for grabs with Poland facing Argentina and Saudi Arabia squaring off with Mexico. Argentina managed to keep itself in the race and avoided a meltdown with a 2-nil win over Mexico. Right now, Poland holds the top spot by one point and one-goal in differential. Although El Tri of Mexico sits Photo courtesy of ABC13 The U.S. Men’s cocker team is through to the next round thanks to Christian Pulisic’s goal in a 1-0 win over Iran. in last with a single point, they are technically not dead in the water just yet. Poland holds 1C with a win over Argentina or with a tie if Saudi Arabia loses to Mexico. Poland would be out of the tournament with a loss and Saudi Arabia win. Argentina guarantees a spot by defeating Poland and wins the group with a loss or tie from Saudi Arabia. If the Arabian Falcons and Argentina wins and are tied at six points each, the tiebreaker would be goal differential—which Argentina leads by two goals. Should the two become tied in goal differential, the tiebreaker becomes goals scored and then head-to-head if the goal tally is also tied. Mexico must beat Saudi Arabia to give itself a chance and a win by four or more goals guarantees a spot. If Mexico wins and Argentina loses, El Tri finishes second. If Argentina ties against Poland, Mexico would need to win by three goals to qualify. If Mexico wins by four or more goals, they would finish second. take 2E with a win and Japan losing to Spain. If Japan ties, Germany needs a multi-goal win to finish ahead of Japan on goal differential. Group F: No. 12 Croatia (4 points), No. 22 Morocco (4 points), No. 2 Belgium (3 points), No. 41 Canada (0 points) Group F also plays on Thursday with Croatia, Morocco and Belgium in contention, and in that order. The Moroccans stunned top-ranked Belgium 2-0 on Sunday, November 27, while Croatia knocked out Canada from contention 4-1 that same day. Belgium, which I had making the semifinals, is looking like their life is in doubt against a tough Croatian side, with Morocco just needing to get the job done versus Canada. A tie won’t be enough for Belgium to make it out of the group, but they can win the group with a win and a Morocco loss or tie. Group D: No. 4 France (6 points, clinched), No. 38 Australia (3 points), No. 10 Denmark (1 point), No. 35 Tunisia (1 point) France is perhaps in the best form of the tournament at 2-0 with a 4-1 win over Australia to open and a strong 2-1 defeat of Denmark. PSG star Kylian Mbappe is a real difference maker, once again, with three goals—two of which coming against the Danes. Already clinched France is set to close the tournament today against Tunisia and is looking like a clear favorite for the Coupe du Monde. Today, Denmark could fight its way to the Round of 16 by defeating Australia, where the Socceroos just require a tie to qualify. Group E: No. 7 Spain (4 points), No. 24 Japan (3 points), No. 31 Costa Rica (3 points), No. 11 Germany (1 points) Thursday’s slate of Group E games include Spain taking on Japan and Germany versus Costa Rica, with each qualification spot available for all four teams. Spain can qualify by tying Japan and can earn 1E with win, or a tie would still earn the top spot with a Costa Rica loss or draw to Germany. Japan can win the group by defeating Spain and will automatically qualify regardless of Costa Rica’s results based on goal differential, where the Japanese holds a six-goal advantage. Germany is on the verge of being knocked out in the group stage for the second consecutive World Cup, but they can still fight from death with a victory against Costa Rica at the bare minimum. The Germans Group G: No. 1 Brazil (6 points, clinched), No. 15 Switzerland (3 points), No. 43 Cameroon (1 point), No. 21 Serbia (1 point) Brazil was the first team to clinch a spot into the next round after beating Switzerland 1-0 on Monday. The second qualification spot will likely come down to Switzerland against Serbia on Friday at 11:00 a.m. with Cameroon taking on the Canaries of Brazil. A tie won’t do it for Serbia, who I had as a potential that that could surprise its way to the quarterfinals. Serbia must win to overtake Switzerland for the second spot, they’ll need a peak performance from Fulham striker Aleksandar Mitrović and require Juventus forward Dusan Vlahović to quickly recover from his injury. Group H: No. 9 Portugal (6 points, clinched), No. 61 Ghana (3 points), No. 28 South Korea (1 point), No. 14 Uruguay (1 point) Portugal has already clinched its spot to the next round and will face South Korea, which needs a win to stay alive, on Friday at 7:00 a.m. The second spot is still up for grabs with Ghana and Uruguay competing at 11:00 a.m., and things can certainly get messy. If Ghana wins, they are in. If they draw and South Korea draws or loses, they finish second. If Ghana draws and South Korea wins by one goal, the two sides will be equal on goal differential and the winner will be determined by goals scored— which Ghana currently leads 5-2. If South Korea wins by two or more goals, South Korea will move to second. If Uruguay wins, they finish second if South Korea draws or loses. Uruguay will be the favorite against Ghana, but have been another disappointment after walking in as the favorite to earn 2H.

articles.text: Competing at the 2022 Division 3 NCAA Championships at the Forest Akers Golf Course in Lansing, Michigan on November 19 were two former standout runners at Piedmont High. Class of 2020 Sophia Zalewski competed with Carnegie Mellon while UC Santa Cruz’s Walter Teitelbaum, PHS Class of 2018, also ran in the event. For Zalewski, her team finished 30th of 32 and she placed 253 of 292 with a time of 24:39.1. Prior to the championship meet, the Tartans competed in the NCAA Mid-Atlantic Regional Championship and finished second of five schools. There, Zalewski finished 42nd of 209 runners with a time of 23:19.9 on the 6K course. She graduated from Piedmont High in 2020 as the Posts Athlete of the Year, was the school Valedictorian, and PHS’ Outstanding Senior Athlete. Walter Teitelbaum helped UC Santa Cruz to finish 19th of 32 schools and individually was 209th of 292 runners with a time at the Nationals of 26:44.5 on the 8K course. His college team placed 3rd at the NCAA West Regional Championship on November 12. Teitelbaum later returned home to compete in the annual Turkey Trot on Thanksgiving morning, winning the 5K race for the second-consecutive year with a time of 16:02. Former PHS running stars Walter Teitelbaum (left) and Sophia Zalewski at the NCAA cross-country championship in Lansing, Michigan, with two more former Highlanders and Athlete of the Year winners, Reece Proctor and Jack Stein.

articles.text: Photo by Drew Altizer Hung Liu speaks at the opening of a retrospective art exhibit honoring her work. De Young Museum celebrates the legacy of Hung Liu with Golden Gate, an exhibition displayed in the museum’s Wilsey Court through January 8. Liu was one of the most important Chinese-born artists working in the United States, and specifically in Oakland. This installation reimagines some of her most iconic paintings through her own personal history as a Chinese-born artist, placing herself among the migrants who arrived in California by both land and sea. The artist died suddenly in August 2021, prompting the museum to extend the exhibition’s closing date to 2023. “Hung Liu was such a vibrant and vital part of the art world in the Bay Area and beyond,” said museum curator Jana Keegan. “Her art practice focused on recovering the stories of people who have been often forgotten in traditional historical narratives. The legacy and wonderful oeuvre she leaves behind will ensure that she too will always be remembered.” Liu tells the story of migration and displacement throughout the United States in her artwork. One of her most iconic paintings, Resident Alien, is the focal point of the exhibition. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/ hung-liu.
articles.title: Hung Liu: Golden Gate exhibition leaves de Young on January 8

articles.text: The annual holiday artisan market returns to Asian Art Museum in San Francisco this Sunday, December 4, featuring a dozen artists this year. The event is free and open to all, and no museum admission is required. The market is held in the lobby of the museum on the main floor. Artists display their one-of-a-kind, custom-made items for purchase for early holiday shopping. Items will include jewelry, ceramics, books, specialty food products, ornaments, cards, fashion, accessories, and gifts for little ones. The market will be operational from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. To learn more, visit https://calendar. asianart.org/event/annual-holiday-artisan-market/. Liu was one of the most important Chinese-born artists working in the United States, and specifically in Oakland. This installation reimagines some of her most iconic paintings through her own personal history as a Chinese-born artist, placing herself among the migrants who arrived in California by both land and sea. The artist died suddenly in August 2021, prompting the museum to extend the exhibition’s closing date to 2023. “Hung Liu was such a vibrant and vital part of the art world in the Bay Area and beyond,” said museum curator Jana Keegan. “Her art practice focused on recovering the stories of people who have been often forgotten in traditional historical narratives. The legacy and wonderful oeuvre she leaves behind will ensure that she too will always be remembered.” Liu tells the story of migration and displacement throughout the United States in her artwork. One of her most iconic paintings, Resident Alien, is the focal point of the exhibition. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/ hung-liu. articles.text: Brass concert, Holiday Blast, this Sunday at 4 p.m. Berkeley Symphony will ring in this holiday season with Holiday Blast, where the Berkeley Symphony Brass Quintet will perform festive favorites at Piedmont Community Hall on Sunday, December 4, at 4 p.m. Holiday Blast is part of the chamber music series in Piedmont and will feature pieces from J.S. Bach to Duke Ellington. Guests are invited to join a free outdoor reception following the concert, where they can enjoy sweet and savory treats and libations, including hot seasonal beverages. Tickets are $35 and are available online at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the box office at (510) 841-2800. The concert celebrates the 10th anniversary of its Chamber Series, and will honor Gray Cathrall, a founding board member of the Piedmont Center for the Arts and editor of the Piedmont Post. Cathrall has been integral to the partnership between Berkeley Symphony. “Ten years ago, Gray came to us with a bold idea to produce a Berkeley Symphony chamber music series at the Piedmont Center for the Arts,” said René Mandel, Artistic Director of Berkeley Symphony. “We are grateful to our eclectic, enthusiastic, and devoted audiences at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. We marvel at the wonderful works of art that grace its walls and enhance our performances. We are profoundly grateful to Gray for his unwavering support and service to this jewel of a series and to the entire East Bay community.” Performing music will be the Berkeley Symphony Brass Quintet, John Pearson (Trumpet), Scott Macomber (Trumpet), Meredith Brown (Horn), Tom Hornig (Tenor Trombone), and Peter Wahrhaftig (Tuba). The big brass sound of the quintet will play a lively program that features J.S. Bach’s “My Spirit Be Joyful,” Music from the Royal Fireworks by G.F. Handel, Morley Calvert’s Suite from “Monteregian Hills,” a selection by Duke Ellington, including “Cottontail Capers,” “Sophisticated Lady,” “It Don’t Mean a Thing if it Ain’t Got That Swing,” and “Boy Meets Horn.”

articles.text: Orchestra to perform Duke Ellington’s Nutcracker Suite The Marcus Shelby Orchestra will perform Duke Ellington’s Nutcracker Suite at SF Jazz this Friday, December 2. A bass player, composer, and arranger, Shelby modeled his Orchestra after Duke Ellington’s and cites the jazz luminary as an inspiration for him musically. Shelby is best-known for his major works for jazz orchestra titled Port Chicago, Harriet Tubman, Soul of the Movement: Meditations on Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., and Beyond the Blues: A Prison Oratorio. He has served as Artist in Residence at Yerba Buena Gardens Festival in San Francisco and Composer in Residence at Intersection for Arts. He Marcus Shelby was appointed to the San Francisco Arts Commission in 2013. He and his orchestra are regular performers at San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/marcus-shelby-orchestra-ellingtons-nutcracker2/

Local artist Michael Stehr will open his newest exhibition, entitled “Lost in the Shadows,” at Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, December 3, at 11:30 a.m. The exhibit includes 42 new paintings, and 80 total works of art, and will be on display through December 18. Stehr will use some of his new paintings to explore the power of shadow in painting. While it is light that often contributes animation and luminosity to a composition, it is the absence of this light, shadow, that makes the presence of that light much more tangible. Without light, there cannot be shadow. But without shadow, the effect of light is greatly mitigated. Indeed, the two must work hand in hand, for it is the contrasts between bright and dark values, light and shadow, that do much to provide visual interest to a painting. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays December 3-4, 10-11, and 17-18. Masks and proof of vaccination are required at the Center.

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s holiday favorite, Nutcracker, premieres on Thursday, December 8, at the War Memorial Opera House. The ballet will be performed through December 27. This special production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks like the Painted Ladies by Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s 90-year history. San Francisco Ballet performs the production every year, with a kaleidoscope of 150 dancers telling the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco. San Francisco Symphony will perform the familiar score of Tchaikovsky. A diverse array of instruments are used by the Symphony, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani – all played by only three musicians. Scenic design is by Michael Yeargan; costume design is by Martin Pakledinaz; lighting design is by James F. Ingalls, and projection design by Wendall K. Harrington. The ballet is especially appropriate for children aged five and older. No children under age three will be permitted. The performance Nutcracker runs two hours with one intermission. Tickets are selling quickly for performances on Christmas Eve, December 24. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker-dec-2022/. Photo by Erik Tomasson Helgi Tomasson’s production of Nutcracker begins on December 8 at the War Memorial Opera House.
articles.title: SF Ballet’s iconic Nutcracker begins Dec. 8

articles.text: Oakland Ballet will present three performances of Graham Lustig’s The Nutcracker at the Paramount Theater the weekend of December 17-18. Tickets are now available for both performances. Oakland Ballet dancers will bring Artistic Director Lustig’s classic holiday ensemble to life with magnificent scenery and costumes. The Oakland Symphony and Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will deliver Tchaikovsky’s magnificent score. Running time is approximately two hours including an intermission. Doors open one hour before showtime. An encore reception will take place following performances at the Paramount Theatre. Performances will be at 1 p.m. on Saturday, December 17, and at 1 p.m. and 5 p.m. on Sunday, December 18. Tickets are available online at https://oaklandballet.org/performances-events/graham-lustigs-the-nutcracker/. Oakland Ballet will present the iconic ballet The Nutcracker on December 17 and 18.

articles.text: Turkey… The very word conjures up a multitude of images. It could be fun activities like the Turkey Trot in Piedmont on Thanksgiving morning. At the opposite end of the spectrum, it is insulting to be called a turkey. But the bird itself is certainly beautiful and conjures up some beautiful thoughts. Some people even consider that its beauty should make it the national bird of America. You may remember that the turkey was the origin of a great national debate. When our Founding Fathers were discussing what bird should be the national symbol, John Adams wanted it to be the eagle. Thomas Jefferson wanted the dove. Benjamin Franklin proposed the turkey and gave many good reasons. The eagle won. However, the turkey is a much more important bird. Please read on. Thanksgiving is over, and the race to the end of the year has begun. I have some thoughts looking back, and also some thoughts looking to the future. A renowned chef in San Francisco gave me his recipe for turkey: Separate the skin from the breast and the leg. Use your favorite seasonings and then pour enough red wine to fill the cavity. Roast and serve. Let’s hope there is quite a bit of turkey left over. Save all the bones and make a soup or broth. Be sure to cook over a low flame or in the oven at about 225 degrees. articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s production of Guiseppe Verdi’s masterpiece La Traviata ends this Sunday, December 3. Tickets are still available for the closing performance. Music Director Eun Sun Kim leads the Opera Orchestra and chorus in Shawna Lucey’s production of the three-act production. South African-born Pretty Yende sings the lead role as Violetta Valéry. Yende has appeared in the same role in the Vienna State Opera, Naples’ Teatro di San Carlo, Royal Opera, Paris Opera productions. Jonathan Tetelman is cast in the lead male role as Alfredo Germont, a young bourgeois from a provincial family who admires Violetta from afar. “Verdi’s masterpiece about one of the most incredible women in history lives at the intersection of sex and money,” said Director Shawna Lucey. “Marie Duplessis, or Violetta as she is known in the opera, through her own ingenuity and tenacity has become Paris’ most famous courtesan.” The opera is set to an Italian libretto by Francesco Piave and is based on the famous play by Alexandre Dumas. The opera us three hours with two intermissions. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfopera.com/operas/ la-traviata/. Jonathan Tetelman and Pretty Yende star in San Francisco Opera’s current production of La Traviata.
articles.title: SF Opera’s La Traviata ends this Sunday, December 3

pages.text: Wednesday, November 30, 2022 19 The Musical Gourmet that comes to mind. It seems that The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Thomas Jefferson did not concoct the recipe. There are as many recipes for turkey a la king as there were for King Louis of France. Here is an easy one: this will serve two diners. To serve four, just double the recipe. Dice half an onion and one clove of garlic and put into a sauté pan to caramelize along with a little oil, a little salt and white pepper. Finally chop some celery and add it to the pan. Add a handful of chopped mushrooms and continue to cook. Cover this with about 8 ounces of your turkey soup and 2 tablespoons of sour cream and about 4 tablespoons of cream sherry. Take two handfuls of chopped leftover turkey and put in the pan and just warm it. You can even add some peas if you like. This mixture can be served with polenta, rice or on top of toast. You can use this exact same recipe to make a turkey pot pie. All you have to do is line an oven-proof dish with polenta, add your turkey mixture, and then top with the remaining polenta. Bake in the oven at 425° for about 40 minutes. Nothing could be easier or more beautiful. If you don’t want to go to this effort, you can always put some barbecue sauce on your turkey and serve it with mashed potatoes. Some Thanksgiving music, please maestro There isn’t a lot of music associated with Thanksgiving. One of the songs that I particularly like is “Bless this house” when sung by the great opera singers of the past. For some strange reason composers didn’t write music about turkeys, and they certainly missed a wonderful opportunity. Bon appetite. Seal the room and wait. But Hugh is far too curious and the idea of finding life on Mars is compelling, bordering on the miraculous. articles.text: Frederich Nietzche once wrote, “…if you gaze long enough into the abyss, the abyss will gaze into you.” As is profoundly depicted in the film 12 Years a Slave, released in 2013. Slavery, in all its malignant cruelty, is that abyss. The institution of slavery was an embedded pathology that gripped our nation for more than a century, initially made manifest in the plantations of the South and buttressed by the virulent prejudice and discrimination that rippled through antebellum and post-antebellum America. The word “holocaust” has been reserved to depict the atrocities of the concentration camps of Germany during World War II, crafted from the darkest parts of the human heart. Slavery is viewed through a different prism, though it too is a nightmare that was abhorrent in the extreme, with human beings reduced to mere chattel. When viewed across history it also seems incomprehensible. 12 Years a Slave is a powerful and unyielding view of one man’s journey into the heart of the South in the year 1841. His name was Solomon Northrup (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a freeman, prosperous, and living in Saratoga, N.Y., with his wife and two children. Kidnapped, he awakens one morning in a dark room, in chains, and soon finds himself sold and resold, ending up on a Louisiana plantation. His master, Edwin Epps (Michael Fassbender), is a ruthless and sadistic slave owner, so unhinged that he is blind to his own depravity, and the depravity of his wife (Sarah Paulson), who urges him to shred the backs of the less productive slaves while knowing that her husband rapes the young women. Solomon soon understands that he has descended into one of the circles of hell and he bears witness to the personal torment of the slaves with whom he shares his existence. It is an existence that is, in every respect, filled with an acute and daily privation that seems unendurable. He faces his new life in the context of the life from which he was snatched. He was a musician, educated, with a family that filled his world and now floods his memories. The power of 12 Years a Slave resides in its unremitting honesty. There are no benevolent owners, not even Master Ford (Benedict Cumberbatch), who, while humane, still views his slaves as forced free labor and not as people. In one wrenching scene he buys a young black woman at auction, but not her two children. In another harrowing scene, Solomon is hung by the neck by an overseer, his toes barely touching the ground, and though Ford eventually cuts him down, he is incapable of viewing that moment for what it is: heinous and monstrous. Like all those involved in slavery, Epps and Ford were incapable of viewing the pain it exacted, or seeing it as an evil of such magnitude that it shriveled the souls of those who perpetuated it and it laid ruin to those who lost more than their freedom. That is what 12 Years a Slave conveys, absent stereotypes and unnecessary melodrama. This film is a spare narrative, based on the story written by Solomon Northrup, a memoir that has stood the test of time and finally has found its way, remarkably, to the screen. 12 Years a Slave. Directed by Steve McQueen. Starring Chiwetel Ejiofor, Michael Fassbender, Benedict Cumberbatch. 2 hrs,, 14 min. Rated R. Released in 2013, Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ HBO MAX.
articles.title: 12 Years a Slave – true story of grim reminder of America’s past

articles.text: The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society I realize is a mouthful as titles go, but it is a film worth finding, charming and an old-fashioned drama with a superb ensemble cast, led by Lily James as Juliet Ashton and Michael Huisman portraying Dawsey Adams. Based on the best-selling novel by Mary Shafer and Annie Barrows, the story opens in London in 1946, and World War II has just ended. Reminders of the damage to the city by German blitzes are seen on street after street; many buildings are mere scorched shells. Yet the Brits are determined to carry on, and much relieved that they have prevailed. Juliet, a novelist who lost her parents in a bombing raid, has just published a book titled Izzy Bickerstaff Goes to War. With the encouragement of her editor, Sidney Stark (Matthew Goode), she is giving readings at small bookshops. After one such appearance she is asked by Sidney to write an essay for the London Times about the importance of reading. It captures her interest, however she wonders where to begin. Simultaneously she receives a letter from Dawsey, a farmer living on Guernsey Island. He asks her if she might be able to find a particular book for him. Though the island is located closer to France than England, and was part of the English Crown, it was occupied by the German forces. Dawsey explains in the letter that during the war he was part of a book club with a strange long name, a group of six or seven people that continued even after the Germans had left. Intrigued, Juliet thinks of her essay assignment and this unusual literary society and convinces Sidney that she should visit the island and interview the club members, focusing on how reading got them through the occupation. As it turns out, just before boarding a ship for the journey, she accepts a marriage proposal by an American officer, Mark Reynolds, who places a stunning ring on her finger. Arriving on Guernsey, she is impressed with its extraordinary vistas. She manages to find the local postmaster, Eden Ramsey (Tom Courtenay), who is the titular head of the society, and is invited to a society gathering where she is asked to give a reading. On a dark evening she meets the members and through a 1941 flashback learns how the eccentric name came about. She assumed her visit to the island would be brief; however, she soon learns that there is a tragic tale needing to be told, a mystery of sorts, and so she extends her time on Guernsey, growing ever fonder of the people, especially farmer Dawsey, though ever reminded of her engagement to Mark. Guernsey is more than engaging as a film. It is both touching, superbly acted, and a perfect period tale, enjoyable to its most satisfying conclusion. The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society. Directed by Mike Newell. Starring Lily James, Matthew Goode, and Michael Huisman. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG. Released in 2018. Now streaming on Netflix. Lily James and Michiel Huisman in a scene from The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society.
articles.title: The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society a charming old-fashioned drama
