articles.text: The children’s classic Black Beauty was written by Anna Swell in 1887 and has managed to endure for well over a century, told and retold in books and on the screen. Note that the film I’m recommending in this review was released by Disney+ in 2020, and represents a complete overhaul of the story. Where the original narrative by Sewell is set in Dickensian Victorian England, and Black Beauty is a male mustang (voiced in the 1994 film by Alan Cummings), this most recent release flips the gender of Black Beauty who is now voiced by Kate Winslet. The story begins in the American West where the young colt (not yet named) roams free with her mother in the Onaqui Mountains of Utah. Free that is until some cowboys round up the wild horses, and in the process separate the youngster from her mother; the two never to be reunited. As it turns out, the young mustang catches the attention of horse trainer John Manley (Iain Glen) who takes her to a horse sanctuary named Birtwick. Though the horse likes Manley, it is nevertheless rebellious and uncooperative, trying the patience of the trainer. At the same time, Manley Mackenzie Foy stars in the Disney remake of Black Beauty. receives the tragic news that his sister and her husband have been killed in a traffic accident and he is asked to care for his young niece, Jo Green (Mackenzie Foy), a teenager. Though Jo makes it clear to her uncle that she is unhappy with the situation, and still grieving, the black mustang catches her attention, and wisely Manley puts the difficult horse in the care of Jo, asking her also to work in the stables. As it turns out, the horse (which Jo names Black Beauty) and the teen become close, recognizing that each has suffered a loss. And so begins act two of the movie. To Jo’s distress, Manley tells her that because Birtwick is in need of money, Black Beauty may have to be sold. Jo makes a deal with the owner of the sanctuary that she will work extra hours and earn enough money to buy Black Beauty. Nevertheless, the horse is sold, and the setting of the film shifts dramatically from Utah to England. The story evolves as Jo searches for Black Beauty. The horse ends up being sold several times, first to an upper class English family, to a farmer, then to a New York carriage driver. Meanwhile the Beauty and Jo yearn to be reunited and the search continues. Black Beauty. Directed by Ashley Avis. Starring Kate Winslet, Mackenzie Foy, Iain Glen. 1 hr., 50 min. Rated PG. Released 2020. Now Streaming on Disney+, Mackenzie Foy and Iain Glen in a scene from Black Beauty.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS Black Beauty – an updated version of children’s classic

articles.text: A scene from Ice Age: Continental Drift. Ice Age: Continental Drift is the fourth installment of what has proved to be a kid friendly (7-8 years-old) franchise, with the familiar characters – Manny the wooly mammoth (Ray Romano), Sid the sloth (John Leguizamo), and Diego the saber-toothed tiger (Denis Leary) – who return for another adventure. Added to this cohort is a new character, Sid’s sassy granny (Wanda Sykes). Of course they encounter natural disasters, predators, engage in wacky antics, and naturally learn life lessons that revolve around friendship and family. There are avalanches, tidal waves, and even a tornado for added excitement. But perhaps the best four minutes of this animated feature belong to the now favorite prehistoric, bug-eyed squirrel called Scrat (Chris Wedge), ever in the hunt for that elusive acorn. He never utters a word; instead, he makes squeaky noises as he remains in hot pursuit of that nut that is always not quite within his grasp. Scrat is a truly inspired character. In this story, the trio and granny navigate the open waters, trapped on a large chunk if ice. Manny is preoccupied with thoughts of his rebellious teen daughter, Peaches (Keke Palmer), who is crushing on a boy wooly mammoth (Drake). And he worries about how she is doing back on solid land, so to speak, wishing he could still lay down parental rules that make Peaches crazy. As it turns out, just as Peaches is wishing to be free of her dad’s restrictions and house rules, off he floats, drifting away into the distance, while she and Ellie (Queen Latifah), Manny’s wife and Peaches’ mom, watch helplessly. And thus begins the ice floe journey of the foursome that involves encountering a bevy of pirates who use chunks of ice as a ship, one commanded by a giant ape (Peter Dinklage). Diego even develops a heart-throbbing crush on one of the pirates, Shira (Jennifer Lopez). The group also meets up with an army of chipmunks (apparently Sid can speak chipmunk). For youngsters, it’s still a hoot, even if older kids may begin to find the Ice Age gang a bit predictable. With the exception of Scrat who steals every scene in which he appears. Ice Age: Continental Drift. Directed by Steve Martino and Mike Thurmeier. With voices of Ray Romano, Denis Leary, John Leguizamo. 1 hr., 27 min. Rated PG. Released in 2012. Now streaming on Disney+/VUDU/ Apple tv. 30 DOORS OPEN AT 3:30 PM

articles.text: It may seem like a lifetime ago when you gazed down at your first grandchild with your eyes tearing up and your heart full of love. Just like the new parents, you looked at the beauty of that innocent little bundle and unconsciously began thinking about the years ahead; how the child would grow, learn, play, make friends, become an active part of your family and a positive member of the community that they live in. Now fast forward five, ten, 15 years. Things have changed and not for the better. You have a troubled grandchild. Maybe your grandchild’s problems began in pre-school when the parents were repeatedly being contacted by the teachers about the behavior of hitting or not following directions. Maybe your grandchild has been identified as being a mean kid in elementary school by the teachers or the principal who feel that they are a ringleader who coerces others into negative behavior in the classroom and after school. Or perhaps you have a grandteen who has been in trouble with the law for drug use, underage drinking, or other anti-social behaviors that have led them into formal interactions with the criminal justice system. There are an infinite number of factors that contribute to children having the kinds of struggles described here, and therefore, just as many ways to approach solutions. Some parents try to cope with their children’s behavior problems with severe consequences or punishment – the Tough Love approach. Others simply bury their heads or throw up their hands, not knowing exactly what to do and fearing making things worse. What’s wrong with the Tough Love approach? One may argue that anything else is coddling, ignoring, and enabling the child’s negative/destructive/dangerous behaviors, and that things will simply get worse and worse by not applying strict boundaries and punishments. Although it’s possible that in expert hands, short-term success can result when troubled kids and teens see that their behaviors have consequences, and that the adults in their lives will hold them to a specific set of behaviors or else they will be punished. Children can be troubled and have dark feelings. As a grandparent, you can help them. In the long run however, this approach may result in breaking the young person’s sense of trust in those who are supposed to love and understand them. The young person may end up having fractured relationships with the very adults who tried to address the issues in this way. Another way to view the troubled child or teen is to try to look beyond their behavior to what is underlying the child’s actions. Most people, children included, are behaving in ways that they believe are advantageous to them in some way, even when it seems paradoxical to the observer. The pressures on young people today are enormous and very different from stresses that the older generation experienced. The possible causes are endless, and it may be that professional help is needed to find the underlying motivation. What’s a grandparent to do? Grandparents play a special role in children’s lives. Unlike the parents, grandparents enjoy a few degrees of separation in a child’s life and can usually be absolved of the disciplinary role in the troubled child’s world. (Grandparents raising grandchildren as primary custodians are the exception, of course). Instead, a grandparent can be the source of unconditional love, compassion, and understanding. Ask your grandchild to share their feelings with you confidentially. Remind them that you love them no matter what and that you will always be there for them. Pose questions such as: • “How has this (insert situation, experience, dilemma) been for you?” • “What were you feeling when that was happening?” • “What might make things easier for you?” • “How can I be part of making things better for you?” • “What if you had a magic wand? What one thing would you wish for?” Many adults who have recovered from severe difficulties in their childhood/teens/young adulthood, such as addiction, abusive relationships, gang membership, criminal activity, and/or incarceration, will point to one person in their life who always believed in them and always made them feel loved and understood. More often than not it’s a grandparent, a person who had the vision to see beyond the behavior to the person inside. It may take years for a person to recognize how that love made the difference for them in their life, but it can and does happen. Be that special person in your troubled grandchild’s life. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Gragrandparents. Dear Macmama: I see there is an update to a new operating system, Ventura, OS 13. I currently have Big Sur OS12.6. Is there any reason to update, any new features? -Geoff, Piedmont Dear Geoff: Each new operating system comes with new features, sometimes responding to customers’ feedback, and Ventura is no different. Most likely, if the applications that you use are working fine with Big Sur, they should work well with Ventura. There are cases of applications that are not Ventura-ready, so it would be important for you to look up the compatibility of the applications that you use the most. But yes, there are some exciting features that many customers have been requesting for a long time. Here are just a few. 1. Get rid of duplicate photos: This is a feature that customers and tech pros I like have been asking to have available for years. It’s finally here. In your Photos app, if there are duplicates available, there will be a “Duplicates”, listed in the sidebar. You can then select the ones you want to merge. This will not remove any photos from your albums, and merge all the copies you may have, and put the extras in “Recently Deleted” in Photos. When I ran this utility, I was able to get rid of almost 2000 photos. 2. Schedule when to send an email, and undo send: Scheduling an email to be sent or undoing a sent email was something we used to have to use a thirdparty app for, but now through the Mail app, these are both possible. You have up to 10 seconds to “unsend” an email message, and you can also select a date and time to remind you to get back to a message that you want to read later in your inbox. 3. Use your iPhone as a webcam: The camera on your laptop is OK, but the camera on your iPhone is much better. As a matter of fact, it’s much better than many of the Webcams that are out there. This function is called “Continuity Camera”. To enable this, you simply bring your iPhone near your Mac, making sure they are both on the same Wi-Fi network, or that Bluetooth is enabled, and your iPhone will appear as an available WebCam in FaceTime, Zoom and other video communication apps. Apple sells a MagSafe stand for laptops for $30 made by Belkin that allows you to clip the stand with your phone magnetically attached to the top of your screen. They will be making one for monitors and desktop computers soon. 4. Enhanced Spotl ight Search: It seems that with every operating system upgrade the search function gets better. This is definitely the case in Ventura. Spotlight now allows you to open an QuickLook item with Preview. To do this, you select the item in the list of search results and press your spacebar. More excitingly, though, spotlight allows you to search for photos by searching their location and by searching their type. For example, you can search “dog” and your dog photos will come up. In my experience this function is pretty good but will definitely need to be improved. There are many features in Ventura, like “undo send” in Messages, Hand-off in FaceTime (switch from your phone to your Mac seamlessly while on a FaceTime call), and a completely refreshed System Settings (previously System Preferences). These features, and some new features to come in further updates, make Ventura a worthy update to the line of operating systems from Apple. articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Seniors in front of the Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito: Jim Ayotte (left), Penny Robb, Tanya Hu, Larry Hu, Susan McCreary, Yorkman Lowe, George Epstein, Irene Westler, Ann Morales, Mona Jamieson, Nancy Hinsch, “Smiley” Seal, Cheryl Stanton, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Fred Pemberton, and Janet Epstein. Fifteen members of the Piedmont Seniors traveled to new, yet nearby destinations on Friday, September 16. The first stop was an out-ofthe-way scenic location at Fort Cronkhite in the Marin Headlands. To get there, one needs to go through an unusual tunnel that only allows traffic to go one way at a time. Those who want to drive the opposite way have to patiently wait for several minutes until the road is clear to proceed. The views are certainly worth the wait. It is a favorite spot for surfers and beachcombers alike. The views of the Golden Gate Bridge and surrounding areas are breathtaking, and the scenery alone merits a visit. The next stop was at the Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito. It had been closed to the public due to COVID. The Seniors felt privileged to be allowed inside as the Mammal Center has only recently opened their doors and are very strict. For example, one must show evidence of COVID vaccinations, show identification, and wear facial coverings. The animals need to be protected as well as people. Founded as a non-profit in 1975, It is home to the world’s largest marine mammal hospital, which provides life-saving care to animals so they can be safely released back to the ocean. It has been acknowledged that marine mammal health, ocean health, and human health are linked. The work of the Center advances medical knowledge and understanding about these links to inspire consumers to try to change their behavior to protect our future. When you visit, sign up for the docent tours; they make all the difference in understanding the work done by the Center. The Seniors saw sea lions, elephant seals, and other sea life needing rescuing. The docents spoke about sustainable seafood and conservation. articles.text: Did you know that gratitude can make you a better caregiver? Being thankful can help reduce anxiety and allow us to cope better with stress. It can also boost optimism, improve focus, increase happiness and improve sleep. The holidays provide the perfect opportunity to count your blessings and practice being grateful. As a caregiver, you may have your fair share of frustrating and exhausting days. However, even in the hard moments, there are many reasons to be thankful for the opportunity to help others. Here are four reasons to be grateful this holiday season for your caregiving experience: 1. Your work is meaningful At the beginning of every morning, you can wake up knowing that you will truly make a difference in someone’s life that day. You may feel like your day is filled with repetitive tasks like helping to cook meals or clean the house. However, all those little things you do result in a huge impact on the lives of those you serve. Without you, they would struggle with physical and emotional challenges and would not be able to live life to the fullest. Since you chose to be a caregiver, you have the power to transform someone’s day, week, and ultimately, their life. 2. Lessons from work can enrich your personal life As a caregiver, you develop many important skills which can also be applied to your personal life. You learn how to speak (and listen) with empathy and patience. You can hone your skills in communication, flexibility, and reading body language. Physical strength can improve from helping others with daily tasks which in turn leads to greater health and well-being. You will likely learn about nutrition, human relationships, efficiency, mindfulness and you will gain knowledge of a plethora of medical terms. All these skills can serve you well in areas of your life outside of work. 3. You Model Generosity You may have a son or daughter, niece or nephew, or other young people in your life who look up to you. As a caregiver, you can show them how to be selfless and value others in their community. You are able to truly lead by example and demonstrate that caring for others is the right thing to do. 4. Insights About Aging If you are given the chance to care for an older adult, you can learn many things about the aging process. It may present you with new perspectives and ways to help prepare yourself or loved ones for that season of life. Not only can it give you a new outlook on how to help others. but it may also help you prioritize your goals and what matters to you. through a lens of gratitude, you will feel more fulfilled. This will translate into you becoming a more effective caregiver. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. Those who want to drive the opposite way have to patiently wait for several minutes until the road is clear to proceed. The views are certainly worth the wait. It is a favorite spot for surfers and beachcombers alike. The views of the Golden Gate Bridge and surrounding areas are breathtaking, and the scenery alone merits a visit. The next stop was at the Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito. It had been closed to the public due to COVID. The Seniors felt privileged to be allowed inside as the Mammal Center has only recently opened their doors and are very strict. For example, one must show evidence of COVID vaccinations, show identification, and wear facial coverings. The animals need to be protected as well as people. Founded as a non-profit in 1975, It is home to the world’s largest marine mammal hospital, which provides life-saving care to animals so they can be safely released back to the ocean. It has been acknowledged that marine mammal health, ocean health, and human health are linked. The work of the Center advances medical knowledge and understanding about these links to inspire consumers to try to change their behavior to protect our future. articles.text: William (Bill) Howard passed away peacefully from cancer at home on November 17, 2022 surrounded by his family. Throughout his nearly two-year journey with glioblastoma, Bill never failed in his courtesy to his family and caregivers. He faced death with his usual grace. Born in San Francisco on October 1, 1950, he was the second child of Henry Howard, founder of the noted San Francisco law firm Howard, Rice, Nemerovski, Canady, Falk & Rabkin. He grew up just below Twin Peaks until the family moved to Hillsborough when he was six because his father was tired of San Francisco’s cold, foggy summers. Bill attended Stevenson School in Monterey and graduated from Burlingame High School. He studied theatre at the University of Seattle, and after graduation, Bill moved to New York City to pursue acting. He wrote to his mother that at 6’6” his one career obstacle was towering over other actors, giving casting directors a Bill Howard with sons Henry and Leland at Crater Lake, Oregon. Bill Howard died on November 17. He was 72. problem if they hired a short hero. He subsequently returned to San Francisco, where he earned his Master of Business Administration from Golden Gate University, and pursued a career in investment management, including managing HighMark Mutual Funds. During this time, Bill continued to pursue his passion in theatre through acting and directing productions in the Bohemian Club. Bill and his wife, Kyung Hee, moved to Piedmont in 1994 and raised two sons. Bill was present in his sons’ lives and enjoyed coaching their sports teams. He shared his love of the outdoors through backpacking and camping trips in the Sierra. Bill applied his woodworking talents in designing and building a beautiful home for his family. In addition to Kyung Hee, his wife of nearly 31 years, he is survived by his sons Henry and Leland Howard and sister Kit Duane. A memorial will be held 11 a.m., Monday, December 5 at Piedmont Community Church. The family suggests that in lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to the Pacific Crest Trail Association (www.pcta. org/donate) and Yosemite Conservancy (www.yosemite.org/ memorial).

articles.text: Runners were treated to music starting at 8 a.m. by a group of seven symphony musicians playing fanfare music on authentic, historic French and Belgian hunting horns organized by Piedmont’s Tom Reicher. What draws musicians to the start of the race each year? “The drive is the ability to play these instruments outdoors, where they are supposed to be played, it’s a unique experience.” Symphony musicians providing musical fanfares at the start of Piedmont’s annual Turkey Trot on Thanksgiving morning included Robert Ward, principal horn, San Francisco Symphony; Piedmont resident Jonathan Ring, second horn, San Francisco Symphony; Daniel Hawkins, utility horn, San Francisco Symphony; Caitlyn Smith, principal horn, Santa Cruz Symphony, Stockton Symphony, and Santa Rosa Symphony; Alicia Mastromonaco, section horn, Marin Symphony, Monterey Symphony, and Carmel Bach Festival; Stuart Gronningen, retired principal horn, Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony; and Tom Reicher, utility horn, Berkeley Symphony and organizer of Les Trompes de Piedmont. A long line of runners kept coming several minutes after the start of the Turkey Trot. For many the Turkey Trot is a time to take your dog for a walk.

Symphony musicians providing musical fanfares at the start of Piedmont’s annual Turkey Trot on Thanksgiving morning included Robert Ward, principal horn, San Francisco Symphony; Piedmont resident Jonathan Ring, second horn, San Francisco Symphony; Daniel Hawkins, utility horn, San Francisco Symphony; Caitlyn Smith, principal horn, Santa Cruz Symphony, Stockton Symphony, and Santa Rosa Symphony; Alicia Mastromonaco, section horn, Marin Symphony, Monterey Symphony, and Carmel Bach Festival; Stuart Gronningen, retired principal horn, Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony; and Tom Reicher, utility horn, Berkeley Symphony and organizer of Les Trompes de Piedmont. Knitted turkey hats were en vogue this year. A father runs with his daughter. A long line of runners kept coming several minutes after the start of the Turkey Trot. Cory Smegal’s brother Jack Texeira (left), father-in law Tom Smegal, sister Kelly Moyer, and sister-in-law Betsy Andersen. For many the Turkey Trot is a time to take your dog for a walk.

articles.text: It’s Thanksgiving morning, and Piedmont’s streets hold a charge of anticipation. 2,300 people stretch their legs and wish each other good luck, their breath forming white clouds in the air with every word in the crisp morning air. As the 8:30 a.m. start time approaches runners at Piedmont’s’ annual Turkey Trot stiffen and silence falls over the crowd. At the crack of starter’s gun , the 2022 Turkey Trot commences. Thousands of participants take off toward the finish line, five kilometers ahead of them. “It’s surreal seeing how many people are running alongside you,” said Piedmont High alum Ana Romanczuk, now a freshman at Chapman University. “I think [the number of runners] is inspiring and really pushes you to keep going and give it your all.” Piedmont’s annual Turkey Trot sees runners going solo as well as entire families completing the three-mile run together. Along the sidelines of the course, citizens set up stations with cups of water and apple juice to keep runners hydrated and refreshed. “People on the sidelines helped out, the firemen helped out, it really felt like the whole community came together to keep a tradition going,” Romanczuk said. Among the Turkey Trot’s challenges is the course itself, riddled with hills and steep climbs that enhance the challenge. “Magnolia hill was pretty hard. About a half-mile into the race it kind of hits you like a truck, and you aren’t quite warmed up yet. The Turkey Trot is notoriously very hilly,” PHS alum Jack Stein said. Piedmont’s natural hilly landscape is part of what gives the run its character and has Piedmonters preparing in the months in advance. “In my opinion Sea View was the hardest part of the run. The first part of the street is pretty brutal if you’re going for a fast time. It’s not a steep climb, but it’s a pretty long stretch uphill. It definitely felt good getting past that point,” said Xander Schulte-Sasse, a PHS junior on the Photo by Sohrab “Seb” Ford Piedmont Post intern Micah Temple reports on the Turkey Trot while running it. cross-country team. In the race, participants cheer each other on and encourage one another to push onward. “There’s not a super competitive or fierce attitude. Everybody just wants to motivate each other to go fast and not quit,” added PHS grad Charlie Lambert. Many of the Turkey Trot runners are current Piedmont residents, but with the race during Thanksgiving break, lots of college students come back home to participate. “My favorite part of the run has been coming back and seeing friends and family. I’ve been missing these guys in college, so it’s great to be able to come back and do something fun together,” Romanczuk said. Aside from the accomplishment runners get from undertaking an arduous endeavor such as the Turkey Trot, it brings Piedmonters and those coming from afar together on Thanksgiving day. “I’m happy to be here and home from college. Everyone comes out here on Thanksgiving morning. It’s a gathering spot where you can see everyone you’ve missed,’ said Stein. Micah Temple is a junior at Piedmont High School and an intern with the Piedmont Post. He ran in this year’s Turkey Trot while taking notes for this story. Photo by Micah Temple Ana Romanczuk gets a little assistance on Mountain Avenue from Holden Temple (left) and Jackson Temple (right). The support from her entourage helped her achieve a time that gave her 39th place overall in the Female age 15-19 division.

articles.text: Jen and I have long been supporters of replacing the community swimming pool. Despite its flaws, our community pool provided a place for residents to gather in the center of town, to interact with one another in a relaxing outdoor environment and to watch our children safely play. But the facility wasn’t ideal for our sports teams and our student athletes (many exited Piedmont as a result). The facility was in disrepair and tired in a way that made it less useful even for its primary purposes. In 2020, voters overwhelmingly supported Measure UU to raise $19.5 million in bonds to build a new pool complex. There was a thorough public process both before and after Measure UU to discuss the scope and features of the new facility that would best serve the needs of our community. Since the passage of UU, a number of things have happened to impact the project. Some broke in our favor (the bonds were issued in a very low interest rate environment), and some not (construction costs skyrocketed the past two years, requiring a $4 million reduction in the project scope). Last month the City wisely rejected the initial construction bids that came in too high and launched a second round of bidding. The second round went much better and the City can now move forward with construction costs consistent with its estimates. But with inflation, the money available from UU is not sufficient to cover a number of very important features of the complex. These include starting blocks, a scoreboard, a poolside room for community events, and importantly making sure the dimensions of the pools don’t have to be cut so we can allow for a full-sized competition option and a shallow end of the recreation pool for swim lessons and play. It’s first edition was on October 20, 1998, a 12-page paper that hardly offered any promise, let alone optimism, that it might be around a quarter century later. articles.text: The American Red Cross of Northern California needs special volunteers to deliver blood products to hospitals in local communities and provide the vital link between blood donors and patients who need blood products. Volunteers in the blood transportation specialist position have two important assignments — to transport blood from our blood collection sites to our labs throughout the region for testing and processing, and to deliver blood products to hospitals in the area using a Red Cross-owned vehicle. WHAT DOES IT TAKE? These crucial volunteers will be asked to fill two to four shifts in their region each month, and the assignment usually taking about four hours to complete. The need for these transports may be scheduled during the day, in the evening, and on weekends. If you have a valid state driver’s license and at least 3 years of licensed driving experience, you can choose regular routes, stand-by emergency deliveries or both. This is a great volunteer opportunity for individuals, couples, friends or family members. Volunteers must be able to lift as much as 45 pounds. Training is provided by the Red Cross. Blood transportation specialists can schedule their own hours while helping patients in need. “It only takes a few hours each week to have an impact on someone’s life. When you join us, as a member of our Blood Transportation Team, you’ll serve as a critical link in getting blood donations to those who need them,” said Patty Montmorency, Blood Services Transportation Team Lead. “Training is free, but the blood you deliver is priceless.” Hear firsthand (https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=X-hTsLecWDk&ab_channel=AmericanRedCross) why others have volunteered in this role: When Red Cross volunteer Mark Merz is asked why he serves as a Blood Transportation Specialist, he says he gets motivated “just knowing that someone is in hospital and might need a transfusion.” Since he is semi-retired, Mark does a shift every other week, picking up boxes of blood donations from blood drives and transporting them to hospitals. What is his impression of the Red Cross since he started volunteering in December 2021? “It’s a top-notch organization!” he says. If helping hospital patients who need blood and blood products during their battle back to health is of interest to you, visit https://www.redcross.org/volunteer/become-a-volunteer/urgentneed-for-volunteers.html for more information.
articles.title: Red Cross needs special volunteers to help deliver blood products to area hospitals

articles.text: Last week, 48,000 unionized academic graduate workers across the 10 campuses in the University of California system began striking for pay increases, enhanced healthcare, longer family leave, public transit passes, and lowered tuition for international researchers. It’s the largest academic strike in U.S. history, and it may be the largest California strike in history. Many of the graduate students – including researchers, postdoctoral fellows, and teaching assistants – live on $24,000 a year and work far longer hours than their maximum quota. They hope for enough of a raise that no more than 30% of their salaries will cover rent/ This means a base salary of $54,000 for graduate students and $70,000 for postdocs. As the statewide strike enters its second week with less than a month before the end of the semester and no smooth end to the bargaining in sight, Piedmont residents who work at UC Berkeley offered their thoughts on the cause of the strike. Patty Dunlap, a Programs and Grants Coordinator at UCB’s Program in Critical Theory, said that her department and many others had postponed all event programming until the spring semester next year. While she admitted to being minimally affected by the strike due to working remotely, she affirmed that most workers she knew stood in solidarity with the strikers and “are not crossing the picket lines,” a sentiment echoed by Piedmont resident Richard Saykally, Professor Emeritus of Chemistry. Ralph Catalano, a professor in the Public Health Graduate School and soon to retire after 50 years at Berkeley, offered his thoughts on the cause of the strike. “As public universities receive less and less money from the government due to budget cuts, they can afford less and less full-time teaching faculty. As this happens, the line between the students who receive an education and the workers who produce it not only moves but blurs. No wonder more graduate workers than ever are fighting for a livable wage.” “Many of the people filling these graduate positions,” added Catalano, “wouldn’t have been able to attain to them in, say, 1925, when a lot of these researchers were people of private means only being paid enough by the school that it wouldn’t distract them from temporary work.” As the demographics of graduate workers have rightfully broadened since then, the function of graduate workers has also broadened to the point where they are now essential to all teaching, research, and grant-writing operations of the University. The critical nature of this role is supported by the fact that, within a week alone, the strike brought many lectures and extracurricular events at Berkeley to a standstill. Nevertheless, as grad students continue to demand higher wages, many local UC Berkeley workers view the disruptions presented by the strike as a welcome price to pay – and a long time coming.
articles.title: UC Berkeley workers in Piedmont reflect on current strike

articles.text: The City of Piedmont Sustainability Division invites community members to complete a brief online survey about their experience of compost, recycling, and trash collection services within the city. The survey is an opportunity for residents, business owners, and property managers to help the City understand what works well today and where there is room for improvement. City staff will use the information gathered to target future improvements and to help shape public education and outreach initiatives regarding available services, waste reduction, and composting. 4 Questions The survey asks community members about their: • general satisfaction with waste collection services in Piedmont • awareness of cost saving opportunities, including annual pre-payment discounts and on-premises service at curbside rates for physically disabled customers • composting habits and understanding of waste sorting guidelines • disposal practices for bulky waste items, such as mattresses, couches, and appliances The survey is available online at piedmont.ca.gov/WasteServicesSurvey and should take less than 10 minutes to complete. It will remain open through December 31. Piedmont entered into a 10-year agreement for solid waste with Republic Services in 2018. The agreement grants an exclusive franchise to Republic Services for the collection, processing, transfer, and disposal of solid waste, recyclable materials, and organic waste in the City. For questions contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman at (510) 420-3058. For waste collection customer service, contact Republic Services at 800-320-8077 or visit their website at republicservices.com/ municipality/piedmont-ca. business hours.

Blood transportation specialists can schedule their own hours while helping patients in need. “It only takes a few hours each week to have an impact on someone’s life. When you join us, as a member of our Blood Transportation Team, you’ll serve as a critical link in getting blood donations to those who need them,” said Patty Montmorency, Blood Services Transportation Team Lead. “Training is free, but the blood you deliver is priceless.” Hear firsthand (https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=X-hTsLecWDk&ab_channel=AmericanRedCross) why others have volunteered in this role: When Red Cross volunteer Mark Merz is asked why he serves as a Blood Transportation Specialist, he says he gets motivated “just knowing that someone is in hospital and might need a transfusion.” Since he is semi-retired, Mark does a shift every other week, picking up boxes of blood donations from blood drives and transporting them to hospitals. What is his impression of the Red Cross since he started volunteering in December 2021? “It’s a top-notch organization!” he says. It’s the largest academic strike in U.S. history, and it may be the largest California strike in history. Many of the graduate students – including researchers, postdoctoral fellows, and teaching assistants – live on $24,000 a year and work far longer hours than their maximum quota. They hope for enough of a raise that no more than 30% of their salaries will cover rent/ This means a base salary of $54,000 for graduate students and $70,000 for postdocs. As the statewide strike enters its second week with less than a month before the end of the semester and no smooth end to the bargaining in sight, Piedmont residents who work at UC Berkeley offered their thoughts on the cause of the strike. Patty Dunlap, a Programs and Grants Coordinator at UCB’s Program in Critical Theory, said that her department and many others had postponed all event programming until the spring semester next year. While she admitted to being minimally affected by the strike due to working remotely, she affirmed that most workers she knew stood in solidarity with the strikers and “are not crossing the picket lines,” a sentiment echoed by Piedmont resident Richard Saykally, Professor Emeritus of Chemistry. Ralph Catalano, a professor in the Public Health Graduate School and soon to retire after 50 years at Berkeley, offered his thoughts on the cause of the strike. “As public universities receive less and less money from the government due to budget cuts, they can afford less and less full-time teaching faculty. As this happens, the line between the students who receive an education and the workers who produce it not only moves but blurs. No wonder more graduate workers than ever are fighting for a livable wage.” “Many of the people filling these graduate positions,” added Catalano, “wouldn’t have been able to attain to them in, say, 1925, when a lot of these researchers were people of private means only being paid enough by the school that it wouldn’t distract them from temporary work.” As the demographics of graduate workers have rightfully broadened since then, the function of graduate workers has also broadened to the point where they are now essential to all teaching, research, and grant-writing operations of the University. The critical nature of this role is supported by the fact that, within a week alone, the strike brought many lectures and extracurricular events at Berkeley to a standstill. Nevertheless, as grad students continue to demand higher wages, many local UC Berkeley workers view the disruptions presented by the strike as a welcome price to pay – and a long time coming. articles.text: With the announcement of Piedmont City Administrator Sarah Lillevand’s planned retirement in Spring 2023, the City Council wants residents to answer the question: “What should City Council look for when selecting Piedmont’s next City Administrator?” The position of City Administrator is appointed by the City Council and is responsible for overseeing day-to-day City operations and addressing the priorities established by the City Council. Upon retirement, Lillevand will have spent nearly four years as City Administrator. Prior to this position she served five years as Piedmont’s Recreation Director. A recruitment survey is available until November 30. It asks the public to consider the skills and experiences most critical to the success of a new City Administrator, what sort of management and leadership the City Council should look for, the way that the candidate should interact with the community, and the most critical challenges and opportunities facing the City of Piedmont that could be helped by the candidate. In speaking of her hopes for the person who would replace her, Lillevand said, ”I am excited for the future of Piedmont and for the next City Administrator to emerge from what is sure to be a deep and experienced pool of candidates. The obvious challenges on the horizon are the completion of the Community Pool project, implementation of the Housing Element and strategizing for future City infrastructure projects. But the day-to-day delivery of service by City Staff is equally important and cannot be lost in the shadow of these large efforts.” Piedmont City Council will use the input gathered from the survey to help guide its decisions during the selection process. The survey is accessible at piedmont. ca.gov/CityAdministratorSurvey, and will remain active until November 30.

articles.text: At its meeting on Monday, November 21, the Piedmont City Council announced that the city received four bids for construction of the new pool. Two of these were well below the two bids the Council rejected at its October 17 meeting. One of the new bids was for $21.35 million and was “in very close alignment” with the cost estimates that the Council reviewed in August. Accordingly, City Administrator Lillevand declared that she issued a Formal Notice of Intent to award a contract for construction. She said that she could bring the award of contract before the Council for consideration as soon as December 5. Extreme construction inflation in the two years since Measure UU passed resulted in significant scaling-back of the Pool Project in Spring 2022, Lillevand said. Even after eliminating the entire second story of the pool building, the estimated cost to build a facility to meet the community’s demonstrated needs still exceeded the available budget by over $2 million. Faced with potential cuts to the project that would have diminished essential dimensions of the pool facilities, Lillevand added, the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization “is committed to a fundraising target of… $2.1 million dollars to help us close that anticipated funding gap and keep the design intact.” She and Council members expressed their gratitude for the PRFO’s critical aid. Other council items The city council approved paving improvements to the Oakland Avenue Rehabilitation Project, a project covering both sides of Oakland Avenue, from Grand Avenue to the east side of the Oakland Avenue bridge, and the area west from the bridge to city limits. The council also introduced a proposed amendment to Chapter 17 of the City Code, regarding the regulation of Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) and the number of bedrooms in a residence. The proposed revisions include changes to development standards regarding building heights and setbacks (open areas between the edges of the building and the edges of the lot). The revisions allow an ADU to be sold separately from the primary residence if the buyer meets certain criteria. The only proposed change which goes beyond state requirements is the removal of owner occupancy deed restrictions on ADUs approved before 2020 if the owner accepts a new 15-year deed restriction. This restriction mandates that if the ADU is rented out, it must be rented to a tenant who meets “very low income” affordability thresholds set by the Association of Bay Area Governments. Normally, an owner occupancy deed restriction prohibits the use of a property for residential purposes by anyone other than the homeowners. Piedmont City Council meets on the first and third Monday of each month at City Council Chambers in City Hall (120 Vista Avenue) at 6 p.m. Interested community members may attend in-person, or over Zoom at the following link: piedmont-ca-gov. zoom.us/j/83863020560.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation invite community members to kick off the holiday season on Wednesday, December 7, at 7 p.m. at Lights Up!, the annual Tree Lighting ceremony in front of Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. The Beautification Foundation is expanding the area near the Community Hall that will be illuminated, with the addition of lights on the Cherry Path near the Japanese Tea House. The tree lighting tradition dates to 1969. Longstanding traditions, including the illumination of the 80-foot redwood tree and Christmas carols being sung by Piedmont High School’s Troubadours, will continue. Changes this year also include the lighting of a menorah, and an interactive activity hosted by Piedmont Girl Scouts inviting attendees to document how they plan to share their own inner light in the new year. A child recipient of the Greater Bay Area MakeA-Wish Foundation will flip the switch for the lights. Piedmont Scouts will serve warm apple cider and hot cocoa, and Chabad Oakland will add to the festivities by serving latkes. Following the tree lighting, families will be invited into the Community Hall for a photo op with Santa Claus. Children are invited to write letters to Santa and deposit them in a special mailbox addressed to the North Pole. Santa will read every letter. Children with special needs will be able to see Santa starting at 6 p.m., ahead of the 7 p.m. lighting ceremony. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation coordinates with the City’s Public Works Department for the installation (and removal) of the LED lights on the redwood tree by the Community Hall. Community members can support the work of the non-profit Foundation by donating to PBF’s 54th Annual Holiday Greeting Campaign (piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/donate). For questions regarding Lights Up! or PBF contact Barbara Love at pbf.piedmont@gmail.com. all award winners. 2nd place age group winners will receive gift certificates from Village Market and Ocho Candy, and 3rd place age group winners will receive gift certificates from Village Market and Yellow Door. articles.text: Bright and early Thanksgiving morning a hardy band of symphony musicians will arrive in Piedmont, set up their music stands in front of the Exedra, and announce –- musically – the start of the 21st annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, a traditional 5-kilometer run on city streets. It’s not a benefit – it’s a fun run embraced strongly by residents and people from throughout the U.S. who come to visit relatives. One of the extra treats for runners (and spectators) will an array of horn players from Bay Area orchestras on hand to play music written for hunting horns more than 100 years ago. “We will have seven or eight hunting horn players who will be playing on authentic trompes de chasse from France,” explained Piedmont resident Tom Reicher, a horn player with Berkeley Symphony and organizer of Les Trompes de Piedmont. “Originally, the trompe de chasse was used as a loud signaling instrument that would communicate to hunters across long distances the various aspects of the hunt. “Over more than two centuries, music was composed for large ensembles of trompes de chasse, and that is what we will be playing. This is music intended to be performed outdoors and thus is appropriate to celebrate the gathering of runners for the Piedmont Turkey Trot.” Onlookers will see large, coiled brass horns, each 14 feet in length pitched in the key of D, that are the primitive ancestors of the modern French horn. Because they have no valves, the hunting horns can play only the notes that are in the harmonic series for the key of D. Performing this year will be Robert Ward, principal horn, San Francisco Symphony; Piedmont resident Jonathan Ring, second horn, San Francisco Symphony; Daniel Hawkins, utility horn, San Francisco Symphony; Meredith Brown, principal horn, Oakland Symphony, Santa Rosa Symphony, Symphony Silicon Valley, and California Symphony; Caitlyn Smith, principal horn, Santa Cruz Symphony, Stockton Symphony, and Santa Rosa Symphony; Alicia Mastromonaco, section horn, Marin Symphony, Monterey Symphony, and Carmel Bach Festival; Stuart Gronningen, retired principal horn, Oakland Symphony and Berkeley Symphony; and Reicher, utility horn, Berkeley Symphony and organizer of Les Trompes de Piedmont. Symphony musicians will provide musical fanfares at the start of Piedmont’s annual Turkey Trot on Thanksgiving morning. Pictured from last year are: Tom Reicher (left), Stuart Gronningen, Alicia Mastromonaco, Caitlyn Smith, Meredith Brown, Jonathan Ring, and Robert Ward

articles.text: The 55th Annual Piedmont Scout Tree Lot opens this Saturday, November 26, at 9 a.m. One day earlier a caravan of trucks and semis will deliver 1400 trees to the Scout Tree Lot at Coaches Field adjacent to the city’s Corporation Yard. The history of the Scout Tree Lot is filled with stories of its earliest day in the Corpus Christi parking lot around 1965, moving to a larger space at Coaches Field, two years ago when the entire operation had to go online. The good news is the Scout Tree Lot is back and inventory looks good. Setup is complete thanks to the Order of the Arrow. All Piedmont Scout troops and parents are scheduled for sales, getting trees on top of cars, and delivery to homes. The Tap-Dancing Christmas Trees are scheduled to arrive, and the ads and social media are buzzing. Wait! It seems simple, but it’s quite Herculean. In 2020, I joined the inner, inner sanctum of the Tree Lot Committee, as the marketing chair. Meetings began in August or September and as the season rapidly approached, we met weekly, addressing every aspect of the lot from ordering, to permits, hiring drivers, organizing Troop participation, building the chute, operating the forklift and power equipment, lighting, marketing, computer systems, training board members to cashier, WiFi, etc…the list makes my head spin. Behind the curtain I found the most dedicated group of people—in fact, two members of the committee have been working on the Tree Lot for roughly 50 years each: Dave Ashton since 1973 and Kevin Fischer since 1968– both started at the lot as Scouts. Right behind them at 40 plus years are Brian Kelleher and Greg Pike. Relative newcomers, Mark Dukas, Troy Alering, and Chris Lee have chalked up 20 or 30 years, but who’s counting? Kevin Fischer is in charge of organizing the Order of the Arrow to set up and take down the lot, including setting up the electrical and lighting plans. Dave Ashton is in charge of ordering all the trees. Beginning in March and April each year, he’s in contact with growers throughout California and Oregon. Brian Kelleher has been ordering all the wreaths – magnolia, mixed cedar and fir, and candle wreaths for many, many years. He likes this role because it’s fun to work with his old Scouting buddies. Greg Pike coordinates the volunteers needed to keep the lot open for 2-3 weeks. He worked on the lot as a Scout and then again when his son was in Piedmont Scouting. The dynamic duo of Chris and Terry Lee traditionally have been in charge of all things marketing, with a little assist now and then. They are able to get the Tap-Dancing Christmas Trees to the lot along with many of the local TV broadcast units. Last year the lot was covered on the 5 p.m. news by KPIX, KABC and KRON. Not incidentally, they’ve been on the committee for over 20 years. When you order your tree and have it delivered – or come to the lot to pick out your tree – remember the thousands of volunteer hours required to make sure you have the best Holiday ever. And thank a volunteer, since all the proceeds support nearly 1,000 Piedmont boys and girls involved in Cub Scouts, Scouts, Explorers, Venturers including the High Adventure and Community Service crews.

articles.text: Millennium High School students fill their plates at the school’s first Gratitude Potluck. On Thursday, November 17, Millennium High School held its first Gratitude Potluck. All student and staff members of the community were invited to bring a dish to share that represented their ethnic, religious or cultural heritage. There was a delicious array of food traditions on display from Ukrainian meatballs to Filipino babinko to Mexican tamales. There were even three competing versions of homemade mac and cheese and a variety of homemade breads and pies. “There was a great diversity of tastes, from sushi to stuffing. It was like having all of my favorite foods,” said MHS teacher Laura Holley. “The food was good and surprising. I liked the contrasts and the decorations,” added MHS 10th grader Andre Bowers. After filling heaping plates, students and staff sat down together at tables decorated by the Parents Club with tablecloths and flowers. While they ate, laughed, and listened to music, they also filled out paper leaves with notes of things for which they were thankful. The leaves are now decorating a gratitude tree in the hall Diana Khushtova, Grace Rego, Adelina Mbise, Charlotte Silver and Angela Enkh-Amgalan give the pre-Thanksgiving meal a thumbs up. MHS 9th graders Bryan Heafy and Ilias Mueller Harley cleared their plates at the Gratitude Potluck, a warmup for Thanksgiving.
articles.title: Millennium High celebrates Thanksgiving early with Gratitude Potluck

articles.text: Sohrab “Seb” Ford A Consent Assembly at Piedmont High School was presented for the 15th year to freshmen and seniors on Wednesday, November 16, in the Alan Harvey Theater. Students also presented the Assembly for an audience of Piedmont parents Monday, November 14, and in San Francisco, at Lick-Wilmerding High School Thursday, November 10. The Consent Assembly consisted of students retelling monologue versions of past stories involving consent and sexual assault. Stories coincided with statistics on sexual assault, explanations of properly asking for consent, and references to student resources. For many years the Consent Assembly was directed by PHS acting teacher Kimberly Taylor. The assembly is now a collaboration with a new student club, Piedmont for Consent (P4C), with hopes of expanding the assembly’s impact. P4C was founded in 2020 after an Instagram account (@ piedmontprotectors) opened a space for Piedmont students to share their experiences of sexual assault and harassment. Since its founding, P4C has provided survivor support groups, in-class consent workshops, and an assembly debriefing. With the consent assembly and additional resources, the club is working to create a shift in Piedmont and Millennium High School’s culture. But with difficult social constrictions, this is easier said than done. “I think people are afraid to say things that can be seen as incorrect by their peers, which kind of creates a stigma around topics like consent,” said senior Tara Kothari, a two-year Consent Assembly presenter. Kothari added, “I think the assembly is just a great thing Junior Bruno Banuelos performs one of the Consent Assembly monologues. that we’re doing, because [sexual assault] is not talked about enough and it’s an uncomfortable topic, but it needs to be put out there more.” The assembly showed consent from a variety of perspectives, from healthy relationships to male victims, and even the perspective of perpetrators. “There are many different facets to consent. It’s not just person on person when someone tries to do something the other person doesn’t like. It’s more complicated, like going too far when someone isn’t ready. I think it’s very important to have multiple perspectives for that reason,” said assembly presenter sophomore Oliver Greenebaum. While the assembly has provided years of consent education to Piedmont students, plenty of work remains to be done. “There is still so much more to do in the consent world and we have some really passionate student leaders who are ready to enact that change,” explained senior Anna Gotto, one of the founding members and President of P4C. “Piedmont for Consent has done so much more than I ever could have dreamed when we started. I am proud of it; however, I also know that it will keep on doing more,” Gotto added.
articles.title: Piedmont For Consent hosts 15th annual Consent Assembly

articles.text: Dear PUSD Community: It’s now been over 90 days since I joined PUSD. In these three-plus months, I’ve spoken with students and staff from all school sites. I’ve attended many meetings of District committees and organizations. I’ve enjoyed introducing myself to parent groups and have met with members of the City Council, Police Department, and other community leaders. I’ve come to know that Piedmont is about relationships. These relationships are essential to the success of the District. During my 90 days of discovery, I noticed that in some areas, our infrastructure doesn’t adequately address our operational needs, preventing us from optimizing our support of students and staff. I’ve identified Curriculum and Instruction, Human Resources, Budget, Facilities, Title IX, Diversity and Inclusion, Technology, Student Services and Special Education as areas needing a build up of infrastructure. In the next three months, we will be developing policies, procedures, and protocols for providing additional layers of support for each area. Throughout the development process, we will hold true to our ‘all means all’ philosophy, where every family will be informed of where to find and access key information to help their child be successful. In listening to the community, we’ve acted on the concerns raised to better serve all of our students participating in our Reading program. The District’s reading curriculum was discussed extensively at the October 12 board meeting. During the meeting, staff gave presentations on students’ progress with Scholastic Reading Inventory and the District’s efforts regarding dyslexia. As a result of conversations with staff, teachers and parents, we’re moving forward with a single screener, Dynamic Indicators of Basic Early Literacy Skills (DIBELS) as our early literacy assessment tool that will be used to identify students at-risk for dyslexia. In addition, we’re reviewing our phonics program for K-2. Thank you to everyone participating in the process. I’ve had conversations with parents and community members on academic excellence, rigor and equity. Regarding academic excellence, Piedmont has built a reputation as one of the top-performing school districts in Alameda County and throughout California. On Monday, the California Department of Education released school, district and state aggregate results from the annual California Assessments of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP). While the results confirmed expected declines state-wide as we recover from the pandemic, PUSD students showed improvement. Over 87% of our students ‘met or exceeded’ the state standards in English Language Arts – second-highest in the state – and 81% ‘met or exceeded’ state standards in Math – third-highest in the state. In addition, PUSD showed a reduction in achievement gaps in student groups and growth in overall distance from ‘met the state standard.’ While that is certainly something to be proud of, we know work remains to be done. To continue the upward trend, my recommendation is to examine “best teaching practices” such as differentiated instruction, Socratic Seminar, and Bloom’s Taxonomy, as tools to be woven into everyday instruction. I want to note that many of our teachers are doing this now, and we will plan to incorporate these tools into our professional development program for the summer. Last January, the District hired Dr. Vanden Wyngaard (Dr. V) as its Director of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. Our equity and inclusion work is critically important to our students being able to navigate and excel in an ever-changing society. What does that work look like in the classroom and in our community? Our goal is to develop and equip a culturally-competent staff that will understand, challenge and motivate all students of all backgrounds. This means narrowing the focus of her responsibilities so that evidence of her work is impactful and meaningful. It is more meaningful now as the country is experiencing an increased level of hate crimes and speech – including in our own community and district. On that topic, based on current events in our nation, I want to be very clear that we stand in solidarity with our Jewish students and families and strongly denounce anti-semitism in all its forms. We are committed to creating an environment where all feel safe and included. Two other items to be aware of... The District started the school year negotiating with the Teachers’ Association, Classified Staff and Administrators. We recently reached an agreement with our teachers including a 7.5% salary increase, $1,500 one-time bonus, and an increase in cap for health care to match a previous agreement with Classified Staff. We [recently reached an agreement with Administrators] and are currently in negotiations with CSEA. We hope to provide an update soon. Finally, at the October 26 meeting, the Board selected Leadership Associates to oversee the process for selecting PUSD’s next Superintendent. The Superintendent position will be posted in the winter with interviews to take place in the winter/spring. PUSD’s next Superintendent will be named in the spring and will assume the new position on July 1, 2023. Other details about the process and timeline [were] discussed at a Special Board Meeting on Wednesday, November 2. I truly believe a successful school district is built on relationships. Teachers, Principals, Staff, Students, Parents/Guardians, and the Community must all work together toward common goals and stand side-by-side to face the challenges ahead. Despite the obstacles of the past three years, I see those relationships at work here in Piedmont and am excited for what lies ahead for the remainder of the school year and beyond. Moving forward, I will be sending out a monthly Superintendent’s newsletter updating our community on what’s happening in our District. –Dr. Donald Evans Interim Superintendent Piedmont School District
articles.title: Supt. Donald Evans’ Oct. 28 update to school community

articles.text: Consultants with the search firm hired by Piedmont School District to find Piedmont’s next permanent school superintendent recently completed as many as 53 meetings with community members. Leadership Associates has a contract with the school district for $23,500 to conduct the search which currently has an applications deadline of January 16, 2023. In a meeting on Wednesday, November 16, Consultant Eric Andrew, who is co-leading the project with Jacki Horejs, met with a group of seven people in Alan Harvey Theater. Andrew fielded comments on Piedmont’s strengths, challenges and desired traits in a new superintendent. His firm has stated that data from 53 meetings and an online survey will orient the search firm as it creates a job description. During the discussion in the theater Andrew explained that Piedmont is six to eight weeks ahead of other districts in the search process as most searches don’t begin until December or January. Piedmont was left without a Superintendent when Randy Booker resigned at the end of the school year on May 13, 2022. In a meeting at Alan Harvey Theater, parents and community members were invited to meet Eric Andrew (right), a consultant with Leadership Associates, the firm selected to lead the search for Piedmont School District’s next school superintendent. Interim Superintendent Donald Evans came out of retirement in Berkeley to serve in a one-year temporary capacity. Andrews, the Superintendent of Campbell Union School District from 2010-2017, explained how superintendent searches have changed in recent years. “One of the very first search criteria is to make sure a candidate is familiar with the cost of living in the Bay Area,” he said. Andrew noted that in the last five years a previously common requirement has been dropped and superintendents are no longer expected to live in the same community. Andrew confirmed his firm’s goal is to find a candidate who will be in place for at least five years. Leadership Associates, a private firm focused heavily on California schools, has been instrumental in hiring current school superintendents in Lafayette, Burlingame, Los Altos, Livermore, and San Mateo Union High School District, the new home of former Piedmont Superintendent Randy Booker. Leadership Associates intends to provide PUSD with four to six superintendent options, but the final hiring decision is that of the school board. “The board has only one employee, the superintendent,” explained Andrew. For more information and to view the preliminary notice about the job posting, visit Leadershipassociates.org/piedmont-unified-school-district-superintendent.
articles.title: Supt. search firm meets with Piedmont community

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School teachers squeaked out a 2-1 victory over the students on Wednesday, November 16, in an exciting game of kickball at Witter Field two days before Thanksgiving break. Students and staff used the new Academy period, which is usually used for extra help, office hours or studying, for some fun. 7th grade teacher, and self-proclaimed Kickball MVP, Ted Scherman had a perfect day at the plate going 3 for 3 including the game winning RBI. Students noted that he ran too slow for it to be an inside-the-park home run. Middle school staff member Michael Wong scored the staff’s first run when Scherman booted Photos courtesy of PUSD 8th grader Alex Hattan-Kutter prepares to kick a ball rolled by a teammate into the defense of teachers Ted Scherman (pitcher), and outfielders Michael Bracamonte (back left), Jessie Hare and Tim Wisniewski. Colin Chang throws the ball as Nikkola Yuen points out that the play should be made to first base. Counselor Amy Sharp applauds the fine play by her teammates while 8th grader Chase Ruegg (right) hopes for an errant throw. the ball over everyone’s heads. This was the first year that kickball was used for student v. staff competition, a school tradition dating back to 1994. PMS educators and administrators have also already battled students in volleyball, and football. Students are licking their wounds from the first three defeats but are hopeful to grow a couple of inches taller over the holidays and beat the staff in basketball and soccer next semester. The Academy period is new this year at middle school and high school. It is scheduled after brunch at the middle school for an hour on Wednesdays and Fridays.
articles.title: Middle school staff v. student kickball game – fun for everyone

articles.text: FireCracker Math, an enrichment math program, is now offering in-person and online small group and private lessons to children in grades K-11. A Math Kangaroo preparation course is being offered during the Winter term. It includes a series of weekly workshops to prepare kids up to 7th grade for Math Kangaroo, a fun, introductory math competition in the U.S. and worldwide. The workshop will include preparation, coaching, and sampling real test problems. “FireCracker Math students have placed first at the national and state levels in 2020, 2021, and 2022. Our small groups of no more than 12 students ensure close teacher-to-student interaction and attention to each child’s needs and pace of learning,” explained FireCracker Math founder and program director Ella Levine. “We employ well-trained, enthusiastic teachers with advanced degrees in math or science.” In-person classes start on January 11 and are held on Wednesdays to March 8. Online courses start January 13. Math Kangaroo test early bird registration is open until December 15 (late registration is through December 31 subject to availability). There are in-person and virtual test center options. For more information and to sign up for Winter and Spring Terms, visit www.firecrackermath.org. Online classes for Algebra Games for grades 4–8 are also available.
articles.title: FireCracker Math available to students in grades K-11

Upcoming Dates in Search December 5: Advertising and active recruitment; ad appears in two consecutive publications of EdCal January 16: Deadline for applicants February 1: Board confers with consultants, reviews all applications and selects candidates to be interviewed February 10-12: Interviews and finalists selected March 8: Board approves contract in school board meeting. July 1: New superintendent begins In a meeting at Alan Harvey Theater, parents and community members were invited to meet Eric Andrew (right), a consultant with Leadership Associates, the firm selected to lead the search for Piedmont School District’s next school superintendent. Interim Superintendent Donald Evans came out of retirement in Berkeley to serve in a one-year temporary capacity. Andrews, the Superintendent of Campbell Union School District from 2010-2017, explained how superintendent searches have changed in recent years. “One of the very first search criteria is to make sure a candidate is familiar with the cost of living in the Bay Area,” he said. Andrew noted that in the last five years a previously common requirement has been dropped and superintendents are no longer expected to live in the same community. Andrew confirmed his firm’s goal is to find a candidate who will be in place for at least five years. Leadership Associates, a private firm focused heavily on California schools, has been instrumental in hiring current school superintendents in Lafayette, Burlingame, Los Altos, Livermore, and San Mateo Union High School District, the new home of former Piedmont Superintendent Randy Booker. Leadership Associates intends to provide PUSD with four to six superintendent options, but the final hiring decision is that of the school board. “The board has only one employee, the superintendent,” explained Andrew. For more information and to view the preliminary notice about the job posting, visit Leadershipassociates.org/piedmont-unified-school-district-superintendent. Students and staff used the new Academy period, which is usually used for extra help, office hours or studying, for some fun. 7th grade teacher, and self-proclaimed Kickball MVP, Ted Scherman had a perfect day at the plate going 3 for 3 including the game winning RBI. Presidio Tunnel Tops is built on top of the Presidio Parkway tunnels, with amazing views of the Golden Gate Bridge. The Academy is open Monday-Saturday, 9:30 a.m.-5:00 p.m.; open late on Thursday nights from 6:00-10:00 p.m. (for ages 18+); and on Sundays from 11:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Tilden Steam Train Redwood-valley-railway.business.site 2481 Grizzly Peak Blvd, Orinda 548-6100 Put the conductor hats on and head to the hills. A Math Kangaroo preparation course is being offered during the Winter term. It includes a series of weekly workshops to prepare kids up to 7th grade for Math Kangaroo, a fun, introductory math competition in the U.S. and worldwide. The workshop will include preparation, coaching, and sampling real test problems. “FireCracker Math students have placed first at the national and state levels in 2020, 2021, and 2022. Online courses start January 13. Math Kangaroo test early bird registration is open until December 15 (late registration is through December 31 subject to availability). There are in-person and virtual test center options. For more information and to sign up for Winter and Spring Terms, visit www.firecrackermath.org. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont School District music teacher Samantha Wilde conducts a practice performance with elementary school musicians at Havens School. In her second year of teaching music in Piedmont schools, Samantha Wilde has more than a full schedule. What was formerly a high school and sometimes middle school orchestra teaching position, the job now includes every grade level from 4th grade through the high school. On Thursday, November 17, the Post caught up with the district’s busiest music teacher while she was teaching the youngest musicians, 4th graders at Havens, in the Ellen Driscoll Theater. The morning’s lesson started with students who have been playing violin for only two months being taught to tune their violins. Wearing a microphone and leading from the piano, Wilde played “The Ant Song,” and sang “Each and every ant, playing in the dirt.” All 4th and 5th grade students have an opportunity to participate in instrumental music, and at the beginning of the school year Wilde demonstrates the different instruments. Students get to select violin, viola, trumpet, trombone, clarinet, or flute and learn to play it for two years. The 4th grade music class meets only once a week for 40 minutes. During Thursday’s lesson Wilde worked on tone production by instructing students to keep the bow perpendicular to First year violinists Mackenzie Ewen (left) and Evelyn Joerger. the string and in the same contact point on the string. “A lot of the ‘aha’ moments come just from drawing attention to mechanics. I also love the connection that music facilitates between people,” said Wilde. “Music isn’t just sound, it’s also something we do. We create, listen, laugh, and overcome challenges together.” General body awareness also received significant attention with a technique of holding the bow likened to “petting the side of a frog.” The day’s lesson worked its way up to playing “Hot Cross Buns”. Kids first plucked the strings with their fingers, known as pizzicato, while holding their instrument like a guitar. “I know it’s very tempting to be a guitar rock star, so we will get it out of our systems,” Wilde said. The temptation for any 4th grader to talk or make noise in a class may be exponentially increased when holding an instrument. Wilde used some creative ways to get their attention. her head at the front of the class, students knew to follow along. “This is the universal unicorn symbol, which means ‘Look at Ms. Wilde,’” she said. Wilde told her class she also does this with her middle school and high school orchestra classes. Wilde herself picked up the violin as her first instrument as a 5th grader. She earned her Bachelors of Music degree from Texas Tech University with a focus on Samantha Wilde leads her class in a rehearsal inside Ellen Driscoll Playhouse.

articles.text: Camp Augusta tells a story. Here at Camp Augusta, we love sharing the wonderful shenanigans we get into each summer. However, there is one program area that is often neglected in our stories because explaining it in a way that makes sense is no easy feat. It’s a shame because this program area happens to be really dang cool. So here it is – a long-overdue love letter to one of our favorite (and weirdest) parts of camp: The Story Experience. Over the course of a session, twenty wildly different storylines will play out within the nooks and crannies of the daily schedule. Here’s how it works. On the first full day of camp, campers are greeted at breakfast with a booklet listing off dozens of potential Story Experiences with only one mysterious line of description to clue them into what may await them on the other side. • Look out! Bandits! – First they came for gold. Then they came for land. Now they’ve come for your counselor • Murphy Family Vacation – Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong • Jurassic Park – You are no longer the King • A Simple Boat Ride… I Hope Nothing Happens – *wink* • Play Your Cards Right – The Devil you know is better than the Devil you don’t All this……and 50 more titles. From only these descriptions, cabin groups select what adventures they are most keen to experience for themselves and vie for a high enough score in that night’s Evening Program to earn them a top pick. When the dust clears, campers are not told what experience awaits them, that is, until a wizard/mad scientist/ secret agent/kooky aunt shows up the next day, starting the storyline - and that’s when the real magic begins. Twenty cabins are launched on twenty different adventures. • Pine 2 was handed a mission to infiltrate enemy territory to steal back a treasured artifact. • Manzi 3 came face to face with an eccentric man who has recreated dinosaurs and has invited them on a ‘perfectly safe’ tour of his facility. • Cedar 1 stumbled into an old-fashioned saloon only to discover the chips they are betting with are months and • years of their life. Oak 5 was delightfully tormented by a family vacation where really no one could have predicted the lost baggage, terrible tour guide or third alligator attack. Story Experiences are the ultimate world of pretend, with incredible props, plot twists, and ambiance built in to create as immersive of an experience as possible. Campers aren’t just swept along, but actively steer, shift and pull the ending of their story as pivotal characters in the action. No matter how old the campers are, Story Experiences reignite a camper’s ability to ‘know’ that what is happening isn’t real and yet still feel completely wrapped up in the outcome. Whether the story is haunting, daring, silly, or magical, the unique mark each cabin leaves on a storyline means no two stories end up the same. In over twenty years of camp, we have had thousands of unique experiences run and we can’t wait to see what stories we can add to our collection next summer. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about our summer program, family camps, and [article reference] can be found at www.campaugusta.org.
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Step Into a story at Camp Augusta
