On the first full day of camp, campers are greeted at breakfast with a booklet listing off dozens of potential Story Experiences with only one mysterious line of description to clue them into what may await them on the other side. • Look out! Bandits! – First they came for gold. Then they came for land. Now they’ve come for your counselor • Murphy Family Vacation – Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong • Jurassic Park – You are no longer the King • A Simple Boat Ride… I Hope Nothing Happens – *wink* • Play Your Cards Right – The Devil you know is better than the Devil you don’t All this……and 50 more titles. From only these descriptions, cabin groups select what adventures they are most keen to experience for themselves and vie for a high enough score in that night’s Evening Program to earn them a top pick. When the dust clears, campers are not told what experience awaits them, that is, until a wizard/mad scientist/ secret agent/kooky aunt shows up the next day, starting the storyline - and that’s when the real magic begins. Twenty cabins are launched on twenty different adventures. • Pine 2 was handed a mission to infiltrate enemy territory to steal back a treasured artifact. • Manzi 3 came face to face with an eccentric man who has recreated dinosaurs and has invited them on a ‘perfectly safe’ tour of his facility. • Cedar 1 stumbled into an old-fashioned saloon only to discover the chips they are betting with are months and • years of their life. Oak 5 was delightfully tormented by a family vacation where really no one could have predicted the lost baggage, terrible tour guide or third alligator attack. Story Experiences are the ultimate world of pretend, with incredible props, plot twists, and ambiance built in to create as immersive of an experience as possible. Campers aren’t just swept along, but actively steer, shift and pull the ending of their story as pivotal characters in the action. No matter how old the campers are, Story Experiences reignite a camper’s ability to ‘know’ that what is happening isn’t real and yet still feel completely wrapped up in the outcome. Whether the story is haunting, daring, silly, or magical, the unique mark each cabin leaves on a storyline means no two stories end up the same. In over twenty years of camp, we have had thousands of unique experiences run and we can’t wait to see what stories we can add to our collection next summer. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about our summer program, family camps, and [article reference] can be found at www.campaugusta.org.

articles.text: Freshman Skylar Best only athlete to qualify for State Piedmont’s boys’ cross-country team placed fifth out of 18 schools at the North Coast Section Championship at Hayward High on Saturday, November 1. The girls’ team finished eighth in a field of 15 schools. Although neither team qualified for the CIF State meet at Woodward Park of Fresno on Saturday, November 26, freshman Skylar Best will represent the school after qualifying for State with a time of 19:24.27. She placed 11th in a field of 110 runners. She was fourth overall among individual runners not on teams that qualified for State. “I feel really good, I’m really proud because of how hard I trained throughout the season. It all paid off. My strategy was to come out fast with the front group and see how close I could stay with them,” said Best. She’s been the lead runner on the team since the first week of the season. Classmate Cora Chun was 26th overall with a time of 20:13.19, an improvement of 22 seconds. Junior Jamie Schwarz in 51st in 21:17.82, Elia Kwong, a third freshman runner, was 55th in 21:28.60, and sophomore Ella Yasar was 59th with a time of 21:45.04, 53 seconds faster than her time from two weeks earlier at the WACC championship “I’m really proud of my team and how we’ll we’re doing, we really support each other. We’re all pretty close and I just really enjoy spending time with them. It’s really fun and we work really hard together, I’m really excited for the next four years because I think we’re just going to keep improving,” said Best. PHS BOYS Over to the boys, they finished fifth with 137 points behind Acalanes and Archie Williams of San Anselmo. “The boys were devastated but faced troubles with illness this season. This group, particularly our four-year team seniors, have been instrumental in shaping the work ethic of our team and made strong impact on our program for years to come,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. Staff Photos Skylar Best finished 11th of 110 runners with a personal best time of 19:24.27. Her time was good enough to qualify for the CIF State Championship. Freshman Cora Chun Chun finished in 26th overall with a time of 20:13.19, a 22 second personal record. Piedmont had four runners place 21st through 24th out of 128 runners. Senior Parker Long was first of the group with a time of 16:16.36, running alongside junior Xander Schulte-Sasse with a near identical time. Senior Christian Taylor came in five seconds later in 16:21.04 and junior Julien Lee was one second after in 16:22.31. Sophomore Evan Byun was 47th in 17:07.18. NEXT UP Piedmont’s Skylar Best will compete in the State Championship for the first time, completing as an individual runner. The meet takes place at Woodward Park this Saturday, November 26. Parker Long (left), Xander Schulte-Sasse, and Parker Lonng (back) make their way to the finish line.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team competed in a preseason scrimmage at Oakland Tech on Wednesday, November 16, drawing 0-0 with the Bulldogs. Despite the scoreless tie, the Highlanders looked strong defensively and had moments on the attack as they executed coach Todd Sullivan’s high-pressing style well. Piedmont controlled possession and dominated the midfield but couldn’t find the finishing touch in the attacking third. “We just want to be a little more connected from the midfield to the forwards, I felt there a little bit of a disconnect there. We got into good positions but couldn’t capitalize on them. I’d like to see the quality improve when we get into those areas; if we can improve our quality, it could’ve been three or four goals for us,” said Sullivan. With 14 player graduating The scrimmage offered a look at Piedmont’s attack alongside striker Aiden Woolwine. last season, Piedmont will obviously take time to build chemistry in several departments. The attack, for example, will have new forwards alongside striker Aiden Woolwine, the Post’s Honorable Mention pick for 2022 Sophomore of the Year last season. Attackers like Sam Shelby, HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY Owen Grippando, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, and Evan Manolis all contributed on Wednesday. “I love who I have next to me,” said Woolwine. “There is a lot of pace up there, it’s wonderful. The people we have are great.” Piedmont had seven shots with two on target against the Bulldogs. Their defense, meanwhile, limited Oakland Tech to no clear looks at goal. “We have a lot of speed in high and wide areas. We’re going to try and use that to exploit those areas to create our chances from those positions,” said Sullivan. In the midfield, senior T.J. O’Neil will wear the captain’s armband and will take over the role of former captain Andre Stankiewicz last year, holding a presence in the middle. “We’ve only had two practices before tonight, we have a lot of new players on the team so we’re just building that connection. It’ll take time but the pieces are there, we have a good foundation. We just have to keep working on the final pieces and that will come with more practice,” said O’Neil. Piedmont was the much stronger side in the first half, drawing five corners due to their high amount of pressure in Oakland Tech’s half. Woolwine had a shot trail wide in the 11th minute, while midfielder William Daniels skied an attempt in the 17th. Soren Dixon had a header from a corner go on target in the 18th, while Daniels connected

articles.text: Staff Photos Tanya Kononova finished fourth in the Div. 2 North Coast Section tennis singles championship. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team traveled 300 miles to McKinleyville for the Division 2 North Coast Section singles and doubles tennis championship tournament on November 14-15. Two players qualified in singles along with three doubles teams. Tanya Kononova and Carolina Romanczuk competed in the singles bracket, with Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini, Emma Eisemon and Cecilia DeFazio, and sisters Anne and Kate Jumper competing in doubles. Kononova, who recently won the League singles championship and was named WACC’ Player of the Year, finished fourth at NCS after reaching the semifinals. The teams of Eisemon and DeFazio, and the Jumper sisters all advanced to the second round, “We had a good tournament. All three doubles teams had some good matches and played well. In singles, Tanya entered as the fifth seed and defeated the fourth seed in the quarterfinals easily and then lost in the semifinals to the first seed,” said coach Jim Landes. Kononova opened the tournament with a 6-1, 6-0 win over Ella Franzese of St, Mary’s, and beat No. 4 seed Eloise Sent of Marin Academy 6-2, 6-1 in the quarterfinals. She lost 6-2, 6-1 to Berean Christian’s Vivian Galloway in the second third round, and in the battle for third place, Kononova lost to Branson’s Anna Rende for the second time, 6-2, 6-3. Nonetheless, it marked a successful debut season for Kononova, a junior who came to Piedmont as a refugee from Ukraine in late summer. She was undefeated in all league matches on her way to the WACC singles title. “I had a great time this season, I thought I would do so much worse at the start of the season and things went so well,” she said. “I’ve learned to let go of things after I lose. I’m enjoying Piedmont; it gets better as I get to know more people and I get used to how things go here. It makes me feel better,” said Kononova. Also in the singles bracket, Romanczuk lost 6-0, 6-2 to Convent’s Anoushka Dadlani. “Carolina lost a tough one to a very steady player. She had a very strong season,” said Landes. In the doubles’ bracket, sisters Anne (senior) and Kate (freshman) Jumper made their first appearance as a team to close Anne’s tennis career at Piedmont High. In the first round, the duo defeated Cardinal Newman’s Suzanna Huxtrum and Sophia Manville in straight sets, 6-3, 6-2. In the second round, they fell 6-0, 6-1 to Lick-Wilmerding’s Alexa DiSabato and Emilia Sisters Anne (pictured) and Kate Jumper were doubles partners in the North Coast Section tennis championships. Junior Cecilia DeFazio (front) and sophomore Emma Eisemon advanced to the second round of doubles at the NCS post-season playoffs. Ozer-Staton. “It was really fun to play with Kate. First of all, I was excited to have her on the team this year given I got to play with her and spend more time with her. It was really a treat being able to cap off my high school career alongside her. We weren’t going into the tournament expecting to win, but it was a lot of fun being able to play together,” said older sister Anne. “It went all full circle because we were always playing as kids, so it was nice to have a send-off for the season being together again. We’ll probably play again, but it was nice to have that last tennis moment together,” added Kate. Also at doubles, Eisemon and DeFazio won their first-round match 6-2, 6-2 over Arcata’s Meta Nave and Kloee Donnelly. In the second round, they lost 7-5, 6-0 to Arcata’s Keona Gutierrez DeArmond and Kyra Alway. Also competing were LaForte and Bini, who fell to DeArmond and Always in the first round, 6-3, 6-2.

articles.text: Those familiar with the extraordinary two-decade success of Piedmont High School’s tennis program will nod in approval when they first see a new sign on the fence above the city’s principal tennis court at Vista and Bonita Avenue. The sign, Rothenberg Heights, is dedicated to longtime tennis coach Neil Rothenberg, who retired a couple of years ago from active coaching. But he shows up match after match to watch the players and cheer them on. “I would always sit up here on the trash cans so I could see all four courts. For years, everyone knew this was my perch up here. This was always the best vantage point, so if I could see something going on, I could go down [and make the necessary adjustments],”said Rothenberg. With the renaming of the courts as the Corey Reich Tennis Center in November 2021, Rothenberg was unaware of the sign after the school’s tennis season was underway. “It had plastic over it. The wind picked up one day and all of a sudden, I could see “Rothenberg.” You know, it’s kind of cool, with gold lettering and the medallion. But I had no idea they were planning it, I think Shahan [Soghikian] was flying under the radar on this. He kept things very low-key,” said Rothenberg. In addition to the commemoration of Rothenberg, Soghikian helped fundraise for the bleachers behind Court 4 and benches along Bonita Avenue. “Two of our kids played tennis with Neil and Corey,” explained Soghikian. “Going back to 2006, there’s a probably a couple of things you would recall—there was only one seating area – the bleachers by the gate. Neil would always walk up to the corner and sit on the garbage can so he could see what was going on. Neil did that as long as he coached, he’d walk up and down along the fence, but then he’d perch on the garbage can.” “When the court renovation was happening,” Soghikian continued, “there were a couple of things we pushed for – benches along the fence and the sign to recognize Neil for all of the work he put in coaching.” Rothenberg ended his tenure as head coach in 2015, helping build a State record of 19 years of undefeated league championships for the girls’ team and non-stop NCS appearances by the boys’ team. To this day, PHS holds the longest streak for consecutive NCS appearances for both boys’ and girls’ teams. “As a coach for the school, I think my favorite moments were working with kids who had some issues going on and helping them navigate to have a great experience in school,” said Rothenberg. Soghikian had some final comments. “Neil was a great tennis coach, but also a great life coach. I would extend that to Corey as well; they were inspirational in different ways. I think Corey’s inspiration speaks for itself with his determination every day, he gives great life lessons. I think Neil brought patience, focus, how to compete in a respectful way, being aggressive while being kind, and how to lose gracefully.” “I think both of my kids learned a lot of lessons from both Neil and Corey along the way,” said Soghikian. Rothenberg was inducted into the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame in 2018. Staff Photos Legendary Piedmont tennis coach Neil Rothenberg at his perch overlooking the tennis courts at Bonita and Vista Avenue, a location now named for him.
articles.title: The story of Rothenberg

articles.text: Kashani, Kononova named League Players of Year Piedmont High School’s’ fall sports season concluded with 25 All-League recipients representing seven teams. PHS had two athletes named :League Player of the Year: water polo goalie Dariush Kashani and tennis player Tanya Kononova in her first year at Piedmont High. Boys’ Water Polo The Boys’ Water Polo team won its second-consecutive Western Alameda County Conference Championship, finishing with a 20-7 overall record and reached the Division 2 North Coast Section Semifinals with the No. 3 seed, losing narrowly 6-5 to No. 2 Marin Academy on November 9. Goalie Dariush Kashani earned the WACC’s Player of the Year award. The squad earned six AllLeague selections, including first-team honors for Kashani and Declan Linnane. Second-team honors were awarded to Peter Krumins and George Stein, while Finn Burke and Quincy Scherman were given Honorable Mentions. Girls Tennis Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team won its first WACC Foothill title since 2018, going undefeated at 12-0 with a 16-3 overall record. They reached the semifinals of the Division 2 NCS Team Championship tournament, falling 4-3 to Branson on November 12. Tanya Kononova was named the WACC’s Player of the Year after winning the league tournament’s singles bracket when defeating Alameda’s Juliana Johnson 6-3, 7-5. The squad earned five AllLeague, including Kononova at singles, while Anne Jumper and Carolina Romanczuk received honorable mentions as singles starters as well. Michaela Bini and Mara LaForte earned AllLeague selections at doubles. Cross Country Piedmont’s boys’ team finished as the No. 2 ranked team at the League Championship at Hayward High on November 5, outscored narrowly by Berkeley. The boys’ earned three first-team selections with senior Christian Taylor finishing third of 71 runners with a time of 15:43.51, junior Xander Schulte-Sasse was fifth in 15:46.92, while senior Parker Long placed sixth, clocking a 15:59.07. The girls’ team placed fourth of seven schools at the WACC Finals and received two AllLeague selections. Freshman Skylar Best earned first-team honors by finishing fourth of 59 runners with a time of 19:25.22, while junior Jamie Schwarz placed 16th in 20:27.05. Girls Water Polo PHS’ girls’ water polo team finished with an 8-11 overall record and finished fifth-place at the WACC Tournament on October 25 by defeating Berkeley in double overtime 13-12. The squad earned four AllLeague selections, including Rosie Feldman and Katarina Melian to the second-team while Annika Nilsson and Friedie Schickendanz were honorable mentions. Girls Volleyball The girls’ volleyball team finished with a 10-14 overall record, which was a considerable improvement from their 3-12 finish in 2021. The team received four All-League selections, including Eden Lorin with firstteam honors, Sadie Town earned a second-team honors, while Bree DeYoung and Klara Zietlow were honorable mentions. Girls Golf Piedmont’s girls’ golf team placed third in the WACC Tournament for the second consecutive year. Sophomore Mai Assalian earned first-team honors Staff photos Mai Assalian earned first-team All-League honors for the girls’ golf team. by finishing eighth at the Monarch Bay Golf Course on October 17 in San Leandro. Assalian went on to place 30th out of 120 golfers at the NCS Championship at Petaluma’s Rooster Run Golf Club on October 24 after shooting a 92. articles.text: Chad Ironside’s Piedmont Rec Soccer team “PSC Barca” took first place in a local Under-17 tournament last weekend, beating the East Bay United Panthers and Alameda Falcons to set up a showdown with the Montclair Stingers in the final. Most of the Barca squad are only 14 or 15, but they outplayed their rivals and held on to win 1-0. “They are a rag-tag bunch, but for six years Chad has taught them the game. They played with heart, skill and grit. Now they have something no one can take away. We couldn’t be more proud of them,” said Assistant coach Neil McKee. articles.text: Photo by Andrew Dunkley A visitor to San Francisco Museum of Modern Art views Nam June Paik’s “Sistine Chapel,” created in 1993. An exhibit titled Contemporary Optics currently is on view at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and will be available for viewing through December 11. Featuring the work of three artists, Olafur Eliasson, Teresita Fernández, and Anish Kapoor, the exhibition expands on color theory developed by painters in the 1960s. The artists use color and light in sculpture. The most widely recognized is Eliasson’s “One Way Color Tunnel,” (2007) a 34-foot-long colorful archway that mimics a kaleidoscope. “Eliasson’s practice is driven by research on human perception and behavior,” explained SFMOMA Curatorial Assistant of Painting and Sculpture Sara Wessen Chang. “The sculptures actively engage the viewer in a sensory experience – triggering a heightened state of awareness and responsibility with regards to our surroundings, specifically the climate.” Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/contemporary-optics/ to learn more. articles.text: After-hours access to museum on December 2 Visit Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) every Friday night for free activities, live music and food truck options on the lawn. “Friday Nights at OMCA” takes place every Friday from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m. at the museum. An assortment of food trucks parked along 10th street between Oakland and Fallon Streets, with food variety changes weekly. Activities and music will be available on the museum’s outdoor lawn space. Use your museum ticket to gain after-hours access to the museum or bring a blanket and enjoy music on the lawn for free. Oakland-based landscape architect and MacArthur Genius award-winner Walter Hood, with architecture firm Mark Cavagnero Associates, led the lawn project design. Renovations were funded by the “All In! The Campaign for OMCA,” which was undertaken to expand OMCA’s role in the community as a public gathering place. The lawn offers direct access to Lake Merritt. articles.text: Movie to be shown concurrently with music San Francisco Symphony will perform the music score of How the Grinch Stole Christmas on December 16 and 17. San Francisco Symphony will perform the music from the movie How the Grinch Stole Christmas in two performances next month, Friday and Saturday, December 16 and 17. The film, directed by Ron Howard with music by James Horner, is a vibrant 2000 adaption of the Dr. Seuss classic. The symphony orchestra will perform the score as the film is being shown – a rare treat for audiences at the Louise M. Davies Symphony Hall. This modern, live-action adaptation still features the reclusive green Grinch, played by Jim Carrey, and all the citizens of Whoville, including Cindy Lou Who. This concert is designed for families of all ages. Joshua Gersen leads the orchestra in both performances. Gersen served as assistant conductor of the New York Philharmonic, where he made his subscription debut in 2017. He has appeared as guest conductor for the Chicago Symphony and Detroit Symphony. To purchase tickets, visit: https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2022-23/How-theGrinch-Stole-Christmas ®
articles.title: SF Symphony to perform music from How the Grinch Stole Christmas

articles.text: Piedmont guitarist and bluesman Jules Leyhe and The Family Jules Band will return to the Sound Room in downtown Oakland this Saturday, November 26, for an 8 p.m. show. Leyhe has shared the stage with blues guitar legends Buddy Guy and Jimmie Vaughan, and has appeared in Guitar Player magazine multiple times, including in the August and September issues in an interview with fellow blues guitarist Taj Mahal. A Berklee College of Music grad who focused on blues and slide Piedmont guitarist Jules Leyhe’s band will perform a show this weekend at The Sound Room in downtown Oakland. guitar, Leyhe has performed with Jimmy Vivino, Fantastic Negrito, has played the National Anthem at the Oakland Coliseum, and been featured in Guitar Player, Premier Guitar, and Vintage Guitar magazines. His album “Your First Rodeo” is a whimsical mashup of blues, hip-hop, fusion, rock and Latin music. Conceived and constructed using vivid fantasy, the Berklee grad imagined what it would sound like to pair signature elements from diametrically opposed artists. Performing with Leyhe at the Sound Room will be Ian McArdle on keyboard, Isaac Schwartz on drums, Andrew Couttie on bass guitar, with guest vocalist Libby Lavella. Tickets are $24 to $28, and are available at https://www. eventbr ite.com /e/jules-leyhe-the-family-jules-band-tickets-446829758837. The Sound Room is at 3022 Broadway in Oakland. Phone (510) 708-9691. (https://www. soundroom.org/).

articles.text: The Marcus Shelby Orchestra will perform Duke Ellington’s Nutcracker Suite in Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz on Friday, December 2. Bassist, composer, and arranger Marcus Shelby modeled his Orchestra after Duke Ellington’s and cites the jazz luminary as an inspiration for him musically. Shelby is best-known for his major works for jazz orchestra, Port Chicago, Harriet Tubman, Soul of the Movement: Meditations on Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., and Beyond the Blues: A Prison Oratorio. He has served as Artist in Residence at Yerba Buena Gardens Festival in San Francisco and Composer in Residence at Intersection for Arts. He was appointed to the San Francisco Arts Commission in 2013. He and his orchestra are regular performers at SF Jazz. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. To purchase tickets to the Friday night performance visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/marcus-shelby-orchestra-ellingtons-nutcracker2/ Bass player Marcus Shelby

articles.text: Call the opera Orphée, Orfeo, or, like the SF Opera, Orpheus and Eurydice. Whatever the name, the production here offers breakthroughs in many directions – a dazzling feast of primary colors and lighting, acrobatic dancers, a goddess descending from heaven on a swing, and the most nimble of males ever in the title role. This reprise of Gluck’s early classical-period opus in this memorable new production is a feast for ears and eyes, despite the severe dramatic limitation of having merely three solo singers. This breakthrough suggests a stunning staging ability at the 90-year old War Memorial Opera House, which shows future producers what can be done in this venerable hall with its stage machinery greatly updated since its floppy-canvas beginnings. Whatever limitations there were in the other voices, nothing could ever top the most memorable Orpheus ever heard here, the Polish countertenor Jakub Jozef Orlinski. With his soaring (presumably amplified) high voice, he could project the score handsomely (from the Vienna He sang the opera’s bestknown aria, “What will I do without Eurydice?” while the dancers played out the famous “Dance of the Blessed Spirits.” (The noted “Dance of the Furies” was omitted, as it first appeared 12 years after the Vienna premiere.) Composer Christoph Willibald Gluck altered the ancient Greek legend of the famous doomed lovers by appending a happy ending, with the goddess Amore pardoning Orpheus for his disobedience and bringing the twice-dead Eurydice back to life to join her disconsolate devoted husband. In the opening sequence, I thought it was all Election Day reenactment, given the vigorously athletic dancers’ red and blue outfits. But no, it was just the wild, eye-popping color scheme under director Matthew Ozawa and choreographer Rena Butler, helped by lighting wizard Alexander V. Nichols. All so bright, we should probably have worn sunglasses. The six lead dancers, who between them could make up a viable gymnastics team, were so versatile, they were given separate credits in the printed program. Countertenor Jakub Jozef Orlinski was brilliant in the role of Orpheus with San Francisco Opera on November 18. premiere of 1762) without transpositions in a seamless clarion voice, as well as shimmy, dance, even wheel and tumble on stage like break dancers. Perhaps we can shelve for good having tenors and mezzos step in, subbing for the thoroughly male title role. Playing the huge dominant part, Orlinski put in the shade the other Orfeos previously in memory or circulation, whether in Gluck, Monteverdi or other operatic versions.

articles.text: Bees are drawn to flowers, bears are drawn to honey, and kids are drawn to the candy shop. Violinists are drawn to violins. That was the scene in Orange County for a full week. The numbers speak for themselves: 300 violin makers, 500 Violins on display. To accompany the violins were enough bows to equip all the archers of the Second Crusade. Wouldn’t King Richard the Lion Heart be happy? But it wasn’t all fun and games at the convention. The makers attended lectures on history and geography. There was a most important one on ecology. It concerned the preservation of Brazil’s Pernambuco forests – that’s the best wood for violin bows. Governments and environmentalists are imposing restrictions. But the real problem is not the violin bow makers. They use very little material. The real problem is organized crime and population growth. There was even a class on publicity and salesmanship. Why was Stradivarius so famous? He was a master of publicity and salesmanship. Oh sure, he was a great violin maker also. But P & S made him famous. Part of the allure for musicians from all over was the convention itself. The other part was the competition. Prizes were awarded for the best tone quality and also for the best workmanship. Three local violin makers were awarded top prizes – Haide Lin, Artur Friedhof and Jay Ifshin of the Ifshin violin shop in El Cerrito. Many of the instruments were sold during the convention. That was the case for the instruments made by Lin. Jay Ifshin has developed his own line of instruments which are known for excellent craftsmanship and tone and available at a very reasonable price. An experienced violin maker of the past always said that young players should have young instruments. In this way both of them mature together. Artur Friedhof’s viola will be heard in the Diluvian Quartet concert on December 4 at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Classical music is a niche market. But it is an enthusiastic one… and is truly international.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre (Berkeley Rep) reimagines Emily Brontë’s gothic masterpiece Wuthering Heights in a new play by Emma Rice. The play premiered on November 18 and will be performed through January 1. The 1847 novel tells the story of the Earnshaws and Lintons, two families living on the West Yorkshire moors, and the compelling relationship between the characters Catherine and Heathcliff. Heathcliff is rescued from the Liverpool docks as a young child, adopted by the Earnshaws and taken to live at Wuthering Heights. He strikes a friendship with Catherine Earnshaw and soon a fierce love ignites. Leah Brotherhead is cast as Catherine. She has performed in Gulliver’s Travels (Unicorn Theatre), Lands (Bush Theatre/ Summer Hall Edinburgh Fringe), and Two Gentlemen of Verona (The Globe Theatre/Liverpool Everyman). Liam Tamne, also with an extensive discography, plays Heathcliff. His theater credits include The Prince of Egypt (Dominion Theatre), and Bonnie and Clyde (Theatre Royal Drury Lane). A post-show discussion on Thursday, December 8, and Tuesday, December 13, will allow audience members to ask questions of the Berkeley Rep staff and actors. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/wuthering-heights/. Photo by Steve Tanner The Emily Bronte classic, Wuthering Heights, is being performed by Berkeley Rep through the end of December.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s Wuthering Heights on stage through December

Peter Whelan’s mostly-strings orchestra was the ready collaborator. In less prominent roles were soprano Meigui Zhang (Eurydice) and Nicole Heaston (the golden goddess Amore, on a swing lowered from heaven). Zhang paired amiably in the duet with Orpheus. Above all, the opera’s message dwells on indecisiveness of the male character, feminine insecurity, and isolation, the latter with the first half-hour showing the lonely Orpheus on stage, meandering about the bier of the expired bride Eurydice. Even though coming from myth, the emotions here ring true millennia later. 30

articles.text: Aurora Theatre premiered Colonialism is Terrible, but Pho is Delicious and ends on Friday, December 4. It is the first play in the company’s 31st season. Dustin Chinn’s newest play, directed by Oanh Nguyen, takes inspiration from two viral moments about cultural appropriation and food: Chef Tyler Akin’s how-to video for Bon Appetit, “PSA: This is How You Should Be Eating Pho,” and Dan Pashman of The Sporkful’s suggestion that you could improve bibimbap, a popular Korean dish, using a bundt pan. Regarding the play’s inspiration, Chinn said he “followed the rabbit hole and wrote a triptych about the ownership and authorship of food following the journey of Vietnamese noodle soup [pho].” The comedy begins in 1880’s Hanoi, Vietnam with a Vietnamese cook who finds herself in the kitchen of wealthy French aristocracy. Then the play jumps to 1999, where Americans taste the culinary fixtures of Vietnam for the first time. Finally, Colonialism is Terrible ends in gentrified Brooklyn, where Photo by Kevin Berne Nicole Tung (left), Anthony Doan and Elissa Beth Stebbins in Aurora Theatre’s current production of Colonialism Is Terrible, But Pho Is Delicious. cultural appropriation and disagreements boil. “Dustin Chinn has built this story from a delightful array of ingredients: witty comedy, an exploration of charged ideas around authenticity and cultural appropriation, and a theatrical approach to language that powerfully centers the Vietnamese characters,” said Aurora Theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello. “It’s been a joy to host [director Nguyen] at Aurora, and to listen to the laughter he draws from cast and crew throughout the process.” A post-show discussion with the cast, playwright and director will follow performances on select dates. To learn more and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.auroratheatre.org/index. php/shows-events/20222023- season /colonialism-is-ter rible-but-pho-is-delicious. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, November 23, 2022 Michael Stehr art exhibit opens Dec. 2 at PCA Sailboat at Lake Tahoe, oil on canvas, 25ʺx31ʺ. Local artist Michael Stehr will open his newest exhibition, entitled “Lost in the Shadows,” at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, December 2. The exhibit includes 42 new paintings, and 80 total works of art, and will be on display through December 18. Stehr will use some of his new paintings to explore the power of shadow in painting. While it is light that often contributes animation and luminosity to a composition, it is the absence of this light, shadow, that makes the presence of that light much more tangible. Without light, there cannot be shadow. But without shadow, the effect of light is greatly mitigated. Indeed, the two must work hand in hand, for it is the contrasts between bright and dark values, light and shadow, that do much to provide visual interest to a painting. Stehr will be describe some of this at the December 2 show opening that will develop the idea of the importance of shadow, while going into the technical devices he uses to articulate the absence of light. articles.text: Daniel Craig (center) stars in Defiance. Some critics have proffered that Holocaust films have become a genre, rather than stand-alone works that use the Holocaust as a context to ponder greater questions about the human condition. Film critic Richard Corliss recently pointed out that there are instances in history where far more people were killed than in the Holocaust: the Great Leap Forward in China (close to 30 million), Russia starving the people of Ukraine (10 million). Yet the Holocaust remains the quintessential archetype of evil and an enduring symbol of man’s inhumanity to man. The question, then, is, Why? Perhaps, unlike other horrific events that have occurred – in the killing fields of Cambodia, Congo, Darfur and Somalia – the German’s Final Solution was, as Corliss points out, deliberate, premeditated and chillingly precise in its plan and execution. Why is it that filmmakers and writers have found in the Holocaust a rich cache of material regarding the nature of evil and the inexplicable absence of a defining morality? What better medium than film to explore the darkest parts of the human soul while begging the question as to why it recurs with such predictability. Films about the Holocaust will continue to be made and should be. While Shindler’s List is a work of art, it is also a stark reminder of what occurred while possessing the embedded admonition that we must never forget, an admonition on a large sign at the entrance to the Nazi camp at Dachau. The films made about the Holocaust, though open to the criticism of being exploitive and even gratuitous, will always be worth the risk. Regarding Defiance, the film opens with grainy, documentary-like footage of German soldiers systematically rounding up and executing Jews. These initial scenes quickly set up the tale of the Bielski brothers, Tuvia (Daniel Craig) and Zus (Liev Schreiber), who take refuge in the forests of Belorussia and are soon joined by hundreds of other Jews, desperate to escape the lethal German juggernaut. Eventually, more than 1,200 men, women and children will hide, forming an ad hoc community that is hunted continuously, until finally liberated by the Russians in 1944. At the heart of the film is the dilemma, framed by Friedrich Nietzsche, when he wrote, “If you gaze long into the abyss, the abyss will gaze back into you.” In other words, if Tuvia and his band of brothers and sisters become too much like their Nazi pursuers will they eventually become the very thing they so deeply despise? As a revenge-resistance film, had the brothers, and those men who joined them, become a cadre of guerilla fighters waging a remorseless war against the Germans, it might have been more satisfying – ambushes, raids and a high German body count. But as a story about a people who struggled with the question of the abyss and yet still prevailed, it is far more interesting. Defiance is a tale that heretofore was likely unknown. Thankfully, the courage of these people, led by Tuvia and Zus Bielski, has now been told and can be added to that archive which asks us to never forget. Defiance. Directed by Edward Zwick. Starring Daniel Craig, Liev Schreiber, Jamie Bell and Alexa Davlos. 2 hrs., 16 min. Rated R. Released in 2009. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Defiance a remarkable story of courage, morality during the Holocaust

articles.text: Keir Gilchrist, Zach Galifianakis, Lauren Graham and Emma Roberts in It’s Kind of a Funny Story. Review by Chris Honoré It’s supremely difficult to make a good movie about adolescents. It’s the equivalent of trying to capture lightening in a bottle: years of emotional riptides, dramatic changes, layered with confusion and clarity and idealism. Which is why so many Hollywood teen movies seem shallow, trivial, and too often buried beneath an avalanche of stereotypes and clichés. Unexpectedly, It’s Kind of a Funny Story gets it just about right. It’s sweet and poignant, certainly relevant, and it’s aimed directly at young people who should instantly recognize the existential crisis of 16-year-old Craig (Keir Gilchrist) who is definitely one of their own. Craig, nudged by depression (he’s seeing a therapist, taking some Zoloft), feeling overwhelmed by the pressures of high school and the expectations of his parents, and stalked by thoughts of suicide, heads toward the George Washington bridge in New York one morning, contemplating jumping off. Instead he detours to Argeron Hospital, in Brooklyn, and, after a cryptic conversations with one of the Docs, unwittingly checks himself into the psych ward. Because the children’s ward is closed for renovations, he finds himself among the general population and quickly realizes – whoops! — perhaps it would be better if he just, like, went home. No harm, no foul. Plus, well, he’s got school the next day and a paper is due. But he soon learns that he is there for a five-day evaluation. His parents, as it turns out, agree, and thus begins Craig’s very strange and enlightening odyssey. Writers and directors Ryan Fleck and Anna Boden walk a precarious line between the dark tragedies that define severe mental illness and the comedic and the light-hearted moments encountered by Craig as he navigates the ward. He is mentored, in a touching and heartfelt way, by Bobby (Zach Galifianakis), who has a wife and young daughter, and who not only has suicide ideation, but has tried to kill himself several times. And of course there is a love interest, Noelle (Emma Roberts), who is hospitalized because she is a cutter. Craig is also gently guided and helped by the resident psychiatrist, Dr. Minerva (Viola Davis), who gives him increasing support and insight as he sorts out his feelings. While watching the relationship between Craig and Noelle grow, as they reach out to one another for understanding and tentative love, it begs an interesting question: can adolescents truly help one another through their long and often painful rite of passage? The answer is probably yes - and no. The fact is that turning to one another is the default response of most teenagers to the exigencies of growing up. Adults, in contrast, have to tenaciously insert themselves into the lives of adolescents, no matter the reflexive resistance – which is what happens to Craig, in a kind of a wonderful way during his remarkable five days on the ward. It’s Kind of a Funny Story would be a great movie to see with a teenager, a son or daughter, hopefully resulting in a conversation post-screening. Know that the film strikes just the right note between the realities of teen suicide (much in the news of late), and the ability of a young, intelligent kid to realize that the gestalt of emotions that seem so perplexing and contradictory can ultimately be understood and dealt with. It’s Kind of a Funny Story. Starring Keir Gilchrist, Emma Roberts, Zoe Kravitz, Zach Galifianakis and Viola Davis. Written and directed by Ryan Fleck and Anna Boden. 1 hr. 41 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDUU/Prime/ Apple tv.
articles.title: It’s Kind of a Funny Story a wonderful film for older teens

articles.text: Photo by Melissa Rivers Santa Claus shown visiting last year’s Montclair Village Holiday Stroll Montclair Village celebrates its 20th Annual Holiday Stroll on Thursday, December 8, from 5:30-8:30 p.m. The heart of the event is located at 2050 Mountain Boulevard with local artists, professional photos with Santa, giant puppets, children’s crafts and activities, Oakland Fire Department’s big rig and toy drive, choirs and live music performances, libations, and holiday shopping at more than 40 businesses. Highlights: • Winter Wonderland including professional photos with Santa. • Giant Puppets by a collaboration of puppeteers, builders, and performance artists. • Live performances with local youth and school groups including Pacific Boychoir Academy, Jazz Education Ensemble, Edna Brewer Band Carolers, and Montera Cheer Squad. • Holiday entertainment provided by The Tap Dancing Christmas Trees, Oakland Ballet, and Renegade Orchestra. • Special discounts and promotions offered at over 40 locally-owned, independent merchants who stay open late to greet guests with music, food, and drinks. • Opportunity to donate to Oakland Fire Department’s Random Acts Toy Drive. Decked out in bright lights and cheerful decorations, Mountain Boulevard and Antioch Court will welcome visitors. Santa will be there for family keepsake photos with kids. Adults will enjoy delicious food and libations while visiting shops that will be open until 8:30 p.m. As a special feature, Oakland’s famous Tap Dancing Christmas Trees return with their choreographic tap dance routines in tree costumes. More information is available at MontclairVillage.com.
articles.title: Montclair Village Holiday Stroll returns for 20th year

articles.text: T he Pied mont Sen iors recently collected a record amount of toys for the Fire Department’s annual Toys for Tots drive, filling two large bins. The toy drive has been strongly supported for the 26 years the Seniors group has been in existence since 1996. The Seniors also are active contributors to the “Socks for Seniors” program, in which they provide pairs of socks which, according to Pastor Ned MacDonnell, who was on hand to pick up the socks, are distributed to the “poorest of the poor” in Oakland nursing homes. These pairs of socks are usually the only gifts the seniors in these nursing homes will receive during the holiday season and are the most requested items on their wish lists. Members of the Piedmont Seniors group gather at a recent meeting to make donations to the Piedmont Fire Department’s annual Toys for Tots drive and to the Socks for Seniors program.
articles.title: Piedmont Seniors take lead in donating for the holidays

articles.text: Walnut Creek garden & nursery offers free admission The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek is partnering with the global movement “Giving Tuesday” by offering free admission to everyone next Tuesday, November 29. Bancroft Gardens is a preservation project of The Garden Conservancy. The mission of the nonprofit is to preserve and expand its collection of water-conserving plants for the education and enjoyment of the public. The Giving Tuesday campaign was created in 2012 and encourages individuals and businesses to give back to their communities. The Garden, a local nonprofit, is giving back by allowing free entry to the gardens between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. Visit the garden on November 29 and tour the many examples of garden design with drought-tolerant plants, hailing from desert and Mediterranean climates. Visit https://www.ruthbanc rof tga rde n.org /eve nt /g iving-tuesday-2/ to learn more about the event.
articles.title: Bancroft Gardens to participate in Giving Tuesday on Nov. 29

articles.text: Piedmont volunteers at Peralta Hacienda: Mike Adams (left), Dana Low, Debra Constantine, Patty Reed, Mary Ireland, Holly Hanke, Christiana Macfarlane, Susan Hill, Lisa Dell’Osso, Cathy Glazier, Jan Zovickian, Lori Adams, tommy Adams, Lindsey Meyersieck, Holly Alonso, Rich Leon, Jean Jarvis, Gayle Lambert, Scott Lambert, and Taos and Jesse Hadden. On a sunny Saturday, 10 wheelbarrows, 15 rakes, 12 shovels, and 30 people turned 34 cubic yards of wood chips and over 6,000 square feet of cardboard into a tidy, sheet-mulched garden, ready for winter planting. Wearing “Dressed for Success” shirts from Rebuilding Together Oakland, a mighty team of volunteers from Piedmont Garden Club, Peralta Hacienda, California Bank and Trust, and RTO performed like a symphony of gardeners. Just as each orchestra instrument is essential, each volunteer team carried out an important job. The cardboard “quality controllers”, operating under time pressure, removed tape and labels; the “installers” laid cardboard on the ground, overlapping seams & cutting to accommodate existing plants. The “kings & queens of the mountain” shoveled wood chips from giant piles into wheelbarrows, and the “movers” maneuvered wheelbarrows throughout the garden bed where “distributors” raked out the wood chips. Hearts were singing. Everyone was in tune, and the all-out physical effort was matched by positive, can-do attitudes. The abundant food kept everyone humming along, as did the camaraderie. And the best part? The joy felt by all for a job well done that will benefit such a deserving community. Special thanks to California Bank and Trust for providing lunch, to Rebuilding Together Oakland for providing all the tools, and to Oakland Public Jan Zovickian and Julia Burke literally dig in to help. Works and Peralta Hacienda for the many hours spent creating the log border and preparing for the sheet mulching. Piedmont Garden Club is partnering with Peralta Hacienda Historical Park to create a native plant garden at their site. The Fruitvale District has few green spaces but has the highest percentage of children of any Oakland district. In addition to community members’ help, the City of Oakland is assisting in preparing the site for planting, and representatives of the Ohlone are providing valuable input on the planting plan. Peralta Hacienda Historical Park provides a vibrant gathering space for various cultural communities in the area, and serves as a bridge between people and nature, people of different cultures, and people of different generations and different abilities. Through its ACE summer camp, teen Water Keepers year-round program, and Oakland Naturalists and Welcome to Wildlife programs, Peralta Hacienda serves more than 300 youth. Other programs focusing on the arts, cultural heritage, community gardens, and building youth leadership skills involve an additional 4,000 community members. “Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful committed citizens can change the world: indeed, it’s the only thing that ever has.” ~ Margaret Mead Gayle Lambert and her grandson, Dylan, Lori Adams.
articles.title: Community digs in to support Peralta Hacienda

By Lori Adams On a sunny Saturday, 10 wheelbarrows, 15 rakes, 12 shovels, and 30 people turned 34 cubic yards of wood chips and over 6,000 square feet of cardboard into a tidy, sheet-mulched garden, ready for winter planting. Wearing “Dressed for Success” shirts from Rebuilding Together Oakland, a mighty team of volunteers from Piedmont Garden Club, Peralta Hacienda, California Bank and Trust, and RTO performed like a symphony of gardeners. Just as each orchestra instrument is essential, each volunteer team carried out an important job. The cardboard “quality controllers”, operating under time pressure, removed tape and labels; the “installers” laid cardboard on the ground, overlapping seams & cutting to accommodate existing plants. The “kings & queens of the mountain” shoveled wood chips from giant piles into wheelbarrows, and the “movers” maneuvered wheelbarrows throughout the garden bed where “distributors” raked out the wood chips. Hearts were singing. Everyone was in tune, and the all-out physical effort was matched by positive, can-do attitudes. The abundant food kept everyone humming along, as did the camaraderie. And the best part? The joy felt by all for a job well done that will benefit such a deserving community. articles.text: Part 57 Certainly the most famous carfree city in the world is Venice, Italy. Its strategic northern position on the shores of the Adriatic Sea, within reach of the Byzantine Empire and traders from the Near East, facilitated the city in becoming the main hub of trade connecting East and West starting in the Middle Ages. This trade was the source for the wealth which financed the incredible built environment that we can see and experience there today. Although Venice with a population of over 262,000 is comprised of over one hundred islands in a shallow lagoon and extends over the water to the mainland of Italy, most people think of the pedestrian island “centro storico” (historic center) with 60,000 inhabitants as “Venice”, where there are no automobiles or roads, just pedestrian footpaths plus water taxis on the main canals. As we have discussed before, to be truly walkable a city has to be dense, with important destinations close enough to make walking efficient and convenient. In Venice most of everything is easily within easy, flat walking distance and the pedestrian “streets” themselves are a large part of the charm. They are lined with beautiful Piazza San Marco, Venice’s main public square and the heart of the city, is one of the most famous examples of Urban Design in the world. The asymmetry of the skewed colonnaded walls, the offset campanile and the sense of enclosure give this large “outdoor room” an incredible richness and interest. The size of the piazza is made especially dramatic by the narrow pedestrian streets through which you must pass for access from the city side. This traditional urban design tool, the red “figure-ground drawing” shows the relations between solid buildings and the exterior spaces formed around them—the streets, courts, canals and piazzas. (Can you spot the Piazza San Marco with campanile?) When viewed in three dimensions, another whole layer of design is revealed, such as the numerous view corridors that frame important vertical building elements as show in the sketch. The rich pedestrian street texture of Venice includes such things as the decorative, landscaped residential balconies and buildings that bridge over streets and passageways. Mixed use is everywhere.

Its strategic northern position on the shores of the Adriatic Sea, within reach of the Byzantine Empire and traders from the Near East, facilitated the city in becoming the main hub of trade connecting East and West starting in the Middle Ages. This trade was the source for the wealth which financed the incredible built environment that we can see and experience there today. As we have discussed before, to be truly walkable a city has to be dense, with important destinations close enough to make walking efficient and convenient. In Venice most of everything is easily within easy, flat walking distance and the pedestrian “streets” themselves are a large part of the charm. They are lined with beautiful multi-colored buildings and palaces of different eclectic architectural styles. And in the tangle of narrow back-paths walkers can find hidden plazas, quaint shops, and restaurants that many visitors never see. It is a real town, a real community, a real place. What impresses me as much as the pedestrian character of the island is the considered and well thought out urban design found virtually everywhere, at all different scales. I have never seen anything like this anywhere else in the world. The huge Piazza San Marco contains a number of Venice’s most famous buildings, such as the Byzantine mosaic tiled, multi-domed St. Mark’s Basilica and the “Venetian Gothic” Doge’s Palace. The square is actually an outdoor forecourt or vestibule of sorts for these incredible buildings. Napoleon called the piazza “the world’s most beautiful drawing room”. The approaches to the large piazza are the opposite – narrow and a little dark. They make the sudden arrival at this large civic space a dramatic surprise by contrast. It represents Urban Design at its finest. “Venice and its Lagoon” was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987, in recognition of its unique historical, archaeological, urban and artistic heritage and exceptional cultural traditions, integrated into an extraordinary natural landscape. And just as scientists and inventors necessarily draw on past work and past accomplishments as the building blocks of their work going forward, so, too, do architects, landscape architects, urban designers and planners in their work on the built environment. The question here is, what can we learn from Venice? What can we emulate and reasonably translate to our own cities and towns in this era? articles.text: Temporary house jacks are a short-term fix for a failing foundation. Dear Jim: I have seen problems developing in my house in the last few years, and I’m getting concerned. I’ve been getting more cracks inside, the floors are out of level, and I have some water in the crawlspace. Can you help me figure out if these problems are serious, and if so, what I need to do about them.? -George H. Are your problems serious? Starting with the pandemic, when people were hanging out at home most of the time, homeowners became focused on the issues that they never paid attention to before. A large percentage of the inquiries I have been getting started with the question “do I have anything to worry about?”, or “is this problem serious?”. Since homeowners typically do not venture down in their crawlspaces or basements where the actual evidence lies, this concern was based upon the cosmetic evidence inside the living areas of their homes. The answer depends on your timeline. For a majority of the inquiries I provide them with some degree of reassurance. Most structural issues develop slowly and are unlikely to lead to catastrophic failure. Many settlement issues are caused by drainage problems that are accelerating somewhat with climate change and erratic weather. These typically take many years, sometimes decades to develop. Small cracks are common and are not concerning. Large cracks that develop in short time frames are more problematic, but these are not the norm. The focus should be on the proper solution, not just the budget. If the problems are minor, and you may be moving in a few years, then maybe you defer the work. Simple solutions, such as directing downspouts away from your house to slow down settlement and water issues, can be helpful sometimes. The reality is that most people stay in their homes for a lot longer than they anticipate, and once they hear their house is not falling down, they tend to forget about the structural issues, which can be a mistake. Sometimes they patch Failing support piers are begging for help. together quick fixes, but over time those can cause bigger problems down the road. Many of the foundations and drainage systems in our typical 1920’s homes nearing the end of their lifespans may require substantial and expensive foundation and drainage replacement and repairs. When the quality of the concrete is poor or there is substantial cracking or major drainage problems, it is time to consider the bigger fix – especially if the home is going to stay in the family for a while. The proper long-term fix should last a lifetime and end those nagging concerns once and for all. articles.text: Many wine experts have noted that South African wines form sort of a bridge between the “Old World” wines of Europe and the “New World” wines of America. They have been making wine in South Africa since 1655, well before we got in the game here in America. While they make most of the standard French varietals like Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, and Syrah, there are two grapes that in my mind really stand out for their exceptional quality and rarity – Chenin Blanc and Pinotage. Chenin Blanc originally hails from the Loire Valley in France, In the regions of Savinnierres, Vouvray, Montlouis and Coteaux du Layon they make wines of tremendous complexity and character. They range from bone dry to opulently sweet. Some of the producers, like Huet and Nicholas Joly, are highly sought after. The grape found a home away from home in South Africa where (often under the name Steen) it became the most planted grape in the country, a status it still occupies. As in much of the world, Old and New, the fate of winegrowing and making and marketing wine in South Africa through the centuries was tied to colonization, international relations, wars and politics. A deep dive leads to the important English market drying up as the island nation’s ties to France warmed. In modern terms, however, it’s important to know that the Apartheid regime in South Africa did no favors for the quality of the country’s wine. With democracy prevailing in 1994, producers have put that New World pace of evolving wine quality on steroids. mouth-filling and textured with oak treatment, even sparkling and as fodder for good brandy (a use to which it has generously been put in the past). Pinotage The other South African grape that needs exploring is Pinotage. It was created in 1925 by a South African chemist who crossed Cinsault with Pinot Noir creating what is essentially South Africa’s signature red grape. For many people, Pinotage grape is a love/hate thing. Those that hate it find something in the nose that offends them. That was mostly in the earlier versions of the wine. Today, the average quality of Pinotage is far better than 20 years ago and is also better understood and respected. The most outspoken people that do not like Pinotage have not enjoyed the great examples of this grape. Presently, South Africa’s third most planted red variety is experiencing a renaissance. More experience in growing and producing Pinotage has led to better understanding of the various factors that ultimately impact the final wines. Classically bold, concentrated and powerfully structured examples still abound, and offer better overall balance and complexity than those from a decade or more prior. While attractive and young, these well-crafted bottlings also showcase the great longevity that the grape can possess, often maturing well for 10-plus years from release. If you are looking for a place to start with Pinotage, I would suggest Kanonkop or Beyerskloof, two of the best producers. In addition, I had a chance recently to try some excellent South African wines, and my tasting notes for them follow. Chenin Blanc There’s no better place to start than with Chenin Blanc. Ken Forrester, dubbed “the godfather of South African Chenin” for his role in steering the conversation about the white toward quality, said “We believe Chenin Blanc was one of the first grapes delivered to the Cape some 350 years ago. But we didn’t know it was Chenin until about 1960.” Now, with some 60 percent of the world’s vineyards of the variety – and bottles that can go up against any of the greats in the Loire Valley – South Africa pretty much owns Chenin Blanc. Forrester describes the malleability and the potential of the white variety, calling it almost a “mystical grape” in its ability to mirror the conditions where it’s grown: “If it’s a cool place, the wine is all about green apples, pears and white blossoms; if it’s warmer, it can show impressive minerality.” Getting to Chenin’s best self, he says, is akin to “calling cats.” It’s a wine, too, that takes to a variety of styles, from bone-dry to a touch sweet (a range it displays in the Loire as well), crisp and stainless-fermented to more • 2021 Terre Brulee “Le Blanc” Hailing from the Swartland region of South Africa, this wine comes from 40-year-old vines that are grown on sand and granite soil. Medium straw in color it shows aromas of lemon, peach, melon and pineapple. Medium to full-bodied, the palate is broad and slightly oily in texture with good tension, vibrant acidity and lush fruit. The wine continues to unfold its complex layers as it evolves over a long, satisfying finish.

articles.text: After sitting around the dinner table with friends and family, professing gratitude for the life they have, millions of Americans will rush to big-box stores and online retailers to find deals on electronics, toys, clothes, and more. It’s more than a little ironic that Thanksgiving has become a precursor to Black Friday’s mass consumption. Last year, 190 million Americans visited a store over the course of Thanksgiving weekend and Cyber Monday sales hit $10.7 billion. In addition to generating irony, Black Friday generates a lot of waste. According to a report from Green Alliance, 80% of everything bought during Black Friday will end up in a landfill, incenerator, or at best, in low-quality recycling – often after a short life. Nor is the consumer waste limited to Black Friday. Shopping makes up a significant portion of our carbon footprint. A report from C40 Cities found that 10% of the carbon footprints of North American city-dwellers come from purchases of items such as electronics, home goods and clothing. This percentage doesn’t factor in the emissions generated from producing, manufacturing, and shipping products before they come into our possession. Consumption (more accurately, over-consumption) is one of the primary drivers of the climate crisis. If everyone on the planet lived like Americans, we would need more than five Earths to support everyone. The U.S. population has grown 60% since 1970, while consumer spending is up 400%. Many know that our purchases have a negative impact on the environment, and we try to find eco-friendly alternatives. Brands know this, and many label their do is to buy nothing at all. If you’re looking to reduce your consumption, take care not to be a passive recipient of advertising. Rather than allowing yourself to be a marketing target, buy with intention. Seek out products that you need, and only when you need them. Reframe your thinking around sales. If you buy an item worth $100 at 20% off, it’s important to remember that you aren’t saving $20, you’re spending $80. Last year, 64% of Black Friday shoppers bought something on sale that they later regretted (according to finder. com/black-friday-statistics). When shopping for the holidays, there are many ways you can reduce your carbon footprint. If shopping online, you can buy in advance and allow time for slower shipping. Consider supporting small businesses and shopping locally. Lastly, gifts don’t always have to be consumer goods. Experiences, classes, baked goods, and homemade crafts make great gifts and have a negligible carbon footprint. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions on electrification, plant-based eating, or hiking. products as “green” or “ecofriendly” regardless of their environmental impact. This is known as greenwashing. Greenwashing leads consumers to believe that they don’t need to change their consumption habits; that they don’t need to be buying less, they just need to buy the right products. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, November 23, 2022 How Black Friday hurts the planet By Sophie Roberts After sitting around the dinner table with friends and family, professing gratitude for the life they have, millions of Americans will rush to big-box stores and online retailers to find deals on electronics, toys, clothes, and more. It’s more than a little ironic that Thanksgiving has become a precursor to Black Friday’s mass consumption. Last year, 190 million Americans visited a store over the course of Thanksgiving weekend and Cyber Monday sales hit $10.7 billion. In addition to generating irony, Black Friday generates a lot of waste. According to a report from Green Alliance, 80% of everything bought during Black Friday will end up in a landfill, incenerator, or at best, in low-quality recycling – often after a short life. Nor is the consumer waste limited to Black Friday. Shopping makes up a significant portion of our carbon footprint. A report from C40 Cities found that 10% of the carbon footprints of North American city-dwellers come from purchases of items such as electronics, home goods and clothing. This percentage doesn’t factor in the emissions generated from producing, manufacturing, and shipping products before they come into our possession. Consumption (more accurately, over-consumption) is one of the primary drivers of the climate crisis. If everyone on the planet lived like Americans, we would need more than five Earths to support everyone. The U.S. population has grown 60% since 1970, while consumer spending is up 400%. Many know that our purchases have a negative impact on the environment, and we try to find eco-friendly alternatives. Brands know this, and many label their do is to buy nothing at all. If you’re looking to reduce your consumption, take care not to be a passive recipient of advertising. Rather than allowing yourself to be a marketing target, buy with intention. Seek out products that you need, and only when you need them. Reframe your thinking around sales. If you buy an item worth $100 at 20% off, it’s important to remember that you aren’t saving $20, you’re spending $80. Last year, 64% of Black Friday shoppers bought something on sale that they later regretted (according to finder. com/black-friday-statistics). When shopping for the holidays, there are many ways you can reduce your carbon footprint. If shopping online, you can buy in advance and allow time for slower shipping. Consider supporting small businesses and shopping locally. Lastly, gifts don’t always have to be consumer goods. Experiences, classes, baked goods, and homemade crafts make great gifts and have a negligible carbon footprint. articles.text: Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls was a small but important part of Piedmont’s history. It was the first school to offer a college preparatory high school education in Piedmont. Somewhat isolated in Hazel Lane, yet accessible by streetcar, the school enjoyed a reputation as one of the prestigious private schools in the Bay Area. It all started with Amy Requa Long, who wanted her daughters to have a good education. When the girls were old enough for school, Isaac Requa built a one-room schoolhouse on his property, and Amy hired a school teacher for her daughters and a few children from the neighborhood. It was the first school in Piedmont. Interest in a private school in Piedmont grew, and in 1905 Amy leased the rambling Fridheim house at the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane and hired Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges, both teachers from Anna Head School in Berkeley. The school accepted day and boarding students and attracted the daughters of many of Piedmont’s and California’s prominent families. It quickly outgrew the Fridheim site, and in 1908, Amy Requa Long hired Julia Morgan to design a modern school with classrooms and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that today is Hazel Lane. The new school opened in 1913 as the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls. It was strictly a college preparatory school, not a finishing school. Morgan returned in 1913 to build additional classrooms, and in 1916 added a gymnasium for the growing school. The curriculum included History, Math, English and foreign language classes in French, Latin and German. The school also offered special courses in Music, Drawing and Oral Expression. The Music class included piano, singing, harmony and Glee Club. The Drawing class taught painting, costume design, architecture and sculpture. The Oral Expression class ended with a full-dress presentation of a Shakespeare play in the school’s courtyard. Athletics were also important, and the school had basketball, field hockey, tennis and baseball teams, and even hiking and riding clubs. It also sponsored outings to plays and concerts, hiking and riding on trails in the East Bay hills, and picnics at local beaches. Ransom-Bridges offered classes from first grade through high school. The younger girls lived in Piedmont, Oakland and Berkeley and attended as day students. The school had dormitory rooms for up to 70 students. Some of the high school girls who boarded came from as far away as Washington, Oregon, Washington, D.C. and Maine. Almost all the graduates went on to the University of California in Berkeley, Stanford and other comparable colleges. Uniforms were required for the older girls – white middy blouses, dark ties and dark or white pleated skirts. (Piedmont High School continued the tradition of school uniforms when it Ransom Bridges students performed a production of Romeo and Juliette in 1915. Each year students performed a different Shakespeare play. Ransom Bridges girls wore white middy blouses with ties and white or dark pleated skirts. Pictured, a student enjoys her morning hot chocolate. Note the Julia Morgan Della Robbia ceramic. Ransom Bridges School for Girls in 1914 at the end of Hazel Lane. The path in the lower left corner leads to Highland Avenue. opened in 1921.) The younger students attended classes from 8:30 to 12:45; the older students were in class until 1:15. The school served bouillon or hot chocolate and crackers at morning recess and lunch at 1:15. The afternoons were for study, music, drawing and outdoor activities. For the boarding students, dinner was served at 6:30, and lights out were at 8:30, 9:30 for the older girls. Ransom-Bridges School flourished into the prosperous 1920s. In 1924 there were 186 students; 123 in high school and 63 in the lower school (grades 1-8). In 1928, there were 21 instructors and 42 graduating seniors. The school struggled financially after the Stock Market Crash of 1929 and the Depression that followed. Many families could no longer afford to send their daughters to private school. Piedmont High School was built in 1921 and offered a less expensive opportunity for education. Ransom-Bridges enrollment declined, and by 1932, there were only 12 graduating seniors. Shortly after graduation in June that year, the school closed. In 1936, the school was demolished, and the land was developed by architect Albert Farr as Ransom Gardens. The first house was built at 152 Hazel Lane. Today, the redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane marks the entrance to the former Ransom-Bridges School. Redwood trees between 100 and 114 Hazel Lane lined the entrance to the school and mark the eastern edge of the school property. The main school building was built where 141 Hazel Lane stands. The path from Hazel Lane into Piedmont Park was called Ransom Way, named for the school. For more information on Piedmont’s history, please visit our website: Piedmonthistorical. org. If you enjoy reading these biweekly columns on the history of Piedmont, consider becoming a member of the Piedmont Historical Society. For more information, contact Gail Lombardi at 501-0118 or by e-mail at lombardg@pacbell.net. The Ransom Bridges Riding Club in front of the school in 1915. Julia Morgan designed a symmetrical façade with open arches, wrought iron balconies, arched windows and a central entry with columns for the Ransom Bridges School.

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department invites community members to donate toys for children whose families have trouble affording holiday gifts as part of the 75th year of the Toys for Tots Drive. The Toys for Tots Foundation, a not-for-profit public charity, is sponsored and organized by the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve. Donations of new, unwrapped toys may be dropped off at the Piedmont Fire Department through December 9. Donation bins are located in the Fire Department adjacent to City Hall, at 120 Vista Avenue. “Although Fire Department business hours are 8 a.m.-5 p.m.,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, “the Station is open for non-emergencies 24 hours a day and locals are encouraged to make a donation in the bins, located next to the Station entrance, at any time.” “The Piedmont Fire Department is proud to partner with the Alameda County Marine Toys for Tots Foundation,” said Brannigan. “Every year the generosity of the Piedmont community brings hope and joy to children throughout Alameda County.” Speaking on the donation drive, Fire Captain John Fitzpatrick said, “The intent of the program is to provide toys for children whose parents wouldn’t be able to afford them otherwise.” Since it takes the Marines several weeks to distribute the gifts, he urged community members to donate by the second week of December. “We’ll always do our best to distribute last-minute gifts,” said Fitzpatrick, “but the sooner, the better.” In a longstanding tradition, each member of the Piedmont City Council will donate a toy to the Toys for Tots program. Their donations will take place at the Monday, December 5 council meeting in City Council Chambers at City Hall, beginning at 6 p.m. For more information on donating a toy in Piedmont, please call Fire Captain Jon Fitzpatrick at (510) 420-3030, or email him at jfitzpatrick@piedmont.ca.gov. don’t know what we have ‘til it’s gone’? articles.text: Thousands of people from Piedmont and beyond are expected to converge near Piedmont Park on November 24 for the 21st annual Turkey Trot. The 5-kilometer race will begin at 8:30 a.m. The popular Thanksgiving morning event is celebrating its 21st year. Runners, joggers. Dog walkers and families with strollers will gather on Highland Avenue in front of the Exedra at the corner of Highland and Magnolia Avenues. Coffee and hot chocolate will be served at Corcoran Group, formerly Highland Partners, at the beginning and the end of the race. There will also be plenty of refreshments afterwards. The race begins on Highland Avenue and continue onto Wildwood Avenue and La Salle Avenue, before looping back along Sea View and Mountain Avenues. The route is considered a good workout for serious runners and a benchmark for hundreds of others looking to improve their time or just get some morning exercise with a lot of friends and neighbors. Although anyone can join the race, those who have registered are in the running to win some sweet prizes. All registered runners should plan to pick up their race bib and official Piedmont Turkey Trot jersey on Wednesday, November 23 at the Veterans Hall between 3:00 and 5:00 p.m. Winners will be announced at an awards ceremony in front of the Exedra after the last runner crosses the finish line. Prizes are awarded to the top three runners in each age category, from youth to seniors over 80. All winners will receive a racing cap, a fresh bouquet of flowers from J. Miller Flowers, and a pumpkin pie from Piedmont Grocery. The overall male and female winners will receive a turkey from Village Market, and running shoes from Transports. Proceeds from the Turkey Trot support Piedmont High School cross country and track-and-field teams and the City of Piedmont’s sorts facilities maintenance fund.

articles.text: At a Special City Council Meeting on Tuesday, November 15, Piedmont’s city staff received council authorization to submit Piedmont’s Draft Housing Element, with several proposed updates, to the California Department of Housing and Community Development. The updates include: • maximizing the use of Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) from 140 to 160 to meet State-mandated housing production targets • relocation of affordable units in the housing sites inventory from the Civic Center area to the mixed-use zone on Grand Avenue • keeping Above Moderate Income units on Grand Avenue at or below five stories • expanding the Moraga Canyon Plan area to include all cityowned property along Moraga Avenue, including Blair Park. Each city in California has an allocated Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) number, which specifies the target number of homes to plan for at various income levels. Piedmont’s housing target is 587 units. This includes 163 Very Low Income units, 94 Low Income units, 92 Moderate Income units, and 238 Above Moderate Income units. California law requires cities to update their Housing Element every eight years. articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department invites community members to donate toys for children whose families have trouble affording holiday gifts as part of the 75th Anniversary Toys for Tots Donation Drive. Donations of new, unwrapped toys may be dropped off at the Piedmont Fire Department during regular business hours now through December 9. Donation bins are located in the Fire Department adjacent to City Hall at 120 Vista Avenue. “The Piedmont Fire Department is proud to partner with the Alameda County Marine Toys for Tots Foundation,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Every year the generosity of the Piedmont community brings hope and joy to children throughout Alameda County.” In a longstanding tradition, each member of the Piedmont City Council will donate a toy to the Toys for Tots program. Their donations will take place at the December 5 council meeting in City Hall. The Toys for Tots Foundation, a not-for-profit public charity, is sponsored by the U. S. Marine Corps Reserve. For more information on donating a toy in Piedmont, please contact Fire Captain Jon Fitzpatrick at (510) 420-3030 (jfitzpatrick@piedmont.ca.gov).
