articles.text: Bring back the original 19th century Blair Park Editor: Blair Park, along Moraga Ave, is a perfect place for high density housing. The site is easily accessible for developers. Everyone who drives on Moraga Ave, past Blair Park knows that it is very underused. Who wants to be in a park with such heavy traffic speeding past? Please move the new Blair Park from its current 4.85 acre location in Moraga Canyon. The park, not housing, would be better located on a portion of the original 75 acre Blair Park site, above Coaches Field-high on the hillside (see historyofpiedmont. com search Blair Park)! All Piedmont residents could enjoy this superior park location high on the hill with its mature trees, some of the original graded trails, and unsurpassed views. Following is a description of our magnificent hillside from the San Francisco Morning Call newspaper, dated Sunday, March 22, 1891. Page 8: “a splendid view is had over the whole Bay Area, that ranges from the Golden from Berkeley to Alameda on this shore and from Mount Tamalpias down along the Coast Range” Isn’t it better for our climate issues if Piedmonters just walk out of their houses to a majestic new Blair Park on the mountain for exercise, rather than jumping into their cars to drive somewhere else? It was a highly desired destination for people in 1891 and it could be again. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. articles.text: Building electrification is a shift away from gas appliances and a move towards clean electric appliances for heating, cooling, and cooking. Gas, oil and propane used for heating and cooking generates 600 million tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the United States each year. When factoring in methane leakage, that number rises to the equivalent of 1 billion tons of CO2. That’s equal to the emissions from 215 million gasoline cars being driven for one year. In Piedmont, residential buildings account for 49% of in-territory greenhouse gas emissions, with the overwhelming share of these emissions coming from natural gas used for heating and cooling. Building electrification has the potential to significantly reduce Piedmont’s greenhouse gas emissions, especially since Piedmont’s grid operates on renewable energy through East Bay Community Energy. Electrification can help Piedmont meet its goal of reducing emissions within City boundaries by 40% by 2030. In addition to contributing to the climate crisis, gas appliances can create unhealthy living environments. Air pollutants from gas appliances such as carbon monoxide, particulate patter and formaldehyde gas can create indoor air pollution. articles.text: Piedmont Scouts from Troop 11 helped collect and sort food. Pictured are: (front) Carter Brookfield (left), Gus Leonard, Henry Stein, Theo Ferguson; (standing on truck) Will Myers, Colin Amen, Zach Osborn, and Drew Kobal. Piedmont Council Scouts stepped up on Saturday, November 12 in its 38th annual Scouting for Food drive, providing support for the Alameda County Community Food Bank and the people it serves. “Alameda County has one of the highest incidences of hunger in the nation,” said Anne Hauss Davies, Piedmont Scout Council’s Scouting for Food Chair. “One of every five residents of the County calls upon the Alameda Food Bank for assistance, and two-thirds of those requiring assistance are children and the elderly. More than half of those served by the Food Bank have jobs but aren’t earning enough to make ends meet.” The service project, done by Scouts across the nation for decades, incorporates Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, and Venturers. The prior weekend, November 5, Cub Scouts distributed door hangers reminding Piedmont residents to place donations of non-perishable outside. Piedmont Scouts followed up last weekend throughout the city to pick up the donations and bring them to the parking lot at Piedmont Community Hall where Venturers from the Piedmont Community Service Crew helped sort the donations and load them onto a truck from the food bank. “It’s a huge lift, but it’s made lighter because so many people step in and step up,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “This wouldn’t happen without the generosity of the greater Piedmont community.” Each Pack and Troop’s route was mapped out in advance for both the door hangers and food pickup. One of this year’s highlights was Troop 4’s coordinator Kevin Blodgett. “Kevin is a recent Eagle Scout,” said Benson, “and it’s great to see him continuing to lead in his troop.” In a sign of the community’s generosity, the truck was fully loaded with donations when it left for the Food Bank. Scouts also brought in over $3,000 in cash and checks and the virtual food drive raised an additional $6,000 as of November 14. Scouting in Piedmont Are you interested in Scouting for your family? Programs are available for youth in grade school (Cub Scouts), youth 11-18 (Scouts BSA), and youth 14-21 (Venturing and Exploring). To learn more, visit www.PiedmontBSA.org, call the Scout office at 844-1752, or reach out to contact@piedmontbsa.org. #AdventureOn! articles.text: Symphony horn players will be returning to the Piedmont Turkey Trot again this year on Thanksgiving morning starting at 8 a.m. for a festive fanfare that officially launches the race in the middle of town. Last year’s musicians included Tom Reicher(left), Berkeley Symphony; Stuart Gronningen, Oakland Symphony (retired); Alicia Mastromonaco, Marin Symphony; Caitlyn Smith, Santa Cruz Symphony; Meredith Brown, Oakland Symphony; Jonathan Ring, San Francisco Symphony; and Robert Ward, San Francisco Symphony. They will be joined this year by an eighth brass player, Daniel Hawkins of San Francisco Symphony. “We will have eight hunting horn players who will be playing on authentic trompes de chasse from France,” explained Piedmont resident Tom Reicher, a French Horn player with Berkeley Symphony. “Originally, the trompe de chasse was used as a loud signaling instrument that would communicate to hunters various aspects of the hunt. However, over more than two centuries music was developed for large ensembles of trompes de chasse, and that is what we will be playing. This is music intended to be performed outdoors and thus is appropriate to celebrate the gathering of runners for the Piedmont Turkey Trot.”

articles.text: Due to California’s ongoing school funding crisis, many school districts have cut the hours of their libraries or closed them altogether. Thanks to the Piedmont community’s support of the Giving Campaign, Piedmont’s libraries are stronger than ever, serving as hubs of literacy, interactive learning, and connection for students. These active, multi-faceted spaces and the librarians and aides that run them depend in large part on support from the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) and its Giving Campaign. At every Piedmont school, dedicated teacher librarians and aides help students develop a love of reading along with critical thinking and research skills. A significant portion of the funding for aides in the libraries comes from funds raised by the Giving Campaign. “The tri-school elementary teacher librarians are so grateful to PEF for its ongoing library funding,” said Havens Elementary teacher librarian Laura Remer. “We couldn’t do our work without having the support of our library assistants. They take care of some of the nitty gritty so that we can focus on teaching and helping our students find just-right books for their reading level, for their personal interests, and for supporting who they are as individuals.” Beyond encouraging a love of reading, school libraries and librarians provide students with the tools they need to develop critical thinking skills and media literacy. In a recent middle school project led by teacher librarians Jennifer Gulassa and Carolyn White, students selected one Amendment from the Bill of Rights. Using online databases, they researched and read three news articles about current events and considered how they impacted their chosen amendment. “This project helped students understand how our founding documents still impact current events and their own lives,” said Gulassa. “It integrated the use of key words for database searches, citations, extraction of key ideas, reflection, and collaboration.” Piedmont school libraries also serve as calm spaces for students during lunch hour. When previous library staff members retired, the school district lacked the budget to replace them, so all three elementary schools were forced to close their libraries during the lunch hour. Last year’s Giving Campaign prioritized funds for library aides to allow the district to continue to offer students the respite and opportunities the libraries provide. With new funding, the district has reopened the libraries during the lunch hour. “We are so happy to now be able to serve our students nearly every recess of the week,” noted Remer. “We know that for some students a quiet space to relax, read, and do a variety of activities is important to their social-emotional well-being.” During lunch, elementary school library staff offer activities like Legos, puzzles, coloring, origami, board games, and chess. Havens library aide Christina Wagg knows firsthand the value of having a welcoming library in which to spend free time. “I lived in the Montclair library as a kiddo,” she says. Piedmont Middle School teacher librarians Carolyn White (left) and Jennifer Gulassa. “Going there every day after school, I knew I would always be welcome. It was a godsend for me.” Funds from the Giving Campaign cover 10%-15% of the costs of librarians at each school. “That funding is the difference between librarians being able to teach five versus six classes,” said PEF director Heather Frank. “Our librarians make these libraries into places kids want to come and learn.” Thanks to the Giving Campaign, Piedmont school libraries will continue to be a space for learning and growth. “I believe libraries are a safe haven for all, where we make connections, learn about our world, read, write, draw, create, and take a break from the busyness,” said Wagg. “I’m so glad the Piedmont community values its beautiful libraries.” To learn more about the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign or to donate, please visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org.
articles.title: School libraries a rich resource for Piedmont students

articles.text: Community members are invited to the new Alan Harvey theater tonight to contribute to the search for a permanent school superintendent. A public forum will be held tonight, Wednesday, November 16, at 6 p.m. allowing residents to provide input towards Piedmont School District’s search for a permanent school superintendent. The meeting will be held in the new Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus. Residents will have an opportunity to interact with consultants from the search firm, Leadership Associates, which has been hired by the school board to lead the search. Residents are asked to provide input about desired personal and professional qualities anticipated in the incoming superintendent. Comments from the public will be used in the development of the candidate profile, recruitment process, and reference checking. The consultants will compile a summary of all comments received and share the report with the School Board and with the future superintendent. “The search firm has a great reputation for finding excellent candidates for school districts,” said Interim Superintendent Donald Evans. “You can’t create the candidate profile without listening to the Piedmont community. Piedmont is about relationships. They have to be involved and engaged in the process. This is how parents stay connected to the superintendent search.” During the forum, consultants will share an overview of the process, and ask audience members the following questions: • What are the desirable qualities, characteristics, background and professional and personal experiences for the next superintendent? • What do you see as the strengths of the district and the major challenges facing the district in years ahead? There is no need to RSVP. Those unable to attend may provide feedback and responses to these questions on an online survey at: Surveymonkey.com/r/53FDH9S. The survey will remain open until November 21 at 4:00 p.m.
articles.title: Public forum on school superintendent search tonight at 6 p.m.

articles.text: This year Piedmont and Millennium High School are offering a new class, Affinity Mentorship, after school hours in the 8th period. A total of 36 high school mentors have enrolled in the diversity-focused course which aims to make an impact on middle and elementary school students in Piedmont schools. The class trains high school students to create effective and age-appropriate lessons on identity. The mentors put their work into action by offering mentoring sessions to younger students of similar cultural, ethnic, religious, gender-expansive, and neurodiverse backgrounds. Neurodiverse is an umbrella term that includes people with autism, dyslexia, ADHD, or other neurological differences resulting in varying perspectives of the world. Mentors meet with their students two to three times each month creating fun, safe spaces for young mentees to explore and celebrate their identities. The Affinity Mentorship program has seen growth since it began in 2020, allowing mentors to expand services to middle school students. This year also brought the capability to deliver sessions to the district’s neurodiverse and gender-expansive Photo by Jean Takazawa Sage Mosley (left), and Julia Banuelos (right) with 3rd graders Isaac Pelletier and Ramon Fierro. students. “To be able to recognize that there are students, neurodivergent students, and gender expansive students that would really benefit from actually having mentors in those identities, has been really amazing for the younger students,” said Jean Takazawa, who teaches the Affinity Mentorship class. “I didn’t know it was going to go this far. pages.text: Wednesday, November 16, 2022 7 Public forum on school superintendent search tonight at 6 p.m. Community members are invited to the new Alan Harvey theater tonight to contribute to the search for a permanent school superintendent. By Jay Russell A public forum will be held tonight, Wednesday, November 16, at 6 p.m. allowing residents to provide input towards Piedmont School District’s search for a permanent school superintendent. The meeting will be held in the new Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus. Residents will have an opportunity to interact with consultants from the search firm, Leadership Associates, which has been hired by the school board to lead the search. Residents are asked to provide input about desired personal and professional qualities anticipated in the incoming superintendent. Comments from the public will be used in the development of the candidate profile, recruitment process, and reference checking. The consultants will compile a summary of all comments received and share the report with the School Board and with the future superintendent. “The search firm has a great reputation for finding excellent candidates for school districts,” said Interim Superintendent Donald Evans. “You can’t create the candidate profile without listening to the Piedmont community. Piedmont is about relationships. They have to be involved and engaged in the process. This is how parents stay connected to the superintendent search.” During the forum, consultants will share an overview of the process, and ask audience members the following questions: • What are the desirable qualities, characteristics, background and professional and personal experiences for the next superintendent? • What do you see as the strengths of the district and the major challenges facing the district in years ahead? There is no need to RSVP. Those unable to attend may provide feedback and responses to these questions on an online survey at: Surveymonkey.com/r/53FDH9S. articles.text: Piedmont School Board came to a tentative agreement on November 9 to give administrators a 7.5% raise retroactively to July 1, 2022. and a one-time stipend of $1,500. CSEA Classified employees include paraeducators, maintenance workers, custodians, tech support, food service providers, and office staff. The agenda of last week’s meeting even had an agendized item to approve the new agreement. However, a “significant misunderstanding,” sent the agreement back to CSEA members for revision and revoting. “Unfortunately we became aware of a significant misunderstanding between the negotiating teams regarding an item on the agreement. As a result CSEA was not able to submit to the board a tentative agreement approved by our membership as we had hoped,” explained Kylie Bennett at November 9 board meeting. Due to Thanksgiving Break, the November 9 board meeting is the only regularly scheduled meeting this month. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. articles.text: Piedmont Scouts in Troop 15 spent the rainy weekend of November 5-6 on an overnight adventure at Cassini Ranch campground along the Russian River. With lunches in daypacks, the Scouts set out in rain on Saturday on a four-mile loop trail known as Island in the Sky. “It was like taking a big shower, but cooler,” noted Scout Oscar Van Gelder. Adelina Mbise noticed that “the rain cleaned the dusty air which then smelled nice. The plants looked healthy and perky.” After hiking about three miles, the Scouts paused for a wet but satisfying lunch. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont coach Dan Chubbock and the girls’ soccer team return with a roster that includes 10 seniors. Piedmont girls’ soccer coach can hardly wait for the winter season to begin. His team includes 10 seniors and five other players who earned varsity time last year. “We have a lot of returning players and a couple of freshmen; there’s a lot of familiarity across the board and returning cohesion. There’s a lot of competition for places, so there’s a lot of good headaches at each position,” he said. “We had our first practice since tryouts and everyone looks good. A lot of players are fighting for spots. We have a strong team and there are a lot of opportunities for players to earn a spot,” said coach Chubbock. Starting with the attack, fouryear starter Emily Fitzgerald and two-year starter Audrey Lam are back in the fold. Fitzgerald recently committed to play Division 1 soccer at UC San Diego after graduation from Piedmont. Lam was invited to train with the United States U-17 team in Europe this summer, and is committed to play for Brown. “Audrey is great for the team. When you throw in a player like Audrey, she’s just going to raise the level of play even more. For Emily, she’s an even stronger player than last year and will have a big impact on the league,” said Chubbock. Last year’s striker Zenobia Pellissier-Lloyd is likely to be replaced on the front line by Fitzgerald and possibly freshman Miranda Liu. “Miranda Liu is a center forward by trade, and she’ll be fighting for a spot. I think we’ll be stronger going forward this year. Miranda can fill that striker role; the same for Emily,” he added. On defense, Piedmont returns a group of center backs who saw a lot of action last season: Sofie Hebert, Charlotte Davis, Elle Ruegg, Audrey Harmon, and Amy Derr. Eliza Hammond, a JV call-up, has been impressive this offseason. “There’s definitely competition at center back. Honestly we have two or three options at every position this year, which is great,” said Chubbock. With the amount of returners, PHS s likely to have a balanced team in all phases of the game. “I think it’s a strong team this year. Everyone will play a role, even if they aren’t getting a lot of minutes. We’re going to get straight into the season right after Thanksgiving and won’t have much time in the preseason. So, we’ll know a lot more after the first couple of games,” said Chubbock. Piedmont opens its season on Monday, November 28 with a non-league game against Miramonte. A week later it jumps straight into the league season with a critical match at Bishop O’Dowd on December 7. Emily Fitzgerald, the team captain, is a four-year starter for Piedmont.

articles.text: PHS falls to No. 2 Branson in NCS Semifinals Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team reached the Division 2 North Coast Section semifinals as the No. 3 seed, but lost 4-3 to No. 2 Branson in the semifinals on Saturday, November 12 at the Goldman Tennis Complex in Golden Gate Park. To reach the semis, PHS defeated No. 6 Lick-Wilmerding 5-2 on Thursday, November 10 at home. Against Branson, Piedmont battled to a 3-3 tie on with No. 1 singles starter Tanya Kononova on the court. After winning the first set 6-2, she but dropped the next set 6-2. The third set was battle. Tied at 6-6 it went to a tiebreaker before Branson’s Anna Rende powered to a 6-1 win. In the quarterfinals with Lick-Wilmerding, PHS won two of four singles matches and swept all three doubles matches. Tanya Kononova fell in a heated three-set match to Branson in the NCS semifinals, but shutout LickWilmerding’s No. 1 starter. Freshmen Arianna Krotum (left) and Kate Jumper won their No. 2 doubles matches against Lick-Wilmerding and Branson. Staff Photos Michaela Bini and Mara LaForte reeled in the clinching fourth victory in Piedmont’s 5-2 win over Lick-Wilmerding in the NCS Quarterfinals. “We split the singles with Lick and won all three doubles. We also won all three doubles against Branson but lost all the singles. Tanya came out on fire against Branson and won the first five games of the first set. Branson’s No. 1, Anna Rende, came back in the second after trailing 4-2, and then won 6-1 in the tiebreaker. It was a great match,” said PHS coach Jim Landes. In the 5-2 win over Lick-Wilmerding, the clinching fourth match victory came down to the No. 1 doubles team of Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini winning in straight sets 6-2, 6-3. In the second set, the duo trailed 3-0 but won six straight games to take home the win. “It’s a pattern sometimes,” said Bini. “We get so cocky and confident in the first set, then we slack. I told Mara, ‘we cannot slack off.’ And then Jim got on our case and woke us up,” she added. a bit in the second set. Coach Jim told us, ‘Play better.’ So I guess we just played better. Soon after, Cecilia DeFazio and Emma Eisemon won 6-4, 4-6, 6-2 at No. 2 doubles. Lick-Wilmerding then scored its first win at No. 4 singles, where Ellie Broscow lost 7-5, 6-3. articles.text: Piedmont enters season as defending NCS Champion Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team comes into the upcoming Winter season as the defending Division 4 North Coast Section champions and winning the WACC’s Shoreline Division with undefeated records for two years. The high-level results have earned the Highlanders a promotion to the WACC’s Foothill Division. “This is for sure going to be a transition year. We’ve had a lot of success over the last three years and were able to cap it off in the right fashion by winning NCS. But with success comes new challenges. Being moved up into the [more competitive] Foothill Division will be a huge challenge,” said coach Todd Sullivan. With the loss of 14 seniors from last year’s team, Sullivan is forced Aiden Woolwine, the Post’s 2022 Honorable Mention for Sophomore of the Year, is back to lead the front line. Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team returns as the defending Division 4 NCS champions and have been moved up to the WACC Foothill Division. to replace several key starters, including former captain and midfielder Andre Stankiewicz, forward Conner Curtis, center back Ian Work, and winger Russell Tan, currently in Spain with Atletico Madrid’s Academy. Last year, Piedmont defeated Bishop O’Dowd 1-0 and San Leandro 2-0 but lost narrowly 1-0 to Castro Valley and Berkeley. “Playing the likes to Berkeley, Bishop O’Dowd, San Leandro, and Castro Valley twice in a season will definitely take a toll on our record. It’s going to be important to focus on our Div. 4 games to clinch a playoff position,” said Sullivan. Sullivan’s attack is characterized by a possessive style, high pressing, and keeping the ball in the opponent’s half. With the large amount of changes to the roster, he expects a more direct style that utilizes their speed and athleticism. Three-year starter Aiden Woolwine, will be back to lead the front line. “The style of play may be tweaked as a result of the changes. We likely won’t play the attractive brand of soccer that we’ve been used to seeing, but we’ll still be a high intensity pressing team that looks to keep the tempo high. We’ll have a more direct attack this year and we have a few pacey players who can go up there, like Sam Shelby and Jack Zirkelbach is quick as well,” said Sullivan. Piedmont will still be able to have a solid defense with returning starters goalkeeper Daniel Malecki, fullback Evan Manolis, and center back Soren Dixon. “We still have a decent amount of starters from last year that make up the defensive shape. There’s still continuity there and then we have to figure out how to build around that. Miles Corcoron is a good center back, Andrew Szerdy is another one and he’s a big boy, so we have some options,” said Sullivan. Moving to the midfield, Piedmont will have to replace last year’s captain, Stankiewicz, which is no easy task. Inheriting the captain’s armband will be fellow midfielder T.J. O’Neil, who earned a first-team All-League selection last season. “T.J. is going to be our mainstay, he’s a big part of the team this year and we’ll be able to build around him in the midfield. articles.text: John Savage is a well respected and well liked chemistry teacher at Piedmont High School, his alma mater. He’s also a water polo coach at the school. He is also an accomplished triathlete who qualified this fall for the famed Ironman World Championship in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii. On Saturday, October 8, Savage finished in 538th overall out of 2,376 athletes, and placed 154th out of 419 athletes in the 35-39 age division. To qualify for the prestigious event, Savage raced in Ironman Texas on April 23, where he was fifth of 221 athletes in his age group, and 39th overall in a field of 2,273 triathletes. His race in Hawaii featured a 2.4 mile swim in Kailua Bay followed by a 112 mile bike course that had 5,814 feet of elevation gain, and finished with a 26.2 mile run, which included a total elevation gain of 1,009 feet. He clocked times of 54:38 in the swim, 5:03:03 on the bike and 3:44:55 in the run for a total of nine hours, 55 minutes, and 15 seconds. “Somewhat unsurprising as a water polo coach, I’m a pretty good swimmer. My goal for the swim was to get in the front group of guys and let them pull me along as I draft on their feet. I came out of the water in 16th position for my age group. The bike is essentially a 50-mile outand-back. You’re riding through lava fields, and it got pretty hot and windy. My goal for that was to stay in control and as comfortable as I could. It’s very hot and humid in Hawaii, so I made sure to stay hydrated,” said Savage. “The strategy on the bike is to go easier because you have to run next. If you bike too hard, there’s no coming back from that, so I rode as controlled as I could. The run is a mixed bag. You do the first six or seven miles through the town of Kona, so you’re right next to the ocean, there’s a nice breeze and a lot of spectators. But from there, the remaining 20 miles are along the highway. It’s away from the ocean, it was rolling hills, it’s really hot and there’s no shade,” he added. Savage explained that he began to feel fatigue on the run and that his team, Every Man Jack, helped push him toward the finish. “The temperature was getting hotter and there’s no protection from the shade. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California is drawing upon its extensive collection to feature the works of late Oakland-based artist Hung Liu, who passed away in August, 2021. The museum has regularly showcased Liu’s work during her lifetime, including during Women’s History Month alongside other famed female artists like Mine Okubo, Helen Nestor, and Favianna Rodriguez. The museum had a longstanding partnership with the artist and commissioned her installation at the Oakland Airport, Going Away, Coming Home. Oakland Museum is also featuring a survey of her works in the exhibition titled Summoning Ghosts: The Art of Hung Liu in 2013. That installation opened in October, 2021 and features four of Liu’s works in the Gallery of California Art: Still Point (1998), Heroine of Gu Yanxiu (2012), Bindlestiff (2015) and Portrait of Dorothea Lange (2017), inspired by photographs by the famous Depression Era photographer Lange. To learn more about the exhibition and artworks, visit https:// museumca.org/on-view/remembering-artist-hung-liu/.
articles.title: Exhibit honoring artist Hung Liu now on view at Oakland Museum

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco has opened an exhibition titled The New Black Vanguard: Photography between Art and Fashion and will be on view through March 5, 2023. In its West Coast premiere, the exhibit highlights the work of 15 contemporary fashion photographers from London, Lagos, New York, Johannesburg, and beyond. Each artist’s work showcases a fresh perspective on fashion, beauty, race, gender, and aesthetics. The New Black Vanguard is curated by Antwaun Sargent and organized by Aperture, New York. Visitors will see over 100 select works from international artists and photographers, including Tyler Mitchell, the first Black photographer hired to shoot a cover story for American Vogue. To learn more and to purchase tickets to MoAD, visit https:// www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/thenew-black-vanguard. Photographs displayed in current exhibit at MoAD in San Francisco. In its West Coast premiere, the exhibit highlights the work of 15 contemporary fashion photographers from London, Lagos, New York, Johannesburg, and beyond. articles.text: The irrepressible Vitamin Em music ensemble is returning to town for a concert this Sunday, November 20, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 4 p.m. Celebrating jazz, funk, R&B, soul and fiddle music with verve and enthusiasm, the band is a musical collective of award-winning symphony musicians and friends from throughout the Bay Area, inclduing Matt Szemela, Evan Price and emily Onderdonk of Berkeley Symphony The band is serious about having fun and its members - steeped in an abundance of musical traditions – bring a wealth of experience, creativity and fearless improvisation to each performance. Musicians performing include Emily Onderdonk, Matt Szemela Evan Price, Paul Hanson, Dan Cantrell, Joe Hébert, Michael Graham and Philip Brezina. Composers and some of the pieces that will be played include: • Fables of Faubus by Evan Price. Evan takes the Mingus tune and gives it a personal spin. Waltz for the Wee Hours, a composition by Price that captures the peace and mystery of the midnight hour. • Seven Corners Country by Paul Hanson – an original jazz tune with a Balkan flair. Hanson’s Focal Points is an original fusion tune that takes the listener on a grand harmonic journey. • The Phoenix, a wholly original and unexpected version of a popular fiddle tune by Emily Onderdonk. • Onderdonk’s is an original funk tune reminiscent of Prince, Tower of Power, and Bruno Mars. • Hold the Phone by Casey McGill is a wonderful swing tune in the classic style. Audience members are invited to meet the musicians at a wine reception following the concert. For tickets, click on: https:// www.simpletix.com/e/117752. Photo by Jim Orsetti Vitamin Em musicians Paul Hanson (left), Matt Szemela, Evan Price, Emily Onderdonk, Dan Cantrell, Joe Hébert, and Michael Graham. Not pictured: Philip Brezina, violin.
articles.title: Vitamin Em concert this Sunday at PCA

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse will premiere a production of Shakespeare’s As You Like It tomorrow, November 17. The epic tale is adapted for stage by Shaina Taub and Laurie Woolery, and follows the same basic story, illustrated by eight characters who all marry at the end of the play. A major theme in Shakespeare’s classic is love – disguised, blind and even manipulated. Duke Senior and his followers are forced from their homes, then escape to the Forest of Arden where they are welcomed by a utopian vision of society. Will Springhorn Jr. plays the title role of Duke Frederick, and Abigail Esfira Campbell makes her San Francisco Playhouse debut as Celia. Ryan Torres plays Oliver, and Johann Santiago Santos, Jillian A. Smith, Renee Rogoff, and Göran Norquist complete the cast, performing a number of roles between them. This musical adaptation features a score by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The play is directed by San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English. San Francisco Playhouse is located at 450 Post Street. Purchase tickets online at www. sfplayhouse.org, or call the box office at (415) 677-9596.
articles.title: As You Like It opens tomorrow at SF Playhouse

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s production of Guiseppe Verdi’s masterpiece, La Traviata, is being performed now through December 3 at the War Memorial Opera House. Music Director Eun Sun Kim leads the Opera Orchestra and chorus in Shawna Lucey’s production of the three-act opera. SF Opera casts South African-born Pretty Yende as protagonist Violetta Valéry. Yende has appeared in the same role with the Vienna State Opera, Naples’ Teatro di San Carlo, Royal Opera, and Paris Opera productions. Jonathan Tetelman will sing the role of Alfredo Germont, a young bourgeois from a provincial family who admires Violetta from afar. “Verdi’s masterpiece about one of the most incredible women in history lives at the intersection of sex and money,” said Lucey. “Marie Duplessis, or Violetta as she is known in the opera, through her own ingenuity and tenacity has become Paris’ most famous courtesan.” The opera is set to an Italian Photo by Cory Weaver Jonathan Tetelman and Pretty Yende sing the principal roles in Verdi’s La Traviata with San Francisco Opera. libretto by Francesco Piave, and is based on a play by Alexandre Dumas. The opera is three hours and includes two intermissions. To view performance dates and times and purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfopera.com/ operas/la-traviata/.
articles.title: SF Opera unveils Verdi’s masterpiece, La Traviata

articles.text: Piedmont Community Church and Music Director Stephen Main invite the public to a magical performance and reception that has become a holiday tradition in the Bay Area for more than a decade. Main is currently composing a movement to add to his original cantata, For All This Night, he wrote in 2011. The concert will feature the Piedmont Church choir and full orchestra. There will be two performances, Saturday, December 17 and Sunday, December 18, both at 7:30 p.m., followed by a gala reception. Tickets are on sale now at PiedmontChurch.org/concert. General admission tickets are $50 and patron tickets with special seating are $150. Past concerts have sold out completely, so get your tickets while they last. Piedmont Community Church is located at 400 Highland Avenue. For more information, visit PiedmontChurch.org/concert, or contact the church at (510) 547- 5700.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Church concert, reception whets holiday appetite

articles.text: Bay Area favorite James Carpenter returns in role of Ebeneezer Scrooge A Christmas Carol returns to San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater (ACT) on Wednesday, November 30 with performances through Christmas eve, December 24. The production stars Bay Area favorite James Carpenter as Ebeneezer Scrooge, a role strongly identified with him, and which he has performed with ACT for 15 years The play is based on Charles Dickens’ famous story that captures the zeitgeist of the mid-Victorian era, with main character Ebenezer Scrooge at its center. Dicken’s novella has been recounted onstage and in film for nearly a century; ACT’s production is adapted by Carey Perloff and Paul Walsh and directed by Peter Kuo. Music is scored by Karl Lundenberg with choreography by Val Caniparoli. The cast is once again led by James Carpenter, with Anthony Fusco in alternating performances as Ebenezer Scrooge. Dan Hiatt plays the Ghost of Jacob Marley, Jomar Tagatac and Sarita Ocón are cast as Bob and Anne Cratchit; Brian Herndon and Sharon Lockwood are Mr. and Mrs. Fezziwig; B Noel Thomas is the Ghost of Christmas Past; and Catherine Castellanos as the Ghost of Christmas Present. Also featured are Tasi Alabastro, John Chukwudelunzu, Evangeline Edwards, Steven Flores, Cindy Goldfield, Jeremy Kahn, Adam KuveNiemann, Paige Mayes, James WDL Mercer II, Emily Newsome, Amanda Le Nguyen, Anna Marie Sharpe, and Howard Swain. A Christmas Carol has been a mainstay of ACT’s repertory for decades. Performances will take place at the newly-named Toni Rembe Theater at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. The production uses theatrical haze and lighting that may not be appropriate for photosensitive groups. A sensory-friendly performance of A Christmas Carol will be performed on December 18 at 6 p.m. Visit https://www.act-sf.org/ whats-on/202223-season/christmas-carol/ to purchase tickets. James Carpenter in a scene from Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol from an earlier production at ACT in San Francisco.
articles.title: Dickens’ Christmas Carol opens Nov. 30 at ACT

articles.text: “There’s good news“ is how a famous news program used to begin. These days all new sources except for the Piedmont Post tell us that it’s the bad news that sells. I don’t buy it…and apparently neither do the voters. They passed proposition 28 by a whopping majority. This proposition will increase the spending in California’s public schools for music and the arts. The public, in its wisdom, realizes that music and the arts are important. They are pledging about $1 billion in the hopes that society will benefit. It will, but I don’t trust the big shots in education. This subject requires an in-depth analysis which will follow very soon. Heard recently at the PCA The unique San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra played a delightful concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last Saturday afternoon. I arrived just in time to hear a Suite of compositions by one of the most unique figures in music history… a Frenchman by the name of Erik Satie. The featured soloist was the noted opera singer/narrator Twila Ehmcke. Satie always had a unique way of looking at everything. In this piece, he writes music for children; and as you might expect, his way of looking at things is very childish. He sees children as annoying even though he loves them. Needless to say, the audience loved it all. Violinists take over Orange County The Violin Society of America is hosting its 24th annual convention in Anaheim. It is fun to renew old friendships and begin new ones. Hundreds of violin makers are in attendance. In addition to technical workshops, there will be a number of concerts and some very important discussions involving ecological concerns. My taxi ride from the airport to the hotel was most informative. The taxi driver filled me in on all aspects of the area. It turns out that he is a knowledgeable gourmet, so he told me about the best restaurants. Southern California is quite different from Northern California as most of us know. The strip malls in Southern California have restaurants which actually feature good food. Little Arabia is a perfect example. Even though it is surrounded by corporate vapidness, I felt as if I were in Beirut, Lebanon. Service was excellent and friendly. The restaurant was filled with young families and well-mannered kids. I looked into the kitchen and saw the owner-chef busy at work. He has the grizzled face of culinary wisdom. My son and I shared a huge combo plate filled with flavorful and fragrant delicacies of the Middle East. It was so large that my son and I couldn’t finish it all. A brief conversation with the owner and the management convinced me that these people love what they are doing. People line up for workshops and concerts at the Violin Society of America’s 24th annual convention in Anaheim.
articles.title: Hear and there

articles.text: Second children’s book in a series Longtime Piedmont residents Connie and Mark Herrick released Ripley’s Missing Locket, the second book in an illustrated children’s series based on the adventures of their late rescue cat, Ripley. Connie, the author, and Mark, the illustrator, saw an opportunity to bring Ripley’s adventures to life in a published story during the “quarantine” months of the COVID-19 pandemic. Now retired from decades of working in the finance and tech industries, the couple said it was a project they had discussed for years, especially during COVID-related shelter-in-place mandates. When Ripley’s World was released in October 2021, they Ripley’s Missing Locket was released in October. Mark Herrick shown illustrating Ripley’s Missing Locket, the newest book he and wife Connie have had publshed. Children’s book authors Mark and Connie Herrick of Piedmont. immediately began plans for book number two. Ripley was the Herrick’s calico cat, the runt of a litter of kittens abandoned at a construction site in Oakland. Connie and Mark describe her as “feisty and funny.” She “ruled the house for a good 18 years,” they said, until her passing in July 2018. The joy she brought the Herricks, their family, and friends was described in numerous anecdotes and funny stories the couple would retell over the years. And naturally, the setting for the Ripley series is Piedmont. “Our Greenbank home and backyard are the settings for both books and many of the illustrations are inspired by our family photo albums,” Mark explained. “Book two expanded to include one of our favorite places, the Oakland Rose Garden.” Creating each book took about nine months, start to finish. The couple researched the self-publishing process in order to publish their first book and enlisted the help of friends who serve as graphic designer and copy editor for the series. The process has become easier since the October release of Ripley’s Missing Locket. “We really enjoyed making the second book, feeling like we found a good rhythm of working together, and seeing that we are getting better at what we do,” Connie said. “Ripley’s Missing Locket is a more engaging story. The watercolor illustrations are more vibrant and their compositions more complex.” “Our creative process is very organic and collaborative and starts with Mark and I brainstorming the story concept and flow, usually as we are out on our daily walks around Piedmont,” Connie said. “Then Mark begins composing possible illustration concepts and I write a first draft. As Mark begins painting and I see my words come to life, the story grows and develops.” Proceeds from the series are donated to charities that support animal adoption, wildlife preservation, and children’s literacy. This year’s profits from book sales will be donated to the East Bay SPCA and the International Bird Rescue. “We have a special fondness for the East Bay SPCA because that’s where we adopted Ripley. The music will be performed by Shira Kammen, Patrice Haan, and Margaret Davis on harp, Marla Fibish on mandolin, and Kristoph Klover and Tony Marcus on guitar, Healing Muses provides live, therapeutic harp music to support patient care & recovery in hospitals, hospices, cancer wards, & children’s palliative care centers throughout the Bay Area. All proceeds from the concert support their musical programs as above. A wine reception and silent auction will begin at 6:30 p.m. with the concert at 7:30 p.m. For tickets see: www.TicketStripe.com/HealingMuses. Founded in 2016 by violist Emily Onderdonk, Vitamin Em presents a broad and exciting range of styles of music to audiences in the Bay Area and beyond. Performers include Matt Szemela, Evan Price, Michael Graham, Paul Hanson and Emily Onderdonk, with compositions by Onderdonk, Price, Hanson and McGill. A wine reception will follow the concert. For tickets, go to www.simpletix.com/e/117752.

Note that this concert will be at the Piedmont Community Hall, 701 Highland Avenue, not the Center for the Arts. For advance tickets, see: http://bit.ly/3UMABtG. Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events. All public events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require photo ID and valid proof of full vaccination including booster shot for entry, as well as proper masking while inside.

articles.text: Empire of the Sun, released in 1987 and directed by Steven Spielberg, is extraordinary. It was adapted by screenwriter Tom Stoppard from the autobiographical novel by J.G. Ballard, and earned six Oscar nominations at the 60th Academy Awards ceremony. It is a must-see classic that will appeal to a wide audience, from older kids to adults. Its moving score is by John Williams with a recurring thematic leitmotif solo by James Rainbird, backed by the Ambrosian Junior Choir. The story focuses on a young, privileged British boy, Jamie Graham (Christian Bale), who lives with his parents in a cloistered expat Shanghai community that is convinced it is immune from the gathering storm of World War II, until it isn’t. The Japanese invade Shanghai, and in a remarkable, surging scene, Jamie is separated from his parents. He suddenly finds himself surrounded by crowds of panicky Chinese. The last words he hears his mother yell at him as she is swept away by a surge of humanity, are to go home and wait. Which he does. His parents never return, and Christian Bale stars in Empire of the Sun. Jamie soon runs out of food. Desperate, he decides to bicycle to the urban center of Shanghai. Through a series of circumstances, involving two American expats, Basie and Frank (John Malkovich and Joe Pantolino), the three are captured and sent to a British prisoner of war camp where they are interned by the Japanese for the duration of the war. Jamie (called Jim by Basie) soon learns that if he is to survive the harsh conditions of the camp he must emulate Basie who has an array of side-hustles. He also learns that nothing in his Christian Bale and Takatarô Kataoka in a scene from Empire of the Sun. previous affluent, sheltered life prepared him for what he is now confronting. Meanwhile, Jim struggles to remember what life was like with his parents. He also dreams of airplanes (the camp borders a Japanese airfield where he bonds with a Japanese boy about to become a Kamikaze pilot). There are more than a few compelling scenes where Jim views the Japanese Zero through romantic eyes and not as instruments of death and destruction. There is also an extraordinary scene when, with the war concluding, a squadron of American P-51s bomb and strafe the airfield as Jim watches from the top of a crumbling building. Empire of the Sun is episodic with magical, wonderfully created moments that can border on the surreal. The conclusion is compelling beyond expectation, and the photography throughout is breathtaking. Empire of the Sun. Directed by Steven Spielberg. Starring Christian Bale, John Malkovich, Joe Pantoliano. 2 hrs., 32 min. Rated PG. Released into theaters in 1987. Now streaming on Roku/ Prime/VUDU. articles.text: Ewan McGregor with Winnie the Pooh in Christopher Robin. Christopher Robin is a live-action/animated fantasy film inspired by the books of A.A. Milne, replete with the iconic illustrations of E.H. Shepard. If I had to select an ideal age for this movie, I would pick tweens and early teens, despite the strong animated opening. The tale begins with a young Christopher Robin in the 100 Acre Woods with his friends, Winnie the Pooh, Piglet, Tigger et.al. The lad is about to leave for boarding school, and the gang is giving him a farewell tea party. Christopher comforts Winnie (Jim Cummings), reassuring the honey-loving bear that he will never forget him. And so begins the transition from animation to live-action. As it turns out, the boy has a difficult time in school. His father unexpectedly dies, and he soon puts the 100 Acre Woods behind him. He grows up (now played by Ewan McGregor), marries an architect, Evelyn (Hayley Atwell), has a daughter, Madeline (Bronte Carmichael), and serves in World War II. After the war, he finds a demanding job with Winslow Luggage Co. as an efficiency expert, working long hours while increasingly neglecting his family. In other words, Christopher is losing perspective, putting his work before everything else, including a promised family vacation. This commitment to his job takes the story to that one day when Christopher is sitting on a bench in London’s Langdon Park, staring off into the distance, feeling somewhat dejected when suddenly, on a bench behind him, appears the long-forgotten Pooh. And so, Winnie attempts to remind his old friend about what really matters. Initially, Christopher disagrees with the small bear, insisting that “there’s more to life than balloons and honey.” Pooh responds by asking, “Are you sure?” Meanwhile Christopher suggests that perhaps he should take Winnie back to the 100 Acre Woods, and so their adventure begins with Christopher hiding the bear under his coat hoping he won’t be seen by ordinary people. Along the way the pair confront the much-feared Heffalumps and the Woozles. All the while the pair exchange ideas as to how to keep Christopher’s luggage company afloat. Gradually, Christopher begins to recover his sense of joy and slowly realizes what is important in life. He reconnects with Pooh, who reminds him, “there’s always time for wonder.” Christopher Robin is a whimsical story, value-laden with a strong anti-bullying message, and conveys countless life-lessons about the strength of the human spirit. Older kids will be entertained by the seamless merging of real life action and CGI. Christopher Robin. Directed by Marc Forster. Starring Ewan McGregor, Jim Cummings, Haley Atwell. 1 hr., 44 min. Rated PG. Released in 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: Mitch Winters as a young boy receives a kiss from his younger sister, Elizabeth. A foundation was just launched to assist children of first responders in Alameda County. The foundation honors the memory of Mitch Winters, a Piedmont native and 2016 Piedmont High School graduate, who died by suicide one year ago in November 2021. Being a first responder (military personnel, law enforcement officers, firefighters, paramedics, emergency medical technicians, and emergency room doctors and nurses) is a noble calling. Their jobs often require them to see humanity at its worst, and they are expected urgently to address and fix the many terrible and ugly things that people can do to each other or themselves. Society expects those first responders to carry the heavy burden of virtue. Their families share in that burden. That burden can be generally unspoken as revealed readily by some of the following statistics. Between 9/11 (September 11, 2001) and May 2021, approximately 30,177 active-duty personnel and veterans of the post- 9/11 wars died by suicide. That obscene and tragic number is more than four times the number of military personnel killed in military operations, including training accidents. In 2019, more law enforcement officers died by suicide than by felonious killings or accidental deaths in the line of duty. In 2018, firefighters died at higher suicide rates than police officers—and firefighter suicides exceeded the rate of on-duty deaths by approximately 30%. Healthcare first responders aren’t spared from these gruesome statistics. Even leaving aside the devastating effects of the COVID pandemic, emergency room doctors and nurses, and emergency medical technicians, face significantly higher suicide risks than members of the general population. Like his first responder brothers and sisters, Mitch was all about public service. In Piedmont, he earned the rank of Eagle Scout, received the Public Service Award from his high school graduating class, and served as a Sergeant in the city’s Police Explorer program. He received multiple Presidential Volunteer Service Awards from the President of the United States. Mitch’s Eagle Scout project benefitted the Oakland Police Department’s K-9 officers. Mitch turned down college admission because he wanted to start serving his country right away. He honorably served for four years in the United States Marine Corps, where he was an infantryman and a Combat Marksmanship Coach. He served seven months of that enlistment overseas. When he died, he was serving as a police officer in Arizona. Recognizing the outsized role that first responders play in our society and that society owes them much more than they receive, the Mitch Winters First Responders Foundation provides annual grants to children of first responders in Alameda County. Through donations and support from the public, the foundation grants may be used for trade school (which Mitch thought society undervalued), community college, college or university, or graduate school. Applications are due November 30, and successful applicants will be notified on January 31. For more information about the foundation, including how to donate and how to apply, visit https://mitchwintersfirstrespondersfoundation.org/. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223

articles.text: Construction of a new house or a remodel of an existing house can be a long drawn-out and stressful process. What can one do to improve the likelihood that a construction project is a successful one? Who you hire to guide you through the project can have a big impact on reducing the stress and unpredictability of any given project. Another aspect of the process that can make a big difference in the results one achieves is to initially engage in a thoughtful and thorough design process, and then develop and document the design in sufficient detail to create a clear road map for construction. Contrary to Robert Burns’ statement, “The best-laid plans of mice and men often go awry”, I have always found that the best laid plans actually make for a more successful project. It is so important in any construction project to have a thoroughly thought-out design that has been studied carefully. This involves looking at multiple design iterations of different ideas. There is nothing more disruptive and expensive than second guessing a plan in the middle of a construction project. Shifting gears during construction can often end up being very expensive and most likely extend the construction schedule. The extra time and effort looking at various design options at the start makes for a more confident process moving forward. Once a general design has been settled upon, after careful study of various ideas, the selected design approach needs to be developed three dimensionally. The three-dimensional aspects should be considered during the two-dimensional layout but then fleshed out after one preferred layout has been selected. All design considerations, interior and exterior, should be thoughtout thoroughly in tandem. What I have described above are the ‘design phases’ of the project. Once the preliminary design and the design development phases are complete, more detailed drawings for the regulatory agencies as well as for the execution of construction need to be developed. I like to make the case that the design process doesn’t really end until the project has been completely constructed, because during this phase of the work, many detail decisions that may affect the design are made and imbedded in the construction drawings. The more care and thought one has applied to these design decisions and then documented properly, the better the road map for construction. Again, to my way of thinking, there is nothing like the best laid plans. Doing a project in this way A preliminary design sketch showing one of many layouts considered, a 3D model, and a page from the construction drawings. Drawing by Kaplan Architects

articles.text: Piedmont Seniors pose in front of a stunning floral display at the Ritz Carleton Hotel in Half Moon Bay during a special group tour of this luxurious site. On a delightful fall day in October, the Piedmont Seniors made an excursion to the beautiful coastside town of Half Moon Bay. Usually, the town is overcast and foggy, but the Seniors lucked out and the weather was beautiful. The Seniors decided to take the scenic route, going from San Francisco to Pacifica to Highway 1 on the coast instead of the more common route on Highway 92 through San Mateo. Back in the day the small towns along the coast were popular with bootleggers during Prohibition, where alcohol could be secretly delivered to coastal restaurants with little chance of being caught. The Seniors’ first stop was the luxurious Ritz Carleton Hotel, located on a bluff of Half Moon Bay overlooking the Pacific Ocean, located approximately 30 minutes from both San Francisco and San Jose. It truly was a highlight of the day to see the elegant resort up close. The Ritz Carlton is proud of merging luxury with nature and has fire pits, two 18 hole golf courses, including one designed by Arnold Palmer! The hotel is known for its spa treatments as well as outstanding dining at the Navio Restaurant, which is rated one of the top brunches in Northern California. As the Seniors entered the hotel lobby, they saw a large, sumptuous pink silk flower display to acknowledge breast cancer awareness month. The group was given a private tour of the property, inside and out. The hotel hosts numerous weddings and social events due to its beautiful location on the ocean. The Seniors next explored the historic, quaint downtown of Half Moon Bay, where some of the brave souls visited the town’s jail. The jail once housed local lawbreakers in its two small cells. Today it houses the Half Moon Bay Coastside History Museum, telling the story about the Ohlone Indians, the first Coastsiders, Spanish and Mexican eras, the California Gold Rush, the Prohibition Era, and World War II. There are historians available for tours, with advance notice. The town is incredibly busy during weekends in October due to the many fields of pumpkins and the well known pumpkin weighing contest, along with rides and special events for children. The Seniors then had a delicious lunch in the heart of Main Street at Fattoriaemare, an authentic Italian restaurant with inside and outside seating. After lunch the Seniors headed to Pastorino Farms, one of the many nurseries on the outskirts of town on highway 92. They had a field of pumpklns from which to choose, along with gift items, plants and cut flowers. Some of the Seniors opted to take a short train ride around the property. On weekends in October, they offer a haunted house, face painting, hay rides, ponies, and opportunities to feed farm animals. Just a short walk away is Half Moon Bay Lavender Farm and Half Moon Bay Nursery, also with enticing gifts and, of course, more pumpkins. The Seniors couldn’t have asked for a more perfect day to celebrate this year’s Fall season. To find out more about the Piedmont Seniors meetings and their activities, contact Janet Epstein, the group’s coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Piedmont Seniors celebrate fall with trip to Half Moon Bay

articles.text: Suffering from life-threatening health issues, a bear cub is now undergoing rehabilitation efforts at Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. An orphaned black bear cub, estimated to be eight months old and weighing 28 pounds, was brought to Oakland Zoo on Friday night, November 11, by wildlife biologists from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW). The cub is suffering from multiple health issues, including a severe skin infection that has caused extreme hair loss, pneumonia, a viral infection, internal parasites, and a deeply infected bone in his left front foot, causing lameness in walking. The cub was named “Nixon” by the concerned citizens who reported him wandering into a retail shop called Nixon in South Lake Tahoe last week. CDFW received the cub from the Bear League in Lake Tahoe after the group posted a story about the bear on its Facebook page. CDFW conducted a veterinary assessment treatment, performed initial examinations, and contacted Oakland Zoo for further care and hopeful rehabilitation at the Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. “It’s touch and go right now. This cub is a tough little guy; despite his physical state, he’s eating well and is in good spirits,” said Dr. Alex Herman, Head of Veterinary Services at Oakland Zoo. “We are putting our best efforts into practicing next-level medicine on him, and hope we can save his life.” Nixon has been receiving treatment at the Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital since his arrival, and on Tuesday morning, November 15, underwent an extensive medical examination by the Zoo’s veterinary team. Bloodwork was sent to several labs, x-rays, an ultrasound, dermatology assessment, dental exam, and more were also completed during the hours-long medical procedure. Currently, his prognosis is extremely guarded, but hopeful. Nixon is being administered antibiotics, antifungals, and special baths to treat his infected skin. Due to his lack of fur, he’s being kept warm by heat lamps at the veterinary hospital and being fed a special diet of “bear chow” soaked in formula, various produce, and browse. Oakland Zoo’s veterinary team will continue to monitor him daily and alter his treatment as needed. The primary concern is the infected bone in his foot and his severe pneumonia. If he recovers, he will not be released back into the wild due to being orphaned at such a young age and being unable to learn how to survive in the wild from his mother. ®

articles.text: Miriam and Jerry Friedkin at home in Piedmont Gerald S. Friedkin, a Piedmont resident for 49 years, passed away peacefully at home from cancer on October 14 surrounded by his family. He was 79. Born on May 9, 1943, Jerry grew up in Oakland and graduated from Oakland High School in 1960. From an early age, Jerry took on all sorts of odd jobs – delivering the Oakland Tribune, distributing Kosher meat, working the night shift at the main post office, restoring used cars – which gave him a lifelong appreciation for hard work. After graduating from San Francisco State, Jerry built a successful real estate investment company and became known for his honesty and integrity. He loved the art of negotiation and generously mentored many young professionals. Jerry was a loyal and wise counselor to his family and friends. He nurtured lifelong relationships over many Shabbat dinners, rounds of golf, Sunday walks to Montclair, and Scotch happy hours in his backyard. Always welcoming and inclusive, Jerry was a builder of community. He served as president of Beth Jacob Congregation and the Jewish Foundation of the East Bay, co-founded the Oakland Hebrew Day School, and supported countless other organizations throughout the Bay Area and beyond. A quiet philanthropist and leader, he was a pillar of the East Bay Jewish community who lived his values of charity, kindness, and repairing the world. In addition to his wife of 51 years, Miriam, he is survived by his brothers Stephen (Terry) and Morton (Amy); his children Julie (Reuven Kahane), Ilana (Reed Bennett), Yael (Matthew Kovner) and David (Sarah Marder-Eppstein); and his grandchildren David, Gabriela, and Annika Kahane, Aaron, Ariana and Abigail Bennett, Eve and Jacob Kovner, and Noam Friedkin. Above all his many accomplishments, Jerry was a wonderful husband, father, brother and friend. As humble as he was generous, Jerry truly lived a life of meaning, purpose, and love. May his memory be a blessing. The family has established the Gerald S. Friedkin Memorial Fund (℅ JCF, 121 Steuart St, San Francisco, CA 94105) to receive charitable contributions friends may wish to make in his memory. Grants from this fund will support the causes that mattered most to Jerry.
articles.title: Community builder Gerald Friedkin dies October 24

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group seems to be charmed when it comes to the weather. It had rained on Tuesday but was clear by the time the group assembled at the Exedra last Wednesday morning. It was great walking weather, and a strong turnout of 40 walkers showed up for a morning together. It was announced that Piedmont historian and walker Meghan Bennett has created a Walking on Wednesday website. It contains the stories of Walking on Wednesdays walks going back to group’s start in 2018 (https:// www.walkingpiedmont.com/). The group has a goal of walking every traffic-safe street in Piedmont each year, and has walked all but a few this year, including the upper parts of Palm and Nova Drives, as well as Dale Avenue and Sylvan Way. Getting to them would allow the group to walk through Piedmont Park, and see how much water was in Bushy Dell Creek after the recent rain. At the top of the park, behind the Community Hall, the group checked the water level in the creek. It was still good to see water flowing after the long. dry season and the drought we are experiencing. The group took the lower park trail to be closer to the creek, stopping at the cascades that Frank C. Havens built when he created the park in the 1890s as an attraction for his real estate sales. The stairs overlooking the cascades that provided tiers for the walkers to pose on for a group photo. The walkers continued on the path in a long line, and regrouped at the former sulphur spring grotto where Mark Twain visited the park in about 1868 during a writer’s tour and sampled the mineral water. Matt Gerhardt asked why there isn’t a sulphur smell now. It was explained that in the mid- 20th Century the neighbors didn’t like the smell, and had the City cap the spring. As the walkers went through the park, they had a pleasant surprise when they came upon former Piedmont Recreation supervisor Michael Murphy who was walking his dog. Emerging on Wildwood Avenue, they went past Wildwood School to the 5-W intersection of Wildwood, Wallace, Winsor and Warfield. They went down Winsor Avenue to Park View Drive, and then to the top of Palm Drive. There the story of Havens planting palm trees as a grand entrance to his park was also told. There are still some of Havens’ palm trees in people’s front yards, but most are now gone. The group went down Palm to Wildwood where it intersects with Sylvan Way and started its short by steep assent. The walkers seemed to enjoy the climb and the extra exercise it provided. They went down Sylvan to Boulevard Way and then past the office of the Piedmont Post near the corner of Grand Avenue. The walkers turned up Wildwood Avenue, past the Nova Circle, and came to the one-block, little-traveled Dale Avenue. From there it was on to Fairview, Jerome, and Oakland Avenues. A home on Oakland Avenue had Japanese maple trees with striking, beautiful red leaves. The street also provided another climb for the walkers before they came to the 300 block of El Cerrito Avenue. It is a level walk until Magnolia Avenue, which gave the group one last uphill challenge nefore arriving back at the Exedra. It turned out that all these hills and the almost a three mile walk were not that much of a challenge for the group. They have been climbing almost all of Piedmont’s streets all year long, and the walkers are confident they will finish the Turkey Trot route first in a couple of weeks on the day before Thanksgiving. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Members of Walking on Wednesdays pose for a photo near the cascades bt Bushy Dell Creek in Piedmont Park. Pictured are Ian Morgan, Ann Quinby, Karen Palmer, Dave DeRoche, Elizabeth Richter, Pat Keller, Kathy Rolefson, Martin Levy, Alicia Rivera, Nancy DeRoche, Sherry Jacobs, Rob Smith, Stella Houston, Kat Lang, Phil Witte, Alan Goldhammer, Nadine Guffanti, Brenda Ferrero, Sarah Johnson, Mike Gallant, Priscilla Wanerus, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Jasmine Cai, Quincy Dong, Elane Rehr, Christine Calliste, Pat McMahon, Helen Dong, Charlene Louie, Matt Gerhardt, Bob Wong, Will Adams, Aaron Katzel, Lisa Euphrat, Jen Peltzer, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Kathy Rolefson brought Joanne Larsen to walk with them for the first time.

articles.text: On Monday, November 7th, fall weather finally arrived for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group. It was cool, so instead of meeting outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park, they moved inside the Piedmont Community Hall. There was an excellent turnout of 18 readers, including Dale Benveniste, Adrienne Hamlin, Sarah Johnson, Mike Henn, Mike Bandrowski, Jerry Gragg, Darby Gragg, Bob Hall, Martin Levy, Laura Goldman, Pat McMahon, Lois Price, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Carol Long and Priscilla Wanerus. Treats provided by Carol Long were largely from Japan to recognize Kazuo Ishiguro, the author of the group’s November selection, Klara and the Sun. It was published in 2021 and is science fiction. This is the eighth novel by the Nobel Prize-winning, British writer. Ishiguro’s story is set in the U.S. in an unspecified, dystopian future where some children are genetically engineered, or “lifted,” to enhance their academic ability. Schooling is provided entirely at home by on-screen tutors, so opportunities for socialization are limited and parents who can afford it often buy their children androids as companions. The book’s narrative is told by Klara, a solar-powered AF (Artificial Friend), who is chosen by Josie, a sickly, 14-year-old to be her companion. Josie lives with her mother in a remote region of prairie. Soon after joining them, Klara learns that the lifting process carries some risk. Josie’s older sister Sal had earlier died, and Josie herself is gravely ill. Josie’s only near neighbor and childhood friend is Rick, a boy of about her own age. Although academically able, Rick has not been lifted and faces discrimination and reduced career prospects. In spite of this, Josie and Rick have always known that they will be together forever. Although Klara is exceptionally intelligent and observant, her knowledge of the world is The prose and story development also disappointed them. Others found it simplistic, but still eloquent, creative, and cleaver. However the group did believe the book presented a possible future that their grandchildren may have to face. As machines become more like humans, it is a potential, scary future with moral questions that Ishiguro wants us to consider today. Klara and the Sun got the group thinking and talking about related issues. The questions of upper income parents providing extra tutoring for their college-aspiring children, and the appropriateness of the SAT exam and Affirmative Action in college admissions were also considered before the readers refocused on the book for some final thoughts. The group seemed to agree that Klara and the Sun was a worthwhile book to read, and it had been a good discussion. Ishiguro was able to make this science fiction future and Klara’s plight seem real for readers. Some found Klara’s being treated like a “vacuum cleaner” at the book’s end to be sad, and they were left with feelings of melancholy. The readers also agreed the moral issues Ishiguro raises are ones we should be thinking about now and working on solutions because our decedents may have to grapple with them in the not-too-distant future. With their discussion complete, the readers considered their next books. The group tries to alternate monthly between fiction and non-fiction books. They had previously selected the non-fiction Priestdaddy by Patricia Lockwood for December and Afterparties by Anthony Veasna So for January. After some consideration, the group picked Prisoners of Geography: Ten Maps that Explain Everything About the World, by Tim Marshall for their February read. The group’s next meeting will be Monday, December 5 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by calling the Recreation Department at 420- 3070. limited. Through an experience, Klara comes to believe that the sun has great kindness and a special kind of nourishment that can save Josie. The novel tells how Klara works to get the sun to help Josie regain her health, as Klara believes it can. Klara and the Sun generated a lot of discussion, which the group enjoyed. There were those who really enjoyed the book, and those that didn’t, with the former being in the majority. One reader felt the book was a “remarkable achievement” that contained many concepts and moral choices for the reader to contemplate. There was the relationship between humans and machines, the place of artificial intelligence in our society as it increases its power and dominance over human intellect, humans’ responsibilities to machines that contribute to our lives in personal ways, the development of religion to help make sense of the world, the importance of programming and misinterpretation of experience, the consequences of loneliness, and more. Ishiguro doesn’t answer the questions he raises, but rather leaves them for the reader to consider, interpret, discuss, and decide. There also were those who were not so enchanted with the book. Some said it was “junior fiction” that 9th graders would find interesting. It was a little long and dragged for some, and was like “the autobiography of a machine,” one said. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03
