Treats provided by Carol Long were largely from Japan to recognize Kazuo Ishiguro, the author of the group’s November selection, Klara and the Sun. It was published in 2021 and is science fiction. This is the eighth novel by the Nobel Prize-winning, British writer. Ishiguro’s story is set in the U.S. in an unspecified, dystopian future where some children are genetically engineered, or “lifted,” to enhance their academic ability. Schooling is provided entirely at home by on-screen tutors, so opportunities for socialization are limited and parents who can afford it often buy their children androids as companions. The book’s narrative is told by Klara, a solar-powered AF (Artificial Friend), who is chosen by Josie, a sickly, 14-year-old to be her companion. Josie lives with her mother in a remote region of prairie. Soon after joining them, Klara learns that the lifting process carries some risk. Josie’s older sister Sal had earlier died, and Josie herself is gravely ill. Josie’s only near neighbor and childhood friend is Rick, a boy of about her own age. Although academically able, Rick has not been lifted and faces discrimination and reduced career prospects. In spite of this, Josie and Rick have always known that they will be together forever. Although Klara is exceptionally intelligent and observant, her knowledge of the world is First Monday Reading Group discusses Klara and the Sun The prose and story development also disappointed them. Others found it simplistic, but still eloquent, creative, and cleaver. However the group did believe the book presented a possible future that their grandchildren may have to face. As machines become more like humans, it is a potential, scary future with moral questions that Ishiguro wants us to consider today. Klara and the Sun got the group thinking and talking about related issues. The questions of upper income parents providing extra tutoring for their college-aspiring children, and the appropriateness of the SAT exam and Affirmative Action in college admissions were also considered before the readers refocused on the book for some final thoughts. The group seemed to agree that Klara and the Sun was a worthwhile book to read, and it had been a good discussion. Ishiguro was able to make this science fiction future and Klara’s plight seem real for readers. Some found Klara’s being treated like a “vacuum cleaner” at the book’s end to be sad, and they were left with feelings of melancholy. The readers also agreed the moral issues Ishiguro raises are ones we should be thinking about now and working on solutions because our decedents may have to grapple with them in the not-too-distant future. With their discussion complete, the readers considered their next books. The group tries to alternate monthly between fiction and non-fiction books. They had previously selected the non-fiction Priestdaddy by Patricia Lockwood for December and Afterparties by Anthony Veasna So for January. After some consideration, the group picked Prisoners of Geography: Ten Maps that Explain Everything About the World, by Tim Marshall for their February read. The group’s next meeting will be Monday, December 5 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required by calling the Recreation Department at 420- 3070. limited. Through an experience, Klara comes to believe that the sun has great kindness and a special kind of nourishment that can save Josie. The novel tells how Klara works to get the sun to help Josie regain her health, as Klara believes it can. Klara and the Sun generated a lot of discussion, which the group enjoyed. There were those who really enjoyed the book, and those that didn’t, with the former being in the majority. One reader felt the book was a “remarkable achievement” that contained many concepts and moral choices for the reader to contemplate. There was the relationship between humans and machines, the place of artificial intelligence in our society as it increases its power and dominance over human intellect, humans’ responsibilities to machines that contribute to our lives in personal ways, the development of religion to help make sense of the world, the importance of programming and misinterpretation of experience, the consequences of loneliness, and more. Ishiguro doesn’t answer the questions he raises, but rather leaves them for the reader to consider, interpret, discuss, and decide. There also were those who were not so enchanted with the book. Some said it was “junior fiction” that 9th graders would find interesting. It was a little long and dragged for some, and was like “the autobiography of a machine,” one said. This finding arose from the facts, cited in the EIR, that (1) Caltrans assumes a sight distance of 385 feet to allow vehicles traveling at 35 MPH to stop safely, (2) at least 15% of vehicles on Moraga Avenue at Blair Park exceeded 35 MPH, and (3) no location at Blair Park provided a 385-foot sight distance for drivers traveling in either direction. Building a footbridge seemed an intuitive solution to the sight-distance problem for pedestrians. As the EIR reported, however, experience with footbridges showed that pedestrians, particularly children, “dash” rather than use a bridge if opportunities to cross appear at street level. Footbridges reduced deaths only when a wall at street level forces pedestrians to cross on the bridge. A wall on Moraga Avenue was, however, thought ineffective because it would have had to include dash-inducing gaps for vehicular left turns into and out of Blair Park. A footbridge, moreover, would not have solved the sight distance problem for vehicles entering and exiting parking lots at Blair Park. Slowing vehicles on Moraga Avenue to the 25 MPH speed limit by enforcement, roundabouts, and road narrowing was considered in 2010. These options were rejected because they would have created a dangerous, rush-hour “back up” at the Highway 13/Moraga Avenue interchange which has a short sight distance for vehicles traveling south on Highway 13. Impeding traffic on Moraga would also have shifted travel to Oakland Avenue creating congestion and safety problems along its entire route through Piedmont. To assign 60 or more extremely and very low-income families to Blair Park would be not only dangerous but also uncivil. An extremely low-income neighborhood accessible only by a thoroughfare known unsafe for drivers and pedestrians would be, to say the least, stigmatized and isolated. This isolation would be made worse if, as is likely, parents rightly fearful of the unsafe conditions on Moraga Avenue, kept their children from visiting friends in Blair Park. Assigning extremely low-income families to Blair Park is not only unsafe and uncivil, but also unnecessary given the obviously better solution of integrating them into the new neighborhood of market-rate housing planned for the area around Coaches Field. The first draft of the Housing Element included 60 very and extremely low-income units in that neighborhood and showed no housing in Blair Park. We should return to that plan because it would tempt no one to cross Moraga Avenue. The Corporation Yard, which attracts no pedestrians and generates few vehicular trips, could be moved to Blair Park to make room, if needed, for added housing. Rather than becoming a segregated community, Piedmont could celebrate a new, safe, and inclusive neighborhood.

This finding arose from the facts, cited in the EIR, that (1) Caltrans assumes a sight distance of 385 feet to allow vehicles traveling at 35 MPH to stop safely, (2) at least 15% of vehicles on Moraga Avenue at Blair Park exceeded 35 MPH, and (3) no location at Blair Park provided a 385-foot sight distance for drivers traveling in either direction. Building a footbridge seemed an intuitive solution to the sight-distance problem for pedestrians. As the EIR reported, however, experience with footbridges showed that pedestrians, particularly children, “dash” rather than use a bridge if opportunities to cross appear at street level. Footbridges reduced deaths only when a wall at street level forces pedestrians to cross on the bridge. A wall on Moraga Avenue was, however, thought ineffective because it would have had to include dash-inducing gaps for vehicular left turns into and out of Blair Park. A footbridge, moreover, would not have solved the sight distance problem for vehicles entering and exiting parking lots at Blair Park. Slowing vehicles on Moraga Avenue to the 25 MPH speed limit by enforcement, roundabouts, and road narrowing was considered in 2010. These options were rejected because they would have created a dangerous, rush-hour “back up” at the Highway 13/Moraga Avenue interchange which has a short sight distance for vehicles traveling south on Highway 13. Impeding traffic on Moraga would also have shifted travel to Oakland Avenue creating congestion and safety problems along its entire route through Piedmont. To assign 60 or more extremely and very low-income families to Blair Park would be not only dangerous but also uncivil. An extremely low-income neighborhood accessible only by a thoroughfare known unsafe for drivers and pedestrians would be, to say the least, stigmatized and isolated. This isolation would be made worse if, as is likely, parents rightly fearful of the unsafe conditions on Moraga Avenue, kept their children from visiting friends in Blair Park. Assigning extremely low-income families to Blair Park is not only unsafe and uncivil, but also unnecessary given the obviously better solution of integrating them into the new neighborhood of market-rate housing planned for the area around Coaches Field. The first draft of the Housing Element included 60 very and extremely low-income units in that neighborhood and showed no housing in Blair Park. We should return to that plan because it would tempt no one to cross Moraga Avenue. The Corporation Yard, which attracts no pedestrians and generates few vehicular trips, could be moved to Blair Park to make room, if needed, for added housing. Rather than becoming a segregated community, Piedmont could celebrate a new, safe, and inclusive neighborhood. Climate Corner Continued from page 2 in the next five years. For us, it is not about who we agree with 100% of the time, or who is most popular in our community, but who do we trust? Who do we believe has the thoughtfulness to make the best decisions, the intelligence to seek creative solutions, and the integrity to stand up for their beliefs. For Piedmont school board, the person we trust is Ruchi Medhekar. As active volunteers with the Beach Parents Organization, we met Ruchi not long after her family moved to town when she began her involvement with the parent club. What was immediately apparent was her genuine interest in our schools and her priority in putting students first. Fast forward to 2022. Ruchi is very clearly a valued member of our community as evidenced by her school and district level leadership roles, and her involvement with the Piedmont Education Foundation and the City Recreation Commission. She has earned a reputation for working hard, listening with an open mind, and having the kind of can-do attitude that we all know PUSD needs. Her impressive career as a scientist and business leader provides a unique perspective on evaluating curriculum priorities, strategic planning, and the need to balance competing demands with constrained resources. As our district moves beyond COVID, students and families deserve to have leaders who bring broad perspectives, demonstrate foresight, think independently, and have the courage to lead. We trust Ruchi to be this kind of leader. Ruchi Medhekar will be a champion for educational excellence and student wellness, ensuring that our kids are academically and socially supported and inspired. We are lucky and proud to have her represent us on the school board. –Linda & Andrew Wendel Parents of students at PMS and Beach Elementary electric appliances in a cost-effective manner. articles.text: Piedmont voters re-elected Betsy Andersen and Jennifer Long, and elected veteran Planning Commission member Tom Ramsey to four-year terms on City Council based on partial voting results late last night. Three seats were available with a total of six candidates running – Andersen, Long, Ramsey, Bridget Harris, Jeanne Solnordal, and Nancy Bostrom. As of 10:42 p.m. Tuesday night, November 8, Andersen was the top vote getter with 1,701 votes, Ramsey received 1,431 votes, and Long received 1,418. Harris Was fourth with received 639 votes, Solnordal a distant 435, and Bostrom with 81 votes. In-person voting took place at the Veterans Memorial Building and was staffed by poll workers for four days, Saturday through Tuesday. The number of tallied votes represented ballots cast in-person and by mail. Voters not registered by the October 24 deadline had the option to register same-day and vote provisionally. Piedmont voters also had the option to vote with a Piedmont Photo Credit Julie Reichle Betsy Andersen was re-elected for a second 4-year term on Piedmont City Council Jennifer Long was re-elected to a full 4-year term on the city council. Planning Commissioner Tom Ramsey won easily in his first Piedmont City Council campaign.

articles.text: Catalytic converter thefts have risen dramatically in the last few years. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers and Captain Chris Monahan have recently focused on plotting each theft on a GIS (Geographical Information System) map to determine data trends to see where and when the thefts are happening. Despite concentrations in lower Piedmont and at night, however, Bowers said, “It’s truly all over the map.” The challenge in catching the thieves is structural and twofold. On the one hand, it’s a matter of economics: there’s a motivation for thefts as long as there’s a market for precious metals used in the converters (platinum, rhodium, and palladium). On the other hand, these thefts are hard to track because there is no identification on the converters. The auto industry generally opposes legislators’ attempts to require that identifying information be etched onto converters, due to the extra cost for manufacturers. articles.text: In partial returns late last night, Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson have commanding leads in the race for two open seats on the Piedmont School Board. At 8:36 p.m., approximately 1,700 ballots had been cast in the school board and city council election. The city has a total of 8,804 registered voters. At approximately 11 p.m. Tuesday night, Medhekar is the leading vote getter with 41.39% of the vote, and Thomasson was at 39.62%. Shirley Hooi trailed Thomasson by roughly 20% of the vote. “The campaign was a great experience. I got to meet and talk with so many people around town, which made me feel even more connected to our community,” said Medhekar. “I am grateful for the confidence the voters have shown in me tonight, and most importantly, I am excited to get to work on the school board to help foster positive dialogue and advocate for a high-quality and nurturing school experience for our kids.” There are no incumbents in this race, and all three candidates were first-time candidates. “The campaign has been challenging yet incredibly informative,” said Thomasson. “Tonight I am grateful for each constituent who came out to speak with me, share their perspectives, insights, and experience. Now we get to work. The challenges are significant and yet I am confident that we have the knowledge and determination in this community to come together and solve them,” said Thomasson. Ruchi Medhekar Lindsay Thomasson
articles.title: Medhekar, Thomasson heading to school board victories

articles.text: The following is an abridged version of a letter sent to Piedmont City Council on November 6 by residents on Oakland Avenue. Editor: As Piedmont residents directly affected by the new plans for the Oakland Avenue Bulb-Out at Jerome Avenue we are writing to protest and object to certain aspects of the new plans. The new plans include for the first time the removal and relocation of two long existing AC Transit Bus stops at the corners of Oakland Avenue and Jerome Avenue and Oakland Avenue and Latham Street and the loss of at least 4 parking spaces that are used every day by residents. The new plans differ in material and substantial ways from the Bulb-Out and flashing Lights plans and proposals previously presented in City Staff reports and in the plain language of the City Council minutes and resolutions on which residents relied for their information. Many of the signatories to this Notice are long-time residents of the local area, and some of us have lived here for over 45 years. We are fully cognizant of the AC Transit bus traffic patterns and bus stops in our area, as many of us have for decades used the buses running up and down Oakland Avenue. We are also very familiar with the vehicular traffic patterns and parking needs on Oakland and Jerome Avenues and Latham Steet. We are approaching these new City proposed traffic measures not as idealogues but as practical people and residents who know what is going on in our neighborhood. At no time prior to the revelation of the current plans on October 29, 2022, were residents informed of the removal of the bus stops and parking or the relocation of bus stops, nor does it appear that this proposed radical change in the plans was discussed in public or addressed in staff reports or in open City Council meetings. The April 15, 2019 Piedmont Council Agenda Report contained a recommendation submitted by Public Works Director Chester Nakahara to the Mayor and City Council regarding “Review of Preliminary Designs for Traffic Calming Measures at Oakland Ave. at El Cerrito Ave. and Oakland Ave. at Jerome Ave. ”The recommendation attached a plan and commented that the 4 corner bulbout design would include rapid flashing beacons, new pedestrian ramps and refreshed street paint. articles.text: Staff photo Resident and architect Chuck Oraftik measures driveways at Oakland and Jerome Aves. to compare with city bulb-out plans. A year ago, on October 4, 2021, Piedmont City Council first approved design plans for the construction of bulb-outs on Oakland Avenue at the intersections of El Cerrito Avenue and Jerome Avenue. At an on-site meeting on November 1 a week ago, as directed by the city staff, the plans were shared with neighbors. The proposals were based upon the Piedmont Safer Streets Plan, adopted in December 2021, which listed the Jerome and El Cerrito intersections as among the 10 high priority crossings for pedestrian safety improvements. The current plan calls for four permanent “bulb-outs” at each intersection where the sidewalk extends and the street shrinks, to make the pedestrian crossing shorter and safer. In addition to the bulb-outs, the plan provides for high-visibility crosswalks, pedestrian ramps, yellow flashing beacons, new street paint, and new signs at each intersection. Despite the public engagement plan prescribed by the Piedmont Safer Streets Plan, however, the bulb-out proposal has received low support from those it affects. Residents overwhelmingly agree with the need for slower traffic on Oakland Avenue, as is reflected in community surveys by city staff. Oakland Avenue residents Jonah Levy and Helga Ying, as example, have called for more pedestrian safety measures like speed bumps, signage, and bicycle infrastructure. However, many neighbors of the targeted intersections on Oakland Ave. feel that they have been hastily and scantily informed of some of the consequences – the elimination of 10 street parking spots and the relocation of four bus stops. As one resident explained, “Our community doesn’t call it the bulb-out problem, we call it the bus stop problem.” The intention behind the bulb-out plan — pedestrian safety on the busiest street in Piedmont — may present little problem. Residents initially saw a benefit to the installation of bollards at the intersection on Greenbank Avenue in April 2019. But a better solution was found” installing two newly designed speed bumps on the narrow street. Bollards, one resident said, “is like putting a Band-Aid on a wound.” Another resident, perusing weeks of City Council meetings regarding the bulb-outs, found nothing about bus stops; nor are buses mentioned in the Piedmont Safer Streets plan, except for a statement ensuring that “neighborhood traffic calming measures do not negatively impact [bus] access.” Some of the existing crosswalks along these intersections already empty onto private driveways. Given that the impacted homes will lose parking spots, many residents contend that the bulb-out plan will create more pedestrian traffic, not less, on a busy street. Nor is there a precedent for this parking spot displacement, given that the other bus stops along Oakland Avenue are placed in deliberately non-invasive areas — where houses don’t face the street, and nearly always along a shrub wall. Oakland Avenue residents are hoping the City can describe how the current plan benefits those it will directly affect. business hours.

articles.text: The Piedmont Post has begun its 25th year of publishing the community’s weekly newspaper. It’s first edition was on October 20, 1998, a 12-page paper that hardly offered any promise, let alone optimism, that it might be around a quarter century later. In a small town with only a few commercial businesses, the outlook for its survival was somewhat bleak. Ten years later we began reading stories in the New York Times about the large number of local newspapers going out of business – over 2,000 at last count. And yet here we are – thriving and finding ways to thank the residents for so strongly supporting The Little Newspaper That Could. During the next several weeks and months, you will read comments of some of the people who were there at the beginning – the optimists and pragmatists.
articles.title: 25th Anniversary of Piedmont Post

articles.text: Editor: How is it possible that the Post is already 25 years old? Very few would have taken up the challenge of starting a serious, subscription-based newspaper in a small town. Too many chances to fail. But the Post has survived and flourished. From the beginning, it has covered stories often overlooked by the large regional papers but important to our multi-generational community (and especially to the parents of school-age children!). in a well-written, evenhanded manner, and – where appropriate – a self-deprecating sense of humor Hats off to the Post, our hometown paper. –Rick Eigenbrode and Pat Nicholas, Palm Drive
articles.title: 25 years? How is it possible?

articles.text: Join the City of Piedmont on Wednesday, November 9, for an informational open house about the City’s updated Draft Housing Element. The open house will take place from 5:00-6:30 pm on Wednesday at Community Hall (711 Highland Avenue). This event is an opportunity for you to learn more and speak directly with Planning & Building staff about: • proposed changes to the Draft Housing Element sites inventory based on direction from City Council at their August 1, 2022 meeting • timelines for Housing Element adoption and implementation • what to expect over the next three years as the City implements the policies and programs outlined in the Draft Housing Element The open house will also provide information about consequences for non-compliance with State deadlines and how they impact Piedmont, including the process known as the “builder’s remedy,” which limits a city’s ability to deny applications for new development while its Housing Element is out of compliance. articles.text: Healthy donors needed to give now The American Red Cross urges blood and platelet donors to give now and help fight the potential impact of seasonal illnesses and a potentially severe flu season on the blood supply. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention predicts a serious spread of flu this year and is already reporting an early spike in cases in several states. When seasonal illnesses increase, the number of healthy donors tends to decrease, leaving the Red Cross blood supply vulnerable to a potential shortage over the holidays. Paired with busy holiday schedules, seasonal illnesses may make it harder to collect the blood hospital patients require this winter. Donors − especially those with type O blood and those giving platelets − can help bolster the blood supply now by making an appointment to give in the coming weeks. There is no waiting period to donate blood or platelets after receiving a flu shot. Schedule an appointment by using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org or calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733- 2767). As thanks, the Red Cross is offering several opportunities to donors this month: • Everyone who donates until November 22 will receive a $10 e-gift card to a merchant of choice. Details are available at rcblood.org/perks. • Those donating who come to give over the Thanksgiving holiday, November 23-27, will get a Red Cross knit beanie, while supplies last. Details are available at rcblood.org/together. For more infromation, call the Oakland Blood Bank at 6230 Claremont Avenue. Tel. (510) 594-5210.
articles.title: Flu season may impact Red Cross blood supply

articles.text: On Monday, November 7, the City Council met to approve the following: the continued use of Zoom as a remote option for meetings, the consolidation of three parcels of land into two in the Piedmont Community Pool Project, and an agreement to provide crossing guards at the intersections of Oakland and Grand; Oakland and Bonita; Oakland and Highland; and Oakland and El Cerrito. articles.text: NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that at 5:30 p.m. on November 14, 2022, the Planning Commission will review an ordinance amending Chapter 17 (Planning and Land Use) of the City Code to conform the City’s regulations regarding Accessory Dwelling Units to new state laws and make a recommendation to the City Council. The ordinance also includes a new division 17.42 to address CA Assembly Bill 916, which requires ministerial review for the development of new bedrooms within existing residential units. NOTICE IS FURTHER GIVEN that at 6:00 p.m. on November 21, 2022, the City Council will consider the proposed ordinance and the recommendation of the Planning Commission and could approve the first reading of the ordinance. Background On January 1, 2022, new state laws come into effect which further limit a local jurisdiction’s ability to regulate Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs). The provisions affected by the changes to state law include but are not limited to: street (front) yard setbacks, unit height limitations, approval of existing conditions inconsistent with current Building Code requirements, interior connections between a Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit and the Primary Dwelling Unit, and the separate conveyance of ADUs. City staff is also recommending an incentive for the development of affordable ADUs in exchange for the release of owner-occupancy restrictions. Local laws which do not conform to these new state standards are preempted and cannot be enforced. The ordinance also proposes a new City Code division 17.42 that establishes a ministerial review process for projects that develop no more than two additional bedrooms within an existing dwelling unit, in conformance with AB 916 (2022). City staff has developed the proposed ordinance which will be considered by the Planning Commission and the City Council to conform Piedmont’s ADU regulations to the new state law. Documents on the City Website Documents related to this effort are available on the City website at piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Steven Pifer, former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine, joined the League of Women Voters of Piedmont on November 2, 2022 to discuss the current situation and prospects for Ukraine. The live audience included members from 16 different Leagues from California, Oregon, and Michigan. Topics included a brief recap of the current war in Ukraine, options for ending the war, the effects of the war within Russia, the risk for Europe and other neighboring countries, U.S. involvement and public opinion, and nuclear threats. Ambassador Pifer first talked about some of the surprises from the war, including the effectiveness of the Ukrainian military and the poor state of the Russian military’s logistics, command structure, military tactics and training. He broke down the war into three main phases. The first was from February 24 through March. Russia’s initial attack was from the East, intended to capture Kiev and occupy the eastern half to Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Steven Pifer. two-thirds of Ukraine. It was not successful. In the second phase, from April through July, the new goal was to capture all of the Donbas region. This push resulted in seizing Luhansk but not Donetsk. The third phase, from August to the present, has seen Ukrainian counter offenses in which Russian forces have been pushed out of formerly occupied territories. Asked how the war might end, Ambassador Pifer talked about the unlikely possibility of a negotiated settlement between Ukraine and Russia. He discussed the reasons why a settlement is unlikely and what the West can do to support Ukraine both in its current and post-war efforts. He highlighted societal influences within Ukraine and Russia that led to the conflict, which are currently affecting its resolution. He said he would like to see Russia “come to terms with the fact that it’s no longer the Russian empire – the Soviet Union – and that it ought to be finding ways to live in peace with its neighbors.” He also discussed perception of the war inside Russia both with the general public and within Putin’s inner circle; the risk to other countries, including Georgia, Kazakhstan, and the Baltic states; war crimes and the potential for Russian accountability; past corruption in the Ukrainian government; movement of Europe away from a dependency on Russian oil and gas; and the potential effects of the U.S. midterm election on America’s support of Ukraine. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) student’s standardized test scores for the 2021-22 school year earned the district top three rankings in California. All public school districts are required to take the California Assessments of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP) test, which tests subject matter, critical thinking, analytical writing, and problem-solving skills. The CAASPP is a collection of computer-based assessments in English Language literacy and Mathematics and Science. The CAASPP replaced the paperbased Standardized Testing and Reporting (STAR) program in 2014. Last spring, Piedmont students in grades 3–8, and grade 11 participated in the 2021-22 CAASPP for English Language Arts (ELA) and Math. Students in grades 5, 8, and 12, participated in a Science test. The California Department of Education released school, district and state aggregate results on October 24. Piedmont students demonstrated a high level of achievement overall on the CAASPP, ranking second among California unified school districts in English Language Arts and third in Math. Overall, more than 87% of Piedmont students met or exceeded state standards in English, marking a 2% increase from 2021, as well as a return to the district’s pre-pandemic score. In Mathematics, 81% of students met or exceeded state standards, 5.5% below pre-pandemic levels. In Science, nearly 75% of PUSD students met or exceeded state standards. To see Piedmont’s full test results visit Tinyurl.com/pusdcaaspp2022 for ELA and Math, and Tinyurl.com/ pusdcast2022 for Science. State results show that approximately 47% of students met or exceeded standards in English Language Arts (down four points from 2019), 33% in Math (down seven points), and 29% in Science (down one one point). “This is exciting news from the state and another wonderful testament to the hard work of Piedmont students, teachers and staff,” said Interim School Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. “To show such resiliency in reaching or approaching the District’s preCOVID results, despite everything they’ve gone through, demonstrates students’ willingness to learn and educators’ dedication to supporting them in every way.” The CAASPP assessments are one gauge of student progress, providing information to schools, teachers, and parents about how students perform relative to California’s goals for both learning and college and career readiness. The results will be used as one of several means to determine and meet student needs and guide discussions among parents and teachers. Individual scores were made available in the fall and can be seen online on the Infinite Campus Parent Portal. Directions are available on the district website.

articles.text: For over 30 years, Scouts have collected non-perishable food for the Alameda County Community Food Bank. The tradition continues this Saturday morning, November 12, when Piedmont Scouts will go door-to-door to pick of bags of non-perishable food being donated by residents, and which will be delivered to the Food Bank. Last year’s food drive generated more than 9,000 pounds of food and raised over $4,500 through the Scout virtual food drive. One week ago Piedmont residents received door hangers reminding them of the citywide food drive. Residents are encouraged to leave donations of nutritious, non-perishable food in recycled boxes or bags outside their doors before 9:00 a.m. this Saturday morning. Alameda County has one of the highest rates of hunger in the nation. One of every five Alameda County residents rely on the food bank for assistance, and two-thirds of those are children and the elderly. Help eliminate hunger by donating non-perishable foods such as: canned fruits, vegetables, and meats; canned soup; peanut butter; pasta and canned sauce. Troop 6 Scouts Charlie and JD Sellman shown last year with bags of donated food. Door hangers were left at residences throughout Piedmont last week reminding them that Saturday, November 12, is the annual Scouting for Food citywide campaign In addition, residents can participate in the virtual food drive by visiting the website (https:// donate.accf b.org/vfd/Member/ MyPage/5806787/Boy-Scoutsof-America?tab=MyPage), where $1 becomes 2 meals for children, adults, and seniors in the community. Help the Scouts reach their goal of $10,000. For more information contact Eris Turner at the Scout office at 510-844-4752. Visit the website www.piedmontbsa.org for additional information about the annual food collection program.

articles.text: Meeting scheduled for Nov. 16 at Alan Harvey Theater A public forum has been scheduled for residents to provide input in the Piedmont School Board’s search for a permanent school superintendent. The meeting will be held on Wednesday, November 16, at 6:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. Residents will have an opportunity to interact with consultants from the search firm, Leadership Associates, which has been hired by the school board to lead the search. Residents are asked to provide input about desired personal and professional qualities anticipated in the incoming superintendent. Comment from the public will be used in the development of the candidate profile, recruitment process, and reference checking. The consultants from Leadership Associates will also compile a summary of all comments received during these sessions and share the report with the School Board and with the future superintendent. During the forum, consultants will share an overview of the process, and ask audience members the following questions: • What are the desirable qualities, characteristics, background and professional and personal experiences for the next superintendent? • What do you see as the strengths of the district and the major challenges facing the district in years ahead? There is no need to RSVP. If unable to attend, individuals will have an opportunity to provide feedback and responses to these questions on an online survey. The survey will activate on November 14 and remain open until November 21. articles.text: Photos by Sohrab “Seb” Ford Children’s Fairyland Fairyland.org 699 Bellevue Avenue, Oakland, 452-2259 Fairyland is a mid-century 10-acre fantasy world for young children. The park has new puppet shows in its open-air Children’s Storybook Theater. Tam and Cam, a popular Cinderella tale from Vietnam is coming in November, along with the Lewis Carrol classic, Alice in Wonderland. Fairyland is open five days a week, Wednesday to Sunday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Lawrence Hall of Science Lawrencehallofscience.org 1 Centennial Drive, Berkeley 642-5132 The Hall is open for visitors to explore the wonders of science and the universe Wednesday–Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. For more than 50 years the Hall has enabled kids to discover something new with hands-on exhibits for all ages. See Sunstones II, the 3-D theater and explore the Cambrian Explosion. Exploratorium Exploratorium.edu Pier 15, San Francisco (415) 528-4444 The Exploratorium has interactive exhibits that are outof-the-world and invite participation. You will be amazed at the dozens of exhibits ready for kids and parents. Among the mind-blowing exhibits are the Aeolian harps, anamorphic benches, the Bacteriopolis, and the chaotic pendulum. The Exploratorium has more exhibits, features and activities than can be seen in one day, so consider a membership. Open Wed.-Friday, 10 a.m.–5 p.m. Thursday nights for ages 18 & older from 6–10 p.m., and Sunday from 12 noon to 5 p.m. Academy of Science Calacademy.org Golden Gate Park, 55 Music Concourse Dr., S.F. (415) 379-8000 California Academy of Science in Golden Gate Park has a four-story rainforest with everything from butterflies to the bioluminescent depths of the “twilight zone.” The Academy’s newest exhibit, “Bugs”, was created by Te Papa Tongarewa Museum of New Zealand and Weta Workshop (the creative studio behind the Lord of the Rings films’ sets). It reveals the secrets of insects and arthropods in delightful, dazzling ways. The Academy is open Mon. to Saturday, 9:30 a.m.-5:00 p.m., Thursday night for ages 18 & older from 6 - 10 p.m., and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. “We were really excited this year because we have a new theater. It opened up lots of new possibilities,” said Lorin. “Everyone just had a new level of excitement, which I think made this show better than usual.” The play, set in 19th century England, follows Elizabeth “Lizzy” Bennet and her sisters as they struggle in the game of love. The sisters encounter strict gender constructs, class conflict, and a persistent mother, Mrs. Bennet, set on marrying her four daughters off to the richest bachelors. Though Lizzy is insistent she will never marry, she ends up falling for Mr. Darcy. Lizzy navigates this dynamic switch while attempting to retain her strength of character. The play is “empowering but also hilarious,” commented Lorin adding that the story suggests “you can have a man, but still be a feminist.”

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Part 2 of Sally the Witch As the midnight wind blew through Sally’s hair, she looked down to see the lights of Salem glowing and twinkling beneath her. Flying over the magic district, Sally could see the old, empty building at the corner of Looking Glass Way, and breathed a heavy sigh. It had been her dream to own an enchanted bookstore ever since she was able to cast a spell – usually around two or three years old. (Witches and wizards are fast learners.) Sally figured her bookstore would be filled with texts of worlds long forgotten, spellbooks, and potion journals that had been in her family for hundreds of years. The store would even have books on enchanted cooking. Sally’s grandmother had owned a bookstore centuries ago, and as a young girl she would go with her mother to sit in a favorite corner by the fireplace. The bookstore was filled with soft lights of all colors and with plants from around the world. Sally would sit and read her favorite book, “The Tales of Agatha the Wise.” It was about the adventures of a witch who could wield the elements. Contrary to popular beliefs about witches, Agatha helped people. Sally always remembered the fireplace with green flames and the shelves with thousands of books. She also remembered the terrible day that the bookstore caught fire and burned down. The books were saved, but not the building, and since that day Sally had a dream of recreating her grandmother’s bookstore as her own. Out of the corner of her eye, Sally noticed a “For Sale” sign. She slammed the brakes on her broom, almost knocking Lucinda, her cat, out of the pet passenger seat. Whooshing down to Looking Glass Way, Sally jumped off her broom and ran to the building. But before we go on with Sally’s story, I must inform you that buying property as a magical being is a different process than for mere humans. Sally walked up to the building and began bargaining for the price. After many different offers both parties came to the agreement of 300 gold coins. A moderately cheap price, considering that there were curses on the building and it was inhabited by ghosts. But those were part of Sally’s everyday life. Nonetheless, Sally excitedly picked up the key, opened the door, and walked inside. The main floor was a big open space with gothic style windows and a fireplace. The floors were wooden and creaked when stepped on. The second level was reached by a spiral wooden staircase with ivy on the railing and steps, the level itself was a loft that included more gothic windows. Eager to create her dream store, Sally decided to start renovating that same day. She hopped onto her broom and flew home as fast as she could. Arriving at her cottage she put a charm that levitated anything that it was cast on, and she cast it on all of the books and some of the shelves to make it easier to transport them. As she flew through the early morning sky she looked behind her and started to laugh; s30 flying bookshelves and thousands of books following her. As she made it back to the bookstore the furniture and books followed her in. She started to arrange the bookshelves and the books began to find their designated sections and shelves. While the books and furniture were arranging themselves, Sally noticed that there were sofas tucked away in the back of the store. She put a Gemini charm on it and suddenly there six couches appeared. The bookstore was coming together, the books were exactly where they were supposed to be, the couches had been placed strategically near the windows and corners. Sally enchanted the ivy on the stairs to help decorate all the shelves and windowsills. Remembering her grandmother’s bookstore, she pulled a book off the shelves named “103 Ways to Light Up A Room, Literally.” The final thing she did was to light the fireplace with green flames. And just like that, The Bookstore On Looking Glass Way was open for business. Larissa Edel, a student at Bentley School, sent this story as a post-Halloween treat.
articles.title: A GHOSTLY TALE The bookstore on Looking Glass Way

articles.text: Piedmont’s Fire and Police Departments held a Wildfire Evacuation Drill on Saturday morning, November 5, the first of its kind in the city. Despite some morning rain, participation was high in both the evacuation of residents in high risk-homes and the debriefing at Community Hall afterwards. Approximately 50 homes above Coaches Field (Maxwelton Road, Abbot Way, Echo Lane, Nellie Avenue) were identified as the area at the highest risk for wildfire due to the isolated locale and wooded surroundings. Historically, large wildfires in Oakland have come over the hill near the Piedmont border. “The police department was able to knock on every door in the evacuation neighborhood in about 45 minutes,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “I thought it was a great accomplishment. They were able to physically check on every single house in the area.” Brannigan mentioned that there were 615 downloads of the at-home fire-drill activities and over 1,000 visits for the fire evacuation exercise. During the drill Piedmont’s Public Works Department was called on to clear the Corporation Yard of critical equipment that might have been in harm’s way during an emergency and to redirect the equipment to firefighters at the top of the hill on Maxwelton Road. “The city staff that participated got a lot out of it. We did have some good lessons learned, and not everything went perfectly. We have some things to figure out and improve, and that’s the whole point [of the drill],” Brannigan added. Photo Credit Tamarack Management Piedmont Fire Department simulates fighting a wildfire above Coaches Field. Photo Credit Piedmont Police Fire Chief Dave Brannigan (right) talks with Piedmont Police officers during the November 5 wildfire evacuation drill. Photo Credit Tamarack Management Community members from Maxwelton Road are briefed by police and fire after having their doors knocked on in the 9 a.m. hour to simulate a fire evacuation. Photo Credit Piedmont Police Chief Brannigan communicates via radio with other first responders. Photo Credit Piedmont Police Community members met at 711 Highland Avenue’s Community Center for a debriefing Saturday morning at 10 a.m.
articles.title: Rain doesn’t dampen turnout for Wildfire Evacuation Drill

Eager to create her dream store, Sally decided to start renovating that same day. She hopped onto her broom and flew home as fast as she could. Arriving at her cottage she put a charm that levitated anything that it was cast on, and she cast it on all of the books and some of the shelves to make it easier to transport them. As she flew through the early morning sky she looked behind her and started to laugh; s30 flying bookshelves and thousands of books following her. As she made it back to the bookstore the furniture and books followed her in. She started to arrange the bookshelves and the books began to find their designated sections and shelves. While the books and furniture were arranging themselves, Sally noticed that there were sofas tucked away in the back of the store. She put a Gemini charm on it and suddenly there six couches appeared. The bookstore was coming together, the books were exactly where they were supposed to be, the couches had been placed strategically near the windows and corners. Sally enchanted the ivy on the stairs to help decorate all the shelves and windowsills. Remembering her grandmother’s bookstore, she pulled a book off the shelves named “103 Ways to Light Up A Room, Literally.” The final thing she did was to light the fireplace with green flames. And just like that, The Bookstore On Looking Glass Way was open for business. Larissa Edel, a student at Bentley School, sent this story as a post-Halloween treat. DEREK McBREARTY PLUMBING Residential Plumbing Services Sewer line repair Gas lines Water heaters Earthquake shutoff valves Plumbing repair service 415-377-3841 Lic #795277 Rain doesn’t dampen turnout for Wildfire Evacuation Drill By Jay Russell Piedmont’s Fire and Police Departments held a Wildfire Evacuation Drill on Saturday morning, November 5, the first of its kind in the city. Despite some morning rain, participation was high in both the evacuation of residents in high risk-homes and the debriefing at Community Hall afterwards. Approximately 50 homes above Coaches Field (Maxwelton Road, Abbot Way, Echo Lane, Nellie Avenue) were identified as the area at the highest risk for wildfire due to the isolated locale and wooded surroundings. Historically, large wildfires in Oakland have come over the hill near the Piedmont border. “The police department was able to knock on every door in the evacuation neighborhood in about 45 minutes,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “I thought it was a great accomplishment. They were able to physically check on every single house in the area.” Brannigan mentioned that there were 615 downloads of the at-home fire-drill activities and over 1,000 visits for the fire evacuation exercise. During the drill Piedmont’s Public Works Department was called on to clear the Corporation Yard of critical equipment that might have been in harm’s way during an emergency and to redirect the equipment to firefighters at the top of the hill on Maxwelton Road. “The city staff that participated got a lot out of it. We did have some good lessons learned, and not everything went perfectly. We have some things to figure out and improve, and that’s the whole point [of the drill],” Brannigan added. articles.text: Both veteran and new Petal It Forward ambassadors gathered at J. Miller Flowers on Wednesday, October 19, to begin their 8th Annual Petal It Forward celebration – and what a celebration it was. Petal It Forward is a national program sponsored by the Society of American Florists that shares the emotional and healing power of flowers. There are more than 450 events in more than 400 cities in the U.S. and in Canada and India. In each country it is quite an undertaking. Quite simply, it is a random-acts-of-kindness event, with flowers as the focal point of interest for all involved. More than a dozen volunteers trimmed, assembled, and wrapped hundreds of bouquets with flowers donated by Santa Rose Wholesale, Pacific Coast Evergreen, Mt. Eden Floral, Neve Brothers, Torchio Nursery, Rafas Floral, and Repetto’s Nursery. Many growers have donated year after year, and their beautiful blooms are a huge part of what makes Petal It Forward such a meaningful day every year. Two bouquets are given to each recipient – one to keep, and one to give to someone else. The group’s first stop was UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital in Oakland. The flowers were barely unloaded and volunteers just fanning out when a mom arrived alone, her shoulder down and her heart in her throat. She was given two bouquets, and tears were shed by all as the mom told the groud her child came to Children’s a week ago as a trauma patient. It was clear by the pain on her face that this had been the hardest week of her life. She said that this small act of Gisele Rainier (left), Shari Santos, Stacey Hanover, Danielle Baca, Valerie Lee, and Bob Otsuka in front of UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital in Oakland. kindness was a beautiful, unexpected gesture in such a difficult time. Although she couldn’t take the flowers to her child’s room, she promised to take a picture and show her daughter how total strangers had given the bouquets to her and how appreciative she was. There were many moments like that, with worried parents receiving a moment of beauty when they were least expecting it but needing it most. Children were bringing the second bouquet to their grandparents or someone else important to them, and their pride at bringing flowers home brought smiles to all everyone’s faces. The group then brought flowers to Mountain Music on Piedmont Avenue, a store had recently robbed, and whose owners appreciated a bright spot in their day. They also brought flowers to the Piedmont Avenue Holistic Veterinarian and their office puppy. The last stops were Pizza Violetta, whose owner, Violetta’s dad Jonathan, had provided delicious pizzas to the hungry volunteers making bouquets the day before. Another wonderful visit was to the dedicated team across the street from the flower shop on Piedmont Avenue at Chapel of the Chimes. As is done every year, each volunteer is asked to share their favorite moment. More than one mentioned the first woman they met, whose tears reminded them how important Petal It Forward is, especially to those with sick or injured children. Another volunteer said that she loved how unexpected and appreciated every recipient found the small act of giving. Another said that Petal It Forward reminded them of how such a small act can bring such an emotional moment for someone who truly needs it. Valerie Lee, co-owner of J. Miller Flowers, said that one of her favorite reasons for putting in the extra hours and extra work year in and year out is that it’s for her community – as a person and as a member of the Piedmont, Oakland, and Contra Costa community. Marisa Anderson and Cynthia Aguirre at Chapel of the Chimes. Jada Brown at RIDE Cycling Studio. Shari Santos (left), Julie Moreno, Carey Boisvert, Linda Henson, Jacqueline Angel, Mark Frattine, Monica Kelsey, Gisele Rainier, and Bob Otsuka at Chapel of the Chimes.

articles.text: Emma Eisemon, Cecilia DeFazio place 2nd in doubles Staff Photos Tanya Kononova won the WACC Tennis Singles title on November 5 with a victory over Alameda’s Juliana Johnson. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team had a successful showing at the 2022 Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament at Chabot College last weekend, November 4-5. Firstyear student Tanya Kononova, a junior, won the singles championship, and the doubles team of junior Cecilia DeFazio and sophomore Emma Eisemon placed second. Kononova defeated Alameda’s Juliana Johnson on Saturday in straight sets 6-3, 7-5, and marked her third win of the season over Johnson. “I just waited until the moment I could make myself calm and in the mood where I could win. I didn’t want to play a third set because I was unsure if I could handle the pressure,” said Kononova, who arrived from Ukraine in late summer. But though But though seeded No. 1 in the tournament, she admitted she had some concerns. She had to fight through some frustrating moments in the second set to win 7-5, but was able to hammer home the win with her usual array of powerful serves, forehands, and backhands. For the final point, Johnson was unable to return a strong forehand by Kononova, forcing the Alameda starter to commit an error on an attempt that flew out of bounds. “It feels strange; I was so emotional today. It felt like was playing against myself. I just need to practice and gain more experience, because this match was good experience to gain. When I play in a similar situation, I’ll know that I’ve already been through a tough challenge and Emma Eisemon and Cecilia DeFazio (not pictured) finished second in the WACC doubles bracket. Michaela Bini (front) and Anne Jumper took third-place in the doubles ladder.

articles.text: After receiving a first-round bye, the No. 3 seeded Piedmont High boys’ water polo team defeated No. 6 Novato in the Division 2 North Coast Section quarterfinals on Saturday, November 5 at Amador Valley in Pleasanton. PHS advances to the semifinals and will face No. 2 Marin Academy today, Wednesday, November 9 in San Rafael. “It was kind of a shootout. We were scoring goals and Novato was scoring goals. We had a really balanced attack. Everybody was involved and that’s what really carried us through the game. It wasn’t our best defensive effort. It was our balanced scoring attack that got it done,” said coach Rik Krumins. It was a big match for juniors George Stein and Peter Krumins, who recorded five goals and four goals respectively. “Peter was hitting shots from the outside and a lot of those were going in. George is an all-around player. He was scoring inside, scoring on 6-on-5 chances, and scoring on the counter attack. George was doing it all. It was a good game for him,” said coach Krumins. No. 3 Piedmont faces the second-ranked Wildcats of Marin Academy tomorrow, a rematch from the 2021 NCS Semifinals. The Highlanders will have the opportunity to avenge last year’s 7-4 postseason loss. “We know they are a really good team,” said Krumins. “Their players play on clubs yearround. We also know they are a good team of swimmers, and they are a team who has been at this level before. We expect them to be very confident and wellcoached. We have to bring our best to advance into the championship round. “We are confident and excited. If we execute our game plan, then I think we have a pretty good shot,” he said. “I think last year’s game is somewhat in the minds of our players, but it’s a different team for us and for them. They’ve lost some key seniors, and we lost three key seniors. We are a more balanced team than last year and we’re able to handle the counter attack, I think the boys are pretty confident going in,” Krumins added. PHS will face Marin Academy goalie Ezra Trost-Goldhammer, who is a Piedmont resident and competed in the Junior Olympics with club-team CC United alongside other PHS students. “They have a really good goalie who is actually from Piedmont. A lot of the players know each other from clubs, it’s going to be a good game,” said Krumins. Semifinals recap After conceding the opening goal of the game after 38 seconds, Piedmont gained a man-advantage at 6:05, leading to Stein scoring 13 seconds later. Novato scored again at the 5:24 mark, but it was the last time the Hornets held the lead. Just 22 seconds Staff Photos George Stein had five goals in Piedmont’s 15-12 win over No. 6 Novato in the NCS Quarterfinals. Peter Krumins scored four goals against Novato. Daniel Banin had three goals on the Hornets. later, Stein scored again to tie it at 2-2 and then landed a first-quarter hat trick with 1:44 to go. Daniel Banin made it 4-2 with 38 seconds left in the first. In the second quarter, Novato narrowed the gap to 4-3 after 40 seconds of action, but Piedmont responded after drawing a penalty at the 4:08 mark and Declan Linnane scoring 13 seconds later. Finn Burke added another for PHS with 1:47 left in the half, 6-3, and then #2 scored with another man-advantage. Novato tacked one on with 32 seconds left to make it 7-4 going into the half. Novato scored 45 seconds into the third quarter but it only took Piedmont’s Banin to increase the advantage just 30 seconds later. Banin scored another in a 6-on-5 opportunity with 4:46 to go. Novato added one to their tally 18 seconds later, but Peter Krumins answered just 13 seconds later. The Hornets scored the next two goals to make it 10-8 with 2:31 left in the third, but Krumins scored at the 2:08 mark and Stein sent one in with 52 seconds on the clock. In the fourth quarter, Burke scored after a minute and a half, which led to three consecutive scores by Novato to put themselves within striking distance at 13-11. However, Stein scored with a man-advantage with 2:54 on the clock. Novato scored 52 seconds later, 14-12, but it was their last time to get on the scoreboard. With 23 seconds left in the game, Stein scored the game’s final goal to make it 15-12. Final stats: Stein scored five goals, and had one steal and one assist. Krumins had four goals and one assist. Banin had three goals and one assist. Burke scored twice with one assist and steal. Linnane had a goal, assist, and steal. Goalie Dariush Kashani had five saves and one assist. NEXT UP No. 3 Piedmont (20-6) heads to No. 2 Marin Academy in San Rafael today, Wednesday, November 9 at 3:30 p.m. for the North Coast Section semifinals. With a victory, PHS will face the winner of No. 1 Terra Linda and No. 4 Clayton Valley in the finals.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross country teams had a strong run at the Western Alameda County Conference Championship meet on Saturday, November 5 at Hayward High. The boys’ team finishing second out of seven schools, and the girls’ team was fourth. Berkeley’s boys’ team won with 98 points, and Piedmont was second with 115 points. Senior Christian Taylor finished third of 71 runners with a time of 15:43.51, which marked his fastest time this season by 22 seconds. Junior Xander Schulte-Sasse finished fifth with a time of 15:46.92, ahead of senior Parker Long in 15:59.07. Rounding out their top-five was junior Julien Lee in 19th with a time of 16:51.33, and senior Alex Ware in 22nd at 17:03.04. “The boys had a great run to finish second. Christian Taylor, Xander Schulte-Sasse, and Parker Long all made first-team all-league with their results. Alex Ware ran his best race ever, shoring up our number five position,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. There is notably a bug going around the Highlanders’ cross country team that forced some athletes to miss time and recover. Now that students are progressing from some sickness, “Coach B” Holmlund is hopeful that their best race is ahead of them at North Coast Section on November 19 at Hayward. Freshman Skylar Best was fourth of 59 runners. Parker Long finished in sixth place in 15:59.07. “Not everyone has completely recovered from our batch of illness going around. But if the stars align, NCS is calling for us to run well,” Holmlund added. Freshman Skylar Best continued to lead the girls’ team with a 4th place overall finish in a field if 59 runners on Saturday in a time of 19:25.22. Behind her were junior Jamie Schwarz in 16th in 20:27.05 and freshman Cora Chun 17th, 20:34.96. Rounding out the top five were freshmen Elia Kwong in 21:11.12, a 50-second improvement, and Quincy Antaya in 21:31.24, a 37-second improvement. “The girls finished fourth in the league and have made a lot of improvements this year and putting a lot of effort. Skylar Best was first-team All-League and Jamie Schwarz made the second-team; we had a lot of personal records. We couldn’t be more thrilled to see so many girls making a huge effort,” said Holmlund. Piedmont now looks ahead to the Division 4 North Coast Section Championship Meet at Hayward High on Saturday, November 19. The top three teams will qualify for the CIF State Meet at Woodward Park in Fresno on Saturday, November 26. NEXT UP Piedmont returns to Hayward High on Saturday, November 19 for the North Coast Section Championship. The girls’ event starts at 8:30 a.m. and the boys one hour later at 9:30 a.m. Christian Taylor (right) placed third, and Xander Schulte-Sasse (left) was fifth in the League championship cross-country championship.

articles.text: JV team ends season with 41-8 rout of Kennedy Piedmont High’s junior varsity football team closed its season on a high note by defeating Kennedy 41-8 on Thursday, November 3 at Witter Field. It was their third consecutive blowout win. Coach Jordan Seiden reflected on the season, pointing out that this is the energy they need to bring into their offseason program. Although Thursday’s game marked the season-finale for football, it seemed to represent the start of a new era of football in Piedmont. In the final three games of the season, the JV team outscored opponents 126-20. “These are the kids that are going to be the foundation of the program. We have some great building-blocks with a strong group of freshmen, sophomores, and juniors. They are all leadership-type kids at each level. This is a unique group, it’s exciting to be a part of,” said coach Seiden. Prior to the game, PHS honored its nine seniors on the varsity roster after having their season canceled after playing only four games. The players graduating are Bailey Cain, Ryan McConathy, Bautista and Matteo Costa, Marcos Filho, Aiden Hickman, Jack Nelson, Liam Campbell, and Luka Rivas Cate. Seiden was the head coach of the varsity team prior to its closure and then stepped to the JV team after the school decided to terminate the varsity season. Seiden has seen considerable progress from several players, giving high praise to tight end Albert Bellingrath, lineman Adrian Kondakov, running back and linebacker Tommy Ashton, and receiver and defensive back Marius Arno. “The thing we preach about football is about developing. Football is a developmental sport where you start at a baseline and grow from there. We spent a lot of time in the summer and preseason working out together and I got to know a lot of them, but then when you see the light bulb go on, it’s exciting. Albert never played tight end before and has been so excited to learn that spot. Tommy hadn’t played much running back until coming down to JV, now we’re looking at him being a feature back. Adrian is another kid who never played football and is a world-class chess champion. His development to starting both ways makes us view him as a staple. Marius is a player I talked to directly and his growth has been amazing,” said Seiden. Players like quarterback MarStaff Photos Quarterback Markos Lagios gets ready for a snap with Tommy Ashton behind him at running back. Receiver Sam Shelby scored three touchdowns against Kennedy. Photo by Chuck Wolf cos Lagios and Ashton got time at the varsity level and were able to see the speed from top-level teams like Del Norte and St. Mary’s. Their message to players who did not gain varsity experience is to play with confidence, don’t over complicate things, and take what’s in front of you. “This is really our future right here. It was good to get time together and build chemistry with everyone. I really think that adjusting to varsity is dealing with bigger players, the lights, and more pressure, but it’s really the same game. The advice I’d give is to treat it like every game, don’t overthink it, and stay relaxed,” said Lagios. “It was a tough season but we really came together and gained some momentum. I’d tell players that the pressure can get to you sometimes, but keep fighting and you’ll be fine. Play your best and always give your best effort,” added Ashton. Game Recap Piedmont started the game by recovering an onside kick and scored after just two plays including a 40-yard catch and run by receiver Sam Shelby—which was the first of three scores by the sophomore. PHS led 6-0 after a missed extra point at 8:34 in the first quarter. From there, Piedmont recovered a fumble at the Kennedy 48 yard line and scored after four plays on a 17-yard touchdown run by Ashton, who punched across a two-point conversion, 14-0, at 3:24. After a Kennedy punt to the PHS 44 yard line, the Highlanders capped off a seven play drive with a seven yard run by Ashton—an extra point made it 21-0 with 6:45 left in the first half. On the Eagles’ next series, they drove to the Piedmont 28 but failed to convert a fourth-andfour when Vince Arbit broke up a pass. The Highlanders drove six plays for the score on a 45-yard pass to Shelby—making it 28-0 with six seconds left. In the third, PHS scored with Ashton’s third touchdown, which was a 25-yard run to make it 34-0 after a missed extra point at 7:19. In the fourth, Kennedy finally got on the board with a long touchdown run with 9:34 left in the game—34-8. pages.text: Wednesday, November 9, 2022 13 PHS cross-country teams finishes 2nd, 4th at WACC Championship By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s cross country teams had a strong run at the Western Alameda County Conference Championship meet on Saturday, November 5 at Hayward High. The boys’ team finishing second out of seven schools, and the girls’ team was fourth. Berkeley’s boys’ team won with 98 points, and Piedmont was second with 115 points. Senior Christian Taylor finished third of 71 runners with a time of 15:43.51, which marked his fastest time this season by 22 seconds. Junior Xander Schulte-Sasse finished fifth with a time of 15:46.92, ahead of senior Parker Long in 15:59.07. Rounding out their top-five was junior Julien Lee in 19th with a time of 16:51.33, and senior Alex Ware in 22nd at 17:03.04. “The boys had a great run to finish second. Christian Taylor, Xander Schulte-Sasse, and Parker Long all made first-team all-league with their results. Alex Ware ran his best race ever, shoring up our number five position,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. There is notably a bug going around the Highlanders’ cross country team that forced some athletes to miss time and recover. Now that students are progressing from some sickness, “Coach B” Holmlund is hopeful that their best race is ahead of them at North Coast Section on November 19 at Hayward. Freshman Skylar Best was fourth of 59 runners. Parker Long finished in sixth place in 15:59.07. “Not everyone has completely recovered from our batch of illness going around. But if the stars align, NCS is calling for us to run well,” Holmlund added. Freshman Skylar Best continued to lead the girls’ team with a 4th place overall finish in a field if 59 runners on Saturday in a time of 19:25.22. Behind her were junior Jamie Schwarz in 16th in 20:27.05 and freshman Cora Chun 17th, 20:34.96. Rounding out the top five were freshmen Elia Kwong in 21:11.12, a 50-second improvement, and Quincy Antaya in 21:31.24, a 37-second improvement. “The girls finished fourth in the league and have made a lot of improvements this year and putting a lot of effort. Skylar Best was first-team All-League and Jamie Schwarz made the second-team; we had a lot of personal records. We couldn’t be more thrilled to see so many girls making a huge effort,” said Holmlund. Piedmont now looks ahead to the Division 4 North Coast Section Championship Meet at Hayward High on Saturday, November 19. The top three teams will qualify for the CIF State Meet at Woodward Park in Fresno on Saturday, November 26. NEXT UP Piedmont returns to Hayward High on Saturday, November 19 for the North Coast Section Championship. The girls’ event starts at 8:30 a.m. and the boys one hour later at 9:30 a.m. Future of Piedmont football looks bright JV team ends season with 41-8 rout of Kennedy By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s junior varsity football team closed its season on a high note by defeating Kennedy 41-8 on Thursday, November 3 at Witter Field. It was their third consecutive blowout win. Coach Jordan Seiden reflected on the season, pointing out that this is the energy they need to bring into their offseason program. Although Thursday’s game marked the season-finale for football, it seemed to represent the start of a new era of football in Piedmont. In the final three games of the season, the JV team outscored opponents 126-20. “These are the kids that are going to be the foundation of the program. We have some great building-blocks with a strong group of freshmen, sophomores, and juniors. They are all leadership-type kids at each level. This is a unique group, it’s exciting to be a part of,” said coach Seiden. Prior to the game, PHS honored its nine seniors on the varsity roster after having their season canceled after playing only four games. The players graduating are Bailey Cain, Ryan McConathy, Bautista and Matteo Costa, Marcos Filho, Aiden Hickman, Jack Nelson, Liam Campbell, and Luka Rivas Cate. Seiden was the head coach of the varsity team prior to its closure and then stepped to the JV team after the school decided to terminate the varsity season. Seiden has seen considerable progress from several players, giving high praise to tight end Albert Bellingrath, lineman Adrian Kondakov, running back and linebacker Tommy Ashton, and receiver and defensive back Marius Arno. “The thing we preach about football is about developing. Football is a developmental sport where you start at a baseline and grow from there. We spent a lot of time in the summer and preseason working out together and I got to know a lot of them, but then when you see the light bulb go on, it’s exciting. Albert never played tight end before and has been so excited to learn that spot. Tommy hadn’t played much running back until coming down to JV, now we’re looking at him being a feature back. Adrian is another kid who never played football and is a world-class chess champion. His development to starting both ways makes us view him as a staple. Marius is a player I talked to directly and his growth has been amazing,” said Seiden. Players like quarterback MarStaff Photos Quarterback Markos Lagios gets ready for a snap with Tommy Ashton behind him at running back. Christian Taylor (right) placed third, and Xander Schulte-Sasse (left) was fifth in the League championship cross-country championship. Receiver Sam Shelby scored three touchdowns against Kennedy. Photo by Chuck Wolf cos Lagios and Ashton got time at the varsity level and were able to see the speed from top-level teams like Del Norte and St. Mary’s. Their message to players who did not gain varsity experience is to play with confidence, don’t over complicate things, and take what’s in front of you. “This is really our future right here. It was good to get time together and build chemistry with everyone. I really think that adjusting to varsity is dealing with bigger players, the lights, and more pressure, but it’s really the same game. The advice I’d give is to treat it like every game, don’t overthink it, and stay relaxed,” said Lagios. “It was a tough season but we really came together and gained some momentum. I’d tell players that the pressure can get to you sometimes, but keep fighting and you’ll be fine. Play your best and always give your best effort,” added Ashton. In the fourth, Kennedy finally got on the board with a long touchdown run with 9:34 left in the game—34-8. But on the ensuing kickoff, Shelby took the return to the house for the game’s final score, 41-8 with 7:59 to play. Piedmont honored its nine seniors from the varsity roster prior to Thursday’s game. articles.text: Staff Photos Trinity Zamora announces that she’ll continue playing basketball at San Diego State, a Div. 1 program. Piedmont senior Trinity Zamora, the basketball team’s leading scorer, intends to attend San Diego State and play for its Div. 1 team. Piedmont High School is hosting a ceremony today, November 9, for the senior to sign her Letter of Intent for her selected college team. “I think what drew me to the school the most was the coaches, the staff, and the team itself. It was very much like a family and San Diego is a place I could see myself living for a while, growing, and becoming a woman,” said Zamora. Zamora is a four-year starter at Piedmont High. In addition to her Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year as a junior, we named her our 2021 Sophomore of the Year and 2020 Freshman of the Year. She’ll undoubtedly be a front runner for 2023 Athlete of the Year honors. “We are so proud of Trinity; she is everything you want in a basketball player and leader,” said veteran Piedmont High coach Bryan Gardere. Zamora said she has felt a strong connection to the Aztecs’ coaching staff for two years, including head coach Stacie Terry-Hutson. “They’ve watched me play AAU and high school ball, and we connected very well. I’ve always been able to have good, comfortable conversations with them. It just felt like home; whenever I talked to them it felt like I was speaking to a family member. I really appreciate that about the school,” said Zamora. After making an official visit to the school, Zamora felt like the college and its facilities fulfilled her immediate dreams. “I took an official visit, and it’s beautiful. The campus is beautiful and it’s pretty big. Their gym is amazing; the practice facilities and locker rooms are nice. It’s just a beautiful facility allaround. And there’s a bunch of beaches in San Diego, of course,” she said with a laugh. Zamora said she also considered schools like Nevada, Sacramento State, and Loyola Marymount, but San Diego had many factors that drew her to Southern California. “Nevada and San Diego State were really my top-two. I’d say the facilities and the coaching set San Diego State apart. I could just see myself there compared to the other schools. San Diego just felt like home,” said Zamora. She is planning on exploring San Diego State’s Fowler College of Business. With the high school basketball season soon to begin, Zamora and her teammates are setting lofty goals. The starting five is likely to include AllLeague Natalia Martinez, Maddie Hill, Perseas Gioukaris, and Eva Levingston. The Highlanders fell narrowly short of winning their first WACC title since joining the league 11 years ago, yet they advanced in State post-season competition. “Our number one goal is to win state. We want to keep a strong record and go out with a bang. We have a lot of seniors and some transfer students from last season (Gioukaris and Levingston) who didn’t get to play. There is certainly a lot of built up tension ready to let off,” said Zamora. Other student-athletes who are announcing their college intent, please reach out to The Post at News@PiedmontPost.org and JonathanCX525@gmail.com to keep us informed. Trinity Zamora was the Post’s 2022 Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year, its Sophomore of the Year and 2021, and Freshman of the Year the year prior.

articles.text: Visit the park’s famed ladybug swarms on the Stream Trail From now through February, it is the prime time to witness the swarms of ladybugs at Redwood Regional Park in the Oakland hills, where the common Coccinellidae beetle is annually called to the fence posts and plants residing along the Stream Trail for mating season. “Here in Redwood, Ladybugs wait out the winter, often along the creeks. They are likely attracted to the area by chemicals in the air, or from pheromones, or scent markers, left behind in their footprints,” wrote East Bay Regional Parks on their informative panel describing the phenomenon. About 1.7 miles down the Stream Trail are bushels of ladybugs. Scientists determined that their behavior is a mechanism for the species to reproduce and cope with a limited food supply during the winter months as they lay eggs on the underside of leaves. Because the Stream Trail is mostly flat, it’s a great location for children and senior walkers. To reach the location, start at the Canyon Meadow Staging Area off of Redwood Road and take the Stream Trail which starts at the end of the parking lot. At 1.5 miles you’ll reach a Continue to the Tres Sendas and Starflower Trails to add some ascent to your day. Take the Madrone Trail, venturing right, to make your way to Redwood Peak.
