pages.text: Wednesday, November 9, 2022 15 HIKING WITH JON Ladybug season has returned to Redwood Regional Park Visit the park’s famed ladybug swarms on the Stream Trail By Jonathan Comeaux From now through February, it is the prime time to witness the swarms of ladybugs at Redwood Regional Park in the Oakland hills, where the common Coccinellidae beetle is annually called to the fence posts and plants residing along the Stream Trail for mating season. “Here in Redwood, Ladybugs wait out the winter, often along the creeks. They are likely attracted to the area by chemicals in the air, or from pheromones, or scent markers, left behind in their footprints,” wrote East Bay Regional Parks on their informative panel describing the phenomenon. About 1.7 miles down the Stream Trail are bushels of ladybugs. Scientists determined that their behavior is a mechanism for the species to reproduce and cope with a limited food supply during the winter months as they lay eggs on the underside of leaves. Because the Stream Trail is mostly flat, it’s a great location for children and senior walkers. To reach the location, start at the Canyon Meadow Staging Area off of Redwood Road and take the Stream Trail which starts at the end of the parking lot. At 1.5 miles you’ll reach a Continue to the Tres Sendas and Starflower Trails to add some ascent to your day. Take the Madrone Trail, venturing right, to make your way to Redwood Peak. bridge and intersection with the Mill Trail. Take the bridge to continue down the Stream Trail and .2 of a mile later you will encounter the swarms of ladybugs. Turning around from this point will end your day at slightly over three miles of hiking. Hikers wanting to continue for an added workout, can walk uphill to Redwood Peak, where you will see a collection of boulders with initials and dates etched into their surface. It is a great location to relax and hydrate while you scour the boulders to find the oldest date. The oldest year I was able to find was more than 100 years ago, in 1918. To reach Redwood Peak, travel an additional half-mile to the Tres Sendas Trail, which will intersect with the Starflower Trail. Continue on the Starflower Trail for nearly a half-mile until you reach the Madrone Trail, taking the route on the right. You’ll venture on the Madrone Trail for nearly a half-mile until it becomes the Redwood Peak Trail, walking straight for .2 of a mile until reaching the boulders at the trail’s end. The venture from the Stream Trail to Redwood Peak will add 1,000 feet of elevation gain to your day. To return to your car, take the West Ridge Trail from Redwood Peak for 1.1 miles until reaching the Chown Trail, which you will take for another mile as it descends back to the Stream Trail. The Chown Trail has five switchback turns as you descend and is much narrower than the other trails, but surrounds you in beautiful redwood trees and ferns. You’ll occasionally hear a woodpecker knocking around trees for food. Once you’re back on the Stream Trail, venture to the right and walk for another mile back to the trailhead. That rounds out your day at slightly under seven miles of hiking and 1,100 feet of elevation gain. It’s worth mentioning that the Stream Trail is one of the most popular trails at Redwood Regional due to the ladybug swarm and the general easiness Staff Photos From now through February, Redwood Regional Park’s famous ladybug swarm is underway. Millions of ladybugs are found about 1.6 miles down the Stream Trail from the Canyon Meadows Trailhead. A closer look at the ladybugs on the Stream Trail. of the walk. On a Sunday morning around 11:00 a.m., we passed approximately 122 people on the trail as we made our way to the Tres Sendas Trail. On the Tres Sendas and Starflower Trails, we passed only 20 people on the way to Redwood Peak and passed another 41 people while on the West Ridge Trail. The Chown Trail is one of the most secluded and perhaps the most underrated, passing just six people on the 1-mile descent. Back on the Stream Trail, we passed another 51 hikers while making our way back to the car. The collection of boulders at Redwood Peak has names, initials, and dates from several generations etched into the rocks. One of the oldest dates found on the Redwood Peak boulders. A woodpecker at work in a tree on the Chown Trail.

articles.text: City Council member Betsy Andersen adds some star power Piedmont’s hometown orchestra, the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, enjoyed a sold-out concert hall on Sunday afternoon, November 6. The orchestra performed the music of Franz Schubert (written at age 14), Romanian Dances, by Bela Bartok, and one of Mozart’s signature pieces, Symphony No. 40 in G minor. Tucked neatly into the program was Alan Ridout’s lighthearted piece about Ferdinand the Bull. The children’s story was recounted musically by violinist Joseph Gold, and theatrically by City Council member Betsy Andersen as the story’s narrator. Following the concert, she confirmed that Sunday’s concert was not her musical debut in Piedmont. articles.text: Special treat for kids at the Symphony San Francisco Symphony will present Fantasia in Concert on Tuesday, November 22, with Tim Davies as guest conductor. This special performance showcases the Symphony performing the music scores from two of Walt Disney’s most beloved animated feature films, Fantasia (1940) and its sequel by the same name made in 2000. Disney’s 1940 film introduced young children to the orchestral sounds of strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion, much as did Peter and the Wolf by Sergei Prokofiev in 1936. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s holiday favorite, Nutcracker, opens December 8 at the War Memorial Opera House, with performances through December 27. This special production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks such as the Painted Ladies by Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. San Francisco Ballet performs the ballet every year and features “a kaleidoscope” of more than 150 dancers to tell the story of the Sugarplum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco, accompanied by the Opera Orchestra performing the familiar music score by Tchaikovsky. A diverse array of instruments are played during performances, including the glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam tam, ratchet, and timpani -- all played by three musicians. The scenic design is by Michael Yeargan; costumes by Martin Pakledinaz; lighting design by James F. Ingalls, and projection design by Wendall K. Harrington. Nutcracker is appropriate for children aged five and older; no children under the age of three will be permitted. The ballet runs two hours with one intermission. Tickets are selling quickly for performances on Christmas Eve, December 24. The production will end on December 27. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/nutcracker-dec-2022/. Photo by Erik Tomasson San Francisco Ballet dancers perform in Helgi Tomasson’s production of Nutcracker.
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Nutcracker performances begin December 8

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre reimagines Emily Brontë’s gothic masterpiece, Wuthering Heights, in a new play by Emma Rice, premiering on November 18. The 1847 novel tells the story of the Earnshaws and Lintons, two families living on the West Yorkshire moors, and the compelling relationship between the characters Catherine and Heathcliff. Heathcliff is rescued from the Liverpool docks as a young child, adopted by the Earnshaws and taken to live at Wuthering Heights. He strikes a friendship with Catherine Earnshaw and soon a fierce love ignites. Leah Brotherhead is cast as Catherine. Her theatre credits include Gulliver’s Travels (Unicorn Theatre), Lands (Bush Theatre/Summer Hall Edinburgh Fringe), Two Gentlemen of Verona (The Globe Theatre/ Liverpool Everyman), Wolf Hall and Bring Up the Bodies (RSC/ Aldwych Theatre/The Winter Gardens on Broadway), and As You Like It (Lamb Players). The male lead of Heathcliff will be performed by Liam Tamne, whose performances included The Prince of Egypt (Dominion Theatre), Bonnie and Clyde (Theatre Royal Drury Lane), The Light in the Piazza (Royal Festival Hall/ LA Opera), Spamilton (Menier Chocolate Factory), and Mack and Mabel Concert with LMTO (Hackney Empire). The New York Times called the reimagining “a feat of storytelling that wraps itself around the audience, pulling us into its silliness and sorrow.” Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/shows/wuthering-heights/ to obtain tickets.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep reimagines Wuthering Heights

articles.text: The punchline usually comes at the end. There is nothing like a walk-off home run in baseball, or a sudden knockout in boxing, or a field goal at the end of a championship football game. In this case, the punchline comes at the very beginning. We need music education… now more than ever. My attendance at a recent concert made me do some real soul-searching. The concert itself was a distressing affair. Knowing how to respond in a diplomatic way was equally distressing. The advance publicity of a highly touted ensemble was indeed impressive. To liven things up, their enthusiastic fan club filled the auditorium. The atmosphere was charged with energy. I think my readers know that I am a fan of excellence. It is also important to keep an open mind. We must not only know history, but we must learn from history. Many of the great artists of the past deserve their reputation. That is why they are immortals. But it is not a good idea to have a love affair with the past. I appreciate honest and sincere effort, but I also believe, as a philosopher once said, that the closer humanity gets to perfection, the farther we get from humanity. In the past, performers were inspired by the emotion of the moment. Their performances were unpredictable. Today’s performers achieve perfection in almost every performance. How wonderful is that? But they pay the price. So do we in the audience. I can hear many of you asking: “what is the point of this?” An enthusiastic audience must be able to discern between the good and the bad. Our educational system has a responsibility to encourage the public to think and analyze. All of us need to learn from history. We must be Robin Sharp (left), Natasha Makhijani, Ben Simon and Eric Gaenslen

articles.text: Legendary jazz saxophonist John Coltrane. Sax player John Coltrane studied with Philadelphia jazz guitarist Dennis Sandole from 1946 through the early fifties, upon being discharged with honors from the U.S. Navy. Sandole taught him a polytonal concept that combines portions of scales and arpeggios from different keys. Coltrane used this concept with four, five or six-note melodic cells. These cells can be conceived as simple chords with a neighboring tone. Study this subject further in Guitar Improv, which you can download for free at the link below. See the chapters “Triads with Neighbors”, “Bebop and Other Octatonic Scales” and “Substitution”. Coltrane later studied with Hasaan Ibn Ali (pianist), Thelonius Monk and Ornette Coleman, developing his ability to play tonally and harmonically more freely, listening to feeling rather than just logic. Coltrane helped to pioneer modal jazz and free jazz. Modal and cool jazz were a backlash to bebop, which for many jazz enthusiasts had gotten too complex, undanceable and lacked the feeling of blues and other more sensitive components of jazz. Modes are created by assigning the key to various tones of a scale. Playing a C major scale (C-D-E-F-G-A-B-C) from “D” to “D” (D-E-F-G-AB-C-D) establishes a new scale or mode (“modus” is Greek for “mood”). Pythagoras is credited with introducing the modal concept, though he likely got it from Egyptian music scholars. The ancient Greeks thought of math, astronomy and music as one body of work. Rather than rapidly changing scales to follow frequent chord changes in bebop, modal jazz compositions use fewer chords and reside in fewer modes. Along with Miles Davis, Coltrane was instrumental in introducing modal jazz on the Milestones album. One of the examples for this column is Joe Pass’ solo on the song Milestones (see link below). Coltrane excelled at bebop, modal and cool jazz and free jazz. His later work became increasingly more spiritually based with cascading soundscapes of scales and arpeggios that have been called “sheets of sound”. He was a humble man. Jazz journalist Nat Hentoff said, “Trane struck such a spiritual chord in so many listeners that people started to think of him as being beyond human. He was just a human being like you and me – but he was willing to practice more, to do all the things that somebody has to do to excel. The real value in what Coltrane did was that what he accomplished, he did as a human.” Coltrane remains influential today. He posthumously received a special Pulitzer Prize and was canonized by the African Orthodox Church. Listen to and read my improvised examples for this column and music for my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/PostColumns.pdf. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. Call (510) 923-9522, text (510) 435-3997, or email jim@guitarencyclopdeia.com for videoconference or in-person lessons. His course is available for free online at www. guitarimprov.com.
articles.title: John Coltrane and modal jazz

It is not a good idea to smash the recordings of deceased performers. We must be able to compare the good and the bad of the past with the good and the bad of the present. The performance in question was notable for its perfection. It was also notable for artistic qualities which were completely absent. Absent was any sense of artistic sensibility. Absent was any attempt at dynamics. The playing was loud and heavy-handed from beginning to end. It was unrelenting in its loudness. Though the program contained music from many different time periods and stylistic periods, everything was played exactly the same. All great artists of the past maintained high personal artistic standards. I remember hearing the famous guitarist Andres Segovia. He bungled one of the pieces on his program but apologized to the audience for his poor performance. He then said respectfully, “Let me try it again”. The listening public also needs to expect high personal artistic standards. We need to educate ourselves and speak up. In some countries the audience will boo an inferior performance. articles.text: Orchestra to perform this Saturday at Center for the Arts The San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, November 12 for a concert at 5:00 p.m. This will be the fifth time the orchestra has performed in Piedmont. The concert theme is “Anticipation” with music inspiring expectation, hope, and the promise of musical enchantment. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Still Mine is a sensitively made, superbly acted film, starring two veteran actors, James Cromwell and Genevieve Bujold, portraying Craig and Irene Morrison. They have been married for 61 years, and live on a family farm in rural St. Martins, New Brunswick, Canada Based on true events, Still Mine is in many ways an elegiac drama, a metaphor for mortality, and a nuanced love story, suffused with intimacy, and written and directed by Michael McGowan. It is that rare film in which elderly people are not all but invisible. As old age begins to define them, Irene and Craig slowly begin to realize that their twostory farmhouse is showing decades of wear. Irene, is also revealing signs of early dementia, growing ever more distracted, forgetful, and incautious. Falling twice, the second accident results in a broken hip and a hospital stay. Resisting the worried bickering of their middle-aged children regarding what to do with Irene (a retirement home?), Craig decides to build a smaller, single-story house on a nearby 200- acre plot of open land. He is a master craftsman, owns a bevy of tools, knows quality timber, and was schooled in carpentry by his shipwright father. He sees no problem with constructing a cottage on his own land; that is, until he soon learns that he must meet government codes and submit drawn plans as well as paying what he regards as an unnecessary, bureaucratic fee of $400. He is informed of these requirements by an obstinate, unsympathetic building inspector (Jonathan Potts) who eventually places a “Stop Work” order on Craig’s newly framed house. He is told in the harshest terms that to ignore the codes and fail to submit his plans amounts to breaking the law and could result in standing before a municipal judge or even going to jail. Irascible as always, laconic in the extreme, Craig continues to build. When one of his sons suggests that perhaps Craig is too old (87) for such a project, he points out that “age is an abstraction and not a straightjacket.” But what Craig gradually begins to understand is that when it comes to Irene, aging is not an abstraction; rather, time is of the essence as is finishing the cottage. Still Mine. Written and directed by Michael McGowan. Starring James Cromwell, Genevieve Bujold, Julie Stewart. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2013. Now streaming on Prime/ VUDU/Peacock. articles.text: Review by Chris Honore’ The question that often comes to mind when watching a film such as Run All Night is, who is the audience? Films of this genre – call them pulp cinema – are dark and gritty and usually edged with nihilism. Run was shot in the boroughs of New York City and takes place over some 16 hours with hardcore shoot-outs and one prolonged chase scene on Jamaica Avenue in Queens that will take your breath away for all the destruction of public and private property involved. At the center of Run is Jimmy Conlon (Liam Neeson), a once mobbed-up hit man who was so good at what he did he was nicknamed “the gravedigger.” Over the years, his life has evolved into a train wreck and he’s finding it hard to live with his past and the price he has paid in terms of family, especially his estranged son, Mike (Joel Kinnaman), who has a lovely wife and two daughters. Profoundly alone, broke, and as much a part of the detritus of the streets as the isolated homeless huddled under blue plastic tarps, Jimmy lives off the generosity of Shawn Maguire (Ed Harris), the ex-gangster he once worked for, who is also his boyhood friend. They share a bond and repeatedly swear to cross the final finish line together. Of course, relying on that familiar line from Neeson’s Taken (a movie worth finding), Jimmy still has skill sets. In other words, he’s a blunt instrument. And for reasons far more complicated than is possible to detail here, his son, a limo driver suddenly, violently, finds himself in need of the father he has angrily pushed away. As circumstances would have it, Jimmy shoots a young man before he can shoot his son. Tragically, he is the only son of Shawn, Danny (Boyd Holbrook), who is into some very bad drug dealings with an Albanian cartel. Apparently, the Albanians are the new Sicilians. Shawn pledges that the only thing that will balance the scales is if he, or one of his hired thugs, kills Mike. Nothing Jimmy can say to Shawn will dissuade him. All he can promise is that he will do all within his power to stop Shawn and his men (one in particular, portrayed by Common). As a result, lots of people die badly. Which takes us back to the question regarding the audience. There is a solid fan base for these B-movies. Even when they feature middle aged actors who still have their mojo. Run All Night is well done and for the intended moviegoers who find these stylized, urban movies engaging, they will not be disappointed. The film is intense, a game clock of sorts is ticking, and time is telescoped into one night that happens to be Christmas Eve (the irony is not lost). Action-thriller? Definitely. Is it a cliché? Indeed. But in the best sense of the word. Run All Night. Directed by Juame Collet-Serra. Starring Liam Neeson, Ed Harris and Joel Kinnaman. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated R. Released in 2015, Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Run All Night – action and mayhem non-stop

articles.text: Shailene Woodley stars in Insurgent. Short and sweet: Insurgent is the second installment in what will be a four-part series based on the Divergent trilogy (two movies from the third book, Allegiant), written by Veronica Roth. Its premise is strikingly similar to The Hunger Games films and possesses a young, resourceful heroine, Tris Prior, played by Shailene Woodley. The setting is also post-apocalyptic (locale is Chicago), and distinctly dystopian. If you missed Divergent, which had a lot of exposition in act one, then you will be trying to fit the pieces together, an impossible task. Truth be told, these films only make sense to those who have likely read the books and are way ahead of the plot before taking that first bite of popcorn. Demographic: tween-teen girls who revel in the story of Tris, a rogue character of extraordinary courage and athleticism who challenges the stratified conformity of her world. Is Insurgent a good movie? The question is incidental. This story, like The Hunger Games, captures the young imagination completely. And if you have a tween-teen girl in your household, one who considers Tris Prior exceptional and the books riveting (involving romance-lite), she’s already seen it. Or really, really wants to. Reading is a good thing, and if it’s the Divergent trilogy, then no worries. Ditto the movies. Suggestion: tag along, sit in the back and enjoy. Two more to go. Insurgent. Starring Shailene Woodley, Theo James and Kate Winslet. Directed by Robert Schwentke. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG-13, Released in 2015. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/HBO Max. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Freaky Friday is a family-friendly comedy, ideal for kids (8+), tweens and teens, but not to forget that parents will find lots to smile at as well. At the center of the story is single mom Tess (Jamie Lee Curtis), widowed several years ago and now on the brink of marrying Ryan (Mark Harmon). Her daughter, Anna (Lindsay Lohan), just 15, is a surly teenager. The two frequently find themselves at odds. Actually, they couldn’t be more different. Tess is a multi-tasking, stressed-out psychologist, who is either on her cell phone, checking her Palm Pilot, or seeing patients. Anna plays the guitar, is failing English, generally feckless and often in detention. One evening they go out for a Chinese dinner, the meal followed by a fortune cookie. While all seems benign, we soon learn that it wasn’t. Inexplicably, they wake up the next morning having discovered that they have, in effect, well, body-swapped. While it isn’t a new premise, as films go in Hollywood (recall Big with Tom Hanks, for example), Lohan and Curtis do a superb job trying to adjust to this remarkable change. Both stand before the mirror and have that expected “Good grief, what’s happened to me?” moment. Both actors are having fun with their roles, conveying that Jamie Lee Curtis and Lindsay Lohan in Freaky Friday. neither is prepared to walk in the other’s shoes. Tess can’t play the guitar, nor can she do algebra, nor navigate school. Anna stumbles through Tees’ neurotic patient appointments, and even attends a talk show where she tries to sell her mom’s recently published book on aging. Tess has a hilarious problem when she is confronted with the very awkward attention of Anna’s hunky, motorcycle riding boyfriend, Jake (Chad Michael Murray) who doesn’t want to take “no” for an answer. All of this amounts to one hilarious moment after the next, using the fulcrum word “empathy”l while the story unfolds. Though they were both in constant disagreement, slowly they develop lots of insights into one another. Anna comes to understand what it means to be a mom, and her mom realizes that being a teen is no walk in the park, what with all the changes in moods that define what it means to be an adolescent. Reconciliation is not far off. Freaky Friday. Directed by Mark Waters. Starring Jamie Lee Curtis, Lindsay Lohan, Mark Harmon. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 2003. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+.
articles.title: Freaky Friday – lots of fun for kids (and parents)

articles.text: Part 56 in a bi-weekly series Croatia’s Dubrovnik, the Dalmatian Coast city dubbed “the pearl of the Adriatic”, is an incredible place. It was included early at the start of the UNESCO World Heritage Listings in 1979. The old city is filled with a beautiful range of different architectural styles appropriate to the local tradition and geography – the very definition of the word “eclectic”. Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque buildings give it a wonderful rich and interesting visual texture. But the totality of the place, the designed combination of buildings, streets, courtyards, plazas, pathways, light fixtures, landscaping and paving, in short, the Urban Design, is what ultimately make it the place it is. Contributing greatly to this specialness is its pedestrian function and character. The entire walled Old Town is a car-free zone! What also is endearing to me about Dubrovnik has to do with why I write this column: encouraging people to become educated relative to our built environment, and as a result to care about it. In 1991 during the Croatian war of independence, an ISIS-like bombardment of the Old Town during the Siege of Dubrovnik provoked immediate international outrage and condemnation over the senseless destruction of the priceless cultural heritage. The following diplomatic and economic reaction actually changed the course of the war. It is encouraging to recall that many people do care – many a great deal. Ljubljana Slovenia, Croatia’s Balkan neighbor to the north with its relatively small (p 280,000) yet remarkable capital city of Ljubljana (loo blee ah nuh), is another wonderful gem of urban design and pedestrian accommodation. It was included early at the start of the UNESCO World Heritage Listings in 1979. The old city is filled with a beautiful range of different architectural styles appropriate to the local tradition and geography – the very definition of the word “eclectic”. Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque buildings give it a wonderful rich and interesting visual texture. But the totality of the place, the designed combination of buildings, streets, courtyards, plazas, pathways, light fixtures, landscaping and paving, in short, the Urban Design, is what ultimately make it the place it is. articles.text: If you receive Social Security, you’ve probably already heard that your checks in 2023 will be bigger – considerably bigger, in fact. How can you make the best use of this extra money? Here’s what’s happening: For 2023, there’s an 8.7% cost-ofliving adjustment (COLA) for Social Security benefits – the largest increase in 40 years. Also, the monthly Medicare Part B premiums are declining next year, to $164.90/month from $170.10/ month, which will also modestly boost Social Security checks for those enrolled in Part B, as these premiums are automatically deducted. Of course, the sizable COLA is due to the high inflation of 2022, as the Social Security Administration uses a formula based on increases in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). So, it’s certainly possible that you will need some, or perhaps all, of your larger checks to pay for the increased cost of goods and services. But if your cash flow is already relatively strong, you might want to consider these suggestions for using your bigger checks: • Reduce withdrawals from your investment portfolio. When you’re retired, you will likely need to withdraw a certain amount from your portfolio each year to meet your expenses. A boost in your Social Security may enable you to withdraw less, at least for a year. This can be particularly advantageous when the markets are down, as you’d like to avoid, as much as possible, selling investments and withdrawing the money when investment prices are low. And the fewer investments you need to sell, the longer your portfolio may last during your retirement years. • Help build your cash reserves. When you’re retired, it’s a good idea to maintain about a year’s worth of the amount you’ll spend from your portfolio in cash, while also keeping three months’ of your spending needs in an emergency fund, with the money kept in a liquid, low-risk account. Your higher Social Security checks could help you build these cash reserves. (Also, it’s helpful to keep another three to five years’ worth of spending from your portfolio in short-term, fixed-income investments, which now, due to higher interest rates, offer better income opportunities.) • Contribute to a 529 plan. You could use some of your extra Social Security money to contribute to a tax-advantaged 529 education savings plan for your grandchildren or other family members. • Contribute to charitable organizations. You might want to use some of your Social Security money to expand your charitable giving. Your generosity will help worthy groups and possibly bring you some tax benefits, too. While it’s nice to have these possible options in 2023, you can’t count on future COLA increases being as large. The jump in inflation in 2022 was due to several unusual factors, including pandemic-related government spending, supply shortages and the Russian invasion of Ukraine. It’s quite possible, perhaps even likely, that inflation will subside in 2023, which, in turn, would mean a smaller COLA bump in 2024. Nonetheless, while you might not want to include large annual COLA increases as part of your long-term financial strategy, you may well choose to take advantage, in some of the ways described above, of the bigger Social Security checks you’ll receive in 2023. When opportunity knocks, you may want to open the door. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. Edward Jones, Member SIPC. T.J. Stevko is a Financial Advisor at the Piedmont office of Edward Jones, 370 Highland Avenue, Suite 201. Phone (510) 547-4589.

articles.text: It’s Saturday afternoon, and I am enjoying all the things about my home that I try to create for my clients. It feels welcoming and quiet, orderly and beautiful, and it’s the perfect place to be after two weeks of traveling abroad to Switzerland and Cape Town, South Africa. I feel grateful not only for shelter, but for one that welcomed me home with such a feeling of lightness and comfort. It feels like me. I love it for how it has supported me throughout my darkest days and my happiest moments, as we have raised a family and grown a business. It is a place where a stranger can feel welcome and be invited to go deep. When I think about it, my home has evolved along with me, and has supported me on my journey to becoming the version I am now. Before I left on the trip, I asked Gray Cathrall for a reprieve from writing my column in the Post, A Life By Design, for a month. I wanted to make sure my clients and staff had what they needed before my departure. I intended to create space to get things done in advance of my trip. But the moment I made the request, I realized what I really needed was more space for new creative endeavors to germinate. Life is asking for something novel and different for me right now, and I’m feeling called to pivot toward some of the other projects that fuel my multi-passionate self. I have a desire to let go of some things to make room for what’s next. I don’t know exactly what it is, but life has taught me to get still so I can hear it speak. Even though this is my last column for the Piedmont Post, it’s not a goodbye. LMB Interiors is thriving, and my intention is that it keeps evolving, serving, and connecting to this community. When I asked Gray if I could write a column for the Piedmont Post seven years ago, I had no idea it would become such a fulfilling experience. Through the years, I have made new friends through this outlet. I’ve crossed paths with incredible people who appreciate interior design as a way to create connection through heart-centered living. For those of you who have become regular readers over the years and have reached out to comment and share their insights, I am grateful. My intent has always been to take you on a My friend, the Klein Constantia bull. Photos by Laura Martin Bovard Stained glass art at Cape Town’s Norval Gallery. journey into your hearts, through deep thoughts about the value of beauty, and how it all brings us into soulfulness. I hope you will continue to follow me on social media, and through my newsletter which you can sign up for on lmbinteriors.com. In the meantime, LMB Interiors will continue to serve the community through our design services, and by sourcing curated, local, artisan-crafted interiors that reflect the value of conscious consumerism and thoughtful details we have become known for. I invite you to engage with me on Instagram, my preferred platform, for all things interior design and updates on our projects. The photos with this column are from my most recent trip to Nyon, Switzerland, and the Klein Constantia Winery, where I stayed in Cape Town. South Africa. Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. Since 2002 she has helped clients create beautiful, joyful, and functional homes. The firm has garnered numerous awards and recognition as one of the Bay Area’s most sought after interior design agencies. articles.text: Rebecca Burgess was the guest speaker in the Climate Speaker Series on Wednesday, October 19, presented jointly by Piedmont Connect and the League of Women Voters of Piedmont. Her informative talk focused on the sustainability and future of textiles. Burgess is Executive Director of Fibershed, an organization that invests in regenerative agricultural research and practices and advises on regional sustainable fiber production systems. Burgess explained that approximately 60% of wardrobes in developed nations consist of textiles made from fossilized carbon, also called synthetic fibers. These fibers include acrylic, nylon, capilene, polyester and their synthetic dyes and finishing agents which are also derived from fossil sources. To stem climate disruption, Burgess advised the first step residents of wealthier nations can take is to wear clothes made of 100% natural fibers such as cotton, linen, hemp, silk and animal wools. According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change IPCC, land-use activities like agriculture and forestry currently account for 23% of total net human greenhouse gas emissions. Research by Dr. Rattan Lal and other top soil scientists, estitheir personal textile fossil footprints. Burgess pointed out that 80% of the clothes are seldom worn. “Textile industries become unsustainable mainly due to high consumption levels. When we reduce our consumption rate, existing fiber systems are less compelled to mine– soil, labor, and fossilized carbon, extractively and exploitatively,” she said. Asked whether there were clothing or textile brands to look for or avoid, Burgess suggested avoiding volume-based, fast-fashion businesses like Shein, H&M, and Zara. She recommended smaller, climate-conscious fashion labels such as Coyuchi (based in Marin County), Mara Hoffman (NYC), and Veja (Brazil) for athletic shoes. articles.text: Editor: In last week’s Viewpoint, Bernard Pech asked whether it is now time to seriously consider climate engineering as a way to give more time for transitioning to clean energy. Packed into that sentence, and into Pech’s whole article, are a number of assumptions and principles that are not generally understood. Most importantly, even if we are able to zero out greenhouse gas emissions by, say, 2050, the earth’s average global temperatures would not, at that point, revert back to those at some earlier date. As David Keith, professor of applied physics and public policy at Harvard and one of the leading experts on climate engineering, has pointed out in a NY Times guest essay (“What’s the Least Bad Way to Cool the Planet?” October 1, 2021), “Average temperatures will stop increasing when emissions stop, but cooling will take thousands of years as greenhouse gases slowly dissipate from the atmosphere.” Consequently, average global temperatures will be much higher by the time emissions reach zero, and this past summer, the summer of 2022, may be the coolest for many years to come. Thus, the idea of climate engineering (which also goes by the names of “geoengineering” and “solar radiation management”) is to provide us with a mechanism for actually cooling the planet and so reducing the inevitable temperature increases, buying us time to get our carbon house in order. In other words, it is a transitional technology, injecting a sulfur compound or engineered particles into the stratosphere to prevent a certain amount of solar radiation from reaching the earth. Climate engineering is not without its potential risks, and Pech alludes to a rogue nation deciding on its own to engineer the climate. Last year, I chaired a program on solar radiation management, and David Keith was one of the speakers. What Keith and others working on this technology advocate is support for international research to determine whether solar radiation management can be effective, what its potential risks might be, and how, if it proved both effective and with benefits that far outweighed its risks, its utilization could be governed in a way that allowed all nations of the world to have some say in its deployment. This technology is opposed by some environmentalists who fear that it will lessen our resolve to reduce emissions to zero, thereby extending our reliance on fossil fuels, and that its risks are not well known. I understand such opposition but do not think that it should impede research efforts to fully understand solar radiation management and to determine whether it might be a useful tool in our efforts to control climate. It may well prove to be an important tool in managing the transition to zero greenhouse gases and in avoiding the inevitable damage caused by unchecked increases in global temperatures.
articles.title: Cooling the Planet

articles.text: Support received from Beautification Foundation, Education Foundation The Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) has announced that fundraising is successfully continuing for the Piedmont Community Pool Project. To date, over $500,000 has been raised towards PRFO’s goal of $2,000,000 in their pledge to assist the City of Piedmont. “We truly appreciate everyone who has donated to the Piedmont Community Pool Project to date,” said Steve Collins, PRFO President. “We are fortunate to live in a generous community that believes in supporting City projects. But we still have a long way to go. We hope the greater community will help ensure Piedmont has the funding needed to create a state-of-the-art facility for our athletes, our aquatic enthusiasts, and our families.” In addition to individual community members, the project has received significant support from groups such as the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) and the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF). “PEF voted unanimously to support this project from our reserve funds. This is a very leveraged contribution that will support athletics and recreation for Piedmont students for years to come,” said Rick Smith, Treasurer of the Piedmont Education Foundation. In November 2020, with support of more than two-thirds of the vote, Piedmonters approved Measure UU, a $19.5 million bond measure to pay for the replacement of the Piedmont Community Pool. Since Measure UU passed, however, extreme inf lationary pressures have driven up costs. Earlier this year, the pool building design was substantially revised to reduce the overall costs by $4 million. But construction costs continue to be high, and a $2 million shortfall is anticipated. Without raising additional private funds, key elements of the project design will be lost. The City of Piedmont rejected the first two bids received for construction of the pool and put the job out to bid again this month with hopes for better pricing. The council hopes to award a contract by year-end, and break ground in 2023. The community is invited to learn more about the Piedmont Community Pool Project and donate at PRFO.org. Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO), a non-profit, actively supports the development of public recreational facilities that serve residents of Piedmont. PRFO strives to work collaboratively with the City of Piedmont to bring private financial support to assist in the funding of projects that invest in healthy spaces within the city.
articles.title: PRFO fundraising going strong

articles.text: On October 22, Chabot Space & Science Center’s annual Starlight Gala raised $325,000 for STEM education. The event featured live music, one-of-kind art and the premiere of Chabot’s new exhibition, Astrolight. The star-studded event was attended by many local political leaders, including Oakland Mayor Libby Schaaf. Chabot recognized 2022 Champion of Science Awardees, including CFO and longtime volunteer Fred Patton, and Retired Deputy Director of NASA’s Ames Research Center Lewis Braxton III. Additionally, Fremont High School teacher Rowan Driscoll was named recipient of the Carole C. Quan Excellence in Science Education Award. Guests at Chabot Space & Science Center’s annual Gala in front of the Space Mirror, an art piece created by local artist Colin Bowring.

As David Keith, professor of applied physics and public policy at Harvard and one of the leading experts on climate engineering, has pointed out in a NY Times guest essay (“What’s the Least Bad Way to Cool the Planet?” October 1, 2021), “Average temperatures will stop increasing when emissions stop, but cooling will take thousands of years as greenhouse gases slowly dissipate from the atmosphere.” Consequently, average global temperatures will be much higher by the time emissions reach zero, and this past summer, the summer of 2022, may be the coolest for many years to come. Thus, the idea of climate engineering (which also goes by the names of “geoengineering” and “solar radiation management”) is to provide us with a mechanism for actually cooling the planet and so reducing the inevitable temperature increases, buying us time to get our carbon house in order. In other words, it is a transitional technology, injecting a sulfur compound or engineered particles into the stratosphere to prevent a certain amount of solar radiation from reaching the earth. Climate engineering is not without its potential risks, and Pech alludes to a rogue nation deciding on its own to engineer the climate. Last year, I chaired a program on solar radiation management, and David Keith was one of the speakers. What Keith and others working on this technology advocate is support for international research to determine whether solar radiation management can be effective, what its potential risks might be, and how, if it proved both effective and with benefits that far outweighed its risks, its utilization could be governed in a way that allowed all nations of the world to have some say in its deployment. This technology is opposed by some environmentalists who fear that it will lessen our resolve to reduce emissions to zero, thereby extending our reliance on fossil fuels, and that its risks are not well known. I understand such opposition but do not think that it should impede research efforts to fully understand solar radiation management and to determine whether it might be a useful tool in our efforts to control climate. It may well prove to be an important tool in managing the transition to zero greenhouse gases and in avoiding the inevitable damage caused by unchecked increases in global temperatures. Internationally renown organist and choral director Ben Bachmann, has joined St. Paul’s as its new Director of Music. Bachmann comes to St. Paul’s after leading the music and chorus programs at Grace Cathedral in San Francisco for 17 years. “St. Paul’s has a rich 150-year history of spiritual outreach,” said Bachmann. “I hope to continue that tradition by expanding the role of sacred music in the way we interact with our whole community.” Bachmann will perform organ recitals, create opportunities for young voices, and open St. Paul’s to even more musical organizations for concerts. Paraphrasing an African American Spiritual, Bachmann said, “Ev’ry time people hear our music, I hope the spirit will move in their hearts.” Bachmann was born into a musical family in Akron, Ohio. articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident, Wai Bong Lok, M.D., passed away in August at the age of 71 due to complications of Parkinson’s disease. Born in Shenzhen, China, he was the youngest of five children and spent his childhood in Hong Kong. When he was 17, he and his mother immigrated to the United States. He completed his senior year of high school and undergraduate degree in New York City. Wai Bong moved to the West Coast to attend the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). It was during medical school where he met and eventually married his wife, Bessie. His residency, fellowship, and training to become a cardiologist was also in the Bay Area and allowed him to establish deep roots in the community. Dr. Lok devoted his life to helping others. He ran a private cardiology practice for more than 30 years on Pill Hill in Oakland and served on the medical staff of Alta Bates Summit Medical Center. He also held a clinical teaching role and enjoyed allowing UCSF medical students to shadow him on Fridays. During his career, Dr. Lok was honored by community health centers, including Asian Health Services and La Clinica de la Raza, for providing their patients excellent quality care regardless of their income level or insurance coverage. Outside of his medical Dr. Wai Bong Lok passed away in August at the age of 71 due to complications of Parkinson’s disease. practice, he enjoyed golf, tennis, painting, traveling, and exploring good food. The Lok family has lived in Piedmont since 1980 and raised their two sons here. Despite his diagnosis with Parkinson’s, he continued to enjoy many active years and was even doing uphill neighborhood walks until the end. Wai Bong is survived by his wife Bessie, his older son Justin and wife Robin, and his younger son Michael and his wife Jessica. He is also survived by two sisters and a long list of nieces and nephews. The Lok family is planning a Celebration of Life on November 13 at 2 p.m. at the Piedmont Community Hall. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests memorial donations in the name of Wai Bong Lok to Asian Health Services, or to the UCSF Medical School student scholarship fund, or taking the time to mentor someone. Wai Bong was always passionate about sharing knowledge and skills with others, and access to health care and public education.

articles.text: Taking pride in your home reaches new heights around the winter holidays. During this time, we want our homes to look their absolute best as we all take a moment to appreciate family and friends, with dinners and get-togethers. So, as the leaves turn color, it is the time to consider projects around your home that you’ve been aiming to complete. Although it’s unlikely you’ll have time to turn that rarely-used basement into a home theater in 2022, there’s quite a bit you can achieve in the short term. Gutter cleaning, weatherproofing and roof inspections are crucial now to prevent any leaks and water damage that could put a damper on your upcoming celebrations. The rains can create maintenance issues with French doors sticking, and sump pumps or deck drains overflowing. It’s also a good time to change out furnace filters, smoke/CO detector batteries, have your fireplace serviced and your windows cleaned. Other projects which make a huge impact, while at the same time not being overly intrusive and time consuming, are freshening up the paint in the common areas and updating light fixtures. Of course, even the most minor of home repairs and continual maintenance can be daunting to take care of on your own. A A comfortable chair in front of the fireplace is the perfect spot on a chilly day. qualified contractor could accomplish most of these smaller projects in less than a week’s span. You may not be comfortable hiring an unlicensed handyman and with good reason. Homeowners are looking for someone they can trust with a service background that is more attention-oriented – a white glove service, so to speak. Few General Contractors offer maintenance services and therefore demand is high this time of year. Reach out to yours now to get on their schedule before your festivities begin. They may even be able to help you put that bicycle together or install your holiday lights. Whatever you decide to upgrade in your home in preparation for the winter holidays, be sure to allow yourself plenty of time. That way, once the work is complete, you can appreciate the new look and add the final touches of décor. After all is set and done, you can relax for some much-needed alone time before you gather with loved ones. If you call 911, we’ll come, intercede, and take every possible safety measure,” Bowers said. He encourages two measures that civilians can take to prevent thefts. “If you have a garage, park in it. If you can afford after-market bracing, get a shield welded onto your converter. It’s all about hardening the target, making your car less appealing to thieves than someone else’s car.” READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: A new tradition began at Piedmont High this year as its Student Body leaders in ASB followed the middle school and elementary schools by hosting a costume contest on Halloween. The students obliged with animated participation, and two winners were named, earning goodie bags with candy from ASB. Freshman Jerry Jialin Yu was named Best Overall winner, dressed as Russell from the Pixar film Up. Zachary Feldstein, a junior, was given the title Mr. Worldwide dressed as Reggaeton Rapper Pitbull. “The contest brought a lot of spirit to campus and students were able to show off their creativity by dressing up. I think everyone really enjoyed the costume contest, and it will definitely be put on next year as well,” said Junior Class Vice President Hailey Marshburn. Walking through the city, neighborhoods are subtly defined by the varying quality of different buildings and, by what I will call “urban landscaping” – paving, light fixtures, ironwork, and subtle signage. A very sensitive response to its geography, especially the central river and surrounding hills, is what characterizes Ljubljana, the capital of Slovenia. Its extensive central core consists of a series of public spaces and buildings: squares, parks, streets, promenades and bridges – and all limited to pedestrians and bicycles. It is considered a model of pedestrian success and remains the only European capital whose city center is completely car-free.

articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Department will host an informational open house on proposed housing and the City’s Housing Element on Wednesday, November 9 from 5:00 to 6:30 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. articles.text: The Cain family in Wildwood Gardens received a special delivery early Saturday morning, two days before Halloween. Their son, 1st grader Timothy Cain, was the winner in guessing the weight of the 1006-pound jumbo pumpkin, the centerpiece of the Wildwood Dads Pumpkin Patch. Timothy guessed 1004 pounds, narrowly beating out the next closest guess, 1003 pounds, and more than 200 other guesses. The gourd arrived at the Cain residence at 4:00 a.m. and was dropped off on a pallet via forklift by the Fuji Melon, the supplier for this year’s patch. The delivery was due at 7:00 a.m. but, like all things Halloween, the drop off occurred in the dark of night and by surprise. When asked for his secret strategy in guessing the mass of the gourd, Cain held his cards close to the chest. Despite the prying efforts of this reporter asking if he picked it up, used a tape measure, a phone app or skills from math class Cain stated, “I just looked at it.” Wildwood dads gave fair warning to the Cains that the pumpkin had started to decompose a little early this year. Wildwood Dads Club President Adam Fishman used some quick thinking and filled up a gash in Jack with some expansion foam. All things considered, the Cains were not sure quite what to do with the pumpkin. Timothy’s brother, William, a 5th grader at Wildwood School, considered carving a jack-o-lantern face into the pumpkin with shovels. Fuji Melon agreed to return this week to cart off whatever is left of Giant Jack.
articles.title: 1st grader Timothy Cain’s guess wins 1006-pound Giant Jack

articles.text: Piedmonters will receive an Alameda County Alert at approximately 9 a.m. this Saturday, November 5, as part of the city’s first-ever wildfire evacuation drill. The drill will directly affect about 50 homes located on streets above Coaches Field off Moraga Avenue. For most residents, the alert will include instructions for an at-home wildfire readiness activity. However, residents on Maxwelton Road, Abbot Way, Echo Lane, and Nellie Avenue will receive an alert instructing them to evacuate their homes and go to Piedmont Community Hall, at 711 Highland Avenue. Emergency responders will knock on doors in this neighborhood around 9 a.m. Alerts will arrive via text and email. All residents are invited to a post-drill debriefing and preparedness event starting at 10 a.m., at Piedmont Community Hall. After remarks from city officials, participants are encouraged to ask questions and share their own experiences. The drill, which Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan conceived last spring and has been planning for the last four months, will help the readiness not only of residents but of responders as well. Because emergencies like earthquakes and wildfires can cut power lines, Brannigan is pushing for the use of walkie-talkies among responders. He also seeks to optimize communications between collaborators like the city of Oakland, Mountain View Cemetery (as an evacuation site), and the Piedmont Police Department, which is primarily responsible for organizing wildfire evacuations. The only prospective problem which Brannigan fears is low participation of local residents on account of the light rain which is forecasted on Saturday. Otherwise, in his words, “The time to have problems is during an exercise. If we have any problems, I’ll be happy about that.” “Our changing climate means wildfires are more frequent and destructive than ever,” said Brannigan. “By taking the time now to prepare our homes and practice evacuation, we will all be better prepared to take lifesaving actions quickly when a fire comes our way.” Piedmont and Alameda Counties use AC Alerts for evacuation warnings and information in the event of a fire, earthquake, or other emergency. All Piedmonters are encouraged to register for AC Alert at acalert.org, or texting their zip code to 888-777. To register in advance for the Community Hall debriefing and for information, visit piedmont. ca.gov/WildfireDrill.
articles.title: Fire Dept. to hold wildfire emergency drill on Saturday

articles.text: Editor: The United Nations has announced that under the current Paris agreement pledges of 166 nations, the earth is on track to warm 2.5 degree Celsius by the end of the century. Is it time to seriously consider climate engineering as a way to give more time for transitioning to clean energy? It is relatively cheap and quite effective as demonstrated by historical volcanic eruptions. Any modern nation can do it on its own without the authorization of the UN. China is likely to do it someday regardless of international opinion to avoid civil unrest and to maintain in power its harsh communist regime should the impact of warming be as bad as predicted by the climate models. Rather than worrying about “moral hazard”, let’s put this technology on the forefront of discussion and research. As an alternative to spraying sulfur aerosol in the stratosphere, could Elon Musk redirect his Mars effort towards deploying a 1000 square kilometer shield (for example as one thousand one square km shields) at the L1 Laplacian point between the sun and the earth? It would cool the earth by one degree Celsius.
articles.title: As the earth heats up, what to do

articles.text: The Piedmont Post has begun its 25th year of publishing the community’s weekly newspaper. It’s first edition was on October 20, 1998, a 12-page paper that hardly offered any promise, let alone optimism, that it might be around a quarter century later. In a small town with only a few commercial businesses, the outlook for its survival was somewhat bleak. Ten years later we began reading stories in the New York Times about the large number of local newspapers going out of business – over 2,000 at last count. And yet here we are – thriving and finding ways to thank the residents for so strongly supporting The Little Newspaper That Could. During the next several weeks and months, you will read comments of some of the people who were there at the beginning – the optimists and pragmatists. years of the Piedmont Post every Wednesday afternoon. –Kent & Kathy Penwell generations. When you introduced yourself to me 25 years ago, we had a very compelling conversation that I had heard many times before growing up at the dinner table. You stood for open, safe communication and the integrity of a story (just like my father and grandfather). We instantly hit it off. You needed advertising and I needed a trusted venue that would continue to embrace my company’s legacy and the story of Piedmont itself. Perhaps it was selfish, but it was a terrific trade! Your insights and pushbacks are as refreshing today as 25 years ago. Your ability to run from the playing field to a night at the Symphony and every nuance in between is pretty remarkable. Thank you again. –DJ Grubb The Grubb Company

articles.text: Editor: We live at 1211 Oakland Avenue at the corner of Jerome. We received a public notice Saturday about a proposed bulb-out in front of our house. The bulb-out would eliminate all three parking spaces in front of our house as well as the two spaces in front of the neighboring property at 1209 Oakland Avenue. A bus stop would also be relocated in front of our house. These are very significant costs. While sharing the City Council’s commitment to safer streets, we disagree with the proposed measures to slow traffic and make crossing safer on Oakland Avenue. Recently, speed bumps were installed on Greenbank and seem to be working well. Putting speed bumps on Oakland Avenue would be significantly less expensive and disruptive than constructing eight bulb-outs at the Jerome and El Cerrito intersections, eliminating a net of 10 parking spaces, relocating four bus stops, and removing two mature trees, as the current plans provide. Traffic lights would be another less disruptive option. We applaud the city’s commitment to making Piedmont’s streets safer. We do not agree with the proposed solution, however. There are significantly less expensive and disruptive alternatives available that do not require the destruction of mature trees. Killing trees in order to build concrete bulb-outs could not be further from the agenda of protecting nature and combating global warming. We urge the City Council to reject this over-engineered, costly, disruptive, and anti-environmental proposal. -Jonah Levy and Helga Ying
articles.title: Proposed bulb-outs not the solution to slow traffic on Oakland Ave.

articles.text: Before there was “social media” there was the Piedmont Post. Starting in 1998, the new hometown newspaper provided more than the sports scores, want ads and a few newsy items; it became a public forum for controversial items in town, providing detailed coverage (sometimes not appreciated by all) as well as unrestricted space for the residents to present their ideas, clarifications and objections. A couple of examples that come to mind are stories about undergrounding of utilities in some neighborhoods, and Measure E, the earthquake retrofitting of Piedmont schools. pages.text: Wednesday, November 2, 2022 3 25th Anniversary of Piedmont Post The Piedmont Post has begun its 25th year of publishing the community’s weekly newspaper. It’s first edition was on October 20, 1998, a 12-page paper that hardly offered any promise, let alone optimism, that it might be around a quarter century later. In a small town with only a few commercial businesses, the outlook for its survival was somewhat bleak. Ten years later we began reading stories in the New York Times about the large number of local newspapers going out of business – over 2,000 at last count. And yet here we are – thriving and finding ways to thank the residents for so strongly supporting The Little Newspaper That Could. We received a public notice Saturday about a proposed bulb-out in front of our house. The bulb-out would eliminate all three parking spaces in front of our house as well as the two spaces in front of the neighboring property at 1209 Oakland Avenue. A bus stop would also be relocated in front of our house. These are very significant costs. While sharing the City Council’s commitment to safer streets, we disagree with the proposed measures to slow traffic and make crossing safer on Oakland Avenue. Recently, speed bumps were installed on Greenbank and seem to be working well. Putting speed bumps on Oakland Avenue would be significantly less expensive and disruptive than constructing eight bulb-outs at the Jerome and El Cerrito intersections, eliminating a net of 10 parking spaces, relocating four bus stops, and removing two mature trees, as the current plans provide. Traffic lights would be another less disruptive option. We applaud the city’s commitment to making Piedmont’s streets safer. We do not agree with the proposed solution, however. There are significantly less expensive and disruptive alternatives available that do not require the destruction of mature trees. Killing trees in order to build concrete bulb-outs could not be further from the agenda of protecting nature and combating global warming. We urge the City Council to reject this over-engineered, costly, disruptive, and anti-environmental proposal. -Jonah Levy and Helga Ying Piedmont Post news racks at 2 locations Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at Mulberry’s Market, and Piedmont Shell at Grand & Wildwood Ave. Copies of the paper may be purchased for $1 at all locations during business hours. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters is hosting a public discussion today on the invasion of Ukraine by Russia. The guest speaker is Steven Pifer, Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine. The discussion will be held on Zoom at 5 p.m., Wednesday, November 2. The war in Ukraine is the largest land war since World War II. Listen to the latest about the current situation from a diplomatic, military, and economic viewpoint, as well as possible trajectories for the war. Ambassador Pifer will address implications for international security, not only for Ukraine and Russia but also for the US and the EU. Ambassador Pifer is an affiliate with the Center for International Security and Cooperation at Stanford and a nonresident senior fellow with the Brookings Institution. A retired Foreign Service officer, in a career of more than 25 years with the Department of State, he served as deputy assistant secretary with responsibilities for Russia and Ukraine, U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine, and special assistant to the President and senior director for Russia, Ukraine and Eurasia on the National Security Council. He also served at the U.S. embassies in Warsaw, Moscow and London as well as with the U.S. delegation to the negotiation on intermediate-range nuclear forces in Geneva. He is author of The Eagle and the Trident: U.S.- Steven Pifer, former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine, speaks about the invasion by Russia in a Piedmont League of Women Voters Zoom discussion today at 5 p.m. Ukraine Relations in Turbulent Times. This event is co-sponsored by the League of Women Voters of Solano County and Portland, Oregon. The talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube streaming and will include an audience question and answer session moderated by Lorel Plimier, president of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont. Visit the website (lwvpiedmont.org) to learn more and to register for the discussion. Once you have registered, you will receive the Zoom link by email. The event is free and open to the public.

articles.text: The scheduled talk by Ford Roosevelt, grandson of former U.S. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt, at the Piedmont Seniors meeting on Wednesday, November 16 at Piedmont Community Hall has been postponed and will be rescheduled to February 22, 2023. articles.text: Final of an 8-part series The Post wraps up its election preview series this week. With the election just days away residents are now entrusted to do their civic duty by voting by November 8. Piedmont is always at the top of voter turnout in Alameda County, and among the highest in the state. The Post thanks all candidates City Council and School Board for their willingness to answer questions each week for a period of two months. Every week, two questions are sent out on Thursday and candidates are instructed to limit their answers to 150 words per question. City Council 3 open seats, 6 candidates. Week 8 QUESTIONS 1. If elected, what is on your short list of what you hope to accomplish in the first two years? 2. This is the last week of questions from the Post prior to the November 8 election. Do you have any final comments? JENNIFER LONG Incumbent 1. Accomplish in First Two Years If elected, my first two years will be focused on helping to select our next City Administrator, bringing critical infrastructure projects like the pool and dispatch center to fruition, further developing a vision for our City’s growth, and creating a robust community engagement process outside of chambers. 2. Final Comments As a current member of the Council it has been a privilege to serve. Over the course of my campaign I have had the opportunity to get to know our community better and to hear about issues that concern our residents. This campaign has only strengthened my commitment to continue in my role, should I be fortunate enough to be elected. I would like to thank the Piedmont Post, my fellow candidates, and the Piedmont community for the part each has played in making this a positive and informative campaign season. On November 8th, please make your voices heard. Think of our city as a tiny nation. We are 1,000 acres, the same size as Central Park. Love your neighbour as you do yourself, visit the sick and the prisoners. Protect the animals and the babies and children and elderly in particular. delayed their Housing Element. The State also accelerated the timeline to complete Santa Monica’s updated design guidelines, taking away even more local control from the city. Let’s work together and avoid a costly fight with the State. Let’s also complete our due diligence process and create a detailed facilities condition assessment report of our civic buildings outlining options and costs for repair/replacement or a combination of both to protect our critical facilities. 2. Final Comments Thank you to the Post for providing this weekly Q&A forum throughout the campaign and it’s also worth recognizing (and appreciating) that politics in Piedmont have a different tone than what is considered the “norm” these days on the national stage. So, thank you to all the candidates and all our neighbors for being involved, being respectful, and voting! This experience gives me one more reason why I think Piedmont is a great town. Feel free to contact me at tom@ vote4tomramsey.com JEANNE SOLNORDAL 1. Accomplish in First Two Years My two-year short list is as follows: • Submit a resident approved version of the Housing Element plan. I support a vote before any rezoning. • Obtain pool bids that meet the needs, not desires, of Piedmont residents. Over building and excess costs need to be avoided. It is my experience that Piedmont tends to be overcharged by contractors. Costs should be carefully compared to those being charged in other cities. • Getting design reviews completed for the infrastructure needs at the Civic Center is critical. Time is of the essence to avoid inflated costs. • Assess school and park crosswalk safety. Safer crossings are needed to avert potential dangers to our youth. • Work with the administrators at the PUSD to ensure our excellent test scores are sustained. • Connect with the Climate Action team to re-promote the rideshare to work program. • Establish two EV charging stations centrally located in City Center. 2. Final Comments I want to thank all residents for taking the time to listen to many candidates. Being involved in politics, I understand the enormous amount of campaign materials received daily. An important fact to remember: in 1868 the Fourteenth amendment established equal protections for all citizens. In 1870 the Fifteenth amendment ratified that all citizens regardless of race, origin, etc. had the right to vote. Our state constitution also grants us this right. The Piedmont City Charter specifically gives residents the right to vote on rezoning changes. Voting is such an important right that any attempt, by anyone, to circumvent that right should be met with great skepticism and scrutiny. Demand your right to vote on all rezoning changes. Circumventing voting rights sets our history back more than a century. This is digressive not progressive. Many thanks to Jay Russell at Piedmont Post for providing this platform to candidates. NANCY BOSTROM 1. Accomplish in First Two Years I plan to enlist Piedmonters to help me continue to formulate plans to keep them and their property and pets safe as I have done already. My house was ransacked and thieves stole a vellum edition of the Gutenberg Bible and a set of Audubon’s Birds of America, among other things. Our crime rate was escalating so I promoted cameras at every entrance [to the city] and augmenting license plate readers. Every week our police catch another person with a stolen car, guns, and warrants, thanks to this applied technology. 2. Final Comments Our school and City need a motto. Piedmont High School’s is “Achieve the Honourable.” A better one I think is “Be Kind.” All a teacher has to do is point. TOM RAMSEY 1. Accomplish in First Two Years Let’s get our Housing Element approved and then work together to update our design guidelines over the next 18 months. This next phase is our tool to put guardrails on the state mandates and have more control over what gets built and where. Other California jurisdictions have seen the consequences of not approving the Housing Element on time. For example, the State approved thousands of housing units in Santa Monica without the city’s input because city officials BETSY ANDERSEN Incumbent 1. Accomplish in First Two Years My short list includes hiring a new City Administrator, renovating the 911 Dispatch Center, and rebuilding the Piedmont Community Pool. City Administrator Sara Lillevand is retiring, and the City Council has begun the search for her replacement. Please complete the community survey (launching this week) to provide input on the qualities and qualifications you would like to see in our next City Administrator. Second, renovating the 911 Dispatch Center is a necessary first step to bring our public safety facilities to current standards. Our community generously supported Measure UU to rebuild the community pool. We did not anticipate that California construction costs would increase 30% from July 2020 to July 2022. Council has already scaled back the building plan and is currently re-bidding the project. The Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO) is raising additional funds. To learn more and to make a tax-deductible donation, please visit www.prfo. org. 2. Final Comments We all care deeply about our community. Over the past five years on the City Council, I am grateful to have worked with so many talented residents, community volunteers, and council members who strive to understand the nuances involved in the complex matters before us. Looking ahead, we need to continue to collaborate. The state-mandated plan for potential new housing in Piedmont is one of many important long-term issues we need to address constructively as a community. We also need to work together to improve core city services, prepare for wildfires and earthquakes, increase pedestrian and bicyclist safety, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, optimize recreational spaces and opportunities for all ages, and recruit and retain top-notch

articles.text: The Alameda County Registrar of Voters is seeking poll workers for the November 8, 2022 election. Poll workers play a critical role in making voting accessible to all community members – and get paid to do it. Workers are needed throughout Alameda County from Saturday, November 5 through Tuesday, November 8, election day. Interested community members can sign up online to volunteer at acgov.org/rovform_app/ewapply. The application is simple and takes just a few minutes to complete. Job details Poll workers are paid volunteers who perform tasks including: • Setting up and closing a polling place • Helping voters understand their rights • Protecting ballots and voting equipment The County Registrar of Voters office provides training for poll workers. Individuals are paid for training and time served as a poll worker. No special skills are required to be a poll worker. Eligibility requirements: • Must be a registered voter in California • Must be a legal permanent resident or green card holder • An eligible high school student Bilingual Poll Workers Sought Bilingual poll workers are especially needed. In Alameda County, assistance is provided to voters in Burmese, Chinese, Hindi, Khmer, Korean, Laotian, Mien, Mongolian, Punjabi, Spanish, Tagalog, Telugu, and Vietnamese. Residents fluent in any of these languages are urged to consider volunteering. Interested residents can find more information about volunteering as a poll worker at acvote.org/community/become-anelection-worker or by calling the Alameda County Registrar of Voters office at 510-272-6973.
articles.title: Poll workers needed for Nov. 8 Election

In Alameda County, assistance is provided to voters in Burmese, Chinese, Hindi, Khmer, Korean, Laotian, Mien, Mongolian, Punjabi, Spanish, Tagalog, Telugu, and Vietnamese. Residents fluent in any of these languages are urged to consider volunteering. Interested residents can find more information about volunteering as a poll worker at acvote.org/community/become-anelection-worker or by calling the Alameda County Registrar of Voters office at 510-272-6973. If elected, what is on your short list of what you hope to accomplish in the first two years? 2. This is the last week of questions from the Post prior to the November 8 election. This campaign has only strengthened my commitment to continue in my role, should I be fortunate enough to be elected. articles.text: Michael Malione ALPS (Advancing Learning for Piedmont Students) is a parent support group that advocates for more solid academics at PUSD and provides families with resources and opportunities to engage their children in deeper and more joyful learning. The group has been gaining steam and making impactful strides in advancing academic focus in the community. As the 2022 school board election race comes to a close, we wish to remind the community that as a parent support organization, we cannot directly endorse candidates. Our members and officers have, as individuals, taken a variety of positions on matters relating to the current state of academics at PUSD and the school board candidates. We firmly believe that strong academics and DEIB improvements can and should coexist to help all children reach their full potential while making the world a better place for all. While in theory the school district can achieve both, in practice there are people in PUSD who’ve proffered an unbalanced approach that undermines students’ academic potential. All three candidates for school board care strongly about academics. We hold that it is critical to select high-quality curricula and provide the right professional development opportunities for our teachers. Given that more than 30% of PUSD students are high-performing, we consider the guidance from the state of California to be a floor, not the ceiling for our district. Our district has in recent years lurched in directions that are not in sync with the great expertise that exists among the various sectors of our community—teachers, professionals, and parents alike. We urge you to vote for candidates whom you think will be able to stand up to the administration and advocate for the needs of our children. Parent Sharing Forum We held our first Parent Sharing Forum in October. It was a chance to welcome new parents, and how to get the most from differentiated instruction, early reading and mathematics. Registration will soon be opening for the longest-standing enrichment program, Math Kangaroo, an international competition for grades 1 to 12 that focuses on problem-solving. We will host a virtual Q&A session about it on Monday, November 14 at 8 pm. We also offer Learning Circles, which we’ll be promoting in advance of the next session. Many of our officers and board members participated in both special school board meetings, to provide feedback on the drafted mission and vision statements. They’ve expressed that the district’s mission should include academic focus and opportunities for each child to reach their full potential. We had a productive discussion with Dr. Evans about education at PUSD and academic rigor in our schools. We welcome his bold support for improving the differentiated instruction and academic curriculum throughout PUSD. With exciting work happening in the district on literacy and rewriting its mission and vision, there is increased optimism that academics will once again become a priority. To get the latest information about ALPS programs and opportunities, visit the Piedmont Store (piedmontstore. org), and click on Parent Support Groups. Ella Grossberg and Michael Malione are co-Presidents of Advancing Learning for Piedmont Students.
articles.title: What is ALPS and how does it help kids?

articles.text: Eden Lorin plays Lizzie Bennet and Jack Gross Whitaker is Mr. Darcy in Piedmont High School’s production of Pride and Prejudice. Members of the Piedmont High School Advanced Acting class will perform Jane Austen’s classic, Pride and Prejudice, the first weekend in November. All seats are General Admission. Online tickets are $18 for General Admission and $12 for Students and Seniors. Tickets are an extra $2 when purchased at the door, so patrons are encouraged to purchase tickets in advance online at https://www.showtix4u. com/events/PHSPride. For more information contact Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@ piedmont.k12.ca.us.
