articles.text: The Piedmont School Board will discuss its search process for a new superintendent at a Special School Board meeting tonight, Wednesday, November 2, at 5 p.m., in the Council Chambers at City Hall. The board will designate a liaison and spokesperson to meet with Leadership Associates, the educational executive recruitment firm expected to provide guidelines for the search for a permanent school superintendent. The Board will also issue its recommendations regarding the participation of Piedmont community and staff groups for input to the search process. The Board intends to describe the input it will use in developing a job profile for prospective candidates, with comments from school support groups, board members, and results from an online survey sent to parents, teachers, staff, and community members. After the job description is refined, a majority of board members will review and respond to it before it is posted on the websites of the school district, Leadership Associates, and Edjoin.com. At this meeting, the board will specify dates for publication of the position with the Association of California School Administrators, dates for future input sessions, and two closed session dates: one for application review, and another for interviews. The application review session is expected to last two to two-anda-half hours. The interviews are expected to last all day. The interviews are expected to take place in venues other than the School District office. Alongside its candidate recruitment process, board members will refine a “Worksheet of Contract Parameters” to be completed by interviewing candidates. The board will request input regarding the desired qualities, characteristics, and experiential background of candidates, the school district’s strengths and challenges in recruiting, and questions or problems regarding the recruitment process. While interested community members can participate in the regular school board meetings in-person or on Zoom, this Special School Board meeting will be held in person only (no Zoom). The public is invited to attend the meeting tonight at City Hall. Details of the meeting can be found at: us06web.zoom. us/j/81035778105.
articles.title: School Board to describe Supt. search tonight

articles.text: A free screening of two Academy Award winning shorts on Title IX, Queen of Basketball and Mink, will be shown on Thursday, November 3 at 7 p.m. at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on the Havens School campus, 325 Highland Avenue. • Queen of Basketball Lucy Harris scored the first basket in Olympic women’s basketball and was drafted by the NBA. If not for Title IX, she couldn’t have gone to college and had either opportunity. In The Queen of Basketball, Lucy tells her own story, from being “too tall and that’s all” to finding her place in sports. The film won an Academy Award in 2022 as Best Short Documentary. Queen of Basketball is about Lucy Harris, arguably the greatest women’s basketball player. Mink! focuses on Patsy Takemoto Mink, the first woman of color elected to Congress. • Mink! Ironically, TitIe IX almost didn’t pass because one of its key sponsors, Patsy Mink, was called away for a family emergency. Mink! tells the story of Rep. Patsy Mink’s path as the first woman of color to serve in Congress, and the crucial role she played in the passage of Title IX. The two films will be followed by a conversation with Chelle Putzer and Eva Phalen of the Piedmont Recreation Department. Masks are required. Title IX is the federal legislation that prohibits sex-based discrimination in any school or other education program that receives federal funding.

CSEA employees are pushing the school district to pay a greater share of healthcare premiums through the same general fund which it used for the recent teachers’ pay raise. If the district does not do this, it will amount to a 10-15% decrease in take-home pay for classified workers. Piedmont CSEA President Christine Petersen, a Piedmont native who has worked in the school district for more than 30 years, advised that this will double and even triple many classified employees’ share. Until now, PUSD paid 92% of healthcare costs with an 8% split for employees, including teachers. Petersen has stated that, although healthcare costs are rising for the district by 9.9%, it will be paying only 50-75% of premiums in 2023. Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) President Elise Marks, who led the charge for a 7.5% raise for teachers throughout the district in October, came to the defense of the classified California School Employees Association. CSEA and APT both received raises in October as contracts were negotiated, but APT won extra protection against health care costs, and CSEA workers did not. “The Kaiser increase of up to $200 a month would more than wipe out” this pay raise, given that many full-time classified workers earn less than $30,000 a year. As a result, Marks said, many employees will make less in January than they made before the pay raise. articles.text: ASB and Affinity Mentorship Class host forum on campus Photo by Sohrab “Seb” Ford Eleven students from ASB and the Affinity Mentorship Class hosted a forum for all three school board candidates on October 28 in the new Alan Harvey Theater Sohrab “Seb” Ford Members of the high school student government (ASB) and the Affinity Mentorship Class hosted a panel discussion for the three candidates running for Piedmont School Board on Friday, October 28 in the new Alan Harvey Theater. Each student on the questioning panel asked a question and each of the three candidates had 90 seconds to answer. The candidates were Ruchi Medhekar, Lindsay Thomasson and Shirley Hooi. Although few students at PHS are age 18 and eligible to vote, the forum is the first to date of any Piedmont Candidates that has been held in person. Although attendance was optional for the 10:15 a.m. forum, students, teachers and administrators filled the theater. “It’s important that students become aware and involved in local elections like the school board because they directly impact our day to day lives, more then they impact anyone else. Students need to get their voices heard.” said Ruby Guzdar after the event. With the theater’s wifi not working, the forum felt like an old-time town hall meeting with speakers relying on the strength of their voices to be heard. Students on the questioning panel included student board member Cleo Tahawi, Junior Class President Jack Cramer, Ruby Guzdar, Elena Stevens, Inaya Majid, and Meher Bachher. Medhekar answered a question about discrimination by saying, “There is a debate between diversity and academics that’s been going on. And I think that it’s just not either/ or,” she said. “I think that one thing that the district is not doing well is talking about incidents that happen, we have to respect students privacy, but we need to also talk about what is happening,” Medhekar added. In response to a question over a controversial curriculum, Hooi suggested providing multiple options to students and parents in order to let them decide which readings and opinions they felt were most important. Thomasson emphasized the importance of opening up discussion between students and board members, Thomasson suggested re-implementing “school board listening sessions” or “office hours” that the school held during the pandemic shelter-in-place order. The Affinity Mentorship program began in 2020 and in 2022 was recognized as a class in the 8th period. The year-long course currently has 33 students. Mentors offer sessions to elementary and middle school students of similar affinities in order to explore and learn about themselves and their identities. Piedmont residents will go to the polls on Tuesday, November 8 to select two of the three candidates to join the school board. Photo by Jay Russell The lower section of the theater was filled with students to hear from school board candidates vying for two seats.
articles.title: Students ask school board candidates some tough questions

articles.text: A man walks as if he has the weight of the world on his shoulders. He lives in a house at the end of the street. He walks hunched over. Head down. Never talking to anyone. Each day he walks hunched over to the park at the end of his street. He stays there for hours, sitting on a bench, staring aimlessly at the pond. He doesn’t bring bread for the birds. He just sits. The sun will go down and finally, he will leave. The trees, the birds and the stars watch him. He doesn’t notice, he’s hunched over. It is dark, he doesn’t see the path in front of him. He knows he doesn’t need to; he has walked the path many times and knows where it leads. It ends at the playground where he sits on a swing and lights his pipe. He pulls his coat tighter around his aging body. Only the embers of his tobacco are seen in the dark night, momentarily reflecting his sunken face and faded blue eyes. But alas there is no one to see him. He scans the darkness as if waiting for someone to appear, perhaps to come to him. Someone to see him. Someone to bear the weight of the world with him. The stars watch the wisps of smoke rising toward them. The man sits, hunched over, dreaming of a life that could’ve been. He gets up from the swing and begins to walk home. His feet carry him to the lonely house at the end of the quiet street. He sleeps, though no dreams come to him. The next day he walks with the world on his shoulders, hunching him once more. Larissa Edel, a Piedmont resident, is a sophomore at Bentley School.

Each student on the questioning panel asked a question and each of the three candidates had 90 seconds to answer. The candidates were Ruchi Medhekar, Lindsay Thomasson and Shirley Hooi. Although few students at PHS are age 18 and eligible to vote, the forum is the first to date of any Piedmont Candidates that has been held in person. Although attendance was optional for the 10:15 a.m. forum, students, teachers and administrators filled the theater. “It’s important that students become aware and involved in local elections like the school board because they directly impact our day to day lives, more then they impact anyone else. Students need to get their voices heard.” said Ruby Guzdar after the event. With the theater’s wifi not working, the forum felt like an old-time town hall meeting with speakers relying on the strength of their voices to be heard. Students on the questioning panel included student board member Cleo Tahawi, Junior Class President Jack Cramer, Ruby Guzdar, Elena Stevens, Inaya Majid, and Meher Bachher. Medhekar answered a question about discrimination by saying, “There is a debate between diversity and academics that’s been going on. And I think that it’s just not either/ or,” she said. “I think that one thing that the district is not doing well is talking about incidents that happen, we have to respect students privacy, but we need to also talk about what is happening,” Medhekar added. In response to a question over a controversial curriculum, Hooi suggested providing multiple options to students and parents in order to let them decide which readings and opinions they felt were most important. Thomasson emphasized the importance of opening up discussion between students and board members, Thomasson suggested re-implementing “school board listening sessions” or “office hours” that the school held during the pandemic shelter-in-place order. The Affinity Mentorship program began in 2020 and in 2022 was recognized as a class in the 8th period. The year-long course currently has 33 students. Mentors offer sessions to elementary and middle school students of similar affinities in order to explore and learn about themselves and their identities. Piedmont residents will go to the polls on Tuesday, November 8 to select two of the three candidates to join the school board. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.title: Halloween Costume Contest prevails at Piedmont High

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School held its annual Halloween Carnival during an extended lunchtime on October 31. Jamie Van Kleeck’s ASB class organized Carnival games on the Bern courts which kept the entire middle school on a sugar buzz. Games included Candy Corn Take Out, Mystery Cups, Pumpkin “Booling,” and Swamp Fishing. A costume contest solicited dozens of entries, in what turned out to be a nearly impossible task for judges. Swamp Fishing and Donuts on a String garnered long lines the entire afternoon. A raffle ramped up the fun for middle school Halloween revelers and costumed games of basketball and cornhole never ceased. Justus Shreiber appears as a bottle of “Mr. Maple’s Syrup”. 8th grade ASB member Ruben Cohen spins the wheel for the cake hop game. Nearly every student wore a costume to school on Monday.

articles.text: The Highlander boys’ water polo team swept through the Western Alameda County Conference Championship Tournament at San Leandro High on its way to a second consecutive league title, defeating San Leandro in the opening round 20-3 on Tuesday, October 25, Lick-Wilmerding 11-6 in the semifinals on October 27, and s 13-4 drubbing in the finals on Saturday, October 29. PHS was undefeated and the clear favorite entering the post-season playoffs. Last year Piedmont narrowly defeated No. 1 Berkeley 12-8. “This is a testament to the kids coming and working every single day, the leadership we had from our juniors and seniors, and the way they grew into the program,” said assistant coach John Savage, who stepped aside from the lead role after being head coach for the previous nine years. Piedmont was able to lean on its defense against Alameda, and allowed no goals until the third quarter. Goalie Dariush Kashani had 15 saves, and the PHS defenders forcing the Hornets to attempt scoring from long range. “It all comes down to defense; that’s what we stressed the most. We have the best goalie in the league, but it comes down to team defense. We run press defense and then we run a drop, which basically forces players to cover 2-3 guys at once. It’s really a team effort, and that’s what’s really carried us through the season,” said head coach Rik Krumins. “These guys keep me on my toes. We all work hard and get the job done. I’d like to highlight our chemistry, we worked very well together. We executed well in the second half. Quincy Scherman did great coming back on defense, same for Finn Burke,” said Kashani. Much of this year’s team contributed on 2021’s league title as well, but the Highlanders entered the league tournament as the No. 3 seed last time around. This time, the postgame celebration was a bit more subdued with the Highlanders, far and away the better side. Staff Photos Goalie Dariush Kashani had 15 saves in the finals against the Hornets. Peter Krumins led the rout of Alameda with six goals – a double hat trick. Piedmont water pollo players and coaches with their second consecutive WACC Championship banner after defeating Alameda 13-4 in the finals. “Last year, we focused on shutting down one guy for Berkeley. Now, coming into this game, we were the No. 1 team. It felt a lot different. Our practices were much more like swim-team practices. We’ve been countering and you wouldn’t see us counter like that last year. We’re in a lot better shape,” said Peter Krumins, who led the team in scoring with six goals. “We flipped the script this year,” added Declan Linnane. “We weren’t supposed to win it last year; we were the underdogs. This year, we had a dominant league season and we just continued that to the championship game,” Piedmont will enter the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs on Saturday, November 5. as the No. 3 seed and a first-round bye. 13-4 win over Alameda In the first quarter, PHS was first on the board when Krumins assisted George Stein 40 seconds into the match. However, Alameda tied one minute later. The Hornets had an opportunity to take the lead with a 5-meter penalty shot at the 4:46 mark, but Kashani came through with a big save. From there, Piedmont recorded eight shot attempts, which included throws by Krumins and Stein hitting the crossbar. The second quarter started with Kashani stopping three shots in the first two minutes of action, leading to Krumins scoring at 5:13 to give Piedmont the lead. Stein scored 30 seconds later to put PHS ahead 3-1, while Stein assisted Krumins at 3:22 to make it 4-1. In the remaining time, Alameda scored twice but Kashani had two saves, including a big stop on a breakaway opportunity. In the third, Piedmont scored five unanswered goals to put the match out of reach at 9-3. Krumins assisted Farris Saffouri 45 seconds into the quarter, followed by Linnane drawing a 5-meter penalty 30 seconds later, enabling Krumins to score. Krumins scored again with 3:33 to go, while Linnane assisted Krumins at the two-minute mark. Stein scored once more with 10 seconds on the block. Daniel Banin scored in the fourth quarter to make it 10-3 with 5:15 to play, while Krumins assisted Quincy Scherman 45 seconds later. Finn Burke then scored on another assist by Krumins with 3:55 remaining. Alameda scored its first goal of the second half with 3:05 on the clock and added one more at 1:45 with Piedmont rotating bench players in. Krumins scored the final goal of the match at 1:32. Final stats: Krumins had six goals and two assists. Stein had three goals, an assist and steal. Burke, Saffouri, and Scherman had individual goals. Kashani had 15 saves and two steals. 11-6 win over Lick-Wilmerding PHS led 5-1 by the end of the first quarter and 7-3 by halftime. It scored two goals and allowed one in the third period to lead 9-4 before scoring twice in the fourth period, 11-6. Final stats: Linnane had three goals, an assist and a steal. Krumins scored three and had an assist. Saffouri had two goals and a steal. Burke had two goals. Stein had a goal and a steal. Kashani had nine saves. 20-3 win over San Leandro Piedmont led comfortably 7-0 by the end of the first quarter and 10-0 by halftime. It extended the gap to 14-1 in the third and closed out with six more goals in the fourth. PHS finished with 10 different goal scorers. Final stats: Hayden Jahn had four goals and two steals. Elles Krieckhaus had four goals, an assist and steal. Burke and Banin had two goals. Stein had two goals, an assist, and steal. Leo Hurwitz had two goals, an assist, and four steals. Evan Dickason had a goal and two assists. Spencer Barlow had a goal, assist, and steal. Scherman scored once. NEXT UP Piedmont (19-6 overall, 9-0 league) play the winner of No. 6 Novato and No. 11 Lick-Wilmerding on Saturday, November 5. Location and start time is To Be Determined.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team return to its tradition of winning every match every year. Last week it defeated Berkeley 4-3 at home on Tuesday, October 25, and rolled over Bishop O’Dowd 6-1 at Merritt College on Thursday, October 27. It was the team’s first league title since 2018. In the process, the Highlanders were a perfect 12-0 against WACC schools, something they achieved for 19 consecutive years between 2000-2018. It was the third win of the season against O’Dowd after defeating the Dragons 4-3 on October 11 and 5-2 at the California Tennis Classic in Fresno in September. This time, BOD was without two players, which forced them to pack their No. 1 doubles team with their usual top-two singles starters. Piedmont’s clinching fourth victory on match day was at No. 2 doubles with Cecilia DeFazio and Emma Eisemon winning 6-4, 6-2. “To be honest, I was kind of expecting us to win the title. We’ve beaten O’Dowd before and I knew we could do it again. Our Emma Eisemon (front) and Cecilia DeFazio captured the clinching win against Bishop O’Dowd to solidify Piedmont’s undefeated league championship season. Photo by Jacque Jumper Piedmont honored its five seniors on the roster on October 25 against Berkeley. Pictured are: Sophia Kalamas (left), Anne Jumper, Mara LaForte, Talia Blumberg, and Michaela Bini. team is really strong this year,” said DeFazio, a junior. She and Eisemon were a breakout doubles team last year, and this year they are even better. “As a doubles partner, I feel like we’re a lot closer now. I think we have a better mentality this season and we come back stronger. Because we’re so close as a team and we’re so eager to win, it pushes us through our wins. With the title, it proves that we earned everything we worked towards,” said sophomore teammate Emma Eisemon. Piedmont the WACC Individual Tournament on Friday and Saturday, November 4-5, where they will compete with two singles starters and two doubles teams. 6-1 win over O’Dowd Against Bishop O’Dowd, Anne Jumper at No. 2 singles was the first win on the day, cruising to a 6-1, 6-3 victory. Quickly following was Carolina Romanczuk winning easily 6-0, 6-0 at No. 3 singles. No. 1 doubles Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini lost 6-4, 6-2 as the third match to close on the day, but soon after, Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum at No. 3 doubles won 6-4, 6-1. Eisemon and DeFazio then reeled in the clinching victory at No. 2 doubles, 6-4, 6-2. Finishing the day was Anika Gilliland winning in three sets at No. 4 singles 6-4, 3-6, 10-8, while No. 1 singles starter Tanya Kononova won comfortably 6-3, 6-0. 4-3 win over Berkeley Piedmont defeated Berkeley 4-3 on October 25 and took time to honor their five seniors: LaForte, Bini, Anne Jumper, Sophia Kalamas, and Talia Blumberg. PHS won all three doubles matches and the No.1. singles match. Playing in her usual spot as No. 1 singles, Kononova won 6-1, 6-0 at No. 1. Anne Jumper lost in three sets at No. 2, 6-2, 4-6, 10-3. Romanczuk fell 6-2, 6-3 at No. 3, and Gilliland lost in three sets at No. 4, 6-3, 6-7 (8-6), 6-2. In doubles, LaForte and Bini won 6-3, 7-5 at No. 1. Eisemon and DeFazio cruised 6-1, 6-1 at No. 2. Kate Jumper and Kortum won 6-1, 6-2 at No. 3. NEXT UP Piedmont (16-3 overall, 12-0 league) play in the WACC Individual Tournament (Singles and Doubles) on Friday and Saturday, November 4-5 at Chabot College in Hayward. Matches start at 10:30 a.m. The Highlanders will also compete in the Division 2 NCS Team Championships, starting Tuesday, November 8. Staff Photo Staff Photo Arianna Kortum was all smiles in a 6-4, 6-1 win with Kate Jumper at No. 3 doubles.

articles.text: Piedmont High football fans got a preview on Thursday, October 27 of what they can expect in the future from Piedmont’s football program after its Junior Varsity team routed Tennyson 34-0 in Hayward. It was the second consecutive decisive win for Piedmont’s JV team after thrashing St. Patrick 41-12 on October 21. Tennyson got the first possession of the game and the Lancers drove all the way to Piedmont’s 30-yard line. However, a costly penalty helped the Highlanders force a turnover on downs. Although the first quarter ended scoreless, Piedmont drove downfield with a mix of runs by sophomores Tommy Ashton, Brandon Dickie and Miles Silver, and freshman Cash Panico, to go along with sophomore quarterback Vince Arbit completing a pass to receiver Sam Shelby. Ashton put Piedmont on the scoreboard with a one yard touchdown run to break the deadlock and a 6-0 lead. PHS missed the extra point attempt. On Tennyson’s next possession, sophomore linebacker Cash Elmquist made a sensational onehanded interception and took it all the way to the end zone for a pick-six. Ashton made the twopoint conversion for a 14-0 lead. Freshman Marius Arno recovered a Lancer fumble on its next possession deep on Tennyson’s side of the field. Shortly after, Ashton sprang loose for a 17-yard TD run. Freshman Ryan Riddell converted the extra point attempt for 21-0 to end the first half. The second half started with a bang when sophomore receiver and defensive back Miguel Long took the opening kickoff all the way to the Tennyson 35-yard line. Sophomore quarterback Markos Lagios followed with a 17- yard touchdown pass to freshman Dash Waters Worthen and a 27-0 lead. In the fourth quarter, Tennyson drove to the Piedmont 20-yard line, but the defense Tommy Ashton had a pair of touchdown carries against the Lancers. made a big stop with help from sophomores Jordan Alemania, Nick King, and Logan McGilloway, as well as freshmen Adan Sotelo, Adrian Kondakov, George Bishop, and Jason Shum. Not finished for the night, the Highlanders started another drive with a 25-yard run by Ashton, and then back-to-back completions from Lagios to freshman tight end Albert capped by a 21-yard touchdown pass on a post route to make it 34-0. The winning streak gives Piedmont momentum going into the season finale on Thursday, November 3 against Kennedy of Richmond at Witter Field at 6:00 p.m. Prior to the game, PHS will honor the nine seniors on the varsity team, Jack Nelson, Ryan McConathy, Matteo and Bautista Costa, Liam Campbell, Marcos Filho, Luka Rivas Cate, Bailey Cain, and Aidan Hickman. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-3) hosts Kennedy at Witter Field on Thursday, November 3 at 6:00 p.m. with senior night festivities starting at 5:30 p.m. Markos Lagios (4) had two touchdown passes on Tennyson.

JV football team shuts out Tennyson 34-0 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High football fans got a preview on Thursday, October 27 of what they can expect in the future from Piedmont’s football program after its Junior Varsity team routed Tennyson 34-0 in Hayward. It was the second consecutive decisive win for Piedmont’s JV team after thrashing St. Patrick 41-12 on October 21. Tennyson got the first possession of the game and the Lancers drove all the way to Piedmont’s 30-yard line. However, a costly penalty helped the Highlanders force a turnover on downs. Although the first quarter ended scoreless, Piedmont drove downfield with a mix of runs by sophomores Tommy Ashton, Brandon Dickie and Miles Silver, and freshman Cash Panico, to go along with sophomore quarterback Vince Arbit completing a pass to receiver Sam Shelby. Ashton put Piedmont on the scoreboard with a one yard touchdown run to break the deadlock and a 6-0 lead. PHS missed the extra point attempt. On Tennyson’s next possession, sophomore linebacker Cash Elmquist made a sensational onehanded interception and took it all the way to the end zone for a pick-six. Ashton made the twopoint conversion for a 14-0 lead. Freshman Marius Arno recovered a Lancer fumble on its next possession deep on Tennyson’s side of the field. Shortly after, Ashton sprang loose for a 17-yard TD run. Freshman Ryan Riddell converted the extra point attempt for 21-0 to end the first half. The second half started with a bang when sophomore receiver and defensive back Miguel Long took the opening kickoff all the way to the Tennyson 35-yard line. Sophomore quarterback Markos Lagios followed with a 17- yard touchdown pass to freshman Dash Waters Worthen and a 27-0 lead. In the fourth quarter, Tennyson drove to the Piedmont 20-yard line, but the defense Tommy Ashton had a pair of touchdown carries against the Lancers. made a big stop with help from sophomores Jordan Alemania, Nick King, and Logan McGilloway, as well as freshmen Adan Sotelo, Adrian Kondakov, George Bishop, and Jason Shum. Not finished for the night, the Highlanders started another drive with a 25-yard run by Ashton, and then back-to-back completions from Lagios to freshman tight end Albert capped by a 21-yard touchdown pass on a post route to make it 34-0. The winning streak gives Piedmont momentum going into the season finale on Thursday, November 3 against Kennedy of Richmond at Witter Field at 6:00 p.m. Prior to the game, PHS will honor the nine seniors on the varsity team, Jack Nelson, Ryan McConathy, Matteo and Bautista Costa, Liam Campbell, Marcos Filho, Luka Rivas Cate, Bailey Cain, and Aidan Hickman. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-3) hosts Kennedy at Witter Field on Thursday, November 3 at 6:00 p.m. with senior night festivities starting at 5:30 p.m. Markos Lagios (4) had two touchdown passes on Tennyson.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ water polo players celebrate following the game-winning goal to capture fifth-place at the WACC Tournament. Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team concluded its season with a fifth-place finish in the WACC Tournament at San Leandro HS. They opened with a 13-5 loss to Castro Valley on Tuesday, October 25 but followed with a big 19-4 win over Lick-Wilmerding on Thursday, October 27. In the battle for fifth-place on Saturday, October 29, the game went into double overtime before PHS topped Berkeley 13-12 in sudden death. Katarina Melian scored the golden goal 49 seconds into the period. “In the last overtime period, and my thought going in was, ‘If I get the ball, I’m shooting.’ When they passed it down to Julia [Montes], I called for the ball and then the ball worked to Annika [Nilsson], then she passed it to me. I saw space between my defender and I knew it was the time to shoot it,” said Melian of the game-winner. It was a big game for goalie Friedie Schickedanz in Saturday’s match against the Yellowjackets, recording 11 saves on the day including three pivotal stops in overtime. “Starting out, they were shooting a lot of lobs, which have been difficult for me. They scored a bunch early, but I try to reset mentally every quarter. We switched our defense and it worked well. That helped me dial in for the rest of the game,” said Schickedanz. PHS had to battle back from a 4-1 deficit at the end of the first quarter and 7-5 disadvantage to start the fourth. “I think the main thing that brought us the win was our teamwork and our spirit. Even when we were down, everyone kept playing hard and no one gave up. We worked really well as a team just communicating,” said Melian. Piedmont concludes its season with an 8-11 overall record and watches seniors like Rosie Feldman, Odessa Dando, Annika Nilsson, Macie Gard, and Molly Ashton depart. PHS will have considerable players returning like leading scorer Melian, Schickedanz in goal, Sonja ten Grotenhuis, Kate Keyjes, Vivian Burke, Sydney Olson, Julia Montes, Sage Gilbert, and Alicia Bernales. 13-12 over Berkeley Gard scored the first goal of the game after just 15 seconds in the first quarter, but Berkeley went on to score four unanswered goals to lead 4-1 to start the second. In the second, Melian scored the second goal 30 seconds into the quarter. After a save by Schickedanz, Nilsson assisted Melian for a goal at 5:16. Berkeley then scored with 4:51 to go and the two sides traded possessions, including two saves by Schickedanz before #7 assisted Melian for a goal at 2:21. With just four seconds left in the half Melian scored again to make it 5-5 going at halftime. In the third quarter, Berkeley scored twice at the 4:10 and 3:07 marks to jump ahead 7-5 while PHS was unable to get on the board. The Yellowjackets scored two more unanswered goals in the fourth quarter to lead 9-5 with 6:13 to play, but that’s when the comeback started. From there, Gard scored on an assist by Nilsson with five minutes on the clock. After two minutes, Melian scored on a rocket from distance to make it 9-7. Melian scored once more on a five-meter penalty shot with 1:59 on the clock, and then Melian assisted Gard to tie the match 9-9 with 1:20 remaining. Berkeley regained the lead 13 seconds later, but with 38 seconds left in the fourth, Feldman assisted Gard to make it 10-10. After that, Schickedanz had a big save with 30 seconds left while Gard nearly won the game with seven seconds left, but her shot rang off of the post. In the first of two 3-minute overtime periods, Dando had a steal and breakaway goal with 2:20 left to give PHS its first lead of the game. After a pair of penalty stops by Berkeley, Gard scored on an assist by Meyjes with 1:39 remaining. Berkeley cut the deficit to 12-11 with 40 seconds remaining, while Schickedanz thwarted a pair of shots in the final five seconds. Into the second overtime period, Nilsson had a shot attempt stopped with 1:55 left but Berkeley was able to score in a 6-on-5 opportunity with 1:01 remaining. After back-and-forth possessions, the two sides finished 12-12. In the third sudden-death period, Piedmont stopped the opening possession by Berkeley and turned the ball up-pool. Julian Montes had the ball on the lower wing and worked it to Nilsson, who sent a pass to Melian to fire the game-winning score. Final stats: Melian finished with seven goals, Gard had five goals, Dando had one. Schickedanz had 11 saves on the day. 19-4 over Lick-Wilmerding Piedmont led 6-1 by the end of the first quarter and 11-3 by halftime. PHS scored twice in the third to lead 13-4 and closed out with five goals in the fourth, 18-4. Final scorers include Melian and Gilbert with three goals. Gard, Feldman, Burke, Dando, and Meyjes scored twice. Nilsson, Anne Reardon, and Mary Schickedanz had individual goals. 13-5 loss to Castro Valley Against Castro Valley, Piedmont briefly held a 2-1 and 3-2 lead in the first quarter, but only scored twice in the final three quarters. CV tied 3-3 to start the second and lead 5-4 at the half. In the third, the Trojans went ahead 9-5 to start the fourth and added four more in the final going. Final scorers include Melian with four goals and ten Grotenhuis with one. Katarina Melian had seven goals including the gamewinner against Berkeley. Goalie Friedie Schickedanz had 11 saves against Berkeley.
articles.title: Girls water polo team rallies to win 5th in league tourney

articles.text: Piedmont team now accepting new riders In the spirit of building community, Piedmont Mountain Bike Team recently gave four of its older loaner bikes to Skyline High School in an effort to help invigorate the Oakland school’s new program. “We have many riders of color who needed bikes in the Skyline High School bike club this year. We’re thrilled to partner with the Piedmont team and give new life to these bikes. We’re getting our program off the ground and it was great to get support from an established team,” said Skyline HS head coach Jen Ryden. In addition, the co-ed Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is currently recruiting new riders for the upcoming spring season. The team practices on local trails and competes in the spring semester against other East Bay high schools in the Norcal Mountain Bike League between December and May. Piedmont MTB has two “Fun Rides” planned in the upcoming weeks at Oakland’s Joaquin Miller Park on two consecutive Sundays, November 6 and November 13. Rides are designed to be inclusive and open to anyone. There are no registration requirements prior to the start of the racing season. Interested riders can email Piedmont MTB at Piedmontbiking@gmail.com. For more information, visit www.piedmontmtb. com. Jonathan Carmona, Skyline High School junior riding a bike donated ny the Piedmont Mountain Bike team. Piedmont’s Jasper Schuetz competes in an earlier race.
articles.title: PHS Mountain Bike Team donates bikes to Skyline riders

articles.text: November is here, which means Turkey day is right around the corner! If you are planning to do the Piedmont Turkey Trot, it’s time to really lace up those shoes and get in some runs before the big race on Thanksgiving morning. This week, plan to run two days of easy running using the walk/run approach and then add in a hill workout. This hill workout is specific for the last .2 mile of the race, a very sneaky hill placed right before the finish line. Do a short warm up jog (5-10 minutes) over to the Magnolia Ave and Hillside Ave intersection. Once you feel nice and warmed up, run up Magnolia Ave to Highland at a speedy pace, stop and walk back down the hill. You will repeat this a total of four times. These should be all-out sprints, as hard as you can run without stopping. This is a good time to start visualizing race day and how good it will feel to finish fast up that last stretch of the course on race day. Staff photo More than 2200 runners sped down Highland Avenue on Thanksgiving morning 2021 at the start of the annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, a 5-kilometer run along city streets. WEEK DAY WORKOUT November 7 Monday Run 6 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 6x Add 5 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 5x Wednesday Run 4 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x Saturday Hill workout: 5 min jog warm up 4 x run up Magnolia Ave (Start at Hillside, run to Highland) Walk down hill between reps 5 min jog cool down
articles.title: Training for hills in Turkey Trot

articles.text: Piedmont High sophomore Mei Assalian had a strong performance at the 2022 North Coast Section championship tournament on Monday, October 24 at the Rooster Run Golf Club in Petaluma, finishing 30th of 120 golfers with an 18-hole round of 92 strokes. “Mei earning her way to NCS should be exalted around school and in the community. Mei’s a player, the moment is never too big for her,” said coach Howard Oliver proudly. “She enjoys the game for the right reasons. In reaching NCS, she sees what she can aspire to if she chooses.” Assalian, a sophomore standout, was named a team captain before the start of the season and frequently was the team’s low medalist. She qualified for the prestigious tournament by finishing eighth at the WACC Tournament at Monarch Bay on Monday, October 17. The Rooster Run course is characterized by long fairways on a collection of par-four and par-five holes, along with difficult greens that are fast and sloping, Assalian had a solid round off of the tee to hit the fairways and focused on having a productive approach on the greens. “I try to play safe, straight shots. Most of my play off of the tee got onto the fairway… One thing that was really challenging were the greens due to the slopes, so even the short puts were really difficult,” said Assalian. Mei Assalian finished with an 18-hole score of 92 strokes at NCS. Mei Assalian, a sophomore, finished 30th of 120 at the North Coast Section Championship Tournament at Rooster Run Golf Club in Petaluma. She was able to convert a birdie opportunity on the par-four 16th hole, using an eight iron on her approach shot. “One of my better holes was on the 16th. I hit a good drive and used my eight iron to get onto the green,” described Assalian. To prepare for the tournament, Assalian traveled to Petaluma one day early to get a feel of what was ahead of her. “My dad and I played there the day before. I got to know the course; I didn’t know anything about it before, so it helped me understand the angles to take and how to approach different holes,” said Assalian. League Tournament As for her day at the WACC Tournament, Piedmont competed at Monarch Bay on multiple occasions throughout the season, giving her a good familiarity with the course. They played two rounds on the nine-hole course, where she shot a collective score of 74. “We played the course twice. I think playing it the second time went a lot better, I shot a 40 and then a 34. I think going over the second time helped with my tee shots and knowing what to do,” said Assalian. “I feel like I know how to visualize better, I think that helped me a lot. After a bad hole, I began visualizing how to do better shots. I just need to keep getting out and playing,” said Assalian.
articles.title: Piedmont golfer Assalian finishes 30th of 120 at NCS

articles.text: Rugby. Fast paced, muddy, physical. Great long-sleeve shirts. A ball that resembles an American football but is bigger, and is thrown backwards. The kind of sport that builds physical strength and character in men and women the world over. You may think about countries like England, Scotland, Wales, Ireland, South Africa, France, New Zealand, Samoa, Australia, as the centers of the sport. With its growing popularity in America and in Northern California, rugby is one of the fastest growing youth, amateur and professional sports. It attracts thousands of kids and young adults from middle school through high school, college and beyond. No regional youth rugby club demonstrates this growing trend toward the high energy sport more than Lamorinda Rugby Club, drawing players from throughout the East Bay. The sport is becoming so popular that the U.S. has won the bid to host the Men’s 2031 World Cup and the Women’s 2033 World Cup, gaining support from President Biden in April 2022 and winning the bid in May from the World Rugby governing body. This is an exciting time for the sport. Two of America’s leading universities offering college level rugby for both men and women are both local – St Mary’s College in Moraga and University of California in Berkeley. The current Division 1A rankings for men’s rugby in 2021 had Cal Berkeley at #1 and St Mary’s at #2. The Lamorinda Rugby Club has a long history in the area. The program started in 1980 by Pat Vincent, a former captain of the New Zealand All Blacks rugby team, first as a high-school-only team through 2001. Then, due to Tommy Ashton is one of the Piedmont players with the Lamorinda Rugby Club. the demand in the area, and the need to prepare young athletes to compete at a high level, teams of younger players were formed. The Lamorinda Rugby club now has teams for boys and girls starting at the U8 level. High School Director of Rugby Tom Lee says, “Touring and travelling as a rugby team provides some amazing benefits for the players. Obviously, team-bonding and camaraderie, but it also provides skills for life: commitment, leadership and self-reliance. Above all, though, it’s fun.” This season, the high school boys team plans to travel to Portugal and Spain during Spring Break to compete in a youth tournament with teams from Europe. The resumption of international travel after two years of lockdown due to Covid means rugby life is returning to normal. Registration for the 2022-2023 season is underway. More information can be found at https:// lamorugby.sportngin.com/register/form/625128496 Check out the Club’s “Open Days,” a great opportunity for experienced players to continue developing their skills and for new players to try out the sport. Open Days are scheduled for November 5, 12 and 19 from 10 a.m. to 12 noon at the Orinda Sports Field. Those interested can contact admin@lamorugby. com for details.
articles.title: Lamorinda Rugby – fast, physical and open to all

articles.text: Olafur Eliasson’s “One Way Color Tunnel”, 2007, at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. Contemporary Optics is currently on view at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) through December 11. Featuring the work of three artists – Olafur Eliasson, Teresita Fernández, and Anish Kapoor – the exhibition expands on color theory developed by painters in the 1960s. The artists use color and light in sculpture – the most widely-recognized is Eliasson’s “One Way Color Tunnel,” (2007) a 34-footlong colorful archway that mimics a kaleidoscope. “Eliasson’s practice is driven by research on human perception and behavior,” said SFMOMA Curatorial Assistant Sara Wessen Chang. “The sculptures actively engage the viewer in a sensory experience—triggering a heightened state of awareness and responsibility with regards to our surroundings, specifically the climate.” To see more, visit https://www. sfmoma.org/exhibition/contemporary-optics/.

articles.text: Youth Musical Theater Company (YMTC) opens its 18th season with Matilda the Musical, with performances November 4–13 at the Malonga Casquelourd Center for the Arts in downtown Oakland. Roald Dahl’s beloved story of an extraordinary little girl is brought to dazzling, high-energy, and hilarious life in Matilda the Musical. Overlooked and unloved by her parents and bullied at school by the cruel Headmistress Trunchbull, 6-year-old genius Matilda finds solace in stories – in the pages of the books she devours and the tales that come tumbling out of her mind. With the help of a vivid imagination, her kind teacher Miss Honey, and an army of rebellious schoolchildren, Matilda decides to change her own story and rewrite her destiny. Matilda the Musical pays perfect tribute to the absurd humor and profound heart of Roald Dahl’s original story. The book was written by internationally acclaimed playwright Dennis Kelly, and the music and lyrics by Tim Minchin (Groundhog Day the Musical). Matilda premiered in the UK in 2011 and on Broadway in 2013, winning Dahlia Saffouri of Piedmont is in the YMTC production of Matilda. Addison Au performs the lead role of Matilda in the show of the same name by Youth Musical Theater Company. five Tony Awards, as well as more than 50 international awards, including the Olivier for Best New Musical. The show features a cast of 26 student performers and five apprentices (ages 12–18) from cities throughout the Bay Area. Dahlia Saffouri, a 10th grader at Piedmont High School, plays the role of a “Big Kid” and is the understudy for Mrs. Wormwood. They are led by a team of professional directors, designers, and musicians, including Directors Jennifer Boesing and Celeste Kamiya, Music Directors Diana Lee and Eric Walton, and Choreographer Nicole Helfer. The production features an 11-piece orchestra playing the original musical score. Matilda opens Friday November 4, with 7:30 p.m. performances on November 4-5 and November 11-12. Two matinee performances at 2 p.m. are scheduled for Sundays on November 6 and 13. Tickets are available online at www.ymtcbayarea.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Ticket prices are $16– $34, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. YMTC history YMTC is dedicated to providing exceptional training to young theater artists through the production of exceptional musical theater. The organization brings together the Bay Area’s most talented and dedicated young performers – as well as students of technical theater – with professional directors, designers, choreographers and musicians. They take on challenging and sophisticated musical and dramatic themes. Productions are always accompanied by a full, live orchestra. YMTC takes young artists on adventures that will inspire them for the rest of their lives.
articles.title: YMTC to present Matilda the Musical November 4-13

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s production of Giuseppe Verdi’s masterpiece La Traviata opens on Friday, November 11. Music Director Eun Sun Kim leads the Opera Orchestra and chorus in Shawna Lucey’s production of the three-act opera. La Traviata casts South African-born Pretty Yende as protagonist Violetta Valéry. Yende has appeared in the same role in the Vienna State Opera, Naples’ Teatro di San Carlo, Royal Opera, Paris Opera productions. Jonathan Tetelman is cast as Alfredo Germont, a young bourgeois from a provincial family who admires Violetta from afar. The opera is set to an Italian libretto by Francesco Piave, and is based on a play by Alexandre Dumas. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfopera.com/operas/ la-traviata/.

articles.text: Review by Jaime Robles In front of the stage’s black curtain a man rings a bell. He continues to ring, calling onto the stage 10 dancers, similarly dressed in black. Then the curtain opens and the dancers cluster, seething darkly into groups, only their faces, bare feet, hands and arms reflecting the dim light of Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. Thus begins Cloud Gate Dance Theatre of Taiwan’s performance, the second of Cal Performances’ dance programs for the 2022–23 season. The program, 13 Tongues, was choreographed by the company’s current artistic director, Tsung-lung Cheng. Cheng took his inspiration from the neighborhood where he grew up, Bangha, Wanhua, in Taipei. There he sold slippers as a child, navigating the chaotic streets of Taipei’s oldest district. Cloud Gate Dance Theatre, which began in 1973 under the direction of choreographer Hwaimin Lin, takes its name from the oldest dance form known in China, but the company was the first modern dance company in Taiwan and Asia. As contemporary dance, the group’s choreography is firmly based in Asian movement, both the indigenous forms of dance and martial arts. And, as the opening bell-ringing suggested, there is much of mediation and worship in their dance. There are also suggestions of ballet and Western modern dance, but the spirit of Asian movement predominates and energizes. Although Giong Lim’s electronic music accompanies much of “13 Tongues,” the music is primarily made by the dancers as they stomp, yell, scream and vocalize. Occasionally folk songs break through, melodic and choral, or the hum of Taoist chants. The use of the dancers’ voices reminded me of Jackie Chan fight scenes. Chan’s tightly choreographed fights are full of groans, cries and shouts. Though it sounds simply like random noises, the grunts and groans are a language, telling the fighters where each of them is, how close they are and what move will be made next. It’s fair to say that 13 Tongues is similar in visual effect as well. The dance is built around chaos, its unloosening and its reigning in. Chaos to order, order to chaos, chaos to order. There are comic moments and terrifying ones. These transitions are also notable in the use of color. The performance begins in darkness, with the dancers dressed in black tunics and baggy black pants, a few exposed bare arms here and there. The skin of faces and bare feet and hands becomes brighter as the lighting increases. Only the energy of the dancers’ bodies and their emphatic cries draws in the viewer. With the slow entrance of abstract green projections on the upstage scrim, the world of 13 Tongues takes on color, moving toward the bright and geometric, and more clearly defining the dancers. Then the goddess appears among them, dressed in bright fluorescent colors. She is exalted, the black-clad dancers lifting her upwards, and seemingly she floats across the stage. She removes her robes, and they are coveted by everyone, taking on a life of their own. Eventually everyone is covered in bright fluorescent colors. And the luminous skin of bare hands, feet and faces is increased by a bare chest here and there wrapped and accented by pinks, greens, yellows and reds. But these colors are oddly subterranean. The use of blacklight to set the colors glowing in the dark gives a slightly psychedelic spin to the dance, as if these figures were threads escaping from the obscure brocade of the collective unconscious. Special kudos to projections designer Ethan Wang. In the midst of this landscape of dynamic movement an enormous orange and silver koi languidly swam across the surfaces of the stage, passing through and over the clusters of black figures. The designers wisely chose to end the piece with the fish reappearing for a final lap across the stage, calmly swimming upward toward the heavens. Coming soon Cal Performances’ next dance performance is by New York– based choreographer, dancer and director Camille A. Brown, who returns with ink, the final installment of her dance trilogy on December 14-16. For information and tickets, visit calperformances.org.
articles.title: Cloud Gate Dance Theatre of Taiwan comes to Berkeley

articles.text: Oakland Symphony will present a special program entitled “Psalms by Bernstein” at the Paramount Theater in downtown Oakland on Friday, November 4. The program includes Mary Lou Williams’ Zodiac Suite, Erich Korngold’s Much Ado About Nothing Suite, and Leonard Bernstein’s Chichester Psalms. Holly Hyun Choe will be the guest conductor. John Kendall Bailey will give a pre-concert talk from the stage beginning at 7 p.m. The concert begins at 8 p.m. For tickets, visit https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/event/ psalms-by-bernstein/.

articles.text: Revelations of the liquid kind. Are you a gourmet or a gourmand? Most of us enjoy good food. That is the gourmand in us. But there is more to life than just eating well. This was clearly demonstrated to me a few years ago when I was invited to a banquet. It was a multi-course affair with every plate selected with great care. Each course was paired with a wine designed to bring out the best. All of the diners were advised to take a bite of the first course and then sip the accompanying wine. The flavor literally exploded in our mouths. What a revelation it was. Just recently I attended a class on the enjoyment of wine. The expert told us that it is better not to drink the wine but to enjoy it in other ways. He suggested that we conjure up a vocabulary to describe the wines. In wine appreciation the nose is the best sense we have, followed by the taste buds. Our instructor told us that there are no taste buds in the throat, so don’t swallow the wine. The eyes play an important part also. The first wine we sampled was from Hungary. The person next to me was a Hungarian, who observed that the wine had the color of Tokay. Soon after that, our instructor said the very same thing. The next thing we were told to do was to use our nose to breathe the wine in deeply and conjure up descriptive words. My uneducated pallet sensed citrus overtones. I was right. Our instructor used the word “linden” which is the German word for lime. A person nearby was a recovering alcoholic, but he was an enthusiastic participant. He sniffed every wine, but the wine did not touch his lips… Ever. A sensational discovery Almost 100 years ago the tomb of king Tut was discovered by Howard Carter. The date was November 4, 1922. The discovery spawned every sort of Egyptology. You can get yourself in the mood by listening to Ballet Egyptian by Luigini, selections from Aida, or Africa by St-Saens. Chamber music at Piedmont Center for the Arts The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco presented its 10th anniversary concert in Piedmont on Sunday afternoon. They showcased one of the pieces they played in their very first concert in 2012, the monumental Beethoven String Quartet Op. 132. But there were other musical pieces to admire. To begin the concert, the quartet performed a new composition by Carolyn Shaw entitled Valencia. The composer has a unique way of looking at things. Her composition was about the Valencia orange not the city in Spain. It embraced every aspect of the orange from planting to eating. It was colorful, flavorful, piquant, with zesty eruptions of juicy chords. There was even a dark section where I envisioned a chef broiling the orange. Mozart’s unique “Dissonant” quartet came next, and then the Beethoven quartet brought the concert to a conclusion. The chamber music Society of San Francisco plays with incredible technical bravado. It can become intoxicating in its perfection. Their ensemble is tight. The word “perfection” comes to mind as I listened in amazement. But then I began to think that in the headlong zeal to play all the notes perfectly, other aspects of music can suffer, with nuance, dynamics and tone color neglected. I remember reading a book on the interpretation of music. The author was a noted scholar. He warned his readers not to delude themselves. Dynamics, when used wisely, create sensational musical effects. I urge readers to listen to the great cellist of yesteryear, Ennio Bolognini, playing his own composition the Echo Serenade. His dynamics were achieved through genuine artistry. They were not done by somebody twisting the knobs in the control booth. I heard him play this piece in person when I studied with him. As a final thought, I also realize how lucky we are to have the Piedmont Center for the Arts. There is no better place than the PCA to enjoy chamber music. In general, it would be nice to see young folks attending concerts. Do teachers in the schools require their music students to attend concerts? In my day, students were required to attend concerts. They were also encouraged to write reviews. It was part of their grade. A city of culture An orchestra legitimizes a city. Piedmont has its own Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, which will present a gala concert this Sunday, November 6 at 4 p.m. in the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. As one of the performers, I invite all of you to attend… And please bring the kids. A generous underwriter stepped forward recently, and the concert will be free for everyone.
articles.title: Living the good life

articles.text: As reliable as the swallows returning each year to San Juan Capistrano, A Christmas Carol returns to San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater (ACT) with performances from November 30 to December 24. The play is based on Charles Dickens’ famous story that captures the zeitgeist of the mid-Victorian era, with main character Ebenezer Scrooge at its center. Dickens’ novella has been recounted onstage and in film for nearly 100 years. ACT’s production is adapted by Carey Perloff and Paul Walsh and directed by Peter Kuo, with music scored by Karl Lundenberg and choregraphy by Val Caniparoli. A Christmas Carol has been included in ACT’s repertory for decades. Performances will take place at its theater at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco, recently named the Toni Rembe Theater. For tickets. visit https://www. act-sf.org/whats-on/202223-season/christmas-carol/. Cast members of a past production of A Christmas Carol by American Conservatory Theatre.
articles.title: A Christmas Carol returns to ACT on November 30

The featured soloist is pianist Aaron Diehl, who appeared in the New York Philharmonic’s online presentation of “An All-American Program” and in selections from the chamber-orchestra version of the Zodiac Suite. John Kendall Bailey will give a pre-concert talk from the stage beginning at 7 p.m. The concert begins at 8 p.m. For tickets, visit https://www. oaklandsymphony.org/event/ psalms-by-bernstein/. Living the good life By Joseph Gold Revelations of the liquid kind. Are you a gourmet or a gourmand? Most of us enjoy good food. That is the gourmand in us. But there is more to life than just eating well. This was clearly demonstrated to me a few years ago when I was invited to a banquet. It was a multi-course affair with every plate selected with great care. Each course was paired with a wine designed to bring out the best. All of the diners were advised to take a bite of the first course and then sip the accompanying wine. The flavor literally exploded in our mouths. What a revelation it was. Just recently I attended a class on the enjoyment of wine. The expert told us that it is better not to drink the wine but to enjoy it in other ways. He suggested that we conjure up a vocabulary to describe the wines. In wine appreciation the nose is the best sense we have, followed by the taste buds. Our instructor told us that there are no taste buds in the throat, so don’t swallow the wine. The eyes play an important part also. The first wine we sampled was from Hungary. The person next to me was a Hungarian, who observed that the wine had the color of Tokay. Soon after that, our instructor said the very same thing. The next thing we were told to do was to use our nose to breathe the wine in deeply and conjure up descriptive words. My uneducated pallet sensed citrus overtones. I was right. Our instructor used the word “linden” which is the German word for lime. A person nearby was a recovering alcoholic, but he was an enthusiastic participant. He sniffed every wine, but the wine did not touch his lips… Ever. A sensational discovery Almost 100 years ago the tomb of king Tut was discovered by Howard Carter. The date was November 4, 1922. The discovery spawned every sort of Egyptology. You can get yourself in the mood by listening to Ballet Egyptian by Luigini, selections from Aida, or Africa by St-Saens. Chamber music at Piedmont Center for the Arts The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco presented its 10th anniversary concert in Piedmont on Sunday afternoon. They showcased one of the pieces they played in their very first concert in 2012, the monumental Beethoven String Quartet Op. 132. But there were other musical pieces to admire. To begin the concert, the quartet performed a new composition by Carolyn Shaw entitled Valencia. The composer has a unique way of looking at things. Her composition was about the Valencia orange not the city in Spain. It embraced every aspect of the orange from planting to eating. It was colorful, flavorful, piquant, with zesty eruptions of juicy chords. There was even a dark section where I envisioned a chef broiling the orange. Mozart’s unique “Dissonant” quartet came next, and then the Beethoven quartet brought the concert to a conclusion. The chamber music Society of San Francisco plays with incredible technical bravado. It can become intoxicating in its perfection. Their ensemble is tight. The word “perfection” comes to mind as I listened in amazement. But then I began to think that in the headlong zeal to play all the notes perfectly, other aspects of music can suffer, with nuance, dynamics and tone color neglected. I remember reading a book on the interpretation of music. The author was a noted scholar. He warned his readers not to delude themselves. Dynamics, when used wisely, create sensational musical effects. I urge readers to listen to the great cellist of yesteryear, Ennio Bolognini, playing his own composition the Echo Serenade. His dynamics were achieved through genuine artistry. They were not done by somebody twisting the knobs in the control booth. I heard him play this piece in person when I studied with him. As a final thought, I also realize how lucky we are to have the Piedmont Center for the Arts. There is no better place than the PCA to enjoy chamber music. In general, it would be nice to see young folks attending concerts. Do teachers in the schools require their music students to attend concerts? In my day, students were required to attend concerts. They were also encouraged to write reviews. It was part of their grade. A city of culture An orchestra legitimizes a city. Piedmont has its own Piedmont Chamber Orchestra, which will present a gala concert this Sunday, November 6 at 4 p.m. in the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. As one of the performers, I invite all of you to attend… And please bring the kids. A generous underwriter stepped forward recently, and the concert will be free for everyone. Oakland Symphony’s guest soloist on November 4 is pianist Aaron Diehl. A Christmas Carol returns to ACT on November 30 By Allyson Aleksey As reliable as the swallows returning each year to San Juan Capistrano, A Christmas Carol returns to San Francisco’s American Conservatory Theater (ACT) with performances from November 30 to December 24. The play is based on Charles Dickens’ famous story that captures the zeitgeist of the mid-Victorian era, with main character Ebenezer Scrooge at its center. Dickens’ novella has been recounted onstage and in film for nearly 100 years. ACT’s production is adapted by Carey Perloff and Paul Walsh and directed by Peter Kuo, with music scored by Karl Lundenberg and choregraphy by Val Caniparoli. A Christmas Carol has been included in ACT’s repertory for decades. Performances will take place at its theater at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco, recently named the Toni Rembe Theater. For tickets. visit https://www. act-sf.org/whats-on/202223-season/christmas-carol/. Cast members of a past production of A Christmas Carol by American Conservatory Theatre. Tickets are now available for both performances. Oakland Ballet dancers bring the holiday classic to life with magnificent scenery and costumes. The Oakland Symphony and Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will perform Tchaikovsky’s magnificent score. The performance is approximately two hours including intermission. Doors open one hour before showtime. An encore reception at the Paramount will take place following both performances. Tickets are now available for 1 p.m. performances on Saturday and Sunday, December 17 and 18. To purchase tickets, visit https:// oaklandballet.org/performances-events/graham-lustigs-the-nutcracker/. The Nutcracker, performed by Oakland Ballet, returns to Paramount Theatre in Oakland next month.

articles.text: The California Society of Printmakers will be celebrating its 108th anniversary with an exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, opening Sunday, November 6. An artists’ reception will be held on Friday November 11, from 6:00 to 9:00 p.m. The exhibition features the work of more than 80 printmakers and highlights a wide variety of printmaking techniques, including serigraphs, monotypes, lithographs, etchings, woodcuts, and aquatints. The talented artists represent CSP members from throughout California. Some examples of the myriad of forms of printmaking include Oakland artist Luz Marina Ruiz, whose work is a handmade artist Tunnel Book. Within the three-dimensional work, Luz incorporates linocuts embellished with watercolor and gouache on BFK paper. Another artist, Toru Sugita from Albany, depicts the changing or transitional monuments of the Bay Area using his own photographs and sketches of his surroundings to capture these spaces and textures through screen printing. Alicia Persaud, from Santa Cruz, also creates work influenced by their environment. In her work on display she uses photo-intaglio with digital chine collé, to generate both sharp and blurred qualities layered together. Toru Sugita, Bridge Composit, Screen print, 11.5” x 17”, 2022 She describes her process as, “depicting movement and motion of my memories both aesthetically through the imagery as well as emotionally through the physicality of the photo intaglio-process itself, highlighting how memories often blend together and change over time”. Some printmakers like Katherine Levin Lau from San Jose create images by hand painting on a zinc plate and then running the piece through the press many times. In Katherine’s detailed and dreamy scenes of nature, the original paintings are monochromatic. She enhances them with color layers using viscosity techniques. A final example of the breadth of techniques that will be on view is a work from Los Angeles artist Roxanne Sexauer, who utilizes a combination of printing methods including relief, monoserigraph, stencil, and chine collé to develop rich layers of abstract images. Only a small sampling of the unique work has been described here. To see these and more than 80 other visually compelling prints, visit the display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue at the corner of Bonta Avenue. The exhibit will be on view Saturdays and Sundays from November 6 to November 27. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. For more information visit http://www. piedmontcenterforthearts.org/ or http://www.caprintmakers.org/.

articles.text: Come enjoy the many music events in the next month, and stay for an art exhibit. Saturday, November 5, 5:00 p.m. Ambroš Duo concert The Ambroš Duo, a renowned mother-son music duo from the capital city of Prague in the Czech Republic will perform a concert featuring works by Mozart, Sarasate, and Czech composers Dvořák and Smetana, among others. The concert will conclude with the lively “Monti Czardas.” A light reception to meet the artists follows. This concert is co-sponsored by the Czech and Slovak cultural associations Sokol San Francisco, BayCzech and the Czech School of California. Tickets are $20, at https://bit. ly/3yO9i9t. Sunday, November 6, 11 a.m.–2:30 p.m. Opening of CA Printmakers exhibit The California Society of Printmakers returns for their 108th anniversary exhibition, a show that will include more than 80 works by members of the of the oldest continually operating association of printmakers in the United States. CSP is a non-profit arts organization with an international membership of print artists and supporters of the art of fine printmaking. The show will be open to the public on Saturdays and Sundays through November 27, from 11 a.m.–2:30 p.m. Free. There will be an opening reception on Friday, November 11 from 6 to 9 p.m. Sunday, November 6, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Piedmont’s own orchestra presents a varied and unusual program for its Fall concert, conducted by Sue Crum and Martha Stoddard. The rarely heard Overture to Johann Albrecht’s comedy Der Teufel als Hydraulicus, composed by Franz Schubert at age 14, opens the concert, followed by Béla Bartók’s delightful Romanian Folk Dances. Concertmaster Joseph Gold will perform Ferdinand the Bull, a lighthearted piece based on Munro Leaf’s children’s story. The guest narrator is Peidmontn City Council member Betsy Andersen. The concludes with Mozart’s orchestral masterpiece, Symphony No. 40 in G minor. Thanks to an anonymous underwriter, the concert is being offered free to the public. Doors open at 3:30 p.m. Saturday, November 12, 5:00 p.m. SF Mandolin Orchestra San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra begins its 2022 concert season with Anticipation, a concert featuring music by Beethoven, Erik Satie, and the orchestra’s conductor, Achille Bocus. A plucked string orchestra with 15-25 members will play instruments of the mandolin family (mandolin, mandola and mandocello), as well as guitar, viola da gamba and double bass. Their musicianship and style have pleased PCA audiences many times. Tickets are $20 General and $15 for students and seniors and are available at the door and online at https://sfmandolin.square.site/. Sunday, November 13, 4:00 p.m. (new start time) In the Tradition Piano Trio In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Rich Trevor, and Anthony Pegram – will perform a concert paying tribute to Duke Ellington, known as the greatest jazz composer and bandleader of his time. One of the originators of big-band jazz, he led his band for more than 50 years, composing thousands of scores. The concert is a benefit for the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, showcasing the magnificent Steinway grand piano. Tickets $20 at the door, or at https://bpt.me/5316993. Seating limited to the first 70. Saturday, November 19, 6:30 p.m. Healing Muses Benefit Concert The professional musicians of Healing Muses provide live, therapeutic harp music to support patient care & recovery in hospitals, hospices, cancer wards, & children’s palliative care centers throughout the Bay Area. This event includes music from Dublin to Dubrovnik, with Shira Kammen, Patrice Haan, and Margaret Davis on harp, Marla Fibish on mandolin, Kristoph Klover and Tony Marcus on guitar. All proceeds support their musical programs as above. A wine reception and silent auction will take place at 6:30 p.m. one hour before the start of the concert. For tickets and additional information, go to www.TicketStripe.com/ HealingMuses.

articles.text: Photo courtesy Danae Mattes and Christel Dillbohner. Sylvia Brownrigg reads in front of imagery by Danae Mattes and Christel Dillbohner from the performance “Lightfast” at the Museum of Craft and Design in San Francisco. Cellist Monica Scott was the instrumentalist in this four-woman collaboration of multimedia performance and installation. Review by Jaime Robles Theater, with its melding of text, performance, music and dance, has long depended on collaboration, but among artists working in forms that are most often practiced separately and individually collaboration takes on a very personal dimension. And its relationship to the audience is also less formal and more approachable. Lightfast, a multimedia performance and installation at the wonderful Museum of Design and Art in San Francisco, explores the realm of collaboration between artists. The result was a performance that was intimate, multi-faceted and elegant. The four artists behind Lightfast are novelist and short story writer Sylvia Brownrigg, cellist Monica Scott, and visual artists Christel Dillbohner and Danae Mattes. Beginning in 2020 the four women began conversing and collecting the images – musical, verbal and visual – that they ultimately shaped into last weekend’s performance. The program to Lightfast lists the elements of the piece, which can be thought of as movements, or facets, of a coherent and blended portrait of the world shared by the four collaborators. The space Lightfast inhabited at the museum was a large rectangular room, with chairs for an audience of about 50 viewers placed in rows along one of the long sides of the room. Two sets of deciduous tree branches were suspended in diagonal corners of the room. The branches looked like they had been dipped in thick pale gray paint. The lights above them caused their shadows to fall in soft blurry pink and greenish traceries across the white walls. The performance began with the entrance of the cellist. Scott placed herself and her instrument inside a gauzy cone of white mosquito netting that cascaded to the floor in front and to the right of the wall to the audience’s left. As the deep sounds of the cello resonated in the gallery space, a film of waves on sand plays was projected across most of the wall behind her. These were not the large rolling waves of surf, but waves after they have broken and become a simpler sheen of water over sand, expanding and retracting like breath. This imagery assembled by visual artists Dillbohner and Mattes was overlaid with other less distinct patterns of grays and lights, giving the play of water an abstract and dreamlike quality. Within the pale netting, the cellist became a ghostly figure, blurred and indistinct like the light on the waves. Like most of the imagery used in Lightfast, the colors used in the two films and a later series of projected stills were muted, as close to grays as possible. The deep sounds of the cello anchored the figure and images. Later in the performance the images shifted to another wall, the waves replaced by organic forms that were familiar but not clearly recognizable. Trees, grasses. A woman’s body appearing, disappearing, and reappearing seemed to float among the layered images. No story was told, instead emotions were evoked. There was no need for explanation of the beauty of the imagery or the sounds of the music. Instead, they formed an environment that was tender, meditative and nuanced. Into this shadowy and palely abstract world walked writer Brownrigg. In four monologues spaced in between shifting abstractions of music and image, she talked about the mysteries of family and the life on our green and blue planet. She talked about light and dark and silence: “It is not that the shadow knows, it is that the shadow speaks.” And finally, she talked about following a path, a trail where children, adults and elders walk, through a forest, across dry river bed of leaves, accompanied by the music of heat and insects. The museum’s space favored the cello over the spoken voice, but even so, the human voice has a music of its own, its words composed of a palette of sounds that, like the projected images, is subtle and serene. All performance is ephemeral, disappearing even as we watch. However, Lightfast has been recreated in book form, both as a large-format artists’ book and as a chapbook. Videos from the performance can be found on YouTube at https://m.youtube. com/playlist?list=PLHvdJYFqI- 4Ve3kLVy3Jo48GAjq6bqRYnj
articles.title: Lightfast creates a world of beautiful shadows

articles.text: Visit the Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside throughout the month to see the 16-acre estate illuminated for the holidays. The non-profit and historical landmark will be celebrating “Holidays at Filoli” through January 2. An impressive myriad of decorations and over a dozen festooned Christmas trees enhances the estate’s historic and renowned elegance. Filoli has a designated holiday decor team responsible for installing decorations inside and outside the mansion and miles upon miles of string lights that drape the interior. Last year Filoli installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreates the original holiday placement that is indicative of Agnes and William Bourn, the house’s first residents. The Bourns decorated with natural materials from the gardens, including pinecones and evergreen wreaths. Realistic artificial trees and garlands were not yet available in the early to mid- 1900s. More original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene, one of her favorites, is displayed in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively in the daylight. Daytime admission provides access to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. To learn more about “Holidays at Filoli” and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/events/holidays/. Filoli House and Garden will begin its holiday festivities on November 19.
articles.title: Holiday festivities at Filoli begin November 19

All performance is ephemeral, disappearing even as we watch. However, Lightfast has been recreated in book form, both as a large-format artists’ book and as a chapbook. Videos from the performance can be found on YouTube at https://m.youtube. com/playlist?list=PLHvdJYFqI- 4Ve3kLVy3Jo48GAjq6bqRYnj
