articles.text: Members of the Cancer League, Inc. gathered at the home of Lisa Settlemier, its president, to assemble invitations for the 49th annual Holly Ball celebration on December 2. The Cancer League, a local nonprofit that funds groundbreaking research in cancer’s early stages, has announced details for the 49th annual Holly Ball, its largest annual fundraising event. This year’s Holly Ball will be on December 2 at Claremont Country Club and will have a Scottish theme. Holly Ball: Great Scot! will whisk guests away to the Scottish Highlands for a night of, eating, drinking, dancing and general merriment. Guests are encouraged to come dressed in their finest Highland formal attire, including kilts and tartan. The black-tie event commences with a cocktail reception, where guests will meander through an enchanted forest followed by a dinner in a Scottish castle. Entertainment includes Scottish Fiddlers, Highland dancers, and a Bagpipe serenade. The night would not be complete without a live auction, raisethe-paddle, a raffle and dancing into the night. “This year we are particularly excited about our live auction prizes,” said Brooke Wall and Rebecca Heywood, Holly Ball co-chairs. “We have a pair of fullbody health scans from Prenuvo, a shooting and dinner experience for 10 at Wing & Barrel Ranch, an exciting golf vacation in the Scottish Highlands, and much more.” Individual tickets for the event are $425, and sponsorship at any level is welcome. Sponsors at the $1,500 level and above will be invited to the Sponsor Party on November 9. This year’s sponsors include John Muir Health/UCSF Health, J.P. Morgan Private Bank, the David & Susan Martin Foundation, Oakland KIA, and Gary Kovacs, and Rebecca & John Carlo Heywood. Cancer research is normally funded by large nonprofit organizations that require a significant proof of concept. But getting the funding required to develop this initial data set can be challenging, leading cutting-edge ideas struggling to get noticed. Just like technology startups, these research startups need seed funding to get off the ground. 100% of funds raised at the annual Holly Ball event help The Cancer League find and fund these breakthrough research projects, accelerating us all towards the cure. “The Cancer League has been seeding bold, new research at UCSF for over 20 years,” said Dr. Alan Ashworth, President at UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center. “These projects have gone on to earn funding from hugely competitive sources so they can yield meaningful changes in how we treat cancer with investigational therapies and clinical trials.” To purchase tickets and to learn more about The Cancer League, visit the website at www. thecancerleagueinc.org/hb22. The Cancer League The Cancer League is a San Francisco Bay Area nonprofit that funds groundbreaking cancer research at its early stages. Since inception in 1973, The Cancer League has raised and donated more than $5 million toward the fight against cancer. The organization has an average yearly budget of over $300,000 in allocations, and an average grant size between $10,000-50,000. The Cancer League’s grants support early-stage researchers creating the datasets necessary to get their ideas off the ground. The Cancer League is a charitable nonprofit 501(c)(3) organization (www.thecancerleagueinc.org).

articles.text: Costieres de Nimes is a wine growing region between the ancient city of Nimes and the western Rhone delta. Formerly part of the Languedoc region of France it is now considered part of the southern Rhone family of wines. Wines from the region have been produced for over 2,000 years, and were consumed by the Greeks in pre-Roman times, making it one of the oldest vineyards in Europe. The area was settled by veterans of Julius Caesar’s campaigns in Egypt, and bottles of Costieres de Nimes bear the symbol of the Roman settlement of Nimes, a crocodile chained to a palm tree. The soil is a mixture of round river rocks similar to Chateauneuf du Pape and sandy alluvial soil and red shale. The climate is Mediterranean, like that of the Rhone valley, but is characterized by its proximity to the coast and sea breezes. The vast majority of wines that are produced are red from Syrah, Mourvedre, Grenache, Carignan, and Cinsault. The white wines are made from Bourboulenc, Clairette Blanc, Grenache Blanc and Roussanne. Some refreshing Rose wines are also produced. The Costieres de Nimes is a region that is transitioning from mainly a producer of low-priced bulk wines to a source of genuinely characterful, well-made wines. One of the things I like about the region is that unlike other regions, the prices have not skyrocketed, and the wines often represent great values. For more information on where you can access Costieres de Nimes wines contact Marion Helluy of Colangelo and Partners at mhelluy@ colangelopr.com. • 2021 Mas Carlot “L’irresistible” A pale pink rose made from mostly Grenache with a touch of Mourvedre. It gives up lots of juicy peach, citrus and pineapple in its clean, quaffable and delicious profile. This is the perfect picnic wine, and as the name suggests, would be pretty irresistible on a warm day. • 2019 Chateau Grand Escalion “Safranee” Operated by the Maison Gabriel Meffe, the is vineyard is sustainably farmed on ancient marl soil. The cuvee is 75% Syrah and 25% Grenache. Offering big, bright berry fruits, pepper, olive and hints of meatiness, it is a medium-bodied, elegant and rock-solid Cotes du Rhone style wine that has tons of character. A perfect companion to grilled burgers or ribs. • 2021 Chateau Mourgues du Gres “Galets Dores” This delightfully refreshing white wine is made from Roussanne, Grenache Blanc, Vermentino, Marsanne and Viognier – quite a vinifera cast. It has loads of tropical fruits, pineapple and floral notes in its medium-bodied, thrillingly pure crisp and lengthy personality While it doesn’t skimp on texture, it has beautifully integrated acidity and will be versatile on the dinner table. I’d drink it over the coming year or two but wouldn’t be surprised to see it drink well longer. • 2020 Mas des Bressades “Cuvee Tradition” This wine is a 50/50 blend of Syrah and Grenache from one of the more famous producers in the region. It presents gorgeous aromas of plum, blackberry, crushed rocks, pepper and violets win a medium to full-bodied, fresh, focused, impeccably balanced style. I love its fruit and this rocking effort will drink nicely in its youth and keep through 2028. Like the other three wines, this wine offers great value to the consumer.
articles.title: Gems from the South of France – Costieres de Nimes

articles.text: In the last couple of years, police departments across the country have been in the news. Tensions have risen, and many departments have had challenges connecting with their communities in a positive way. Social distancing has made those connections even more difficult. Across that backdrop, Piedmont Police has restarted their Exploring program, Post 911. Open to young men and women ages 14-20, Exploring helps youth learn about law enforcement as a potential career. In the case of Post 911, youth receive training in law enforcement policy and procedures, tactical and physical training, and forensics. They also learn life skills and career development that are transferable across career fields- including team building, communication, character education, and leadership. “There are a lot of controversial thoughts around law enforcement,” said Explorer Douglas Chu. “I wanted to learn more and get a different perspective.” “I’m interested in law enforcement. This gives me a chance to learn more about it,” said Explorer William Tretola. Exploring is also a lot of fun and provides opportunities for local and national competitions. “We’re looking forward to the competitions” said several of the Explorers. The Scouts have been to the national Law Enforcement Competition in Chandler, Arizona six times. It usually happens in February, and they’re preparing for a return to the event in 2024. In the meantime, they will prepare for regional competitions in CaliExplorer Lucas Chau practices cuffing Officer David Cutler with Explorer William Tretola as backup. Sgt. Casalnuovo gives instructions to Explorer Douglas Chu before starting the scenario practice. Explorer William Tretola assesses the situation at the beginning of the scenario practice. fornia. Competitions can include different scenarios such as hostage negotiation and building searches, as well as marksmanship. Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo serves as one of the advisors for the Post, along with Officers David Cutler and Hugo Diaz. “My favorite thing about this program is the camaraderie that builds among the participants,” said Casalnuovo. “Kids from all walks of life who might not otherwise hang out together develop really great bonds.” “The opportunity to be a mentor to youth in our community is important to me. I had a lot of great mentors as I was growing up, and this is my way of giving back,” added Officer Cutler. At a recent meeting, Explorers walked through a felony stop scenario. With the advisors, they discussed how to approach a suspect, how to communicate with them and with each other, and how to keep the situation from escalating. Then they walked through a mock scenario. Officer Cutler served as a mock suspect (who was remarkably helpful for someone afoul of the law), while Sergeant Casalnuovo provided feedback from the side. “Exploring is an important program,” said Piedmont Scout Executive Kate Benson. “While it carries the character development that is central to all Scouting programs, Exploring is unique in how it prepares youth for different career paths. Youth will develop a lot of transferable skills, but more importantly they’ll get a jump start if they find that a given field is a great fit. We are proud to partner with the Piedmont Police Department and of the leadership they provide to this program.” Interested in Exploring? Reach out to Officer Cutler at dcutler@ piedmont.ca.gov, Sergeant Casalnuovo at NCasalnuovo@piedmont.ca.gov, or Officer Diaz at hdiaz@piedmont.ca.gov. Or contact the Piedmont Scout office at 547-4493. Explorers Douglas Chu and Bo Droga approach Officer Cutler, while Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo provides commentary.
articles.title: Post 911: Piedmont Scouts thrive in police Explorer unit

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Piedmont Persimmon Coffee Cake – a Fall classic. • • Persimmon trees are very common in Bay Area backyards. I’m fortunate to have neighbors on two sides with persimmon trees. One is the Fuyu variety, round and squat, best eaten crunchy like an apple and usually raw as well. The other is the Hachiya variety that is oblong with a pointy bottom and must be ripened until it is very soft and squishy. The soft pulp from the Hachiya variety is what is typically used in baking. Eaten raw they are a dessert in themselves with a pudding-like texture. Make the spice blend ahead for the streusel topping the cake batter. There will be a bit extra to add it to either the streusel or cake to use all of it. Substituting a ready-made pumpkin pie spice works too. • • • • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 2 cups all-purpose flour 1 teaspoon baking soda 1/2 teaspoon baking powder 1-1/2 teaspoons spice blend 1/4 teaspoon sea salt INSTRUCTIONS Piedmont Persimmon Coffee Cake Adapted from Gemma Stafford’s Apple Snack Cake Makes one 8-inch square cake INGREDIENTS For the spice blend: • 1-1/2 teaspoons cinnamon, suggest a “baker’s variety” for robust flavor • 3/4 teaspoon nutmeg, freshly ground is best • 1/2 teaspoon ground ginger • 1/4 teaspoon ground allspice • 1/4 teaspoon ground cloves • Pinch of freshly ground black pepper For the streusel topping: • 1/2 cup walnuts, chopped to about 1/4” pieces • 1/3 cup old-fashioned oats • 1/3 cup brown sugar • 1-1/2 teaspoons spice blend • 2 tablespoons butter, melted For the persimmon cake: • 2 eggs, extra-large, room temperature • 1/2 cup granulated sugar • 1 cup persimmon pulp, from 2 – 3 very ripe Hachiya persimmons, slightly drained of their liquid • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly • 2 tablespoons olive oil, extra-virgin (“fruity” or “grassy “profile, but try a “peppery” one too) • 2 teaspoons apple cider vinegar Place an oven rack in the center position of the oven. Preheat to 350° F. Line an 8-inch square pan with baking parchment, covering up the sides with some extra above the rim to lift out the cake when ready. Set aside. For the spice blend: Combine all the ingredients in a small bowl. Stir to combine. Set aside. For the streusel topping: Combine the oats, brown sugar, walnuts, and spice blend in a small bowl. Add the melted butter and stir to combine. Set aside. For the persimmon cake: Whisk together the all-purpose flour, baking soda, baking powder, spice blend and salt in a medium bowl. Set aside. In a large mixing bowl, beat the eggs and granulated sugar on medium speed until light and fluffy, using an electric hand-held mixer, or a stand mixer with the paddle attachment. This will take 3–5 minutes. Beat in the melted butter, olive oil, apple cider vinegar and vanilla. Slowly add the persimmon pulp and mix well. Add in the flour mixture and mix on low speed. Use a spatula to scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl to finish incorporating the dry ingredients into the wet mixture, taking care to not overbeat the batter. Pour the batter into the prepared pan. Sprinkle on the streusel topping evenly, making sure to get to the edges and corners of the pan. Bake for 30–35 minutes or until a toothpick or wooden skewer inserted in the center comes out clean. Rest the cake in the pan for at least 20 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack to cool. Serve slightly warm or at room temperature. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

pages.text: 24 Wednesday, November 2, 2022 It’s Fall – time for fresh persimmon coffee cake Photo by Deborah Quok Piedmont Persimmon Coffee Cake – a Fall classic. By Deborah Quok • • Persimmon trees are very common in Bay Area backyards. I’m fortunate to have neighbors on two sides with persimmon trees. One is the Fuyu variety, round and squat, best eaten crunchy like an apple and usually raw as well. The other is the Hachiya variety that is oblong with a pointy bottom and must be ripened until it is very soft and squishy. The soft pulp from the Hachiya variety is what is typically used in baking. Eaten raw they are a dessert in themselves with a pudding-like texture. Make the spice blend ahead for the streusel topping the cake batter. There will be a bit extra to add it to either the streusel or cake to use all of it. Substituting a ready-made pumpkin pie spice works too. • • • • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 2 cups all-purpose flour 1 teaspoon baking soda 1/2 teaspoon baking powder 1-1/2 teaspoons spice blend 1/4 teaspoon sea salt INSTRUCTIONS Piedmont Persimmon Coffee Cake Adapted from Gemma Stafford’s Apple Snack Cake Makes one 8-inch square cake INGREDIENTS For the spice blend: • 1-1/2 teaspoons cinnamon, suggest a “baker’s variety” for robust flavor • 3/4 teaspoon nutmeg, freshly ground is best • 1/2 teaspoon ground ginger • 1/4 teaspoon ground allspice • 1/4 teaspoon ground cloves • Pinch of freshly ground black pepper For the streusel topping: • 1/2 cup walnuts, chopped to about 1/4” pieces • 1/3 cup old-fashioned oats • 1/3 cup brown sugar • 1-1/2 teaspoons spice blend • 2 tablespoons butter, melted For the persimmon cake: • 2 eggs, extra-large, room temperature • 1/2 cup granulated sugar • 1 cup persimmon pulp, from 2 – 3 very ripe Hachiya persimmons, slightly drained of their liquid • 6 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly • 2 tablespoons olive oil, extra-virgin (“fruity” or “grassy “profile, but try a “peppery” one too) • 2 teaspoons apple cider vinegar Place an oven rack in the center position of the oven. Preheat to 350° F. Line an 8-inch square pan with baking parchment, covering up the sides with some extra above the rim to lift out the cake when ready. Set aside. For the spice blend: Combine all the ingredients in a small bowl. Stir to combine. Set aside. For the streusel topping: Combine the oats, brown sugar, walnuts, and spice blend in a small bowl. Add the melted butter and stir to combine. Set aside. For the persimmon cake: Whisk together the all-purpose flour, baking soda, baking powder, spice blend and salt in a medium bowl. Set aside. In a large mixing bowl, beat the eggs and granulated sugar on medium speed until light and fluffy, using an electric hand-held mixer, or a stand mixer with the paddle attachment. This will take 3–5 minutes. Beat in the melted butter, olive oil, apple cider vinegar and vanilla. Slowly add the persimmon pulp and mix well. Add in the flour mixture and mix on low speed. Use a spatula to scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl to finish incorporating the dry ingredients into the wet mixture, taking care to not overbeat the batter. Pour the batter into the prepared pan. Sprinkle on the streusel topping evenly, making sure to get to the edges and corners of the pan. Bake for 30–35 minutes or until a toothpick or wooden skewer inserted in the center comes out clean. Rest the cake in the pan for at least 20 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack to cool. Serve slightly warm or at room temperature. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. Post 911: Piedmont Scouts thrive in police Explorer unit By Kate Benson In the last couple of years, police departments across the country have been in the news. Tensions have risen, and many departments have had challenges connecting with their communities in a positive way. Social distancing has made those connections even more difficult. Across that backdrop, Piedmont Police has restarted their Exploring program, Post 911. Open to young men and women ages 14-20, Exploring helps youth learn about law enforcement as a potential career. In the case of Post 911, youth receive training in law enforcement policy and procedures, tactical and physical training, and forensics. They also learn life skills and career development that are transferable across career fields- including team building, communication, character education, and leadership. “There are a lot of controversial thoughts around law enforcement,” said Explorer Douglas Chu. “I wanted to learn more and get a different perspective.” “I’m interested in law enforcement. This gives me a chance to learn more about it,” said Explorer William Tretola. Exploring is also a lot of fun and provides opportunities for local and national competitions. “We’re looking forward to the competitions” said several of the Explorers. The Scouts have been to the national Law Enforcement Competition in Chandler, Arizona six times. It usually happens in February, and they’re preparing for a return to the event in 2024. In the meantime, they will prepare for regional competitions in CaliExplorer Lucas Chau practices cuffing Officer David Cutler with Explorer William Tretola as backup. Sgt. Casalnuovo gives instructions to Explorer Douglas Chu before starting the scenario practice. Explorer William Tretola assesses the situation at the beginning of the scenario practice. fornia. Competitions can include different scenarios such as hostage negotiation and building searches, as well as marksmanship. Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo serves as one of the advisors for the Post, along with Officers David Cutler and Hugo Diaz. “My favorite thing about this program is the camaraderie that builds among the participants,” said Casalnuovo. “Kids from all walks of life who might not otherwise hang out together develop really great bonds.” “The opportunity to be a mentor to youth in our community is important to me. I had a lot of great mentors as I was growing up, and this is my way of giving back,” added Officer Cutler. At a recent meeting, Explorers walked through a felony stop scenario. With the advisors, they discussed how to approach a suspect, how to communicate with them and with each other, and how to keep the situation from escalating. Then they walked through a mock scenario. Officer Cutler served as a mock suspect (who was remarkably helpful for someone afoul of the law), while Sergeant Casalnuovo provided feedback from the side. “Exploring is an important program,” said Piedmont Scout Executive Kate Benson. “While it carries the character development that is central to all Scouting programs, Exploring is unique in how it prepares youth for different career paths. Youth will develop a lot of transferable skills, but more importantly they’ll get a jump start if they find that a given field is a great fit. We are proud to partner with the Piedmont Police Department and of the leadership they provide to this program.” Interested in Exploring? Reach out to Officer Cutler at dcutler@ piedmont.ca.gov, Sergeant Casalnuovo at NCasalnuovo@piedmont.ca.gov, or Officer Diaz at hdiaz@piedmont.ca.gov. Or contact the Piedmont Scout office at 547-4493. Explorers Douglas Chu and Bo Droga approach Officer Cutler, while Sergeant Nicole Casalnuovo provides commentary.

articles.text: Spencer Strellis passed away at the age of 88 on October 19, 2022. Smart, funny, generous, and kind, Spencer and Judy, his wife of 48 years, moved to Piedmont in 1973. Almost immediately he set about championing community events and organizations. He was a fixture in Fourth of July parades and block parties. He taught wine-making classes through the Piedmont Adult School at their home for many years. Bottles of home vintages still line their wine cellar. Spencer was always quick to volunteer in support of his family. When his children Eric, Lauren, and Keith took an interest in judo, Spencer took to the mat himself, earning an honorary black belt and opening a dojo. Later, Spencer served as the President of the Piedmont Swim Club where his stepdaughter Anne Patterson launched a long and successful swimming career. He also coached his daughter Paisley’s softball teams. He delighted in entertaining friends and family, hosting many parties at their home on Bonita Avenue. He loved arts and was a longtime supporter of Berkeley Repertory Theater, American Conservatory Theater, the Oakland Symphony, and San Francisco Opera. He enjoyed reciting the poetry of Kipling, Wordsworth, and Robert Service, among others. Born in Chicago on January 10, 1934, the son of Milton and Billie Strellis, Spencer moved around the country and world for his father’s work as an Army Engineer, including attending high school on Guam. While studying History and Political Science at the University of Illinois at Champaign Urbana, he spent breaks visiting his parents in Morocco, Italy, and other farflung destinations. Spencer attended Berkeley Spencer Strellis Spencer Strellis with daughters Anne Patterson (left) and Paisley Strellis. Judy and Spencer Strellis. At age 25, Spencer Strellis received his first photo ID as a member of the Alameda County Public Defender’s office. Law (then Boalt Hall). He truly found his calling as a criminal defense attorney, beginning his career at the Alameda County Public Defender’s Office in 1959. In private practice, Spencer tried more than 300 felony cases before a jury, including defending members of the Free Speech Movement, the Black Panther Party, and Chinese American community leaders. However, most of his clients were not known to the public. He worked tirelessly to ensure they were given a fair trial. Some of his proudest legal accomplishments took place outside of the courtroom. In 1973, Spencer co-founded California Attorneys for Criminal Justice and served as a director for many years. Later Spencer co-founded the Criminal Courts Bar Association, which gave defense lawyers, District Attorneys, and judges a chance to connect outside of the courtroom. Spencer shared his expertise as a professor of criminal law and trial skills at Hastings College and the Oakland College of the Law. More recently, Spencer served as the 2004 President of the Alameda County Bar Association. In addition to his wife and children, Spencer is survived by nine grandchildren and countless friends and family members who will miss him dearly. A memorial will be held on Saturday, November 12 from 1-4 p.m. at the Colombo Club where he was a member for more than 30 years, The location is 5321 Claremont Ave, Oakland, CA 94618. In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the American Parkinson Disease Association, the ACLU, or the Oakland Library.

articles.text: Editor: As we head towards the home stretch of the November 8th election, and for those who have not yet voted, let me share with you my thoughts of why I support and voted for Betsy Andersen, Jennifer Long, and Tom Ramsey for Piedmont City Council. As a 40-year Piedmont resident, longtime volunteer for the City, former Mayor and City Council member, I know what it takes to effectively serve on the City Council. Betsy and Jennifer, as incumbents, have demonstrated their ability to listen to all viewpoints, provide thoughtful analyses of issues, be collaborative and demonstrate effective leadership. Both hav a commendable history of volunteering in our community. I have met with Tom and am impressed with his professional background as an architect, his service on the Planning Commission for seven years, and his many other volunteer activities, His professional experience and skills will strongly benefit the community. Tom’s colleagues and neighbors have nothing but praise for his expertise, fairness, problem-solving and decision-making abilities, and leadership. Tom will be a strong addition to the Piedmont City Council. -John Chiang is a former Piedmont Mayor

articles.text: Editor: As mayor of the great city of Piedmont, I know first-hand what makes an outstanding public servant. It takes patience, intellect, devotion to the common good and a keen eye for details. Most importantly, a great public servant has vision for a better future. I am writing to strongly urge my fellow Piedmonters to vote for Councilmember Betsy Andersen for Piedmont City Council and Dr. Cindi Reiss for Peralta Community College Trustee. Betsy Anderson is a joy to serve with on the Council. Her calm demeanor and skilled intellect – honed as a practicing attorney – results in Betsy’s best work. Her passionate commitment to good government, fiscal restraint and excellent city services preserves the best of our small town. And, Betsy is dedicated to making Piedmont cleaner and greener for future generations. She’s taken a lead on ensuring our city is walkable, bikeable, and ready for the transportation challenges of the 21st century. And it’s because of Betsy’s leadership that Piedmont will enjoy a state-of-the-art pool in the near future. For many similar reasons, I am offering my strong support to Dr. Cindi Reiss for Peralta Community College District Trustee. Cindi is completing her first term on the college board, and she goes toe to toe with entrenched interests constantly to promote sound fiscal management in this sprawling – and critical – community college district. Many Piedmonters - kids, adults, seniors – benefit from community college access. Cindi Reiss’s commitment to excellence in financial leadership and thoughtful long-range planning, make her the stand-out candidate for this role. Please vote to reelect Betsy Andersen for Piedmont City Council and Dr. Cindi Reiss for the Peralta Community College District. –Teddy Gray King Mayor, City of Piedmont
articles.title: Mayor King voting for experienced leaders

articles.text: Editor: I write to endorse Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson for Piedmont School Board. Put simply, both Ruchi and Lindsay have done their homework and demonstrated their commitment to serving the entire community. They have spoken and listened to the teachers, parents, students, administrators, and local organizations. During the Tri-School Parent Club School Board forum on October 25th, when asked about their qualifications, both Lindsay and Ruchi stated that they “show up.” Yes, they do show up. I am the mother of an autistic boy with an IEP at Beach. His brothers go to Wildwood. We are grateful for the special education resources at Beach, but we are deeply concerned about what lies ahead for our son when he will be in middle school and high school. Inclusion is extremely important to our family. Because special education, especially at the middle and high school levels, is extremely important not just to my family, but to so many other Piedmont families, I am proud to serve on the board of PRAISE (Piedmonters for Resources, Advocacy, & Information in Special Education). PRAISE had a School Board Candidate forum on October 17. Twenty minutes before the forum, candidate Shirley Hooi emailed to say she would not be attending. Ruchi and Lindsay came prepared, and they were inspiring. I admit that only since the pandemic and schools closed did I realize how important it is to have people on the School Board with young school children. It is important to have people on the Board with diverse learners, and people who understand the importance of inclusion in our schools. As school board members, I believe that Ruchi and Lindsay will continue to show up and continue to thoughtfully engage with PRAISE and all of the other school district stakeholders who care so much about Piedmont’s amazing schools. They have my vote. –Amber Brumfiel

articles.text: Editor: In Piedmont’s upcoming election, there are two open seats for School Board and three for City Council. The candidates getting my votes are those who are most experienced, thoughtful and collaborative. Having served on our School Board for the last six years, currently as its president, I’ve found that – while members each bring different perspectives and talents – the most effective members are those who collaborate and work well with others. To be successful, members need to learn about the issues by listening carefully, asking questions and talking with stakeholders. But the true key to success is working as a governance team. If a member comes into the role thinking they have all the answers, or they can do this alone, they will not be effective. In the School Board race, I am supporting Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson. They both have been engaged with school issues for several years. Serving as parent club presidents during the height of the pandemic gave them each a deep understanding of the issues the district faces and the complexity of balancing stakeholder interests. But what has impressed me more than their volunteerism is their willingness to learn and collaborate to develop solutions. For City Council, I am supporting Betsy Andersen, Jennifer Long and Tom Ramsey. These three candidates have experience, either from serving on Council, or serving on our Planning Commission, and will strengthen our community’s strong foundation. They are currently doing the hard work, and moreover understand how to work with their peers to get things done.

Her passionate commitment to good government, fiscal restraint and excellent city services preserves the best of our small town. And, Betsy is dedicated to making Piedmont cleaner and greener for future generations. She’s taken a lead on ensuring our city is walkable, bikeable, and ready for the transportation challenges of the 21st century. And it’s because of Betsy’s leadership that Piedmont will enjoy a state-of-the-art pool in the near future. For many similar reasons, I am offering my strong support to Dr. Cindi Reiss for Peralta Community College District Trustee. Cindi is completing her first term on the college board, and she goes toe to toe with entrenched interests constantly to promote sound fiscal management in this sprawling – and critical – community college district. Cindi Reiss’s commitment to excellence in financial leadership and thoughtful long-range planning, make her the stand-out candidate for this role. I am the mother of an autistic boy with an IEP at Beach. His brothers go to Wildwood. We are grateful for the special education resources at Beach, but we are deeply concerned about what lies ahead for our son when he will be in middle school and high school. Inclusion is extremely important to our family. Because special education, especially at the middle and high school levels, is extremely important not just to my family, but to so many other Piedmont families, I am proud to serve on the board of PRAISE (Piedmonters for Resources, Advocacy, & Information in Special Education). Ruchi and Lindsay came prepared, and they were inspiring. articles.text: NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that at 5:30 p.m. on November 14, 2022, the Planning Commission will review an ordinance amending Chapter 17 (Planning and Land Use) of the City Code to conform the City’s regulations regarding Accessory Dwelling Units to new state laws and make a recommendation to the City Council. The ordinance also includes a new division 17.42 to address CA Assembly Bill 916, which requires ministerial review for the development of new bedrooms within existing residential units. NOTICE IS FURTHER GIVEN that at 6:00 p.m. on November 21, 2022, the City Council will consider the proposed ordinance and the recommendation of the Planning Commission and could approve the first reading of the ordinance. Background On January 1, 2022, new state laws come into effect which further limit a local jurisdiction’s ability to regulate Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs). The provisions affected by the changes to state law include but are not limited to: street (front) yard setbacks, unit height limitations, approval of existing conditions inconsistent with current Building Code requirements, interior connections between a Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit and the Primary Dwelling Unit, and the separate conveyance of ADUs. City staff is also recommending an incentive for the development of affordable ADUs in exchange for the release of owner-occupancy restrictions. Local laws which do not conform to these new state standards are preempted and cannot be enforced. The ordinance also proposes a new City Code division 17.42 that establishes a ministerial review process for projects that develop no more than two additional bedrooms within an existing dwelling unit, in conformance with AB 916 (2022). City staff has developed the proposed ordinance which will be considered by the Planning Commission and the City Council to conform Piedmont’s ADU regulations to the new state law. Documents on the City Website Documents related to this effort are available on the City website at piedmont.ca.gov. A staff report to the Planning Commission dated November 14, 2022, is provided on the website. It includes the proposed changes that will bring the City’s regulations for ADUs and additional bedrooms into compliance with the new state laws. The Planning Commission’s responsibility is to make a recommendation for consideration by the City Council, which is the decision-making body. The City Council staff report for this item will be posted on the City website no later than 12 noon on Friday, November 18, 2022. Public Engagement The opportunity for public input is available throughout this process. Interested members of the public are encouraged to attend the public meetings. Both the Planning Commission meeting on November 14, 2022, and the City Council meeting on November 21, 2022, will be televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government access TV station and available through streaming video on the City’s web site at piedmont.ca.gov/. Written comments regarding the proposed ordinance may be sent to the City Council and Planning Commission via email to: citycouncil@piedmont.ca.gov. Comments intended for the Planning Commission’s consideration should be submitted by 5 p.m., Thursday, November 10, 2022. To send comments via U.S. Mail, please use the following address: Piedmont City Council c/o City Clerk, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. If you have questions about the applications, please contact Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov. Any correspondence sent to the City will be considered a public record. John O. Tulloch City Clerk City of Piedmont 120 Vista Avenue Piedmont, CA 94611 November 1, 2022

City staff is also recommending an incentive for the development of affordable ADUs in exchange for the release of owner-occupancy restrictions. Local laws which do not conform to these new state standards are preempted and cannot be enforced. The ordinance also proposes a new City Code division 17.42 that establishes a ministerial review process for projects that develop no more than two additional bedrooms within an existing dwelling unit, in conformance with AB 916 (2022). City staff has developed the proposed ordinance which will be considered by the Planning Commission and the City Council to conform Piedmont’s ADU regulations to the new state law. Documents on the City Website Documents related to this effort are available on the City website at piedmont.ca.gov. A staff report to the Planning Commission dated November 14, 2022, is provided on the website. It includes the proposed changes that will bring the City’s regulations for ADUs and additional bedrooms into compliance with the new state laws. The Planning Commission’s responsibility is to make a recommendation for consideration by the City Council, which is the decision-making body. The City Council staff report for this item will be posted on the City website no later than 12 noon on Friday, November 18, 2022. Public Engagement The opportunity for public input is available throughout this process. Interested members of the public are encouraged to attend the public meetings. Both the Planning Commission meeting on November 14, 2022, and the City Council meeting on November 21, 2022, will be televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government access TV station and available through streaming video on the City’s web site at piedmont.ca.gov/. Written comments regarding the proposed ordinance may be sent to the City Council and Planning Commission via email to: citycouncil@piedmont.ca.gov. Comments intended for the Planning Commission’s consideration should be submitted by 5 p.m., Thursday, November 10, 2022. To send comments via U.S. Mail, please use the following address: Piedmont City Council c/o City Clerk, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. If you have questions about the applications, please contact Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov. Any correspondence sent to the City will be considered a public record. John O. Paraeducator Pam Deluca, who has worked in the school district for ten years, shared her own experience of this financial lag. In 2012, her starting salary was $19.67 an hour. Today, it’s $24.88 an hour. “That’s a difference of $5.21 in ten years,” said Deluca. “The average hourly salary across industries here in the U.S. is $32.46.” As discussions concluded, CSEA members were clear: if PUSD does not authorize a higher level of employer contribution to classified employees, these workers will have to choose food or housing over healthcare and hope that another pandemic or personal health crisis “doesn’t bankrupt us,” Deluca noted. articles.text: Teachers Union President Dr. Elise Marks (left) and a group of parents in discussion on core values. The Piedmont School Board hosted a public workshop on Wednesday, October 19 at the high school Student Center to receive comments and work on rewriting the District’s current core philosophical ideologies. The district’s Mission Statement was up for discussion and editing, as were the Vision and Core Value statements. The workshop attracted a diverse range of stakeholders, including student board members, school board candidates, parents, and teachers. Ahead of the workshop, in a September Student School Board member Gianna Yan Halloween Parade...................1 Letters. .....................................2 Post at 25. ................................3 Turkey Trot training. ................5 Schools. ...................................6 Candidates Q&A................7, 10 PPD Blue. .................................9 Cubs Webeloree....................11 Sports....................................12 Theater, Dance. ......................16 Music.....................................17 Musical Gourmet. ..................18 PCA events............................19 Movies...................................20 Walking Piedmont.................22 Climate Corner......................23 USS Potomac.........................24 Wed. Walkers. ........................25 Real Estate............................26 Where in the World. ...............32 16 board meeting, the board produced a draft version of key declarations for the community to analyze and edit. The draft Mission Statement stated: “Piedmont Unified School District provides all students with an excellent education that includes a broad-based academic and social-emotional curriculum, delivered by exemplary staff in an environment that is caring, equitable, and inclusive.” It was originally written in 1999 and updated in 2011. The board will be hiring a permanent superintendent within the next year, and it wants to establish accurate representations of the school district’s main focuses before interviewing potential candidates. Workshop attendees read and reflected on the drafts, then moved to different tables to share opinions on the mission, vision, and core values statements. Attendees emphasized the inclusion of “curiosity,” “resilience,” and “empathy” in the statement. St u d e nt s cho ol b o a r d member, senior Gianna Yan expressed a desire for the district to work towards encouraging students to have a “genuine interest in learning that goes beyond getting an A.” Impassioned discussion emerged over definitions of “Equity” and “Critical Thinking.” Students and parents shared their experiences with Piedmont schools, and what they wish to see more of, whether in academics or leadership. The workshop ended with a one-word check-out, such as “excited,” “pumped,” and “motivated.” The input will be reworked into the next draft of the mission statements and is expected to be presented at the October 26 board meeting tonight, with a goal of finalizing it by November 9. articles.text: The 35th annual Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade takes place this Saturday, October 29, starting at 11:00 a.m. at the corner of Montell Street. Dave Larson, owner of Piedmont Grocery will be the Grand Marshal for the fifth time but in a brand new costume. Merchants created the parade in 1986 as a way to celebrate Halloween on the popular street in a safe manner. It has evolved into a celebration that brings the community and merchants on the Avenue together. The street will be closed west of the Piedmont Theater from 10:30 a.m. until 1:00 p.m. Kids can start stocking up on candy two days before Halloween this year by trick or treating at participating merchant’s shops and designated stations. Spooky storytime for the very young at the Piedmont Avenue Branch Library precedes the parade at 10:15 a.m. West Wind
articles.title: Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade this Saturday

articles.text: Only a few more days are left to buy a pumpkin as the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch enters its final weekend of sales. This Saturday, October 29, the Patch will be open from 10 a.m.to 6 p.m., followed by a special twohour sale from 10 a.m. to 12 noon on Sunday, October 30, the day before Halloween. The deadline for guessing the weight of the giant pumpkin is Thursday, October 27. So far more than 200 people have submitted guesses. The guess closest to the actual weight will win free delivery of Giant Jack to their home. More than 50 Wildwood Dads have volunteered this year at the Patch. Under the guidance of their fearless leader, Dads Club President Adam Fishman, they are on track to exceed their goal of raising $30,000 to help fund projects at Wildwood Elementary School. The patch still has some gorgeous gourds available including carving pumpkins, swan gourds, decorative mini pumpkins, and a handful of specialty pumpkins. At 12 noon on Sunday the pumpkin patch will be dismantled in preparation for the big day. Staff photo Hundreds of guesses have been made to correctly guess the weight of Giant Jack, the centerpiece of the Wildwood Dads Club annual pumpkin patch at Coaches Field.
articles.title: Final weekend for Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch

articles.text: Last week I read a letter to the editor from “ new neighbor,” Tu Ngoc Nguyen, who stated that the PiedmontVotes.com website had created a smear campaign against school board candidate Shirley Hooi. I opened PiedmontVotes.com and ironically the “smear campaign” is composed of words Ms. Hooi used in her multiple letters to the editor and commentaries she wrote to the Piedmont Post. The core of her opinions came down to PUSD staying in their lane and not teaching anything about critical race theory, racial oppression or related material that would run the risk of her mixed race children feeling white guilt or questioning her white husband’s beliefs towards people of color. Tu Ngoc Nguyen then went on to bash Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign for their perceived part in the PiedmontVotes.com profile and how they were targeting the only Asian American candidate. That opinion is clearly debunked on PREC’s facebook page. [An example of] racial bias from teachers came when my black son was encouraged to “aim lower” for his academic goals in his first year in Piedmont. That same son was stopped 10 years later for the audacity of walking while black (200 yards from my front door) in a community policing encounter by two officers of color. (PPD was swift to respond, held two separate meetings with me and my son and admitted to racial bias being present across all races of peace officers, and antibias training was mandated by Chief Bowers.) It was a best-case scenario and radically different from police encounters in other neighborhoods that we have witnessed via our media. Please vote for the candidates who understand the importance of educating our children about our past mistakes as a country. articles.text: This week marks the 25th anniversary of the Piedmont Post. It’s first edition was 12 pages and hardly offered any promise, let alone optimism, that it might be around a quarter century later. In a small town with only a few commercial businesses, the outlook for its survival was somewhat bleak. And then we began reading stories in the New York Times about the escalating number of local newspapers going out of business – over 2,000 at last count. And yet here we are – thriving and finding ways to thank the residents for so strongly supporting The Little Newspaper That Could. Over the next several weeks, you will read comments of some of the people who were there at the beginning – the optimists and pessimists. my core belief that the Post had taken its place in that long line referred to as the Fourth Estate which defines our democracy and the First Amendment, It would be not only essential to the vitality of our city government but would be a means to inform the community about a broad spectrum of “news” and opinion, and a forum for information and debate. I have always preferred ink on paper, loved holding a newspaper in my hands, even relishing its smell. And here it was, the Post, the first of many to come. Finally, let me say that the denizens of Piedmont should take pride in this weekly paper, for without their generous support it would not have flourished, grown in the number of pages (including color), and, in keeping with the times, is now available online. Without a doubt, after twenty-five years, week after week, it has become an integral part of the Piedmont community. May it continue for another quarter of a century. Chris Honore’ is the Post’s movie reviewer with occasional pieces on the Opinion page. He is married to Judi Honore’ and lives in Ashland, Oregon. license plate readers. I’m remembering bringing the Piedmont Post with us on vacation, then not remembering to send in the photo of us reading it. And now we see the names of people who were in school with our kid, and who are now running the city. Remembrances of the early days of the Piedmont Post, give way to the bigger picture – why it’s important to have a hometown newspaper. It’s not just to read about your kid, the activities of the community and local politics. It’s reading about the issues and challenges facing our town, some which seem to have stayed the same over 25 years. It keeps us up to date on the city and schools, and reminds us it’s important to be an active member of the community. As the Post has grown from 12 pages to 32 pages, it has not only survived, but prospered, maybe even beyond Gray’s initial vision. I’ve said to him that the Post is the only paper I know that’s growing instead of shrinking. I’d like to thank him and the Post for unwavering support of Piedmont, of the school fundraisers and other philanthropic community events. The Post has been an important voice for our community. Congratulations and thanks. Here’s to the next 25 years. Cheers! Sheryl and Bob Wong Manor Drive

articles.text: Russian-American author Anastasia Edel, a Piedmont resident, will present a four-week illustrated lecture titled Russia’s War on Ukraine, with classes starting on Thursday, October 20 at 2:30 p.m. The course is being offered by Osher Lifelong Learning Institute at the University of California in Berkeley, where Edel conducted an eight-week illustrated lecture in 2018 on Understanding Russia, a course that intertwines the country’s political and cultural developments with historical perspectives expressed in film, music, and literature. The last four years have proven to be a busy time for Edel. In 2018 she gave the keynote address at OLLI and to the League of Women Voters in Piedmont on The State of US-Russian Relations. One year later she delivered talks at the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco, the University of Washington, and Berkeley City Club. Due in part to the publicity generated by op ed pieces she wrote for the New York Times between February and May this year, she was an invited commentator on CNN, MSNBC and Bay Area NBC. In the past five years, six of her guest essays and opinion pieces have appeared in the New York Times, with a spike of interest since Russia began its move to wage war on neighboring Ukraine. The course fee for Russia’s War Russia: Putin’s Playground, by Anastasai Edel, was published in 2016. Piedmont author and social historian Anastasia Edel, is teaching a four-week course on the Russia vs. Ukraine war at the University of California in Berkeley through Osher Lifelong Learning Institute. on Ukraine through OLLI is $90 for the four lectures, each of which will be from 2:30 to 4:00 p.m. on consecutive Thursdays, October 20 to November 10. Signups are still being accepted. The course will stream live on the scheduled day and time and will also be recorded. Videos will be available on Friday each week. When Russian missiles struck multiple cities across the sovereign nation of Ukraine in February 2020, Russia became an aggressor bent on destroying a neighboring nation with whom it shares centuries of common past. How did it happen? Why does Putin’s regime refuse to call war “war”? What’s behind Ukrainians’ resilience and Russians’ acquiescence? And where does this all end for Russia, Ukraine, and the world? Edel provided some perspective on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine earlier this year with a lecture at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in April. To register for the current course, click on: https://olli.berkeley.edu/programs/courses/russia%E2%80%99s-war-ukraine. Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel is a writer, social historian, and New York Times contributor. She’s the author of “Russia: Putin’s Playground,” a concise guide to Russian history, politics and culture. “Did the IRS let you get away with your wife’s fat farm deductions?”

articles.text: The Alameda County Registrar of Voters is seeking poll workers for the November 8, 2022 election. Poll workers play a critical role in making voting accessible to all community members – and get paid to do it. Workers are needed throughout Alameda County from Saturday, November 5 through Tuesday, November 8, election day. Interested community members can sign up online to volunteer at acgov.org/rovform_app/ewapply. The application is simple and takes just a few minutes to complete. Job details Poll workers are paid volunteers who perform tasks including: • Setting up and closing a polling place • Helping voters understand their rights • Protecting ballots and voting equipment The County Registrar of Voters office provides training for poll workers. Individuals are paid for training and time served as a poll worker. No special skills are required to be a poll worker. Eligibility requirements: • Must be a registered voter in California • Must be a legal permanent resident or green card holder • An eligible high school student Bilingual Poll Workers Sought Bilingual poll workers are especially needed. In Alameda County, assistance is provided to voters in Burmese, Chinese, Hindi, Khmer, Korean, Laotian, Mien, Mongolian, Punjabi, Spanish, Tagalog, Telugu, and Vietnamese. Residents fluent in any of these languages are urged to consider volunteering. Interested residents can find more information about volunteering as a poll worker at acvote.org/community/become-anelection-worker or by calling the Alameda County Registrar of Voters office at 510-272-6973.

pages.text: 4 Wednesday, October 26, 2022 Local Items Poll workers needed for Nov. 8 Election The Alameda County Registrar of Voters is seeking poll workers for the November 8, 2022 election. Poll workers play a critical role in making voting accessible to all community members – and get paid to do it. Workers are needed throughout Alameda County from Saturday, November 5 through Tuesday, November 8, election day. Interested community members can sign up online to volunteer at acgov.org/rovform_app/ewapply. The application is simple and takes just a few minutes to complete. Job details Poll workers are paid volunteers who perform tasks including: • Setting up and closing a polling place • Helping voters understand their rights • Protecting ballots and voting equipment The County Registrar of Voters office provides training for poll workers. Individuals are paid for training and time served as a poll worker. No special skills are required to be a poll worker. Eligibility requirements: • Must be a registered voter in California • Must be a legal permanent resident or green card holder • An eligible high school student Bilingual Poll Workers Sought Bilingual poll workers are especially needed. In Alameda County, assistance is provided to voters in Burmese, Chinese, Hindi, Khmer, Korean, Laotian, Mien, Mongolian, Punjabi, Spanish, Tagalog, Telugu, and Vietnamese. Residents fluent in any of these languages are urged to consider volunteering. Interested residents can find more information about volunteering as a poll worker at acvote.org/community/become-anelection-worker or by calling the Alameda County Registrar of Voters office at 510-272-6973. articles.text: Registration is now open for the 21st Annual Piedmont Turkey Trot, a 3-mile run-walk-jog on Thanksgiving morning, November 24. articles.text: The Piedmont Turkey Trot is notorious for its hilly course, so if you want to feel your best on race day, you need to train for the hills. If you are following the official Piedmont Turkey Trot training plan (see below) or just want to get in a good workout, head over to Sea View Avenue for a hill repeat workout. Run up Sea View from Hampton to the end at Mountain Avenue three times at an uncomfortably hard pace. Once you reach Mountain, stop and walk back down the hill to start again. It is only .35 of a mile, but it feels much longer. If you use a watch, try to run it faster each time. This is a great workout to prepare for race day. This hill comes at the end of mile 2 of the 5K race, which is the Photo by Kaitlin MacLean A group of runners ascending at the crest of Sea View during the 2016 Piedmont Turkey Trot. hardest mile of any 5K. If you can master this point in this race, it’s (mostly) all downhill to the finish line. WEEK DAY WORKOUT October 31 Monday Run 3 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday Run 3 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Add 3 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 3x Saturday Hill workout: 5 min jog warm up 3x run up Sea View Dr (Start at Hampton, run to Mountain) Walk down hill between reps 5 min jog cool down

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, October 26, 2022 SchOOLs Millennium students spend day on the Bay On Friday, October 14, a group of Millennium High School students and staff chaperones spent the day on San Francisco Bay with the Blue Water Sailing Foundation. The all-volunteer nonprofit organization is dedicated to bringing the joys and challenges of sailing to under-served youth in the Bay Area. MHS students had the chance to steer the sailboat, put up the sails and learn some sailing fundamentals. The outing was financially supported by the MHS Parents Club. MHS is grateful to Piedmont resident Eric Downing who volunteers with the group and helped bring the opportunity to MHS. Senior Alex Guevarra enjoyed the chance to be out on the Bay, saying, “it was so peaceful out on the water.” Junior Andre Bowers commented, “The crew was nice. They taught me how to steer. It was hard at first but then I got used to it.” For more information on the Blue Water Foundation and to make a donation, see website https://www.bluewaterfoundation.org/. articles.text: Big educational changes are coming to PUSD. Here are some examples: At PUSD’s recent Professional Development Day, teachers were lectured that “Perfectionism is a characteristic of white supremacy culture.” They were also shown videos from the “Gender Sexuality Alliance”– videos PUSD won’t share with parents. The agenda for the day lists seven lecture hours on DEIB (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging) topics. No time was allocated for certified teachers about issues with dyslexia, academics, filling the student knowledge gap from the COVID era, or school safety. Also this month, the Piedmont Middle School presented a video to all its students about why grade achievement isn’t that important – a video intended for parents. During the first week of school, at least one of the 2nd grade teachers instructed children on being able to change their pronouns at any time. DEIB has a place in academics, but it seems quite imbalanced now. See for yourself at the school board meeting at 7 p.m. tonight. PUSD’s values, mission, and vision are in the process of being redefined. A progress report on PUSD’s educational action plan will be presented.
articles.title: Wake up to the changes at the school district

articles.text: Members of the Piedmont High School Advanced Acting class will perform Jane Austen’s classic, Pride and Prejudice, the first weekend in November. Directed by Kimberly Taylor and adapted by celebrated contemporary playwright Kate Hamill, the show will be performed in the new Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus, 800 Magnolia Avenue. Performances are Thursday through Saturday, November 3-5 at 7:00 p.m. Watch the Bennet sisters navigate the silly game of marriage through plenty of obstacles. Will they negotiate the strict rules of gender and class in order to fit in and “win the game”? The cast includes Jack Gross Whitaker, Jake Hanke (Thursday, Friday), Maya Hollinsworth, Milani Juarbe (Friday, Saturday), Jasper Kra-Caskey (Saturday), Miranda Long (Thursday), Eden Lorin, Callan Mitchell, Emma Nielsen, Ella Puckett, Macy Puckett, Andres Roberts (Saturday), Xander Schulte Sasse, Sadie Shoop (Saturday), Eve Tellegen, Charles White (Thursday/Saturday), Isabella Wire. All seats are General Admission. Online tickets are $18 for General Admission and $12 for Students and Seniors. Tickets are an extra $2 when purchased at the door, so patrons are encouraged to purchase tickets in advance online at https:// www.showtix4u.com/events/ PHSPride. For more information contact Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@ piedmont.k12.ca.us. articles.text: On Friday, October 21, purple-clad Giving Campaign volunteers celebrated Spirit Day, sharing goodies and good cheer at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood elementary schools, and outside Piedmont Middle School, Piedmont High School and MillenBalloons, purple pom-poms, leis, and green “I’m In” stickers greeted students as they headed “It’s been one month since the Giving Campaign launched, so spirit day is about raising awareness and celebrating the success thus far,” said Laura Jacobs, Beach School’s Giving Campaign representative. So many families have donated and shown their support, and we want to continue the momentum.” Students and teachers also dressed in purple to show their commitment to Piedmont schools and the Giving Campaign. This year’s event also drew attention to the critical date of Tuesday, November 1st – the last day for families to make their Giving Campaign donation and receive a lawn sign highlighting their family’s support of Piedmont schools. “Early participation and the lawn signs are a strong signal to the community that we are committed to the ongoing success of our schools,” said Giving Campaign co-chair Julia Ruthven. “The Giving Campaign donations are essential to funding the gap between what state funds cover and what PUSD is able to offer.” With a solid first few weeks of community support, the Giving Campaign is nearly halfway to this year’s goal of raising $3.5 million for Piedmont’s students and schools. All Piedmont Education Foundation and PUSD board members have already made their donations. Other ongoing events include the annual grade-level competition, where each grade level will vie for the highest family Giving Photo by Julia Ruthven Max White, Mookie White and Lola Ruthven join the spirit day celebration. Photo by Meghan Bennett Beach volunteers Laura Jacobs and Zeena Fakoury show their Giving Campaign spirit Photo by Meghan Bennett Carson Jacobs passes out candy Photo by Carolyn Pan Mia Parker and Eden Allessio Photo by Carolyn Pan Kathy Derrigo and Karla Gudino Campaign participation rate. The friendly and fun rivalry encourages all families in the school district to donate. This year’s winning grade level will be invited to a special event. The Giving Campaign aims for 100% participation from Piedmont families. “A big part of the campaign this year is participation – ‘I’m In!’ is our tagline,” explained Jacobs. “We’re encouraging everyone to participate. The donation amount is not as important as showing your support for your community and your schools.” The Giving Campaign team also hopes that spirit day serves as an opportunity to educate families about why the Giving Campaign is such a critical fundraiser for Piedmont schools. “The idea behind spirit day is to draw attention to the Giving Campaign and answer questions, especially for new families or people unfamiliar with how the funds are used,” said Beach Giving Campaign representative Zeena Fakoury, “We’re so fortunate to live in Photo by Katie Sharafi Rita Fabi hands out spirit day swag at Havens. a community that places so much value on music, library, and extracurriculars that other school districts may not have the opportunity to fund,” continued Fakoury. “We feel very lucky that everyone comes together to make those things available to our students. At the end of the day, the Giving Campaign is all for our kids.” To learn more about the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign or to donate, visit www.piedmontedfoundation. org. www.cindireiss2022.com PAID FOR BY CINDI REISS FOR PERALTA BOARD OF TRUSTEES, 2022. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. articles.text: In our elementary schools school counselors are the primary point of contact for students with mental health needs or social-emotional challenges, including those flagged on the BESS screener. They also focus on proactively giving students tools to manage stress, deal with friendship challenges, and prevent bullying. RUCHI MEDHEKAR 1. School Traditions I love our traditions around the performing arts. My kids are at Beach, which has an annual Beach Revue, and has a high degree of participation amongst students. Parent volunteers made a Herculean effort to bring back the Revue last year by staging it outside to prevent it from being canceled. This weekend, I went to the middle school performance of The Addams Family at the new theater. It had a large cast and crew, and parents told me that students were devoting 3-4 hours of practice a day for the last month and a half which resulted in an incredible show. And during the pandemic, my family really enjoyed the brilliantly creative stay at home version of Clue put on by PHS students. These performances are incredibly important for our community and are directly tied to how much we collectively value a well-rounded student education. 2. Mental health of youth The middle school also benefits from the wellness center, which is an important resource for these students. The new Academy aspect in middle school also allows for evidence-based skill building around emotional self-regulation and developing healthy relationships. I recently sat on a PMS parent club meeting which talked about extending health education to middle school - this will be invaluable to educating students on how to have healthy relationships with peers and dating partners. At the elementary level, at risk students are identified through a BESS screener (Behavior and Emotional Screening System). They also learn from a robust social-emotional curriculum. Though it is hard to know every reason, youth suicide is highly tied to social situations like peer or romantic rejection. It is really important to equip young people with tools to navigate social situations in a healthy and affirming way in addition to helping them manage their mental health.

Most impactful proposition We have multiple propositions that are important. Roe v. Wade was overturned leaving states to make important decisions on abortion rights. California already had these rights in place; therefore, I do not consider this proposition a high priority. I strongly believe it is our duty as voting adults to be critical thinkers for our youth. The two gaming propositions 26 and 27 impact our youth. Youth spend excessive amounts of time online. It is not a stretch for youth to easily find their way onto gambling sites. Gaming has been proven to be addictive for both children and adults. Both propositions encourage gambling and on-line gaming. We should oppose both. Proposition 30 provides funds for more arts in the classrooms. The State’s heavy taxation has caused an exodus of taxpaying businesses and residents. Piedmonters cannot afford any new taxation as we work to fund the pool, infrastructure, and Housing element. 2. Walkability in Piedmont Most of Piedmont residents do not work within the City of Piedmont. Therefore, it is hard to promote bicycling or walking to work. However, I have noticed that rideshare to work pick up spots are no longer functioning at the capacity they were prior to covid. Now that the covid pandemic is no longer an emergency the city could begin to promote the rideshare program again. An online survey could be done to determine if the city’s needs have changed since Covid. Pickup and drop off locations could be changed accordingly. It is free and simple to promote the rideshare program. Posting the information in the in media sources, such as the Post could greatly increase participation. TOM RAMSEY 1. Most impactful proposition For proposition measures, it is BETSY ANDERSEN Incumbent 1. Most impactful proposition From my perspective, there are two propositions that are most important and impactful for Piedmonters: Proposition 1 and Proposition 31. Proposition 1 will constitutionalize current California law regarding reproductive freedom. Proposition 31 will uphold a previously-approved state law to ban the sale of flavored tobacco at gas stations, grocery stores, and other places. The City Council recently voted 5-0 to ban the sale of flavored tobacco in Piedmont to protect our youth from becoming addicted to nicotine through the use of sweet-flavored tobacco products. During my tenure, the City Council has supported funding and staffing for a dedicated Juvenile Liaison Officer with the Piedmont Police Department, and partnered with the PUSD on efforts to reduce teen smoking and vaping. I encourage all Piedmont voters to visit www.votersedge.org to learn more about all of the state ballot propositions, including pros/cons, financial impacts, campaign contributions, and endorsements. 2. Walkability in Piedmont The City Council can promote walking by making it safer and easier to walk around town. During my time on Council, we have allocated funding to upgrade sidewalks, crosswalks, and pathways throughout Piedmont, and to slow traffic and improve pedestrian safety, specifically on Scenic, Greenbank, and the Oakland Avenue Bridge. In 2020, the Council appointed a citizen-representative PedesRUCHI MEDHEKAR 1. School Traditions I love our traditions around the performing arts. My kids are at Beach, which has an annual Beach Revue, and has a high degree of participation amongst students. Parent volunteers made a Herculean effort to bring back the Revue last year by staging it outside to prevent it from being canceled. This weekend, I went to the middle school performance of The Addams Family at the new theater. It had a large cast and crew, and parents told me that students were devoting 3-4 hours of practice a day for the last month and a half which resulted in an incredible show. And during the pandemic, my family really enjoyed the brilliantly creative stay at home version of Clue put on by PHS students. These performances are incredibly important for our community and are directly tied to how much we collectively value a well-rounded student education. 2. Mental health of youth The middle school also benefits from the wellness center, which is an important resource for these students. The new Academy aspect in middle school also allows for evidence-based skill building around emotional self-regulation and developing healthy relationships. I recently sat on a PMS parent club meeting which talked about extending health education to middle school - this will be invaluable to educating students on how to have healthy relationships with peers and dating partners. At the elementary level, at risk students are identified through a BESS screener (Behavior and Emotional Screening System). They also learn from a robust social-emotional curriculum. Though it is hard to know every reason, youth suicide is highly tied to social situations like peer or romantic rejection. It is really important to equip young people with tools to navigate social situations in a healthy and affirming way in addition to helping them manage their mental health. articles.text: The biggest family camp of the year for Piedmont Scouts took place at Bort Meadow last weekend with the Cub Scout Overnighter and Webeloree. “This is an important event for our council,” explained Scout Executive Kate Benson. “Our Scouts BSA troops, Piedmont Community Service Crew, and Order of the Arrow do a great job supporting this overnighter for our younger Scouts. It’s one of the few events where all the programs weave together.” A total of 90 Cub Scouts and parents landed at the campground in Chabot Regional Park on Friday evening, ready for adventure. They selected their campsites, set up their tents, and played at full speed in the fading light. The Order of the Arrow – an honor society for Scouts BSA – arrived to make dinner for everyone before leading a campfire program. By 8:30 p.m., the Cubs were ready for bed and crawled into their sleeping bags for a night outdoors. They awoke Saturday morning to a continental breakfast and headed out for a one-mile hike. “This was the best part,” said one Cub during their roses-andthorns debrief. “I wanted to keep going.” As the younger Cubs packed up their tents and headed home, the older Cubs arrived on Saturday for their Webeloree. They started the day with a three-mile hike and set up camp upon their return. Piedmont Community Service Crew – a Venturing unit – showed up with lunch organized by Theo Ferguson. Webelos and their parents dined on pulled pork sandwiches, mac and cheese, fruit salad, chips, and banana boats cooked over hot coals. “Theo did an excellent job organizing the lunch,” said PCSC Crew advisor Ken Li. “The marshmallows and chocolate were tasty and sticky!” enthused several Webelos. Afternoon activities for the Webelos included first aid, knot skills, flag practice, and an engineering adventure. Scouts Samantha Pell and Madeleine Poon of Troop 1 led the First Aid section, walking the Webelos through the correct response for nose bleeds, hypothermia, abrasions, and more. Scout Alex Younger Cub Scouts in grades K-3 form a circle for a roses-and-thorns debrief after their Saturday morning hike. Madison Jung and Anna Benson enjoy some laughs in between activities. Rob Ashton (center) scopes out the 3-to-1 pulley system his den used to raise him up, while Troop 11 Scoutmaster Rob Kobal explains how it works. Troop 15 Scouts Thomas Moision (left), Henry Ciriacruz, and Abigail Taylor Collins watch over the coals while cooking foil packet dinners prepared by the Webelos. Piedmont Community Service Venturer Theo Ferguson (left) helps a Cub Scout cook a banana boat dessert after lunch. Jim Crawford-Jakubiak prepares hot chocolate for a pair of excited Webelos on a cold Sunday morning. Alex Wolff of Troop 4 demonstrates how to tie a square knot to Webelos from Pack 3. Gabe Ross (left) lowers the flag as Ben Cole prepares to fold it at a flag ceremony at the Camporee. CHAPEL OF THE CHIMES - OAKLAND

articles.text: Tennis team beats Alameda, Castro Valley, St. Mary’s In a triumphant week, the Piedmont tennis team walking away with three victories in as many days including a pair of Western Alameda County Conference foes. They defeated Alameda narrowly 4-3 on the Hornets’ home courts on Thursday, October 20, beat St. Mary’s 6-1 the previous day, and bashed Castro Valley 6-1 at home on Tuesday, October 18. The most critical match was with Alameda, which had an opportunity to prevent the Highlanders from claiming a league championship outright. But the 4-3 victory kept Piedmont undefeated and on track for its first WACC crown since 2018. Matches remain against Berkeley and Bishop O’Dowd. The team is now 14-3 overall and a perfect 10-0 in league. An undefeated league season would be a return to tradition for the Highlanders’ girls’ tennis program, which went undefeated in league matches for 19 years, a state record. Thursday’s match with the Hornets wasn’t settled until Carolina Romanczuk at No. 3 singles defeating Allison Quan in three sets, 6-4, 3-6, 6-3. “The whole team is incredibly excited. We’re running a really good lineup this year with a good attitude, and I think that’s what’s going to push us through league,” said Romanczuk after her critical win. Trailing 4-1 in the first set, she won the next five games to win the set. She also won five straight games in the third set after trailing 3-1. “When I was down 3-1, I was just thinking back to my first set and how I was down 4-1. I was just pushing through and taking it one point at a time. I was just taking deep breathes and thinking of, not even about my own match, but just thinking about my team and trying to win it for my team,” said Romanczuk. 4-3 win over Alameda Against the Hornets, No. 1 singles starter Tanya Kononova won the first match of the day handily, 6-2, 6-4. Soon after, the No. 3 doubles team of Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum won 6-3, 6-2, while Emma Eisemon and Cecilia DeFazio won 6-4, 7-6 (6-4) at No. 2 doubles to put PHS up 3-0, one win away from clinching the match. At No. 1 doubles, Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini lost a 5-set barnburner, 6-3, 5-7, 7-6 (7-5), and soon after, Annika Gilliland lost 6-3, 6-1 at the No. 4 singles spot. Suddenly the match was tied at 3-3. Romanczuk vs. Quan at the No. 3 singles was a long match, with each set highly contested. Romanczuk fell behind 4-1 in the first set disadvantage but pulled off a remarkable rally by winning five games in a row for a 6-4 victory. In the clinching third set, she also won five straight games to win 6-3. Her match featured several long rallies and Quan couldn’t maintain the same consistency as Romanczuk. However, Anne Jumper lost 6-3, 6-1 at the No. 2 singles spot. Staff Photos Carolina Romanczuk celebrates with Arianna Kortum after winning in three sets against Alameda, including winning five straight games in the first and third sets. Emma Eisemon and Cecilia DeFazio (not pictured) had wins over Alameda and Castro Valley as the No. 2 doubles team. Tanya Kononova won against Castro Valley, St. Mary’s and Alameda at No. 1 singles.
