articles.text: Piedmont’s boys and girls’ cross-country teams competed last weekend in the prestigious 74th annual Mt. Sac Invitational in Walnut in Southern California on Friday, October 21. The boys’ team placed 10th of 20 schools. The girls also were 10th in a field of 11 teams. The Mt. Sac Invitational is sponsored by Nike and located at Mt. San Antonio College and brings together thousands of runners from middle schools, high schools, and colleges. Senior Christian Taylor led the way with a time of 15:57 to finish 16th of 133 runners. Behind him in 27th was senior Parker Long with a time of 16:10 and junior Julien Lee finished in 16:31 in 48th. Junior Xander Schulte-Sasse returned after missing the previous meet, running to a 54th place finish with a time of 16:37. Rounding out their best five was sophomore Evan Byun in 89th, 17:29. Junior Jamie Schwarz led the girls’ squad by finishing 17th of 83 runners with a time of 20:53. Behind her was freshman Skylar Best continuing her strong debut year by finishing 24th with a time of 21:24. Freshman Cora Chun placed 34th, clocking a time of 21:45. Rounding out the top five were two more freshmen, Quincy Antaya and Ella Kwong. Who placed 61 and 62 with times of 23:08 and 23:09. The Western Alameda County Conference League Championship meet takes place in a week, on Saturday, November 5 at Hayward High. PHS then will compete in the North Coast Section Championship also at Hayward. The top three teams in Piedmont’s Division 4 will qualify for the CIF State Meet in Fresno. NEXT UP Piedmont is set to run at the WACC Championship meet at Hayward High on November 5. Races start 9:00 a.m. Christian Taylor led the way for Piedmont with a time of 15:57 to finish 16th of 133 runners. Quincy Antaya is one of four freshmen on the varsity team.

articles.text: Piedmont’s volleyball team had its season come to an end on Wednesday, October 19 at San Leandro with a victory in three sets, 25-11, 27-25, 25-23. “Just having the team come together and having them focus on team and personal goals. Just reminding that throughout the set of what they can do. It was a really close game; San Leandro’s effort on that side was why it was as close as it was. It was a lot of fun to watch,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. Piedmont compiled a record of 10-14 overall and 4-8 in league, and in spite of the record, marked an improvement from last year when the Highlanders finished 3-12 overall. “I wasn’t with the team last year, but I was around the team. They only won a few games throughout the season, we didn’t have a lot of different players, so it was a huge stride,” sad Cardenas. It marked the final appearance for seniors Bree DeYoung, Lila Town, Tara Kothari, Shelby Cavenaugh, and Eden Lorin. “This year, we have a lot of juniors who got experience. Last year was a building for us and we got to put more pieces into play this year,” said Lorin. In the wake of the Class of 2023, Piedmont will move ahead with players Izzy Grimmer, Maddy Mullin, Elena Stevens, Bauer and Beck Peterson, Molly Wagener, Klara Zietlow and leading outside hitter Sadie Town. “A lot of our seniors are important, so it’ll be interesting to see how their spots get filled up and what the coaches decide. But I’m excited, it’ll be good,” said Town. Game Recap In the first set, Piedmont led narrowly 5-4 but then scored six straight points to go ahead 12-4 and then but put up another eight straight points to lead 20-5. The runs included three aces by Lila Town and kills by Sadie Town, Kothari, Bauer Peterson. DeYoung closed out the set with a block to win 25-11. Photo by Korte Lee Eden Lorin had six kills and two serving aces in her final appearance at Piedmont. In the second set, San Leandro led 6-5 but conceded six straight points for PHS to lead 11-6. From there, SLHS scored four straight to make it 11-10, but PHS powered four straight to lead 15-10. The Highlanders led 21-15, but allowed eight of the next nine points to fall behind 23-22. But from there, PHS pulled ahead 24-23 with a kill by Lorin and ace by Sadie Town to gain set point, but SL tied 25-25. Piedmont closed with the next two points due to an attacking and defensive error by the Pirates. In the final set, PHS battled to a 9-7 lead after starting out in a 4-1 deficit, but San Leandro briefly regained the lead at 10-9. From there, Piedmont scored eight of the next 12 points to lead 18-14. After a few points by San Leandro, PHS scored five of the next eight to lead 23-20. The Pirates battled to a one-point deficit at 24-23, but Cavenaugh killed the game with a mighty spike. Final stats include: Lorin with six kills and two aces. Sadie Town had seven kills, one block, and three aces. Kothari had five kills. DeYoung had five kills, two blocks, and an ace. Cavenaugh had six kills and one block. articles.text: Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team won big against St. Patrick in Vallejo on Friday, October 21. The 51-12 win was one-sided affair by halftime, led by running back and linebacker Tommy Ashton, running back Brandon Dicke, and quarterback Vincent Arbit who threw two touchdowns passes and rushed for one. “We just got back to basics on offense,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “Tommy ran for about 150 yards in the first half. We were up a lot by halftime so people who hadn’t played much saw some action. It was a good response to the team’s 22-14 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on October 14 following their multiple week stoppage after the varsity team canceled the rest of its season. “It was a good game for us to have after having had so much time off and no one was happy with how the O’Dowd game ended,” said Seiden. The defense had a positive day with multiple turnovers and sacks by Brandon Dicke, Arman Kazemi, and Ashton. “Defensively, we had three interceptions, a fumble recovery, and around 4-5 sacks. We lost containment on a couple of plays for touchdowns, but other than that, the guys came to play,” said Seiden. Seiden indicated that he was able to get all of the players some time on the field against St. Patrick. “Brandon was all over the place making tackles. Dash played well, Adrian K played well as a freshman as an offensive and defensive linemen. We got everybody on the team time on the field and everyone contributed,” said Seiden. Seiden also had praise for freshman Albert Bellingrath for Staff Photos Miguel Long had a big game as a receiver and defensive back. his contributions at tight end after originally being listed as an offensive and defensive lineman. “Albert Bellingrath had a couple of nice catches after never really playing tight end before. He made good catches and did well in blocking,” said Seiden. At quarterback Arbit didn’t commit any turnovers and was part of three touchdowns “Vince Arbit had a good game. He took care of the ball really well, and didn’t make any mistakes,” said Seiden. Touchdowns were scored by Worthen, Dicke, Ashton, Jason Shum, Arbit. Interceptions were recorded by Miles Silver and Miguel Long, who also had a big day as a receiver. “Miguel was going crazy. He had a couple of nice receptions on fade balls and also had a big interception. It was a fun to see him play, it’s such a confidence booster when you see kids apply what they do in practice in games,” said Seiden. articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek is celebrating Halloween with a green twist. Visit the gardens on Sunday, October 30, for “Aloe-ween.” Dress up in costume for this family-friendly event, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Dogs on leash are welcome. Kids activities There will be a pumpkin scavenger hunt for kids. Find all the hidden pumpkins in the gardens, and win a prize. Story time read-alouds in both Spanish and English, hosted by the Contra Costa Library, will take place at 10:30 a.m. Kids will enjoy a visit from staff at Papaya Pythons. Herpetologists will teach audiencemembers about reptiles and amphibians and how important they are to their retrospective ecosystems. There will also be a visit from the garden’s resident “Cactus Lady.” Costume contest A youth and family-focused costume contest will be conducted - costumed pets are welcome, too. To enter: 1. Post a picture of you or your furry friends in their costume 2. Tag the garden on Instagram at @ruthbancroftgardennursery @ruthbancroftgarden 3. Hashtag your photo - #2022Aloeween To RSVP, visit https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/ event/2022-aloe-ween/. The event is free and open to all. You can also call the gardens directly at (925) 944-9352 to reserve tickets. “Aloe-ween” and the popular costume contest returns this Halloween to Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek. articles.text: City Council member Betsy Andersen makes cameo appearance in Ferdinand the Bull Piedmont’s hometown orchestra will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday afternoon, November 6, at 4 p.m. Conducted by Martha Stoddard and Sue Crum, the orchestra will perform the rarely heard Overture to Johann Albrecht’s comedy Der Teufel als Hydraulicus, composed by Franz Schubert when he was just 14. Other music includes the delightful Romanian Dances, by Bela Bartok, and Mozart’s orchestral masterpiece, Symphony No. 40 in G minor, composed during some of the artist’s darkest days. The compositions finds its way from the turbulence of the beginning sections into the triumph of the conclusion. As a special audience treat, the humorous musical piece, Ferdinand the Bull by Alan Ridout, based on the children’s story of the same name by American author Munro Leaf, will be performed by violinist Joseph Gold, with narration by Piedmont native and City Council member Betsy Andersen. It is the story of a bull who would rather smell the flowers than be in bullfights. The work Photo by Julie Reichle Piedmont City Council member Betsy Andersen will make her musical debut on November 6. was banned by both Hitler and the Spanish Fascists as “degenerate democratic propaganda.” Admission is free. Doors open at 3:30 p.m. Piedmont Center for the Art is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue at Bonita Avenue. Street parking is available.
articles.title: Piedmont Orchestra in Nov. 6 concert at PCA

articles.text: Cloud Gate Dance Theatre of Taiwan will perform this weekend on October 29 and 30 at Zellerbach Hall in a presentation by Cal Performances. The contemporary dance group performs “13 Tongues” (2016), a work by Theatre Artistic Director Cheng Tsung-lung. “13 Tongues” translates the director’s childhood memories of living in Taipei, Taiwan into a choreographed “fantasy world”, with a distinctive blend of contemporary dance, ballet, martial arts, and qigong that set Cloud Gate Dance Theatre apart from other troupes. Expect to see eclectic and vibrant coloring and costume. Accompanying music is by Lim Giong. “13 Tongues” includes music whose genres range from Taiwanese folk songs Cloud Gate Dance Theatre of Taiwan to Taoist chants to electronica. articles.text: The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday afternoon, October 30, at 1:30 p.m. Tickets are available at: https:// bit.ly/3TpKMUZ. The quartet of Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Beethoven’s Opus 132, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. Beethoven’s String Quartet in A minor, opus 132, is from his collection of “late” quartets, written in the final years of his life. In these works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. The quartet will also perform Caroline Shaw’s Valencia, and Mozart’s “Dissonance” String Quartet in C Major, K465. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco is dedicated to bringing chamber music masterworks to diverse audiences. CMS of SF is passionate about concertizing in intimate settings, creating close connections between performers and listeners, and cultivating a relationship between music and audiences that extends far beyond the perimeter of the concert hall. Drawing listeners into the lives of the composers and the world of the music, CMS of SF concerts are a favorite destination for both chamber music lovers and those new to the genre. Members of CMS of SF can be heard performing with San Francisco Symphony, SF Opera, SF Ballet, San Francisco and New Century Chamber Orchestras, American Bach Soloists, Oakland Symphony and many others. The four founding members came together through their mutual love of the late Beethoven String Quartets. Collaborations have included artists such as Kay Stern, Stephen Prutsman, Jean-Michel Fonteneau, and Jodi Levitz. For more information, see: www.chambermusicsocietysf.org The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday afternoon, October 30, at 1:30 p.m. Pictured are Natasha Makhijani (left), Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton. articles.text: San Francisco Symphony celebrates Dia de los Muertos with festivities and performances on Saturday, November 5. This is the Symphony’s 15th annual celebration of the Day of the Dead, a sacred and ancestral holiday celebrated in Latin America and most widely-celebrated in Mexico. The holiday centers around prayer and remembrance of friends and family members who have died, and includes traditional dance, feast, and costume. Festivities begin at 12:45 p.m., and the concert at 2 p.m. The program includes Sensemayá by Silvestre Revueltas; Kauyumari by Gabriela Ortiz; Concierto de Otoño by Arturo Márquez; Santa Cruz de Pacairigua by Evencio Castellanos Yumar; Danzón No. 2 by Arturo Márquez; and Huapango by José Pablo Moncayo García. Carlos Miguel Preito conducts the symphony, which will open with an Aztec neon serpent procession featuring Casa Circulo Cultural and Cancion de Obsidiana. Trumpet soloist Pacho Flores will accompanies the symphony. To purchase tickets visit www. sfsymphony.org/dia, or call the box office at (415) 864-6000. Tickets are half off for children and young adults under the age of 18.

articles.text: Jason Klein, conductor of the Saratoga Symphony Babe Ruth made more money than the President of the United States. When a journalist asked him how he could justify that, the Babe said simply: “I had a better year than the president.“ Things have certainly changed since then. Salaries earned by big-name sports personalities are in the millions. But in the 1800s, it was the opera singers and classical musicians who made the millions, not sports figures. The great opera singer Jenny Lind made more money than anybody else. Her manager was “the great showman” PT Barnum. It is interesting to note that she demanded her money in advance – before she sang a note. The date was 1850. In 1905 the popular violinist Jan Kubelik made $500,000 in one season in the U.S. Compare that with the peanuts major league baseball players were paid. It is also interesting to note that at that time there was no difference between what we call “pop music“ and classical music. The public flocked to the classical music concerts. The most popular composer of the era was Stephen Foster, whose music was popular all over the world and was translated into many languages. It is sad to note that Stephen Foster died completely destitute. He needed a good lawyer. Food on the music trail If you take a short holiday trip to the Mother Lode in California, you can relive some of those exciting days of yore. You can visit the town of Jenny Lind, named for the great opera singer. Curiously she never came to California. It doesn’t matter where you go – all the towns are interesting and you can find good food everywhere. Be sure to go to the antique shops. Antique jewelry is almost always at bargain prices. Here is another tip: Get off the main street and go to some of the side streets and the back streets. Look at the architecture. Imagine yourself living during those heady days of the 19th Century and early 20th Century. Honor to Ukraine Last Sunday my wife and I went south to hear the Saratoga Symphony conducted by Jason Klein. I have always appreciated the conducting of Dr. Klein. He is a perfect example of an orchestra conductor inspiring his orchestra to play above their ability. In addition, his pre-concert words are not only informative, but they are very amusing. The concert was entitled “Honor to Ukraine”. Dr. Klein explained everything in his inimitable way. Four Ukrainian national composers were featured on the program. Three of them were virtually unknown to this critic, and the orchestra played in inspiring fashion. A piano concerto by Sergei Bortkiewicz featured dynamic playing by pianist Ron Brickman. It was like Rachmaninoff with shades of Wagner. In addition, there was a real swagger to the music. The result was invigorating. All in all, it was a unique program featuring a fine orchestra, a dynamic pianist and a superlative conductor. Some fan mail for Center for the Arts Last week a number of Piedmont residents told me how much they appreciate everything at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. You can’t beat the admission price, AND they frequently feed you. You can always find a parking space. And the quality of the entertainment is fantastic. Art included.

articles.text: Youth Musical Theater Company (YMTC) opens its 18th season with Matilda the Musical, with performances November 4–13 at the Malonga Casquelourd Center for the Arts in downtown Oakland. Roald Dahl’s beloved story of an extraordinary little girl is brought to dazzling, high-energy, and hilarious life in Matilda the Musical. Overlooked and unloved by her parents and bullied at school by the cruel Headmistress Trunchbull, 6-year-old genius Matilda finds solace in stories – in the pages of the books she devours and the tales that come tumbling out of her mind. With the help of a vivid imagination, her kind teacher Miss Honey, and an army of rebellious schoolchildren, Matilda decides to change her own story and rewrite her destiny. Matilda the Musical pays perfect tribute to the absurd humor and profound heart of Roald Dahl’s original story. The book was written by internationally acclaimed playwright Dennis Kelly, and the music and lyrics by Tim Minchin (Groundhog Day the Musical). Matilda premiered in the UK in 2011 and on Broadway in 2013, winning five Tony Awards, as well as more than 50 international awards, including the Olivier for Best New Musical. The show features a cast of 26 student performers and five apprentices (ages 12–18) from cities throughout the Bay Area. Dahlia Saffouri, a 10th grader at Piedmont High School, plays the role of a “Big Kid” and is the understudy for Mrs. Wormwood. They are led by a team of professional directors, designers, and musicians, including Directors Jennifer Boesing and Celeste Kamiya, Music Directors Diana Lee and Eric Walton, and Choreographer Nicole Helfer. The production features an 11-piece orchestra playing the original musical score. Matilda opens Friday November 4, with 7:30 p.m. performances on November 4-5 and November 11-12). Two matinee performances at 2 p.m. are scheduled for Sundays on November 6 and 13. Tickets are available online at www.ymtcbayarea.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Ticket prices are $16–$34, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. YMTC history YMTC is dedicated to providing exceptional training to young Dahlia Saffouri of Piedmont is in the YMTC production of Matilda. theater artists through the production of exceptional musical theater. The organization brings together the Bay Area’s most talented and dedicated young performers – as well as students of technical theater – with professional directors, designers, choreographers and musicians. They take on challenging and sophisticated musical and dramatic themes. Productions are always accompanied by a full, live orchestra. YMTC takes young artists on adventures that will inspire them for the rest of their lives Addison Au performs the lead role of Matilda in the show of the same name by Youth Musical Theater Company.

articles.text: Exhibit at Center for the Arts celebrates society’s 108th anniversary The California Society of Printmakers will be celebrating its 108th anniversary with an exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, with an opening reception on Friday, November 11 from 6:00 until 9:00 p.m. The exhibition features the work of more than 80 printmakers and highlights a wide variety of printmaking techniques, including serigraphs, monotypes, lithographs, etchings, woodcuts, and aquatints. The talented artists represent CSP members from throughout California. Some examples of the myriad of forms of printmaking you can see on display, include Oakland artist Luz Marina Ruiz, whose displayed work is a handmade artist Tunnel Book. Within the three-dimensional work, Luz incorporates linocuts embellished with watercolor and gouache on BFK paper. Another artist, Toru Sugita from Albany, depicts the changing or transitional monuments of the Bay Area using his own photographs and sketches of his surroundings to capture these spaces and textures through screen printing. Alicia Persaud, from Santa Roxanne Sexauer, Carnival Ostinato IV, Relief, Monoserigraph, Stencil, Chine Collé, BFK Rives, grey, 11.5” x 15.5”, 2022 Cruz, also creates work influenced by their environment. In her work on display she uses photo-intaglio with digital chine collé, to generate both sharp and blurred qualities layered together. She describes her process as, “depicting movement and motion of my memories both aesthetically through the imagery as well as emotionally through the physicality of the photo intaglio-process itself, highlighting how memories often blend together and change over time”. Some printmakers like Katherine Levin Lau from San Jose create images by hand painting on a zinc plate and then running the piece through the press many times. In Katherine’s detailed and dreamy scenes of nature, the original paintings are monochromatic. She enhances them with color layers using viscosity techniques. A final example of the breadth of techniques that will be on view is a work from Los Angeles artist Roxanne Sexauer, who utilizes a combination of printing methods including relief, monoserigraph, stencil, and chine collé to develop rich layers of abstract images. Only a small sampling of the unique work has been described here. To see these and more than 80 other visually compelling prints, visit the display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue at the corner of Bonta Avenue. The exhibit will be on view Saturdays and Sundays from November 6 to November 27. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. For more information visit http://www. piedmontcenterforthearts.org/ or http://www.caprintmakers.org/. pages.text: Wednesday, October 26, 2022 19 California Printmakers exhibit comes to Piedmont Exhibit at Center for the Arts celebrates society’s 108th anniversary The California Society of Printmakers will be celebrating its 108th anniversary with an exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, with an opening reception on Friday, November 11 from 6:00 until 9:00 p.m. The exhibition features the work of more than 80 printmakers and highlights a wide variety of printmaking techniques, including serigraphs, monotypes, lithographs, etchings, woodcuts, and aquatints. The talented artists represent CSP members from throughout California. Some examples of the myriad of forms of printmaking you can see on display, include Oakland artist Luz Marina Ruiz, whose displayed work is a handmade artist Tunnel Book. Within the three-dimensional work, Luz incorporates linocuts embellished with watercolor and gouache on BFK paper. Another artist, Toru Sugita from Albany, depicts the changing or transitional monuments of the Bay Area using his own photographs and sketches of his surroundings to capture these spaces and textures through screen printing. Alicia Persaud, from Santa Roxanne Sexauer, Carnival Ostinato IV, Relief, Monoserigraph, Stencil, Chine Collé, BFK Rives, grey, 11.5” x 15.5”, 2022 Cruz, also creates work influenced by their environment. In her work on display she uses photo-intaglio with digital chine collé, to generate both sharp and blurred qualities layered together. She describes her process as, “depicting movement and motion of my memories both aesthetically through the imagery as well as emotionally through the physicality of the photo intaglio-process itself, highlighting how memories often blend together and change over time”. Some printmakers like Katherine Levin Lau from San Jose create images by hand painting on a zinc plate and then running the piece through the press many times. In Katherine’s detailed and dreamy scenes of nature, the original paintings are monochromatic. She enhances them with color layers using viscosity techniques. A final example of the breadth of techniques that will be on view is a work from Los Angeles artist Roxanne Sexauer, who utilizes a combination of printing methods including relief, monoserigraph, stencil, and chine collé to develop rich layers of abstract images. Only a small sampling of the unique work has been described here. To see these and more than 80 other visually compelling prints, visit the display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue at the corner of Bonta Avenue. The exhibit will be on view Saturdays and Sundays from November 6 to November 27. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. For more information visit http://www. piedmontcenterforthearts.org/ or http://www.caprintmakers.org/. Katherine Levin Lau. “Seahorse with Speckled Leaves” Monotype, 22” X 30”, 2021 Luz Marina Ruiz, Ultramarino, Tunnel Book, Linocut with watercolor and gouache on BFK, 12” x 6” x 8.5”, 2021 Piedmont Center for the Arts Come enjoy the many music events in the next month, and stay for an art exhibit. Sunday, October 30, 1:30 p.m. Chamber Music Society of S.F. Opening its 10th anniversary season with a return to Beethoven’s Opus 132, String Quartet in A minor, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago, CMS of SF will also perform Mozart’s Dissonance String Quartet in C Major and Caroline Shaw’s Valencia. Get your tickets now at https://bit. ly/3TpKMUZ for this 90-minute season-opening concert which was postponed from September 17. Saturday, November 5, 5:00 p.m. Ambroš Duo concert The Ambroš Duo, a renowned mother-son music duo from the capital city of Prague in the Czech Republic will perform a concert featuring works by Mozart, Sarasate, and Czech composers Dvořák and Smetana, among others. The concert will conclude with the lively “Monti Czardas.” A light reception to meet the artists follows. This concert is co-sponsored by the Czech and Slovak cultural associations Sokol San Francisco, BayCzech and the Czech School of California. Tickets are $20 at https://bit. ly/3yO9i9t. Sunday, November 6, 11a.m.–2:30 p.m. Opening of CA Printmakers exhibit The California Society of Printmakers returns for their 108th anniversary exhibition, a show that will include more than 80 works by members of the of the oldest continually operating association of printmakers in the United States. CSP is a non-profit arts organization with an international membership of print artists and supporters of the art of fine printmaking. The show will be open to the public on Saturdays and Sundays through November 27, from 11 a.m.–2:30 p.m. Free. There will be an opening reception on Friday, November 11 from 6 to 9 p.m. Sunday, November 6, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Piedmont’s own orchestra presents a varied and unusual program for its Fall concert, conducted by Sue Crum and Martha Stoddard. The rarely heard Overture to Johann Albrecht’s comedy Der Teufel als Hydraulicus, composed by Franz Schubert at age 14, opens the concert, followed by Béla Bartók’s delightful Romanian Folk Dances. Concertmaster Joseph Gold will perform Ferdinand the Bull, a lighthearted piece based on Munro Leaf’s children’s story. The guest narrator is Peidmontn City Council member Betsy Andersen. The concludes with Mozart’s orchestral masterpiece, Symphony No. 40 in G minor. Thanks to an anonymous underwriter, the concert is being offered free to the public. articles.text: Review by Chris Honore’ Last Chance Harvey uses a familiar template that Hollywood has often turned to – estranged father attends daughter’s wedding and after a series of unexpected events, both comedic and dramatic, he finds redemption. What makes Harvey entertaining is not the story, but the fine performances of Dustin Hoffman and Emma Thompson. Both are charming and delightful to watch and raise this film to a new level by their sheer acting ability. They meet in a London bar. When they begin their hesitant, quasi-hostile dance of getting acquainted, they are so engaging it’s impossible not to conclude that Last Chance Harvey is very much a film that possesses a nice glow. At the outset, using deft parallel editing, we are introduced to Harvey Shine and Kate Walker and discover that they are both lonely people. Harvey has lost his job and seemingly his daughter, and Kate is convinced that she is defined by her age and seeming isolation. Without realizing it, they set out to prove others wrong. About so many things. Watching them interact, first as strangers and then as friends, is to observe two consummate actors who can look into the camera and with a look, a smile, a raise of the eyebrows say volumes. It males it hard to bid these two likable people adieu as the credits begin to roll. Last Chance Harvey. Directed by Joel Hopkins. Starring Dustin Hoffman, Emma Thompson, James Brolin and Kathy Baker. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2009. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. Dustin Hoffman and Emma Thompson star in Last Chance Harvey.

articles.text: Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball is about Lucy Harris, arguably the greatest women’s basketball player. A free screening of two Academy Award winning shorts on Title IX, Queen of Basketball and Mink, will be shown on Thursday, November 3 at 7 p.m. at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on the Havens School campus, 325 Highland Avenue. • Queen of Basketball Lucy Harris scored the first basket in Olympic women’s basketball and was drafted by the NBA. If not for Title IX, she couldn’t have gone to college and had either opportunity. In The Queen of Basketball, Lucy tells her own story, from being “too tall and that’s all” to finding her place in sports. The film won an Academy Award in 2022 as Best Short Documentary. • Mink! Ironically, TitIe IX almost didn’t pass because one of its key sponsors, Patsy Mink, was called away for a family emergency. Mink! tells the story of Rep. Patsy Mink’s path as the first woman of color to serve in Congress, and the crucial role she played in the passage of Title IX. The two films will be followed by a conversation with Chelle Putzer and Eva Phalen of the Piedmont Recreation Department. Masks are required. Mink! focuses on Patsy Takemoto Mink, the first woman of color elected to Congress. Title IX is the federal legislation that prohibits sex-based discrimination in any school or other education program that receives federal funding. articles.text: Mulberry’s switching to compostables Mulberry’s is going green. Piedmont’s popular, one-andonly market is now using compostable utensils and is “slowly transitioning” from plastic to compostable cups and deli containers. According to General Manager Sal Viveros, compostable utensils replaced plastic six weeks ago, and compostable cups and deli containers are on order. But, he said, “there’s a supply chain problem. We expect deli containers to arrive in three to four weeks, but the coffee cups may take three to four months.” Viveros estimates Mulberry’s uses a total of 1,000 coffee cups and deli containers a week. The costs for compostable, he says, are almost 35% to 40% higher than the costs of plastic, up from 18 to 25 cents per cup to 30 to 40 cents. “Right now, we’re absorbing the cost, but eventually, we’ll have to pass it on to customers,” he said. “Plastic clamshell containers used for takeout salads are harder to replace,” he said, “because it’s difficult to find a vendor. Eighty percent of the market’s straws are now compostable, except for slushies, which still use plastic because of vendor supply.” Mulberry’s leftover food that is still edible – breads, salads, sushi, anything that cannot be sold the next day – is picked up every day and donated to homeless shelters, schools and other organizations. The market uses Republic Services to recycle its bottles, cans and cardboard, and for composting its food waste. While Mulberry’s offers organic and non-organic products, many packaged goods on the store shelves still come wrapped in plastic. Viveros agrees with the City’s Mulberry’s Market General Manager Sal Viveros. Staff photo goal to have the market transition to 100 percent compostable and biodegradable materials. “It’s what I want to leave for my kids,” he said. He also credits the market’s barista, Jill Ohaviano, for encouraging the transition to compostable materials. “She’s been a tremendous help,” he said. “Eventually, probably a year from now, we will be 100 percent zero waste,” Viveros predicted. Alyssa Dykman, the city of Piedmont’s Sustainability Manager, is delighted with Mulberry’s transition. “I’m thrilled to see a Piedmont local business working to incorporate sustainability into their business practices,” she said, “as well as leveraging resources to reduce food waste and help address food insecurity. People often don’t realize how much food they throw away every day that could be eaten or repurposed. As the sole grocery store in Piedmont, Mulberry’s has an important role in the community.” Dykman notes that the City itself is striving to become more sustainable. “Last December, the Sustainable Procurement Policy was updated to minimize the City’s contribution to solid waste disposal, pollution and climate change through its purchases and practices. Since then “we’ve seen an increase in green waste materials collected and diverted from the landfill,” she added. Piedmont’s Sustainability Division also helps residents reduce their own carbon footprint through City sponsored programs such as the Piedmont Climate Challenge, the induction cooktop lending program, compost giveaways at the Corporation Yard, and an upcoming pilot program for home electrification rebates. The city’s environmental actions are supported and enhanced by Piedmont Connect, a community volunteer organization that advocates for City and School District sustainability policies and raises awareness of actions Piedmonters can take to reduce their impact on climate change. Marjorie Blackwell is a Board Member of Piedmont Connect, a collaborative community organization supporting resident initiatives and city efforts to build a sustainable future. For resources and questions, visit the city website: www.piedmontconnect.org.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is providing residents with a free pickup of compost from the Corporation Yard at Moraga Avenue and Red Rock Road this Saturday, October 29 from 9 a.m. to 12 noon. All households may pick up one cubic yard of compost while supplies last. Preorders are not available. Bring shovels, gloves, and container(s) for the compost. Piedmont Public Works staff will be available to operate a backhoe to lift larger quantities of compost into the back of trucks. While not required, it is strongly encouraged that residents indicate their estimated pick up time on Saturday on the form here: https:// docs.google.com /for ms/d /e/ 1FAIpQLSf1ckpa3i08Hx3bmSYZf-cchcX8OFugf 27qLoKczm_7n6RyZA/viewform. The compost comes from yard trimmings and food waste collected by Republic Services communities participating in curbside organics collection services. Mixing compost with your soil adds nutrients to the soil, aids in water retention and pest control, and helps plants thrive. Learn more about the benefits and uses of compost here: https:// www.stopwaste.org/at-work/ built-environment/landscapes/ compost-mulch-and-soil. More information is available on the City’s news and notifications page (https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/city_ news___notifications). Contact the city’s Sustainability Program Manager, Alyssa Dykman, with any questions at: adykman@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Dear Jim: I have noticed recently what looks like mold in the crawlspace under my home. What is causing this and how can I get rid of it? Is it possible that this could be causing health issues for me? I have noticed lately that I have had a lot of allergies and breathing issues I did not have before, and they seem to be getting worse over time. –Fred S. Mold is a common problem under Bay Area homes, and something I see frequently when I’m inspecting crawlspaces and basements. I’m not a mold expert, but the three most common types we see are black mold (most toxic), yellow or orange mold (house eating mold (fortunately rare), and white mold. White mold is fairly common, and fortunately, it is the least toxic of the three. It can still present problems for those with a chronic low-level exposure. Mold spores can infiltrate through floors and ductwork, and can make their way into livCrawlspace mold develops in moist soil due to lack of proper drainage. Black mold is more common in basement walls and bathrooms. ing spaces from down below. What causes this mold? Primarily it is drainage issues that have not been addressed, with water infiltrating through and under old foundations and getting into the dirt areas, and occasionally into walls and floor structures. Less frequently there are leaks in walls around poorly sealed windows and doors, siding or stucco, roofs etc., but it is mostly the subterranean moisture that is the culprit. You may also see a white substance on your foundations known as efflorescence. This is caused by water migrating through the concrete and depositing salts on the surface. Efflorescence is harmless, but it does indicate there are water issues that can lead to mold. There are a few different approaches to solve the problem. Some companies will put in plastic in the crawlspace to encapsulate the soil, along with other measures to control the humidity. From our perspective, this is not ideal as it doesn’t address the source of the problem and mold will continue to grow under the plastic. Proper drainage is the best first-line defense, consisting of French Drains and downspout drainage along with appropriate ventilation, keeping the water away from your building and improving air circulation. Over time these spaces will dry out and will no longer be breeding grounds for mold. We have had clients report back that their health issues have improved significantly after appropriate drainage is installed, which makes us believe we are on the right track. articles.text: Ford Roosevelt in Piedmont discussion on Nov. 16 The Piedmont Seniors are pleased to announce that Ford Roosevelt, grandson of former U.S. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt, and the son of Elliot Roosevelt, will speak at the Piedmont Seniors meeting on Wednesday, November 16 at 11 a.m. at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. Earlier this year Mr. Roosevelt began serving as Executive Director of the USS Potomac, the former Presidential Yacht. The Potomac is permanently docked on the Oakland Estuary at the foot of Clay Street. Ford has worked as a nonprofit executive and educator, and human rights advocate for nearly 40 years. He is an active member of the Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt Institute, and has represented the Roosevelt legacy in several positions, from the National Democratic Party conventions to serving a surrogate speaker in several presidential campaigns. Annually, Mr. Roosevelt awards the Eleanor Roosevelt human rights award with the San Diego United Nations Chapter to deserving Human Rights activists in . Most recently, the award was presented to California Attorney General Xavier Becerra. Ford’s engagement with the USS Potomac is an on-going link to the Roosevelt legacy and the family itself. Mr. Roosevelt will speak to the Piedmont Seniors about his famous grandparents, how FDR’s New Deal impacted the Bay Area, as well as the USS Potomac’s educational mission. Guests are welcome. Please RSVP to jepstein@piedmont. ca.gov to ensure adequate seating. The USS Potomac was the Presidential Yacht under Franklin Delano Roosevelt from 1936 until his death in 1945. The Potomac is now preserved in Oakland as a National Historic Landmark and is the only presidential yacht open to the public.

articles.text: The Wednesday walkers on October 19 included Jennifer Peltzer, Helene Farber, Pat Keller, Jasmine Cai, Fangfang Lai, Winston Lee, Melba Chen, Christine Calliste, Judith Lee, Adrienne Hamlin, Rob Smith, Quincy Dong, Laura Goldman, Phil Witte, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Jim Kuo, Carole Lyons, Mark Davis, Brenda Ferrero, Peter Persoff, Helen Dong, Stella Houston, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Ann Quinby, Lisa Euphrat, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Judy Wang, Mary Hedley, Kat Lang, Ian Morgan, Jim Kellogg, Nadine Guffanti, Elizabeth Richter, Dave DeRoche, Sarah Johnson, Priscilla Wanerus, Mike Gallant, Karin Fetherston, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Fangfang Lai brought her neighbor, Natalie Nussbaum, to walk with the group for the first time. A warm, sunny Wednesday last week may have encouraged a large gathering of 43 walkers and one K-9 best friend to participate in the weekly Walking on Wednesdays. One street the group hadn’t visited in a long time was Littlewood Drive, and going there offered the opportunity to share Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi’s history of Piedmont’s first and probably last manufacturing industry, silk fiber production. Going up Mountain Avenue they passed front yards ready for Halloween with scary house decorations, and one flying a Ukrainian flag. The long line of walkers stopped in the shade where Caperton Avenue runs into Mountain. This spot also gave them the opportunity to look around and see in a front yard a larger than life statue of a distinguished looking gentleman dressed in what looks like a suit made of leaves. The walkers continued their climb on Mountain to Dudley Avenue, and then up to Littlewood. As group photo was taken, Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont silk farm history was told. At the end the end of the 19th century there were only three types of cloth, cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government thought silk could be produced in America, and funded groups to create experimental silk producing stations. It was believed that silk production could provide employment for women, reduce unemployment, and increase family income. In the early 1880s the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society purchased 15 acres of land at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue, where Dudley and Littlewood Avenues are today. The society planted mulberry trees, whose leaves are the principal food of silk worms, and built a two-story, eight-room cocoonery. The locals called it the “Silk Farm.” The trees and this history provided the inspiration for the name of today’s Mulberry’s Market. By 1885 the grove was thriving, and an additional seven acres were purchased. About 100 women were employed. During their lives, silkworms consume 50 times their weight in mulberry leaves. The women harvested and chopped them and fed them to the worms in trays four times a day. The worms reached maturity in 35 days and spun their cocoons. At the Silk Farm the cocoons were fumigated to kill the pupa, softened in hot water, and unreeled as separate silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament up to 300 feet long, almost the length of a football field. Several filaments were spun together to form one silk thread. Natalie Nussbaum and Fangfang Lai said they had visited silk farms on trips to China. The Silk Farm in Piedmont didn’t prosper. The canyon was not warm enough for the worms and the women would not work for less than a dollar a day, while Chinese workers were only paid six cents a day. So, in 1895 the farm closed. The group of walkers descended own Littlewood and its canyon to where the Silk Farm’s mulberry trees had been planted, however no trees survived. The walkers came to the dead-end of Littlewood, but a long driveway continues on. Just before a home’s large gate at the driveway’s end is a surprising, old, red, London telephone booth. Some members of the group had seen it on past visits, but there was still no explanation of how it got there. The group then began tracing its steps and made the climb back up Littlewood. Returning the city center it was all downhill. It had gotten warm, and the walkers were pleased to be returning to the Exedra. For a variety they visited Poplar Way, which doesn’t seem to have any poplar trees, and then on to Lakeview, Sheridan, and Highland Avenue. The two-mile walk was completed in a little over an hour. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Editor: We are writing to enthusiastically endorse Ruchi Medhekar for School Board. As we have the good fortune of being Ruchi’s next-door neighbors, we’ve known her and her family since they moved to Piedmont in 2016. Upon moving in, Ruchi got right to work, helping to organize our neighborhood Fourth of July block party…and she just kept going. While balancing a busy professional life and a growing family, she stepped up to volunteer for the three-year commitment as Beach Parents Organization Vice President and then President. She took on her pandemic-era presidency as a growth opportunity, leading to a hybrid-based approach to community building, and finding creative ways to ease the isolation for both kids and parents. She was able to adjust the role and processes of the BPO to fit our circumstances, intuitively knowing what to prioritize. Her contributions to the BPO, will endure. Ruchi’s character is perfectly suited for a position on the School Board. A scientist by training, she is thoughtful and analytical in her approach to problems. We never hear he complain about an issue; instead, she sets her mind at work to figuring out the problem and then fixing it. We have witnessed her unflappable patience on many occasions, whether it pertains to home, school, or community, and have also marveled at her ability to be able to talk to anyone about a diverse variety of issues. Ruchi believes that a strong sense of belonging, in concert with a high standard of academic excellence, will lift up all of our students. And knowing Ruchi, she’ll still have time for our neighborhood block party in July. Please vote for Ruchi in November. –Leila Hebshi (BPO President 2018-2019) and Peter Udovch
articles.title: Praise for Medhekar from neighbors

articles.text: Editor: When I met Jen Long three years ago, I soon realized that we had more than a few things in common. Neither of us was a California native. We had each moved to Piedmont around the same time and felt welcomed here. Our teenage children, back then, were both high school sophomores. As I got to know Jen better, though, it became clear she was a kindred spirit. She values community service and working to address unmet needs. She is an upstander who leans into civic engagement. She sees the promise and potential of an inclusive Piedmont and is willing to do the necessary work to get us there. Jen won unanimous support when she was appointed to fill a vacant seat on City Council earlier this year. That’s not surprising because she connects easily with others in social and civic leadership spaces. I saw this when Jen partnered with young leaders from Piedmont Middle School to lead a community march. I saw it when she stepped up to serve as co-president of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee and hit the ground running with popular new programming. I also saw it when she managed my School Board campaign. With Jen at the helm, our campaign team meetings were equally strategic and inspirational, setting the stage for success. Jen listens closely and sees beyond the surface. She cares deeply and invests time and brain power to find solutions to challenges. Piedmont needs Jen Long on City Council. She is an effective, informed, and visionary leader. I know she will serve the city well. I am excited to vote for her. I encourage you to vote for her, too. –Veronica Anderson Thigpen
articles.title: Long an upstander who leans into civic engagement

articles.text: Amidst PSATs, college applications and waiting on college admission notifications, we invest in our children’s education because we understand the direct link between a good education and a good future. By extension, we also understand the link between thriving educational institutions and a thriving society. In the last decade, community colleges have played a vital role in California’s economic trajectory by educating and transforming the lives of 2 million students across the state. For us, the Peralta Community College District colleges (Merritt, Laney, Berkeley, and College of Alameda) have been our neighborhood institutions. Whether for high school dual enrollment classes, concurrent enrollment, college credit transfer classes, grandparents’ art classes, language classes, or swimming at the Laney pool, these institutions have been our community’s colleges. In a post-COVID landscape however, where societal effects are not yet fully discernible but are palpably precarious, we need our community colleges to be structurally stronger and more financially stable. We need colleges who will meet students where they are, build their skills, give them hope, create opportunities and transform their lives. In sum, we need Peralta’s colleges to thrive.
articles.title: Re-elect Cindi Reiss for Peralta Community College Board

We need colleges who will meet students where they are, build their skills, give them hope, create opportunities and transform their lives. In sum, we need Peralta’s colleges to thrive. For this reason, I recommend that you re-elect Cindi Reiss for Peralta Community College Board Trustee, Area 5. Cindi was first elected in 2018 with the goal of strengthening and stabilizing Peralta in the areas of finance, governance, and accountability, areas of grave concern for about two decades. In these last four years, Cindi Reiss has achieved much, starting to finally bring Peralta out of its financial hole, including staving off state takeover of the District, moving the District off accreditation probation, and no longer being considered a high risk financial district by FCMAT. But there is still more work that needs to be accomplished. We do not yet know how critical a role community colleges will play in shaping society as longer-term pandemic effects become more manifest; however, as an educator and an accreditation commissioner, Cindi Reiss has the expertise, knowledge, and proven track record to ensure Peralta will be the strong, stable, fiscally responsible district that our communities will very much need. Please join me in voting to re-elect Cindi Reiss on November 8th. –Melissa Wilk Long an upstander who leans into civic engagement Editor: When I met Jen Long three years ago, I soon realized that we had more than a few things in common. Neither of us was a California native. We had each moved to Piedmont around the same time and felt welcomed here. Our teenage children, back then, were both high school sophomores. As I got to know Jen better, though, it became clear she was a kindred spirit. She values community service and working to address unmet needs. She is an upstander who leans into civic engagement. She sees the promise and potential of an inclusive Piedmont and is willing to do the necessary work to get us there. Jen won unanimous support when she was appointed to fill a vacant seat on City Council earlier this year. That’s not surprising because she connects easily with others in social and civic leadership spaces. I saw this when Jen partnered with young leaders from Piedmont Middle School to lead a community march. I saw it when she stepped up to serve as co-president of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee and hit the ground running with popular new programming. I also saw it when she managed my School Board campaign. With Jen at the helm, our campaign team meetings were equally strategic and inspirational, setting the stage for success. Jen listens closely and sees beyond the surface. She cares deeply and invests time and brain power to find solutions to challenges. Piedmont needs Jen Long on City Council. She is an effective, informed, and visionary leader. I know she will serve the city well. I am excited to vote for her. I encourage you to vote for her, too. –Veronica Anderson Thigpen READ IT IN THE POST

articles.text: At 4:17 a.m. on Thursday, October 20, Piedmont Police were notified of the first of four fires that morning believed to have been started by one arsonist. One trash can, a stack of wooden pallets and two different Halloween scarecrows were set on fire. The suspect remains at large. The first call was for a trash can in flames on Grand Avenue in Oakland, which was extinguished by the police. Minutes later at 4:21 a.m. patrolling officers observed multiple wooden pallets on fire in the Ace Hardware parking lot on Grand Avenue. Officers immediately notified the fire department and worked to put the fire out with fire extinguishers to prevent the flames from spreading. “Just before 4:30 a.m., I noticed light flickering on my bedroom windows,” said resident Don Dare of nearby Wildwood Avenue. “I looked out the window to see a raging fire at least 15 feet tall with sparks flying high into the night sky.” Officers were able to extinguish the fire and were later assisted by the Piedmont Fire Department to confirm the fire was out. Later in the morning, Halloween decorations were lit on Photo of a suspect in four arson fires on October 20. fire in the 300 block of Wildwood Avenue and the 100 block of Sierra Avenue. At both sites a scarecrow was set on fire. Police received notification of the Wildwood Avenue fire at 6:55 a.m. and at 7:20 a.m. on Sierra Avenue. The resident on Sierra was able to extinguish the fire himself. Minimal property damage was reported. The photo of a suspect was captured on video at the involved locations. Residents who have any information related to this or video of unusual activity related to the events are asked to contact the Piedmont Police Department at (510) 420-3000. articles.text: Sophie Roberts began work for the City of Piedmont on October 3 as the new Climate Action Fellow in the City’s Sustainability Division. Roberts is working with the City through Climate Corps AmeriCorps, a national fellowship program that places individuals with local governments and nonprofits to advance sustainability programs. Roberts is paid a stipend by AmeriCorps. She takes over the 11-month post held the past year by Annie Wenslow. Piedmont has a long history of young, active, and bright fellows, now being overseen by Alyssa Dykman. The Climate Corps program requires individuals to serve an average of 40 hours a week. More information on the national program is available at Climatecorps.org. Roberts hails from Connecticut and earned her undergraduate degree in Environmental Studies and Global Studies at UC Santa Barbara. Prior to working in Piedmont, she was a Legal Assistant at the environmental law firm of Lozeau Drury in Oakland. Roberts said that she relishes the opportunity to work in a city where there is a strong sense of community. articles.text: There are limitations on Housing Element input by residents Editor: On October 12, the Piedmont Post published two letters stating that the 6th Cycle Housing Element, or implementation thereof, should be subject to a vote of all residents. It is important that Piedmonters understand the limitations on what a vote can accomplish. Planning for the potential addition of up to 587 housing units is an obligation imposed on Piedmont by state and regional entities. The Housing Element must be adopted by the City Council and certified by the state by May 2023. No vote by Piedmont residents can alter this obligation. California Government Code Sections 65100 et seq. state (as applied by Piedmont) that the City’s general plan, of which the Housing Element is a part, is to be created by the City Council, with specified responsibilities assigned to the Planning Commission and the Housing Advisory Committee. The role of Piedmont residents is to provide input to the process; there is no statutory provision that allows residents to accept or reject a Housing Element approved by the City Council. Furthermore, it is unrealistic to believe that useful resident input to a Housing Element of more than 300 pages could be provided via an election ballot. The letters allege that changes to Zone B (allowing duplexes and multi-family dwellings on City-owned land) would constitute reclassification of that zone, thus would require voter approval. The City states otherIn my opinion, the City has the stronger argument based on a straightforward reading of the cited Code Section. Given certain residents’ hope to delay or derail the Housing Element, I believe that the City Council needs to do a better job of assessing all Piedmonters’ desires and concerns with respect to implementation thereof. Such an assessment could be done via a carefully designed, thorough online survey made available to all adult residents, who would receive notice of the survey by email, on the City’s website, and via postal service. The City Council should publish the results of the survey and, if it does its job correctly, should proceed with implementation in a manner that reflects the survey results to the greatest extent possible. –Dana H. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, October 19, 2022 Opinion LETTERS TO THE EDITOR There are limitations on Housing Element input by residents Editor: On October 12, the Piedmont Post published two letters stating that the 6th Cycle Housing Element, or implementation thereof, should be subject to a vote of all residents. It is important that Piedmonters understand the limitations on what a vote can accomplish. Planning for the potential addition of up to 587 housing units is an obligation imposed on Piedmont by state and regional entities. The Housing Element must be adopted by the City Council and certified by the state by May 2023. No vote by Piedmont residents can alter this obligation. California Government Code Sections 65100 et seq. state (as applied by Piedmont) that the City’s general plan, of which the Housing Element is a part, is to be created by the City Council, with specified responsibilities assigned to the Planning Commission and the Housing Advisory Committee. The role of Piedmont residents is to provide input to the process; there is no statutory provision that allows residents to accept or reject a Housing Element approved by the City Council. Furthermore, it is unrealistic to believe that useful resident input to a Housing Element of more than 300 pages could be provided via an election ballot. The letters allege that changes to Zone B (allowing duplexes and multi-family dwellings on City-owned land) would constitute reclassification of that zone, thus would require voter approval. The City states otherwise, citing Piedmont City Code Section 17.02.010.C, which provides that “reclassify” means to change a property from one zone to another, rather than to change regulations within a zone. In my opinion, the City has the stronger argument based on a straightforward reading of the cited Code Section. articles.text: Russian-American author Anastasia Edel, a Piedmont resident, will present a 4-week illustrated lecture titled Russia’s War on Ukraine, with classes starting on Thursday, October 20 at 2:30 p.m. The course is being offered by Osher Lifelong Learning Institute at the University of California in Berkeley, where Edel conducted an eight-week illustrated lecture in 2018 on Understanding Russia, a course that intertwines the country’s political and cultural developments with historical perspectives expressed in film, music, and literature. The last four years have proven to be a busy time for Edel. In 2018 she gave the keynote address at OLLI and to the League of Women Voters in Piedmont on The State of US-Russian Relations. One year later she delivered talks at the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco, the University of Washington, and Berkeley City Club Due in part to the publicity generated by op ed pieces she wrote for the New York Times between February and May this year, she was an invited commentators on CNN MSNBC and Bay Area NBC. In the past five years, six of her guest essays an opinion pieces have appeared in the New York Times, with a spike of interest since Russia began its move to wage war on neighboring Ukraine. . Russia: Putin’s Playground, by Anastasai Edel, was published in 2016. Piedmont author and social historian Anastasia Edel, is teaching a four-week course on the Russia vs. Ukraine war at the University of California in Berkeley through Osher Lifelong Learning Institute The course fee for Russia’s War on Ukraine through OLLI is $90 for the four lectures, each of which will be from 2:30 to 4:00 p.m. on consecutive Thursdays, October 20 to November 10. The course will stream live on the scheduled day and time and will also be recorded. Videos will be available on Friday each week. When Russian missiles struck multiple cities across the sovereign nation of Ukraine in February 2020, Russia became an aggressor bent on destroying a neighboring nation with whom it shares centuries of common past. How did it happen? Why does Putin’s regime refuse to call war “war”? What’s behind Ukrainians’ resilience and Russians’ acquiescence? And where does this all end for Russia, Ukraine, and the world? Edel provided some perspective on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine earlier this year with a lecture at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in April. To register for the current course, click on: https://olli.berkeley.edu/programs/courses/russia%E2%80%99s-war-ukraine. Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel is a writer, social historian, and New York Times contributor. She’s the author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, a concise guide to Russian history, politics and culture.
articles.title: Edel 4-week illustrated lecture on Russia’s War on Ukraine begins tomorrow

articles.text: The official Piedmont Turkey Trot training is well underway, but it’s not too late to start training for the big race on Thanksgiving morning. Below is the training plan for next week. The full plan is on the race website: piedmontturkeytrot.com. Police officer Nicole Bolden (right) with McGruff, the cartoon dog that “takes a bite out of crime,” cheered on runners as they made the turn onto Vista Avenue, during the 2018 Turkey Trot Turkey hats are the norm Thanksgiving morning 2018 in Piedmont. Most importantly, don’t forget to register for the race. This next week we are building on your fitness and running more than walking. The run/ walk program is a great way to allow your body to adjust to running longer distances and as the weeks progress you should be able to run more comfortably for longer periods of time. You will also add in another day of speed work so head over to Witter Field during non-school hours and run four fast laps. These should feel uncomfortably fast and you shouldn’t be able to say more than 1-2 words if you were running with a friend. A good goal is to try to run the same pace the full lap and not go out too fast in the first 100 meters. Trust me, it’s easier said than done. These workouts help us build our speed and stamina for race day. Consistent work week over week will allow you to feel your best on turkey day. WEEK DAY WORKOUT October 24 Monday Run 3 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday 5 min jog warm up 4x 1 lap around Witter track, 2 min break between laps 5 min jog cool down Saturday Run 4 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x

articles.text: Join Fire Chief Brannigan for citywide drill on November 5 Many Piedmonters vividly remember the 1991 Tunnel Fire in the Oakland hills, which killed 25 people and destroyed more than 2,500 homes. While Piedmont escaped the devastation 26 years ago the threat is more present now because of climate change, which has made wildfires more frequent and destructive. As your Fire Chief, I strive daily to ensure our City government is poised to protect this community in a disaster. In an emergency, the best efforts of public agencies alone will not be enough. Our community needs to be ready for wildfire, and can do so with three simple steps. 1. First, make first responders can reach you in a disaster. If you aren’t yet registered for AC Alert emergency notifications, sign up now. Piedmont and Alameda County public safety officials will use AC Alert to send evacuation warnings and orders in a fire, earthquake, or other emergency. Visit acalert.org or text your zip code to 888777 to register. Bookmark community.zonehaven.com on your computer and phone. In a wildfire, emergency responders will use this site to post real-time, location-specific evacuation instructions and updates. 2. Everyone should do pack or refresh a “go-bag.” In a wildfire, you could have only moments to leave. Everyone in your household should have a go-bag ready with the items they’ll need if they had to evacuate, like a map, cash, and a paper list of phone numbers for essential contacts. articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has released a video identifying the underlying causes of California’s constant public school funding battles. A short film explains explains how the 1978 passage of Proposition 13 resulted in California having one of the country’s lowest public school funding levels, and why this structural deficit creates a constant struggle for public school funding. The video can be viewed at www.piedmontedfoundation.org. The thoughtful, polished film has all the hallmarks of a highcost presentation from a professional marketing company but was nearly free for PEF. The Palo Alto School Unified District’s Partners in Education foundation created the original video. They then open-sourced it, allowing any California education foundation to customize and use it for a very minimal cost. “Palo Alto is so invested in helping to strengthen the Bay Area’s educational foundations,” says PEF director Heather Frank. “Not only was their idea brilliant, but it also allowed us to develop an educational video for the Giving Campaign that we wouldn’t have been able to afford otherwise. That support is so helpful.” The Giving Campaign is PEF’s largest annual fundraiser, a yearly effort that helps the Piedmont Unified School District combat the gaps created by California’s chronic underfunding of public schools. This year’s campaign aims to raise $3.5 million for Piedmont’s students. Piedmont is not alone in the need for public school fundraising. Because of California’s ongoing school funding crisis, many public school districts have formed their own education foundations similar to PEF. Their misData on state-by-state school funding levels.

Foundation debuts educational video Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has released a video identifying the underlying causes of California’s constant public school funding battles. A short film explains explains how the 1978 passage of Proposition 13 resulted in California having one of the country’s lowest public school funding levels, and why this structural deficit creates a constant struggle for public school funding. The video can be viewed at www.piedmontedfoundation.org. The thoughtful, polished film has all the hallmarks of a highcost presentation from a professional marketing company but was nearly free for PEF. The Palo Alto School Unified District’s Partners in Education foundation created the original video. They then open-sourced it, allowing any California education foundation to customize and use it for a very minimal cost. “Palo Alto is so invested in helping to strengthen the Bay Area’s educational foundations,” says PEF director Heather Frank. “Not only was their idea brilliant, but it also allowed us to develop an educational video for the Giving Campaign that we wouldn’t have been able to afford otherwise. That support is so helpful.” The Giving Campaign is PEF’s largest annual fundraiser, a yearly effort that helps the Piedmont Unified School District combat the gaps created by California’s chronic underfunding of public schools. This year’s campaign aims to raise $3.5 million for Piedmont’s students. Piedmont is not alone in the need for public school fundraising. Because of California’s ongoing school funding crisis, many public school districts have formed their own education foundations similar to PEF. Their misPhotos by Katie Sharafi PMS students supporting the Giving Campaign: Sai Ahuja (left), Lettie Moore, Violet Snyder, and Ellia Sharafi. Data on state-by-state school funding levels. The best quality in all departments Serving our community for 120 years CURRENT STORE HOURS Monday through Saturday – 9:00 am to 8:00 pm Sunday – 9:00 am to 7:00 pm Piedmont Avenue • Oakland, California 94611 • 510-653-8181 Open Seven Days • Free Parking PMS students walking to school: Ben Gitter (left), Rory Hull, and Spencer Lee Tsai. sion is to provide the economic support required to give students a high-quality education beyond the bare-bones elements funded by the state. PEF is part of a group of such organizations, the Bay Area Education Foundations (BAEF) consortium. The 36-member group collaborates in numerous ways, from annual round table discussions to facilitating communication among members to address questions and share policies. Upcoming topics include teacher retention and declining enrollment, both state-wide issues. “It’s a lovely collaboration between all the foundations,” says Giving Campaign co-chair Katie Sharafi. “And a great example of that is the Palo Alto foundation sharing their work with other districts.” PEF also contributes to the consortium, sharing policy and contract structures and its experience on more cutting-edge issues, such as school support organization fiscal sponsorships. “Because we’ve done the work on many things, we can share and help strengthen other education foundations,” says Frank. PEF’s primary purpose continues to be its critical fundraising work for Piedmont schools. “Raising this much money every year is a huge endeavor, and public school districts don’t have the personnel and expertise to put on major fundraising campaigns,” explains Frank. “And because the foundation is separate from the school district, PEF can reflect community priorities when deciding how to distribute funds.” And as the video makes clear, public schools throughout California will continue to contend with funding challenges until the issues underlying the deficits are rectified. “Piedmont is not alone in this fundraising experience,” says Giving Campaign co-chair Sharafi. “All California’s public school districts are trying to find creative ways to fill their funding gaps.” To learn more about the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign or to donate, please visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org.

articles.text: Last summer a cohort of Chabot’s Galaxy Explorer high school students worked at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley as part of a larger partnership between NASA Ames and Chabot Space & Science Center in Oakland. The full-time internships placed each student in a department for project work and close mentorship by NASA staff. Students were paired with scientists and staff based on their interests and future career paths. For Piedmont High senior Sage Mosley, a 3-year Galaxy Explorer, the passion for space began at a young age. She began exploring the cosmos at age nine with a Planet Project and continued to Space Camp during middle school for two summers at the U.S. Space and Rocket Center in Alabama. She has been an intern at Chabot Space & Science Center since her freshman year in high school. “In 3rd grade, I told my parents I wanted to work for NASA,” said Mosley. “Eight years later, I was reading my offer letter to intern at Ames Research Center. I started jumping up and down, and I immediately ran to share the news. My family and friends were beyond proud.” Mosley plans to study Aerospace Engineering after graduation, and ultimately her goal is to become a NASA astronaut. “The most exciting thing about the internship is meeting people with the same passions as mine. While I was nervous to be the youngest in the room on my first day, I was welcomed into a super friendly environment at Ames. Through my example, I hope to encourage others my age to follow their dreams and keep going until they succeed.” Mosley is one of eight Galaxy Explorers who interned at NASA Ames this summer. The interns learned directly from mentors in the field, working on projects in supercomputing, data analytics, rotorcraft aeromechanics, lunar missions, public engagement, computer science and STEM engagement. Megan Hiller is an intern at Chabot Space & Science Center, located at 10000 Skyline Blvd. in Oakland. https://chabotspace. org/events/events-listing/ Piedmont High School student Sage Mosley was an intern at Ames Research Center this past summer.
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom My summer at NASA Ames

articles.text: Part six in a series Three individuals will be competing for two seats on the Piedmont School Board in the election on November 6. The Post continues its weekly coverage of both the school board and Piedmont City Council election. The two questions shown below were sent to the school board candidates on Friday, October 14. Candidates were asked to limit their answers to 150or fewer words per question PIEDMONT SCHOOL BOARD 2 open seats; 3 candidates 2. Teacher Housing in Piedmont? Like many, I was thrilled that PUSD was able to give our teachers a much-deserved raise, as well as a one-time cash bonus! articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont resident and photographer, Steve Zirkelbach, took dozens of photos at Piedmont High’s Homecoming Dance on Saturday, October 1 which captured the electricity of the evening. As is tradition, the Homecoming dance in the Binks Rawlings gym punctuated the end of Homecoming Week (also known as Sprit Week) on campus. All students, from freshmen to seniors, were invited to dance the night away at the disco-themed party organized by Associated Student Body members. Four students were elected by their peers to the Homecoming Court and were presented with crowns at the student Homecoming rally on Friday. Seniors Milani Juarbe and Callan Mitchell were crowned as Homecoming Queen and King, and juniors Bauer Peterson and Shunji Hagashi were named Princess and Prince of the Homecoming Court on Friday, September 30.
