articles.text: The Highlanders’ boys’ water polo team continued its unbeaten run in the Western Alameda County Conference last week with an impressive 12-7 win against rival Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 11 at the Mills College pool. The victory improves Piedmont’s record to 15-4 overall and 7-0 in league. The team will likely be the No. 1 seed heading into the WACC Tournament at Encinal starting next Tuesday, October 25, with games through Saturday, October 29. Piedmont wraps up its regular season in a round robin tournament at Stevenson High in Pebble Beach this Saturday, October 22. “We’re trying to build up for league championships and NCS (North Coast Section playoffs). That was always our goal at the beginning of the season. We are in the driver’s seat, for sure, but we also need to make sure we maintain the pace at practice and work on little tweaks here and there,” said coach Rik Krumins. Piedmont jumped out to a comfortable 4-1 lead by the end of the first quarter with O’Dowd, and went up 7-3 by halftime. They kept a four-goal advantage through the third quarter to lead 9-5 and closed out with three more goals in the fourth, 12-7. In the first quarter, Finn Burke scored the first two goals of the game in less than a minute. O’Dowd cut the deficit to 2-1, but George Stein made it 3-1 with a goal during a man-advantage with 2:05 remaining. PHS then killed two separate penalties before drawing a 5-meter penalty with just four seconds left, allowing Peter Krumins to make it 4-1. BOD narrowed the score to 4-3 at the 3:33 mark in the second quarter, but it was their last goal in the first half. Hayden Jahn scored with 2:44 to play, and scored again during a man-advantage with 33 seconds left. With four seconds left in the half, Quincy Scherman launched a goal into net. In the third quarter, Piedmont’s Declan Linnane scored three seconds after gaining a penalty at the 6:07 mark, 8-3. BOD then converted a man-advantage opportunity with 4:55 left and scored once more with 2:43 to go, making it 8-5. PHS drew another exclusion penalty in the dying seconds, leading to Daniel Banin scoring with two seconds left, 9-5. Photo by Nancy Brahm Daniel Banin had a goal, assist, and steal on O’Dowd. Krumins scored 22 seconds into the fourth quarter to make it 10-5. BOD scored with 4:26 left in the game, 10-6, but it took Stein just 20 seconds and scored once more with a man-advantage with 3:17 to play for PHS’ final goal. Bishop O’Dowd tacked one on with 41 seconds remaining. Final stats include: Stein led the way with three goals. Krumins and Burke scored twice and had one steal, Jahn scored twice as well. Linnane had a goal, two assists, and two steals. Banin had a goal, assist, and steal. Scherman scored a goal. Goalie Dariush Kashani had 10 saves and a steal. Tuesday vs. Alameda Piedmont faced Alameda yesterday, Tuesday, October 18 for its final regular season league match of the season prior to the WACC Tournament on October 25-29. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (15-4 overall, 7-0 league) heads to Stevenson HS in Pebble Beach for a tournament this weekend starting at 3:00 p.m. on Saturday, October 22. Staff Photo Finn Burke had two goals and a steal in Piedmont’s 12-7 win vs. the Dragons. Photo by Nancy Brahm George Stein scored a 3-goal hat trick against Bishop O’Dowd.
articles.title: Boys’ water polo team dispatches O’Dowd 12-7

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls tennis team claimed a big 4-3 win over league rivals Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 11. The victory puts PHS in first place of the Western Alameda County Conference with a 7-0 league record, and on pace for its first WACC title since 2018. “It was like déjà vu. We defeated O’Dowd 4-3; just like we defeated them at the California Tennis Classic (in early September in Fresno), and the same score when we defeated Berkeley the previous week. We are now No. 1 in the WACC League, but we can’t rest. We will be playing all the Foothill teams again, and they were all close matches before, so we need to keep getting better,” said coach Jim Landes. PHS still must face challenging league matches with Alameda, Berkeley, Castro Valley, and O’Dowd once more before the end of the season. With wins over each school, Piedmont would accomplish their first undefeated banner year since the last title in 2018. The Highlanders famously held the longest undefeated streak against league opponents in California high school tennis at 19-years long from 2000-2018. The school also won five consecutive D2 NCS Team Championship titles during that stretch from 2013-2017. PHS could’ve made it six consecutive in 2018 as the No. 1 seed, but smoke from the wildfire in Paradise in late November and rain in early December canceled the tournament. Piedmont’s final three matches of the regular season will be at Alameda on Thursday, October 20, hosting Berkeley on Tuesday, October 25, and then at O’Dowd on Thursday, October 27. 4-3 win over Bishop O’Dowd Against Bishop O’Dowd, Piedmont won all three doubles matches and took one of four at singles to claim the win. At singles, No. 1 starter Tanya Kononova continued her winning streak with a 6-2, 6-0 win. It marked her seventh consecutive win. At No. 2 was Anne Jumper falling 6-1, 6-1, while Carolina Romanczuk lost 6-2, 7-5 at No. 3. Annika Gilliland had a narrow two sets at No. 4 but lost 7-5, 7-5. Over to doubles, Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini continued their strong play at the No. 1 spot, winning 7-5, 6-2. They have now won five consecutive matches as Piedmont’s top doubles team. “I think we’re really good at picking each other up in our low moments. We know how to stay positive when we play together; it’s really important to have a doubles partner who can take things seriously but also be really flexible and supportive,” said Bini. “Michaela is just great. She’s funny and we can make each other laugh even when we hit a ball way too hard out onto the street. We can look at each other, laugh it off, and know everything will be fine,” said LaForte. At No. 2 was Emma Eisemon and Ceclilia DeFazio winning in three sets, 6-2, 4-6, 6-3, while the freshman pair of Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum won 6-2, 6-2 at No. 3. Tuesday vs. Castro Valley Piedmont hosted Castro Valley yesterday, Tuesday, October 18. See next week’s Post for match details. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team lost 7-3 to Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 11 at Mills College in Oakland, snapping a fourgame winning streak by the Highlanders. It was a close for three quarters with O’Dowd holding a 4-3 lead to start the fourth period. The loss brings Piedmont’s record to 6-9 overall and 1-4 in league with one match remaining in its regular season before the start of the Western Alameda County Conference tournament from Tuesday, October 25 through Saturday, October 29 at the Encinal HS pool in Alameda. The Dragons led 2-0 by the end of the first quarter and kept the two-goal advantage by halftime, 3-1. Piedmont ate away at the lead in the third quarter and closed the score to 4-3 but couldn’t maintain the offensive fluidity in the fourth, falling 7-3. O’Dowd came out of the gate hot, scoring its first goal within 26 seconds into the game after winning the opening sprint. Piedmont’s goalie Friedie Schickedanz did well to record two saves in the remaining time, including a pivotal stop of a penalty situation, but the Dragons scored on a breakaway with 58 seconds left in the quarter. In the second quarter, Katarina Melian scored with 56 seconds left in the half, but Bishop O’Dowd answered just 14 seconds later on its next possession. Prior to then, Odessa Dando recorded a steal and drew an exclusion penalty, which led to Melian taking a shot attempt with 5:30 to play, but her ball went to the right of net. Piedmont started the third quarter strongly by drawing an exclusion and scored four seconds later when Melian launched a long-range shot into the net, cutting the deficit to 3-2. However, the Dragons scored with a long shot of its own with six minutes to play. PHS answered 13 seconds later on its next possession Photos by Nancy Brahm Rosie Feldman scored once against the Dragons. with Dando assisting Rosie Feldman on a close-range goal to make it 4-3, but it was the last time they’d get on the score sheet. In the remaining minutes of the third period, Piedmont gained four exclusion penalties against BOD but the Dragon goalie made critical saves and some shots went wide of the net. In the fourth quarter O’Dowd converted a 6-on-5 opportunity with 5:26 left in the game, extending the lead to 5-3. From there, BOD scored at the 3:42 mark by way of a breakaway goal, 6-3, and then tacked on one more with just 39 seconds to play. Final stats include: Melian had two goals, while Feldman had one. Dando had two steals and an assist. Tuesday vs. Alameda Piedmont played a match with Alameda on Tuesday, October 18 at the Encinal pool for its final regular season match of the season. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-9 overall, 1-4 league) is set to play in the WACC Tournament at Encinal. The first round game is on Tuesday, October 25 with semifinals on Thursday, October 27 and finals on Saturday, October 29. Odessa Dando looks for a pass. She had two steals and an assist against O’Dowd. Piedmont are set to play in the WACC Tournament from October 25-29.

articles.text: Piedmont’s volleyball team celebrated its five seniors – Tara Kothari, Eden Lorin, Lila Town, Shelby Cavenaugh, and Bree DeYoung – on Senior Night, a game with Castro Valley on Wednesday, October 12. Facing a league foe at Binks Rawlings Gym, they fell in a five-set barnburner, 25-20, 23-25, 25-16, 20-25, 15-4. “We ran our seniors in a 5-1 rotational play and our setters kind of gassed out. Then we ran a 6-2 zone again. The first couple of points in the second set gave us momentum towards the win. In the fifth set, we just struggled in serve and receive balls, which gave them a lot of free points.” said coach Mariah Cardenas. Piedmont lost to the Trojans 3-1 in their first match of the season on September 21. Shelby Cavenaugh (9) goes up for a block with Bree DeYoung hovering close by. “We fought until the end, it was some of our best play. I think we brought a better mentality. We knew it was going to be a really good game,” said Cavenaugh. “I think our connections were Piedmont celebrates after a point. Everybody was giving it 100 percent and diving for every single ball,” added Lorin. In the first set, Piedmont jumped out to a 5-1 lead but Castro Valley eventually went ahead 8-6. From there, the two sides traded points and PHS was able to tie the set four times before briefly holding a 17-16 lead. It was a close for three quarters with O’Dowd holding a 4-3 lead to start the fourth period. The loss brings Piedmont’s record to 6-9 overall and 1-4 in league with one match remaining in its regular season before the start of the Western Alameda County Conference tournament from Tuesday, October 25 through Saturday, October 29 at the Encinal HS pool in Alameda. The Dragons led 2-0 by the end of the first quarter and kept the two-goal advantage by halftime, 3-1. Piedmont ate away at the lead in the third quarter and closed the score to 4-3 but couldn’t maintain the offensive fluidity in the fourth, falling 7-3. O’Dowd came out of the gate hot, scoring its first goal within 26 seconds into the game after winning the opening sprint. Piedmont’s goalie Friedie Schickedanz did well to record two saves in the remaining time, including a pivotal stop of a penalty situation, but the Dragons scored on a breakaway with 58 seconds left in the quarter. In the second quarter, Katarina Melian scored with 56 seconds left in the half, but Bishop O’Dowd answered just 14 seconds later on its next possession. Prior to then, Odessa Dando recorded a steal and drew an exclusion penalty, which led to Melian taking a shot attempt with 5:30 to play, but her ball went to the right of net. Piedmont started the third quarter strongly by drawing an exclusion and scored four seconds later when Melian launched a long-range shot into the net, cutting the deficit to 3-2. However, the Dragons scored with a long shot of its own with six minutes to play. PHS answered 13 seconds later on its next possession Photos by Nancy Brahm Rosie Feldman scored once against the Dragons. with Dando assisting Rosie Feldman on a close-range goal to make it 4-3, but it was the last time they’d get on the score sheet. In the remaining minutes of the third period, Piedmont gained four exclusion penalties against BOD but the Dragon goalie made critical saves and some shots went wide of the net. In the fourth quarter O’Dowd converted a 6-on-5 opportunity with 5:26 left in the game, extending the lead to 5-3. From there, BOD scored at the 3:42 mark by way of a breakaway goal, 6-3, and then tacked on one more with just 39 seconds to play. Final stats include: Melian had two goals, while Feldman had one. Dando had two steals and an assist. Tuesday vs. Alameda Piedmont played a match with Alameda on Tuesday, October 18 at the Encinal pool for its final regular season match of the season. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-9 overall, 1-4 league) is set to play in the WACC Tournament at Encinal. The first round game is on Tuesday, October 25 with semifinals on Thursday, October 27 and finals on Saturday, October 29. Odessa Dando looks for a pass. She had two steals and an assist against O’Dowd. Piedmont are set to play in the WACC Tournament from October 25-29.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team returned to action on Friday, October 15 after a three-week absence, and fall 22-14 to Bishop O’Dowd. It marked a return to action for the football program after canceling the remaining 5 varsity games on its schedule following a game on September 23. “It was awesome to play a game again. It was our first game in three weeks; the kids have been antsy just waiting to get out there. The kids were super excited and were working hard all week in practice. It’s a great group,” said JV coach Bradley Smet, who also serves as the high school Athletic Director. The JV squad inherited a few underclassmen on the varsity team. “We were able to bring some of the kids down [from varsity to JV]. The sophomores including Brayden Hong and Derek Schleuning as juniors, so we were able to split players up more offensively and defensively. We didn’t have to play all of our kids both ways and we were able to rotate players more. It gave an opportunity for kids to play and exert their energy in their primary role,” explained Smet. The Highlanders trailed 14-0 by the end of the first quarter after allowing a kickoff return for a touchdown, followed by O’Dowd scoring on a 65-yard touchdown pass. “They had two big plays at the beginning of the game. Aside from those, I thought we did a great job controlling the game. That was the downfall in our last game against St. Mary’s, where we suffered several turnovers. Staff Photos Sophomore Tommy Ashton, who had been on the varsity team, scored a touchdown and a made a two-point conversion for the JV football team in its game with Bishop O’Dowd on October 15. JV coach Bradley Smet gives a play call to quarterback Brandon Dicke. Miguel Long goes high for a touchdown reception against O’Dowd. We asked the team to take care of the ball and that’s what they did,” said Smet. Piedmont rallied in the fourth quarter to bring itself within one possession. With 8:16 left in the game, quarterback Brandon Dicke connected with Miguel Long in the end zone pm a 20-yard touchdown pass to make it a 14-6 game following a failed two-point conversion. The Dragons scored with 3:50 left in the game after a long pass to the one-yard line and then punching the ball across. But on Piedmont’s next possession, the Highlanders churned downfield with long runs led by Ashton and Cash Panico, leading to Ashton powering his way on a five-yard carry across the goal line, shouldering his way over an attempted tackle. He also converted a twopoint conversion to make it 22-14. “It was great to be back out there. It wasn’t the result we wanted, but we had a lot of fun,” said Ashton. But Piedmont wasn’t done. On the ensuing kickoff, PHS recovered its onside kick on the right sideline to gain possession and be in great field position and with enough time to tie the game. But on a second down at the 30-yard line, Dicke quarterback suffered a shot to the ribs and had to leave the game. Its once promising drive ended at the 28-yard line. “We caught them by surprise on the onside kick. Albert Bellingrath kicked the ball and Long went streaking down the sideline to get it. They executed their jobs perfectly,” said Smet. The JV team continues with three more scheduled games, at St. Patrick in Vallejo this Friday, October 21, at Tennyson in Haywards on Thursday, October 27, and at home against Kennedy on Friday, November 4. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-3) heads to St. Patrick in Vallejo on Friday, October 21 at 4:30 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont High School is pushing forward with Junior Varsity football after a tumultuous cancellation of the five varsity games remaining on its schedule. JV will continue, but due to a diminished roster and injuries, the varsity season was terminated following a game on September 23. The JV team played its first game in three weeks on Friday, October 14, but there was no varsity game. Although JV head coach Bradley Smet, who also is the school’s athletic director, was calling the offense. Varsity head coach Jordan Seiden has been taking the reins at practice. “Once we decided to make the move with varsity, we talked about bringing our [varsity] staff down to JV and starting the transition for those players who will be getting varsity experience next year. We’re getting them used to our system and expectations. We definitely want to run the same system on both levels (JV and varsity), so we’re building the culture and a true program,” said Seiden. Defensive coordinator Mike Dixon called the plays in Friday’s game and in future games, offensive coordinator Kerry Griffin will take control. “The kids are using the same terminology and all those things, so we thought the natural progression would be for us to be working with JV as a unit. Our defensive coordinator is running the JV defense with assistance of the other coaches who were there. Mike Dixon is running the offense starting this week, last week with coach Smet,” said Seiden. Most of Piedmont’s varsity lineup included sophomores and juniors under Seiden, where a large focus of attention was developing players. That undoubtedly becomes an even greater emphasis going forward on JV, allowing Seiden to learn even more players to his incumbent varsity team in 2023. “It’s been nice having time to work with the team before playing O’Dowd. We are still going through the transition of getting to know each other, I tell the team that it’s almost like starting over again. We have a chance to get a leg-up on next year by getting together this year. We’re keeping the focus on developing and getting better; the focus of JV is more about developing and growth rather than wins and losses, said Seiden. The JV roster has approximately 24 active players, which allows the team to rotate players on offense and defense and keep them fresh. The number of playStaff Photos Piedmont head football coach Jordan Seiden discusses the future of the sport at the high school. The remaining five games of the season were canceled. ers also allows Piedmont to have its first 11-on-11 practices this season. “We haven’t had numbers in order to rotate players effectively. Guys aren’t necessarily having to start both ways, while some guys who are in better shape who can handle it are able to play both ways more, it also allows some guys to play one way. We’re able to sub guys out without there being a drop-off between players and have allowed us to go full 11-on-11 in practice,” said Seiden. The impact of COVID-19 was undoubtedly felt by the football program, which requires a large number of players. As PHS assistant coach Dick Carter wrote in last week’s Post, “interest in football by middle school boys was not sufficiently cultivated in the recent years before 2020. As Seiden describes, Piedmont High is making efforts to get the middle school involved to invigorate the program. “If kids are seeing the high school program struggle, what’s the incentive? The head of the flag football program [Billy Goldstein] came by and said they have around 24 eighth grade kids who are playing football. We plan on coming by and talk to the team about the program, recruiting, summer ball, and opportunities they’ll have when they come to the high school program,” said Seiden. Piedmont’s JV team will play St. Patrick in Vallejo this Friday, October 21, travel to Hayward to play Tennyson on Thursday, October 27, and finish the season with a game at Witter Field with Kennedy of Richmond on Friday, November 4 “We’re hoping for it to be an evening game, but we plan on having a Senior Night to honor the seniors who were on the team,” said Seiden. Jordan Seiden and PHS Athletic Director Bradley Smet (back) talk with JV players during a timeout on Friday.
articles.title: How Piedmont plans to push forward with football

articles.text: Piedmont’s cross-country team raced on the trails at Point Pinole Regional Shoreline on Wednesday, October 12 for its second Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season The boys’ team finished third of 10 schools while the girls were fourth out of nine teams. “As we get to our last meets of the season, we inevitably start calculating results and sometimes get too caught up in a frenzy of beating certain teams. At Point Pinole, we were pleased to see a large number of improvements. This is only the second year that the league has raced on this course,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. The boys’ team finished four points behind Bishop O’Dowd, 64-60, while Berkeley blitzed the field with a team score of 31. Christian Taylor (2507) was third of 91 runners with a time of 16:05.35 in a league meet at Point Pinole. Jamie Schwarz (1683) and Skylar Best (1656) placed fourth and ninth in the recent league meet. Running without Senior Christian Taylor led PHS by finishing third in a field of 91 runners with a time of 16:05. Behind him was classmate Parker Long in fourth in 16:09.84. The team was without lead runner Xander Schulte-Sasse, who placed third overall in the GOAT Invitational in Hercules on October 1. Junior Julien Lee was ninth with a time of 16:33.93, senior Alex Ware in 22nd place in 17:21.40, and sophomore Evan Byun 29th in 17:36.02. Junior Jamie Schwarz led the girls’ team, placing fourth out of 65 runners with a time of 19:52.9. She has finished in the top five in all her race this season. Freshman standout Skylar Best was ninth with a time of 20:25.82. next came a trio of up-and-coming freshman runners. Cora Chun (28th, 21:39.12), Elia Kwong (30th, 21:51.72), and Quincy Antaya in 33rd in 22:08.41. The girls team also was without one of its top runners, Josie Oesterer, who ran a time of 19:51.5 at the league meet on September 21. NEXT UP Piedmont is set to race in another league meet today, Wednesday, October 19, at Oyster Bay Regional Park at 4:00 p.m. Later this week, the squad heads to the prestigious Mt. Sac Invitational on Friday, October 21 in Walnut in Southern California. Elia Kwong, a freshman, finished in 21:51.72 at the league meet.

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California will host its 28th annual Dia de los Muertos Celebration this Sunday, October 23 from 12 noon to 4 p.m. The museum, in collaboration with OMCA’s El Día de Muertos Volunteer Community Committee, explores the culture and heritage of Latin America through music, dance, food, and art. Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is a celebration and appreciation of life and death practiced mainly in Mexico. Visitors will enjoy performances by Ballet Folklorico Mexicano and Mariachi Femenil Orgullo Mexicano, an all-female Mariachi band from the Bay Area. Traditional indigenous dance will be performed by Danza Azteca Nahui Ehekatl. Celebrating Dia de los Muertos at Oakland Museum of California with music, dance, food and art. View the community offerings at the ofrenda (altar) and explore the art of repujado (embossing). The festivities will take place between 12 p.m. and 4 p.m. This is a family-friendly event. Visit https://museumca.org/dia-de-losmuertos/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Oakland Museum celebrates Dia de los Muertos this Sunday

articles.text: Indecent is based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s Broadway debut The God of Vengeance. San Francisco Playhouse is celebrating its 20th season with a performance of Indecent, Paula Vogel’s new play based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s Broadway debut of The God of Vengeance. Although many consider Asch’s work to be a seminal work of Jewish culture, it is also viewed by some as libelous. The play is being performed at SF Playhouse through November 5. “We were lucky enough to be on hand when Paula Vogel’s Indecent opened on Broadway five years ago, and being huge fans of hers already, and galvanized by the production, we began angling to present the play’s Bay Area premiere immediately,” said San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English. “At the time we were a long shot due to strong interest from bigger companies, but after a two-year pandemic and catastrophic changes in the American theatre, a door opened five years later for us to present Indecent.” The play is directed by Susi Damilano, with music direction by Dmitri Gaskin and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The cast includes Dean Linnard, Billy Cohen, Rachel Botchan, and Rivka Borek. The show is co-produced with the Yiddish Theatre Ensemble and features a klezmer music score. “It is both a love song to the Ashkenazi Jewish culture spanning 50 years and a love song to the theatre. It is an odyssey that spins us from Warsaw to Berlin, to NY Yiddish theatre, to Broadway and back to Warsaw as the tumultuous and tragic history of the early 20th Century unfolds around the play within our play,” English said. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfplayhouse.org/ sfph/get-tickets/. Sokol San Francisco in cooperation with the Czech School of California and BayCzech would like to invite you to a live concert performance! The Ambroš Duo, a renowned mother-son music duo from the capital city of Prague, Czech Republic, will be performing at Piedmont Center for the Arts 801 Magnolia Ave. Piedmont, CA 94611 Saturday, November 5, 2022, at 5:00 PM Tickets $20 The concert will feature works by Mozart, Sarasate, and Czech composers Dvořák and Smetana, among others. The concert will conclude with the lively “Monti Czardas.” A light reception to meet the artists will follow. Current COVID safety protocols require that every ticket holder will need to show photo ID and proof of full vaccination for entry. Every attendee is also required to wear a mask during the entire event. We will update you if these mandates change before the event.
articles.title: SF Playhouse presenting Indecent through Nov. 5

articles.text: Zheng Chongbin’s large art installation, I Look for the Sky, is on view now at San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. The installation uses transparency and light to explore how ephemeral changes can alter the viewer’s perception. The exhibition is located in the museum’s Bogart Court. “Art has always been a pathway to this fuzzy world. It’s full of probabilities and chance – and so it was, working on this installation,” Chongbin said. “The assembled fragmented pieces were never about fixing the object itself, but rather about the shifting relationship among the fragments, a resonance, a natural chemistry. Culture and nature need to share the same space; society, all living beings, this physical planet, this earth, are interconnected.” Chongbin is a Bay Area-based artist trained in classical Chinese figurative painting who studied performance, installation, and conceptual art at San Francisco Art Institute. Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/zhengchongbin-i-look-for-the-sky-2/ to purchase tickets. Chongbin’s I Look for the Sky on view now at Asian Art Museum By Allyson Aleksey Zheng Chongbin’s large art installation, I Look for the Sky, is on view now at San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. The installation uses transparency and light to explore how ephemeral changes can alter the viewer’s perception. The exhibition is located in the museum’s Bogart Court. “Art has always been a pathway to this fuzzy world. It’s full of probabilities and chance – and so it was, working on this installation,” Chongbin said. “The assembled fragmented pieces were never about fixing the object itself, but rather about the shifting relationship among the fragments, a resonance, a natural chemistry. Indecent is based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s Broadway debut The God of Vengeance. By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Playhouse is celebrating its 20th season with a performance of Indecent, Paula Vogel’s new play based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s Broadway debut of The God of Vengeance. Although many consider Asch’s work to be a seminal work of Jewish culture, it is also viewed by some as libelous. The play is being performed at SF Playhouse through November 5. “We were lucky enough to be on hand when Paula Vogel’s Indecent opened on Broadway five years ago, and being huge fans of hers already, and galvanized by the production, we began angling to present the play’s Bay Area premiere immediately,” said San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English. “At the time we were a long shot due to strong interest from bigger companies, but after a two-year pandemic and catastrophic changes in the American theatre, a door opened five years later for us to present Indecent.” The play is directed by Susi Damilano, with music direction by Dmitri Gaskin and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The cast includes Dean Linnard, Billy Cohen, Rachel Botchan, and Rivka Borek. The show is co-produced with the Yiddish Theatre Ensemble and features a klezmer music score. “It is both a love song to the Ashkenazi Jewish culture spanning 50 years and a love song to the theatre. It is an odyssey that spins us from Warsaw to Berlin, to NY Yiddish theatre, to Broadway and back to Warsaw as the tumultuous and tragic history of the early 20th Century unfolds around the play within our play,” English said. articles.text: A leader in symphonic innovation and imagination now for six decades, the Oakland Symphony launched its first full post-pandemic season on October 14 with the first of its music-director candidates out front. And, of course, with an innovative program. Through countless setbacks, the ensemble keeps emerging again and again like a phoenix from the ashes; its struggles remain a challenge for the future. Has any ensemble suffered greater adversity? It went bankrupt after the off-season death (accidental drowning) of its highly talented 32-year-old maestro Calvin Simmons precisely 40 years ago. He had been feted as the first Black conductor of any major U.S. orchestra. The more recent Oakland Symphony music director, the exemplary Michael Morgan (also Black), died last year at the age of only 63, having served here indefatigably since 1991. Given the large Oakland Black population, these men were a welcome fit for the community as they presented a very broad-ranging repertory that was rarely predictable. Local commemorations of Morgan are well-deserved. But the charismatic Simmons remains a bit marginalized. Both made immense contributions, each in his own way. And now the new era, with the lead-off batter (it’s still baseball season) Ankush Kumar Bahl as the podium guest, marking the orchestra’s resumption of a normal, full-season schedule. Bahl was a Bay Area product of Indian descent now running the Omaha Symphony and vying for the Oakland directorship. Nurtured by some very prominent conductors, he has a secure stick technique demonstrated in two demanding contemporary works. He is also one of the most adept annotators that the Paramount Theater podium has heard in recent years. Chen Yi’s The Golden Flute Flute virtuoso Demarre McGill performed with Oakland Symphony In its season-opening concert on October 14. was a priceless virtuosity vehicle for flute virtuoso Demarre McGill, the guest soloist, and the orchestra. Despite his modest-size frame, McGill is one powerful flutist with extraordinary breath control, in turns both whimsical and canary-like, able to modulate tones like gentle swells with breath alone. His bird effects were swooping and swarming unerringly, all while imbuing this Western orchestra with techniques from China. They emanate from composer Yi, a remarkable émigré woman, now 69, who had managed to smuggle her violin and clandestine Bach music to the work farms during the Cultural Revolution, “to inspire the peasants working the fields,” more or less as Mao would have it back then. (Bach? With Mao?) Moving on from the cadence that brought down the house, McGill appended James Lee’s Principal Brothers, an unaccompanied showpiece encore. Bahl followed with Berlioz’s Symphonie Fantastique, often cited as the very first romantic symphony. As the personnel here in their six-concert classical series play few romantics, the start was too detached for comfort, like a vintage table that could use some regluing. But the middle movement depicting the shepherd horn calls across the mountains was beautifully wrought by Bahl and cohorts. Buoyed by the sinuous oboe solos of Andrea Plesnarski, the movement lifted up this entire programmatic symphony through the gallows scene, the beheading, and the witches’ sabbath toward an effusive celebration of death by the morbid hero of the symphony. Notable among the sections of this enlarged Berlioz orchestra were the violas and the harp pairing. Three bass players were too few, but on the other hand you had to admire the rarity of paired tubas. Named after Beethoven’s motto “Fate Now Conquers,” composer Carlos Simon, 36, also quoted some harmonies from Beethoven’s Seventh for the brief but profoundly accented curtain-raiser. MUSIC NOTES Yet another Oakland musical luminary, Bob Hughes (Robert Grove Hughes), passed away this summer at 91. He had been a true jack of all trades, as bassoonist, conductor and composer. A longtime collaborator of composer Lou Harrison, conductor Hughes had also founded the Oakland Youth Orchestra and was credited as composer on the Disney film Never Cry Wolf. Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy also writes for the classical-music site www.artsSF.com .
articles.title: Battling Symphonic adversity – and winning

articles.text: City Council member Betsy Andersen makes cameo appearance in Ferdinand the Bull Piedmont’s hometown orchestra will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday afternoon, November 6, at 4 p.m. Conducted by Martha Stoddard and Sue Crum, the orchestra will perform the rarely heard Overture to Johann Albrecht’s comedy Der Teufel als Hydraulicus, composed by Franz Schubert when he was just 14. Other music includes the delightful Romanian Dances, by Bela Bartok, and Mozart’s orchestral masterpiece, Symphony No. 40 in G minor, composed during some of the artist’s darkest days. The composition finds its way from the turbulence of the beginning sections into the triumph of the conclusion. As a special audience treat, the humorous musical piece, Photo by Julie Reichle Piedmont City Council member Betsy Andersen will make her musical debut on November 6. Ferdinand the Bull by Alan Ridout, based on the children’s story of the same name by American author Munro Leaf, will be performed by violinist Joseph Gold, with narration by Piedmont native and City Council member Betsy Andersen. It is the story of a bull who would rather smell the flowers than be in bullfights. The work was banned by both Hitler and the Spanish Fascists as “degenerate democratic propaganda.” Admission is free. Doors open at 3:30 p.m. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue at Bonita Avenue. Street parking is available. ®
articles.title: Piedmont Orchestra in Nov. 6 concert at PCA

articles.text: The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday afternoon, October 30, at 1:30 p.m. Tickets are available at: https://bit.ly/3TpKMUZ. The quartet of Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Beethoven’s Opus 132, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. Beethoven’s String Quartet in A minor, opus 132, is from his collection of “late” quartets, written in the final years of his life. In these works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. The quartet will also perform Caroline Shaw’s Valencia, and Mozart’s “Dissonance” String Quartet in C Major, K465. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco is dedicated to bringing chamber music masterworks to diverse audiences. CMS of SF is passionate about concertizing in intimate settings, creating close connections between performers and listeners, and culThe Chamber Music Society of San Francisco will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday afternoon, October 30, at 1:30 p.m. Pictured are Natasha Makhijani (left), Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton. tivating a relationship between music and audiences that extends far beyond the perimeter of the concert hall. Drawing listeners into the lives of the composers and the world of the music, CMS of SF concerts are a favorite destination for both chamber music lovers and those new to the genre. Members of CMS of SF can be heard performing with San Francisco Symphony, SF Opera, SF Ballet, San Francisco and New Century Chamber Orchestras, American Bach Soloists, Oakland Symphony and many others. The four founding members came together through their mutual love of the late Beethoven String Quartets. Collaborations have included artists such as Kay Stern, Stephen Prutsman, Jean-Michel Fonteneau, and Jodi Levitz. For more information, see: www.chambermusicsocietysf.org

articles.text: The allure of the American dollar has always been great. They used to say the streets were paved with gold. Great European musicians were clamoring to come to America and the American promoters salivated at the prospect. The Gold Rush in the 19th century opened the floodgates. Before the Gold Rush, Colonial America was a rather sedate place. It’s not exactly that we were a backwater society, but we weren’t exactly forward-looking. American music was pretty much confined to churches. If you want to know what colonial music was like, listen to the Benjamin Franklin Suite. Yes, Ben himself was a composer. The American Revolution invigorated American society. Then came 1848. Europe was immersed in political and societal change. Things opened up here, too. Parlor music became popular. The songs of Stephen Foster are a perfect example. Everyone was singing. Nicolo Paganini, along with his supernatural career, would have been perfect in America. Sadly, he never came. But the list of European virtuosos who did come is a veritable Who’s Who of music. They always started in the Northeast (New York and Boston) and worked their way south, then west. They got as far as St. Louis. Anything to the west of it was literally the Wild West. Things changed with the Gold Rush. The sensational Hungarian violin virtuoso Edouard Remenyi was the first to tour all of America. He was escaping the 1848 revolution in Hungary and came to America to avoid being shot on sight in his home country. Remenyi played concerts everywhere, including many in saloons. The miners would throw gold nuggets onto the stage if they liked the performance. If they didn’t like the performance, they would destroy the joint. In this way musicians were urged to play well. They had to please their audience. As always, opera was the most popular form of entertainment. Famous opera singers toured the country with their own opera companies. articles.text: The popular Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy exhibition at Legion of Honor, of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, has been extended to November 27 due to popular demand. The fashion exhibit features the extraordinary designs of Chinese couture designer Guo Pei, who is widely considered China’s first couturier. More than 80 works over the past two decades will be on display, many of them were shown on Beijing and Paris runways. Pei is known for her craftsmanship, embroidery, and unconventional dressmaking techniques. “As a creator and artist, there is no greater honor than to share my creativity with a wider audience,” the artist said. “I hope that, through the artistry of couture and universal language of art, that it will foster cross-cultural appreciation, connections, and ideas.” The exhibition drew over 130,000 visitors in the first 18 weeks. Legion of Honor then extended Guo Pei’s exhibition for 12 more weeks. “Our visitors’ response to Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy has been absolutely extraordinary, and we are delighted that the exhibition’s Chinese couture designer Guo Pei. extension through Thanksgiving will enable more people to experience Guo Pei’s artistry,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Installed in our special exhibition galleries, and amid our holdings of European Art, Guo Pei’s designs encompass rich details both infused with references to a range of cultural traditions and executed over thousands of hours. This presentation represents a singular opportunity to experience exquisite designs that invoke and encourage transcultural dialogue.” Visit https://legionof honor. famsf.org/guo-pei for more information and to purchase tickets to the exhibition.
articles.title: Guo Pei’s couture exhibit at Legion of Honor on view through Nov. 27

Legion of Honor then extended Guo Pei’s exhibition for 12 more weeks. “Our visitors’ response to Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy has been absolutely extraordinary, and we are delighted that the exhibition’s Chinese couture designer Guo Pei. extension through Thanksgiving will enable more people to experience Guo Pei’s artistry,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Installed in our special exhibition galleries, and amid our holdings of European Art, Guo Pei’s designs encompass rich details both infused with references to a range of cultural traditions and executed over thousands of hours. This presentation represents a singular opportunity to experience exquisite designs that invoke and encourage transcultural dialogue.” Visit https://legionof honor. famsf.org/guo-pei for more information and to purchase tickets to the exhibition. Saturday, November 5, 5:00 p.m. Ambroš Duo concert The Ambroš Duo, a renowned mother-son music duo from the capital city of Prague in the Czech Republic will perform a concert featuring works by Mozart, Sarasate, and Czech composers Dvořák and Smetana, among others. Sunday, November 6, 4:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Piedmont’s hometown orchestra presents a varied and unusual program for its Fall 2022 concert, conducted by Martha Stoddard and Sue Crum. The rarely heard Overture to Johann Albrecht’s comedy Der Teufel als Hydraulicus, composed by Franz Schubert at age 14, opens the concert, followed by Béla Bartók’s delightful Romanian Dances. The next piece, for violin and narrator, is based on Munro Leaf’s children’s story “Ferdinand the Bull,” narrated by Piedmont native and City Council member Betsy Andersen, with the violin score played by the orchestra’s concertmaster Joseph Gold. The concert is underwritten by an anonymous donor. Free admission. Doors open at 3:30. Saturday, November 12, 5:00 p.m. SF Mandolin Orchestra SF Mandolin Orchestra begins its Fall 2022 concert season with Anticipation, a concert featuring music by Beethoven, Erik Satie, and orchestra conductor and composer Achille Bocus. A plucked string orchestra with 15- 25 members playing instruments of the mandolin family (mandolin, mandola and mandocello), as well as guitar, viola da gamba and double bass, their musicianship and style have pleased Piedmont audiences many times. Tickets are $20 General, $15 for students and seniors, and are available at https://sfmandolin.square.site/. articles.text: A scene from Touching the Void. Touching the Void is a taut, compelling docudrama, directed by Kevin Macdonald, and based on a book of the same name written by Joe Simpson. The film recounts Simpson’s (Brendan Mackey) and Simon Yates’ (Nicholas Aaron), 1985 successful ascent of the never climbed West Face of the 21,000- foot Siula Grande peak in the Peruvian Andes. Simpson and Yates, both experienced mountaineers, having reached the summit, confidently begin their decent by way of the North Ridge. Unexpectedly the weather turns stormy and not long after leaving the summit Yates plummets some 4,500 feet down an icy slope, stopped only by his climbing rope and ax. After the fall, they decide to bivouac high on the peak, and the next morning resume their downward climb. It was during that decent that the film takes an ominous turn when Simpson unexpectedly drops over an ice cliff and finds himself dangling over a deep crevasse, still roped to Yates, 300 feet above him. Yates, feeling the rope go suddenly taut, digs the heels of his boots into the snow and ice; however, he soon begins to lose both grip and purchase and realizes that if he falls he will also go over the ledge. It is then that he makes a fateful decision and cuts the rope, and it is that act which literally separates the two for the rest of the film. As a result of Yates cutting him loose, Simpson falls into the deep, dark, crevasse, landing on a narrow ledge, his broken leg so painful he passes out. What was a climbing challenge has suddenly become a story of survival, and Simpson’s situation is now starkly untenable. He realizes that Yates most likely thinks he is dead and if he is to prevail, he must do so alone. And so begins his long ordeal, one of impossible odds. First he must find a way off the narrow ledge and out of his icy prison, wondering how, with a shattered leg, will ever find his way back down the face of a massive glacier and back to the base camp. This docudrama is an exceptionally excellent reenactment, and delivers sustained tension, excitement, and intensity, coupled with moments that seem all but hopeless. Touching the Void. Docudrama. Directed by Kevin Macdonald. Cast: Brendan Mackey as Joe Simpson, and Nicholas Aaron as Simon Yates. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated R. Released in 2003. Now streaming on Prime/AMC+/ Apple tv.

articles.text: A scene from Dreamworks’ Shark Tale. Review by Chris Honoré Shark Tale is a Dreamworks animated feature starring a bluestreak cleaner wrasse fish named Oscar (Will Smith) and a timid vegetarian shark named Lenny (Jack Black). This odd-couple hangs out in the Southside reef. Oscar dreams of becoming rich and famous while working at the local Whale Wash, and Lenny has to deal with his mobbed up family, led by his dad, Don Edward Lino, who worries that his son, a shark, prefers not to eat fish. The Don decides that Lenny needs some gangster mentoring and assigns the task to his older son, tough-talking Frankie (Michael Imperoli). When Oscar reports to work, he is called into the office of his boss, Sykes (Martin Scorsese), a puffer fish, who not only owns the Whale Wash, but on the side is a loan shark to whom Oscar owes money. Sykes tells Oscar that it’s time to pay the debt – some 5,000 clams – the next day, or else. Oscar, broke, is rescued by his best friend Angie (Renee Zellweger) who gives him a shiny pink pearl, which Oscar quickly pawns. The next day, Oscar brings the money to the racetrack where he intends to pay Sykes, but hears that there is a sure thing sea horse running, named Lucky Day, and he bets all of his cash to win. It’s an exciting race with Lucky in the lead; however, at the last moment, just before the finish line, Lucky trips and loses – and so does Oscar. Sykes, hearing that Oscar cannot pay him, sends two of his enforcers, Ernie and Bernie (Ziggy Marley and Doug E. Doug), Jamaican jellyfish, to deal with Oscar. And so we’re introduced to Oscar who is always on the verge of trouble. He happens to be in the vicinity of an anchor, which is dropped and hits Frankie, killing him. Suddenly the locals of Southside reef are referring to Oscar as a “shark slayer,” a tale that he doesn’t dispute. After all, fame is fame, and he enjoys his new reputation. Of course, there are lots of machinations taking place, with behind-the-scenes double-dealing, chases and plotting, all involving Angie, Lenny, and a seductive female Lion fish named Lola (Angelina Jolie). She gives Oscar a big kiss, making Angie jealous. And then there is, Don Lino, who believes Oscar killed Frankie and is seeking revenge. At one point he sends his left-hand man, Luca (Vincent Pastore), an octopus, to track down Oscar. Finally, Oscar steps forward and confesses that it was an anchor that killed Frankie and not him. Lenny and Don Lino reconcile, and Oscar becomes the manager of the Whale Wash. It’s all a comedy of errors that the kids will enjoy, highlighted by the jive-talking Oscar. Shark Tale. Dreamworks animation. Directed by Bibo Bergeron & Vicky Jenson. With voices of Will Smith, Robert DeNiro, Renee Zellweger. 1 hr. 30 min. Rated PG. Released in 2004. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: The California Air Resources Board (CARB) recently approved a first-in-the-nation plan to set zero-emissions standards for space and water heaters, effectively banning the sale of gas-powered furnaces and water heaters by 2030. Buildings will be required to install zero emissions alternatives such as energy efficient electric heat pumps. The proposal, approved late last month, is part of a larger plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions and meet federal air quality standards. The full text of the legislation is available at: Arb.ca.gov/ sites/default/files/2022-08/2022_ State_SIP_Strategy.pdf CARB’s plan directs state agencies to draft legislation to phase out gas-fueled heaters and will be subject to a final vote in 2025. The plan also includes further emissions reduction measures for trucks, medium and heavy-duty vehicles, and consumer products. The goal of the plan is to improve air quality and reduce nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions that contribute to particulate matter and ground-level ozone (otherwise known as smog). Control of NOx emissions is critical to improving air quality in California. Currently, more than half of Californians reside in areas that exceed the federal heath-based ozone standards. Low-income and disadvantaged communities are more likely to be impacted by high ozone levels. CARB’s latest plan will speed up the Golden State’s transition away from fossil fuels to cleaner forms of energy. In Piedmont the City’s Sustainability Division is actively pursuing ways to reduce emissions and transition to electric appliances and vehicles. Earlier this year, the City approved replacing all remaining gas-powered water heaters in City facilities with electric heat pump water heaters at no cost to the City. In the spring, the City Council directed that the new Piedmont Community Pool, scheduled to be completed in 2024, be designed as an all-electric facility. The entire facility will be electrified through a combination of electric heat pumps, solar panels, and integration with the clean electrical grid. The City is currently developing an electrification rebate pilot program that will provide incentives for residents to replace polluting gas appliances with clean electric alternatives. Together, these efforts will lessen our carbon footprint and improve our air quality. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions on electrification, plant-based eating, or hiking.
articles.title: California aims to ban gas water heaters, furnaces by 2030

articles.text: Mount Veeder is an American Viticultural Area (AVA) among the Mayacaymas Mountains west of Napa and Yountville. The mountain was named after Peter Veeder a Dutch Presbyterian minister who was one of the first non-natives to explore the area. The area has been producing wines since the 1860’s and is the only hillside appellation in Napa Valley that adjoins the cool, bayside Carneros, benefiting from the cooling influence of San Pablo Bay. Mount Veeder is an island of ancient seabed pushed up into a mountain surrounded by volcanic soils that typify the rest of Napa Valley. The rugged mountain terrain of extremely steep slopes above the fog renders shallow topsoil and minimal water retention, resulting in tiny berries with intense flavor and concentration. The Mount Veeder AVA is small, with only about 35 wineries producing 40,000 cases per vintage (about 1.3% of total Napa Valley production). In September this year the Mount Veeder Winery Association put on a tasting with wines from 29 wineries. The following wines were the cream of the crop – the best of Mt. Veeder. warm plums, black cherries and blueberries with wafts of redcurrants, cedar chest, dried herbs, lavender and spice box. Veeder is as good for Syrah as it is for Cabernet. It wafts from the glass with plush and vibrant dark fruits, black peppercorn, blueberry tones, plum jam and raspberries. Full-bodied, juicy and generous in the mouth, the wine coats the palate with a luscious chocolate and fruit flavors finishing long and rich. www.chateaupotelle.com • 2019 Majuscule Cabernet Sauvignon Mt. Deep ruby, it has generous layers of cassis, violets, chocolate and bouquet garni as it spends time in the glass. The medium bodied palate explodes with floral fruits supported by abundant, fine tannins, fresh acidity, and a long oak-touched finish. • 2018 Anthem Cabernet Sauvignon Mt. articles.text: A series of six Asian cooking classes on Saturdays are being offered by Piedmont Adult School starting on October 29. The course is being taught by Chat Mingkwan, a native of Thailand who was trained in culinary arts in Rayon, France. Mingkwan began preparing Thai food as a child, working alongside his mother and aunt in their successful restaurant and hotel. He has traveled throughout Southeast Asia, studying local cuisines, and currently a cooking teacher, author, food and restaurant consultant. Students will receive instructions on the ingredients and techniques, and then break into small groups to prepare the recipes. The class then comes together to enjoy the meal they have created. pages.text: Wednesday, October 19, 2022 21 Features The Wine Corner The best wines of Mount Veeder By Pierre DuMont Mount Veeder is an American Viticultural Area (AVA) among the Mayacaymas Mountains west of Napa and Yountville. The mountain was named after Peter Veeder a Dutch Presbyterian minister who was one of the first non-natives to explore the area. The area has been producing wines since the 1860’s and is the only hillside appellation in Napa Valley that adjoins the cool, bayside Carneros, benefiting from the cooling influence of San Pablo Bay. Mount Veeder is an island of ancient seabed pushed up into a mountain surrounded by volcanic soils that typify the rest of Napa Valley. The rugged mountain terrain of extremely steep slopes above the fog renders shallow topsoil and minimal water retention, resulting in tiny berries with intense flavor and concentration. The Mount Veeder AVA is small, with only about 35 wineries producing 40,000 cases per vintage (about 1.3% of total Napa Valley production). In September this year the Mount Veeder Winery Association put on a tasting with wines from 29 wineries. The following wines were the cream of the crop – the best of Mt. Veeder. warm plums, black cherries and blueberries with wafts of redcurrants, cedar chest, dried herbs, lavender and spice box. Full, firm, velvety textured, the palate yields mouth-filling black fruits and spicy layers with a very long, perfumed finish. www.yatesfamilyvineyard.com • 2018 VGS Chateau Potelle Syrah Bald Mountain Vineyard This bottle shows that the terroir of Mt. Veeder is as good for Syrah as it is for Cabernet. It wafts from the glass with plush and vibrant dark fruits, black peppercorn, blueberry tones, plum jam and raspberries. Full-bodied, juicy and generous in the mouth, the wine coats the palate with a luscious chocolate and fruit flavors finishing long and rich. www.chateaupotelle.com • 2019 Majuscule Cabernet Sauvignon Mt. Veeder The Majuscule Cabernet shows classic purity of blueberry and blackberry fruit as well as flowers and subtle background oak is followed by a full-bodied, voluptuously textured, multi-layered wine that is stunningly lush, with sweet tannin and beautiful purity and length. This fine wine can be drunk early on or cellared for another 25 years. www.majusculewine.com California aims to ban gas water heaters, furnaces by 2030 By Sophie Roberts The California Air Resources Board (CARB) recently approved a first-in-the-nation plan to set zero-emissions standards for space and water heaters, effectively banning the sale of gas-powered furnaces and water heaters by 2030. Buildings will be required to install zero emissions alternatives such as energy efficient electric heat pumps. The proposal, approved late last month, is part of a larger plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions and meet federal air quality standards. The full text of the legislation is available at: Arb.ca.gov/ sites/default/files/2022-08/2022_ State_SIP_Strategy.pdf CARB’s plan directs state agencies to draft legislation to phase out gas-fueled heaters and will be subject to a final vote in 2025. The plan also includes further emissions reduction measures for trucks, medium and heavy-duty vehicles, and consumer products. The goal of the plan is to improve air quality and reduce nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions that contribute to particulate matter and ground-level ozone (otherwise known as smog). Control of NOx emissions is critical to improving air quality in California. Currently, more than half of Californians reside in areas that exceed the federal heath-based ozone standards. Low-income and disadvantaged communities are more likely to be impacted by high ozone levels. CARB’s latest plan will speed up the Golden State’s transition away from fossil fuels to cleaner forms of energy. In Piedmont the City’s Sustainability Division is actively pursuing ways to reduce emissions and transition to electric appliances and vehicles. Earlier this year, the City approved replacing all remaining gas-powered water heaters in City facilities with electric heat pump water heaters at no cost to the City. In the spring, the City Council directed that the new Piedmont Community Pool, scheduled to be completed in 2024, be designed as an all-electric facility. The entire facility will be electrified through a combination of electric heat pumps, solar panels, and integration with the clean electrical grid. The City is currently developing an electrification rebate pilot program that will provide incentives for residents to replace polluting gas appliances with clean electric alternatives. Together, these efforts will lessen our carbon footprint and improve our air quality. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions on electrification, plant-based eating, or hiking. articles.text: World-renowned conservationist and ethologist (the study of animal behavior) Jane Goodall made a rare appearance at the Oakland Zoo on October 6 for a private event with 350 guests. During her visit Goodall, currently a resident of England, spoke to 100 Oakland School District students and the Zoo’s Teen Wild Guides about her journey and stories of hope for animals, people, and the environment. Dr. Goodall last visited Oakland Zoo 15 years ago for the unveiling of a Gibbon habitat in the process of being built. Goodall’s recent visit was a once-in-alifetime opportunity for Oakland students and was an opportunity for Goodall to see the recent expansion and progress Oakland Zoo has made to become a toptier conservationist institution Also attending the event were youth members of the Jane Goodall Institute’s Roots & Shoots activism program. Roots & Shoots programs support tens of thousands of young people in nearly 100 countries with projects that help people, animals and the environment. Goodall, now 88, is one of 14 people serving as a United Nations Messenger of Peace. She is best known for her 60-year study of social and family interactions of wild chimpanzees which began in the Gombe Stream National Park in Tanzania in 1960. At age 26, Jane Goodall followed her passion for wildlife to Gombe, Tanzania. Photo by Hugo van Lawick Oakland Zoo Primate Keeper Kelly McDonald introduces Jane Goodall to the zoo’s Chimpanzee residents.
articles.title: Oakland Zoo hosts Dr. Jane Goodall

A tortoise rescued from the roadside Tri-State Zoological Park in Maryland walks on grass at Oakland Zoo, likely for the first time. malnourished, and improperly cared for. “We are incredibly grateful to our Zoo and sanctuary partners for helping us. If we didn’t have reputable Zoos, such as Oakland Zoo, these animals would have to stay with neglectful owners where they would be mistreated for years”, said Brittany Peet, General Counsel for PETA Foundation. Oakland Zoo transported a dozen reptiles cross-country to reputable sanctuaries like the Colorado Reptile Humane Society. The reptiles rescued include box turtles, a leopard tortoise, a yellow-legged tortoise, a Madagascar spiny-tailed iguana, a reticulated python, ball pythons, and a Russian tortoise. “Animal welfare is one of our top priorities at Oakland Zoo – both locally and globally,” said Darren Minier, Director of Animal Welfare and Research at Oakland Zoo. “Our involvement in creating and advocating for legislation is vital to combat the illegal wildlife pet trade.” Two of the rescued tortoises, a yellow-footed and a leopard tortoise, have joined the Oakland Zoo family and are now in quarantine at the Oakland Zoo Veterinary Hospital. The vast majority of Oakland Zoo’s animals are rescues, from both private ownership and the illegal wildlife trade. Animals confiscated by officials at San Francisco International Airport and the Port of Oakland have been brought to Oakland Zoo for treatment, care, and permanent sanctuary over the years. articles.text: The Piedmont Walking on Wednesdays group will have a special tour of Mountain View Cemetery conducted by Mountain View docent conducted docent Jane Leroe a week before Halloween on October 26. One year ago at this time she led a similar walking tour for the group, and identified many of the cemetery’s historical sites, some of which date back to the Civil War. This year’s tour will feature Millionaires’ Row, where the most elaborate crypts are located, housing some of the cemetery’s most famous and wealthy residents. Leroe, a long-time cemetery docent, was a ground-breaking trial attorney and is now retried. To join the group, plan to meet in front of Mountain View’s main mausoleum prior to 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday, October 26. The cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue at the end of Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. Parking in the cemetery is available. The tour will last for about 1 hour and 45 minutes. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers paused for a group photo last week at Hampton Park: Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Alicia Rivera, Melba Yee, Gloria DaSilva, Garrett Clifford, Priscilla Wanerus, Larry Olsen, Nancy Olsen, Mary Hedley, Martin Levy, Jim Kellogg, Mike Gallant, Jasmine Cai, Lisa Euphrat, Matt Gerhardt, Jim Kuo, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Jane Holland, Mark Davis, Brenda Ferrero, Kat Lang, Phil Witte, Christine Calliste, Helen Dong, Edith Lee, Stella Houston, Pat Keller, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Tally, Quincy Dong, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Elizabeth Richter, Noemi Alvarado, Laura Goldman with K-9 best friend Vivie, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome three first time walkers, Beth Cary, Mary Borrelli, and Jennifer Peltzen. Another strong turnout of 38 walkers and four K-9 best friends showed up on October 12 for a stroll to the edge of the city by the Walking on Wednesdays group. One area the group had not visited in some time was the Sandringham-Selborne-Estates loop near the top of Hampton Avenue. Additionally, they had not gotten to the uniquely named Wyngaard Avenue. The walkers went up Highland Avenue to Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues. On Sheridan there was a large persimmon tree in a front yard with a bounty of fruit, but not quite ripe. The trees that line Wildwood have some of the city’s best fall colors, and they seemed to be at their peak, as fallen leaves provided a burgundy sidewalk carpet. The walkers went up Crocker and onto Hampton Road Avenue, passing the always lovely Crocker Park (known as Bear Park to neighbors). The group reassembled at Hampton Park at the corner of LaSalle Avenue, where they posed for a group photo before embarking on the long trek to Wyngaard. The walkers ascended Hampton to Sandringham Road and then to the Marlborough Court cul-de-sac, where they were greeted by long-time walker Carol Long and her K-9 best friend Bailey. A half block later they explored Sandringham Place, another cul-de-sac. As an educational footnote, French speaking members of the group informed the others that cul-de-sac, means bottom of the sack. At the intersection of Sandringham and Selborne Drive, everyone enjoyed a wonderful view of the Bay. Going on Selborne the group made its way to Estates Drive and a short walk further brought them to the uniquely named Wyngaard Avenue. It is marked by columns of the original St. James Woods development, though the columns are nearly hidden behind wisteria vines. It was now time to answer the question: Who or what is Wyngaard? The closest to an answer was a search that revealed 86 percent of Wyngaards are found in South Africa which had a large Dutch population. But the connection to Piedmont remains unclear. Going down Wyngaard, the group viewed a home at the end of the street near Sandringham that is on the market for $3.5 million. They passed more beautiful homes, one of a Tudor half-timber of an Elizabethan architectural style, and another Storybook CHAPEL OF THE CHIMES - OAKLAND

articles.text: When you were expecting your first child you probably sought books to help you prepare for what was coming. Best sellers such as What to Expect When You’re Expecting, The Expectant Father, and Dr. Spock’s Baby and Child Care, helped inform millions of new parents about every aspect of pregnancy, birth, and childcare. Updated editions of these books are still on the market today – decades after their first publication. These days, you might be perusing the literature looking at what you can find about becoming a grandparent. Grandparenting books fall into a few general categories: Grandparent journals, personal memoirs, and how-to books for new grandparents. Grandparent journals/memory books are the top sellers on Amazon.com, and there are dozens of choices. Here are just a few: Grandmother’s/Grandfather’s Journal, by Blue Streak (#1 in Grandparenting Books), Tell Me Your Life Story, Grandma, by Questions About Me, Grandma’s Story, by Korie Herold. These books offer grandparents a simple and delightful way to share with a grandchild their personal details, life history, family lore, and other priceless treasures that can sometimes become lost over the years. It’s amazing how many things we don’t know about our grandparents simply because we never thought to ask them before they passed away. (Options for each book allow the grandparent to choose the journal with their correct grandparent name, i.e., Nana, Grandma, Papa, etc.) Personal memoirs seem to be trending for well-known celebrities and/or authors who would like to share the joys and challenges of becoming a grandparent. Many of these books have a humorous tone, such as Granny Diaries by Adair Lara. This is a brilliant and hilarious take on what to do (and not to do) when your millennial child becomes a first-time parent. Anna Quindlen is the author of Nanaville, Adventures in Grandparenting. Quindlen, who is known for her writing about her own experiences as a mother, now writes with humor and insight into her life as a Nana. Journalist Lesley Stahl wrote Becoming Grandma, The Joys and Science of the New Grandparenting. Along with sharing her personal experiences, Stahl interviews scientists and other famous grandparents on a broad range of relevant topics. All of these authors share their wisdom about how they managed to successfully shed the mantle of parent (to the young adults) and gracefully embrace their new Book ideas for grandparents. supportive role of grandparent/ wise elder. General grandparent books offer a broad range of topics to educate and inform new grandparents. The Modern Grandparent’s Handbook: The Ultimate Guide to the New Rules of Grandparenting, by Dr Georgia Witkin, was published ten years ago, but still offers great advice for today’s families. Unconditional Love, by Jane Isay, is a beautifully written book about the special connection between grandparents and grandchildren. It can help any senior in their journey to be a wise and loving grandparent. The Mindful Grandparent, The Art of Loving Our Children’s Children, by Marilyn McEntyre and Shirley Showalter may be the latest (published in May 2022) and greatest resource available for grandparents. These experienced authors provide spot-on advice for grandparents today and do so while always considering the best interests of all three generations in the family. The chapters are alternately written by each author, and each chapter ends with a brief recap of the key messages of the chapter for the reader. It is an exceptional contribution to the genre of grandparenting books. Whether you are expecting your first grandbaby or are trying to stay connected to a growing teenaged grandchild, these books will enhance your journey, warm your heart, and open your mind to your own special role of grandparent. As you read them, you are likely to gain insight into how to support your adult child in optimal ways, and you just may discover what legacy you want to leave for your grandchild. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. articles.text: Homes are places of comfort and safety for the most part, but there are also inherent dangers in every home where risks do exist. As people age, the likelihood of falling and being seriously injured increases due to dizziness, medication side effects, or vision changes. An in-home care evaluation can be a solution by identifying problem areas and suggesting adaptations to minimize the chances of a slip or fall. Studies have found that someone who is living with dementia is at an increased risk for falling and being injured. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) charts falls among older adults and gives advice on how to intervene to prevent these accidents. According to the CDC, “falls among adults 65 and older caused 34,000 deaths in 2019, making it the leading cause of injury and death for that group.” Of the 1-in-4 older adults who fall each year, less than half tell their doctor, the CDC found. Still, 3 million seniors are treated in the ER for fall injuries and 1-in-5 reported falls lead to a broken bone or head injury. The CDC states that there are 800,000 patients hospitalized annually with a head injury or hip fracture. Room by Room The most dangerous room in a house isn’t even a room, it’s the stairs. According to Medical Guardian, a personal emergency response provider, a home with stairs has an added fall risk for seniors. The solution is ensuring there are adequate handrails on both sides of the stairs. These handrails should be secure; not wiggling when grabbed on to. The bathroom is considered the most dangerous room in the house for seniors, based on a CDC report which found that 235,000 people go to the ER each year after a fall in the bathroom and 14% of those are hospitalized. These injuries can happen while bathing or showering, but also when using the toilet. Grab bars can make a bathroom safer, as well as non-skid mats in the shower or tub, and removing any throw rugs. The kitchen has its own hazards, so falling isn’t the top concern in this room. Improper food storage and accidents while preparing food can lead to food poisoning and injuries like cuts or bruises, and possibly fires. Certainly, if someone is using a stepladder to reach a high shelf or liquids are spilled, there is a higher chance of a fall in this room. The living room and the bedroom can also have a high probability of falls, and for unexpected reasons: lighting and stability when standing. These are rooms where people tend to sit or lie down, but when people stand up, there can be sudden dizziness or stiffness in muscles and joints that contribute to falling down. Some solutions to make these rooms safer include remote controlled lighting, removing throw rugs, clearing clutter and cords that could be tripped over. Outside falls The challenges for older adults can also be found outside, so don’t forget about the garden, garage, and driveways. Gardening can be an excellent activity for elders who want a little exercise and time outdoors. But an inadvertently placed rake or shovel can lead to a trip and subsequent fall. Another consideration is the heat and physical exertion, which can leave someone lightheaded enough to fall. The key here is to remain hydrated, rest often, and keep tools safely stored when not in use. Outside walkways can be slippery, not just in winter, like after watering the lawn and plants. The risk for a traumatic brain injury is real with a fall on the driveway, according to Medical Guardian, so take steps to reduce the chance of a fall in this area. For example, install motion-sensor lights, use an assistive device when walking to the car or to get the mail, safely stow-away hoses, and keep pathways clear. Home care can address risks of falling A professionally trained caregiver knows how to look for fall risks in the home and what measures can be used to lessen the likelihood of a fall. Tasks like assistance with bathing or showering, post-surgery care, and dementia care can all be part of mitigating falls as a steady hand will help someone avoid a slip and fall. A complimentary in-home evaluation can help identify potential risks in each room of the house and include considerations for those who are living with memory impairment. You can then save that signature. For example, I have my mother’s signature, for whom I am power of attorney, and my initials, and my full signature. This way, I can just basically paste it wherever I need it, whether it’s in a tax form or a contract. This signature is resizable. So, if it needs to be bigger, I just stretch the box that it is contained in, and I can move it anywhere in a PDF. 6. Keyboard shortcuts are another feature I depend on: I have made several. articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear Macmama: My son was visiting, and he told me there were a lot of features I am not using on my iMac. For example, he said I could take a picture of my screen. Can you tell me how to do that? –Lissa, Oakland Dear Lissa: I wrote about some features in Monterey in March, but here are a few more including how to take a screenshot. 1. To take a picture, or screenshot of your whole screen, simultaneously press Command + Shift + 3. You will then see a small image of your screen appear in the lower left. If you click on that you can save it, share it via email or messages or even annotate it with text and symbols. To take a screenshot of a portion of your screen, press Command + Shift + 4. Then you will see a small target, and you can click and drag the portion you want to save. This is very useful for example, if you need to show your tech professional something that has popped up on your screen that is troublesome. 2. If a notif ication has appeared on your screen on the upper right, and then disappears, you can show it (and all notifications) again by simply clicking on the time and date on the upper right corner of your screen. 3. Spotlight is for more than just searching for files, you can do math equations. Another thing you can do is currency conversion. For example, if you’re going to Europe, you can type in €100, and it will show you the currency of your home country. 4. If you want to preview a file quickly, single click it, and press your spacebar. And to rename a file quickly and easily, highlight it by clicking it once, then click the Return key on your keyboard. When you’re finished, simply press the Return key again, and the new file name will be saved.
