To customize your own, go to System Preferences > Keyboard > Text and click the + icon. You then decide the letter combination that you want, and then enter the text that will expand with this. For example, every time I write my address, I use the shortcut, “strt.” For my email address, cmm , See MacMama on page 32 By Cynthia Kane When you were expecting your first child you probably sought books to help you prepare for what was coming. Best sellers such as What to Expect When You’re Expecting, The Expectant Father, and Dr. Spock’s Baby and Child Care, helped inform millions of new parents about every aspect of pregnancy, birth, and childcare. Updated editions of these books are still on the market today – decades after their first publication. These days, you might be perusing the literature looking at what you can find about becoming a grandparent. Grandparenting books fall into a few general categories: Grandparent journals, personal memoirs, and how-to books for new grandparents. Grandparent journals/memory books are the top sellers on Amazon.com, and there are dozens of choices. Here are just a few: Grandmother’s/Grandfather’s Journal, by Blue Streak (#1 in Grandparenting Books), Tell Me Your Life Story, Grandma, by Questions About Me, Grandma’s Story, by Korie Herold. These books offer grandparents a simple and delightful way to share with a grandchild their personal details, life history, family lore, and other priceless treasures that can sometimes become lost over the years. It’s amazing how many things we don’t know about our grandparents simply because we never thought to ask them before they passed away. (Options for each book allow the grandparent to choose the journal with their correct grandparent name, i.e., Nana, Grandma, Papa, etc.) Personal memoirs seem to be trending for well-known celebrities and/or authors who would like to share the joys and challenges of becoming a grandparent. Many of these books have a humorous tone, such as Granny Diaries by Adair Lara. This is a brilliant and hilarious take on what to do (and not to do) when your millennial child becomes a first-time parent. Anna Quindlen is the author of Nanaville, Adventures in Grandparenting. Quindlen, who is known for her writing about her own experiences as a mother, now writes with humor and insight into her life as a Nana. Journalist Lesley Stahl wrote Becoming Grandma, The Joys and Science of the New Grandparenting. Along with sharing her personal experiences, Stahl interviews scientists and other famous grandparents on a broad range of relevant topics. All of these authors share their wisdom about how they managed to successfully shed the mantle of parent (to the young adults) and gracefully embrace their new Book ideas for grandparents. supportive role of grandparent/ wise elder. General grandparent books offer a broad range of topics to educate and inform new grandparents. The Modern Grandparent’s Handbook: The Ultimate Guide to the New Rules of Grandparenting, by Dr Georgia Witkin, was published ten years ago, but still offers great advice for today’s families. Unconditional Love, by Jane Isay, is a beautifully written book about the special connection between grandparents and grandchildren. It can help any senior in their journey to be a wise and loving grandparent. The Mindful Grandparent, The Art of Loving Our Children’s Children, by Marilyn McEntyre and Shirley Showalter may be the latest (published in May 2022) and greatest resource available for grandparents. These experienced authors provide spot-on advice for grandparents today and do so while always considering the best interests of all three generations in the family. The chapters are alternately written by each author, and each chapter ends with a brief recap of the key messages of the chapter for the reader. It is an exceptional contribution to the genre of grandparenting books. Whether you are expecting your first grandbaby or are trying to stay connected to a growing teenaged grandchild, these books will enhance your journey, warm your heart, and open your mind to your own special role of grandparent. As you read them, you are likely to gain insight into how to support your adult child in optimal ways, and you just may discover what legacy you want to leave for your grandchild. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. articles.text: On a sunny day in August, 16 members of the Piedmont Seniors group visited Historic Ardenwood Farm in Fremont, where they got a glimpse into life on a family farm that was active between 1890 and 1930. Ardenwood was named after a forest area described in Shakespeare’s play As you Like It. Since 1985 this fully functioning farm has been operated by the East Bay Regional Park District. The best way to get one’s bearings is to hop aboard a train that encircles the 205-acre farm. As the train made its journey, the Seniors saw cattle grazing in the pastures, goats, chickens, and eucalyptus groves which surround the property. There is a Deer Park Station, where you can disembark and explore the farm by foot and even have a picnic. After the train ride, the group took a short walk to the Patterson House, home to three generations of the Patterson family. Completed in 1857, the house was later expanded with a Queen Ann addition in 1889. The Seniors explored the remnants of the once vast estate of George and Clara Patterson, whose family farmed the land for over 100 years, beginning in the 1850s. As transportation options were limited throughout the countryside in the 19th century, railroads served as an important way to connect many of the farms in the East Bay. One of the highlights of the day was the tour of the Patterson House, led by a costumed docent in period attire of the time. The docents were eager to explain the social graces of the Victorian era and demonstrate some of the useful gadgets frequently used in this time frame. An interesting gadget Piedmont Seniors with a docent in front of the 100-year old Patterson House. All Aboard. The Piedmont Seniors group in front of the Ardenwood train station before boarding a train for a trip around the farm. Pictured are: (front) Nancy Hinsch, Janet Epstein, Sandra Curach, Mona Jamieson, Madeline Hall, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, and Yorkman Lowe; (back): Penny Robb, Gregory Jurin, Carole Jones, Cheryl Stanton, Irene Westler, and Robert Hall. Not pictured: Jim Ayotle and Rick Luciano. was a bed warmer, consisting of a metal container shaped like a modern frying pan which would be filled with embers and placed under the covers of the bed. The tour was a glimpse into life on a working farm in the mid- 19th century. It is particularly informative for groups of elementary school students who visit, so they can visualize what life must have been like during this period. Students occasionally allowed to assist in the processing of crops including corn, wheat and hay. Other attractions on the farm include a blacksmith shop with an actual blacksmith on duty, a greenhouse, gazebo, a walnut orchard, a milk house and a myriad of farm animals. You can also order food from a café on weekends and enjoy a pleasant picnic lunch on the spacious grounds. During their visit to Ardenwood, the seniors worked up a hearty appetite, so they ventured to Buon Hayward in Hayward Appetito for a delicious lunch. One of the members even provided the group with a special treat of home-made French bread, It was a delightful outing for a group of lucky Seniors. To find out more about the Piedmont Seniors group and their activities, including monthly meetings, or to receive a quarterly newsletter, contact Seniors’ Coordinator Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov or call the Piedmont Recreation Department at 520-/420-3070. In 2019, the city staff began an assessment process to determine the scope (renovation vs. replacement) of improvements that would be necessary to bring our aging public safety buildings up to current standards. Since then, Piedmont was fortunate to receive $2.6 million from the Federal American Rescue Plan, which Council immediately allocated for the renovation of the 911 Dispatch Center. With our city budget almost entirely dependent upon property taxes, identifying funding sources for large infrastructure projects will remain a significant challenge. Council will continue to evaluate the costs and benefits of different financing approaches in this rising interest rate environment. If our community decides to invest in further upgrades to the civic center, I am confident that talented architects will be able to retain the charming exterior aesthetic of City Hall. 2. Costly upgrades to City Center? Funding deferred maintenance is a challenge most cities face. We will need to carefully study our current infrastructure to determine what is needed. These upgrades are needed to modernize and maintain the core essential services that we all value. Finding funding sources to allow improvements to occur in a cost-effective way must be a top priority for our City. Piedmont is known for its beautiful homes and architecture. Many of us chose to move here because of our city’s size, treelined streets, and charming city center. Preserving the architectural aesthetic of our current civic center is essential to any renovations we undertake. JENNIFER LONG Incumbent 1. The two contractors who submitted bids were SJ Amoroso at $24,597,000 and Lathrop Construction at $26,149,000. The city engineer’s cost estimate is $21.6 million. “We are disappointed but not deterred,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand. “By casting a wider net for contractors, I am optimistic that we will find a firm to complete the project within the City’s available resources.” “I think the key thing about this process we are in right now is we need the competition,” said Clarence Mamuyac, President of ELS. “Generally, when we put these types of projects out to bid, we are looking for four or five bidders.” Mamuyac advised against making changes to the design, specifically the electrification of the pool, since so much community effort and staff time has been dedicated to full electrification. He also discouraged the idea of waiting for costs to go down, citing that rarely occurs. Coupled with inflation, steep rises in construction costs have been driven by supply and demand issues and labor shortages beginning in many areas during the first year of Covid and its general disruption to businesses worldwide. According to a press release by the city on October 14, “between July 2020 and July 2022, the California Construction Cost Index increased by 30%. In comparison, the 10-year average annual increase between 2010 and 2020 was 2.4%. The 20-year average annual increase was 2.9%.” New bids are due within 30 days and the city plans to process them by Thanksgiving, November, 24. Lillevand said it may be possible to award a contract at the December City Council meeting. “The thing we got the most right was the timing of the issuing of the bonds,” said Lillevand, explaining that the city saved an estimated $5 million by issuing bonds in 2020 as opposed to issuing them now. The new community pool as designed will include a 27-meter competition pool with diving wells, a 3,177 square foot activity pool with three 25-yard lap lanes, and a one-story building with locker rooms, two gender neutral changing rooms, and a rooftop pavilion. The raises go into effect retroactively from July 1, 2022. Teachers will receive a separate check for their August and September, and raises will be included in their October 31 checks. Most teachers don’t receive a paycheck for July unless they choose the 12-month payment option. Part-time teachers will receive a pro-rated percentage of the $1,500 based on workload. Prior to the raises, the lowest step on the pay schedule for fulltime teachers without teaching experience or additional degrees was around $60,000 per year. articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch is enjoying a bounty of sales this year. The patch received its famous centerpiece, Giant Jack, on October 4 in the middle of the night by Bay Area legend Kevin “the Pumpkin Kingpin.” Pumpkin patch patrons have been busy trying to guess the weight of the enormous pumpkin since it arrived. As of Monday this week, a total of 76 people had submitted their best estimates. One lucky winner will receive delivery of the behemoth to the home and subsequent removal after Halloween. Kids have been busy applying lessons learned in math, botany and physics to try to determine its weight. Some have brought measuring tapes, pen and paper and have taken their empirical calculations to their geometry teachers The French Fairytale pumpkin is a popular choice once again this year. articles.text: For one evening, the Piedmont Center for the Arts turned its focus to one of its most popular events, the Piedmont Artisanal Brewing Competition – the art of making beer. The 10th Annual Piedmont Artisanal Brewing Contest on Friday, October 7 drew a crowd equal to last year’s large turnout of more than 150 people to sample over 20 homebrews from nine local home brewers. The capacity crowd was in no hurry to go home until the awards for best beers were presented and some of the taps ran dry. Oa k la nd Brewe r Kyle Blomseth of Legacy of Brewtality, was the night’s big winner, earning Best Specialty Beer for his “Bill Marzen Lager” and Best Ale with his “Autumnal Rye.” Bob Davis of Hayward brought four concoctions from Happy Girl Brewing and took home the top prize, Best in Show, for “Reflected Glory,” a Trappist Tripel. Best in Show: Bob Davis - Reflected Glory - Trappist Tripel The PCA board took ownership of the annual with excellent organizing efforts by Carter Dunlap and logistical support at every level. Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson was the quiet hero of the night with his remarkable donation of the bratwurst, red cabbage and potato salad to feed the masses. He also helped with the grilling and serving, and in his spare time was one of three beer judges. “Our board was anxious to return the Piedmont Beer Festival

articles.text: Ramsey needed in city’s future housing plans Editor: I am pleased to support Tom Ramsey in the campaign for City Council. Tom and I served at the same time on the Planning Commission so I have witnessed Tom’s dedication to listening to people on all sides of issues, evaluating information, and making solid decisions. Tom has particular knowledge of State requirements for local governments and creating Piedmont plans to meet those State requirements while serving Piedmont citizens’ desires. Please vote for Tom Ramsey so that he can continue work on behalf of all Piedmont citizens. –Susan Ode civic matters of highest consequence. Her natural curiosity is an invaluable asset. She explores questions through multiple lenses and seeks input from people with varied perspectives, so that the decisions she makes as a leader are nuanced and well informed. Jennifer has been a hardworking and approachable member of the City Council since her appointment to fill a vacancy in 2022, and our community would be best served by electing her to remain on the council. –Anna Weber Kneitel

articles.text: When I was five years old, one of the largest hurricanes on record in the Atlantic Ocean, Superstorm Sandy, took the lives of 233 people from the Caribbean to Canada in October of 2012. Since then, over 16 hurricanes (also known as tropical cyclones) have taken the lives and homes of thousands in the United States. I remember the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy when the sidewalk turned to a shore when waves of knee-deep water crashed at my doorstep. I remember the hanging light in the basement which brushed across the water as it swung, and a power outage that lasted weeks. And now, 10 years later, as a sophomore at Piedmont High School, I ask where my mom’s wedding dress or where our childhood photos went. My parents respond: Lost to the flood waters, weren’t they? I am grateful that we were so lucky to remain safe and healthy during the hurricane compared to the thousands of victims who faced personal and financial crises in the aftermath. But I am left to worry in recent days when new hurricanes and disasters occur everywhere in our world, including in the United States as Hurricane Ian has already claimed the lives of more than 80 people. It is difficult for many to imagine the immense loss and pain that millions across the world are facing due to extreme weather conditions fueled by climate change. We have control over our lives and decisions. We must acknowledge our privileges and use them to the advantage of the world. This does not always mean immense strides and doesn’t mean billions of dollars. It means evaluating decisions in our everyday life. When you ask yourself if you are doing what you can to lessen the destruction. Doing your part can include remaining informed, spreading awareness, supporting environmental campaigns, and being aware of your actions and decisions. I am a member of Piedmont High’s Green Club, which is working to do our part. I understand that there are far too many people in the world who are suffering devastations worth a thousand lifetimes, people who no longer have stable access to electricity, and whose childhood homes are turning to ruin under salt water. As a high school student and a member of the next generation I want your attention. I seek understanding and urgency. We, the youth, need your eyes and your humanity for the good of our future, for the lives of billions, and for justice to families who have lost so much. We can no longer bear to read the news every day and hear of disasters that read like a literary tragedy. We can no longer bear the collective burden that grows due to simple habits that have become our liabilities. A first and meaningful step is for residents to join the Piedmont Climate Challenge at piedmontclimatechallange.org. I encourage you to take part in this movement to save not only the earth, but those who walk beside us and who tread closely behind. In the months ahead, I intend to share ways you can contribute to and support our community and beyond to address climate change – the greatest challenge of our generation. Clea Villaluz is a sophomore at Piedmont High School and a member of the school’s Green Club. She plans to write a monthly column on environmental topics. “Is it good management, or are you just having a run of good luck?”
articles.title: Hurricane Ian part of a continuing pattern

articles.text: As a long-time Piedmont resident with extensive development experience, I urge the City Council not to vote on the proposed rezoning plan until after the next election. Serious issues have been raised concerning the plan. These demand more review and community input. This is particularly true concerning planned major construction of 16 new units of housing in the center of town near Havens school, and over 100 units of new housing on a very congested Moraga Ave. The most important issue we can all agree on is that any plan must ensure the safety of our children and all residents. We can also agree that current traffic in the center of Piedmont near Havens school is currently congested and often dangerous at the beginning and end of school days. We can also agree that Moraga Ave. is very congested right now during peak hours. The proposed 16 units of housing, along with the major construction to build the units, poses significant future safety issues for our children. Given the extensive use of Coaches field for youth activities, a proposal for 100+ units of housing in a very congested area poses clear safety issues. In spite of these clear risks, it is my understanding that the City has not had a traffic engineer or safety specialist formally study these plans. The City Administrator recently basically said not to worry; this is just a plan, and any future development can be debated by the City Council. No big deal. But any developer or expert knows this is simply wrong. Once the plan is submitted to the state, it takes on a life of its own based on current state laws. Future City Councils will not be able to block it. We must make sure the plan is sound now. What is the rush to judgement? We have an election coming up. Let the new City Council review the plan and make the final decision on the plan. Finally, the City Charter clearly states that all residents should vote on zoning changes. The City Council and Administrator seem to think they can ignore that and that they know best. What are they afraid of? Let the residents vote on a clearly laid out plan supported by traffic and safety experts. Let’s do this right. Our children deserve it.
articles.title: Let residents vote on housing plan

pages.text: Wednesday, October 12, 2022 3 In response to letter from City Administrator By Bridget Harris Ever yone i n Pied mont received a letter from Sara Lillevand, the City Administrator, dated September 30, 2022. The City Administrator is hired by the City Council and reports directly to the City Council. Therefore, we can assume that the letter was vetted and approved by the five members of the City Council. The letter is extremely misleading. 1 The letter is a not too subtle endorsement of three candidates to the City Council who oppose a vote on the Housing Element; 2. As stated in the letter, the City has been working on the issue for 18 months, yet this citywide letter was sent five weeks before the election; 3. The letter includes the statement that any future development would have to meet Piedmont’s design standards. This is not true, see Schreiber v. City of Los Angeles and Bankers Hill 150 v. City of San Diego. Both cases illustrate that the state’s Density Bonus Law supersedes a city’s local ordinances and zoning laws. The Density Bonus Law provides developers with incentives and waivers of building restrictions for setbacks, parking and height. 4. The letter outlines the plan to include 132 homes on Cityowned land (Moraga Canyon). This land is in Zone B (Park and Public Land). Zone C is zoned for Multi-family units. The plan is a de-facto re-zone which according to our City Charter requires a majority vote of the citizens of Piedmont. Further, once the plan is approved a developer can enforce development using the state’s Density Bonus Law that overrides Piedmont’s design restrictions thereby making development economically feasible. At that point a vote will be too late. 5. Piedmont Municipal Code §17.08.010 provides that “[i]f a use is not permitted or conditionally permitted, it is not allowed.” Piedmont Municipal Code §17.22.020 lists the permitted and conditional uses allowed in Zone B. Multi-family units are not permitted or conditionally permitted in Zone B. To build multi-family units on property located in Zone B requires a vote to re-zone the land pursuant to §9.02 of our City Charter. Adding 587 units to the city of Piedmont will forever change the city. We must delay submission of the Housing Element plan until we understand all ramifications of the plan. We must review available options and then vote on those options. True engagement by the community requires a vote and the result will be a viable Housing Element plan. Bridget Harris is a candidate for Piedmont City Council. articles.text: Steven Pifer, a former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine, will address the current war in Ukraine and the country’s future in a talk sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters. Titled “What Lies Ahead for Ukraine? Current Situation and Prospects,” the discussion will be on Wednesday, November 2 at 5:00 p.m. (Zoom, YouTube streaming). The war in Ukraine is the largest land war since World War II. Listen to the latest about the current situation from a diplomatic, military, and economic viewpoint, as well as possible trajectories for the war. Ambassador Pifer will address implications for international security, not only for Ukraine and Russia but also for the US and the EU. Steven Pifer is an affiliate with the Center for International Security and Cooperation at Stanford and a nonresident senior fellow with the Brookings Institution. A retired Foreign Service officer, his more than 25 years with the Department of State included assignments as deputy assistant secretary with responsibilities for Russia and Ukraine, U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, and special assistant to the President and senior director for Russia, Ukraine and Eurasia on the National Security Council. articles.text: Public invited to special board meeting today at 4 p.m. The Piedmont School Board will hold a Special Board Meeting at 4:00 p.m. this afternoon, Wednesday, October 12, at City Hall to publicly conduct interviews of the two search firms they are considering hiring to help find a permanent School Superintendent. The Board sent out a Request for Proposal (RFP) on August 31 and two firms, Leadership Associates and McPherson and Jacobson, responded with interest. The public is invited to attend, listen and offer input. There will be time for public comment after the firm’s presentations and before the board deliberates in private. The meeting can also be viewed via zoom at: Zoom. us/j/89689031566. The meeting is scheduled from 4:00-5:30 p.m. based upon the following schedule: 4:00-4:40 p.m. – McPherson & Jacobsen (CSBA) represented by Bill Huyett & Nicole Anderson 4:45-5:25 p.m. – Leadership Associates represented by Eric Andrew & Jacki Horejs 5:25-5:30 p.m. – Public Input Representatives from each firm will give a 15-minute presentation followed by questions from board members. After the formal presentations and public comment, the Board will deliberate in private. The school board is expected to announce which firm has been selected at its regularly scheduled board meeting on October 26.
articles.title: School Board begins interviews with search firms for permanent school superintendent

articles.text: The Alameda County Registrar of Voters is seeking poll workers for the November 8, 2022 election. Poll workers play a critical role in making voting accessible to all community members – and get paid to do it. Workers are needed throughout Alameda County from Saturday, November 5 through Tuesday, November 8, election day. Interested community members can sign up online to volunteer at acgov.org/rovform_app/ewapply. The application is simple and takes just a few minutes to complete. Job Details Poll workers are paid volunteers who perform tasks including: • Setting up and closing a polling place • Helping voters understand their rights • Protecting ballots and voting equipment The County Registrar of Voters office provides training for poll workers. Individuals are paid for training and time served as a poll worker. No special skills are required to be a poll worker. Eligibility Requirements: • Must be a registered voter in California • Must be a legal permanent resident or green card holder • An eligible high school student Bilingual Poll Workers Sought Bilingual poll workers are especially needed. In Alameda County, assistance is provided to voters in Burmese, Chinese, Hindi, Khmer, Korean, Laotian, Mien, Mongolian, Punjabi, Spanish, Tagalog, Telugu, and Vietnamese. Residents fluent in any of these languages are urged to consider volunteering. Interested residents can find more information about volunteering as a poll worker at acvote.org/community/ become-an-election-worker or by calling the Alameda County Registrar of Voters office at 510-272-6973.
articles.title: Poll workers needed for Nov. 8 Election

articles.text: On November 8 Piedmont voters will elect three individuals for the City Council, and two people for the School Board. In addition to local elections, the November 8 ballot includes candidates for U.S. Senate, Congress, statewide elected offices, County officials, and seven statewide ballot measures. Voter Registration deadline: October 24 The last day to register to vote for the November 8 election is Monday, October 24. Those already registered are encouraged to check their registration status online at Voterstatus.sos.ca.gov before October 24 to confirm that the information is correct. Residents will need to re-register if they have moved, changed their name, or wish to change their political party preference. Voter registration forms are available at the City Clerk’s Office at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, and from the Registrar of Voters at Acvote.org/voting/register-to-vote. You can also register to vote online at Registertovote.ca.gov. Ways to Vote All registered voters will receive a vote-by-mail ballot for the November 8 election. Ballots were mailed starting Monday, October 10. Voters can turn in their ballots by mail or at the official Registrar of Voters drop box at the corner of Highland Avenue and Highland Way. • Voting by Mail Ballots mailed through the post office must be postmarked by November 8th. • Ballot Drop Boxes Ballots can be turned in 24 hours a day at any of the 66 official Registrar of Voters secure ballot drop boxes across Alameda County. In Piedmont, there is a ballot drop box located near the mailboxes at Highland Way and Mountain Avenue. The Registrar of Voters picks up ballots from the drop boxes every day. The last pickup will be 8:00 p.m. on Tuesday, November 8th. Postage is not required for ballots submitted at the drop box. • Voting in Person Polling booths will be open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. from Saturday through Monday, November 5-7. And from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on election day, Tuesday, November 8. Voting in Piedmont will take place at the Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue. Sample Ballot & Voter Information Pamphlet The Registrar of Voters began mailing Sample Ballot and Voter Information pamphlets to registered voters on September 29. Any voter who did not receive a sample ballot or who has questions should contact the Alameda County Registrar of Voters Office at 272-6933 or Acvote. org/index .

articles.text: Join Fire Chief Brannigan for citywide drill on November 5 Many Piedmonters vividly remember the 1991 Tunnel Fire in the Oakland hills, which killed 25 people and destroyed more than 2,500 homes. While Piedmont escaped the devastation 26 years ago, the threat remains today, even more present now because of climate change, which has made wildfires more frequent and destructive. As your Fire Chief, I strive daily to ensure our City government is poised to protect this community in a disaster. But I also know that in an emergency, the best efforts of public agencies alone will not be enough. Our community needs to prepare, too. Today, I ask every Piedmonter to take three simple steps to be more ready for a wildfire. 1. First, make sure we can reach you in a disaster. If you aren’t yet registered for AC Alert emergency notifications, sign up now. Piedmont and Alameda County public safety officials will use AC Alert to send evacuation warnings and orders in a fire, earthquake, or other emergency. articles.text: Three Piedmont High School students, senior Gianna Yan, and juniors Siddarth Bhatia and Cleo Tahawi, were selected to serve as student school board members through June 30, 2023. They will be able to place “preferential votes,” to show their positions, but they will not be counted amongst the five elected board members’ votes on action items. In years prior, Associated Student Body (ASB) members gave reports to the board at the start of board meetings. The selection of official student members seeks to expand the role and impact of students upon board decisions and direction. They are scheduled to attend every regularly scheduled board meeting in-person and will have a weekly meeting with Superintendent Donald Evans to review each meeting’s agenda in advance. “We’re asking them to bring that information [from the meetings with Evans] back to the student body, and get some input, to actually bring the voice of the students to this governance team,” said Board President Cory Smegal. While he was superintendent at Berkeley Unified School District, Evans worked with student members, and has come with valuable experience to this new endeavor in Piedmont. Students were asked to submit applications by September 16, and after an administrative review, three applicants were selected for interviews. Smegal and board member Veronica Thigpen interviewed them with plans of picking one or two, but after interviews, decided to take all three for the task. “Four or five months ago I never saw myself sitting in city hall and actually seeing this happen,” said Gianna Yan at the September 28 board meeting. “It was more of a pipe dream [then], but now I am seeing it all come into fruition. Thank you so much.” Earlier in the evening Yan talked about some accessibility issues with the new “Academy” study hall period introduced this year at Piedmont and Millennium High. Bhatia and Tahawi spoke during the meeting as well and thanked the board for having been selected. Senior Gianna Yan Junior Siddarth Bhatia Junior Cleo Tahawi
articles.title: Three PHS students to serve on school board

articles.text: From October 24 to November 7 members of the Piedmont 1st grade Girl Scout Daisy Troop, Troop 31318, will be collecting candy wrappers to recycle through the TerraCycle Zero Waste Program – and they have some big requests: As a community we can all help make a difference. Please show the 1st graders the difference we can make when we work together. 1. Trick-or-Treating When buying candy for trickor-treaters this year, try choosing candy wrappers that are compostable, like Nerds boxes, paper Pixie Stix, and paper wrapped chocolates. 2. Saving Candy Wrappers Set up a bag in your home, maybe an old Amazon shipping bag, and start collecting the plastic candy wrappers that would otherwise end up in a landfill (or our parks and bay). 3. Recycling Bring your wrappers to the Troop 31318 TerraCycle Zero Waste collection bin outside of Mulberry’s Market from October 24th to November 7th. 4. Writing letters Does your favorite candy only have landfill destined wrapping? Write to the maker and ask them to change. A bin for candy wrappers will be in front of Mulberry’s Market for a collection drive by Piedmont Girl Scouts.

articles.text: Candidates respond to questions Part five in a series With Election Day less than four weeks away the Piedmont Post has escalated its coverage of the two local elections, school board and city council. Starting this week and until the election on Tuesday November 8, this Candidate Q & A section will feature weekly answers from the school board candidates. Two questions are sent out on Thursday via email and candidates are instructed to limit their answers to under 150 words. SCHOOL BOARD Two open seats; three candidates. QUESTIONS – Week 5 1. Piedmont High School’s football team recently had to cancel its Homecoming football game. The team’s entire season is in jeopardy and the school’s 100-year-old program is in danger. What do you think needs to be done to continue the tradition, and how can you assist? 2. In February 2019, the School Board voted 4-1 against accepting $390,000 in federal funds to staff an armed police officer on campus. Do you see value in having an armed officer on campus? What is your view on campus safety? ment and our school district, but evidence points away from having an armed officer on campus. Instead, I support measures such as ensuring that doors are not propped open and that they lock, that students are protected even as they eat or play outside, and that we have drills with enough frequency so that students will know what to do even in the worst situation imaginable. Ongoing mental health support for our kids can also help them before problems escalate to violence. We want assurances that our children will be safe at school. Continuing to practice our safety protocols and procedures so our kids know what to do in an emergency is essential. RUCHI MEDHEKAR 1. Football program in jeopardy? First and foremost, I want our kids to be safe. I was worried when I heard about the season-ending injuries that occurred on the team, and my understanding is that the number of injuries on the roster drove the decision to cancel the game. I was very excited to hear that the school pivoted and showcased the girls’ volleyball game so that students could still participate in the Homecoming festivities. We’ve struggled with low participation in football at the high school level, but the numbers in middle school are promising and will likely feed the JV and Varsity teams in coming years. There are opportunities to collaborate with the Recreation Department to create early interest in sports. While I think it is important to appreciate our traditions, if students’ interests in sports are evolving, I believe our programs should meet the needs of our current students. 2. Campus Safety and Armed Officer on Campus? With every shooting - including the recent ones in Oakland and Thailand - the need to protect our students and keep our campuses safe becomes more pronounced and fraught. I appreciate the deep collaboration between our police departSHIRLEY HOOI 1. Football program in jeopardy? There is something special about the tradition of cheering on your local high school football team each fall season. It brings students, parents and the community together under the Friday night lights to revel in the hard work of the athletes and coaches on the field. The role of sports is principally to teach our kids invaluable life skills: physical and mental discipline, teamwork, leadership, resilience. Playing competitive sports builds character and allows them to experience a unique camaraderie in so doing, and all sports teams offer this opportunity. Students get to choose what sports they want to play, with their parents permission and support. My understanding is that increasingly, students are opting to play sports other than football, due to the risk of serious injury, and I fully support their decision, whatever that decision may be. 2. Campus Safety and Armed Officer on Campus? Improving student and staff safety is a paramount concern, and merits thoughtful reevaluation, particularly in light of the increasing number and severity of school shootings in the recent past. An SRO appears to be a promising way to both improve campus safety, as well as minimize the time for qualified law enforcement personnel to intercede - a key finding in the aftermath of the tragedy at Sandy Hook. That said, I am cognizant that even in our own District, concerns have been raised about this particular approach to improve safety. I am not sure what the right answer for PUSD is going forward, but I would find out by consulting all the key stakeholders to solicit inputs. Thereafter, I would carefully weigh the pros and cons in consultation with my fellow board members, and with a bias toward action to promote improved health and safety of our students and staff. LINDSAY THOMASSON 1. Football program in jeopardy? It is my understanding, based on conversations with football families, that the cancellation of the homecoming game and premature end to the season was the culmination of a number of factors. The varsity football team has few junior players due to the cancellation of practices during COVID; football was much slower to return than other sports. As players were injured, there wasn’t a sufficient number of substitutes and the team was forced to forfeit games. Fortunately, there is a very strong string of sophomore players, many of whom played in varsity games this year. There is also significant interest in middle school flag football which feeds into the high school football program. This, along with robust community support for high school sports, bodes well for the sustainability of the football program. Football Fridays are one of my favorite Piedmont traditions. It was incredibly disappointing for the entire community for the homecoming game to be canceled. Yet, I appreciate how the high school was able to change to a homecoming girls volleyball game instead, particularly given ongoing discussions about Title IX and recognition that girls sports should receive equal resources and recognition. 2. Campus Safety and Armed Officer on Campus? I reached out to Chief Bowers last month to discuss the relationship between the Piedmont Police Department and Piedmont School District. He explained that the relationship is generally collaborative and strong. However, he would like to see [the district] form a threat assessment team, something districts nationwide are implementing in an effort to identify and prevent violent incidents on school campuses. These multi-disciplinary teams are made up of police officers, school counselors, county mental health professionals, and teachers. The School Board, in conjunction with the district and PPD, should make establishment of a threat assessment team a priority; prevention should be our primary objective. I am unconvinced that an armed officer would make our campuses safer and may, counterintuitively, provide a false sense of security. We’re fortunate that PPD is centrally located in close proximity to our schools; they can and do respond quickly to issues that arise. That said, in addition to the creation of a threat response team, It is essential that we continually review our school safety plans and have regular earthquake, fire, and lockdown drills so that everyone on our school campuses is prepared to act quickly if an incident occurs.

articles.text: Screenagers is an award-winning documentary from 2016 by Delaney Ruston. Piedmont Parents Network (PPN) is showing the award-winning documentary, Screenagers: Growing Up in the Digital Age on Thursday, October 20 at 7:00 pm in the Middle School Multi-purpose room. The viewing and discussion afterwards are offered to all parents in the Piedmont community, as well as high school and middle school students. The event is in collaboration with Piedmont Middle School and the School District Wellness Center The 70-minute documentary follows physician and filmmaker Delaney Ruston as she probes into the vulnerable corners of family life, including her own, to explore struggles over social media, video games, academics and internet addiction. Through poignant, and unexpectedly funny stories, along with surprising insights from authors, psychologists, and brain scientists, the film reveals how tech time impacts kids’ development. It offers solutions on how adults can empower kids to best navigate the digital world and find balance. PPN invites parents to attend even if they have already seen the film, and as a community explore the impact of screens and social media. After the film, small group discussions will take place as PPN provides resources on how to find balance for children in the digital age. Parents and kids age 11 and older are encouraged to attend together. Seating is limited. Please RSVP at forms.gle/ LUw2nTKTfUukwbrj8 The presentation is the first of this year’s PMS Parent Engagement Nights – a series of regular events at the middle school as part of the Connected Learning Initiative. These events focus on issues and challenges facing families and students. PPN’s goal is to support and empower parents in raising kids who behave ethically, think critically, and participate safely and responsibly. PPN holds monthly gradelevel meetings in homes to discuss topics of interest to small parent groups, to include guest speakers. PPN also helps to keep communication lines open with middle school and high school administrators to ensure parent voices can be heard in a coordinated and constructive way. For information on joining Piedmont Parents Network, contact Edit Kincses (kincsesedit1@ gmail.com) or Caroline Santander (carolinesantander@gmail.com). Piedmont Parents Network (PPN) is showing the award-winning documentary, Screenagers: Growing Up in the Digital Age on Thursday, October 20 at 7:00 pm in the Middle School Multi-purpose room. The viewing and discussion afterwards are offered to all parents in the Piedmont community, as well as high school and middle school students. The event is in collaboration with Piedmont Middle School and the School District Wellness Center The 70-minute documentary follows physician and filmmaker Delaney Ruston as she probes into the vulnerable corners of family life, including her own, to explore struggles over social media, video games, academics and internet addiction. Through poignant, and unexpectedly funny stories, along with surprising insights from authors, psychologists, and brain scientists, the film reveals how tech time impacts kids’ development. It offers solutions on how adults can empower kids to best navigate the digital world and find balance. PPN invites parents to attend even if they have already seen the film, and as a community explore the impact of screens and social media. After the film, small group discussions will take place as PPN provides resources on how to find balance for children in the digital age. Parents and kids age 11 and older are encouraged to attend together. Seating is limited. Please RSVP at forms.gle/ LUw2nTKTfUukwbrj8 The presentation is the first of this year’s PMS Parent Engagement Nights – a series of regular events at the middle school as part of the Connected Learning Initiative. These events focus on issues and challenges facing families and students. PPN’s goal is to support and empower parents in raising kids who behave ethically, think critically, and participate safely and responsibly. PPN holds monthly gradelevel meetings in homes to discuss topics of interest to small parent groups, to include guest speakers. PPN also helps to keep communication lines open with middle school and high school administrators to ensure parent voices can be heard in a coordinated and constructive way. For information on joining Piedmont Parents Network, contact Edit Kincses (kincsesedit1@ gmail.com) or Caroline Santander (carolinesantander@gmail.com). Pro-C is for those creators who are wellknown within their field and area of expertise and are at the top of their form. Little-C refers to the day-to-day act of creation that all of us can undertake – a song that is composed around a campfire, a painting that is for the enjoyment of the creator and a few friends on Instagram, a new creative idea for how to move along the pickup lane at school that helps a group of parents. And Mini-C is the creative process that sometimes doesn’t even leave our own minds or, if it does, it is purely for the process of learning and experimenting. Attend a Bay Area Children’s Theatre production or take a class with a teaching artist and you are seeing Pro-C at work. Create an original piece of art with your child that tells the story of your family vacation and post it to your Whatsapp group; that is Try practicing the 4C’s of creativity at home. Little-C. And, look at the challenge of getting your kids out the door on time in the morning from a new perspective, or experiment with a different way to organize the bedtime routine; that is Mini-C. The key from my perspective is that we need all of these types of Creativity in our world. articles.text: ‘Twas the night of All Hallow’s Eve and Sally the witch of Salem was getting ready to enjoy a night of trick-or-treating, feeling the wind blow through her hair as she rode her broom and carved pumpkins with her cat Lucinda. Sally lived in the forest with her cat in a quaint cottage. Her cottage had remained the same and had been passed down from her ancestors who lived in Salem before her. It it was trapped in colonial times. None the less, Sally had made it ghostly and ready for All Hallow’s Eve. Carved pumpkins with candles inside lined the perimeter of her house to cast scary shadows on the ground. Sally also enchanted mini skeletons to dance on the roof of her house through the night. And last but not least, Sally decided to turn the smoke that came from her chimney a smoky green color for extra fright to anyone who might see it. As Sally was getting ready to get on her broom and fly over the town of Salem, she ran into a small problem. She couldn’t find her hat! Oh no, she cried, as she ran around her cottage in search of the most essential piece of her outfit. But the pointed black hat was nowhere to be found. Sally decided to retrace her steps to when she last saw it. She took Lucinda and put her in the pet basket attached to her broom that she had bought at Brooms and Things Emporium, exclusively for witches who need pet accessories for brooms, and took off into the sunset in the direction of the main part of Salem. Sally f lew as fast as her broom could take her, almost breaking the speed limit allowed for brooms. She landed in front of Styles and Creams, the onestop shop for every mysterious baked good and every spooktacular dress that came straight from Milan Witch and Wizard Fashion Week. Sally ran in, out of breath looking for her hat. She looked on every shelf, through every rack of clothes, and every cake case that she could get her hands on. But no such luck. Her fellow witches even helped her look for the hat, because every witch knows how important a black pointed hat is. But after 15 minutes of frantically searching, Sally gave up. Until she remembered there was one last place she could look for her hat, Merlin’s Potion Palace, the most famous potion brewery on the planet. Well not really. The actual title of most famous on the planet was held by some wizard named Nicholas Flammel who had his own potion brewery in England. (But Merlin’s Potion Palace made one mean Time Reverser draught. It comes in handy when you’re running late.) She had been there earlier that day to get the potion that would turn her fire and smoke green. This time Sally walked in, heels clicking and wood creaking on the ancient floors. The hut itself was operated by no one, but ask and you shall receive whatever you need. Every corner was covered in different potions for different occasions. And lo and behold. There on the counter of the dark and musty brewery, sat her hat. Sally couldn’t contain hers excitement and ran straight for her hat. Hugging it as soon as it was in her hands. Lucinda wrapped herself around Sally’s ankles purring in satisfaction that the hat was found. Sally and Lucinda proudly left the potion brewery and hopped on the broom and started their journey back home to the edge of the forest. The night of All Hallow’s Eve had a full moon. As Sally flew, she noticed that she would be flying through the middle of the moon with her witch’s outline visible to everyone looking to the sky. But Sally decided, what, after all, is Halloween without some spooky witch sightings to be reported. And with that she flew through the middle of the moon, pointy hat and all. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and a sophomore at the Bentley School.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

Yet I have found that being an introvert grants me unique skills and strengths as a community leader and council member. Before speaking or taking action on a matter, I listen deeply, reserve judgment, and weigh diverse viewpoints. I work to make everyone feel valued, seen and heard. As a council member, these skills help me to hone in on what is important. They help me seek to understand diverse perspectives when people agree or disagree with a council decision. As someone who listens before she speaks, I strive to hear every voice–not just the loudest–and to value what every stakeholder brings to the conversation. BETSY ANDERSEN, Incumbent 1. Most Critical Fiscal Issues City Council, City staff, and the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee have worked diligently over the last decade to budget conservatively and set aside funds for future liabilities. Going forward, the most critical fiscal issues are: Pensions, Police & Fire, and the Pool. First, we are about to enter a period of substantial pension cost increases. In expectation, during my tenure, Council set aside $3.75M in a pension rate stabilization fund. We anticipate beginning to utilize these funds as soon as next year. Second, Council has allocated Piedmont’s American Rescue Plan (ARPA) funds to renovate the 911 Dispatch Center. This is phase one of upgrades to bring our public safety facilities up to current standards. Third, rebuilding the Piedmont Community Pool during a period of high inflation is challenging. Council has already significantly scaled back the project to keep within our budget and more tough choices may be necessary. 2. Relevant Life Experience Studying public policy at Duke, practicing law for nearly two decades, and serving on the Recreation Commission and Public Safety Committee have all helped me prepare for City Council. But serving on the City Council for the past five years is the specific experience that has prepared me to serve another term. I have learned that no councilmember can accomplish anything on their own. You have to be willing and able to build consensus to be effective. You need at least three votes to move forward on any agenda item or policy objective. I have found that the best way to build consensus is to be informed, listen, ask questions, and seek solutions. It also helps to presume good intent. Even when our views may differ, every councilmember wants to do the right thing for Piedmont.

articles.text: Beats James Logan, Foothill & California Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team continued its strong season with three wins in four games at the Tri-Valley Tournament at Foothill High in Pleasanton last weekend, October 7-8. Following a narrow 9-7 loss to Terra Linda on Friday, Piedmont won the next three games, a 13-6 win over James Logan, and a 9-8 victory over Foothill and 13-7 vs. California on Saturday. PHS also defeated Lick Wilmerding 10-4 on Tuesday, October 4 at City College of San Francisco. The batch of matches brings Piedmont’s record to 14-3 overall as they creep closer toward the end of the regular season and the Western Alameda County Conference tournament on October 25-29. PHS is currently undefeated in league at 5-0 and is set to attain the No. 1 seed in league. 9-8 win over Foothill Piedmont’s narrow 9-8 victory over Foothill came down to the final seconds in an 8-8 tie. In the final minute, PHS killed a man-advantage opportunity for Foothill with two critical saves by goalie Dariush Kashani. With 40 seconds left junior Peter Krumins launched a shot to the top corner of the goal, hitting off of the goalie fingers and into the net for the game winner. It marked the second one-goal win over Foothill this season after beating the Falcons 11-10 in overtime on September 24. Final stats include: George Stein led the way with four goals, while Krumins had three. Declan Linnane had one goal, three assists, and a steal. Farris Saffouri had one goal. Quincy Sherman had two assists. 13-6 win over James Logan Piedmont held a 3-2 advantage to end the first quarter and scored three more in the second quarter without conceding any goals. PHS extended the gap to 10-3 in the third quarter and closed out by scoring three and allowing three. PHS finished with nine different player scoring. Final stats include: Linnane scored four goals and one assist. Photo by Nancy Brahm George Stein scored four goals in Piedmont’s 9-8 win over Foothill. Photo by Nancy Brahm Peter Krumins scored the game-winner against Foothill. Staff Photo Goalie Dariush Kashani had double-digit saves against James Logan and Lick Wilmerding. Stein had a goal, assist, and steal. Finn Burke scored twice. Evan Dickason and Daniel Banin had a goal and assist. Krumins, Hayden Jahn, Elles Kreickhaus and Leo Hurwitz had individual goals. Scherman had an assist and steal. Aloush had an assist and two steals. Kashani finished with 12 saves and five steals. 9-7 loss to Terra Linda Terra Linda jumped out to a 4-1 lead in the first quarter, led 6-2 by halftime, and 9-5 to start the fourth quarter. But Piedmont rallied with two goals in the final period to close the final score to 9-7. Final stats include: Burke had two goals and a steal. Stein had two goals. Krumins had one goal and three steals. Banin had a goal, assist, and steal. Linnane had two assists and a steal. Kashani had nine saves. 10-4 win over Lick Wilmerding In October 4’s win over Lick Wilmerding, Piedmont led 6-2 by the end of the first quarter and 6-2 by halftime. PHS added three more in the third to lead 9-3 and scored one and allowed one in the fourth. Final stats include: Burke scored three goals with one assist. Banin had two goals and an assist. Krumins scored twice. Linnane had two goals and three assists. Stein had a goal and two steals. Saffouri had two assists and a steal. Jahn had an assist. Kashani had 17 saves and two assists. Tuesday vs. Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont traveled to Mills College yesterday, Tuesday, October 11 to face league rival Bishop O’Dowd. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (14-3 overall, 5-0 league) faces Alameda at the Encinal pool on Tuesday, October 18 at 5:00 p.m. They conclude their regular season at a tournament hosted by Stevenson HS in Pebble Beach on Saturday, October 22.

articles.text: Piedmont‘s tennis team took firm control of the Western Alameda County Conference title race on Thursday, October 6 at the Berkeley Tennis Club, defeating Berkeley High in a narrow 4-3 match day. The win improves Piedmont’s record to 10-3 overall; they remain undefeated in league at 6-0. PHS’ last remaining opponent on the league schedule is Bishop O’Dowd, who they defeated 4-2 at the California Tennis Classic in Fresno on September 10. Thursday’s win came down to the No. 1 doubles, which Mara LaForte and Michaela Bini won in three sets with a decisive 6-0 victory in the decisive set/ The scores with Berkeley’s Rowna Kenneth and Malika Treyna were 6-2, 2-6, 6-0. “The Berkeley match was very exciting. It came down to the last match on the court with Mara and Miki. They split sets and at the start of the third set, the Berkeley player mishit an overhead smash and the ball unfortunately hit Mara in the back. I started to award the point to the Berkeley team when Corey [Reich, assistant coach] signaled that the Berkeley girl’s follow through hit the net for a Piedmont point. After that, it seemed like our girls barely lost another point,” said coach Jim Landes. The final set by the doubles team was characterized with outstanding play at the net by both LaForte and Bini with several well-placed volleys, including a match-winner by Bini to close out the day. “We re-focused after that second set and won 6-0. This was our fourth match together this year, but we played freshman year together and then we both played singles. Now we’re reunited as seniors and we’re happier than ever,” said LaForte. “The thing with tennis is that its super easy to get in your head and that digs a hole. We were both getting really frustrated in the second set and it felt like we forgot how to play tennis. And then we woke up,” mentioned Bini. Match Recap Piedmont started the day with a 6-3, 6-2 win at No. 3 doubles with Sophia Kalamas and Arianna Kortum and went ahead by two matches with a 7-6 (6-1), 6-0 win at No. 2 doubles with Kate Jumper and Cecilia DeFazio. But then Berkeley won the next three matches to jump ahead 3-2 with each match going three sets. No. 3 singles Carolina Romanczuk lost 6-1, 2-6, 6-3. Anne Jumper at No. 2 singles fell 4-6, 6-4, 6-3. articles.text: Football continues at Piedmont High School, but for the time being only the junior varsity team will continue playing its scheduled games. Varsity games have been postponed due to roster attrition and injuries. The JV team will face Bishop O’Dowd at the Dragons’ home field this Friday, October 14 at 4:30 p.m. with underclassmen from the varsity added to the roster. It is still unclear what the school’s decision will be on whether the varsity team will return to the field. It is expected that discussion with high school administrators, the athletic director, the head coach and members his staff, and parents are continuing as everyone searches for best outcome and best future for the players. The good news is that the middle school flag football program has at least 20 kids playing at the 6th, 7th, and 8th grade levels. For updates on the future of football at PHS, contact A.D. Bradley Smet, or Principal Sykanya Goswami.
articles.title: Where does PHS football go from here?

articles.text: Editor: I read Jon Comeaux’s “Reflecting on the lifeline of Piedmont’s football program” in the October 5th issue of the Post, in which he summarizes the last 10 years of Piedmont High football. I have coached PHS freshmen and JV football teams for 17 years, so I am familiar with this history. Jon is correct that the football program has struggled over the last two seasons. This is because of low levels of participation by the classes of 2021 (last year’s graduates), 2022 (this year’s seniors), and 2023 (this year’s juniors). There are probably a number of reasons for the low levels, but an important one is that interest in football by middle school boys was not sufficiently cultivated in the recent years before 2020. However, a very good thing happened two years ago for Piedmont football and Piedmont students when the Recreation Department engaged Billy Goldstein and his Skyhawks youth sports program to operate the middle school flag football program. There are 19 sophomores on Piedmont’s football teams this year in large part because of the interest in football that Goldstein’s program generated. There are also 14 current freshmen on the JV team this year, most of whom have participated in the middle school program. The numbers of freshmen and sophomores on this year’s team are solid. It is important that middle school students continue to be exposed to football, so that they want to play in the future. Happily, the football program with Skyhawks continues. There are 68 middle school students participating in the Skyhawks program this fall, and many of them will play PHS football. It is important that there not be a negative perception regarding the future of Piedmont football. A false perception can become reality, if people believe it. Over the next two years, there will be a resurgence of Piedmont High football. The current sophomores are an especially strong class and the classes that are following it are going to be good, too. It is important that Piedmont students have the opportunity to play football because they can benefit greatly from the experience. It is the hardest thing most of them have ever done. My two sons were not great football players, but they played all four years at PHS. Doing so, gave them the confidence that they could accomplish other hard things in life. Football made them stronger and helped them become the fine men they are. Future generations of Piedmont boys must have the same opportunity. –Dick Carter
articles.title: Piedmont football coach predicts bright future for high school team

articles.text: With making mention of the current athletic accomplishments of student-athletes at Piedmont High, it can get easy to lose track of those who have continued their careers after moving on from the small town in the hills. In this article, we take a look at four former Piedmont Post Athletes of the Year who are currently active at the collegiate level this fall season, including distance runners Ellie Black, Jack Stein, and Sophia Zalewski, along with tennis star Makenna Thiel. Ellie Black, University of California Ellie Black, PHS Class of 2022 and the Post’s 2022 Athlete of the Year, is continuing her strong start to her collegiate career with the UC Berkeley cross-country team. She was the top runner for Cal in their most recent event at the UC Riverside Invitational on September 17 and finished 31st of 265 runners. In Cal’s season-opener at the University of San Francisco Invitational at Golden Gate Park on September 3, Black was also her team’s lead runner, fniishing 22nd of 125 runners with a time of 22:03.8. The Golden Bears finished eighth of 13 teams. Cal’s head coach Bobby Lockhart had high praise of Black after her run in Riverside. “Ellie Black keeps impressing us,” Lockhart said. “She’s just getting going, and I see no reason she won’t continue to make significant jumps.” Photo by Walter Teitelbaum Ellie Black, the Posts’ 2022 Athlete of the Year, is leading the charge on the California Golden Bears’ cross country program. Jack Stein, Pomona-Pitzer College Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, also earned the Post’s Athlete of the Year award in June along with Black. He’s been a big part of the Pomona-Pitzer Sagehens’ cross country team’s first four meets this season. Most recently at the Pomona-Pitzer Invitational on October 8, Stein was the third best runner for his college by finishing 29th of 163 runners with a time of 26:09.1. The Sagehens finished fourth of 14 schools. Stein also was 37th of 206 in the Cougar Challenge at CSU San Marcos on September 24 with a time of 25:42.1; his team was third of 17. Stein started the Photo courtesy of Pitzer College Jack Stein (center, behind lead runners) was also the Posts’ 2022 Athlete of the Year. He’s having a strong freshman campaign at Pomona-Pitzer.

articles.text: Filoli Historic House & Garden in Woodside. Filoli Historic House & Garden in Woodside recently was named ‘Best Attraction’ in the U.S. by the Dutch international travel and tourism company Tiqets. The annual awards have served as a tool for helping discerning travelers since 2017. Tiqets’ sixth annual Remarkable Venue Awards program recognizes the best museums and attractions in the world in seven categories, from the best hidden gems to the most remarkable venues. More than 200 nominees competed worldwide to be recognized in the coveted travel awards. The 2022 winners represent the best of the tourism industry. Seven total venues in the U.S. received top honors, including: • Best Attraction: Filoli Historic House & Garden, California’s Bay Area • Best Onsite Experience: Musical Instrument Museum, Phoenix • Best Museum: The National WWII Museum, New Orleans • Most Innovative Venue: Area 15, Las Vegas • Most Remarkable Venue: Titanic Museum Attraction Pigeon Forge, Tennessee • Best Landmark: SUMMIT • One Vanderbilt, New York City Best Hidden Gem: Fotografiska, New York Winners from eight other countries were also announced, including in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, the UAE, and the UK. Voting is currently underway now through October 19 for the Filoli Historic House & Garden to be named as a Global Winner in the same category. To cast your vote, visit: https://www.tiqets. com/blog/best-museums-attractions-in-2022/. The Tiqets Awards The Remarkable Venue Awards celebrate seven categories of awards in nine countries worldwide. Since 2017, the awards have recognised museums and attractions in France, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, the United Kingdom and the United States. For the first time this year the awards program will include Germany, Portugal and the United Arab Emirates. The Tiqets Remarkable Venue Awards were established to celebrate the best attractions and museums in the world. Tiqets is headquartered in Amsterdam with employees throughout the world.
articles.title: Filoli Historic House & Garden Named ‘Best Attraction’ in the U.S.

articles.text: Treasure Island Museum, a nonprofit that preserves the island’s Pacific-themed heritage, has opened a new, free exhibition entitled Little Island, Big Ideas. The museum is also currently exhibiting Portal to the Pacific in War and Peace. Little Island, Big Ideas details the first 70 years of the island’s history. Attendees can visit the gallery in Room 111 and view artifacts, photographs, and other items of historical relevance. The ongoing exhibition Portal to the Pacific presents Treasure Island’s dynamic and unique history in a series of banners and panels on display throughout the Building One lobby. The panels feature many previously unpublished color photographs of the island. This is a permanent exhibit. Before visiting, check the museum’s calendar at https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/exhibitions. Both exhibitions are free and open to the public, Monday through Friday, from 9:00 a.m. to 5 p.m. The museum is located at 1 Avenue of the Palms #111 on Treasure Island. Treasure Island Museum also offers several online exhibitions throughout the month. The ongoing exhibition Portal to the Pacific is located in the lobby of the Treasure Island Museum.
articles.title: Treasure Island Museum offers Portal to the Pacific and Little Island, Big Ideas

articles.text: The celebrated Left Coast Chamber Ensemble invites the community to its annual Gala, A Cabaret of Souls, to be held this Saturday night, October 15, at 3 p.m. Guests will enjoy wine and appetizers as Left Coast friends, old and new, celebrate the ensemble’s 30th Anniversary season. The fundraiser will feature Left Coast soprano Nikki Einfeld and pianist Eric Zivian with selections of music by Stephen Sondheim, Florence Price, and Kurt Weill. Sign up early for the live auction and stay for the Fund-A-Need auction to benefit Left Coast programs. Tickets are $150 per person and available online at: www. leftcoastensemble.org/gala-2022. Soprano Niki Einfeld West Bay Opera; The title role of Lucia di Lammermoor with Syracuse Opera and Green Mountain Opera Festival; Ophelia in Hamlet with Opera Lyra Ottawa; several roles in the world premiere of Dolores Clairborne by Tobias Picker, Gianetta in The Elixir of Love, Papagena in The Magic Flute, Barbarina in Le Nozze di Figaro with San Francisco Opera; Nanetta in Falstaff and as Mabel in The Pirates of Penzance with Edmonton Opera; Rosina in The Barber of Seville, Marie in The Daughter of the Regiment, and Norina in Don Pasquale with Manitoba Opera. A highly adept interpreter of a wide range of repertoire spanning from the baroque to contemporary music, she has made guest appearances on the concert stage with the San Francisco Symphony, Berkeley Symphony, Pianist Eric Zivian Calgary Philharmonic Orchestra, Winnipeg Symphony Orchestra New Music Festival, Montreal Chamber Orchestra, and the Empyrean Ensemble. As a champion of contemporary music, she regularly performs premieres by modern composers. Nikki is a former Adler Fellow and Merola alumna with the San Francisco Opera, and received acclaim as a Grand Finalist in the 2006 Metropolitan Opera National Council Auditions. Eric Zivian, piano Eric Zivian grew up in Toronto, Canada, where he graduated from the Royal Conservatory of Music. At age 15 he left home to attend the Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia, where he received a Bachelor of Music degree. He holds graduate degrees from the Juilliard School and the Yale School of Music. He studied piano with Gary Graffman and Peter Serkin and composition with Ned Rorem, Jacob Druckman, and Martin Bresnick. He has attended the Tanglewood Music Center both as a performer and as a composer. He has given solo recitals in Toronto, New York, Philadelphia, and the Bay Area, and has played concerts with the Toronto Symphony Orchestra, the Santa Rosa Symphony, the Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra and the Portland Baroque Orchestra. Since 2000, he has performed extensively on original instruments, playing fortepiano in the Zivian-Tomkins Duo and the Benvenue Fortepiano Trio. A longtime member of the Left Coast Chamber Ensemble, he has performed with the Empyrean Ensemble and Earplay. He is a frequent guest artist on the San Francisco Conservatory’s faculty chamber music series. His compositions have been performed widely in the United States and in Japan. He was awarded an ASCAP Jacob Druckman Memorial Commission to compose an orchestral work, Three Character Pieces, which was premiered by the Seattle Symphony. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs

articles.text: Live concert by hometown orchestra at PCA on November 6 Piedmont hometown orchestra is presenting a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday afternoon, November 6, at 4 p.m. Performing a varied and unusual program, the orchestra will be conducted by Martha Stoddard and Sue Crum. The rarely heard Overture to Johann Albrecht’s comedy Der Teufel als Hydraulicus, composed by Franz Schubert when he was just 14, opens the concert, followed by the delightful Romanian Dances, by Bela Bartok. As a special audience treat, the humorous Ferdinand the Bull, by American author Munro Leaf and based upon the children’s story of the same name, will be performed by violinist Joseph Gold with narration by Piedmont native and City Council member Betsy Andersen. It is the story of a bull who would rather smell the flowers than fight in bullfights. The work was banned by both Hitler and the Spanish Fascists as “degenerate democratic propaganda.” The program concludes with Mozart’s orchestral masterpiece, his Symphony No. 40 in G minor, composed during some of the artist’s darkest days but finding its way from the turbulence of the beginning sections into the triumph of the conclusion. Tickets at the door are $20 cash or credit card. Doors open at 3:30 p.m. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue at Bonita Avenue. Street parking is available.
articles.title: Piedmont Chamber Orchestra returns

articles.text: Violinist Maxim Venegrov will perform at Zellerbach Hall on Friday, October 14. articles.text: Larry Carlton was born in Torrance in Southern California in 1948 and began guitar lessons at age six. He was introduced to jazz in junior high school after hearing The Gerald Wilson Big Band album, Moment of Truth, with Joe Pass on guitar. It led him to explore jazz by other guitarists, including Barney Kessel, Wes Montgomery and B.B. King. Larry’s first professional gig was at a supper club in 1962. He honed his guitar-playing skills in the clubs and studios of greater Los Angeles. In 1968 through 1970, he toured with the Fifth Dimension and did studio sessions with Vikki Carr, Andy Williams and the Partridge Family. Then he joined the Crusaders. “I got a call to do a session for Donovan, and when I showed up, Joe Sample, the Crusaders’ keyboard player, was already there,” recalled Carlton. “I plugged in and joined Joe on a downbeat he played, and right away we had a moment of musical communication. Monday morning my phone rang, and it was the Crusaders’ office saying, ‘The guys are in the studio starting an album. Can you come in and join them for the next two weeks?’” Larry was invited to join the Crusaders and played on 13 of their albums from 1971 through 1976. Joni Mitchell’s Court and Spark album, the first record she made with a rhythm section, disGuitarist Larry Carlton plays Carlton’s distinctive technique – a style Mitchell referred to as “fly fishing”, which is interesting because Larry actually enjoys fly fishing. Larry did more than 3000 studio sessions by the early 1980’s, including with Steely Dan, Linda Rondstadt, Michael Jackson and Bobby Blue Bland. Other significant studio session players included Steve Cropper, Tommy Tedesco, Chet Atkins, Steve Lukather, Glen Campbell, Lee Ritenour and Brent Mason. Larry’s catalog of work includes film soundtracks, television themes and work on over 100 gold albums. Larry won four Grammy Awards: Theme from Hill Street Blues, 1981; Minute by Minute, 1987; No Substitutions: Live in Osaka, 2001 and his album Take Your Pick, 2010. In his early years, Larry mostly played a Gibson 335 guitar. In the late seventies, he built a home studio, which he named “Room 335” (also the name of one of his compositions). In the seventies, his nickname was “Mr. 335”. Since the late seventies, Larry phased out studio session work and transitioned to recording his own albums, his focus ever since. Listen to and read my improvised example, Kid Charlemagne, for this column and music for my previous columns at: http://www. guitarimprov.com/PostColumns. pdf. Amazingly, Larry’s Kid Charlemagne solo was improvised (according to him), not worked out beforehand. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. articles.text: Fenner Frank Merlick as Pony and Julie Kuwabara as Marie will appear in Cutting Ball Theater’s production of Pony. San Francisco’s Cutting Ball Theater premieres a production of Pony, a play written by Sylvan Oswald, on October 15. The play will run through November 13. The lead character Pony, a formerly incarcerated transgender man, moves to a post-industrial town to start a new life. He falls in love with a woman who may or may not lead him down a path of violence, as he simultaneously reconciles with new feelings of gender identity and belonging. “Pony was the first play I ever encountered that had multiple transgender characters. To this day it is one of maybe three plays I’ve read that has characters in a variety of stages of gender transition,” said Director Kieran Beccia. “I’m thrilled to be able to put characters onstage who manifest stories and experiences that are less frequently recognized or authentically portrayed by the wider industry.” To view showtimes and purchase tickets, visit https://cuttingball.com/productions.
articles.title: Cutting Ball Theater premieres Pony on October 15
