articles.text: Husband and wife artists Claire and David Cunningham will have an art exhibit at Piedmont Center for the Arts on two Sundays, October 16 and 23, from 3-5 p.m. The works in watercolor and oils are by Claire and gouache and acrylic for David’s paintings. Many of the works come from their outings in the high Sierras where they regularly hike and take their painting materials and easels in backpacks. Often the smaller works are used to create bigger paintings, giving the artists the opportunity to explore their subjects on a larger scale. This show also has local themes such as seascapes from the Monterey Peninsula, Bay Area gardens, some still life works, and a few portraits. “We find working together in wild areas with rich landscape to be a transcendent experience. We feel very fortunate to be able to explore and create from the incredible beauty of California,” said David. Claire is a MA graduate from California College of Arts & Crafts in Oakland and has taught both at CCAC and at Skyline College. David holds both a BFA and an MFA. For more information, see their website: www.cunninghampaintings.com. Tuolumne Meadows near Pothole Dome 24X30 Island Bear Lake 9X12

Saturday, October 15, 3:00 p.m. Left Coast Chamber Fundraising Gala The Left Coast Chamber Ensemble invites the public to A Cabaret of Souls, an exclusive musical gala event celebrating its 30th Anniversary Season. Enjoy wine & appetizers while mingling with Left Coast friends old & new, while soprano Nikki Einfeld and pianist Eric Zivian, perform selections by Stephen Sondheim, Florence Price and Kurt Weill. Participate in the Live Auction and Fund-A-Need to benefit Left Coast programs. Tickets are $150 per person, and are available at www.leftcoastensemble. org/gala-2022. Sundays, October 16 & 23, 3:00–5:00 p.m. Cunningham Art Exhibition Husband and wife artists Claire and David Cunningham will have an art exhibit that includes landscapes of the Sierras: Yosemite and the Plumas Lakes Basin; seascapes from the Monterey coast; gardens in Ben Lomond and Rockridge; and still life paintings. The Cunninghams often hike into the high country and paint smaller works, which they then expand into larger pieces at home. Admission is free, and some works will be available for purchase. One of the originators of big-band jazz, he led his band for more than 50 years and composed thousands of scores. The concert is a benefit for the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, showcasing PCA’s magnificent Steinway grand piano. Tickets $20 at the door, or at https://bpt.me/5316993. articles.text: Russian-American author Anastasia Edel, a Piedmont resident, will present a 4-week illustrated lecture titled Russia’s War on Ukraine, with classes starting on Thursday, October 20 at 2:30 p.m. The course is being offered by Osher Lifelong Learning Institute at the University of California in Berkeley, where Edel conducted an eight-week illustrated lecture in 2018 on Understanding Russia, a course that intertwines the country’s political and cultural developments with historical perspectives expressed in film, music, and literature. The last four years have proven to be a busy time for Edel. In 2018 she gave the keynote address at OLLI and to the League of Women Voters in Piedmont on The State of US-Russian Relations. One year later she delivered talks at the Commonwealth Club in San Francisco, the University of Washington, and Berkeley City Club Due in part to the publicity generated by op ed pieces she wrote for the New York Times between February and May this year, she was an invited commentators on CNN MSNBC and Bay Area NBC. In the past five years, six of her guest essays an opinion pieces have appeared in the New York Times, with a spike of interest since Russia began its move to wage war on neighboring Ukraine. The course fee for Russia’s War on Ukraine through OLLI is $90 for the four lectures, each of which will be from 2:30 to 4:00 p.m. on consecutive Thursdays, October 20 to November 10. The course will stream live on the scheduled day and time and will also be recorded. Videos will be available on Friday each week. When Russian missiles struck multiple cities across the sovereign nation of Ukraine in February 2020, Russia became an aggressor bent on destroying a neighboring nation with whom it shares centuries of common past. How did it happen? Why does Putin’s regime refuse to call war “war”? What’s behind Ukrainians’ resilience and Russians’ acquiescence? And where does this all end for Russia, Ukraine, and the world? Edel provided some perspective on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine earlier this year with a lecture at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in April. To register for the current course, click on: https://olli.berkeley.edu/programs/courses/russia%E2%80%99s-war-ukraine. Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel is an acclaimed writer, social historian, and New York Times contributor. She’s the author of “Russia: Putin’s Playground,” a concise guide to Russian history, politics and culture.

articles.text: A turnout of 14 members of the First Mondays Reading group met on October 3 to discuss Unlikely Allies, by Joel Richard Paul. Participating were Phil Witte, Jerry Gragg, Mike Henn, Laura Goldman, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Martin Levy, Bella Almanzan, Adrienne Hamlin, Peggy Rourke, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The author is a professor and associate dean at the University of California’s Hastings College of Law, who recounts a true story of how three men used espionage, betrayal, and sexual deception to obtain France’s help for the colonies in the American Revolution. Silas Deane was a Connecticut merchant and delegate to the Continental Congress. Caron de Beaumarchais was a successful playwright who wrote the librettos for The Barber of Seville and The Marriage of Figaro. Chevalier d’Eon, was a flamboyant and mysterious officer, diplomat, and spy. He had incriminating documents against Louis XVI that helped obtain a crucial Franco-American alliance. The gender of d’Eon was a mystery until the end of the book. Paul’s story is different from what most of the readers learned in school about our Founding Fathers, who, we are told, were not saints endowed with wisdom, moral character, and virtue. Washington is “painfully aware of his own limitations as a military commander.” Samuel Adams is the head of a self-serving political faction. Ethan Allen is a scoundrel. Thomas Paine is a libeler. Benjamin Franklin likes to bounce pretty women on his knee, and the Lees of Virginia are more interested in nepotism than victory. Paul has no hesitation with these representations. “By placing the founders of our nation on a pedestal, we risk setting up an impossible standard for future generations to follow.” For the author, Silas Deane is one of the few selfless characters in the American Revolution. His tireless efforts cost him his fortune, family life, and reputation. Additionally, his doubts about the Americans’ ability to win the war, and his belief that a treaty should be negotiated with Britain, cost him dearly. While the book’s content deals with important historical matters, many of the readers found the book to be a struggle. It was educational, but not particularly entertaining for them. There were too many characters. A common reader complaint was that the book needed a better editor. They felt there was too much detail that detracted from important storylines. However, some readers enjoyed the book, which provides an important historical understanding of why France supported the American Revolution. It was not because the French king believed in democracy, but rather it was his desire to weaken his rival, Great Britain. The honest portrayals of our Founding Fathers with their imperfections is important to understand. The group appreciated Paul showing that political divisions existed among the Founding Fathers, and that and that political polarization is not new. The question of how appropriate the U.S. Constitution is today was raised. Is it outdated and should it be replaced with a new one? The group agreed that Unlikely Allies, like the Founding Fathers, might not be perfect, but the book did provide a more complete understanding of the creation of our country, and thus has value. With their discussion complete the readers considered their next books. They had previously selected Klara and the Sun by Nobel laureate Kazuo Ishiguro for November, and after some back and forth discussions, the readers picked the non-fiction Priestdaddy by Patricia Lockwood for December, and Afterparties by Anthony Veasna So for January. The group’s next meeting will be November 7 at 1:30 p.m. at the Tea House. New readers are welcome and there is no fee to participate. Registration is required by calling the Recreation Department at 510-420-3070.
articles.title: FIRST MONDAYS READING GROUP First Monday Readers dive into Unlikely Allies

articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors are pleased to announce that Ford Roosevelt, grandson of former U.S. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt, and the son of Elliot Roosevelt, will speak at the Piedmont Seniors meeting on Wednesday, November 16 at 11 a.m. at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. Mr. Roosevelt began serving as Executive Director of the USS Potomac, the former Presidential Yacht, earlier this year in March. The Potomac is permanently docked on the Oakland Estuary at the foot of Clay Street. Ford has worked as a nonprofit executive and educator, and human rights advocate for nearly 40 years. He is an active member of the Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt Institute, and has represented the Roosevelt legacy in several positions, from the National Democratic Party conventions to serving as a surrogate speaker in several presidential campaigns. Annually, Mr. Roosevelt awards the Eleanor Roosevelt human Ford Roosevelt, grandson of Franklin Delano and Eleanor Roosevelt, will be the guest speaker at the Piedmont Seniors’ meeting on November 16 at Piedmont Community Hall. rights award with the San Diego United Nations Chapter to deserving Human Rights activists. Most recently, the award was presented to California Attorney General Xavier Becerra. Ford’s engagement with the USS Potomac is an on-going link to the Roosevelt legacy and the family itself. Mr. Roosevelt will speak to the Piedmont Seniors about his famous grandparents, how FDR’s New Deal impacted the Bay Area, as well as the USS Potomac’s educational mission. Guests are welcome. Please RSVP to jepstein@piedmont. ca.gov to ensure adequate seating. The USS Potomac was the Presidential Yacht under Franklin Delano Roosevelt from 1936 until his death in 1945. The Potomac is now preserved in Oakland as a National Historic Landmark and is the only presidential yacht open to the public.

articles.text: One of the most unfortunate side effects of auto use is parking. Surface parking takes up an enormous amount of space, often vacant and often resulting in a “no man’s land” of impermeable paving between users’ parking spaces and their ultimate destination. Structured parking takes less ground space but is much more expensive to build and the aesthetic results are usually lacking. Part 54 in a biweekly series Transportation, the movement of people and goods from one area to another perhaps more than anything else shapes our built environment today. Think of all we build to handle the various ways we travel – airports, rail lines, freeways, roads of all sizes, bicycle lanes, sidewalks and even pedestrian paths. Accommodating these modes of travel have major financial, visual, environmental, and community-shaping effects on the places where we live. In recent times, transportation systems have very often dominated the built environment at the expense of the aesthetics, character, congestion, and community inhibition of the very destinations they are connecting. I find this ironic because logically, the idea of moving as fast as possible from one place to another presupposes a desirable, nice, worthwhile The automobile has dominated planning for decades in many parts of the world. Cars provided incredible individual freedom of movement... but at a price! With increased car usage comes increased air pollution, congestion, cost, and parking problems. Things seem to have come full circle with once convenient car travel becoming a burden in many places. There is now often a sense of freedom without a car. Planning for and permitting even a few alternative means of transportation can mitigate the increasing burdens of auto transportation. Ride sharing has become popular incredibly quickly. Uber and Lift along with traditional taxis are an effective way to share a vehicle among many users. Buses come in all shapes and sizes for different kinds of service. articles.text: Weekly training tips for the Thanksgiving morning 5K run Last week kicked off the official Piedmont Turkey Trot training plan, but there is still time to join in the training. Runner Jessica Freeman, a past winner of the Trot, has developed a weekly training plan for beginners to train specifically for the upcoming 5K on Thanksgiving Day, November 24th. The full training plan can be seen on the race website, piedmontturkeytrot.com. This week we will be adding in a speed workout which is best done at the track. Head over to Witter Field during non-school hours and run 2 fast laps. You want to be running at a pace that feels uncomfortable and you can hear yourself breathing, but not so fast that you can’t make it all the way around the track without stopping. For those new to the track, During the 2018 Turkey Trot, runners fly down Craig Avenue knowing they are within a quarter mile of the finish line. each full circle around the track is called a lap and it is 400 meters, or one-quarter of a mile in length. You should always run counterclockwise and it is most common to start your lap on the start line which is indicated by big bold numbers on the track. If you are standing in the stadium at Witter, you can see the start line on the right side. It is also best to start in the closest lane to the field (Lane 1). Don’t forget to warm up and cool down the body with a slow jog. Have fun out there! WEEK DAY WORKOUT October 10 Monday Run 1 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday Run 2 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x Saturday Run 3 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x Add 3 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 3x October 17 Monday Run 2 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday 5 min jog warm up 2x 1 lap around Witter track, 1 min break between laps 5 min jog cool down Saturday Run 4 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x Add 5 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 5x October 24 Monday Run 3 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday 5 min jog warm up 4x 1 lap around Witter track, 2 min break between laps 5 min jog cool down Saturday Run 4 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x October 31 Monday Run 3 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday Run 3 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Add 3 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 3x Saturday Hill workout: 5 min jog warm up 3x run up Sea View Dr (Start at Hampton, run to Mountain) Walk down hill between reps 5 min jog cool down November 7 Monday Run 6 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 6x Add 5 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 5x Wednesday Run 4 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x Saturday Hill workout: 5 min jog warm up 4 x run up Magnolia Ave (Start at Hillside, run to Highland) Walk down hill between reps 5 min jog cool down November 14 Monday Run 10 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 3x Wednesday 10 min jog warm up 4x 1 lap around Witter track 10 min jog cool down Saturday Run 15 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 2x Add 5 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds November 21 Monday Run 6 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 3x Add 3 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds November 24 Piedmont Turkey Trot! Race 3.1 miles!! 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

pages.text: Wednesday, October 12, 2022 25 Getting ready for Piedmont’s Turkey Trot Weekly training tips for the Thanksgiving morning 5K run Last week kicked off the official Piedmont Turkey Trot training plan, but there is still time to join in the training. Runner Jessica Freeman, a past winner of the Trot, has developed a weekly training plan for beginners to train specifically for the upcoming 5K on Thanksgiving Day, November 24th. The full training plan can be seen on the race website, piedmontturkeytrot.com. This week we will be adding in a speed workout which is best done at the track. Head over to Witter Field during non-school hours and run 2 fast laps. You want to be running at a pace that feels uncomfortable and you can hear yourself breathing, but not so fast that you can’t make it all the way around the track without stopping. For those new to the track, During the 2018 Turkey Trot, runners fly down Craig Avenue knowing they are within a quarter mile of the finish line. each full circle around the track is called a lap and it is 400 meters, or one-quarter of a mile in length. You should always run counterclockwise and it is most common to start your lap on the start line which is indicated by big bold numbers on the track. If you are standing in the stadium at Witter, you can see the start line on the right side. It is also best to start in the closest lane to the field (Lane 1). Don’t forget to warm up and cool down the body with a slow jog. Have fun out there! WEEK DAY WORKOUT October 10 Monday Run 1 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday Run 2 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x Saturday Run 3 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x Add 3 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 3x October 17 Monday Run 2 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday 5 min jog warm up 2x 1 lap around Witter track, 1 min break between laps 5 min jog cool down Saturday Run 4 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x Add 5 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 5x October 24 Monday Run 3 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday 5 min jog warm up 4x 1 lap around Witter track, 2 min break between laps 5 min jog cool down Saturday Run 4 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x October 31 Monday Run 3 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Wednesday Run 3 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 8x Add 3 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 3x Saturday Hill workout: 5 min jog warm up 3x run up Sea View Dr (Start at Hampton, run to Mountain) Walk down hill between reps 5 min jog cool down November 7 Monday Run 6 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 6x Add 5 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds 5x Wednesday Run 4 min, Walk 2 min, Repeat 5x Saturday Hill workout: 5 min jog warm up 4 x run up Magnolia Ave (Start at Hillside, run to Highland) Walk down hill between reps 5 min jog cool down November 14 Monday Run 10 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 3x Wednesday 10 min jog warm up 4x 1 lap around Witter track 10 min jog cool down Saturday Run 15 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 2x Add 5 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds November 21 Monday Run 6 min, Walk 1 min. Repeat 3x Add 3 strides at the end: Run as fast as you can for 20 seconds November 24 Piedmont Turkey Trot! Race 3.1 miles!! Mom can have her independence back. We can help. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, October 12, 2022 By Ellie Somers and Troop 31318 Volunteers Piedmont Girl Scouts in Daisy Troop 31318 have started their second year off strong, with community service projects with an environmental focus. On the heels of a hugely successful beach cleanup at Jack London Aquatic Center for the 74th Annual California Coastal Clean Up Day, the girls have turned their attention to Piedmont’s own streets and trash cans. Comprised of 19 girls ages 6 and 7 from Havens and Wildwood schools, Troop 31318 has a plan for reducing the waste created during Halloween. The girls will have a Zero Waste recycling box outside Mulberry’s Market for one week before Halloween and one week after. Formed in 2021, Troop 31318 was largely unable to participate in community service the past two years due to ongoing COVID concerns. This year the girls have been excited to have a chance to get out in the greater community to increase their positive impact. After recent Troop meetings centered around reducing waste, Girl Scouts planning Green Halloween reusing items that have life left in them, and composting and recycling as much as possible, the girls are excited to introduce their candy wrapper recycling program to the community. With an expected start date of October 24, the Scouts are hoping to prevent the usual uptick in candy wrappers blowing around on streets at Halloween. TerraCycle’s Zero Waste boxes divert items that would otherwise end up in landfill, or in our streets and waterways, into specialized recycling facilities. Troop 31318 Scouts are hoping the community will take this opportunity to be thoughtful about its plastic-based waste. For trick or treating on Halloween, they urge handing out candy with compostable paperbased wrappers, such as candy that comes in small cardboard boxes. Please look for Troop 31318’s TerraCycle box outside Mulberry’s Market and consider saving your wrappers by participating in an important lesson in civic engagement and environmental responsibility for these young Scouts. Not calling it a re-zone or taking action that requires prior voter approval is contrary to any reasonable interpretation of applicable Piedmont law (Section 17.02.010 of Piedmont’s Municipal Code and Section 9.02 of Piedmont’s City Charter). Although developing Piedmont’s response to California’s Housing Element law unquestionably presents many difficult challenges, the City Council’s adoption of its draft Housing Element will only exacerbate those challenges. Such action would be shortsighted, would negatively position the City’s ability to deal with housing issues moving forward and may result in expensive, protracted and divisive litigation. Piedmont residents have done the right thing when they have voted on tough issues in the past and the City Council should trust them to do the right thing as regards the housing issue. The BJC insists that two religious clauses of the First Amendment, no establishment and free exercise, need to be held in healthy tension. The current court seems to be dedicated to advancing a doctrine of free exercise that undermines the equally important principle of no establishment. This concern is represented by the question “Would the court have ruled the same way if the coach in question was Muslim, Jewish, Sikh or Buddhist rather than a conservative white Christian?” If not, under the guise of supporting free exercise, it is actually establishing one brand of Christianity as entitled to unique protection under the law. These are important concerns. Former Justice Sandra Day O’Connor explains it this way. “Government endorsement of religion sends a message to nonadherents that they are outsiders, not full members of the…community, and an accompanying message to adherents that they are insiders and favored members of the primal community.” There is work ahead for those of us who believe that faith is most meaningful when it is a matter of free expression rather than a matter of required behavior. I plan to vote for her and hope you will as well. –Glyn Burge Reasons to vote for Thomasson for School Board Editor: I encourage Piedmont residents to vote for Lindsay Thomasson for PUSD School Board. I met Lindsay five years ago when she had just moved into town. I was organizing parent parties for Spring Fling and a mutual friend connected us. Since the moment she agreed to host a party that year, we have volunteered together in various roles on the board of Havens Parent Club, including Lindsay’s tenure as President. Most recently, Lindsay and I ran the Traffic Committee to address unsafe driving during student drop-off and pick-up at Havens. When Lindsay decided to run for School Board, she asked me to be her campaign treasurer. I agreed to join her campaign for three reasons: 1) I can’t imagine a more qualified person; Lindsay has volunteered in a variety of positions in Piedmont schools throughout district levels 2) She is incredibly dedicated, hard-working and thorough 3) Lindsay is one of the warmest and kindest people that I know. She establishes strong friendships and working relationships. Lindsay has the experience; this means she will hit the ground running. In addition to her role as Havens President, she was the parent representative for the Local Control Accountability Plan and Superintendent Community Advisory Committees. She recently co-led the Wellness Center Support Committee. She knows how the district operates and already has working relationships with many individuals in the district. If Lindsay sees something is not working, she thoroughly investigates, asks thoughtful questions, and makes sure she understands the entire situation before she proceeds. She is creative and insightful. Lindsay is the kind of person that I want to follow because she plans efficiently and works to constantly improve. Lindsay is extremely thoughtful, fair, and moral. She is genuine and I trust her implicitly. Lindsay easily makes friends and establishes strong working relationships. She is transparent, with no hidden agendas. Lindsay is also very collaborative; she wants to understand everyone’s opinions and work together to find a solution. I am proud to be treasurer of her school board campaign, and I encourage you to vote for Lindsay. –Cindy Hinman Medhekar – a commitment to academic excellence Editor: We write to urge Piedmont residents to vote for Ruchi Medhekar for PUSD School Board. Ruchi’s extensive service to the Piedmont community and Piedmont schools over the years makes her incredibly well qualified and exemplifies her dedication to our town. Her commitment to academic excellence and strong collaboration skills can be seen from her years of volunteerism, including serving as room parent to vice president and then president of the Beach Parents Organization, to the Tri-School Site Council, the Local Control and Accountability Plan (LCAP) Committee, and to the district’s Budget Advisory Committee. If that wasn’t enough, Ruchi also serves on the Board of the Piedmont Education Foundation and the Piedmont Recreation Commission. Ruchi is the PUSD board member that we very much need. Rob had the pleasure of serving with Ruchi during the 2021- 2022 school year as a member of the Budget Advisory Committee and the Parcel Tax Subcommittee. Ruchi’s commitment, diligence, budget and financial acumen, willingness to ask the tough questions and challenge assumptions, as well as her strengths as a collaborator, team builder and solution finder all showcase why Ruchi would be an incredible asset to the PUSD School Board.. We encourage everyone to consider her candidacy. Please vote for Ruchi Medhekar on November 8. –Rob Phillips & Elisa Lee Candidates who tick all the boxes Editor: We live in a town with a wealth of talent and we are very lucky to have people who want to step up and volunteer for important civic positions. The work is hard. These volunteers have to listen respectfully to myriad opinions, work in partnership with many different stakeholders, pay careful attention to the regulatory landscape, and, ultimately, think holistically to make a lot of decisions that range from routine to especially thorny. I’ve done a lot of hiring in my career and there are four criteria I look for to make a successful hire: relevant work experience, capacity to learn, ability to be collegial and collaborative, and no bullies or creeps (see the Robert Sutton book for the more colorful reference). I use this same list when I vote. For me, the candidates who score highest in all my criteria are: Betsy Anderson, Jennifer Long, and Tom Ramsay for city council; and Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson for school board. My husband and I have been in Piedmont for almost 25 years and I’m about to end my tenure on the school board after nine years. I know these candidates because I’ve worked with them or have watched them at work. To a person, they are smart, insightful, measured, respectful, and collaborative. They have significant skills from their professional and volunteer work that will serve us. They are thoughtful servant leaders who will ask good questions and will seek to find the best solutions given the many competing interests/viewpoints and the complex regulatory landscape. These candidates are who I would like to see lead us in the next four years, who will honor the work and responsibility, and will be respectful of the offices and staff who support these roles. I hope you will join me in voting for them. –Amal Smith Amal Smith is a member of the Piedmont School Board. articles.text: Early Wednesday morning on October 5, a call was placed to the Piedmont Police about a parked car on fire on the 100 block of Crocker Avenue. The initial call came in at 3:29 a.m., and within five minutes the car, a Mazda CX5, was fully engulfed in flames. Members of the Police and Fire departments arrived on scene, and fire fighters extinguished the flames before it could spread. The car was thoroughly charred and was eventually towed away. Police enacted a neighborhood canvassing effort which resulted in finding some video evidence leading to a suspect vehicle. The license plate of the arson suspect was entered into the automatic license plate reader (ALPR) system. Four days later, on Sunday October 9, the suspect vehicle entered the city around 11:00 a.m. and recorded a hit on an ALPR camera at Grand and Rose Avenues. The suspect parked his car in the Safeway parking lot and walked inside. When the suspect exited the store and returned to the vehicle he was detained and arrested without incident. Piedmont Police Detective George Tucker interviewed the suspect who confessed to committing the arson by using lighter fluid and a match. The suspect had a previous association with the victim and the suspect admitted to the targeting attack resulting from prior disagreements. The suspect is identified as Tyler Gadbois, formerly of Piedmont and now a resident of Healdsburg. Gadbois was arrested for Aggravated Arson and was sent to Santa Rita jail. Piedmont Firefighters pour water on a burning car near Crocker Park in the middle of the night. The remains of an incinerated Mazda CX5 after being set on fire.

articles.text: Homecoming at Piedmont High has always been synonymous with school spirit and a traditional football game. But with the football game canceled, Associated Student Body members called an audible and brought the celebration in full force to the girls’ volleyball game Friday night at Binks Rawlings Gym. articles.text: Piedmont teachers reached a new tentative agreement with Piedmont School District on September 28 which will give teachers a 7.5% raise and a $1,500 bonus for full-time teachers. The negotiations have been ongoing since March 2022 and ended with an agreement prior to the September 28 school board meeting. articles.text: Selling, leasing city land is a bad idea Editor: Following up my communication of September 11, thank you for providing a link to the updated Housing Element FAQs (https://www.piedmontishome. org/faqs). I am pleased to read that the City now is aware of, and intends to comply with, its obligations under California Government Code Section 37380. However, I am disappointed that the City continues to state that it “could sell or lease its land for low cost to an affordable housing developer”. Jessica may not be a certified coach, but she is an avid runner, winner of the 2019 Piedmont Turkey Trot, and a new Piedmont resident and mom. The training kicks off on Monday of every week, starting October 10th, with three days of running each week. This first week is all about moving the body and starting to build running strength and endurance. Each run this week is running for a prescribed amount of time (1, 2, 3 minutes) and then taking walking breaks. articles.text: eq8iQH3Nxiq4SUStmQ/viewform Piedmont’s Sustainability Division is seeking input from residents on a pilot home electrification rebate program, which is anticipated to launch in January 2023. The Piedmont City Council allocated $50,000 in the 2022- 23 City budget to develop a pilot rebate program that would provide incentives for residents to replace polluting gas appliances with clean electric alternatives. The intent of the pilot program is two-fold: to educate residents on available electric appliance options and to help them make the transition in a cost-effective manner. The intention is to offer local rebates beyond what is available through state and regional programs for the proper removal and replacement of natural gas appliances with high efficiency electric units. Eligible low-income residential applicants may qualify for additional funding. The survey is an attempt to gauge Piedmonters’ knowledge about and plans for home electrification, and asks for residents to share their thoughts on questions such as: • Are you planning to replace gas appliances like cooktops, furnaces, dryers, and water heaters with electric alternatives? • What types of information or assistance would most encourage you to electrify your home? • What are your biggest concerns about switching to electric appliances? • Do you support or oppose a local rebate program? How much of a rebate makes sense for each type of appliance? Please take a few minutes to fill out the survey. Responses are anonymous. Docs.google.com/ forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSfcmwRWnnUUCWzjpp2mgM82s-fSqJ2IOne of the largest contributors to Piedmont’s community greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is natural gas use in residential buildings. Natural gas is mostly methane, a GHG that is approximately 84 times more potent than Carbon Dioxide (CO2). The use of natural gas for space heating and water heating in particular, significantly contribute to a household’s GHG emissions (~90%). In addition, leaks in the natural gas distribution infrastructure are common, thereby releasing methane directly into the atmosphere. In the last three years, emissions from natural gas use in Piedmont’s residential buildings exceeded 14,000 metric tons of CO2 equivalent per year. This is equivalent to roughly 14,000 round-trip flights of 3000-miles (from San Francisco to New York and back). In order to reduce natural gas emissions and meet Piedmont’s climate action goals, the community must switch to electric appliances. Electrification refers to the process of replacing everything that burns fossil fuels with efficient electric alternatives. By removing your natural gas appliances, you reduce GHG emissions and improve indoor air quality. Electric alternatives are available, affordable, and market-ready such as heat pumps and induction stoves. Learn more about the costs, benefits, and funding opportunities for electrifying your home on the City’s website. Piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/planning___building/about_building_/electrification. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. “Our CEO is having a downer.”

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host a discussion about the impact of textiles on the climate. Rebecca Burgess, Executive Director of Fibershed, will present an online talk entitled “Understanding the Climate Impact of Textiles” on Thursday, October 19, at 4:00 p.m. Ever wonder about the impact on the climate of the textiles in your closet – from production to manufacturing to retail distribution? Come learn how sustainable fashion and regenerative farming are closely linked, how new programs are making a difference, and what you can do to reduce the carbon footprint of the clothes you wear and the fabrics you use. Burgess has two decades of experience working with ecology, fiber systems, and regional economic development. She is the author of the best-selling books Harvesting Color: How to Find Plants and Make Natural Dyes, and Fibershed: Growing a Movement of Farmers, Fashion Activists, and Makers for a New Textile Economy. She has taught at Westminster College, Harvard University, and California College of the Arts. She is on the board of the Livestock Conservancy and is on the Textile expert Rebecca Burgess leadership council of the Center for Regenerative Agriculture and Resilient Systems at Chico State University. This event is part of the League’s 2022 Climate Speaker Series and is co-sponsored by Leagues in Oakland and Solano Counties. This talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube and will include an audience Q&A session. For details and for access to the Zoom presentation, visit the website lwvpiedmont.org. The event is free and open to the public.

The healthy identities and make responsible decisions. 3) Rebuild trust and accountability, ensuring transparency across the district. 4) Attract and retain excellent, diverse, and engaged educators. 5) Consistently engage with all key stakeholder groups, working collaboratively as decisions are made. articles.text: Part four in a series As the Post’s coverage of the local election enters its fourth week, the school board returns to the focus. Fresh off their League of Women Voters online forum on Thursday night, the three candidates are hitting high gear in their campaigns for the two open seats. Every week, two questions are sent out on Thursday and candidates are instructed to limit their answers to under 150 words. Week 4 QUESTIONS 1. Piedmont schools are constantly making adjustments to class offerings, recent new classes include: Guitar Engineering, Entomology, Financial Literacy and Film as Literature. If you could pitch a new class for any grade level, what would it be? 2. The teachers union just reached a tentative agreement with the district for a 7.5% raise. What else can the school district do now and what needs to be done moving forward to recruit and retain the highest quality teachers in Piedmont? neurship • cryptology • game theory I would also like to explore increasing our foreign language offerings at all grade levels, including in elementary school. 2 Retaining Teachers Research shows that an effective teacher is the most important factor contributing to student achievement. Ensuring we offer competitive teacher compensation packages – both pay and benefits – is critical. We should review PUSD’s budget annually to identify changes and compromises we must make to pay our teachers a competitive wage with PUSD’s limited resources while advocating for the state to provide sufficient funds for all districts to compensate educators adequately. When a teacher leaves the district, we should conduct an exit interview to understand why they are leaving. We should actively work to find solutions to prevent further attrition. Finally, our teachers must feel supported by parents and the community as a whole. The past few years have been divisive; finding our way back to a place of mutual respect and collaboration is essential to ensuring that PUSD is a desirable district for teachers to work in. using different data visualizations as needed. 2. Retaining Teachers The tentative agreement with the district to pay a 7.5% raise and $1500 bonus is positive, but we need to ensure that our teachers and staff are receiving competitive wages. We should be leaders, instead of following what other districts do. PUSD used to be a highly sought after district for teachers. Conducting win/ loss interviews with candidates would help us understand what motivates high quality teachers. We should improve the pay schedule especially for teachers earlier on in their careers with less tenure. Many of our teachers will be retiring soon, and we will struggle to replace them with newer teachers when the wages are less competitive than proximal districts. Finally, having a culture of growth means that we should invest in our teachers by allowing them consistent access to professional development to further their own interests and nurture their careers. LINDSAY THOMASSON 1. Your idea for a new course at PUSD? I would first and foremost engage our secondary students and ask what courses they would like to take that PUSD isn’t currently offering. In developing a list of potential options, I would look to neighboring schools (both public and private), specifically at hands-on, project-based courses with an emphasis on math, science, and engineering courses to take full advantage of our beautiful new high school STEAM building. Some new course ideas I would explore pitching include: • design engineering • mechanical engineering • introduction to algorithms • video game development • software for social good • product design • design for sustainability • climate change and climate action • environmental economics • interdisciplinary studies of science • introduction to entrepreRUCHI MEDHEKAR 1. Your idea for a new course at PUSD? There is a vital need for today’s kids to ask critical questions of data and to recognize when data is being misused - in short to be data literate. Integrating data science into a robust subject matter will benefit all high school students, and there are tools to make these techniques accessible - for example, simplified coding packages (e.g. RStudio) and visualization tools. In Data Analysis in Climate Science, students would learn how the data available to climate scientists has evolved over time, and how computer modeling has facilitated its analysis. Students would develop a specific research question and use free primary data sources (e.g. federal and state government) to aid in the process. One example could be to determine changes in fire severity in Northern California. At the end of the term, students would present a final project using data that supported their findings SHIRLEY HOOI 1. Your idea for a new course at PUSD? I would introduce a Life Skills class which would include teaching the fundamentals of: how to plan and cook meals; basic home cleaning and laundering skills; how to set up utilities; basic automotive skills; basic first aid; along with time management, organization, communication, networking and social skills. Besides financial literacy, I believe these are fundamental needs every student should possess upon high school graduation. 2. Retaining Teachers To recruit and retain teachers, the district will need to continue to offer a competitive compensation package, a supportive workplace and a defined vertical career pathway of advancement within the district. In addition, I believe that the district should empower Piedmont teachers to make decisions on how best to teach their students based upon their own values, while taking into consideration the beliefs and values of students and stakeholders. Starting next week, the Piedmont Post will expand its coverage and ask two questions to each candidate in both campaigns, school board and city council.

articles.text: The weekend of September 24-25 a total of 31 members of Highlander Robotics,FIRST Robotics Team 8033, traveled to San Jose for the annual Chezy Champs Invitational tournament and finished with a 5-5 record before advancing to playoffs where they placed third overall. Chezy Champs is a FIRST Robotics Competition post-season tournament, and was hosted this year by the current World Champions, Team 254, the Cheesy Poofs from Bellarmine Prep. Teams traveled from as far away as Israel to play this year’s game, Rapid React, where robots up to 125 pounds score points by collecting and shooting 9.5-inch balls into an 8-foot high 4-foot wide funnel before climbing a set of inclined monkey bars. The Chezy Champs invitation list is typically a Who’s Who of powerhouse teams, and this year was no different. Of the 38 teams attending, 20 have won their division at the World Championships in the last decade and of those teams six have taken the title. The Highlanders, who were division semifinalists at the World Championship in 2022, their first season in person, showed that they belong among the elite. In Reece Beck and Helena Young work on Selkie between rounds. Highlander Robotics has grown from 11 founding students from 3 schools in 2019 to 47 from 7 schools this fall. their first match against Bellarmine, their 122-pound robot “Selkie” shot with over 95% accuracy and was responsible for more than half of the points scored by their three-robot alliance. The score remained within a single basket until the last 30 seconds when the opposing alliance was able to pull away and clinch the win when all three robots successfully climbed. Over the course of nine subsequent rounds, Selkie had mixed results despite establishing itself as a top-quartile shooter. The team attempted to climb in several rounds using a telescoping-arm climbing mechanism designed and fabricated after Ambassadors Vale Prieto Black and Lewy Seiden help other teams understand Selkie’s capabilities.
articles.title: Highlander Robotics team places 3rd at Elite Invitational

articles.text: Piedmont High School and Millennium High School held a State of California sponsored Mock Election last week. A description of the event is shown on the Secretary of State’s website. “Hoping to inspire a new generation of voters, young people have the potential to be a powerful force in elections, but only if they get involved and make voting a habit. To encourage students to become active voters once they are old enough to cast a ballot, Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber and Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond invite high school and middle school students, teachers, and principals to participate in the 2022 California Student Mock Election which will take place between October 3-11. The Student Mock Election will stir students’ interest in voting by tapping into the excitement of the campaign season. As students learn about the candidates and issues, they discover how government and politics affect every part of their lives. They gain firsthand knowledge of how citizens make their voices heard in our democracy and experience the power of their votes when they are joined by thousands of California students who will vote in the California Student Mock Election this year.” PHS and MHS students began voting via electronic ballots including Governor, Senator, and all the Propositions that will appear on the ballot on November 8. Ballots may be cast through October 11. To generate interest, students posted hand-made signs around the campus. Registering voters is a core mandate of the League of Women Voters, and we are proud to work with Piedmont High and Millennium High to help enable students to participate in the 2022 California State Student Mock Election. Barbara Addleman is a Piedmont resident and Youth Outreach Director for the Piedmont League of Women Voters. Posters and banners were on display at Piedmont High to promote interest in a state-sponsored mock election.
articles.title: State conducting mock election for students

articles.text: Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball is about Lucy Harris, arguably the greatest women’s basketball player. Title IX, the federal legislation enacted 50 years ago, is a 37-word snippet tucked into the Educational Amendments of 1972: “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” It is no exaggeration to say that those 37 words led to a revolution in women’s education – from middle school shop class to graduate school admissions – but nowhere more visible than in women’s sports. The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series will return to in-person screenings this November with two award-winning short films that trace both the drama of the law’s passage, and the effect it had on athletes: Mink! and Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball. Both films were directed by Canadian filmmaker Ben Proudfoot, a multiple Oscar nominee for his documentary shorts. He won an Oscar in 2022 for Queen of Basketball. Mink! focuses on Patsy Takemoto Mink, the first woman of color elected to Congress, who faces racial and gender discrimination at every stage of her career. The film begins with Mink’s daughter’s words: “The future of equality in some large way was on the table that day when the personal and political collided,” setting up the drama that is the film’s centerpiece. Director Proudfoot recounts learning about the history of Title IX, and the formidable campaign to dilute or erode the law. The film portrays Mink’s compelling fight to save the crucial language, and how it almost lost for lack of a single vote – her own. Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball is a similarly inspiring short film about a remarkable athlete who came of age just after Title IX was passed. Lucy Harris was arguably the greatest women’s basketball player: she won three national trophies; she played in the ’76 Olympics; and she was drafted to the NBA. None of that would have happened without Title IX. But have you heard of her? Her story is told in her own endearing words. NBA players Steph Curry and Shaquille O’Neal served as executive producers. Both films will be shown in person on Thursday, November 3, at 7 p.m. at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School, 325 Mink! focuses on Patsy Takemoto Mink, the first woman of color elected to Congress. Highland Avenue. Following the films, Chelle Putzer and Eva Phalen of the Piedmont Recreation Department will discuss their efforts to bring equality to girls’ sports, and the effect of Title IX on women’s sports today. After the screenings, Chelle Putzer, Director of Piedmont Recreation Department, and Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen will speak about what’s working to promote equal opportunities for girls in sports, and why it matters throughout life. As always, the screening and discussion are free. Masks will be required to help ensure the safety of the audience. Appreciating Diversity Film Series is an all-volunteer nonprofit organization that has presented free screenings to the community for 25 years. For more information, visit diversityfilmseries.org, or contact Deborah@diversityfilmseries.org
articles.title: Diversity Film series returns on Nov. 3

Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball is about Lucy Harris, arguably the greatest women’s basketball player. Diversity Film series returns on Nov. 3 Title IX, the federal legislation enacted 50 years ago, is a 37-word snippet tucked into the Educational Amendments of 1972: “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” It is no exaggeration to say that those 37 words led to a revolution in women’s education – from middle school shop class to graduate school admissions – but nowhere more visible than in women’s sports. The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series will return to in-person screenings this November with two award-winning short films that trace both the drama of the law’s passage, and the effect it had on athletes: Mink! and Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball. Both films were directed by Canadian filmmaker Ben Proudfoot, a multiple Oscar nominee for his documentary shorts. He won an Oscar in 2022 for Queen of Basketball. Mink! focuses on Patsy Takemoto Mink, the first woman of color elected to Congress, who faces racial and gender discrimination at every stage of her career. The film begins with Mink’s daughter’s words: “The future of equality in some large way was on the table that day when the personal and political collided,” setting up the drama that is the film’s centerpiece. Director Proudfoot recounts learning about the history of Title IX, and the formidable campaign to dilute or erode the law. The film portrays Mink’s compelling fight to save the crucial language, and how it almost lost for lack of a single vote – her own. Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball is a similarly inspiring short film about a remarkable athlete who came of age just after Title IX was passed. Lucy Harris was arguably the greatest women’s basketball player: she won three national trophies; she played in the ’76 Olympics; and she was drafted to the NBA. None of that would have happened without Title IX. But have you heard of her? Her story is told in her own endearing words. NBA players Steph Curry and Shaquille O’Neal served as executive producers. Both films will be shown in person on Thursday, November 3, at 7 p.m. at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School, 325 Mink! focuses on Patsy Takemoto Mink, the first woman of color elected to Congress. Highland Avenue. Following the films, Chelle Putzer and Eva Phalen of the Piedmont Recreation Department will discuss their efforts to bring equality to girls’ sports, and the effect of Title IX on women’s sports today. After the screenings, Chelle Putzer, Director of Piedmont Recreation Department, and Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen will speak about what’s working to promote equal opportunities for girls in sports, and why it matters throughout life. As always, the screening and discussion are free. Masks will be required to help ensure the safety of the audience. Appreciating Diversity Film Series is an all-volunteer nonprofit organization that has presented free screenings to the community for 25 years. For more information, visit diversityfilmseries.org, or contact Deborah@diversityfilmseries.org

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, October 5, 2022 Thinking Outside the Classroom Put me in, Coach! By Kymberly Miller There are many things a leader needs to do to make an organization hum. From financial acumen to skilled communication, a leader needs the skills to guide an organization through smooth and rough seas. As a leader of a small non-profit organization, I have found that the most essential skill is the care and development of people. For me, this manifests as coaching. At Fairyland our sweet spot is the smallest of children, and our aim is to provide an experience where imagination is sparked and a desire to learn is fostered while fully immersed in play. But that is just the beginning of the arc for us. At the other end of the arc we aim to be one of the first employers for young people, giving them an opportunity to learn what it means to be part of a team and to apply skill and effort to aid an organization in its mission. Young folks, between the ages of 16-25, are at an amazing time in their lives. Learning to become an active and thriving member of society is a tall order. Lately, I have found myself in the role of not just a leader but also a coach. Leading by example is just one way we can set expectations and to develop staff, but coaching is another. Sometimes I find that “leading” beside staff instead of in front is the best way to support their growth, and it also allows me to learn. There are few things we can do to coach our youth at this delicate stage: Listen and be curious As leaders we often tend to try and solve all the problems as they are presented. A coaching approach wouldn’t be to provide the answer but to provide the space. I have found it’s better to listen, ask questions and be ok with the silence that it creates. It helps them to generate their own possible solutions – they are probably better than yours. The most essential leadership skill is the care and development of people. Meet folks where they are Everyone enters the work force with different skills and gaps. A good coach knows how to see and assess this and make a unique connection with each individual and develop a personalized plan. This is so helpful with young people who are learning at different paces, have different barriers and are at different places emotionally. Support leadership in others. Not everyone needs to be a leader of a team or department. This age group does benefit, however, from understanding that they are the leaders of their own lives. A good coach can help them learn how and when to advocate for themselves to ensure that they are participating in a thriving community that supports them. At Children’s Fairyland we specialize in delighting our littlest visitors, but we understand the assignment, Youth development is a long arc, and we are also responsible for taking care of them on the other end so they emerge confident, vibrant contributors to society. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. articles.text: The famous PMS Medieval Banquet started with KFC. When our beloved Yearbook and broadcasting teacher Anne Smith started teaching at Piedmont Middle School when she was a core teacher. Her students were learning about the Medieval times and decided they should celebrate that part of history in style and theme. So they ordered KFC and sang Medieval songs with a music teacher. Each year the festival has grown. It’s size and robustness is a testament to the great PMS teachers and parent volunteers. This year’s festival, held on Thursday, September 29, featured multiple booths including the ever-popular Soak the Bloke stocks, as well as the marriage booth and donut on a string. All the booths had long lines. Other booths included the diet of worms, strange gummy worms buried in whipped cream – to be eaten without hands, similar to another popular booth, donut on a string. Other activities such as sword fighting were absolutely all hands on. articles.text: Staff Photos Declan Linnane had two assists against Encinal. He talks about the team’s outlook while rolling 5-0 in WACC competition. Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team continued a strong start to its season with a 10-7 win over the Encinal Jets in Alameda on Thursday, September 29. The Highlanders remain undefeated in league at 5-0 and 10-2 overall. They still have to face league opponents Alameda and Bishop O’Dowd. “We’re trying to build up for league championships and North Coast Section. Our goal in the beginning of the season was to do well in both of those tournaments. I think we are in the driver’s seat,” said first-year head coach Rik Krumins. “We also need to continue maintaining the pace at practice and working out little tweaks here and there. We’re doing some new things on offense, working on the defense, and working on the fundamentals. When we get to the postseason, hopefully we’ll be ready to go,” Declan Linnane has been a huge part of the team’s success this season. “Right now, we’re just trying to get better each game. A lot of guys are getting reps right now and we’re going to need them down the road,” said Linnane. In Thursday’s game, Piedmont led 7-2 by the end of the first quarter with their starters in the pool and then gave younger players the remaining three quarters to gain experience. “We want to let our starters begin the game and then get our subs and bench players to get time and play the entire game. It’s a great experience; it’s building up those guys to give them match experience,” said Krumins. Game Recap Piedmont opened the game with Encinal with six goals and 7-2 lead after one period. Encinal cut the deficit 8-5 by halftime and continued to narrow the score at 9-7 at the start of the fourth quarter. Piedmont’s defense stepped up in the end to concede no goals and win 10-7. Within the first 1:15 of action George Stein scored a goal. Twenty seconds later Daniel Banin scored on an assist from Declan Linnane. Following a Finn Burke had three goals against Encinal. Evan Dickason had two goals against the Jets. save by goalkeeper Dariush Kashani, he threw a long pass to Linnane, who sent a pass into Finn Burke in the hole set for a close-range goal. With 4:29 left in the quarter, Burke scored on a five-meter penalty shot. A minute later, Banin scored, followed by Elles Krieckhaus getting on the scoreboard on an assist by Stein a minute and a half later. After allowing two goals by Encinal, Kashani made a save in the closing seconds of the first quarter and scored by sending a shot the length of the pool into an open net for a 7-1 lead. Evan Dickason opened the second quarter with a goal in 13 seconds on a five-meter penalty shot. It was the last time PHS would score in the half. Piedmont scored once in the third quarter with Leo Hurwitz assisting Burke with 3:54 left in the third. Starting the fourth quarter with a tenuous 9-7 lead, PHS peppered the Jets goal, forcing their goalie to make three saves in close quarters. Dickason scored by netting one with 1:32 on the clock. Final stats: Burke scored three goals. Banin and Dickason scored twice. Stein had a goal and an assist. Linnane had two assists. Krieckhaus scored once. Hurwitz had an assist. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team continued its strong season last week with two victories at their home courts; a 5-2 win over NCS rival College Prep on Tuesday, September 27 and 4-3 over Western Alameda County Conference opponent Alameda on Wednesday, September 28. The win over College Prep will help boost Piedmont in the Division 2 NCS standings, while the victory over the Hornets comes against perhaps their best competition in the WACC. “We had two good victories this week defeating CPS and Alameda Wednesday. CPS is a D2 school, so this win will help our NCS position. Alameda may be our toughest league opponent, them and possibly Bishop O’Dowd, so this is good for us,” said coach Jim Landes. Against Alameda, the clinching fourth victory came from the No. 3 doubles team of freshmen Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum with dominant scores of 6-1, 6-1. “We were in a good mindset and were really positive, I think that helped. I try not to focus too much on the score, but it feels good to know that we could do something good for the team as a whole,” said Jumper. “I think it went really well because we were both hitting well and went out there with the same goal of hitting volleys and being more aggressive. Winning was really encouraging, not just for us Staff Photos Tanya Kononova is on a winning streak at No. 1 singles. She defeated Alameda’s top player, Sonam Manghai, 6-1, 6-2 and College Prep’s No. 1 singles player 6-2, 6-2. but for the entire team. The fact that everyone has so much potential, it feels good to get this done,” added Kortum. No. 1 singles starter Tanya Kononova was victorious in both of her matches, defeating College Prep’s Juliana Johnson 6-2, 6-2 and Alameda 6-1, 6-2. The matches mean she’s won her last five in a row since the California Tennis Classic. Through it all, Kononova mentions that she’s been working on staying composed through the frustrating moments. “I like winning,” said Kononova with a laugh. “When I have some bad moments, like with anger, I’m working on just playing through those.” Kate Jumper (back) and Arianna Kortum got the clinching fourth win over Alameda. Mara LaForte (back) and Michaela Bini are instilling themselves as Piedmont’s No. 1 doubles team.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ varsity cross-country team placed second in a league meet. Pictured are Julien Lee (left), Xander Schulte-Sasse, Parker Long, Alex Ware, Evan Byun, and Miles Antaya. Piedmont High hosted the second annual Be The G.O.A.T. (Greatest of All Time) Invitational at the Pinole Multi-Use Trails outside of Hercules on Saturday, October 1. Competing with seven other schools, the Highlanders’ boys’ and girls’ teams placed second behind Berkeley. The race was sponsored by sports equipment company Salomon Group, Ocho Candy of Piedmont, and sports nutrition company GU Energy Labs. Individual medals were awarded to the top 15 runners in each race. The top three teams in each event received plaques, and Salomon running shoes were given to the individual runners. The race included six events: freshman boys, sophomore boys, junior varsity boys, JV girls, boys varsity and girls varsity. “Race day was a big day for our team. I heard good reviews about the organization of our meet… Our girls are running stronger and it was a great race for our boys. Our varsity team placed second with Xander Schulte-Sasse, Julien Lee and Parker Long finishing 3rd, 4th and 5th,” said coach Jeanine Homlund. Junior Xander Schulte-Sasse continued leading the way for the squad, placing third overall among 61 runners with a time of 15:50.3 on the three-mile course. He was second in a WACC meet on September 21 and was 21st of 222 in the Lowell Invitational on September 10 to start the season. The Purple Train rolled behind Schulte-Sasse with junior Julien Lee finishing fourth in 16:15.6. Senior Parker Long was in fifth overall in 16:21.9 and sophomore Freshman Skylar Best continues to impress in her debut season on the varsity cross-country team. She was 2nd out of 42 runners in last week’s league meet. The PHS girls’ cross-country team also placed second: Jamie Schwarz (left), Skylar Best, Quincy Antaya, Elia Kwong, and Cora Chun. Evan Byun finishing 15th in 17:24.7. Rounding out PHS’ topfive times was senior Alex Ware in 21st in 17:36.3. Piedmont was competing without one of its top runners, senior Christian Taylor. One week earlier, PHS beat Berkeley at a league meet on September 21. The girls’ team also placed second to Berkeley with team scores of 29 (Piedmont) to 43. It marked another fine performance by freshman Skylar Best who led the team and finished second out of 42 runners with a time of 19:33.4. Behind Best was junior Jamie Schwarz in fourth with a time of 20:14.9. Following Schwartz was a trio of freshmen, Cora Chun 14th in 21:40.4, Elia Kwong 15th in 21:57.2, and Quincy Antaya in 19th, 22:28.5. The team was without standout runner Josie Oesterer. NEXT UP Piedmont competes at another WACC League Meet on Wednesday, October 12 at Point Pinole Park. The varsity race starts at 4:10 p.m.

articles.text: Beats El Cerrito 11-5, Moreau Catholic 8-7, falls to Marin Academy Photos by Nancy Brahm Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team won two of three games at the Battle of the Bay tournament at Encinal on the weekend of September 30 - October 1. The girls’ water polo team had a successful run at the Battle of the Bay tournament at Encinal High in Alameda last weekend, September 30-October 1. It won two of its three games, defeating El Cerrito 11-5 and Moreau Catholic 8-7 on Saturday, after losing 14-5 to Marin Academy on the opening day. The tournament proved to be a showcase for Katarina Melian and Rosie Feldman, each of whom scored 10 goals in two days of action. 11-5 win over El Cerrito Piedmont was first on the board after a minute and a half when Feldman assisted Annika Nilsson on a fast break. Following a Gaucho five-meter penalty shot with 3:14 left in the first, Odessa Dando took advantage of a 6-on-5 opportunity with 2:25 left for a 2-1 score. In the second quarter, Katarina Melian scored on a five-meter penalty. El Cerrito scored two minutes later to make it 3-2, but with a man-advantage, Melian made it 4-2 with just 34 seconds on the clock. Melian scored once again as time at halftime to take a 5-2 lead. It was all Rosie Feldman in the third quarter. The PHS sharpshooter scored four consecutive goals to boost Piedmont’s lead to 9-2 heading into the last period. El Cerrito scored 30 seconds into the fourth, and Melian scored on a five-meter penalty shot for a 10-3 lead. The Gauchos scored 30 seconds later, but Kate Meyjes responded with a goal at the 1:55 mark. El Cerrito scored the game’s final goal with 18 seconds left to play. 8-7 win over Moreau The Highlanders opened with a goal by Feldman within two minutes. Moreau equalized 30 seconds later, followed by Melian’s goal on a man-advantage. Feldman scored again at 3:23 mark to go up 3-1. Moreau made it 3-2 less than 20 seconds later but Feldman kept PHS on top at 4-2 with 1:56 to play in the quarter. Both teams were scoreless in the second quarter with strong defense by both sides. In the third quarter Moreau battled back to tie the match at 4-4 with 5:10 left in the period, but Feldman scored on a lob shot at 4:14 mark to regain the lead. Melian extended the advantage to 6-4 on another 6-on-5 opportunity with two minutes left. At the 1:23 mark, Moreau scored a five-meter penalty to cut it to 6-5. One minute later Melian responded to take a 7-5 lead. In an exciting, tension-filled fourth quarter, Moreau came to life with 4:31 left in the game, scoring two consecutive goals to tie the match at 7-7. But 20 seconds later, Melian scored what proved to be the winning goal, 8-7. In the remaining four minutes, goalie Friedie Schickedanz made a number of big stops, including saving a final shot at the buzzer. Katarina Melian scored 10 goals in three games.

pages.text: Wednesday, October 5, 2022 13 Piedmont’s boys’ varsity cross-country team placed second in a league meet. Pictured are Julien Lee (left), Xander Schulte-Sasse, Parker Long, Alex Ware, Evan Byun, and Miles Antaya. Piedmont harriers 2nd to Berkeley in G.O.A.T. Invitational By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High hosted the second annual Be The G.O.A.T. (Greatest of All Time) Invitational at the Pinole Multi-Use Trails outside of Hercules on Saturday, October 1. Competing with seven other schools, the Highlanders’ boys’ and girls’ teams placed second behind Berkeley. The race was sponsored by sports equipment company Salomon Group, Ocho Candy of Piedmont, and sports nutrition company GU Energy Labs. Individual medals were awarded to the top 15 runners in each race. The top three teams in each event received plaques, and Salomon running shoes were given to the individual runners. The race included six events: freshman boys, sophomore boys, junior varsity boys, JV girls, boys varsity and girls varsity. “Race day was a big day for our team. I heard good reviews about the organization of our meet… Our girls are running stronger and it was a great race for our boys. Our varsity team placed second with Xander Schulte-Sasse, Julien Lee and Parker Long finishing 3rd, 4th and 5th,” said coach Jeanine Homlund. Junior Xander Schulte-Sasse continued leading the way for the squad, placing third overall among 61 runners with a time of 15:50.3 on the three-mile course. He was second in a WACC meet on September 21 and was 21st of 222 in the Lowell Invitational on September 10 to start the season. The Purple Train rolled behind Schulte-Sasse with junior Julien Lee finishing fourth in 16:15.6. Senior Parker Long was in fifth overall in 16:21.9 and sophomore Freshman Skylar Best continues to impress in her debut season on the varsity cross-country team. She was 2nd out of 42 runners in last week’s league meet. The PHS girls’ cross-country team also placed second: Jamie Schwarz (left), Skylar Best, Quincy Antaya, Elia Kwong, and Cora Chun. Evan Byun finishing 15th in 17:24.7. Rounding out PHS’ topfive times was senior Alex Ware in 21st in 17:36.3. Piedmont was competing without one of its top runners, senior Christian Taylor. One week earlier, PHS beat Berkeley at a league meet on September 21. The girls’ team also placed second to Berkeley with team scores of 29 (Piedmont) to 43. It marked another fine performance by freshman Skylar Best who led the team and finished second out of 42 runners with a time of 19:33.4. Behind Best was junior Jamie Schwarz in fourth with a time of 20:14.9. Following Schwartz was a trio of freshmen, Cora Chun 14th in 21:40.4, Elia Kwong 15th in 21:57.2, and Quincy Antaya in 19th, 22:28.5. The team was without standout runner Josie Oesterer. By Jonathan Comeaux The girls’ water polo team had a successful run at the Battle of the Bay tournament at Encinal High in Alameda last weekend, September 30-October 1. It won two of its three games, defeating El Cerrito 11-5 and Moreau Catholic 8-7 on Saturday, after losing 14-5 to Marin Academy on the opening day. The tournament proved to be a showcase for Katarina Melian and Rosie Feldman, each of whom scored 10 goals in two days of action. 11-5 win over El Cerrito Piedmont was first on the board after a minute and a half when Feldman assisted Annika Nilsson on a fast break. Following a Gaucho five-meter penalty shot with 3:14 left in the first, Odessa Dando took advantage of a 6-on-5 opportunity with 2:25 left for a 2-1 score. In the second quarter, Katarina Melian scored on a five-meter penalty. El Cerrito scored two minutes later to make it 3-2, but with a man-advantage, Melian made it 4-2 with just 34 seconds on the clock. Melian scored once again as time at halftime to take a 5-2 lead. It was all Rosie Feldman in the third quarter. The PHS sharpshooter scored four consecutive goals to boost Piedmont’s lead to 9-2 heading into the last period. El Cerrito scored 30 seconds into the fourth, and Melian scored on a five-meter penalty shot for a 10-3 lead. The Gauchos scored 30 seconds later, but Kate Meyjes responded with a goal at the 1:55 mark. El Cerrito scored the game’s final goal with 18 seconds left to play. 8-7 win over Moreau The Highlanders opened with a goal by Feldman within two minutes. Moreau equalized 30 seconds later, followed by Melian’s goal on a man-advantage. Feldman scored again at 3:23 mark to go up 3-1. Moreau made it 3-2 less than 20 seconds later but Feldman kept PHS on top at 4-2 with 1:56 to play in the quarter. Both teams were scoreless in the second quarter with strong defense by both sides. In the third quarter Moreau battled back to tie the match at 4-4 with 5:10 left in the period, but Feldman scored on a lob shot at 4:14 mark to regain the lead. Melian extended the advantage to 6-4 on another 6-on-5 opportunity with two minutes left. At the 1:23 mark, Moreau scored a five-meter penalty to cut it to 6-5. One minute later Melian responded to take a 7-5 lead. In an exciting, tension-filled fourth quarter, Moreau came to life with 4:31 left in the game, scoring two consecutive goals to tie the match at 7-7. But 20 seconds later, Melian scored what proved to be the winning goal, 8-7. In the remaining four minutes, goalie Friedie Schickedanz made a number of big stops, including saving a final shot at the buzzer. See Girls’ Water Polo on page 32 Katarina Melian scored 10 goals in three games.

articles.text: Photo by Rob Peterson The girls’ volleyball team defeated San Leandro 3-1 on Homecoming Night. It was standing room only at Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday night, September 30. The occasion was the girls’ volleyball team playing a match with San Leandro, and more importantly taking the place of the football team for Homecoming night. With the cancelation of the football team’s game on Friday, the volleyball team happily rescheduled a match with the Pirates to Piedmont and delighted the packed house with a 3-1 victory. The win was made even more special with PHS pep band, cheerleaders, and decorations throughout the gym. “We fed off of our amazing crowd; we had the band there, cheerleaders there, and a packed student section,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. “The girls came in super strong. We started with our strongest rotation, Bauer [Peterson] as setter, Shelby [Cavenaugh] right side, Bree [DeYoung] middle, Sadie [Town] as DS, and Klara [Zietlow] as libero. Eden [Lorin] has been playing libero, but the past couple of games it’s been pretty evident that Eden is a killer on the outside. I’m definitely utilizing Eden playing front and back row. Klara is the only sophomore on the team, and she has taken over the role of libero.” In the first set, Piedmont trailed 2-0 but turned the tide to score six straight points to jump ahead 6-2 and then scored eight of the next 11 points gain a commanding 14-5 lead with help from an ace by Sadie Town and kills by Tara Kothari, Eden Lorin, and Shelby Cavenaugh. From there, Piedmont went ahead 19-9 and then at 20-12, scored five of the next six points to win 25-13 with the help of strong serving by Lorin and a finishing kill by Town. Piedmont lost the 2nd set 27-25. The two sides traded points in the early going but Piedmont eventually pulled away to hold a six-point 15-9 lead. The Pirates inched away at the lead at 19-15, where Town gained two more kills during that span. Following a kill by Kothari, PHS held set-point at 24-21 but conceded four straight points to trail 25-24. PHS tied at 25-25, but San Leandro earned the final two points in long rallies to tie the match at one Photo by Rob Peterson Bauer Peterson sets up Bree DeYoung (3) for a spike. Photo by Sophie Hess Molly Wagener goes up for a block against the Pirates.
