articles.text: Piedmont’s football team reached the North Coast Section Semifinals in 2014, won the won a WACC Shoreline title, and finished with a 12-1 record. It’s been a tumultuous time for Piedmont High’s football program for several years. Wrought with low roster turnout, the team has faced problems of being able to field a complete varsity team for three years. Since the departure of former coach James Holan after the 2017 season, there’s been a sharp downturn for the Highlanders. Long gone are the days of consistent North Coast Section appearances. Covid and the pandemic pretty well knocked the football team off its mooring for at least two years, with a residual effect in this, the third year of a struggle for survival. Holan left Piedmont High with an overall record of 24-13 from 2015-2017, and was 18-7 as a coordinator in 2013 and 2014 under Scott Coats. Piedmont has qualified for the post-season North Coast Section playoffs every year from 2011 until 2018 under John Trotman. Between 2013-2017 Piedmont never finished with a losing record. In 2014 under Coats, its most successful coach in a5 years, PHS went 12-1 overall, reached the Division 4 NCS Semifinals, and won the WACC Shoreline championship. The following year Piedmont went 9-3 overall, reached the quarterfinals of the NCS playoffs, and won a second consecutive WACC Shoreline championship. The team then was bumped up to the WACC Foothill Division, where they resided until the spring of 2021 when the Mission Division was created during a topsy-turvy Covid-impacted sports year. 2014 marked the first time in 38 years Piedmont won a league title. Gabe Watson, the school’s All-Time leading rusher, went on to play for the University of Sioux Falls and was a candidate for the Harlon Hill Trophy, considered the Heisman Trophy for Div. 2 schools. In 2016, Piedmont posted a 8-5 record and advanced to the Div. 4 Former Piedmont football coach Jerome Johnson. Staff Photo Staff Photo Piedmont last reached the NCS postseason in 2019 under coach John Trotman, now the head coach at St. Mary’s in Berkeley. NCS semifinals before falling to No. 1 seed Cardinal Newman. In Holan’s last year at the school in 2017, PHS went 7-5 and reached the quarterfinals of the NCS playoffs before losing to No. 3 Harker in San Jose. In 2019 under Trotman, Piedmont had a 5-6 record and qualified for the NCS playoffs as a No. 7 seed. They were upset by No. 10 Justin-Siena in the first round. Trotman resigned, which opened the door for former defensive coordinator Jerome Johnson to be promoted to head coach from defensive coordinator. PHS went 3-7 the following season with a roster of largely JV players. But in the spring of 2021, the hybrid Covid-impacted high school sports season when football was played in the spring, the Highlander varsity was undefeated at 5-0 under Johnson. It was the first winning season since 2017. However, the impact of Covid resulted in a low turnout of players, leading to the high school canceling the junior varsity program. In the fall of 2021, the team finished with a 2-7 overall record with only 17 players. PHS Athletic Director Bradley Smet informed other teams in the Western Alameda County Conference that Piedmont would be canceling its varsity program and let coach Johnson go. The decision, when parents heard about it, led to an effort to revive football. Now at 0-5 for the current season, the varsity program is on the verge of a full cancelation. The Homecoming game was canceled due to mounting injuries and a depleted roster of a team that began the season with 20 players. Football began at Piedmont High in 1921, and for the first time in 100 years it played the season without a league, scheduling games as an independent school. And now, Piedmont High must again look for answers to revive interest in the sport.
articles.title: Reflecting on the lifeline of Piedmont’s football program

articles.text: It was an electric night for Piedmont High School’s volleyball team when it hosted Homecoming Night for the first time on Friday. The traditional football game had been canceled earlier last week for the first time in 100 years. It was a standing room only in Binks Rawlings Gym, with the students from Piedmont High responding to a volleyball game instead of football. Provided are photos which capture the energy from the rare night on which the volleyball team defeated San Leandro 3-1 in front of a roaring crowd. With a packed house, the student section had to be restrained on the sideline. articles.text: Allyson Aleksey Aaron Sorkin’s play adaptation of To Kill a Mockingbird is in its final week at the Golden Gate Theatre in San Francisco. Sorkin’s adaption of Harper Lee’s famous 1960 novel opened on Broadway in 2018 and has been the highest-grossing American play since its debut. Set in Alabama in 1934, Lee’s novel is widely considered an American classic and an enduring story of racial injustice. The cast includes Richard Thomas as Atticus Finch, Melanie Moore as Scout Finch, Jacqueline Williams as Calpurnia, Justin Mark as Jem Finch, Yaegel T. Welch as Tom Robinson, Steven Lee Johnson as Dill Harris and Mary Badham as Mrs. Dubose. They are joined by Joey Collins as Bob Ewell, Richard Poe as Judge Taylor, Luke Smith as Horace Gilmer, Arianna Gayle Stucki as Mayella Ewell, David Christopher Wells as Sheriff Heck Tate. Tickets can be purchased at www.broadwaysf.com. The Golden Gate Theatre is located at 1 Taylor Street in San Francisco. Photo by Julieta Cervantes Steven Lee Johnson as Dill Harris (left), Melanie Moore as Scout Finch, and Justin Mark as Jem Finch in To Kill a Mockingbird, now playing at the Golden Gate Theatre in San Francisco.
articles.title: To Kill a Mockingbird at Golden Gate Theatre ends this Sunday

articles.text: Paula Vogel’s new play is based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s Broadway debut of The God of Vengeance. Although many consider Asch’s work to be a seminal work of Jewish culture, it is also viewed by some as traitorous libel. “We were lucky enough to be on hand when Paula Vogel’s Indecent opened on Broadway five years ago, and being huge fans of hers already, and galvanized by the production, we began angling to present the play’s Bay Area premiere immediately,” said San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English. “At the time we were a long shot due to strong interest from bigger companies, but after a two-year pandemic and catastrophic changes in the American theatre, a door opened five years later for us to present Indecent.” The play is directed by Susi Damilano, with music direction by Dmitri Gaskin and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The principal cast members include Dean Linnard, Billy Cohen, Rachel Botchan, and Rivka Borek. Indecent is co-produced with the Yiddish Theatre Ensemble and features a live klezmer score. “It is both a love song to the Ashkenazi Jewish culture spanning 50 years, and a love song to the theatre. It is an odyssey that spins us from Warsaw to Berlin, to NY Yiddish theatre, to Broadway and back to Warsaw as the tumultuous and tragic history of the early 20th Century unfolds around the play within our play,” English said. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/get-tickets/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: SF Playhouse celebrates 20th season with Indecent onstage through November 5

articles.text: The acclaimed Broadway hit Moulin Rouge! The Musical is showing at San Francisco’s Orpheum Theater through November 6. The 10-time Tony award-winning musical is directed by Alex Timbers and designed by Derek McLane. The production features Aaron Tveit as Christian and Karen Olivo as Satine from the 2001 film of the same name and directed by Baz Luhrmann. The film is widely popular and has been nominated for more than 100 awards, winning two Academy Awards and three Golden Globes. Choreography for the production is by Sonya Tayeh. To see times for showings at Orpheum theater between now and November 6, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.san-francisco-theater.com/ theaters/orpheum-theater/moulin-rouge-the-musical.php. The 10-time Tony award-winning musical, Moulin Rouge! The Musical, is playing at Orpheum theater through Nov. 6.

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, October 5, 2022 Arts & Entertainment To Kill a Mockingbird at Golden Gate Theatre ends this Sunday Allyson Aleksey Aaron Sorkin’s play adaptation of To Kill a Mockingbird is in its final week at the Golden Gate Theatre in San Francisco. Sorkin’s adaption of Harper Lee’s famous 1960 novel opened on Broadway in 2018 and has been the highest-grossing American play since its debut. Set in Alabama in 1934, Lee’s novel is widely considered an American classic and an enduring story of racial injustice. The cast includes Richard Thomas as Atticus Finch, Melanie Moore as Scout Finch, Jacqueline Williams as Calpurnia, Justin Mark as Jem Finch, Yaegel T. Welch as Tom Robinson, Steven Lee Johnson as Dill Harris and Mary Badham as Mrs. Dubose. They are joined by Joey Collins as Bob Ewell, Richard Poe as Judge Taylor, Luke Smith as Horace Gilmer, Arianna Gayle Stucki as Mayella Ewell, David Christopher Wells as Sheriff Heck Tate. Tickets can be purchased at www.broadwaysf.com. The Golden Gate Theatre is located at 1 Taylor Street in San Francisco. Photo by Jessica Palopoli Rivka Borek (left), Matthew Stein (on violin), Rachel Botchan, Dean Linnard, Dmitri Gaskin (on accordion) and Ted Zoldan appear onstage in San Francisco Playhouse’s production of Indecent. SF Playhouse celebrates 20th season with Indecent onstage through November 5 By Allyson Aleksey Paula Vogel’s new play is based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s Broadway debut of The God of Vengeance. Although many consider Asch’s work to be a seminal work of Jewish culture, it is also viewed by some as traitorous libel. “We were lucky enough to be on hand when Paula Vogel’s Indecent opened on Broadway five years ago, and being huge fans of hers already, and galvanized by the production, we began angling to present the play’s Bay Area premiere immediately,” said San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English. “At the time we were a long shot due to strong interest from bigger companies, but after a two-year pandemic and catastrophic changes in the American theatre, a door opened five years later for us to present Indecent.” The play is directed by Susi Damilano, with music direction by Dmitri Gaskin and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The principal cast members include Dean Linnard, Billy Cohen, Rachel Botchan, and Rivka Borek. Indecent is co-produced with the Yiddish Theatre Ensemble and features a live klezmer score. “It is both a love song to the Ashkenazi Jewish culture spanning 50 years, and a love song to the theatre. It is an odyssey that spins us from Warsaw to Berlin, to NY Yiddish theatre, to Broadway and back to Warsaw as the tumultuous and tragic history of the early 20th Century unfolds around the play within our play,” English said. articles.text: SF Symphony masters Mahler Review by Paul Hertelendy Mahler’s “Resurrection” was a revelation, leaving us in the audience limp and giddy, as if, in a euphoric state of ecstasy, we had just been led through the Pearly Gates into the great beyond. It was the finest hour yet for Maestro Esa-Pekka Salonen in the bows when the orchestra remained steadfastly seated, deflecting the cheers to the conductor himself. The audience too responded with an inordinate five-minute ovation for the San Francisco Symphony and Chorus for their rousing concert. In a budget-be-damned September 27 concert, it ran 24 minutes beyond the two-hour norm, most likely unleashing overtime rewards for all concerned in the oversize ensemble. Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 does require oversize forces – two harps, five percussionists, close to a score of brass players, with various brass sounding from offstage sites above and outside the Davies Hall auditorium, adding to a sense of some reimagined fourth-dimension wonderworld. The disappointment was that all this magnificence overshadowed a significant world premiere by Trevor Weston, Push, that had gone before. The genius of Gustav Mahler lay not so much in the Resurrection choral-vocal text that he himself had penned in the late 19th century. It was in the entire 90-minute structure of a dozen moods culminating in that euphoric finale rivaling in impact Beethoven’s parallel Ninth Symphony (cum chorus) of some 75 years earlier. In the build-up, Mahler leads us through a welter of emotions of a very real life and world, overemotional yet precise in his scores: a serene sunrise on violins, then on to the charming Austrian forerunner of the waltz called Lȁndler, on to fullthroated, exuberant outpourings on brass and percussion at deafening levels. It was an excitement akin to jumping off a high diving board willy-nilly without checking if the pool contained water. On the podium, Salonen paid inordinate attention to dynamics – not only loud, but also with some of the softest and most intimate sonics heard at Davies Hall. This was a throwback to unadulterated romanticism with visceral effect as rarely heard in our very rational 21st century. There came too the Mahler-tradeSan Francisco Symphony music director Esa-Pekka Salonen. marked stimulus of pulse-quickening up-bows on violins, the bells-high positioning of French horns, and amazing crescendos. This was a quasi-religious experience comparable to high mass at a reverberent Gothic cathedral in Mahler’s own Bohemia-Austria habitats. Much of the impact came from the 110 voices of the Symphony Chorus sounding out as rarely before under Salonen and guest chorus leader Jenny Wong. Just the male contingent alone had emerged with such robust strength that the walls of Davies may still be reverberating. In far more restrained solos came soloists Michelle DeYoung and a newcomer from South Africa, Golda Schultz. One lamented that none of the night’s singing of consonants was well enough enunciated to enable following the German text in the printed program. Trevor Weston’s Push Almost lost in the night’s embers was the world premiere that went before, Trevor Weston’s Push, which deserved a better spotlight. Push refers to a Dvorak quote about Americans’ pushing the envelope in their endeavors. Though teaching on the East Coast, the 55-year-old Black composer Weston has a considerable East Bay history, having earned his Ph.D. with the eminent late Prof. Olly Wilson at UC Berkeley, and having then associated with the Oakland Symphony’s late maestro, Michael Morgan, whose versatile involvement in so many facets of community music demands updating all the monographs on a conductor’s role. His deft threnody in the four-movement piece was dedicated to Morgan, who died last year at 63 shortly before his scheduled SF Symphony debut. (At times it was definitely tougher to make it as a Black musician, whether Morgan, Wilson or Weston. In 1975 I heard the 17-year-old ill-attired Morgan in a young conductors’ competition for the Baltimore Symphony leading a Brahms movement and competing against all-white competition typically five years older and with diplomas from leading institutions. I heard Morgan give an electric reading, evoking play surpassing anything from the other candidates. However, he only got an honorable mention, with a music prof afterward citing to me Morgan’s crude stick technique!) Weston demonstrated an apt versatility, ranging from popjazz influences to subtle orchestral expressiveness. The latter was also evident in his subdued “City Quiet” segment hovering somewhere between Copland and Bartok in pianissimos. The outer movements were boisterous, punctuated by effusiveness akin to John Coltrane, whom Weston could only hear on recordings, as tenor saxist Coltrane had perished at age 40 the year Weston was born. MUSIC NOTES The SFS’ new principal cellist, Rainer Eudeikis, performed in the first chair. Among the remaining unfilled principal chairs are flute and harp, with substitutes filling in each time. A Piedmont resident, Paul Hertelendy also writes on classical concerts at the arts-review web site www.artsSF.com Trevor Weston’s 20-minute world premiere, Push; Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 with the S.F. Symphony and Chorus. Esa-Pekka Salonen, music director, at Davies Hall, San Francisco, September 29 through October 2. For SFS info, call (415) 864-6000, or go online: www.sfsymphony.org.
articles.title: Resurrection = Revelation

articles.text: $35 million donation initiates renaming The American Conservatory Theater (ACT) in San Francisco has been renamed the Toni Rembe Theater after the longtime San Francisco fine arts philanthropist. The renaming is in recognition of an anonymous donor who gifted the theater $35 million, the largest single gift in ACT’s history. The announcement was made on September 20 by the theater’s Executive Director. Jennifer Bielstein, Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon, Board Chair Jeff Minick, and Board President Joaquín Torres. “We are deeply grateful to the generous donor for this extraordinary gift,” said Bielstein. “The funds provided are transformational for the future of American Conservatory Theater and the impact of our programming throughout the San Francisco Bay Area. Toni is a role model, and we are honored to recognize her in such a deserving and significant way. The Toni Rembe Theater will forever serve as a reminder of Toni’s decades-long contributions to the arts community.” Toni Rembe is a longtime philanthropist in the arts and has maintained positions as president of the van Lӧben Sels/Rembe Rock Foundation, a private foundation specializing in the promotion of social justice through legal services; a co-founder and advisory board member of the Rock Center for Corporate Governance at Stanford University; a founding member of the Theatre Communication Group’s National Council for the American Theater; and a member of the board of the Immigrant Legal Resource Center. She currently serves on the board of trustees for ACT for over two decades. “Toni Rembe has been central to the health and well-being of the Bay Area theater scene,” said MacKinnon. “Her wide-ranging artistic taste and appreciation of artists and the special act of audiences coming together for a story make her a true theater lover. Her generosity and commitment to Bay Area culture and artmaking is unparalleled.” Photo courtesy of KQED The ACT Theater has been renamed after fine arts philanthropist Toni Rembe.
articles.title: ACT Theater renamed Toni Rembe Theater

articles.text: Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside is celebrating “Orchard Days” every weekend through October 30. Visit the gardens this fall and stroll through the seven-acre Gentleman’s Orchard, a vital component of self-sustaining estates and a feature of many American country houses at the turn of the century. The acres hold a collection of fruits grown for leisure rather than commercial production. The Bourns, the original owners of the estate, planted their orchard with 1,000 trees – apples, pears, plums, apricots, walnuts, figs, and quinces. Only 115 trees remained when the orchard was restored, but there are now over 500 fruit and nut trees of various species. Filoli staff preserve the historic collection of rare and historically significant varieties. Orchard Days at Filoli feature live music, and food and drink for purchase at the Bluebird Bar. Reservations are required. To purchase tickets, visit https:// filoli.org/orchard-days/. The gardens are open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Filoli House and Garden hosts Orchard Days every weekend through October 30.
articles.title: Weekend Orchard Days at Filoli through October 30

articles.text: Due to popularity Circus Bella has added six more free showings of its newest show, Flip Flop Fly, from October 15-23. This series of performances, featuring some of the dazzling circus talent from the Bay Area, will delight audiences of all ages in a family event for all ages. Flip Flop Fly is directed by Circus Bella co-founder and director Abigail Munn. The performances will celebrate the circus’s 13th year. The 60-minute show is circus arts at its most exuberant, exploring human curiosity and sky-high imagination. Circus Bella is a diverse and talented troupe of acrobats, aerialists, jugglers, and clowns - performing to the live music of Rob Reich and the six piece Circus Bella All-Star Band. Guests are invited to bring picnic blankets and small folding chairs to all locations. A preshow performance by the Stars of Prescott Circus Theatre will also be held. To learn more visit: Circusbella.org/flipflopfly or call 415- 480-4239.
articles.title: Circus Bella adds 6 free outdoor shows in October

articles.text: Opera has always been the most popular form of classical music. It combines every aspect of music drama and art. There is good reason why people love opera. When opera addresses human tragedy, people understand it’s a theater of the absurd. When opera addresses comedy, it’s the other way around. Thus, success is guaranteed. Adding insult to injury, opera singers always made much more money than other musicians. They were the pop stars of days gone by. We have many fine opera companies in the Bay Area, and one of the best is the Livermore Valley Opera. It is now presenting Donizetti’s great comedy opera The Elixir of Love. Opening night was last Saturday and there are two more performances this weekend. What makes the Elixir of Love so good is that it expresses the entire human condition perfectly. The Livermore Valley Opera orchestra got things off to a lively start with a neatly performed prelude conducted by music Director Alexander Katsman. Oh, how I wish that Donizetti had written a longer overture. To say that the entire production was first class is putting it mildly. It was absolutely top rate in every way. All of the singers had good voices and were fine actors. Nemorino, the male lead, was played brilliantly by tenor Christopher Bozeka. He sang the famous aria Una furtiva lagrima beautifully. I don’t think it is possible to do better. Elena Galvan played the female lead of Aldina. She has a beautiful, well modulated voice and all the power that you’d want. The other lead characters are also memorable. Andrew Potter played the arrogant military sergeant to perfection, and Samuel Weiser was the epitome of a snake-oil salesman. The story develops towards its inevitable conclusion. The magic elixir cures all the ills of the world. Hurray! It’s an easy drive to Livermore. Take in the show… You’ll love it.
articles.title: A delightful opera production in Livermore

articles.text: The heartfelt, engaging performances of husband and wife soprano Jenny Matteucci and pianist Daniel Lockert continue to attract audiences throughout the Bay Area. Their music is varied and ranges from Fats Waller to the Great American Songbook with many surprises in between. The Pardee Home Museum in Oakland welcomes them for an afternoon performance in the Pardee Garden on Sunday, October 9. Matteucci is known for her flexibility of style. As a young singer, she was active in the San Francisco theater and cabaret scene, where she continues to perform today. In addition to teaching voice and performance classes, she is currently conductor of the Festival Chamber Chorale, the Festival Chorus of Mendocino County, the FCCPA Chancel Choir, the FCCPA Women’s Ensemble and the Palo Alto Oratorio Society. Lockert, is versatile on the piano, organ and harpsichord. He began formal piano studies at age five. As coach and teacher he has been on the staff and faculty of the Julliard School, the San Francisco Opera, San Francisco Conservatory of Music, Opera San Jose, Chapman College, Cal State East Bay, Mills College, Notre Dame de Namur University and the Aspen Music Festival. He currently serves as coach and collaborator at Santa Clara University. The Pardee garden is a lovely place to visit this time of year with flowering plants and shade from the grand trees. Following the concert, a champagne reception will be held with light refreshments, including savories and sweets and plenty of socializing. COVID protocols will be followed with proof of vaccination required and a safe place to gather. The concert will be held on Sunday, October 9 at 4 p.m. Tickets are $25 per person, and all proceeds go to the Pardee Home Museum. Reservations may be made by calling Richelle Lieberman at 510-381-1973. Entry to the concert is through the white gate on Castro Street between 11th & 12th Streets. Soprano Jenny Matteucci and husband Daniel Lockert will perform a concert of songs from the Great American Songbook at the Pardee Home Museum on Sunday, October 9.

By Martin Gustavson Troop 6 kicked off its Fall camping season with its annual trip to Yosemite on August 12th. We always love camping in Yosemite as it’s a beautiful spot filled with opportunities for Scouts to learn about the Great Outdoors while having a great time. Our journey begins a few days before the drive to Yosemite, when all the Scouts were organized into patrols. The patrol method in Scouting is where you split the Scouts into smaller groups and each group is responsible for setting up tents, equipment, cooking and clean-up. Each patrol planned what they needed to bring and what they were going to eat on the trip, assigning tasks and responsibilities to individual Scouts. Mrs. Gros, one of our Scoutmasters, prepared a patrol competition with goals of being the patrol with the least amount of trash and the best food. articles.text: Individuals participating in Walking on Wednesdays on September 28 included Mike Gallant, Jim Kellogg, Brenda Ferrero, Alan Goldhammer, Sherry Jacobs, Lisa Euphrat, Reneez Goldhammer, Cat Lang, Martin Levy, Phil Witte, Pat Keller, Jim Kuo, Elizabeth Richter, David Haecker, Christine Calliste, Priscilla Wanerus, Melba Yee, Ann Quinby, Ian Morgan, Jasmine Cai, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Lois Price, Nancy and Larry Olsen, Harriette Louie, Sarah Johnson, Will Adams, Elane Rehr, Nadine Guffanti, Mike and Nancy Henn, Gloria DaSilva, Dick Carter, Stella Houston, and her guest, first-time walker Brenda Goodbeer. The Walking on Wednesdays group tries to walk every safe walking Piedmont street during the year, and at the end of September there were only a few streets they hadn’t gotten to. Two of them were Kingston Avenue and the portion of upper Grand Avenue from Oakland Avenue to Pleasant Valley Road. On this section of Grand there is a new home being completed on a lot that was vacant for many years because it seemed unbuildable. Architects Jim Kellogg and Will Adams were on the walk and offered some observations. Kingston and the parallel Rose Avenue have some of the oldest homes in Piedmont. The long line of walkers headed down Magnolia Avenue to El Cerrito Avenue where they saw a forest of lawn signs showing support for school board and city council candidates. At Cambridge Way the walkers came upon a home they had seen on past walks that needed some loving care, and now was getting extensive foundation, window, and landscaping work. On Grand Ave. the walkers came to the new house that is almost completed. They were impressed by its design and construction. It is a large home, built with lots of concrete on a steep slope. Though new and different, Kellogg and Adams felt it fit with the surrounding homes. The group continued to Linda Avenue then to Rose Avenue. They enjoyed the many old homes that were built from the late 1800s to the 1930s, and an historic, beautiful Victorian at 950 Rose that was built in 1894. One block away, two homes on Kingston were built in 1892 by William Vickery and his sister, Elizabeth Vickery Hadden, for $4,300 and $3,300. They were the first homes on this street that was then called Summit Avenue. The houses were built in the fashionable Shingle style of the 1890s. The backyard of the house at 778 is one of the deepest lots in Piedmont. Neighborhood lore says the two houses shared one kitchen and the two families ate their meals together. It was time to head back to the Exedra, so the walkers made their way back via Arroyo and Ramona Avenues and a 107 foot path to Park Way. It was a longer than usual walk of just over three miles, and almost two hours, but the contrast of Piedmont homes built almost 150 years apart was striking and made the extra time and steps worthwhile. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: Autumn in the Bay Area brings delightfully mild, sunny days. While autumn produce has made an appearance at markets, I’m not ready to fully dive into hearty fare just yet. This brown rice salad uses autumn produce but is welcomed on lunch and dinner plates while the weather is still warm. There is textural interest from crisp, diced celery and pomegranate arials. As with any salad, use this as a guide to create variations on the theme. Substitutions and additions beckon. Quinoa, bulgur, wheat berries, couscous, or wild rice can be used in place of the brown rice. Butternut or acorn squash can replace the delicata, although I chose delicata because it cooks quickly, and the skin is edible. (You can skip the peeling, making it easy to prepare.) You can take it in different flavor directions by adding spices such as a chile powder blend, a curry blend, or ras el hanout to the dressing. Speaking of the dressing, I use a 1:1 ratio of vinegar to olive oil as the salad needs the assertive punch from the sherry vinegar. If you substitute a different vinegar, adjust to taste. This recipe scales easily, so make a double batch to enjoy either more servings or plan for leftovers. The flavors will deepen overnight, so this can also be made ahead. For the salad: • 2 cups long-grain brown rice, freshly steamed and still warm • 1 cup delicata squash, roasted and diced into 1/2-inch pieces. One small-medium squash. • 1/2 cup pomegranate arils • 1/2 cup celery, finely diced • 1/4 cup red onion, finely diced • 1/4 cup flat-leaf parsley, chopped INSTRUCTIONS Autumn Brown Rice Salad Makes about 2-quarts INGREDIENTS For the dressing: • 2 tablespoons sherry vinegar • 2 tablespoons olive oil, extra-virgin • 1/2 teaspoon Dijon mustard • 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • 1/4 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground, to taste For the dressing: Combine the sherry vinegar, Dijon mustard, salt, and pepper in a small bowl. Whisk in olive oil until combined and emulsified. Set aside. Steam the brown rice according to package directions. Typically, one cup of raw rice will yield about two cups of cooked. The steamed rice should yield separate grains that are soft but retain a slightly chewy texture. Roast the delicata squash. Cut the squash lengthwise into quarters. Remove the seeds and membrane. Lightly brush with olive oil and roast at 350° F for about 30 minutes until tender and lightly browned. Cool slightly and dice to desired size. There is no need to peel the skin as it cooks up soft and tender. Combine the diced celery, red onion, and parsley in a 3-quart mixing bowl. Add the still warm, steamed rice and stir to incorporate the chopped vegetables. Add the diced squash and about three-quarters of the dressing. Stir to combine. Taste and add more dressing, salt and/or pepper as needed. Serve at room temperature or refrigerate until ready to serve. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

articles.text: Picklers far and near came to watch a pickleball demonstration by top players in the Bay Area at the Piedmont Middle School court last Saturday, October 1. Marcia Neishi, Gold Medalist and IPTPA certified teacher, Elaine Hennessy, Jeannie Lowe, and Debi Chen rounded out a demonstration team that showed everyone how to play pickleball like the pros. They impressed a crowd of over 80 people with their level of play. A delicious potluck that followed the demonstration made the event even more enjoyable. The Recreation Department helped contribute staff and food. Pickleball, introduced to Piedmont by Tom Reicher, has been in town for four years and has grown to over 400 players. The sport of pickleball is growing exponentially in Piedmont and in the country. See the Pickleball Calendar at https://sites.google. com/view/piedmont-ca-pickleball/home. articles.text: Nº 58 in series The Paris rainy season has arrived, but with scattered showers and mild temperatures, an ideal time to enjoy the city’s parks. Paris is a green city, and the autumn foliage is luscious in la ville lumière. Its 20 districts (arrondissements) were drawn in the 1860s, when Prefect Baron Haussmann demolished the ramshackle Right Bank of Paris. He was demonized for destroying the old City and flattening cheap housing stock, but he was ultimately celebrated for rooting out disease, sewage, and criminals. In their place h brought sanitation, water filtration, electrical grids, and planted gardens. Paris tourism now boasts of having 400 parks (places). A favorite is Place des Vosges, built in 1605, and a popular square surrounded by art galleries. Another is Le Square du Temple, a bucolic garden on the site of the fortress monastery built by the Knights Templar, the powerful Medieval brotherhood that bankrolled kings and barons in the age of the Crusades. Those 400 places are neatly fitted squares wedged into arrondissements, plus Paris has at least a hundred large parks. Among the best known are Tuileries Gardens between the Louvre and La Place Concorde, and the Left Bank masterpiece Luxembourg Gardens. “Paris parks are secret gardens with hidden and mysterious corners,” writes Alain Baraton, the head gardener at Versailles, in Mes Jardins de Paris. The truly giant parks are woods containing multiple gardens, fields, lakes, trails for riding horses and bicycles, and paths for runners and hikers. These preserved forests were ancient hunting grounds for the royals and were massively harvested, of late, deforested. The French treasure their bois, “the lungs of Paris,” breathing and cleansing the airstreams and offsetting pollution. To the east, Bois de Vincennes, and to the west, Bois de Boulogne, are equivalent in diversity, beauty, and size, each more than 2,000 acres, and 2.5 times the size of New York’s Central Park. Three Charming Parks My criteria for my favorite parks are three-fold: accessible by Metro and inside Paris proper; a manageable size terrain for a half-day visit; and a place of beauty and charm, off the beaten path. Charmer Nº1 is Parc Monceau, literally a walk in the park good for one hour and easily paired with a complementary activity. Monceau is a compact 20 acres of English gardens in a tony sector northeast of Arc de Triomphe. Enveloped by exquisite mansions (townhouses in French-speak), the park is atypical, where six homes border the park and have the Shangri-La of 24-hour access. Might that be a bit of fun to ferret out which ones? Monceau feels privately appointed, because it is, a folly of the fabulously wealthy Phillippe d’Orléans, Duke of Chartres whose playful décor combines Corinthian pillars, a Dutch windmill, and an Egyptian obelisk. Monceau combines nicely with a café lunch and a museum visit at the nearby Nissim de Camondo, an exceptionally beautiful 18th century French mansion filled with art; or the Cernuschi MuseParc Monceau was built in 1778 as a public park. Parc de Bagatelle measures 25 hectares, nearly 62 acres. View from Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, a 61-acre hilly site in northeast Paris. um’s Asian art collection. O u r ch a r me r N º 2 is Buttes-Chaumont with four bridges to provide astounding city views and connect verdant hilly rises with thick forests, and curving, beckoning footpaths. Three bridges are masonry-built, but Gustave Eiffel’s footbridge rises to a (then) exalted height of 213 feet in suspension across the manmade lake. Buttes is a 19th century feat of “titanic” proportions, said New Paris and Future Paris. The land tract was in poor condition, an abandoned limestone and gypsum quarry mined for making plaster. The site’s topsoil was sterile, worthless for growing crops or planting. The land “absolutely refused any vegetation,” opined Baron Haussmann. He thrusted the project at city builder Adolphe Alphand to oversee a team of engineers and landscapers. Alphand worked the quarry’s rugged landscape into a faux Alpine mountain terrain and fashioned leftover rock into “chalky cliffs of Normandy plunging abruptly into the sea.” A Place, now named Elie-Wiesel-Temple Square honors the writer who studied and lived in Paris after surviving Auschwitz. articles.text: Editor: Elect Tom Ramsey and Re-elect Betsy Smegal Andersen and Jen Long to City Council On November 8, I’ll be proud to cast my vote for Tom Ramsey for City Council. I’ve had the great privilege of working with Tom for four years on Piedmont’s Planning Commission. I’ve been deeply impressed by Tom’s decision-making approach in evaluating renovation and construction projects. Tom emphasizes collaboration and cooperation between neighbors, and balances maintaining the character of the community with being open to design innovation. Tom’s many years of engagement and service in Piedmont reflect his dedication to our community. His professional experience and expertise as an architect and senior leader will be extraordinarily helpful to City Council as Piedmont moves forward with complying with state housing laws and completing major civic projects like the pool and civic center. Finally, Tom’s warm, collegial, and solutions-focused nature will ensure that different viewpoints are respected and reflected in the Council’s decisions on important issues facing our city. I look forward to electing Tom Ramsey to City Council. I also look forward to re-electing Betsy Smegal Andersenrn and Jen Long to City Council. As an experienced attorney, Betsy’s diligence and mastery of details will serve her well in her stewardship of our city. Betsy’s extraordinary dedication to Piedmont is reflected in her decades of service in the community. Betsy knows Piedmont inside and out and we are all better for it. I’ve had the privilege of knowing Jen Long since our children were in elementary school. Jen’s collaborative nature was invaluable in helping our school establish new health and wellness policies. Jen’s professional expertise as an attorney and her personal dedication to helping Piedmont become a more diverse and inclusive community have brought a welcome perspective to City Council. Piedmont will be in good hands with Tom, Betsy and Jen serving on City Council. I hope you’ll join me in casting your ballot for each of them in November. –Rani Batra Chair, Piedmont Planning Commission

articles.text: Editor: I am so inspired and excited about two of the school board candidates this year, Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar! I hope our community comes together to elect this Dream Team to the school board. Lindsay, Ruchi and I served on the Tri-School Site Council together where I saw firsthand their dedication to our schools, our children and to a collaborative process. During Site Council meetings, I was consistently impressed with the insightful questions and comments from each of them. It is clear that they both have taken the time and effort to dive deep into the inner workings of the district, and clear that their intent is always to meet the needs they see and hear from their fellow families. Each displays a level of tact and skill at working with groups, including administrators and teachers, and advocating hard for the families they were there to represent. I saw them patiently and diligently take time for extra meetings and one-on-ones with all the parties involved on issues until there was a clear path forward that worked for everyone. I have the bonus of being a Havens parent working alongside Lindsay and having experienced her incredible leadership when she was the Parent Club president from 2020-2021. We all know how difficult that year was, but Lindsay leaned into her role with kindness and repeatedly reminded the parent community to come together and have compassion for each other. The parent community felt ravaged after that school year, and instead of taking a much-deserved break from it all, Lindsay came back to help us repair and get our kids back on track emotionally and academically. At the same time, Ruchi was the parent club president at Beach School, and she and Lindsay have a history of working together. They worked tirelessly to safely reopen by fundraising to install HEPA filters in all elementary classrooms and served on a district committee to bring symptomatic Covid testing to schools and sports programs. Change is afoot in Piedmont. We are making progress towards a district that embraces excellence and belonging for everyone. What a great benefit for us all, especially for our children. I know that Lindsay and Ruchi are the best candidates to continue moving us forward. I’m excited for what they will bring to our school board and thank them

The formalization of groups like this serving our school board would ensure that we have a forum for parents and other community members to engage in meaningful ways, while also serving to gather stakeholder feedback before decisions are made. For example, a Curriculum Committee would improve transparency into the curriculum selection and adoption processes and allow for teachers and parent subject matter experts to engage throughout the process. This would be a vast improvement over the current opaque, top-down curriculum adoption process. This is just one example of how I would work to bring greater transparency in service of our students, families, teachers, and staff. To learn more about my other campaign priorities, please visit lindsayforpusd.com. –Lindsay Thomasson In support of proven leaders Editor: I encourage all Piedmont Voters to mark their ballots on November 8 for three city council candidates: Jennifer Long, Betsy Andersen, and Tom Ramsey, and two school board candidates: Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar. All five share capabilities that will serve our community well: a solid understanding of the issues that face their prospective roles, experience working with and listening respectfully to all viewpoints, and varied professional backgrounds that will each contribute to and add strength to our governing bodies. Jennifer Long, Tom Ramsey, and Betsy Andersen each would approach their roles as council members with a great deal of common sense and commitment to deal with the complicated issues facing our city government in a thoughtful and reasonable way. One such issue is the state-mandated housing element plan. This is a complex policy document that is still being developed; the plan we send to the State will be in draft form and has the possibility of being returned with revisions, as has happened with other California cities. Jennifer, Tom and Betsy understand that this is an unfolding and dynamic process and are committed to working with the community to maintain our town’s charm and character by retaining local control over Piedmont’s housing policies. As a school board member, I have had the pleasure of working directly with Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar. I was impressed with Lindsay’s work as the Havens Parent Board President to engage many of us to discuss the numerous issues facing our schools during the pandemic. Lindsay connected with stakeholders in positive ways when emotions were running high. While serving as Beach Parent Club President, Ruchi offered her expertise to the district Health Council to help research the best options for COVID testing for PUSD during the pandemic. Both bring knowledge of our school district from their leadership roles and as parents of children currently in our schools. They are well poised to dig in and learn the work of the broader school community and become part of our district governance team. Please vote for Jennifer Long, Tom Ramsey, Betsy Andersen for Piedmont City Council, and Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar for Piedmont Board of Education. –Megan Pillsbury Former Piedmont School Board member How about a School Board Dream Team Editor: I am so inspired and excited about two of the school board candidates this year, Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar! I hope our community comes together to elect this Dream Team to the school board. Lindsay, Ruchi and I served on the Tri-School Site Council together where I saw firsthand their dedication to our schools, our children and to a collaborative process. During Site Council meetings, I was consistently impressed with the insightful questions and comments from each of them. It is clear that they both have taken the time and effort to dive deep into the inner workings of the district, and clear that their intent is always to meet the needs they see and hear from their fellow families. Each displays a level of tact and skill at working with groups, including administrators and teachers, and advocating hard for the families they were there to represent. I saw them patiently and diligently take time for extra meetings and one-on-ones with all the parties involved on issues until there was a clear path forward that worked for everyone. I have the bonus of being a Havens parent working alongside Lindsay and having experienced her incredible leadership when she was the Parent Club president from 2020-2021. We all know how difficult that year was, but Lindsay leaned into her role with kindness and repeatedly reminded the parent community to come together and have compassion for each other. The parent community felt ravaged after that school year, and instead of taking a much-deserved break from it all, Lindsay came back to help us repair and get our kids back on track emotionally and academically. At the same time, Ruchi was the parent club president at Beach School, and she and Lindsay have a history of working together. They worked tirelessly to safely reopen by fundraising to install HEPA filters in all elementary classrooms and served on a district committee to bring symptomatic Covid testing to schools and sports programs. Change is afoot in Piedmont. We are making progress towards a district that embraces excellence and belonging for everyone. What a great benefit for us all, especially for our children. I know that Lindsay and Ruchi are the best candidates to continue moving us forward. I’m excited for what they will bring to our school board and thank them for their service thus far to our schools and children. Two spots are open on the school board and Ruchi and Lindsay are just what we need. –Regina Myers Casting a vote for Ramsey, Andersen, Long Editor: Elect Tom Ramsey and Re-elect Betsy Smegal Andersen and Jen Long to City Council On November 8, I’ll be proud to cast my vote for Tom Ramsey for City Council. I’ve had the great privilege of working with Tom for four years on Piedmont’s Planning Commission. I’ve been deeply impressed by Tom’s decision-making approach in evaluating renovation and construction projects. Tom emphasizes collaboration and cooperation between neighbors, and balances maintaining the character of the community with being open to design innovation. Tom’s many years of engagement and service in Piedmont reflect his dedication to our community. His professional experience and expertise as an architect and senior leader will be extraordinarily helpful to City Council as Piedmont moves forward with complying with state housing laws and completing major civic projects like the pool and civic center. Finally, Tom’s warm, collegial, and solutions-focused nature will ensure that different viewpoints are respected and reflected in the Council’s decisions on important issues facing our city. I look forward to electing Tom Ramsey to City Council. I also look forward to re-electing Betsy Smegal Andersenrn and Jen Long to City Council. As an experienced attorney, Betsy’s diligence and mastery of details will serve her well in her stewardship of our city. Betsy’s extraordinary dedication to Piedmont is reflected in her decades of service in the community. Betsy knows Piedmont inside and out and we are all better for it. I’ve had the privilege of knowing Jen Long since our children were in elementary school. Jen’s collaborative nature was invaluable in helping our school establish new health and wellness policies. Jen’s professional expertise as an attorney and her personal dedication to helping Piedmont become a more diverse and inclusive community have brought a welcome perspective to City Council. Piedmont will be in good hands with Tom, Betsy and Jen serving on City Council. I hope you’ll join me in casting your ballot for each of them in November. –Rani Batra Chair, Piedmont Planning Commission What kind of person do I want on the City Council? At the end of qualifications, Highlander Robotics ranked 23 of 38 and advanced to the playoffs after being drafted as part of the No. 3 seed alliance captained by Team 6800 from Austin, Texas. They won two straight rounds before being eliminated from the tournament after losses to alliances captained by No. 2 seed Team 254 and No. 1 seed and eventual winner Team 1678, Citrus Circuits from Davis. Selkie was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Asha Byers and supported by drive coach Alex Ware, technician Kasper Jansson, and human player Barry Balasingham. Helena Young and Peter Stokes led the pit crew which kept the robot running smoothly through 10 full contact matches with turnarounds as quick as 30 minutes. Jasper Tripp led Scouting operations with a team of 12 who used a team-built app to track robot performance at the tournament, informing match strategy and alliance selection during the playoff draft. Chloe Kessinger led a team of five ambassadors who fielded questions, built connections with other teams, and represented the team with Chezy Champs judges. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by Piedmont High alumni Henry and Charlie Lambert. The team is now composed of 47 high school students from Piedmont, Millennium, Las Lomas, College Prep, Maybeck, Bentley and Head Royce. For more information contact Lead Mentor Kevin Clark at kevin.clark@gmail.com. Drive team members Asha Byers (left) and Barry Balasingham wait with Selkie before their next match.

articles.text: out. Bagatelle is a park within a park, within the Bois de Boulogne. Bagatelle’s origin story has a seamy side of debauchery that has clung to Marie Antoinette’s rumored escapades at Versailles and Bagatelle. Built as a private garden and playground by the youngest brother of King Louis XVI, the wealthy, unbridled Count of Artois. At age 20 in a frivolous bet with the Queen, urgently pressed 900 workmen into service to complete the park and château in an astounding 63 days. Artois, unlike his brother the king, escaped Paris ahead of the revolutionary mobs and lived a long life. A semi-finalist for favorite park is Père Lachaise Cemetery situated on a park-like hillside both historically significant and spiritually bracing for a tranquil stroll. The tract was acquired by the Jesuits and Père La Chaise was confessor to the young King of France Louis XIV, the longest serving monarch in European history. The cemetery opened in Jardin du Luxembourg is a 57-acre park with the Senate building.

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, October 5, 2022 Pumpkin Patch Continued from page 1 pumpkin buyer had already turned its pumpkin into a pie. Wildwood first grader Margot Miller carved up her sugar pie pumpkin and quickly transformed it into a scrumptious dessert. The Patch features many pumpkins renowned for their culinary capabilities, such as the “Peanut,” and “Cheese” pumpkins, which are sought by chefs. The Peanut pumpkin is sweet and delicious, and gets its name from the protuberances resembling peanuts. The pumpkin is ideal for pies, breads and cheesecakes. Whether you want to eat your pumpkin, carve a menacing face into it, or just let it sit on the dining room table, the Patch has everything you need. Varieties also include: XL carving, the “One too Many,” fairytale, French, jarrahdale, American tondo, and the knucklehead pumpkin. Photo by Garrett Miller Wildwood 1st grader Margot Miller’s has already made a pie with a Sugar Pie pumpkin from this year’s Wildwood Dads Pumpkin patch.
